Always and Forever (I Hope You Remember)

by thetalee

Summary

Time moves forwards without mercy. Buck is firmly in the captain's seat. Except this time, he isn't keeping the seat warm for when Bobby returned. With Bobby playing advisor for a Hollywood show that resembles their lives a little too much, the 118 is officially Buck's. And of course, disaster is imminent.

Chapter 1: Meet the New Boss

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The absence of things was what really stuck out to Buck. The desk was the same, the lamp and the office supplies on top of it were the same. The map on the back of the wall, showing their coverage area relative to the city of Los Angeles, was the same one that had been there for years. The couch along the wall was the same, as were the chairs in front of the desk. The furniture, anything that was technically department property, anything that belonged to the captains of B and C shifts, all of that was still present and accounted for.

It was Bobby that was missing. His nameplate was gone, replaced. His plaques and various certificates were all taken from the walls. The various knicknacks he’d collected, like the tiny ladder truck that had been on top of the filing cabinet, were missing. All the signs of Bobby once belonging in this office were completely and utterly absent, boxed up and taken out.

Buck hadn’t sat down at the desk that was now, officially, his. He couldn’t quite bring himself to round it and take that spot, even though he had so many times before at this point. Instead, he stood in front of it, gripping the nameplate that read Captain Evan Diaz and tapping it against the pressed wood of the desk.

So focused on it was he that he didn’t notice anyone else come in, not until they tugged at a strand of his curly hair.

“You’re bringing down the mood, mi sol,” Eddie tutted. He was carrying a cardboard box that he placed on top of the desk. “This is your big day, you should be celebrating!”

“Can’t really bring myself to be in a celebratory mood.”

“We’ll get you there,” his husband assured him, before he opened the box and started unpacking.

“What even is…” Buck’s question trailed off as he got a look at the first thing Eddie set out, a framed photograph of Chris and Gavin. The plaque he got on the day they were awarded their Medals of Valor was also placed on the desk, along with the certificate he received upon graduating the leadership academy. “When did you carry this out to the jeep?”

“While you were stuck in your head this morning,” Eddie told him. “Chris helped pick out the photos.”

“When!?”

“You’ve spent a lot of your time stuck in your head lately. It was getting kinda concerning.”

Buck wasn’t sure it was normal to look at a promotion with something akin to dread. It hadn’t been because he didn’t want it, but entirely because of what it meant. As long as he was merely interim captain, there was still the chance of things going back to the way they had been before, the way they should be. As long as he was merely interim captain, there had still been the chance of Bobby walking into the station and retaking his spot.

But Buck had gotten through the simulation exercises, the test, the interview. He’d gotten through the paperwork. It was him in the captain’s seat, now, and Bobby wasn’t ever going to come back as anything other than a visitor. Instead, he was acting as an advisor for some show about firefighting.

Months ago, at the beginning of summer, Bobby had told Chief Simpson that he was retiring. The problem was, though, that he hadn’t bothered telling any of them. Not when he was contemplating it, not when he decided it, not when he submitted his resignation. Buck only found out when the chief summoned him to his office to offer him the spot, weeks after Bobby’s heart attack.

Several hours in Dr. Copeland’s office were spent untangling all the ways and the whys that Buck was angry with Bobby. Everything from how he was caught by surprise, to how he felt vaguely betrayed, to how the way Bobby acted before his heart attack gave Buck the unsettling idea that retirement had been synonymous with leaving in some vague yet terrible way. He still wasn’t certain if he’d have been as angry, if he’d have been angrier or if he’d have been less angry, if the heart attack hadn’t happened, if he hadn’t nearly lost Bobby forever just prior to finding out about his decision to retire. 

“How did Bobby have everything hanging on the wall?” Eddie held up the plaque from the medal ceremony, glancing between it and the wall behind the desk. “He didn’t nail them up, did he? I’m not sure how I feel about damaging the station on your first official day.”

“There’s some of that Alien Tape in the cabinet there,” Buck told him, gesturing at it. He watched, amused, as his husband jogged over to dig it out. “Are you going to decorate the office for me?”

His husband just shrugged at him before busying himself with making sure the plaque stuck to the wall.

Buck couldn’t say he was very surprised by this behavior. He remembered the first time he’d seen Eddie’s bedroom, how borderline barren it had looked, even after living there for a couple years. Chris’ room was an explosion of life and color in comparison, having clearly been what Eddie had chosen to focus all his time and effort on.

He busied himself going through the box to see what all Eddie brought from home to decorate the place with. There weren’t very many things, not really. Another framed photograph, this one of Eddie helping Jee-Yun mix a bowl of cookie dough. One of Chris’ Lego fire trucks that had been sitting on his dresser for years now. A wooden plaque in the shape of a Maltese Cross with the firefighter’s prayer on it, which was new and almost definitely from Abuela.

It took longer than it probably should’ve to get everything placed. That was almost entirely because of Eddie, who kept changing his mind about where they should go. Buck was reminded of when they saw Carla in-person again for the first time after lockdown, his then boyfriend fretting with and repeatedly rearranging the throw pillows on the couch. It made the time go quickly, and soon it was time for the shift to start.

“Alright, everyone,” Buck called out as he crested the top steps to the station loft. He had his trusty clipboard in hand, which held everything from his notes from Captain Mayfair’s handover to the grocery list for that week’s store run. “Good news first: my ongoing reign of terror shall continue for the foreseeable future.”

“Hey, uh, Cap?” Albert, standing next to Ravi towards the back of the gathered group, raised his hand and then gestured between himself and his boyfriend. “Can we get transfer papers?”

“No. Moving on.” He flipped through the pages until he found the email he printed out. “The chief is getting grumpy about costs, so we’re gonna have to tighten our belts a bit. That means no more name brands when we go to the store, I’m sorry.”

“It tastes the exact same, Buck,” Eddie said, stepping around him to join the others.

“We’ve had this argument before and we all agreed you were wrong,” Buck said, and ignored the way his husband rolled his eyes. “Unfortunately, there’s also no room in the new budget to fulfill my campaign promise of replacing the glass walls of the men’s locker room. But on the bright side, they’re going to put in new cast iron plumbing.”

Maybe they could hold a fundraiser for it? Something to contemplate later.

There wasn’t much left of the briefing after that. A heads up on the weather - hot, hot, hot - and then divvying up chores amongst the masses. Afterwards, Hen surprised him with a cake that she’d gotten for the occasion, which had a drawing of a dalmatian with spots on its face that looked identical to Buck’s birthmark. He got to work on the paperwork that seemed to be constantly piling up as he ate his slice, mostly managing to lose himself in his focus on the mundane minutiae. At least until he heard Taylor Kelly’s voice.

Way back in March, while Bobby and Athena were on their doomed honeymoon cruise and Hen was acting captain, the 118 responded to a motor vehicle accident. An idiot in a sports car had T-boned an SUV and sent it rolling onto a sedan. The idiot collapsed of a brain bleed on the scene and was pronounced at the hospital, and an investigation into it - into Hen - was launched because he was the son of a city councilwoman. She was cleared, because he was on meth at the time of the accident and also very drunk, but his mother, Councilwoman Olivia Ortiz - no relation to Javier Ortiz, the apparatus operator for the 118’s ladder truck - decided to lay all the blame for his death at Hen’s feet regardless.

It started with pressuring the judge to drop the adoption hearing for Mara, which should have just been a formality. Then she had the Wilsons’ license to foster revoked. After that, she leaned on Chief Simpson to prevent Hen from getting the captaincy. Anything and everything that the councilwoman could do to hurt Hen, she did.

In retaliation, Buck went to the one person he knew that could effectively meet her head on and with just as much viciousness. His friendship with Taylor might’ve been a smoldering wreck at this point, but it didn’t take much to recruit her. She’d just about jumped at the chance to add the ruination of a politician’s career to her resume, and she got to work quickly. She started with a refresher on the death of Ortiz’s son that pretty much smeared his reputation entirely in the public eye and she kept going from there, with a general theme of the councilwoman intentionally and gleefully hurting a bunch of children that could not defend themselves because she was angry at other people for her lowlife son getting himself killed.

It was the vilest kind of reporting that Buck had ever seen and if it was happening to anyone else, he’d probably feel guilty for helping to bring it about.

“Councilwoman Ortiz’s office still refuses to comment on her horrific treatment of this city’s children,” Taylor was saying on the TV. It was a repeat of last night’s piece, replayed by her channel’s morning news for the viewership it brought in. Everyone loved a scandal, after all. “A spokesperson for the mayor’s office called her actions highly objectionable and an example of cruelty that is horrific to see coming from someone who claims to represent the people of Los Angeles.”

“Y’know, after months of watching her drag that woman through the dirt,” Hen commented, sitting down across from Buck, “I’m about ready to forgive Taylor for everything she’s ever done.”

“Don’t let Eddie hear you say that,” he joked before glancing around, making sure neither Han was around. “How’re you guys? What’s the update on everything Mara?”

“It’s going… Good, I guess,” she said. “We met with a new foster attorney, she thinks we have a strong case to get our foster license back. Plus, she doesn’t care for Councilwoman Ortiz.”

“After the smear campaign, I don’t think anyone does.”

“Seriously, thank God for Taylor Kelly. And I can’t believe I just said that.” Hen laughed, shaking her head. “We have another meeting with her on Friday, but…”

“But we work that day. It’s cool, we’ll manage without you.”

“Thanks,” she said with a smile and a nod. And then she tilted her head, gaze turning intent. “Have you talked to Bobby lately?”

“Yeah, on Sunday.”

She did not look convinced.

“Did you talk to him or just talk to him?” Hen asked. Buck didn’t meet her eyes, instead dropping them back down to the paperwork he was no longer working on. “C’mon, Buck. You can’t be angry at him forever.”

“I’m not trying to be,” he admitted. “I just am.”

His friend let out a sigh and reached across the table to squeeze his arm.

“You’ll get there,” she told him, and it almost sounded like a promise.

The kitchen was a bit of a mess, as was the dining table. There were little flour paw prints everywhere, from where Senorita decided to walk through like she owned the place. There was a mess of baking ingredients that was spread throughout the entire house, because she also decided to knock everything over onto the dog. And Hoover proceeded to run like his tail was on fire.

Eddie would clean that up before anyone saw it, swear.

Buck had taken Gavin to the park to meet Maddie with Mara and Jee-Yun, to let the tots run themselves into exhaustion. His husband would be gone for a while, Eddie knew, because they would inevitably go somewhere to eat, as well. Meanwhile, Carla had taken Abuela out to spend time with her friends, doing… He actually had no idea what they did when they got together. Besides gossiping their gray-haired heads off, of course. Eddie was just thankful that Carla was around to take her, because those old ladies frightened the hell out of him when they got together. They scared Buck, too, which only made him moderately less embarrassed about it.

The long and the short of it was, though, it was just Eddie and Chris in the house, and a mess of baking supplies.

“I think there’s flour on the ceiling,” Chris remarked, head tilted back as he blinked behind his glasses. There was also flour in his curls, turning the strands powdery white.

“Is there?” Eddie looked up as well. “Huh.”

He dismissed it with a wave of his hand, before tearing off the Saran wrap covering the bowl and taking out the large lump of dough that had been sitting in it for the past half hour. There was parchment paper covering half the table, which was in turn covered in flour that puffed up in a cloud when Eddie dropped the dough onto it. It made them both cough.

“I think you put down too much flour, Dad,” Chris complained, trying to clean his lenses off and only succeeded in smearing them a little.

“I might have,” Eddie agreed. He looked around, spotted a clean wash rag, and handed it to his son. “At least it won’t stick?”

The stink eye that his son gave him conveyed his thoughts quite clearly.

Rolling out all the dough took time, mostly because Senorita decided to return to the scene of her crime. The problem with cats, Eddie was quickly deciding, was that they absolutely understood the concept of no and just didn’t care about it. It was the only explanation for why she sat on the edge of the table and stared him in the eye as she reached a paw out to set it on the dough, even as he told her not to.

“Hoover listens much better than you, little lady,” Eddie lectured her, carrying her out to the living room and dropping her on top of her cat tree. There were white hand prints left all over her black fur. “Take lessons from him.”

“Dad, you’re being weird again,” Chris complained.

“You’re weird,” was Eddie’s lame comeback. “Alright, where are they?”

“Right here.”

His son held up an unopened package of cookie cutters. They actually already had an overly vast collection of cookie cutters in various shapes, pumpkins and stars and snowmen, but these were dinosaurs and had therefore been of the utmost importance to obtain. Chris tore the packaging open with absolutely zero grace, dumping the contents onto the table so that they bounced and skipped and nearly fell to the floor.

Together, Eddie and Chris went about cutting the dough, removing each new dinosaur and placing them onto a nearby plate. There was a lot of dough left over, so Eddie folded and rerolled it and went through the process again. Then he carefully carried the plate into the kitchen and to the stove, Chris following behind him.

“Should I get the first aid kit?” his son asked. “Have Nine-One-One ready?”

“Your pops has more faith in me.” 

“I’d ask him the same thing.”

Eddie dug through the various pots and pans, before pulling out one he felt was large enough and setting it on top of the burner. Then he grabbed the vegetable oil and poured it in, before setting it to boil. When he looked over, he saw that Chris had his phone sitting on the counter, ready to call someone if something happened.

“I am a firefighter,” Eddie argued, carefully dropping the first dinosaur into the oil. It splashed and sizzled and bubbled. “I’m not going to burn myself.”

Chris’ only response to that was to open the fridge and pull out the aloe vera. Because he had zero respect for his father.

The dinosaur shaped sopapillas didn’t take long to cook. They soon had a tray filled with the crispy baked goods, shaped like triceratops and tyrannosaurus rexes and brontosauruses. And Eddie managed it with only a minor burn to his forearm, thanks to a fumbling with the tongs and splashing himself. His son was far too smug as he watched him hold his arm under cool water and then rub the aloe vera onto it.

“Honey or chocolate?” Eddie asked, topping them with powdered sugar.

“Chocolate,” Chris answered, digging out a jar of homemade chocolate sauce from the fridge. Eddie was fairly certain it was one of Bobby’s recent attempts at a peace offering.

(He and Buck would be okay, Eddie knew. It would just take time.)

With the sopapillas set out on a tray, and the chocolate sauce poured into a ramekin, Eddie and Chris did not waste time. There was a minor flurry of activity as they each grabbed a dinosaur and then jostled each other to dip it into the chocolate. Silence fell between them, broken only by the sounds of chewing and the delighted groans at how good it tasted.

“And you had no faith in me,” Eddie groused after his second dinosaur.

“It’s okay,” Chris said, licking chocolate off his fingers before grabbing his fourth. “They’re not bad.”

“Thanks, mijo.” He rolled his eyes. “We should probably clean this up before-”

The door opening up interrupted them, Hoover rushing for it with excited barking. Buck came in, diaper bag dangling from one shoulder and a sleeping Gavin tucked against the other. 

“Hey, babe, we’re-” He froze, taking in the mess that greeted him. “What the fu- What happened here?”

“Uh.” Eddie and Chris exchanged wide-eyed looks and then Eddie grabbed the tray, holding it out. “Sopapillas?”

Buck stared at them for a long, silent moment, and then he shrugged and dropped the diaper bag by the couch.

“Okay, sure.”

Chapter End Notes

Darling, So It Goes has historically been fueled mainly by spite. And this time the spite is coming from how goddang stupid the end of season 7 was and how stupid it is that Chris didn't return immediately in 8x01. So here, welcome to the magical world where that idiocy didn't happen.

Chapter 2: Un-Bee-Lievable

Chapter Summary

In which there are bees on the bridge.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Around three-quarters of crops, and a total of one-third of the global food supply, rely on pollinators such as bees. But with pesticides and climate change and disease, the population of wild bees has declined severely enough that there simply isn’t enough to keep up with the demand. So, farmers rely on hives to be hauled across the country, with millions of bees per truck. The almond trees in California alone require the vast majority of all the honeybees available in the United States. And then after their work is done, they’re packed back up and returned home.

Buck didn’t know the exact statistics or numbers for how many long-haul trucks shipping hives of bees passed through Los Angeles on the regular. He could probably look it up later, if he remembered and cared enough. He did know, however, that the number was high enough that this really was simply a matter of when, not if.

He wasn’t entirely certain on the full details. There was a traffic accident on the 4th Street bridge, causing one of those aforementioned hive-hauling trucks to dump its cargo. According to dispatch - Maddie, in this instance - the driver of the truck was downed and there was an SUV with passengers inside that was covered by a bunch of very angry Africanized honey bees, aggravated by both the accident and the heatwave. When they arrived, there was a churning cloud hovering over the cargo truck and the car, and police were doing their best to evacuate the stranded motorists.

“Stay inside,” Buck told Toby, who was allergic to bees and yet also wasn’t someone they could just leave behind at the station. From Eddie’s barely concealed laughter, Buck knew he accidentally slipped into the tone of voice that he used with Chris and Gavin and Jee-Yun. “Keep that EpiPen close.”

“Got it, Cap.”

The driver-engineer was still nodding as the rest of them piled out, making sure the doors were shut firmly behind them. The buzzing of thousands of pissed off bees filled the air. 

“That is a lot of bees,” Eddie commented with a wide-eyed stare.

“A swarm can generate as much electricity as a storm cloud,” Buck told him.

“Good,” Chimney said, him and Hen joining them. “I forgot to charge my phone.”

“Just try not to get shocked again, capitán.” Eddie’s grin was unrepentant despite the glare his comment rightfully deserved.

“Everyone, get your PPE on,” Buck said, raising his voice to be heard. “Hen, Chimney, you’re on the downed driver. Eddie, Albert, the SUV. The rest of you, on the hoses. I want to hit that swarm with fog streams.”

There was a chorus of affirmations, and then they were breaking into motion. The bee nets that attached to their turnout helmets were one of those odd pieces of gear that was needed more often than one would expect, and so were allowed to take up some of the precious compartment space. They didn’t take much effort to put on, slipping over the helmets and clipping on to the collars of their coats.

Hen and Chimney, once theirs were secured, beelined - ha - for their designated patient, with the latter taking an extinguisher with him. Eddie and Albert weren’t far behind them on their way to the SUV and the people trapped within. Buck, meanwhile, got busy helping Ravi and the others haul out the hoses and hook them up to the engine.

“Dispatch,” Hen radioed. “The driver’s a black tag.”

Buck grimaced, but he was not surprised. All that they could see of him when they pulled up was a vaguely man-shaped mass of angry bees on the road. The average person could survive an average of ten stings per pound of bodyweight. He didn’t need to know how many bees were covering the driver, nor did he need lightning-induced math powers, to know that he’d almost certainly been stung far more than that.

“Trucking company says there should be a second driver,” Josh radioed back. 

After confirming that they received the message, the pair hurried to the truck. There wasn’t another man-shaped mound of angry insects lying on the ground, so they probably assumed, much as Buck was assuming, that the second driver was still in the truck.

“Maddie, we are at the SUV.” Eddie’s voice automatically drew Buck’s attention, as it always did. It would’ve even if he wasn’t keeping an ear on the radio chatter. “It’s completely covered, we can’t see inside.”

“Driver is Julie Watson, thirty-eight. Her eight year old daughter is in the backseat with a severe bee allergy,” Maddie said. “She hasn’t been stung yet, but…”

“Cap!” Ravi shouted for him. “The water’s not flowing!”

“What do you mean, the water’s not flowing?” Buck demanded, joining him at the valves on the side of the engine.

“I mean we turn it on and nothing comes out,” was the answer. “Not even a dribble.”

That was not good. It also wasn’t right. Toby had spent that morning doing the routine maintenance for the engine, there was no reason for it to be failing now. Not unless the driver-engineer missed something or he forgot to refill the tanks, but Buck trusted him enough to firmly toss those possibilities to the side. Unfortunately, the guy was also the best person to help track down the problem in a timely manner.

Buck went to the engine cab, opening the door and flinging one of the bee nets at the driver. Toby caught it, looking bewildered.

“The pump isn't pumping,” Buck explained, giving Hen and Chimney a nod as they rushed for the ambulance with the second driver, who was unresponsive and swollen on the gurney they were pushing. “Not a drop of water is coming out. We need to figure out why.”

“I’ll have to lift the cab,” Toby told him, hurriedly pulling the net on and hopping out.

That, at least, worked as it should. The sound of the hydraulics joined the buzzing as the cab was lifted up and forward, revealing the inner workings of the engine. From there, it became very obvious what the problem was.

“They’re inside my engine!” Toby cried, looking horrified and also a little bit murderous as he and Buck, along with Ravi, took in the sight of the intake valve filled to the brim with bees. “The little stinging bastards are gunking up my engine!”

“Buck, this CO2 isn’t cutting it,” Eddie radioed. “We need more firepower.”

Buck reached up to thumb at his own radio, eyes still stuck on the grotesque sight in front of him.

“Tell me about it,” he radioed back. “Dispatch, we’ve been sabotaged by the bees. What’s the ETA on back-up?”

“You have engines en route,” Josh replied. “But the foam’s stuck in traffic in Van Nuys.”

“Get me what you can.” Buck let go of his radio, dropping his arm. They were on their own for the foreseeable future, which meant they really needed to figure something out to rescue the passengers of the SUV. “Ravi, Toby, do your best to get this cleared.”

“How!?” was Ravi’s perfectly reasonable question.

“Find a plunger or something,” Buck told him. “Don’t get stung.”

There wasn’t really a tool available to them for this kind of situation. Mainly because this kind of situation hardly ever happened, if it happened at all. It wasn’t like angry swarms of killer bees were something that they typically had to deal with, so they never bothered to stock the giant squeegee. The best that they had was the shovels, and Buck grabbed one off the engine before jogging to the SUV.

“Seriously?” Eddie sounded unfairly dubious as Buck joined him and Albert in doing their best to scoop off the bees.

“It’s what we’ve got,” Buck replied, feeling a little defensive. “They got into the intake valve, we can’t use the hoses.”

“How did they get into that?” Albert asked, pausing in his futile efforts to clear away the bees with a halligan.

“I don’t know. Found a hole and crawled in, I guess. Ravi and the others are trying to get it unclogged.”

The problem with trying to clear away the bees was that they couldn’t do it fast enough. They just moved right back into the empty space, buzzing angrily. Buck was a bit concerned that the passengers were in just as much danger inside the car as they would have been outside of it. In Japan, when the giant hornets attacked a hive of one of the native honey bee species, the bees’ response was to pile on the hornets and cook them alive with the heat produced by their vibrating. That took hundreds of bees for one single hornet, but while Buck wasn’t entirely certain on the square-cube ratio when it came to people in cars, he didn’t want to risk the chance that the heatwave the city was currently suffering under would help make up the difference.

92 degree heat, plus pavement, plus hot car, plus swarm of buzzing bees-

“One Eighteen.” Maddie’s worried sounding voice cut through the math problem Buck was trying not to solve in his head. “Both patients have a bee allergy, both have been stung. Julie used the EpiPen on her daughter, but she is experiencing a severe allergic reaction.”

Buck looked to Eddie, who was already shaking his head, both of them in agreement without the question even needing to be asked. There were simply too many bees. Even without the allergy, the mother and daughter both would end up exactly like the driver of the truck. But the mother going into anaphylactic meant they were quickly running out of time. The daughter, too, needed to get to an ER as close to immediately as possible, because there was every bit the chance that she could rebound.

“Okay,” Buck breathed out. “So what can we-”

And then the truck, the one that had been hauling the bees, burst into flames with a small explosion. The three of them flinched and turned to stare at it.

“Now why is that on fire!?” Albert shouted, clearly reaching the end of his patience with everything.

That was a very good question. The answer could be anything from a bee getting into the wrong part, to a leak somewhere and a spark from something, to the heat causing spontaneous combustion. But Buck didn’t particularly care about the cause of the fire, or even the fire itself. What he cared about was the amount of smoke it was putting out.

He felt the smile stretching his face as he reached for his radio.

“Ravi, forget about the intake. Get me the PPV fans from the rig.”

“Uh, okay.” Ravi sounded confused. “Copy that Cap, PPV fans on the way.”

Positive-Pressure Ventilation fans were used to push smoke out of a building after the fire had been put out. They forced air into a structure, increasing the pressure and driving the smoke to where there was less pressure. Which was outside the building, if they were doing it right. Obviously, on a bridge with a burning truck was not the circumstances that the fans would typically be used in. 

“Smoke calms bees. Beekeepers use it to stop ‘em from stinging when they need into hives,” Buck explained to Eddie and Albert, who were both staring at him in silent confusion. “We blow the smoke from the fire over the car, we should be able to get them out without any problems.”

Ravi and Clarke arrived with the fans, and there was no time to waste after that. They got them set up, directed so they blew the smoke right onto the car. The effect wasn’t quite instantaneous and the bees were more driven off than calmed down, but Buck would happily take it. All that mattered was that the little guys were no longer in the way and weren’t posing an immediate danger.

With the mass of insects gone, the handle for the driver’s door was free to grab. He gripped it and gently pulled, easing it open so as to avoiding upsetting any of the stragglers. The relief when the mother and daughter saw him was palpable.

“LAFD, ma’am,” Buck said, reaching in to scoop the woman up. Beside him, Eddie was pulling open the back door and grabbing the daughter. “We’ve got you.”

He jerked his chin at the fans, motioning for Ravi and Clarke to grab them, and then he was jogging away from the burning truck and the bees that were still hovering around. Instead of dropping them off on gurneys to be carted off, Buck opted for them to be carried directly to one of the awaiting ambulances. There was too much of a risk for the bees to get upset again, and he wanted the pair of them to be safely tucked away before that could happen.

“Dispatch,” Buck radioed, thumping the ambulance doors once they were closed. “Both patients are loaded up and ready to be transported.”

“Your foam should be getting there any second,” Josh replied. “I gave it a police escort.”

“Awesome. We have a fire that-”

And then the long-haul truck exploded in a burst of flames. Buck immediately sought out Ravi and Clarke, spotting them ducking beside the rigs where they were in the process of repacking the fans. Any relief from that, however, was ruined by the sight of the swirling swarm of angry bees rising up from the flames like some biblical plague.

“Is that a…?” Eddie’s question trailed off, but Buck nodded all the same.

“It’s a bee-nado.” He ignored the incredulous stare from his husband - it was technically his fault, for letting Chris choose Sharknado for movie night - and went back to his radio. “Dispatch, this swarm is very big and very angry. And it’s moving.”

“Copy that, One Eighteen,” Josh responded. “Do you know in which direction?”

“Uh.” Buck tracked it and grimaced. “Northwest. Ish.”

There wasn’t really any good directions for the swarm to be heading, but northwest was almost the worst possible one. That direction had them going directly through downtown Los Angeles and then Hollywood. It would also put the bees perilously close to Dodgers Stadium.

“Eddie.” Buck didn’t take his eyes off the swarm. “What time’s the game tonight?”

“Seven,” his husband answered, his tone grim.

Bees were diurnal, and the sun had started setting before then. They should start hunkering down for the night around that time, and hopefully they would be long past the stadium by then. Buck did not want to imagine the carnage that would ensue if a swarm of angry bees descended upon that many people all packed into one place.

But of course, he was imagining it. Because that was how his brain worked.

Sometimes, Buck had to remind himself that he chose to sign up for the Parent-Teacher Organization at Chris’ school. That he was excited to do it at the start. Most of the time, he didn’t truly mind it, going in and schmoozing with the other parents and faculty members that bothered to show up. Even though a truly absurd number of the other parents were utterly insufferable and he normally ended up hanging out with a small few that couldn’t stand most of the others, either.

At least Chris was in his last year at Durand. It only taught up to eighth grade, which meant they needed to decide on whether or not they were finding another private school to send the kid or returning him to the horrors of public school. Buck was fairly certain Chris would end up going to the same high school May did, so he and Eddie would have to bother her or Athena about it at some point. Worse come to worse, they’d just keep shilling out tuition money to keep their kid enrolled somewhere fancy.

Either way, he sincerely hoped he wouldn’t have to see some of these parents again.

“Babe!” Buck called out as he barged into the house. Hoover immediately ran up to, so he had to juggle taking off his shoes with giving the dog his customary greeting of pets. “You will not believe what Lyndsay did!”

“Lyndsay-with-a-Y?” his husband guessed from the direction of the dining room.

“Yes!” Buck straightened up after a few more headpats to Hoover and headed for his husband, only to pull up short at the sight he was greeted by. “Oh, we have visitors. Hi!”

“Hi, Buck.” May waved at him from the table, where she sat holding Senorita the cat. In the chair next to her was Amy, Gavin’s biological mother, a freshly blue streak in her hair replacing the pink that had been in it before.

After taking a gap year the year before, Amy ended up going to the University of Southern California, just like May. Despite the three and a half year age difference between them, they’d become close friends. Buck was glad to see it, because Amy was coming out of her shell a bit. He was also more than a bit concerned over it, because coming out of her shell meant that she was often joining May in giving him shit over everything.

“Who’s Lyndsay-with-a-Y?” Amy asked. She had Gavin in her lap, the tot focused intently on the coloring sheet in front of him. There was a mess of crayons spread out over the table top. Chris, sitting on her other side, had his own picture that he was coloring in, because you were never too old for coloring.

“Mom at Chris’ school,” Eddie answered, catching a crayon as it rolled his way and sending it rolling back. “So what did she do?”

“She came up with all these godawful fundraising ideas,” Buck told him. “Tried to recruit me to help her, like she hasn’t spent the last two years insulting me behind my back-”

“And to your face.”

“And to my face! And when I reminded her that I didn’t exactly have time for her stupid fundraiser ideas - seriously, one of her ideas was to do an auction thing with the guys or something. One of those, like, the highest bidder gets to have a cooking lesson or go on a date or something, I dunno.”

“She’s probably hoping I’ll volunteer to be one of them.”

“Wait, what?” May looked between them.

“I don’t go to the PTO meetings because she always starts flirting with me,” Eddie told her. “Usually in really bad Spanish.”

“The only person who gets to flirt with my husband in bad Spanish is me,” Buck firmly declared. Said husband smiled and leaned in his chair to press his head into Buck’s side, and Buck started playing with his hair. “But when I told her I have even less freetime now than I did last year, suddenly she was all, Oh, I guess you don’t actually care about your son, what a shame.”

He pitched his voice up as he mimicked Lyndsay, wagging his head as he quoted her.

“She sounds awful,” Amy commented.

“Her daughter isn’t any better,” Chris said, not even lifting his head up from his artistic endeavors. “I got partnered with her for science last year, and she didn’t want to do any of the work.”

Buck opened his mouth to ask if Lyndsay’s daughter - what was her name? He was certain he knew it - was one of the girls he’d been chatting up back in the spring, before deciding that one, he didn’t actually want to know, and two, Lyndsay would have definitely said something if she was. The PTO meetings after that scandal had been painful to sit through.

“Papa!” Gavin started wiggling until Amy helped him down, clutching the sheet he’d been coloring. He ran around the table until he reached Buck and held it out to him. Buck let out a dramatic gasp and knelt down.

“Is this for me?” he asked, taking it from him. It was a spectacularly multicolored Elmo.

“Yeah!”

“We’ll go stick it on the fridge. How about that?” Buck wrapped an arm around his kid and lifted him, and Gavin squealed in delight as he clutched to his shirt. “What about yours, Chris? Fridge material?”

“Duh,” Chris answered, holding it out for him to grab on the way by. “What’s for dinner?”

“Pretty sure Abuela mentioned a hankering for spaghetti,” Buck told him. He had to juggle things a little bit to keep from dropping either Gavin or the drawings as he stuck them both to the fridge with magnets. “Amy? May? You wanna stay for dinner?”

“Are you gonna use Bobby’s recipe for the sauce?” May asked him.

“One of his.” The one that didn’t take as long to make.

“Then sure,” she said, and then snapped her fingers, like she’d just remembered something. “Oh! Apparently Mom has to go to Arizona for a prisoner transfer or something.”

“Isn’t it usually the US Marshals who do that?” Eddie asked, and Buck turned to see his face scrunched up cutely. “Why is she doing it?”

“Dunno.” May shrugged. “She said she should be back by tomorrow night, though.”

Buck’s skeptical scoff was echoed by Eddie and, for some reason, Chris. Chris shrugged when they both stared at him in question.

“She and Grandpops went on a cruise and the boat sank. After being attacked by pirates,” he pointed out. “We all know something’s going to happen.”

Amy looked around at them and then tentatively asked,

“Pirates?”

“Okay, so,” was how May started the story. Eddie got up and came over to take Gavin from Buck, since the little guy was not showing any interest in being put down. With both his hands free once again, he pulled out the various ingredients for the sauce and started cooking as he listened. “Mom and Bobby went on a cruise for their late honeymoon back in the spring. This was after their first cruise got canceled because Grandpa had a stroke…”

Chapter End Notes

It's kinda fun rewriting this episode with the angle of, "here's how Buck and Gerrard differ as captains..." Also my rebellion against Chris' continued absence. I will hike across the country and meet you outside your house, Tim Minear, I swear to God.

As an aside, now that I've come up with the idea, I'm realizing that "giant swarm of angry killer bees descending on a packed baseball stadium" would have been an Awesome season opener.

Chapter 3: Flight of the Killer Bees

Chapter Summary

In which Eddie plays bait and Bobby has an admirer.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The bees were still causing havoc by the time their next shift rolled around. It felt like every other call since they were released on the bridge somehow involved them, either because they were causing untold mayhem or because of the sheer number of medical calls that the paramedics were sent out on for bee stings. Almost all of them had been stung at least once so far, though Toby had thankfully managed to somehow avoid it. Mostly by sprinting away from every buzzing, bumbling pest and throwing someone else at them in sacrifice. 

That was very literal, too. Buck got to watch as Toby grabbed Ravi and shoved him at a bee that got too close, before fleeing in the other direction. Ravi was still nursing a grudge about that, an understandable one considering that they were at the station and he wasn’t wearing his turnouts to protect himself from being stung.

Worse, the engine and ladder both needed to be inspected when they got back from each and every call. After that first one, when the bees managed to get into the guts of the engine to clog the water intake, Buck didn’t really want to take the risk of them having snuck in to cause any problems that could be missed until someone’s life was on the line. Plus, there were the literal guts that needed wiping off, because representing the department (and the city) to the public meant everything needed to shine.

There were many benefits to being the captain, namely the pay increase, but not having to be one of the people who was stuck getting bits of bee out of the engine’s grill was one of the biggest at the moment.

Plans for lunch got interrupted by yet another bee related emergency. The swarm, or at least part of it, invaded a garden party and started laying siege to the guests now stuck inside the house. All except the one unfortunate woman who found herself trapped in a pool, stuck between drowning or being stung to death.

“Thank God,” the presumed hostess said the moment they entered the backyard in full turnouts and beehoods on. “Sheila’s in the pool, with the rest of this.”

She raised the garden hose she was holding. The end of it had been sheared off; in the middle of the swarm hovering over the pool, the cut off piece could be seen sticking out of the water. An improvised snorkel, clever. Buck was willing to bet it was Maddie’s idea.

“How long has she been down there?” Buck asked her.

“About twenty-five minutes.”

That was a very long time to be trapped at the bottom of the pool.

“We can’t just pull her up into the swarm,” Hen pointed out. “We’ve gotta move the bees.”

“Smoke worked last time,” Buck said, thinking aloud. There apparently weren’t any cookouts happening at this house, because he couldn’t spot any grills that they could use. “Not sure how I feel about intentionally starting a fire for it, though.”

“Probably for the best, Cap,” Albert agreed.

“Ravi, get Toby and the others and go check on the people inside,” Buck ordered, even as he crept closer to the pool’s edge. The bees ignored him completely, along with everyone who followed behind him, which was kinda weird. “Make sure no one was hurt too badly in the rush.”

From the looks of things, with furniture overturned and decorations knocked over, the guests had stampeded for the perceived safety of the house. He wondered if Sheila intentionally jumped into the pool, tripped over the edge, or got knocked into it. They were lucky no one got trampled into the ground.

“How are we getting her out of there?” Chimney asked after Ravi left to get everyone else that had been left to linger by the trucks. He and Albert were pulling the stretcher along. “Without her going full Nicholas Cage, I mean.”

“What does Nicholas Cage have to do with anything?” Buck asked in turn, crouching down beside the pool.

“That one actually makes sense. But I’m still disappointed.”

“I’m sure it’s available to watch somewhere,” Eddie said. “Chris’ll probably get a kick out of it.”

“It’s a Nicholas Cage movie. They’re fun even when they’re awful.”

“Okay, but while we’re discussing bad movies,” Hen broke in, “could we maybe make time for figuring out how to get her out of there?”

“I’m guessing waiting until they get bored is out of the question,” Albert said.

“That could take hours,” Buck informed him.

“And I am not comfortable with leaving her underwater for that long,” Hen said.

“Ah, crap,” Chimney suddenly said. Sheila flailed beneath the pool’s surface and there was a spurt of water out of the makeshift snorkel, like a fountain. “Guys! I think the bees found a loophole.”

“Hey, Cap?” Toby’s voice through the radio was excited. “The garden party was a perfume launch! I remember you said something about bees and scents, right?”

Buck felt himself grin, inordinately pleased that someone besides Eddie paid attention to his rambling.

“Who was wearing the perfume?” he asked, though he figured he already knew the answer to that.

“The lady in the pool.”

Yup.

“Guys,” he told the others. “I have an idea.”

None of them looked particularly heartened by that announcement. Which was perfectly reasonable, because one of them was absolutely going to be sacrificed for the cause.

The perfume apparently had both floral scents as well as banana. The former attracted bees, the latter pissed them off. Both of which explained why the bees acted the way that they did. Buck’s idea was very simple: one of them, wearing their full PPE, would get absolutely drenched in the perfume and lure the bees away, to where a catering tent stood a fair distance from the pool. It even zipped up, which was perfect for containment until a beekeeper arrived.

“Okay.” Eddie was standing in the middle of the room, glaring at absolutely everyone as Buck and Chimney spritzed him. “But why does it have to be me?”

“You’re the fastest runner,” Buck told him with a smile.

“That’s such bullshit.”

“You smell wonderful, by the way,” Chimney told Eddie, and then sprayed him right in the face before setting down the perfume bottle and going outside, where Hen and Albert were still waiting, to get into position.

“You are so making this up to me,” Eddie growled, glaring at Buck.

“I’ve already got tickets to the Dodgers’ play-offs game on the fifth. I’ll get us a hotel or something for after,” Buck told him, unable to keep himself from spraying his husband a little bit more before putting the perfume bottle down. Just in case. “And hey, if anyone ever tries to accuse me of showing you favoritism, I can just remind everyone of the time I used you as bait for a bunch of killer bees.”

“Is that why I’m the one doing this!?”

“It obviously wasn’t gonna be me.”

Eddie grumbled under his breath as they went to the backdoor, Spanish phrases slipping out of his mouth that were not fit for children’s ears. He took a breath, hopped in place for a moment as he hyped himself up, and then threw the door open. He sprinted out, shouting for the paramedics to,

“Go! Go! Go!”

Buck followed him out a bit slower, watching as the bee swarm slowly pulled themselves away from their unavailable target and began to chase after the sprinting firefighter. When the coast was clear, Chimney and Albert splashed into the pool and yanked Sheila out, getting her onto the waiting stretcher.

As they hurried her inside, Buck pulled out his phone and took the moment to record his husband running to and fro, screaming at the top of his lungs with the cloud of bees hounding his every step. When he dove into the catering tent, and the swarm went in with him, Buck stopped recording, checked on the patient - they had a bougie to open her airways and were using duct tape to pull out the bee stingers, but her vitals were good - and then went to check on his husband after radioing dispatch for an update on the beekeeper.

Eddie looked comical, angrily glaring at everything as bees crawled over his turnouts and beehood.

“You look like you need a hook for a hand,” Buck remarked, pausing to zip up the entrance to the tent. There were trays of snack foods sitting out, now covered in buzzing bees. He pulled out his phone and snapped a few pictures of his husband, which did not improve the man’s mood any.

“Maybe I should book us a boat tour or something,” Eddie sniped.

“I’m also putting up a video of you running from the bees,” Buck told him, utterly unperturbed as he cropped and waited for everything to upload to their Instagram page. “I put it to Yakety Sax.”

“Cap.” Ravi’s voice. “Monty’s heading your way.”

“Who’s Monty?” Eddie asked.

The question was answered when Buck unzipped the tent flap and the beekeeper in full gear popped inside to cheerfully announce himself as,

“Monty Moore, beekeeper to the stars. Dispatch sent me.” He had a vacuum, the tank attached to his back, which he pointed at Eddie. “Arms up, please. This won’t hurt a bit.”

“Been shot before.” Eddie’s bitchiness was at full tilt. “I’m pretty sure I can handle this.”

“I was talking to the bees, sir.”

Buck gave his husband a pair of thumbs up as the vacuum came to life, the sound of it competing with the constant droning of the insects. He was actually rather amazed as he watched the guy work, just sucking up the angry stabby creatures like they were dust bunnies, crawling across the ground to get the ones that threatened to escape. It didn’t actually take long before the last one was disappearing down the tube, to join its furious friends.

“That oughta do it,” Monty said, turning off the vacuum; there was a muffled, yet undeniable droning from the canister. He unzipped the flap and let himself out.

“That’s it?” Eddie didn’t sound like he trusted it.

“We beat the bees,” Buck happily declared.

“Well, I got one or two hundred thousand in here,” Monty hedged. “And that’s just from just now. I’ve been a busy little bee the past day.”

“We’ll call you if we ever need you again.”

The beekeeper saluted them with the vacuum before marching off to his van or whatever he arrived in. That just left Buck and a still glowering Eddie.

“So,” Buck started. “Honey-”

“There is a pool right there,” Eddie warned. 

“Buzzkill.” Buck dodged the shove, dancing out of range. “C’mon, let’s go check on Hen and them.”

If there was something to be said for being stuck on the production set of an overly dramatic television show, it was that at least the catering was good. It wasn’t anything to really write home about, nothing amazing, but it was better than the food served at other places Bobby had been. It definitely wasn’t up to the quality he was used to for Sunday dinners. Though at least with the show’s catering, he could get away with eating beef or pork or something fried without any issue.

Sunday dinners had gotten awkward in the months since his heart attack. Or, no, they had gotten awkward in the months since Buck learned of his snap decision to retire. Sure, by that point, Bobby had already decided to take it all back, but the damage was already done. 

It had been a very long time since he’d had Buck that angry with him. It might have been, actually, the first time Buck had ever been angry enough to yell at him like that. The lawsuit had been driven more by hurt feelings and the fear of being abandoned. The time after the mess with Jonah Greenway, after Bobby held him back from going down the cliff, there’d been no yelling involved and the anger had cooled quickly enough after they talked. But this time was different, and it was lingering.

On the Sundays that they had their family dinners, the usual welcome was laced with a chill that would rival the winters Bobby grew up with. Buck would greet him and talk with him, but the usual warmth and closeness was decidedly lacking. And yet, not coincidentally, the food that ended up on the table kept with the same theme as it had since his heart attack: an awful lot of fish, more fruits and vegetables than ever before, beans and whole grain breads. On the rare days that cow and pig ended up on his plate, it was the leanest of cuts.

It was all heart healthy food. Buck was very clearly going out of his way to find new recipes with Bobby - or rather, Bobby’s cardiovascular system - in mind. Because Buck was angry, and he was hurt, but he was still Buck. Hell, Bobby’s doctors hadn’t even been as concerned about his diet as Buck was. The heart attack was caused by smoke inhalation and overexertion, after all. 

The chief was perhaps just as concerned about it as Buck, though. Concerned about his heart and about his back, which still twinged first thing in the morning and complained for the rest of the day if he even thought about skipping his stretches. Simpson might’ve been upset when he was first informed of Bobby’s intent to retire, but it was only very grudgingly that he agreed to allow Bobby to un- retire, with the Medal of Valor and the good publicity around it being perhaps the biggest driving force. But his back injury combined with the heart attack meant a return to active firefighting wasn’t going to happen.

The post he was shuffled into was the on-set technical advisor for Hotshots, an overly dramatic and entirely unrealistic television show about firefighters. The dialogue was unforgivably cheesy - Seriously, what person decided “pump and dump” was a phrase that needed to come out of anyone’s mouth who wasn’t standing on a porn set? - and the writing decisions for the scenes he got to see were questionable at best. He pitied the actors at times, for the way they had to carry through with the most ridiculous storylines and convincingly sell them to the audience. Plus, Taylor Kelly’s god awful book kept popping up, and he nearly decided to retire for real when he realized that it was being used as a source of reference by the people who worked on the show.

And yet, for some reason that Bobby just could not comprehend, people loved this show. Christopher, his precious grandson who grew up surrounded by actual firefighters, loved this show. Then again, maybe that one made sense. Buck did often tease Eddie for his and their son’s shared love for telenovelas, and Bobby figured the writing couldn’t be too terribly different. At least it meant that, when he went over to visit on the Sundays that Buck and Eddie worked, he didn’t have to fight for the teenager’s attention. 

Very few things were as cool as a grandfather that worked on the set of a popular TV show, after all.

“Hollywood glamour, eh, Captain Nash?”

The British accented voice had Bobby looking up from his phone, and from the video of Eddie being chased by part of the swarm of bees that had been uploaded to that FirefightersDiaz account. Brad Torrance, who was now dragging a chair over to sit right beside him with his own tray of food, was one of the lead actors of the show. He played Captain Race Banner, a name that Bobby couldn’t hear without thinking of Race Bannon from that cartoon he watched growing up. The actor still had fake soot brushed strategically around his face from the shoot they just wrapped up.

“Pretty hard to complain,” was Bobby’s polite, noncommittal response.

“And yet,” Brad said, “something tells me you’d rather not be here.”

“I was assigned here, so I’m on duty.”

“The fire department’s run out of fire stations?”

“...sure,” Bobby said after a moment. “Something like that.”

“So, the, uh, grips, they tell me that you’re a bit of a hero,” Brad said. Bobby took a breath and bit back the immediate, knee-jerk responses to that: to snap at the man or to laugh at him. Hero? Him? Please. “Sunken Ferris wheel? Or was it a cruise ship?”

Huh. The cruise ship made sense, with all the publicity that surrounded it with the chief’s encouragement, but the Ferris wheel caught Bobby by surprise. That hadn’t even been in that awful book, so he wondered where that story spread from. One of the people they rescued, maybe? One of the other firefighters that was there?

Why was it being credited to him, anyways? Eddie had been the one who scaled it to help everyone, and Lena Bosko was the one who survived the wave and helped everyone she sheltered there with.

“Both, actually.”

“So the rumors are true. You’re an LAFD legend.” Brad ended the sentence with an odd little noise, almost like a growl. It was weird.

“Hardly.” Bobby couldn’t bite back the scoff this time. “I’m just a civil servant.”

“You know De Niro?”

“Not personally.”

“He trained with the real Jake LaMotta for Raging Bull,” Brad continued, like Bobby hadn’t said anything.

“I have never actually seen it,” he admitted.

“You are my LaMotta, Captain Nash.” The actor was staring at him rather intensely, and Bobby found himself leaning away from the man. “I’m gonna study you tip to tail.”

“Why?” Bobby could not help but ask.

“Because from where I’m sitting, your job’s the glamour one.”

Uncertain how to take that statement, and more than a bit unnerved, Bobby decided to go back to his food. He picked up his untouched roll and brought it up to his mouth, only to catch Brad watching him closely, almost anticipatorily. When he did take a bite, the actor nodded, acting like the way that Bobby ate was the most intriguing thing he had ever seen.

Maybe if he begged hard enough, Bobby could get reassigned to somewhere far, far away from any Hollywood actors.

Chapter End Notes

Not pictured: Chris forcing his grandpops to tell him everything that he did on set since the last time he saw him.
I know that there's a lot of flack for how season 7 and 8a open and close with heavy focus on Bathena, but 8x01 really puts the spotlight on Buck, too. More specifically, on the fact that he's actually very smart. Because both times, he's the one who comes up with the plan that saves the victims from the bees.

Chapter 4: Hollywood Glamour is Like Pyrite

Chapter Summary

In which Bobby is not at all surprised about what his wife has gotten up to without him.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

A bell rang and one of the crewmembers - Bobby thought his title was the assistant director - announced that the film was rolling and told everyone to turn off their phones. Bobby pulled his out to do just that, noting the lack of notifications from Athena, and prepared himself for the indignity that he was about to suffer through. They were actually watching it on the screens: currently, it was from the point of view of the camera stuck at the bottom of a toilet, though there was one in the wall right above it, too. Two of the actors dressed up as firefighters - and God on high, that one wasn’t even wearing his turnout coat properly - were staring down at the camera so they were framed by the bowl and the seat. The bathroom mockup was just out of view from where Bobby was standing, too cramped for anyone but the actors that needed to be in the shot.

“Cap,” one of the actors - What was his name? What was his character’s name? Did Bobby actually care about the answer to either of those questions? - said in the flattest delivery ever. “You better give a listen here.”

From out view of the camera, just behind the fake bathroom wall, which was probably constructed to the same level of quality as the actual bathroom wall of Bobby’s last apartment, someone said,

“Help me, help me. I’m in here.”

Nevermind, that was the flattest delivery ever. Bobby really hoped it was going to be dubbed over with someone a bit more lively or something, because he’d been to school plays with better acting. Truthfully, that was a statement that held true for this show in general, but there had to be standards somewhere. Surely the bar they were aiming for here was not on the same level as a preschool rendition of Old MacDonald Had a Farm.

(Who was Bobby kidding? Brooke’s lone line of “oink, oink,” almost shouted into the mic between giggles, was more worthy of an Emmy than anything he’d been forced to listen to on this set.)

“Owners said they retiled the bathroom floor yesterday,” said the second actor, the one with his turnout coat open. To his credit, he may have actually been in a school play once or twice, because his delivery was much better than his scene partner’s. “And no one’s seen the plumber since.”

Wait. What? Bobby clearly needed to actually pay attention to the scripts, because he didn’t realize that was the scenario here. A plumber comes in to retile the bathroom - and why was a plumber doing the retiling? He could swear that he remembered Michael once mentioning a contractor specifically for the tiles. - and they… What? Managed to fall down the pipes that clog if a paper towel gets flushed? Or did they somehow fall through the floor and- No, that still didn’t explain how the plumber was stuck in the pipes from the bathroom end.

“All right, everyone, stand back.” There was Brad Torrance, coming to stand behind the pair, using his passable American accent. “I’m gonna Roto-Rooter this guy out the old-fashioned way.”

The two actors parted for him, and Brad lifted up a sledgehammer. He was going to sledgehammer the toilet. That someone was supposed to be trapped in.

“Whoa, whoa, whoa!” Bobby cried out, before that could go wrong. “Can we cut?”

“What now?” The director sounded annoyed as the bell rang, signalling a pause in filming, but Bobby didn’t really pay him any mind as he went to Brad and the others.

“I’m sorry, everybody,” Bobby said, not feeling very sorry at all. “It’s just that- First, you’d never swing that thing anywhere near where the victim might be, ‘cause you could hurt him. You could even kill him.”

“Hey, tech advisor,” the director snapped, the man having followed him. “It’s a TV show, not reality.”

Wasn’t Bobby’s job here to help them be as realistic as possible when it came to the firefighting stuff? Bobby was fairly certain that was the job description. It definitely wasn’t anything to do with actual safety, because there was a whole host of people here who took care of that.

“Copy that,” he said after a moment, before turning to Brad and the other actors. “So, if it’s a TV show and you have to use a sledgehammer-” Though Bobby, personally, would not use a sledgehammer for this one. It would be less destructive to just shut off the water and remove the toilet from the floor. Both the department and the owner’s insurance preferred that, too. “-then you want to remember that you’re hitting into tile.”

“Yeah.” Brad nodded, laser focused on Bobby. The other two actors, not so much. The one with his turnout coat open, the one who seemed to have better acting skills than a dead fish, had his face scrunched up in confusion.

“And sharp shards of porcelain could come flying back at you,” Bobby continued. “So you’d put your visors down or you might go home blind.”

“They’re not putting their visors down, because then the audience won’t see their faces,” the director argued. Bobby was pretty sure his name started with an M. “And this is not actual porcelain. It’s plaster of paris, not real.”

“But we want it to look real,” Brad broke in, staring the director down. “Don’t we, Marcus?”

The director, Marcus, huffed and glared at Bobby. Then he turned and stormed off, snapping at the assistant director that he needed his script.

“I think maybe that guy hates me,” Bobby remarked as he watched him go.

“Oh, don’t worry about it,” Brad told him. “He’ll be gone by the end of the week, off to another show. But you? You’ll still be here.”

It was probably meant to be comforting. It sounded anything but.

If there was one reason to be thankful for the heatwave that was doing its very best to slow cook the city and all its inhabitants, it was this: for as much as it aggravated the bees, it also sent them flying higher and out of the city. Maddie, when they touched base earlier, said there hadn’t been a bee-related call in hours. Which meant, in turn, that they had a bit of uninterrupted downtime. 

They got the necessary stuff out of the way, cleaning the trucks (again) and restocking the ambulances. Buck managed to bully through some of the paperwork that came with the job title while Eddie continued to sulk about being used as bait for the bees. His mood was not helped by the fact that Marjan, way down in Texas, had captured his flight in both GIF and still image form and turned him into a meme. It was already being spammed in their groupchat with TK, because the paramedic was as much of a little shit as Buck was. The latest one was a screenshot of Eddie, labeled “Me,” fleeing from the swarm of bees labeled “My Responsibilities.”

At the moment, they were sitting down to eat. Or at least, that had been Buck’s plan. Except that as soon as his butt hit the chair, his phone began to ring. The ringtone had him frowning even as he pulled out his phone to look at the caller ID. He wasn’t the only one, because down the table, Chimney lifted his head up to look his way.

“Is that Maddie?” he asked.

“Yeah. I thought she just had her break,” Buck wondered aloud, because that was when they’d touched base. He swiped his thumb over the screen, accepting the call with, “Hey, Mads.”

“Captain Diaz,” was how his sister greeted him. He immediately sat up in his seat, the expression on his face showing enough to have everyone else doing the same. “We’re taking the One Eighteen out of rotation for the rest of shift.”

“Why?”

“I have some people on the line who need to talk to you,” Maddie said. “To all of you. Put me on speaker, I’ll explain.”

“Uh, okay, hold on.” Buck did as she asked, holding the phone out in front of him. The others leaned in, concern and curiosity clear as day on their own faces. “Okay.”

“Hi, everyone. I need your help with multiple casualties from a midair collision.”

“We’re nowhere near the airport,” Hen pointed out.

“And I’d like to think we’d notice a plane crashing outside,” Ravi said.

“They’re still in the air,” Maddie said. “ATC’s working on bringing them down safely. For now, I’m gonna patch them through to each of you individually for triage.”

“Why us?” Eddie managed to ask before anyone else did, since they were all undoubtedly wondering the same thing.

“Because you’re their best hope,” was the dispatcher’s very biased response. “And because Athena’s on that plane.”

Buck felt his heart skip a beat and his stomach drop to his knees. Maddie didn’t stay on the line for long, hanging up so she could start patching through calls. Chimney’s phone rang first, then Hen’s, then Eddie and Albert’s. Each of them stood from their seats as they answered, falling seamlessly into work mode, even if they hadn’t exactly been trained for tele-triage in the academy. Or, in Eddie’s case, at boot camp.

There was nothing for Buck to do, not with his basic level of EMT training. At least, not when it came to the people on the plane. He swiped his thumb over Fire Dad ICE in his contacts; it went straight to voicemail, not even bothering to ring even once.

“You’ve reached Bobby Nash. I’m not available to take your call right now. Please leave a message.”

Buck did not bother leaving a message, hanging up with a huff before the tone even sounded. He’d just have to go about it another way, then. It was a good thing his life was the kind of weird that led to him having the phone numbers of assistants on a television set. Although, when Bobby had given them to him and Eddie, it probably wasn’t with this exact scenario in mind.

Then again, their cruise ship got attacked by pirates and then sunk in a hurricane earlier in the year, so maybe he was thinking of such outlandish scenarios.

The shouting was audible the moment Bobby stepped out of the trailer bathroom. There was a constant flurry of motion, with people rushing past as they focused on their own specific job that kept the entire thing going like a poorly oiled, constantly grinding machine. None of them, he noticed, even looked towards the direction of the shouting, so it was evidently not that rare of an occurrence. Whether it was specifically the person doing the shouting or whether it was because working in Hollywood was just like that, Bobby wasn’t certain and dreaded being here long enough to find out.

“No, no! You listen to me.” It was Brad doing the shouting, his British accent growing thicker with his anger. He was nearby, off the path and out of everyone’s way, poorly hidden behind trees and shrubbery as he paced. Bobby couldn’t see the other person he was shouting at - the actor had a phone to his ear. “You come near her again, and I mean even the same state, you even glance in her direction, and I will know. And the next time you happen to lower your guard just for one moment, just know that I’m gonna take that moment to end your bloody, pathetic-”

Brad stopped in his tracks, eyes going wide as he spotted Bobby watching him.

“Hello, Bobby, mate.” It was like a switch had been flipped, the actor waving and smiling all cheerful-like. Bobby continued to stare in bewilderment as the man came out from behind the greenery, heading for where an assistant sat waiting, young and blank faced, in a golf cart. “Sandy, I’ve got to call you back, darling, yes. Somebody’s, uh, just shown up… Alright darling, toodle-oo. Bye.”

“Are you good?” Bobby asked, somewhat concerned.

“Yeah, yeah, yeah,” Brad assured him. The assistant in the golf cart handed him a drink and something wrapped in foil. “I was just, uh…”

“Doing a scene?”

“Yeah, yeah, yeah. But not for this. Sit down.”

“Yeah, alright.”

There were a pair of rear facing seats on the back of the golf cart. Brad sat down and so did Bobby, mainly because he knew that Brad would be headed the same way as him and also because curiosity was not a trait that Buck had a monopoly on. There was a reason, after all, that Athena made cracks about him dumpster-diving.

“Not for this,” Brad said again. The golf cart started to move, making them both sway in their seats.  “Been rehearsing for a play. I wrote it. Cowrote it. That was my writing partner. Have you seen the movie Platoon?”

“Is that the one with Wilford Brimley?” Bobby asked, just to mess with the man. A pang went through him, because he missed watching Buck purposefully wind Chimney up in the downtime between calls by pretending that he had never seen some movie or show. “At the retirement center and the aliens take him away?”

“That’s Cocoon,” Brad corrected. “Platoon’s-”

“Vietnam. Oliver Stone. I remember,” Bobby told him. “I was making a joke.”

“Oh.” Brad nodded. “The deadpan, seen-it-all irony kind of thing. Yeah, yeah, I’m gonna use that.”

God, this man was weird.

“So, Platoon?” he urged, to get away from the fact that this person was apparently looking to him for character inspiration.

“Yeah, yeah, right. So, before the cast went to the Philippines to film the movie, right?” Brad paused; Bibby nodded, and kept nodding with every actor he listed. “Charlie Sheen. Willem Dafoe. And a really young Johnny Depp.”

The golf cart came to a stop in front of the building that housed the set they were needed on. It was not that far from where they’d started, they could’ve easily walked it and probably made it in the same amount of time. Bobby wondered how much the golf cart kid got paid to drive people ten feet down the lane.

“They all got to work with a real-life drill sergeant,” Brad said as they went inside. “Two or three weeks. It really helped them feel like what it feels like to be in the jungle.”

“Right, right,” Bobby agreed, nodding along.

“So it really, really helped with their performance and everything.”

“Yeah.” Wait. “Oh, so you want to do that. But with firefighting.”

They passed a banner for the show that had Brad Torrance’s face on it and no one else’s. It was things like that which really explained the size of this guy’s ego. It also made no sense: Hotshots was an ensemble show, supposedly, but no one would ever think that if they only saw the promotional material.

“Exactly!” the actor exclaimed. “A weekend up in the mountains, just the men. Or we could do it at my place in Malibu.” 

Bobby was caught on the just the men part and had to give himself a mental shake before this conversation got too far away from him. On the one hand, he had Hen’s voice in his head, talking about how sexist that came across. On the other hand, he had Hen’s voice in his head pointing out the obvious jokes.

“But anyway, you can be the, uh, the drill sergeant,” Brad told Bobby, sitting down on a foldout chair and unwrapping the foil covered sandwich the assistant gave him. “And, I don’t know, berate us to your heart’s content.”

“Well, I love berating people.”

He really didn’t. This whole idea sounded like Hell.

Brad took a bite of the sandwich and immediately spat it out. Bobby jumped to get away from the firing line.

“This is disgusting!” Brad shouted, that anger from earlier making its return.

“I’ll have a think on it,” Bobby told him, eager to away.

“Yeah, take your time.” Once again, that again was gone like it had never been there. “Yeah, yeah, yeah, you mull it over.”

“I am absolutely going to mull it over.” For long enough that he could truthfully say he mulled it over before giving an emphatic no. Which would be about the length of time it took him to walk somewhere else.

“Oh, wait, Bobby!” Brad’s voice caught him again before he even took three steps. “Just one more idea, alright?”

“Alright…”

“I think that my character should use a catch phrase.” Oh, God. “So imagine, all the bells are going off, we’re running to our firetruck and everything. And then I stand there and I say something like, ‘Let’s saddle up, boys.’”

Brad dropped into the American accent he put on for the show, deeper than his normal voice. Bobby stared at him.

“What do you think?” the actor asked. “Did you like it?”

“It’s got a real Western flavor,” Bobby told him.

“That is exactly what I thought! I’m gonna try it.”

“You… Yeah, you do that.”

An assistant director shouted for everyone to get to their places just as the bell rang to signal the start of filming again. It was only as Bobby was following Brad that he remembered he meant to check his phone before he got distracted. Too late now, though.

The loft of the fire station was filled with voices, each of them calm and professional and full of unwavering support. While the paramedics got assigned the more serious cases from the plane - Chimney was talking one group through a fasciotomy to treat a girl’s compartment syndrome; Hen was apparently saving someone’s life over the phone through the use of erectile dysfunction medication - several of the others were now instructing people in basic first aid. Buck was proud of them, each and every single one of them, for the way they’d stepped up without fail. Or at least he would be later.

Right now, his prevailing emotion was frustration.

The person on the set of Hotshots that he called, some assistant of an assistant, was severely road blocking him. They were apparently filming at the moment and God forbid someone violate the sanctity of a live set to pass on a message. It didn’t matter to this person that there was an emergency - in fact, there were several emergencies stuffed into one big one, like an EMS turducken - they would not budge on their refusal to get Bobby for him. And Bobby’s phone was still going straight to voicemail, as if the man hadn’t learned to just put his phone on vibrate instead of turning it off completely for just an occasion such as this one.

The call ended and Buck glared at the screen. He had another number that he could try, but he doubted they would go any differently. One by one, the others finished their calls as well. Albert flopped into a seat at the table beside Ravi, setting his phone down beside the other’s. Eddie, his own phone tucked back away, came to stand next to Buck.

“Remind me to get a cake to bring in for everyone,” Buck told him.

“We’ll all appreciate that,” his husband said. “Any luck getting through to Bobby?”

“Nope. They’re filming right now, so his phone’s off. I gave someone a message to pass on, but I don’t think they’re gonna bother. They pretty much just brushed me off.”

“One of my people made a shiv while I was on the phone with him,” Chimney said as he joined them. “Seems like a useful skill to have, maybe we should request a workshop. Any word from Maddie on what’s gonna happen now?”

“Not yet. She said air traffic control’s working on getting them down safely.” Buck shrugged and stuffed his phone into his pocket. “I guess we just wait and see. Dunno if Fifty-one will be able to handle it themselves, with how many-”

The alarm rang, cutting them off. Overhead, a dispatcher started rattling off station numbers - a lot of stations, including the 118 - and directing them towards one of the LAX runways. There was a pause and then a flurry of motions as everyone ran for their turnouts.

“That’s like half the department,” Eddie commented when he met them downstairs; he’d taken the pole.

“From across the city, too,” Buck said. They probably didn’t want to take too much of the resources directly around the Los Angeles International Airport; the people living and working in that area wouldn’t suddenly stop needing first responders just because they were all busy responding to a plane making an emergency landing. As it was, a bunch of other stations were about to have their workload doubled, the poor bastards. “Hen!”

Hen stopped halfway to their gear and turned.

“I’ll meet you all at the airport,” he told her.

“Where are you going?” she demanded.

“To get Pops!” Buck shouted back, already sprinting across the bay for the entrance that let him out to the parking lot. “You’re in charge until I get there!”

There wasn’t any time for them to argue, and they thankfully didn’t try. The trucks pulled out of the station and headed towards LAX. Buck got into the jeep and pulled out of the parking lot, following behind them until it was time to turn towards Hollywood. He knew where the studio was that Bobby worked at, and he had no problem physically bullying his way past anyone that tried to obstruct him.

Bobby needed to be at the airport to meet Athena, the man wouldn’t forgive himself if he wasn’t.

The acting was not improving. Bobby sat in his assigned seat, stuck watching and listening to it as he glanced through his own copy of the script and wished he was doing literally anything else. He winced as Brad - as Captain Race Banner - brought the sledgehammer down on the toilet to free the unseen victim, only partially gratified that they indeed had their visors pulled down. 

The bell rang for a break to eat and Bobby practically jumped out of his chair. Before he could flee, though, Brad intercepted him, already having shed the coat and helmet.

“Bobby, Bobby, do you have a second?”

“You were great in that last scene,” Bobby lied as he tried to escape. The actor was stuck to his heels, though. “It was compelling stuff.”

He’d seen better acting from Ravi and Albert when they tried to pretend like they hadn’t devoured half of a box of doughnuts brought into the station.

“I was wondering if you had the chance to think about what we talked about?” Brad eagerly asked.

“I did, but I want to think about it some more,” Bobby told him as they got to the exit. The sliding garage-like door was pulling up, releasing them into the outside world where the show’s fully functioning fire engine was parked. “Right now, I’ve got to check in with my wife.”

He held up his phone, screen coming to life as it came back on.

“Well, happy wife, happy life,” Brad said. “And in my case, wives. Five.”

He held up a hand with the fingers splayed.

“You must be a happy guy, then,” Bobby said, entirely unsurprised by this development.

Some of the actors and crew were gathered around a laptop, a live news broadcast playing. The anchor was talking about a small plane colliding in midair with an airliner, but he only paid it half a mind as saw that he had a voicemail from Athena.

“Bobby.” There was wind in the background, a lot of wind, and his wife sounded anxious. “I love you, baby.”

The message ended and Bobby had a horrible thought as he heard the news anchor say that a passenger was now flying the airliner.
