“Did they say where that flight took off from?” he asked the people who’d been paying attention to the story. They weren’t the ones who answered him, though.

“Pops!”

He turned, spotted Buck - in uniform - running for him. And if Buck was here, as frantic looking as he did, then that meant his horrible thought was a reality.

“Athena’s on that flight, isn’t she?” he asked, meeting his son halfway.

“Ma’s flying it.”

“Of course she is.” Bobby couldn’t even find it in himself to be surprised at this point. “What else would she be doing?”

“They dispatched, like, every company in the city to LAX for an emergency landing.”

“Where’s your car?”

“It’s this way,” Buck told him. That ribbon of anger and hurt, present in all their interactions over the summer, was entirely absent from the younger man now as he focused on Athena and the emergency at hand. It was probably inappropriate to be thankful for it, considering the circumstances that brought it about. “Streets were jammed, took me forever to get here.”

That wouldn’t do.

“Then we’re taking this,” Bobby said, pointing at the show’s fire engine. 119 was emblazoned on the side; he once wondered if the person who chose that for the characters’ station number thought they were being clever with it. 

“Seriously?”

“Yeah. Get in, let’s go.”

Buck hesitated for a moment and then rushed to do just that, pulling open the side door and climbing in. Bobby did the same, hopping into the driver’s seat. He barely noticed that one of the back doors was opened and someone else was joining them, not until they spoke up.

“Alright, boys.” Brad was sitting in the back, American accent in place. “Let’s saddle up.”

“Brad.” Bobby cut himself off with a sigh, because there wasn’t really any time to argue about this. “Whatever.”

As he started the engine and they started on their way, he idly wondered if stealing it for this would get him fired from the show.

Chapter End Notes

This chapter was really long because I had no clue where a good spot was to cut it off without awkward chapter lengths.
A note on Lone Star in regards to Darling, So It Goes: I have no damn clue what the hell is going on with the timeline or when the episodes for season 5 are supposed to be taking place. 5x01 is supposed to be a year after the season 4 finale, except Tarlos' wedding anniversary isn't until 5x05? The wiki says TK's birthday is in December, but his birthday is in 5x07, two episodes after the wedding anniversary. Coincidentally, that episode was written by Molly Green, who also decided that a child born in 2011 turns 14 in 2024.
But anyways, this is a (mostly) happy AU and I can do what I want, so just know that in my universe, Grace is still with Judd and wasn't written off to avoid paying an actress what she is deserved.

Chapter 5: Turbulent Landing

Chapter Summary

In which Buck throws himself into traffic, Athena manages the difficult part of flying a plane, and Bobby has faith.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

“Call her for me.”

Bobby was holding out his phone, already unlocked, for Buck to take. He took it, going into the contacts and locating Athena’s number. Unfortunately, when he dragged his finger across her name and called her, it went straight to voicemail. A second and third attempt got the same results.

“Damn it, Athena,” Bobby huffed.

“Okay, Maddie was on the phone with people from the plane earlier,” Buck said, switching over to the keypad and typing in the next three-digit number. “I dunno if she talked to Ma, but maybe someone at Dispatch-”

“Nine-One-One. What’s your emergency?”

“Linda!”

“...Buck?”

“Linda, it’s Captain Bobby Nash.” Bobby glanced between the road and the phone in Buck’s hand as he spoke. “My wife is on that plane and I need to get a hold of her.”

“Okay. Okay, hold on.”

There was dead air as Linda, presumably, handled things on her end. Despite only playing one on TV, the fire engine they were in was serving them well. Its sirens were blaring as they sped down the road, Bobby manhandling the steering wheel with determination. 

“Bobby.” Maddie’s voice. “I just hung up with Athena. Don’t worry, she’s okay.”

“Talk to me,” Bobby requested. Begging, almost. “Tell me what’s going on. Her phone’s going straight to voicemail.”

“Yeah, ATC’s been tying up that line. A flight instructor is coaching her down to the airport.”

“Yeah,” Buck broke in. “That’s where we’re headed.”

“Buck?” His sister sounded surprised. “Bobby, are you with the One Eighteen?”

“No,” Bobby answered. “We’re in a stolen truck.”

“Buck! You stole another fire truck!?”

“Why is your first thought that I did it?” Buck demanded.

“You know why.”

Yeah, he did. It was a very fair accusation.

From the backseat, Brad Torrance - the fucking actor, what the hell was Buck’s life - leaned forward to stick his head between the front seats and said,

“We borrowed it.”

Buck could not help but stare at him, utterly perplexed. That was not how the man sounded on that television show Chris watched. Since when was he British?

“Who is that?”

“Brad Torrance,” the actor said, cheerful as could be. “Nice to meet you, love.”

“Listen, Maddie,” Bobby broke in. “I need to speak to Athena, she’s been trying to reach me all day. I need her to hear my voice. And I need to hear hers, in case…”

His voice broke with the words and he let them trail off.

“She already knows.”

“Not good enough,” Bobby argued. “Buck said that you’ve been in contact with other people on that plane. Can you try one of them?”

“Don’t hang up,” Maddie instructed. “I’ll start dialing numbers.”

While his sister was busy trying to get in touch with one of the passengers on the plane, Buck let his curiosity take over.

“Say that again,” he told Brad. “We borrowed it.”

“We borrowed it?” Brad repeated, a bit of confusion in the words.

“Man, that’s crazy.” Buck chuckled a little as he turned back to Bobby. “I never knew he was British, I would never have guessed.”

“It’s called acting, son,” the actor said, dropping into the American accent that Buck was more used to hearing coming from his mouth.

“Hey, I- I can do a British accent,” he said, and then, “To be-”

“Please don’t,” Bobby cut him off. 

“C’mon, Pops, it’s- it’s a good accent.”

“No.” Bobby firmly shook his head. “It really isn’t.”

Buck pouted in silence as they drove. The longer that time went without Maddie getting back to them, the more agitated Bobby became. This translated to his driving getting a little bit more reckless.

“I’m sorry, Bobby.” That was not the thing they wanted Maddie to say when she got back to them. “I’m not getting through.”

“Not to anyone? What’s going on up there?”

“I don’t know, nobody’s picking up. Maybe they’re all strapped in?”

“What about the manifest?” Bobby asked. “Can we try that? There’s gotta be somebody up on that plane that’ll pick up.”

“I’ll see what I can do,” Maddie promised.

The current state of the Los Angeles International Airport was unnerving. All the other times Eddie had been here, for emergencies or for trips, it had been in a constant flux of activity. Planes taxiing to take off, planes landing, people hurrying to get on, baggage carriers ferrying luggage across the tarmac.

At the moment, though, it was all absent. The runways were clear, the sky was clear. The everpresent cacophony of jet engines was gone.

“Never heard the airport so quiet before,” he commented as he climbed up to the top of the engine, where everyone else had gathered to wait. It was parked in one of the hangers, along with a whole line of other trucks, each from one of the stations that was called. Behind those was the equally long line of ambulances.

The hangar was packed with emergency response vehicles of all kinds.

“They must’ve cleared the airspace,” Hen told him. “Halted all other air traffic.”

“Why do I get the feeling someone doesn’t think this landing is gonna go so smooth?” Chimney asked, twisting around where he sat to look at the ambulances behind them.

“That might be the crash trucks,” Ravi said, pointing them out. 

There was a pair of them at the ends of the lines. They were designed specifically to deal with aviation fuel fires, using cannons to shoot streams of foam to smother the flames where water alone was simply not enough. Because aviation was generally so much safer than driving, the crash trucks were rarely used for the purpose they were meant for.

And now there were two in the hanger with them on standby.

“Any word from Buck yet?” Albert asked.

“No.” Eddie pulled his phone out to check. There was a message from Chris, complaining about the homework one of his teachers had assigned; a message from TK, which was just yet another image of himself turned into a meme; and a message from Stan, the guy who led the veterans group, which contained the recipe for the muffins his wife made for the last meeting. “Not a word.”

“Hopefully he’ll get here before the show starts,” Hen said. “It would be awkward if our captain misses it because he’s stuck in traffic.”

“I’ve got someone. A woman named Pru.”

Buck watched as Bobby sat up excitedly in the driver’s seat.

“Well, put them on!” he said.

“Hello?” said another voice.

“My name's Bobby Nash. I need to talk to Sergeant Grant.”

“She’s a bit busy right now,” the woman told him. “Maybe I could take a message? Give it to her at a more convenient time?”

Buck couldn’t help the snort of laughter.

“Please, I need to talk to her right away,” Bobby just about begged. “It’s important.”

“She’s flying the plane right now. Is it really that important?”

“Yes.” His voice shook. “Please, she needs to hear from me.”

There was an aggrieved, put upon sigh on the other end, followed by a “hold on.” They waited anxiously, the only noise the still blaring sirens on their end and the increasing wind on the other. An increasing wind that was very worrying to Buck, because planes should not have wind like that. They could hear the woman talking to someone, and then,

“Bobby?”

“Athena!” Relief dripped from every syllable of her name. Just hearing her voice again seemed enough to make Bobby relax, just a little bit. “Thank God, are you okay?”

“I’ve had better days. Do I hear sirens?”

“I’m sorry I missed all your calls. Baby, you’ve been all over the news,” Bobby told her. “Listen, I’m headed to LAX right now. There’s just one problem, the 110 is kind of back up, so I might have to meet you at the luggage carousel.”

“Save yourself the trip, we’re gonna miss LAX.”

That did not sound good to Buck. Not one bit.

“What are you talking about?” Bobby didn’t sound as if he liked that ominous statement, either.

“We’ve lost our ability to turn,” Athena said. “In about six minutes, we’re gonna be waving to LAX as we pass over it.”

“Okay.” Bobby shared an uneasy look with Buck. “What do you need from me?”

“Do you have a runway in your pocket?”

Bobby’s entire demeanor shifted. Buck had seen it before, when they were out on a scene together. The way the captain would take a problem handed to them and work through it in his head like a puzzle. Bobby was taking the problem in front of them now and was thinking it through as they drove.

“What direction are you headed?” he asked Athena.

“Due north, to God knows where,” she answered. They were currently in the southbound lane of the 110. “We’re running out of fuel. They’re worried this thing’s gonna take out a lot of people, and I don’t just mean the ones in it.”

“That’s not gonna happen,” Bobby assured her. “How much do you need?”

“How much of what?”

“Runway.”

There was a moment of stupefied silence.

“...a mile?” was Athena’s uncertain answer.

“I’ll give you more than that,” Bobby promised her.

“You’re on the 110.”

“And you’re headed right for me.”

Bobby took the problem that was handed to them and worked it through. A runway needed to be long and straight for the plane to come to a stop; the 110 just happened to have a very long stretch of (mostly) straight road. Buck wasn’t certain if the plane’s current trajectory would put it over them, but Bobby certainly seemed to think so. Enough that he was going to somehow turn it into an emergency runway.

“Buck,” Bobby said. “Get Maddie back on the phone.”

Buck hurried to switch lines, careful not to hang up on Athena. Meanwhile, Bobby’s driving had gotten a bit more reckless. He was treating the truck they were in like a sports car instead of ten tons of engine, jerking the steering wheel into submission as he weaved them through traffic. It earned him blared horns and screeching brakes, not that he seemed to care. If he even noticed at all.

“Jesus, Bob!” Brad complained from the back, clinging onto anything he could to not be thrown about.

“Maddie, we need PD to shut down a mile and a half section of the 110 northbound to the…” He peered at a road sign. “King Boulevard exit.”

“Why? Has there been an accident?”

Technically yes, but…

“There might be.”

“Wait, what’s going on?”

“I’m not meeting Athena at the airport. She’s meeting me here,” Bobby explained and then jerked the wheel. The engine jackknifed across the lanes. The cars behind them came to sudden stops and made their unhappiness with it known to the world. “Southbound’s done. Can you handle north?”

They got out, Bobby taking the phone back from Buck, to the sound of very angry drivers. Buck ignored them as he started searching through the engine’s compartments for something, anything, they might be able to use. But the compartments were turning out to be disappointingly empty.

They always seemed to have exactly what they needed whenever Chris watched the show.

“Alright, we’ll handle it ourselves,” Bobby was declaring as he rounded the engine to the side Buck was on. Buck hadn’t heard his sister’s side of the conversation, but it seemed like they weren’t getting help any time soon. “Brad, is there a roadside kit on this thing?”

“I don’t know,” the actor said, the shrug almost audible in his words. “That’s the teamsters’ job.”

Buck let out a victorious cry as he opened another compartment. It was almost as empty as the others, but this one contained a box of road flares, of all things. He wondered what they might’ve needed them for. Probably not to shut down the freeway for a plane to make an emergency landing.

“I got what we need!” Buck said, waving a pair in the air.

“We’re gonna need those about a mile down the freeway,” Bobby said, pointing down the road.

“A mile?” How was Buck gonna make it a mile before… From behind came the sound of someone who did not care about the rules of traffic. Buck turned, spotted the motorcyclist weaving through the stopped cars, and grinned. “Copy that, Pops.”

He slipped the road flares in his pocket and hurried to wave the motorcycle down. It came to a stop, the driver taking off his helmet to demand,

“What!?”

“Los Angeles Fire Department,” Buck told him, gesturing at his badge. “I need to commandeer that bike.”

“Seriously?”

“And the helmet, come on.”

The guy unhappily cleared the seat for Buck, who swung his leg over and pulled on the helmet. Riding the motorcycle after so long was, well, like riding a bike. He revved the engine and gunned it down the road, the wind pulling at his uniform. 

A mile down the road was not very long at the speeds Buck was going. He reached the exit, which had no police presence, and came to a stop, kicking out the stand so it didn’t just fall over. After tearing off the helmet and dropping it carelessly onto the pavement, he leaped over the dividing wall and yanked out the flares, lighting them up.

“Hey! Hey!” Buck waved the flares frantically, doing his best to get the drivers to stop. They ignored him, though, and drove on past. A couple even swerved around him. He’d forgotten that getting behind the wheel in Los Angeles turned a person into a selfish asshole.

He was going to have to do something reckless to get them to pay attention. The kind of thing he’d need to apologize to Eddie for doing.

“Stop!” Buck yelled, and flung himself in the path of a car. It came to a halt, tires and brakes squealing, as it came just short of hitting him. The cars behind them did the same, and then the ones in the next lanes. He breathed out a sigh of relief as he moved to the middle of the road, still waving the flares. “LAFD! I need you to stay in your cars!”

It was up to Athena, now.

Eddie had no idea what was going on. They’d been sent here to help with the plane when it landed, but the plane hadn’t landed. Instead, it had flown over them, so close that the noise from the engines had them all covering their ears and cringing. And now they were standing around at a loss, unsure of what to do.

“Still no word from Buck,” Eddie told the others as they paced. “And nothing from Bobby.”

Somehow, deep in his gut, he was absolutely certain that the two of them had something to do with whatever was going on.

“Well I didn’t hear a huge explosion,” Chimney said. “So that plane’s still flying.”

“Pretty low,” Toby said, craning his neck to look up at the sky like he was still going to see it. “Where is it going to land?”

“Attention all companies at LAX hanger,” a man’s voice suddenly said over the hanger’s loudspeakers. “Respond to the 110 Freeway.”

As he rattled off the station numbers, they all ran to get back into the trucks. Ravi and Albert sprinted for the ambulance while Eddie and the rest of them scrambled into the engine.

“Who in their right mind takes the 110 at this hour?” Chimney complained.

In the captain’s seat, Hen turned to glare at Eddie.

“What did your husband do?” she demanded.

“I’m gonna guess that he took the 110,” Eddie answered.

This probably also answered Toby’s question.

The cars taking the northbound lanes slowed to a trickle. Until finally, the last one went by and no others followed it.

“I think your boy shut down the road,” Brad said. The actor sounded almost surprised, and Bobby found himself insulted on his son’s behalf.

“Of course he did,” he told him, and then refocused on the matter at hand. Or rather, the phone in his hand. “Athena, can you hear me?”

“I’m here, baby.”

“Buck got the northbound shut down. We have ourselves a runway.”

“Of course he did,” she said. “Best news all day.”

Now, the other matter they had to deal with.

“Brad.” Bobby turned back to the man. “We need to get everybody out of these cars. Tell them to run.”

“Why?”

That was a stupid question.

“There’s a plane coming,” he said. Brad laughed and then his eyes went wide, as if it only just dawned on him just what they were doing here. “Come on.”

It turned out that anger at being held up in traffic melted away in an instant once told there was a plane about to come down right where they were. It also turned out that, once enough people got out to run for their lives in the opposite direction, those in the cars behind them started to do the same without even needing to be told what was going on. The survival instinct of the average Angelino might’ve been poor, as evidenced by literally everything Bobby had seen people do while a firefighter here, but it was not nonexistent.

Once that was done, once he was certain that everyone else was safe, Bobby scaled the stolen fire truck to stand on its roof. His back twinged, reminding him that he had neglected his stretches and exercises a bit with his new job. But it was fine.

“Athena, are you still there?”

“Bobby, they tell me it's gonna get a little complicated up here when we come down. So I’m gonna keep you connected, so you can hear.”

“And I will be right here waiting for you.”

“Maybe you shouldn’t be there.”

“Why? You’re gonna do great,” he told her. There wasn’t any chance in Hell that he wouldn’t be here. No matter the outcome. “I’ll hold up a card with your name on it.”

“Oh, be quiet, you.”

In the sky, Bobby could see the shape of the plane as it dropped through the clouds. Its lights made them glow. It was coming at him fast, and Bobby could not help but pray.

(The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want.)

“I see you,” he said.

“I see you, too,” she said. “I love you.”

“Tell me in person, after you land. And I’ll tell you the same.”

(He leads me beside still waters, he restores my soul.)

Athena didn’t respond, but that was okay. He could hear her talking to air traffic control, able to make out some of her words.

“210 knots… 180 knots…”

The plane wobbled in the air.

(He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.)

“At four hundred feet and falling.”

Athena shouted at someone, though Bobby did not know who.

(Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I fear no evil.)

The nose of the plane tilted up, its belly showing as it came down.

(For thou art with me. Thy rod and thy staff, they comfort me.)

The wheels touched pavement and then exploded, becoming a fountain of sparks as the plane skidded.

(Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of my enemies.)

The tail tore through one of the signs that hung across the freeway, sending shrapnel through the air. Somewhere in the distance, an onlooker screamed.

(Thou anointest my head with oil, my cup overflows.)

And then the plane came to a gentle stop, its nose mere feet away from where Bobby stood on top of the engine. He could not resist lifting up a hand and waving at his wife through the window.

(Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.)

“Welcome to Los Angeles,” he told her. “I hope you enjoyed your flight.”

“Go to hell, Bobby.”

Their laughter, shared over the phone and through the broken window of the plane’s cockpit, was nothing but relief.

(And I shall dwell in the house of the Lord forever. Amen.)

Chapter End Notes

Can we start a GoFundMe to give everyone in this show's writers' room a remedial course on geography and how to use Google Maps, because there is NO EXCUSE for what's going on in 8x03. Go on, look at a map of Los Angeles. Look at where the 110 is at, look at where LAX is at. I don't think anyone who works on this show has ever actually even seen the Los Angeles wikipedia page, much less actually stepped foot in the city itself.

(They also repeatedly refer to the 110 as the busiest road in the country or whatever. It's not, that title goes to the I-5, also in LA. The 110 actually ranks below several stretches of road, and half of those go through Los Angeles. ~The more you know~)

Chapter 6: The Devil Works Hard, But...

Chapter Summary

In which a plane is evacuated, two firefighter fathers are not as cool as a guy who plays one on TV, and a geriatric bigot is not getting their redemption arc in this universe.

Buck had watched, ducking instinctively, as the plane flew over his head and came to a rough looking landing. More than a few people in the cars that he was holding up craned their heads out of their windows or got out entirely to gawk. It seemed that actually seeing (and hearing, it was very loud) the jetliner did wonders for taking the wind out of their sails, considering they were no longer loudly casting aspersions upon his maternal ancestry.

The police were just arriving, cruisers coming up both the on- and off-ramps with their lights flashing. More than a bit late, in Buck’s opinion, but at least it meant that they were there to take over as he dropped the flares and got back on the bike, making sure to grab and put on the helmet as he went. After snapping at one of the cops to park out of the way instead of just in the middle of the empty southbound lane - any fire trucks or ambulances coming to help would undoubtedly be using that lane to get to them - he sped back to where Bobby, and hopefully Athena, would be waiting.

The sight of a plane parked in the middle of the interstate, almost nose-to-nose with the Hotshots fire engine, was a daunting one. Buck left the motorcycle and the helmet off to the side, by the concrete barrier, and jogged over to where Bobby and Brad were standing in the plane’s shadow.

“They’re about to start disembarking,” Bobby told him. “According to Athena, the flight attendants are pretty sure the escape slide should be fine. If it’s not, I’ll have the engine ready to bring it around.”

Buck nodded and Bobby went to the engine, just in case they needed it. The cabin door was flung open and the slide popped out, unfurling to land just short of where Buck stood with Brad, and quickly inflating.

“We’re good!” Buck yelled, gave the ruffled looking flight attendant a thumbs up, and prepared to start receiving the passengers. The first couple ones were jumping out and sliding down when Bobby rejoined them with what looked for all the world like the same kind of first aid kit that would be found on their actual engine.

“I’ll send any injured your way,” Bobby said, handing him the bag.

Buck didn’t argue, he just nodded and took the bag, selecting a nice, out of the way patch of pavement for triage. The kit was surprisingly well stocked, with labeled IV bags that he hoped were just filled with water, actual bandages and gauze, a stethoscope, and an open box of nitrile gloves. He left the IV bags where they were, pulled on a pair of the gloves, slung the stethoscope around his neck, and put the bandages and gauzes aside for if they needed them.

Most of the passengers were left to amble around somewhere out of the way, but more than a few were sent Buck’s way. With his limited supplies, there wasn’t much that he could do for them except put actual coverings on their injuries. For some, like the guy who Hen saved over the phone with erectile dysfunction medication and was desperately clinging to a blanket for modesty, there was even less that he could do.

“Buck!” Bobby sounded more than a little exasperated. “We’ve got another one.”

“On it, Cap- Um.” Buck came to a stop to stare down at Brad, who was passed out on the pavement. “What happened?”

“I asked him to look at my leg.” A teenage girl, who looked like she belonged to a high school sports team of some sort. Her leg had the handle to a rollaway luggage tied to it in a makeshift splint. The calf looked horribly misshapen, and there was a gaping tear along the side that he was fairly certain showed muscle. “He said he was a firefighter.”

“He’s, uh. He’s new.” He shared a look with Bobby and then bent down to lift Brad up, throwing him over his shoulder in a fireman’s carry. “We’re going right over there, do you need help?”

The girl looked to where Buck was pointing, which wasn’t very far, and shook her head. He led the way, matching her hobbling pace.

“I think I know you,” she said. When he looked over, she was staring up at him in concentration. Then she glanced down to his chest - to his name tag - and her face lit up in recognition. “Oh! I follow your Instagram!”

“Um. Thank you?” Buck wasn’t quite sure how to reply to that, even though it wasn’t the first time it had happened since he and Eddie started that account. He laid Brad down on the ground and felt around his head, grimacing when his fingers came back with blood smeared on them. He tugged the glove off, dropped it to the ground, and pulled another one from the box. “What’s your name?”

“Donna.”

“Nice to meet you, Donna.” He rolled Brad onto his side, adjusting the position of his limbs and his head. The bleeding didn’t seem to be very heavy, at least. “What happened to your leg?”

“I broke it,” she explained, lowering herself down and stretching out the aforementioned leg. “Then it swelled up and a guy made a shiv to slice it open. Which helped for some reason? The guy on the phone said it was compartment syndrome.”

“Something about the pressure,” said a woman that he hadn’t even realized had followed them. “I’m her coach.”

“The guy on the phone was my brother-in-law, I think,” Buck told her, using the gauze and bandages to wrap her leg up. He was about to do the same to Brad’s head when there was an explosion on the plane and screams from the passengers who were still onboard. “Okay, I need you two to keep an eye on him. Check his pulse and his breathing, make sure he doesn’t get up if he wakes up. Can you do that?”

The moment he got a pair of nods, he was rushing back to Bobby’s side. The pair of them herded everyone away from the plane and helped the ones who were still trying to escape from it, many of them explaining that there was a fire at the tail end. Athena, of course, was not one of them. Bobby was still on the line with Maddie, who was able to get them an update on what they were dealing with.

“We think it’s the APU,” she explained. “The auxiliary power unit at the tail, it’s a gas turbine generator.”

Bobby’s eyes went wide.

“As in gasoline?”

“Jet fuel. It’s connected to lines running the length of the plane.”

“We’re not dealing with hydrazine again, are we?” Buck asked her, mind flashing back to the military jet from the beginning of the year.

“No, this fuel is less reactive and less hazardous to be around,” Maddie answered. “But it is still jet fuel.”

“And I’m guessing there’s not any water on that rig.”

“No.” Bobby shook his head, looking frustrated. “We need the real thing.”

“All the units that were at the airport were redeployed to you. They should be there soon.”

Unless they were there five seconds ago, it wouldn’t be soon enough.

Another passenger came sliding out of the plane, coughing as he got to his feet. Buck and Bobby rushed to him.

“How many are still up there?” Buck asked him.

“Two,” the man answered. That would be Athena and someone else. “I got to find Bobby.”

“That’s me, I’m Bobby.” And then, “You’re Dennis Jenkins.”

It took a moment for Buck to place the name. Dennis Jenkins was the guy who Athena went off the rails a bit to hunt down and arrest, years ago. Back when Eddie was still doing the stupid fight club, before he and Buck figured their shit out. What was Dennis Jenkins doing on this plane? Was he the prisoner that Athena was transporting?

“Where’s my wife?” Bobby demanded.

“She’s up there doing CPR,” Jenkins said, gesturing back up at the plane. “She won’t come down, says you got to come up there and get her.”

Almost as soon as he said that, there was a click as the emergency slide detached from the plane and fell to the ground. Bobby reached out and pulled Buck out of the way as it did, even though there was no danger of it landing on Buck at all. They stared at it for a moment, and then back to where it had been attached.

“Alright,” Bobby said. “Buck, I want you to pull the rig around. Bring it right over here.”

“You’re gonna use it to climb up?” Buck asked, the two of them already moving. They stopped in their tracks at the sound of approaching sirens.

“That was the plan. Got a better one now.”

They both hurried to where the fleet of trucks and ambulances were pulling to a stop. The 118’s engine and ladder were at the head of them, and Buck saw Albert and Ravi getting out of the ambulance that parked just behind them.

“Grab cans, charge those lines with class-A foam,” Bobby immediately started ordering the moment their boots hit the ground.

“Bobby.” Hen looked both relieved and worried. “Is Athena…?”

“She’s still in there,” he answered. “There’s a patient up there who needs nonstop CPR.”

“Eddie, Albert, the patients everyone teletriaged are over there.” Buck half-turned and pointed to where they were all gathered. “Brad Torrance is with them, he passed out and hit his head.”

“Brad Torrance,” Eddie repeated, already doubling back for a medical bag. “The actor?”

“He’s a better firefighter on TV. Ortiz!”

Javier Ortiz, the apparatus operator for the ladder truck, snapped to attention.

“We need to reach that cabin door,” Bobby said, pointing at it. “Go raise the aerial. Hen, Chim, gear up.”

As the ladder got into position, paramedics from the other stations joined Albert and Eddie with the injured plane passengers, putting down blankets so no one was just sitting on the hard pavement. Buck saw his husband looking over Brad, who was awake and trying to sit up. Once the ladder was extended to the cabin door, Hen and Chimney scurried up it, followed by Ravi and Clarke with Bobby right on their tail. Moments later, Bobby was helping Athena climb down.

“Cabin fire’s out, Cap,” Ravi reported.

“Thanks, Ravi,” Buck responded, at the same time Bobby radioed back with, “Good job, Ravi.”

“Awkward.” Eddie had come to stand beside him, since there were more paramedics to handle the patients now. “Hey, uh. How hard did Brad Torrance hit his head?”

“Dunno, I didn’t see it happen,” Buck answered. “He was standing and passed out, so… Why?”

“He’s British?”

“Oh yeah, no, that’s not the head injury.”

“Huh.”

“Pops and Chimney once responded to a call about a woman who woke up British. Turned out she was having a stroke,” Buck told him. “I’m gonna go check on Ma.”

Eddie nodded, gave him a pat on the back, and returned to the various patients that needed tended to. Bobby and Athena were climbing down from the ladder truck when Buck met them, and he reached out to help steady them both. Athena’s cough told him everything he needed to know.

“C’mon, let’s get you some O2.” Buck was already guiding her towards where he’d seen the 118’s ambulance.

“Where’s Dennis?” she asked.

“I’ll grab him and send him your way,” Bobby said. “Pretty sure I saw him over there.”

“So,” Buck said, breaking the silence once Bobby was gone. “How was your flight?”

Athena smacked him, which was well-deserved.

“How did you two end up coming here together?” she asked, sitting down on the back  of the 118’s ambulance. The gurney was missing from inside, presumably being used for a less ambulatory patient. “Does this mean you’re ready to let go of that grudge?”

Buck shrugged. He was still pretty angry. Or rather, he was still hurt, and that was translating into being angry, however much he was trying not to be.

“He wasn’t answering his phone,” he told her, reaching into the vehicle and grabbing an oxygen tank to drag over. He took the attached mask and shoved it onto her face. “So I went to get him. We ended up borrowing the engine from Hotshots.”

“Borrowing,” she repeated, prying the mask off and glaring at him.

“Technically, Bobby and Brad both work there, so it’s fine,” Buck said, and watched her mouth ‘Brad?’ to herself. He wrapped her up in a hug. “I’m glad you’re okay.”

“Thanks to you and Bobby,” she said, hugging him back just as tightly.  “And that flight instructor. And a kid who likes planes very much.”

“We all need our hobbies.”

“That is so cool!”

Because their shift didn’t end until Chris was already going to school, the teenager hadn’t the chance to interrogate him about what went on the night before. Now, though, while Buck and Abuela fixed dinner, Chris was free to do so while he worked on his homework at the table. It was very similar to when he’d been younger, back when he would hang onto every word of their (edited for children) work stories. It would be nice, except for one thing:

Chris wasn’t so excited to hear all about it because of them.

“Brad Torrance is actually British!?”

“I miss when you thought I was cool,” Eddie mourned, stepping into the kitchen to steal a piece of pepper. He had Gavin in his arms, the toddler grabbing for the pepper until Eddie gave in and let him have it. “At least Gavin still does.”

“You were never cool, babe,” Buck happily informed his husband, leaning in to kiss away his insulted pout. “That’s not too hot for him, is it?”

“It’s a poblano,” Abuela said with a wave, smacking Eddie’s hand when he went to grab another piece. “You lost your chance.”

“You’re both cruel people,” Eddie complained, nose in the air. “Gavin and I don’t need your kind of negativity.”

“Yeah, yeah,” Chris impatiently cut in. “Brad Torrance! What was he like? Did you really steal their engine?”

“We ride in an actual fire engine every day,” Buck reminded the kid. “You’ve ridden in it. Because we’re actual firefighters.”

“Yeah, but you’re not actors.”

“We’re acting like our oldest son isn’t hurting our feelings right now,” Eddie announced as dramatically as possible. “Isn’t that right,  mi sol?”

“We’re big, tough firefighters,” Buck said, with a pointed sniff. “We don’t have feelings.”

“You’re not good actors,” Chris amended, going back to his homework. “Did he rescue anyone?”

“Okay, I helped make an impromptu runway for a plane by throwing myself into traffic, where is my adoration?” Buck demanded, and then, “Shoot. Eddie, pretend you didn’t-”

“You did what!?” Yeah, Eddie didn’t sound happy. Neither did Abuela, who tutted and shook her head as she tasted the enchilada sauce she was making.

“They weren’t stopping!” Buck defended himself, turning back to the food. And then he frowned when he saw Abuela staring at the pot, a look of frustration on her face. “What’s wrong?”

“It doesn’t taste right,” she said with a scowl. “I can’t figure out what it needs.”

Buck reached over and took the wooden spoon that she was using to stir, lifting it up to give it a quick lick. He realized what was missing right away.

“Oh, it’s the chili powder.” It wasn’t on the counter with everything else, so he padded over to the spice rack to grab it.

“The chili powder,” Abuela repeated, taking it from him and adding it to the sauce. Her recipes were all to taste, and she was very liberal with the spices. “I forgot the chili powder? Ay, memoria de teflón…”

“But about you throwing yourself into traffic,” Eddie said, obviously not ready to let it go.

“I was trying to get them to stop,” Buck said.

“By turning yourself into a speed bump? Again!?”

Buck needed a way to get his husband to shut up and let it go. Sadly, the best solution was currently not available to him, since they were in the kitchen with Abuela and the kids instead of alone in the bedroom. So he went with the second best option. He grabbed one of the larger pieces of pepper and stuffed it into Eddie’s mouth.

But even the irritated chewing came across as judgmental.

The shift following the plane was more than a bit irritating. Not because they were unusually busy, because they weren’t. It wasn’t because the calls themselves were unusually stupid, because they were all perfectly average. It wasn’t because anyone they ran into was being particularly obnoxious that day, not anymore than every other day.

No, it was irritating because it turned out that a passenger jet, once parked in the middle of an interstate, was not so easily removed. Plus there was the damage incurred on the road due to its non-standard use, something that the city was particularly paranoid about following the bridge collapse. This all meant that section of 110, right in the middle of Los Angeles, was closed for the foreseeable future. And while it wasn’t the busiest road in the city, it was definitely up there.

Traffic had been absolutely hell all shift. Even Toby, who was generally even-mannered, was reaching the ends of his temper every time they were sent out to the wrong part of the city. It turned out that he could road rage with the best of them, once pushed to that point, and they were all left more than a bit shellshocked.

At the moment, though, they weren’t out on a call. It had actually been rather Q-word for a couple hours now, and Buck was taking advantage of that by working through paperwork. After action reports, mainly, and there was a heavy push from Chief Williams to get the one for the plane done as quickly, but as nicely, as possible. He wondered if Bobby was being forced to fill one out, or if he managed to escape that responsibility.

Everyone else was scattered around the station. Ravi was downstairs, hitting the gym. Albert - who was no longer allowed to be in the gym while Ravi was using it, and vice versa, after The Incident - and Chimney were at the pinball machine. Eddie and Hen were sitting in the lounge area, the latter doing her own reports while the former had a book checked out from the library.

“Hey, Cap?” And Toby was coming up the stairs. “We uh, have a visitor?”

“Alright.” Buck dropped his pen and stood up. “Who- Oh.”

“This place hasn’t changed,” Taylor Kelly said, looking around. Her voice had Eddie leaping to his feet.

“No, no!” He held his hands up in front of him, fingers making a cross. “Begone, foul demon! You have no power here! The power of Christ compels you to get the hell out!”

“He’s as dramatic as you are,” Taylor told Buck as the commotion drew in a crowd. “You’re perfect for each other.”

“Thanks,” Buck drawled. “And what brought you here for a visit?”

“Well, there is the matter of the passenger who piloted that plane, if you could give me a name.” Taylor gave him her prettiest smile, holding it for a moment while batting her eyes before dropping it with a sigh when he just stared. “That’s what I figured. I actually came here to make sure you were watching TV.”

“Why?” Hen drew the word out, curious but hesitant.

“Channel Eight,” was all the reporter said.

Eddie didn’t move to do it, even though the remote was right by where he’d been seated. Hen ended up reaching around him to grab it and change the channel. On the screen, Councilwoman Ortiz - of no relation to their Javier Ortiz - was standing behind a podium, looking mournful.

“-and I regret that it has come to this. I have spent my entire career trying to help the people of this city, but I see now that I have lost sight of that. The decision to step down from the city council was not an easy one, but I cannot continue to work for you all as long as the shadow of my mistakes lingers over-”

“She’s resigning?” Hen sounded awed. “She’s resigning!?”

“And dropping out of the mayor’s race, obviously,” Taylor said, examining her nails. “All credit to me, of course.”

“I’m surprised you’re not there,” Buck said. 

The biggest drive to her doing those hit pieces on the councilwoman, which were undoubtedly the driving force behind the resignation, had very little to do with actually wanting to help Hen and Karen, and more to do with getting a feather in her cap for ruining a politician’s career. Not being there in person for the finale seemed out of character.

“She’s not going to take any questions,” she pointed out. “I didn’t see the point in standing around and-”

She got interrupted by Hen suddenly rushing her, the paramedic wrapping her arms around the reporter and lifting her up. Taylor’s face was the epitome of shock, eyes wide and jaw hanging loose, as she hung limply in the other woman’s grip.

“Thank you!” Hen gushed, dropping her back to her feet. “Thank you! I have to go tell Karen! And then call our attorney! Thank you, Taylor!”

She rushed off, pulling out her phone as she went. Taylor Kelly was left a little shell shocked and a lot speechless. There was silence, broken only by Hen excitedly greeting her wife, until Eddie spoke.

“I still think you’re the devil,” he told the reporter.

“Please.” Taylor sniffed and straightened her clothes. “I have better hair.”

Chapter 7: All Twisted Up

Chapter Summary

In which a cheerleader does the twist.

Chapter Notes

Happy New Years!

It was never a good thing, in Eddie’s experience, when his husband decided to be a recluse. Buck was a people person, someone who took every excuse he could to be around others. It was like sunlight and water for a flower, and much like a flower, he had the tendency to wilt if isolated for too long. 

Normally, when they worked, Buck would be at whichever part of the station everyone else had gathered. Even if he wasn’t actually interacting with them, he still did his best to be in the middle of them all. Eddie wasn’t certain how much use the captain’s office saw during their shifts, because Buck did almost all the paperwork he had to do at one of the tables up in the loft. He once even did it on the benches that lined the edges of the bay, when everyone was busy cleaning the trucks of bee guts.

At the moment, though, Buck was not with the rest of them. No, he’d gone into the captain’s office to check emails and hadn’t come back out. That was an hour ago. Worse, even, the door was closed. Even if Eddie didn’t have a good excuse, he would’ve burst in there to find out what was wrong. And something was wrong.

When he let himself into the captain’s office, he found Buck sitting behind the desk. He was looking stressed, clutching at his hair as he stared down at a bunch of files he’d spread out on the surface of the desk. At the sound of the door opening, he looked up.

“Oh, is it that time?” he asked, dropping his hands to gesture at the blood pressure cuff that Eddie was holding.

Shortly after the lightning strike, after the coma, Buck was given a pair of diagnoses and put on bupropion as a two-birds-one-stone deal. 150 milligrams, extended release. One of the side-effects to watch out for was increased blood pressure, and Eddie was more than a bit anal about checking it.

He knew why he was so insistent on it. Buck knew why, too, because any complaints he had about it was purely for show as he went along with it, unresisting. They’d talked about it with Copeland, just before the bridge collapse. Just like his husband, Eddie was a doer. Copeland referred to it as “caretaking behavior,” back in the early days of the meds, when he was doing the driving and constantly shoved water into Buck’s hands whenever they were empty. All three of them knew it was an attempt to grab any bits of control over the situation that he could find. At least he wasn’t trying to find it in an illegal fight club. Again.

It was just an attempt, though. Taking Buck’s blood pressure was more of a ritual to make Eddie feel better about a situation he had very little control over. Because what could he do, after his husband admitted that he once tried to kill himself long before they ever met? That sometimes he simply didn’t see the point in getting out of the way of the bus when it was coming? That a part of him hadn’t wanted to wake up from that awful coma?

Eddie would never say it aloud, but a not inconsequential part of himself was glad that Buck was the captain now. Not because of the pay increase, though it was nice, or because authority looked attractive on his husband. He was glad for it because as captain, Buck was less likely to be in situations where he might decide, even with the bupropion, to simply stand there and wait for the bus to barrel into him.

Not to say Buck didn’t still somehow find a way to be in the middle of everything, and an opportunity to throw himself in front of the bus. Or a car, as the case had been.

“Are those our personnel files?” Eddie asked, frowning down at them.

“Yeah,” was Buck’s gruff answer. He flipped closed the one he was looking through, Darrell Hendrix’s, and unbuttoned the cuff of his sleeve so he could roll it up. “Gotta warn ya, it’ll probably be a bit high today.”

Eddie directed the frown at his husband, even as he wrapped the cuff around his arm and started squeezing the pump. The needle on the gauge went ‘round and ‘round, and his frown grew heavier at the numbers it gave.

“One twenty-nine over seventy-nine.” Elevated, almost hypertension. He took the cuff off and wrapped it up. “That’s higher than it normally is.”

“Not surprised,” Buck grumbled, dragging his hands down his face.

“What’s going on, mi sol?” Eddie asked, perching on the edge of the desk. 

“Chief Williams called me earlier,” his husband said, slumping back in his chair. “Y’know how the department’s doing budget cuts?”

“‘Cause Councilwoman Ortiz didn’t like the fact that Gerrard wasn’t made captain and fucked over the department’s budget for the year.”

The chief’s office was in the same building as metro dispatch, and Josh had befriended the chief’s secretary, which meant Buck and Maddie had a direct line to some of the gossip. This piece of gossip also came from Taylor Kelly - and Eddie fought hard not to sneer just thinking of the woman - who had managed to find out about it while digging up everything she could for her smear campaign. But apparently it was the (former) councilwoman who was pushing for Gerrard to retake the captaincy that Bobby left vacant.

Even though Eddie had seen the pair buddying up at the medal ceremony back in the spring, he still didn’t understand how the two were friends. From everything he’d heard about the guy, he would’ve assumed a woman of color being in a position of authority would’ve made Gerrard apoplectic.

“Yeah, well. She’s the gift that keeps on giving.” Buck sounded miserable and bitter. “Switching to off-brand stuff when we shop isn’t enough, apparently. Now they’re thinking about layoffs.”

“Layoffs.” Eddie’s eyes drifted to the personnel files. “Oh.”

“They’re pushing the ones that qualify into retirement,” Buck said. Eddie wondered if that included Bobby, though the man hadn’t said anything on Sunday. “But Williams wants me to- Not just me, apparently it’s every captain. Dunno if she’ll be telling Reynolds and Mayfair herself, or if I have to. But she wants me to make a list of people for the brass to choose from, if they decide that they still need to cut more.”

“How big of a list?”

“Five names. She wants me to choose five people that they can pick from,” Buck answered. “How the hell am I supposed to do that, Eds? I’ve worked with all these people for years! I’ve literally run through fire with them. I mean, seriously, how am I supposed to choose one person, much less five? And how am I supposed to look them in the eye afterwards?”

This certainly explained the elevated blood pressure. It was honestly a surprise that it wasn’t higher.

“Put my name on the list,” Eddie told him.

Buck whipped his head up to stare at him, mouth gaping a bit.

“What?”

“Put my name on the list,” Eddie repeated. “Very top. No matter who they end up picking, the others can’t be pissed at you if you put your own husband on the list, too. It’s why you chose me to play bait for the bees, wasn’t it?”

“This isn’t running from bees while wearing full gear, babe,” Buck said, shaking his head. “‘Sides, Williams already said the Medal of Valor recipients were all safe. Otherwise, I would’ve started the list with my name.”

Eddie wasn’t surprised, and to be honest, he might’ve been banking on that when he made his suggestion. Just a little. Chief Simpson was very PR oriented, and it would be bad publicity if one of them got the ax.

“When does she want the list?”

“As soon as possible.”

“Maybe you could-”

Eddie’s suggestion - to go to Bobby for advice, which was only partially motivated by the desire to get them to talk - was interrupted by the station’s alarms going off. It was with a look of great relief that Buck got to his feet and sprinted for the bay, Eddie on his heels. They could hear Maddie’s voice just above the alarm as she rattled off information about an injury at a high school, so they didn’t bother with tugging on their turnouts before getting onto the trucks.

“Looks like there was a collision at a football game,” Buck told them, concentrating on the tablet in his hand. “Turn left here, Toby. Player collided with a cheerleader. The caller said that, uh… They’re ‘ass-backwards.’”

“Hey, Cap,” Ravi piped up from next to Eddie. Albert was sitting across from him, their legs tangled up together. Hen and Chimney were in the ambulance, just behind them. “You played football, didn’t you?”

“He was a tight end,” Eddie answered for his husband, which invoked a round of sniggering from the others in the engine’s cab.

“Yeah, yeah, laugh it up.” Buck’s eye roll wasn’t visible, he was facing the windshield, but Eddie didn’t need to see it to know it happened. “That was low hanging fruit.”

That also led to a very obvious joke, but they were pulling onto the scene which meant it was time to at least pretend like they were all professionals. They hopped out, Eddie and Albert grabbing their med kits from the compartments, and met up with Hen and Chimney, who were already pulling the gurney along. There were anxious on-lookers dotting the field in clumps. A large huddle, consisting of football players, cheerleaders, and officials, were surrounding who Eddie assumed to be the patient, on the track that circled the football field.

One of the coaches met them half-way, looked at each of them like he wasn’t sure who to address, and then just started talking to them as a group.

“Uh, the cheerleader’s name is Weston,” the guy said. “Look, I’m EMT certified, but this is… This is beyond my scope of practice.”

“That’s what these guys are for,” Buck assured him.

The small huddle parted for them. The moment that Eddie got a glimpse of their patient, Weston, he immediately understood what the caller had meant by ‘ass-backwards.’ The kid was laying face-down, but his toes were pointing towards the sky, body twisted at the waist. There was a woman kneeling beside him, maybe Weston’s mother.

“Please,” the woman begged the moment she saw them coming. “Please, can you help?”

“We’re gonna do our best, ma’am,” Chimney assured her. “If you can just give us some space to work?”

With the aid of one of the cheerleaders, the paramedic managed to coax her to separate from the patient. Now that they had room, the three paramedics got to work.

“Have you two ever seen this before?” Albert asked, keeping his voice low.

“Does a medical textbook count?” Hen asked in turn, pulling out a stethoscope, while Chimney shook his head.

“I have. In Afghanistan.” Specifically, Eddie had seen people - soldiers and civilians alike - twisted like this because they were thrown by a concussive blast. Usually because they were caught in the blast radius of an IED. “That’s an open book pelvic fracture.”

An open book fracture was a fracture of the pelvic ring, which consisted of the hip bones and the base of the spine. It earned its name for the way the bones broke, resembling a book that had been dropped to land with its pages splayed out.

“Problem with that is the pelvis is lined with arteries,” Hen pointed out, pressing the head of her stethoscope to Weston’s back.

And if those arteries were torn, then Weston could bleed out right there or lose circulation to his legs. Eddie had seen both happen.

“So we need to be quick and careful,” Buck said. “Eds, it’s your show. Ravi, Toby, go see if anyone else was injured.”

“Got it, Cap,” Ravi said with a nod, before stepping away with Toby

“Weston, hi, I’m Eddie,” Eddie said, kneeling next to the poor kid as he finished pulling on his gloves. “I’m gonna check you out, okay?”

“Okay.” Weston’s voice trembled, and his fear was palpable as Albert got a c-collar around his neck. Hen was strapping a blood pressure cuff to his arm. “Is- Is it bad?”

“You’re talking,” Eddie assured him, glancing at Hen. She was frowning at the gauge. “And that’s good news.”

“His BP’s ninety over sixty,” Hen announced. That was right on the cusp of being hypotensive. It could be worse, but it definitely wasn’t good. “Heart’s racing at one-twenty. Let’s give him something for the pain.”

“Copy that,” Chimney said, digging into his bag. He pulled out everything needed for an IV and got started on that.

“What’s happening?” the mother desperately demanded from where Buck was making sure she stayed back. “Is he going to be paralyzed?”

“We have to move him very carefully,” Eddie told her. “We don’t want to shift anything else.”

“C’mon,” Buck said, before she could ask anything else. “We need to let them focus on your son, okay?”

“Where’s the pelvic sling?” Eddie asked.

“Right here,” Albert said, holding it out to him.

“Alright, Weston.” Eddie took the pelvic sling and unrolled it as he jerked his head for Buck to come help. He and the others got into position, except for Chimney; he was still holding the IV by the kid’s head. “We’re going to lift you up on three.”

He counted and then, right on three, they lifted Weston up. Just enough for Eddie to slide the sling under him and strap it around his pelvis. It was also enough to have the kid crying out in pain through gritted teeth.

When Eddie was done, and he was sure the strap wasn’t going anywhere, he had Buck grab the backboard off the nearby gurney. Buck laid it down next to them, and then went back to his spot.

“We’re going to roll you over, now, Weston,” Hen warned him. “On three. One, two, and…”

They rolled him onto the backboard, Chimney maneuvering to keep the IV from getting tangled. Weston was panting in exertion as they strapped him in, Hen hooking him up to a LifePak, and then they lifted both him and the board onto the gurney.

Chimney handed the IV off to Albert, tasking him with getting it situated on the pole attached to the side of the gurney, and went to Weston’s feet. He pulled off a shoe and took out his pen, running it along a sock-covered sole.

“Weston, buddy, can you feel this?” he asked.

“Yeah.”

“That’s good, right?” the mother asked.

“It’s great,” Eddie told her. It meant that there wasn’t a spinal injury. “Can you make a thumbs up for me?”

“Yeah,” was Weston’s shaky response. His hand, as he did as he was asked, was equally shaky. 

“Perfect. Can you lift your arm up? As high as you can.”

Again, a shaky answer in the affirmative and an equally shaky limb. Weston’s arm trembled as he raised it, but he was raising it. The crowd of onlookers cheered. The cheering followed them as they started rolling Weston to the ambulance, his mother keeping pace.

“I’m right here, baby,” she assured her son. She held up her phone. “I’m calling your dad to tell him to meet us at the hospital.”

“Don’t.” Weston tried to shake his head, but the c-collar did its job to prevent him from moving too much. “Don’t, mom.”

Eddie frowned at him, and caught Buck doing the same.

“He needs to be here,” she insisted.

“It’s fine, he wouldn’t…”

His words trailed off, his eyes fluttered. As his mother tried to rouse his attention, the LifePak began to screech.

“Guys, his BP is bottoming out,” Eddie called out. “He’s probably bleeding internally.”

Those arteries that Hen mentioned, they could’ve been damaged when Weston initially got hurt or it could’ve been something they did as they transferred Weston onto the gurney. There was no way to be sure, and there wasn’t anything they could do about it now.

“We can’t treat him here,” Hen said.

“Then we do it on the rig,” was Chimney’s answer to that. “Let’s go, double time!”

They rushed for the ambulance, the mother sprinting beside them. Whether or not she would’ve tried to climb in with them, Eddie didn’t know. Buck stopped her just a couple feet away, telling her to let them do their jobs and which hospital they’d be headed for. Moments later, the doors were closing and they were speeding down the streets with sirens blaring.

They needed to be going faster, though.

“That’s two liters,” Eddie remarked, taking off the second bag of saline they’d gone through.

“Liquids aren’t working,” Hen said, even as she handed him a fresh bag. “He’s losing too much blood.”

“Chim!” Eddie called to the front, where both Han brothers were sitting. Albert twisted around in his seat to look back at them. “How long until we’re at Presbyterian?”

“About twelve minutes to the trauma bay doors,” Chimney answered.

That was entirely too long.

“Can you make it four?” Hen requested.

“I’ll see what I can do.”

They rocked as the ambulance picked up speed. The LifePak was still screaming at them and Eddie did not want to keep sitting there, twiddling his thumbs. Through the sliding glass of one of the compartments, he sees a possibility.

“You’ve done a REBOA, right?” he asked, leaning across Weston to pull out the kit. He distinctly remembered her using one for the lady impaled by the stop sign, during the short time that Jonah Greenway was at the station.

“On solid ground.” She sounded and looked incredulous. “Threading a balloon through an aorta in a moving vehicle, though? Eddie, that’s insane.”

“At least these streets are paved.” He pulled the scissors from his medical bag and started cutting into Weston’s pants. “I did two in a convoy in Kandahar.”

“How’d that go for you?”

Eddie paused, shrugged at the question.

“Fifty-fifty,” he admitted.

The LifePak was still screaming. Hen glanced at it and then at the still unresponsive Weston, lips drawing into a thin line.

“It’s better than zero,” she said, grabbing the ultrasound.

While Eddie widened the hole he’d made in Weston’s pants and held the fabric out of the way, Hen spread the gel and started searching for an artery with the wand. Once it was found, she kept the wand in place to mark as Eddie got the REBOA out and ready. Just as he was about to insert the needle of the catheter, though, the ambulance bounced and jarred.

“You’ve got to keep it steady!” Eddie snapped towards the front.

“I’m doing my best,” Chimney shot back.

“These streets are not the best maintained,” Albert remarked, twisting around again to look back at them.

That was Los Angeles, for you. A budget of nearly thirteen billion dollars, but God forbid that it went towards things like making sure the roads weren’t crumbling. Eddie got to listen to Buck’s ranting about the city’s budget not too long ago, around the time the brass started coming down on them about the department’s. Such a tiny part of that pie was for the roads, even after the bridge collapse that took Jones.

Eddie held his breath as he inserted the catheter into Weston’s thigh. When it went in without issue, and nothing came spurting out, he heard Hen’s breath come out in a soft sigh. But Eddie didn’t relax just yet, because they were just getting to the tricky part.

“His pulse is barely registering,” Hen reported.

“How am I looking?” Eddie asked, focusing instead on threading the balloon through the catheter.

“It’s hard to say.” She was staring down at the ultrasound in her hand, tracking his progress. “Everything’s twisted- Wait.”

He froze, glanced up at her.

“You’re in the aorta,” Hen said. 

Eddie held out the end of the REBOA to her. There was a hiss as she used a syringe of saline to inflate the balloon. A moment later, a very long moment later, the LifePak calmed as Weston’s vitals stabilized. Eddie let out a cheer.

“BP’s back!” he announced, watching as the teen’s eyes fluttered open. “And so’s our boy.”

“Dad…?” the kid mumbled.

Eddie felt his heart clench, remembering Weston’s insistence to his mother not to call his father. Like the man had better things to do than come rushing to check on his injured son. It was unfortunately not a foreign concept to Eddie.

“You’re gonna be okay, kid,” he assured Weston, unable to help himself from brushing his hand through the kid’s hair.

The mom was at the hospital already when they arrived, anxiously waiting at the trauma bay doors. Eddie wouldn’t be surprised if Buck had gotten her a police escort, for her to have gotten there so fast.

The dad was nowhere to be seen, and he didn’t show up before they returned to the station.

Chapter 8: Listen To Me Now (Redux)

Chapter Summary

In which Buck (finally) clears the air with Bobby.

“It just pisses me off,” Eddie ranted, stuck on the same topic he’d been on for the past day. Buck felt he was doing an admirable job not cooing in affection over it. “I mean, here’s a kid who actually wants his dad in his life, and he doesn’t even bother to show up?”

They were in the kitchen while Buck and Abuela fixed dinner. Eddie wasn’t actually helping, instead getting in the way while he complained about the unseen father of the cheerleader from the call the day before. He had Senorita, their fluffy black cat, in his arms and was absentmindedly petting her as he watched Chris and Gavin.

The two boys were in the living room, playing tug-o-war with Hoover. Chris had Gavin in his lap, helping him hold on to the piece of rope while the dog held the other end in his mouth. Gavin was squealing with giggles the entire time, clearly having the time of his life even though he was getting nowhere.

“Some dads just suck, babe, you know that,” Buck told his husband, shaping meatballs before dropping them onto a baking sheet. A thought struck him. “Hey, this isn’t like… This isn’t about something else, is it?”

Eddie turned his head to give him a flat look.

“Not everything is about you, mi sol.”

“Rude thing to say to a man who’s handling your meat,” Buck retorted. Abuela, stirring a pot of spaghetti sauce, let out a snort. “I’m just saying, you’ve been nagging and nagging me to talk to Pops-”

“Because you should. This is getting old.”

“Yeah, I know.” Buck let out a sigh. “I was thinking I’ll go see him tomorrow.”

“Gracias a Dios,” both Eddie and Abuela said.

“Yeah, yeah.”

“But I just can’t get over it,” Eddie said, going back to that dying horse. “His kid was seriously hurt. But he just didn’t bother to show up? I mean, last year, you dropped everything and raced over because Gavin had a popcorn kernel up his nose.”

“To be fair, you just told me you’d taken him to the ER,” Buck pointed out. “You didn’t tell me why.”

“Because you hung up before I could,” Eddie retorted. Buck shrugged. “And when you were struck by that lightning, Bobby pretty much abandoned his post. But this guy…”

“Perhaps he is on a work trip,” Abuela said, taking a taste of the sauce. She let out a hum and grabbed the sugar to add more in. “You should be familiar with that, Ramon.”

Buck matched Eddie’s frown and the pair of them slowly turned to direct those frowns at Abuela. She didn’t even seem to notice, taking another taste of the sauce and nodding in approval.

“‘Buela?” Eddie hesitantly asked, bending down to gently place Senorita onto the floor.

“Yes?”

“You just-”

Knocking at the door interrupted the question. Hoover dropped his end of the rope to trot up to the door, ears and tail sticking up in alert. Chris moved Gavin off his lap and onto the couch, before getting up to answer the door for them.

“Hi, Chris!” Albert said as he stepped inside, holding out a fist for the teen to bump. He spotted Gavin on the couch and jogged forward to toss the squealing tot over his shoulder.

“Hello, Diazes.” Ravi followed his boyfriend inside, patting Hoover’s head only absentmindedly as he went by. He sniffed the air and frowned. “We’re early, aren’t we?”

“Little bit.” Buck not-so-gently moved his husband out of the way of the preheated oven to slide the sheet of meatballs inside. He set the timer on his phone and sat it on the counter. “Have you heard anything yet?”

“Nope.” Albert was spinning around in place with Gavin. If he made the kid puke, Buck was absolutely going to make him clean it up. “Howie hasn’t mentioned anything, either.”

That afternoon, Hen and Karen were in court to get their foster care license reinstated. They were all hopeful that, with ex-Councilwoman Ortiz hopefully no longer able to be a problem, that it would be a simple matter of going through the motions. Since Mara was with Maddie and Chimney, it would make sense that they would hear the news, good or bad, first.

“Did you see that Taylor did an interview with Brad Torrance?” Ravi asked as he took a seat at the breakfast bar. The mention of the reporter’s name had Eddie sneering in distaste. “Right, my bad. We don’t say her name in this house, I forgot.”

“She’s a vile witch,” Eddie declared. Buck looked to the side, caught Abuela’s amused eye, and had to look away before they both started laughing.

“I saw it,” Chris said, taking the stool beside Ravi. In the living room, Albert took a seat on the floor. Gavin promptly began using him as a jungle gym. “He talked about the plane and how he helped rescue all those people.”

“He didn’t help all that much,” Buck pointed out, still a bit sore that his kid thought someone playing a firefighter on TV was cooler than him. Then he frowned. “Was there any mention about who was piloting the plane when it landed?”

He knew the media, in general, had been more than a bit interested in finding out who it was. Taylor herself made a minor attempt at getting their identity when she swung by the station on the day of the councilwoman’s resignation. Brad knew that it was Athena, he’d been in the Hotshots engine with them the entire time they were on the phone with her.

And yet, Athena hadn’t mentioned anything about being hounded by reporters.

Ravi frowned and looked to Chris beside him. The teen shook his head.

“No,” he said. “Nana ‘Thena wasn’t mentioned at all.”

“Maybe Athena just scares her,” Ravi suggested.

“I doubt that,” Buck said. She had seemed entirely unperturbed when faced with both Athena and Lou Ransone in the past. 

“She’d have to be capable of feeling things to feel scared, the vile-” Eddie cut himself off with a glance at Chris, and then finished with, “Witch.”

“You were gonna say bitch,” Chris said, grinning at them.

“Ay, language,” Abuela tutted, brandishing the mixing spoon at him.

“Sorry,” the teen said, then repeated himself in Spanish, “Ibas a decir perra.”

“The cheek!” Abuela cried. Ravi was doing a poor job covering up his laughter.

“For your information,” Eddie said, nose in the air, “that was not the word I was going to use.”

“I hope you’re not speaking like that in school, kid,” Buck said.

“I don’t have Spanish this year,” Chris assured him.

“Swear to God…”

On the counter, Buck’s phone chimed. After a brief moment of confusion, because he knew the meatballs hadn’t been in the oven long enough to flip, he realized that his phone hadn’t been the only one to go off. Ravi pulled his own out and Albert, with Gavin hanging off his neck like a murder attempt, did the same.

(Eddie’s phone was charging in the bedroom.)

“Hey!” Albert cheered. “Looks like it’s good news.”

Curious, Buck checked his own phone and saw that Maddie had sent a picture to one of the group chats. It showed Hen and Karen, both of them smiling as they hugged Mara in Maddie and Chimney’s living room.

Buck made a note to himself to bring a cake in for their next shift.

Buck hesitated in front of the apartment door, more nervous than he had any right to be. But this really had gone on far too long, he’d dragged this on for too long. Everyone - from Copeland and Eddie, to Hen and Chimney, even to TK and Carlos - spent the summer telling him to just talk to the man. Now he was here, and his nerves were playing havoc.

He took a breath and rapped his knuckles on the door. A few scant seconds later, Bobby was opening it. His face dropped in surprise when he laid eyes on his visitor.

“Buck.”

“Hi, Pops.” Buck gave a timid wave. “Can… Can I come in?”

“Yeah! Of course.” Bobby hurriedly stepped out of the way, opening the door wider. “Take a seat. I’ll- I’ll get you something to drink.”

Buck had never once stepped foot in this apartment before. It looked less like a home and more like the model pictures put up for listings. He was reminded of Bobby’s original apartment, when they found him passed out drunk that one day. The furniture and electronics were fancier, newer, more expensive - thanks to Bobby and Athena’s salaries, plus the insurance payouts - but everything was just as impersonal. The only pictures hanging up were generic landscapes, the kind found in home decor aisles. Buck knew that some of their photos were saved digitally, but it seemed they hadn’t bothered printing them out to display here.

Covering the dining table, some small thing straight out of a box, was a set of blueprints. Buck allowed his curiosity to take center stage as he sat down, eyebrows twitching upward when he first recognized the shape and then saw “House for Mr. and Mrs. Grant” at the top. 

“Gave up trying to find a new place?” Buck asked.

“Seems it.” Bobby set a cup of coffee down in front of him. “Too much sugar and a little cream.”

“Thanks.” Buck picked the coffee up, suddenly feeling nervous again as Bobby took the seat across from him. 

“Athena didn’t like any of the places we looked at,” Bobby said with an awkward laugh. “The real estate agents we tried didn’t help. Especially the woman with the ugly brooch, I thought Athena was gonna shoot her.”

“Oh, God, Marcy.” Buck remembered her clearly, along with all the racist and homophobic asides she made as she showed them around. “She was the worst.”

“Yeah…”

They fell into awkward silence, Buck shifting uncomfortably in his set as he clutched at the coffee. He never knew how to start these things, what to say. So he did what he always did, and simply blurted out the first thing on his tongue.

“I don’t want to be angry anymore.”

“I’m… Glad to hear that,” Bobby said. “I understand why you were, though. I should’ve told everyone I was planning to retire, instead of hiding it like that.”

“But you weren’t planning to retire,” he snapped, and then felt guilty for it. He set the coffee back down and dropped his hands into his lap as he tried to find the words without hurling them like daggers.

Across from him, Bobby sat, quiet and patient.

“You were planning to leave.” Buck kept his gaze focused on his hands, his fingers twisting anxiously together. “If you’d just decided to retire, you would have told us. You’d have given us a date, and we’d be sad but we’d throw you a party when the day came. But you didn’t. You told the chief, decided to do it right away, and didn’t say a word to any of us except to tell us goodbye without saying the word or even letting us know that it was goodbye. You gave Eddie your Book of Prayers, and there was no reason for that unless you thought you wouldn’t need it anymore. You weren’t planning to retire, you were planning to leave.”

He risked a glance at Bobby. The man’s face was a mask of pain and regret.

“You’re important,” Buck told him. “To Chris and Gavin. To Eddie. To me. I’ve told you before how important you are to me, that I wouldn’t know what I would do if anything happened to you. You’re my pops. And you were planning to leave.”

“I’m sorry,” Bobby whispered. “My past caught up to me again and I let myself drown in the guilt of it. I wasn’t thinking about… I was being selfish. I was focused on how much I was hurting, and I didn’t care that I would be hurting others.”

He got up and changed seats, pulling the chair closer to Buck, and reached out to cover Buck’s hands with his own.

“I’m sorry,” he repeated, a bit more firmly.

“I forgive you,” Buck said, and then screwed up his mouth. “I want to forgive you. I don’t want to lose you.”

“I figured that out from all the heart-healthy meals you started serving on Sundays,” Bobby teased. Buck felt himself flush.

“So- So, um.” He cast about for a topic and landed on the blueprints again. “You’re planning to rebuild, instead?”

Buck was more than a bit relieved about that. Part of what he liked about his current home was that it was so close to Bobby and Athena. He’d been a little worried that they would end up halfway across the city.

“Yeah.” Bobby didn’t quite manage to hide the grimace quickly enough. “She had Michael send these over. He designed it for her.”

“You don’t sound too thrilled about that,” Buck hesitantly pointed out. He glanced at the blueprints again, at the “Mr. and Mrs. Grant” at the top. “Maybe you could ask him to design a house for the two of you.”

“Maybe.” Bobby sat up a little, head tilted as he stared at the blueprints in thought. Then he looked back to Buck and asked, “So how is being captain? No probies starting arsons, I hope.”

“God, I wish,” Buck groaned. He started to lay his head on the table, only to remember his barely touched coffee was in the way. “We’re having budget cuts.”

“So I’ve heard,” Bobby said. “Rumor through the grapevine is that Gerrard was pushed into retiring.”

“Hen and Chimney threw a dance party in the locker room at the news,” he said. “But I have to give them names to choose from.”

“Names? Oh.” Bobby’s face fell.

“I don’t know how the hell I’m supposed to do this, Pops,” Buck said. Whined, more like. “I’ve been through actual hell with these people, and I’m supposed to just look five of them in the eye after shortlisting them to be fired?”

“Yes.” Bobby shrugged at the wide-eyed stare Buck sent him for his bluntness. “This part of the job might not be the worst, but it’s up there. I’m sorry I didn’t prepare you for it better.”

“How am I supposed to choose anyone?”

“I haven’t had to do it often, but when I do, I like to think of it as triage,” Bobby told him. “We’re trained for that, to decide who has the better chances and the more pressing need for treatment.”

“I’ve never been good at that, either,” Buck said, remembering the train crash and Abby’s fiancé.

“I know.” From the man’s smile, he was probably flashing back to the same thing. “But let’s start with who you can’t choose.”

“Williams already said everyone who got a medal is safe.”

“There you go. That’s Hen, Chimney, Eddie, and Ravi off the list.”

“And we only have three paramedics on shift…” A couple years ago, at Hen and Karen’s vow renewal, Buck had brought up the idea of Eddie becoming paramedic certified. It had been tabled, but now seemed like a good time to bring it back up.

“That means Albert’s in the clear,” Bobby said, bringing Buck back to the task at hand. “Anyone else?”

“Javier and Toby,” he said after a moment. “We don’t have anyone else qualified to fill in for them. Just me.”

That was also something he needed to bring up. They couldn’t afford to be down the ladder or the engine if something happened to one of those two men. He wasn’t sure how to go about taking care of that, though, especially since they were talking about lay-offs. Maybe he could annoy Williams about it.

“Unless you’ve gotten new people since I’ve been gone-”

“We haven’t,” Buck said with a shake of his head.

“Then you’ve narrowed it down to five people.”

He frowned as he realized that he had. And by sheer virtue of deciding who on their shift was more important than the others. It made him feel unclean.

“Do I… Do I tell them?”

“Why?” Bobby asked. “What good would that do? They don’t need to know unless the brass makes a decision. Make the list, send it in. Then it’s out of your hands.”

“I don’t like it.”

“I know,” the other man said. “I’ve always hated it when I had to do it.”

Buck groaned and dragged his hands down his face. Bobby looked both sympathetic and amused.

“So I’ve been meaning to ask,” Bobby said. “Since Chris is a fan of the godawful show, do you think he’d like to visit the set at some point?”

Buck let out a bark of laughter.

“Pops,” he said, “I fear for our lives if he realizes it was an option and it didn’t happen.”

Chapter 9: Tyger, Tyger

Chapter Summary

In which, to quote Tweety Bird, "I did! I did see a putty tat!"

Owners of exotic pets were not exactly a rare commodity in Los Angeles, thanks to its nature and the nature of some of its more affluent residents. One of Buck’s calls as a probie was a good example, the lady with all the snakes. The laws in California were actually surprisingly stringent in some ways compared to its neighbors, with animals such as ferrets and even gerbils and certain species of hamster being illegal to own, due to the perceived threat they posed to the native wildlife. Buck presumed the late beloved hamster once owned by one Christopher Diaz was not one of those certain species.

However, what was legal to own was just as surprising as what wasn’t. Zebras, for example, were perfectly fine. As were actual wolf dogs, as long as they were second generation. Ostriches and bison, too, were legal to own, though Buck had no clue why anyone would. So too were various hybrid cats, with the Savannah cat and the Bengal cat being especially popular with certain breeds of LA residents.

Tigers, though, were most definitely and understandably illegal for a private citizen to own. The reasons for that should have been obvious, except that one of Buck’s earliest lessons in this job was that people were kinda dumb at times. Unfortunately, this particular pet owner and his landlady were both learning this lesson today.
