“Alright, we have an estimated ten minutes before she goes into hypovolemic shock,” Buck informed everyone as they got out of the trucks. One of the cops on the scene handed him a tranquilizer gun and the ammo cartridge that went with it. “Animal control will get here in seventeen minutes.”

The group gave a collective wince as they were faced with the unfavorable math there. Buck grabbed a Halligan out of one of the engine’s compartments, ignoring the looks the others gave him for it, and led the way through the apartment entrance and then out into the courtyard.

“According to dispatch-” Maddie. “-the apartment is on the eighth floor. It should be the second window from the right there.” Buck pointed as the others squinted to see. “One of you is going to repel from the roof and use this tranq gun to put the kitty to sleep.”

He expected Eddie to volunteer to be the one to do it, all things considered. His husband even started to take a step forward to do just that. But before he could, Chimney took the gun from Buck’s hand.

“Uh, maybe you should let me do that,” Eddie suggested. 

Chimney gave him a look, judgment and sarcasm evident even from behind his sunglasses, and did something to the tranq gun that filled the air with the sound of electronics coming to life and the laser sight turning on. 

“Or not,” Eddie conceded.

“And where did you learn to do that?” Buck asked.

“I have layers,” Chimney told him.

“Like an ogre,” Eddie said at the same time as Buck. They grinned at each other, before Eddie turned to Ravi. “Help me grab the gear.”

“Are you sure about this?” Hen asked Chimney, appearing very uncertain.

“Hell yeah,” he answered. “I just wish I was trying to hit him with a paintball.”

“He is very good at paintball,” Albert commented with a sagely nod.

“Okay then.” Buck wasn’t going to argue, not that they had the time. “Hen, Albert, you’re coming up with me. As soon as the cat’s down, we’re popping the door open and getting the vic out to safety. Then we get her stabilized.”

The paramedics gave him dubious looks, but they didn’t argue, either. The stairwell gave access to the roof, so they climbed it as a group until they reached the eighth floor, where Buck and the two paramedics got off with him. It was easy to find the right apartment, seeing as 8C was the only door with cops flanking it, neither of whom he recognized. Also, the snarls and growls coming from just the other side was a bit of a clue, as well.

“Dispatch,” Buck radioed. “We’re outside the apartment.”

“Copy that, One Eighteen,” Maddie replied.

“It’s just the tiger and the landlady in there,” Buck told Hen and Albert. “She’s hiding in the bathroom, but Maddie didn’t say where that is. It’s a studio apartment, though, so it can’t be too hard to find.”

“Where’s the person who lives here?” Hen asked, eying the door warily.

“Apparently he went to the ER claiming his dog attacked him. Ma has him in custody,” Buck said, and then grabbed his radio again. “How are we doing out there?”

“He’s going down now,” Ravi responded.

“Why are you here with us?” Albert asked him. “Instead of out there where you could see what they were doing?”

“I figure if I’m sending you guys up here to get mauled, I might as well go with,” Buck answered with a shrug.

“I don’t see anything,” Chimney suddenly complained over the radio.

“Are you sure you’re on the right floor, Chim?” Eddie asked. Several seconds went by without an answer, and then Buck suddenly heard a growl and a muffled shout.

“Yeah,” Chimney responded, a bit breathless. “It’s the right floor.”

“Everything okay?” Buck asked.

“Peachy. Just got jumpscared by Shere Khan.”

“Shere Khan is the tiger from the Jungle Book,” Hen told Buck with a smirk.

“Thanks,” Buck told her, putting as much sarcasm into the single word as he could.

“You’re welcome.”

“One Eighteen, be advised,” Maddie cut in. “Patient is going into shock and is about to open the bathroom door.”

“Try to talk her outta it,” Buck replied to her. “Chim, hurry it up.”

Through the door, he heard the following sounds: a door creaking open and the thump of someone flopping onto the floor; claws tapping against hardwood, reminding him of Hoover, but much larger; an angry, hair-raising yowl that was followed first by tense silence and then plaintive cries from a distressed tiger.

And then the loud thump as something fell onto the floor.

“He’s down! He’s down!” Chimney excitedly relayed.

Buck didn’t bother responding, instead grabbing the handle and giving it a try. The door opened easily and he stepped through first, halligan raised, with the cops right behind him. They found the tiger lying unconscious in the middle of the floor and the landlady half out of the bathroom, looking pale and unsteady. The inside of the apartment was a disaster, with bits of wood and parts of what was hopefully a toy strewn all over the place, along with the occasional splatters of blood.

“No pets,” the woman declared very seriously, even as she panted out the words.

“No pets,” Buck agreed, shoving the Halligan haphazardly through his belt. “Help me move her.”

He very much did not want to try and treat a patient right next to an animal that had already proven itself prone to attacking people. Even though it was currently knocked out, Buck wasn’t sure how long it would stay that way and he did not want to push their luck. Together, he and Albert, along with one of the cops, picked her up and got her moved to the building’s elevator, because being trapped in a large metal box actually sounded safer for once.

Plus, it meant they could treat her while transporting her to the ground floor and the gurney waiting for them.

“Dispatch,” he radioed, because he still remembered Abby’s complaints that they didn’t often get to hear how the calls ended. “The patient is out and being treated.”

Hen and Albert barely looked up from where they were wrapping the woman’s thigh in gauze, replacing the makeshift tourniquet she’d put on.

“Copy that, One Eighteen,” Maddie responded, sounding relieved. “Animal control should be arriving there in a few minutes.”

“Copy that,” Buck replied, before letting go of the radio as the elevator doors opened again. “And for your information, Hen, Maddie took me to see the second Jungle Book when it was in theaters.”

Hen just rolled her eyes.

This probably, technically, almost definitely counted as minor stalking. It was the kind of thing Athena would sigh and roll her eyes and call someone an idiot for. Buck was usually the one who, once he latched onto something, simply could not put it down, but Eddie wasn’t a stranger to it, either. This thing with the cheerleader and his father, for example.

A bit of invasion of privacy and a little searching on the internet, and Eddie managed to locate Weston’s father, Mike. Not his home address, but his place of employment. A bit of impulsiveness later, which he would absolutely blame on Buck’s influence, whether or not it was true, and Eddie was pulling into a small but apparently popular auto repair place. There were several classic cars parked out front, but he didn’t allow himself the luxury of admiring them before heading inside.

Eddie couldn’t really say why he went to all this effort to find the guy, or what he was doing here. Maybe he saw himself in Weston, or maybe he saw Chris, or maybe he was just tired of fathers disappointing their sons. Maybe he was just tired of sons having reasons to be disappointed with their fathers.

Inside the garage proper were a pair of cars being worked on. As Eddie walked in, he heard a clattering of tools and a loud curse, before Weston’s father slid out from beneath one. He got to his feet, more focused on his injured palm than his surroundings, so he was startled when Eddie spoke up.

“Mind if I take a look at that?” he offered.

“You a doctor or something?” Mike asked, sounding dubious. There was a resemblance between the man and his son, but Eddie thought Weston might’ve taken more after his mother.

“Firefighter,” Eddie answered, already going back to his truck for the first aid kit he kept in there. “Well, army medic before that.” 

A rolling cart of tools served as an impromptu table, with Eddie tossing the kit down on it before looking at Mike’s hand. There was an ugly gash across his palm, not deep enough to need stitches, but more than painful looking. Eddie was familiar with the kind of injuries received from working on cars, and had known people who joked that nothing worked until there was a proper amount of blood shed in the process.

“Today must be my lucky day,” Mike commented, eying the bottle of saline in Eddie’s hand with wary eyes.

“It’s gonna sting,” Eddie warned him, before washing out the wound. Mike hissed with pain and tried to jerk his hand away on instinct, stopped only by Eddie’s grip on his wrist. “Hazard of the job?”

“One of many.”

“I can relate,” he told him, switching out the saline for a roll of gauze and tape to wrap up the man’s hand.

“I bet,” Mike said, watching him work. It didn’t take long to do.

“You might need to get that changed later,” Eddie said, putting away the supplies he pulled out. “But that should stop the bleeding.”

“You got a vehicle here?” Mike asked him. “Least I can do is knock something off your service charge for you.”

“Not necessary.” Eddie zipped up the kit. “I actually came here to talk to you.”

The change in demeanor was instant. All of Mike’s friendliness dropped away, replaced with hostility and suspicion. He tilted his chin up, puffed up his chest.

“What? You Stacy’s new boyfriend or something?”

Laughing at that was probably rude. Eddie did it anyway.

“No.” He raised up his hand and showed off his ring. “I’m the firefighter who saved your son’s life the other day. Mind if we sit down and talk?”

Mike was confused, that much was clear, which meant that maybe Eddie had leaped farther in his assumptions than previously thought. The mechanic led him to a pair of lawn chairs outside, where Eddie told him the abridged version of what had occurred. It was heartening to see that the guy at least appeared to be worried.

“Stacy didn’t tell me that Wes was in the hospital.”

“She wanted to,” Eddie said. “Weston told her not to.”

“And yet,” Mike scoffed, “he blames me for staying away.”

“You’re the adult. Would you have come if she had called?”

Just before his blood pressure dropped, Weston had told his mother that “he wouldn’t-,” though he didn’t get to finish the sentence. Was he going to say that his father wouldn’t care? Wouldn’t want to be bothered? Wouldn’t show up anyway?

Mike’s gaze dropped, discomfort clear. Maybe Eddie’s assumptions about things hadn’t been entirely off-base. Unfortunately.

“Me and Weston, we don’t have the best relationship.”

“I get that. But sometimes a son just needs his dad.” Or his pops, as the individual case may be. He took a moment to be thankful and relieved that Buck was talking to Bobby again. “But you don’t miss him?”

Eddie had wanted to ask his own father that question more than once growing up, with the man so often gone on his work trips. He never quite worked up the nerve, before it was him who was gone all the time with a son left at home. His own answer to that question was a resounding, yes, always, all the time.

“All the time,” Mike said, unknowingly echoing his own sentiments. “I just got tired of arguing.”

Buck would probably tell the guy to just stop arguing, then. But Eddie liked to think he had a bit more tact than his husband. Even if he really wanted to tell the guy to stop being an idiot and just stop arguing with his teenage son.

“So you’ve decided to just not be there, ever?” Eddie asked him. “To miss watching him grow up?”

“You think I want to watch my only son be a cheerleader?” Mike angrily shot back.

Eddie stared at him, feeling an echo of the heartbreak he felt at his father’s reaction over himself and Buck. There was also anger, simmering just beneath his skin, because this was the problem? The man couldn’t handle that his son was a cheerleader?

“Does he enjoy it? Does it make him happy? Do you love him?” Eddie asked him, leaning forward to glare at Mike as he spoke. “‘Cause those are the things you should be focusing on, not whether or not what he’s doing is manly enough.”

“Who are you to judge me?” Mike demanded, hands clutching the arms of his chair.

“A guy whose sons want him there when they’re hurt,” Eddie answered, shutting the man up. He reached into his pocket to pull out his phone and bring up a video. “You think being a cheerleader makes Weston weak? Let me show you something.”

Eddie hadn’t even known that someone was recording them and Weston at the time, not until someone tagged him and Buck on Instagram. He couldn’t say he was surprised, though, with people being how they were and everyone having a camera in their pocket. Mike’s face as he watched the video, as he watched his son in pain, became drawn, tight around the eyes and his jaw going stiff.

“I’ve seen soldiers die from what he went through. Your son almost died,” Eddie told him. “And he was telling his mom not to call you. Maybe because he either didn’t think you’d bother to show. Or maybe he didn’t think you cared what happened to him.”

“I appreciate what you did for my kid,” Mike said, shoving the phone out of his face and getting to his feet. “But you need to leave.”

He went into the garage without looking back, the dismissal clear and concise. Eddie sighed and watched him go, not at all feeling like this had gone the way he wished it would have.

The place that Buck would’ve chosen for this had apparently gone out of business while he wasn’t looking, which was disappointing. It had been close to home, right on West Jefferson, so that had been convenient. Instead, he’d had to find another diner with a suitable wine menu that wasn’t going to murder his wallet.

He got there first and luckily didn’t have to wait long. Taylor Kelly showed up to take the seat across from him at the tiny table he’d chosen.

“I haven’t ordered yet,” Buck told her, looking over the menu. “Wasn’t sure what you’d want to drink.”

“Water.”

Buck paused, then he slowly lowered the menu to stare at her.

“What?” Taylor demanded, picking up her own menu.

“Water?” Buck repeated, then gestured at the laminated wine selection that she was glancing at but hadn’t picked up. “Just water?”

“I might have a coffee,” she said. “What of it?”

“An Irish coffee?”

“No. Just coffee.”

“I once watched you make breakfast for yourself that was just a mimosa with a side of aspirin,” Buck reminded her. “Then you complained there was too much orange juice. You once offered me a thermos of soup that was just gin with noodles. You put whiskey on your frozen waffles instead of syrup. Your idea of a salad is vodka with a thimble of tomato juice.”

“And now,” Taylor said, smiling with far too many teeth, “I’m going to just have a coffee.”

“Blink twice if you’re being held hostage.”

“What am I doing here?” Taylor asked, rolling her eyes.

“I’m not even sure if you are here. I might be talking to a pod per-”

“Buck.”

“Fine, fine.” Buck let it go for the moment. “Mara’s with Hen and Karen.”

“A happy ending, yay.” Taylor went back to looking over the menu. “Is that why I’m here? So you could tell me that?”

“I wanted to, I dunno. Thank you, I guess. In person,” Buck said. “You didn’t have to help her. Especially since, y’know, things between us have been kinda…”

“You called me, told me I was a miserable, horrid cunt, got upset with me for being upset, and then hung up.” Taylor sniffed. “And you said I had awful hair.”

“Well.” Buck couldn’t deny that, because he distinctly remembered saying worse things to her after reading her book. He wasn’t about to take it back, though. Most of it anyways. “I’m sorry about insulting your hair. I like the color, I shouldn’t have called it ugly.”

“Seriously? That’s it?”

“You wrote a book about us and didn’t even give us a heads up,” he said. “You wrote about Eddie being shot like you had any right to it. You wrote about Pops and the brownies. You wrote about everything that happened with Jonah.”

“Those things happened,” Taylor said, glaring at him from across the table. “We’ve had this argument before. I thought everyone deserved to know the truth about what was happening around them.”

“They deserved to know that you think I’m broken?” Buck asked her. She dropped her gaze. “It’s never been about the truth with you, Taylor, not really. We both know that. I mean, you didn’t even bother to tell the truth about yourself in that book.”

For as much as she wrote word after word and page after page about them, her short foreword hadn’t mentioned her mother or her father, or even her actual last name. Though this argument did remind him of the other reason he’d invited her out to lunch.

“I heard you interviewed Brad Torrance about the plane,” he said with forced casualness.

“He was eager to talk to me,” Taylor said, brushing her hair out of her face. “Couldn’t say enough about Bobby or how exciting it was to rescue people for real. That man has an ego the size of this city.”

“The name of the pilot wasn’t included. Did he not tell you?”

“No, he did.” She wasn’t looking at him.

“Taylor.” Buck waited until she raised her eyes to his. “Why didn’t you tell everyone it was Ma?”

“Maybe I’m trying new things,” Taylor said with a flick of her wrist.

Buck let out a hum, eyes flickering to the neglected wine menu again.

“Do you need me to ask Bobby about sponsors or…?”

“Let it go, Diaz.”

When Eddie mentioned to Buck what he was doing, he’d teased him mercilessly for it. Probably well-deserved, all things considered. Here he was, sitting on the other side of the sliding doors with a pair of crutches, waiting.

He got up when he spotted Weston being pushed in a wheelchair around the corner by a nurse, his mother, Stacy, on their heels. The kid smiled when he saw him coming, and Eddie helped him get his feet under him with the crutches.

“Nice and easy,” Eddie advised as Weston wobbled a bit. “There you go. Not as fancy as the ones my son uses, but they’ll do.”

Weston took a tentative hop-step forward, smiling from ear to ear, as his mother fretted at his elbow.

“I got it,” he told them both, taking another one.

“Just like that,” Eddie said. “You’re doing it.”

“He’s always been a quick study.” Mike’s voice was a surprise. Eddie twisted around to see him standing awkwardly a few feet away.

Weston’s face lit up at the sight of him.

“Dad!”

“I’m sorry it took me so long to get here,” Mike said, coming closer.

“You’re here now,” Weston said. He leaned forward, settling for bumping his head into his father’s shoulder since he couldn’t manage a hug without falling over.

“Let’s get you home,” Mike said, and then looked between Eddie and Stacy. “My truck would probably be easier for him to get in and out of, right?”

“Probably,” Eddie agreed.

“Alright, come on, then.”

Mike hovered at Weston’s elbow as he hop-stepped towards the doors, just as Stacy had been doing moments prior. Stacy, for her part, lingered behind to mouth a “thank you” to Eddie before following after them.

So maybe things had gone the way Eddie wished, after all.

Chapter 10: FirefightersDiaz_LAFD

Chapter Summary

Some transcripts of videos posted by @FirefightersDiaz_LAFD.

Chapter Notes

Did something a little bit different this time. It was fun, and I tend to focus a lot on dialogue anyway.

Transcript from a video captioned, “Caught him singing the Beautiful Milk song to Senorita. 🤣🤣🤣”

[Interior shot of the Diaz living room. Eddie stands in the middle of the room, back to the camera, as he sways and sings. He is holding something in his arms which is mostly blocked from view, except for a fluffy black tail flicking in the air.]

Eddie, singing: -leche linda que la traigo aquí, es para esta niña que se va a dormir.

[Laughter from off screen but close to the camera, muffled as if the person is covering their mouth.]

Eddie, singing: Arrorró mi niña, arrorró mi sol, arrorró pedazo-

[Eddie turns as he sings, revealing the black, fluffy cat draped in his arms. The muffled laughter gets louder and he looks up. The change in demeanor is instant.]

Eddie: Buck!

[Eddie opens his arms and drops the cat to the floor.]

Buck, from off-screen, laughing: Babe, were you singing to the cat?

[A pause.]

Eddie: No.

Buck, OS: Are you sure?

[The camera pans down to the cat brushing against Eddie’s leg and then back up. Eddie’s face is turning very red.]

Eddie: Are you recording this?

[A pause.]

Buck, OS: No?

Eddie: Buck.

[A pause.]

Buck, OS: I thought it was very cute. I bet everyone else will, too.

Eddie: Buck!

[Eddie takes a step towards the camera. The image blurs as the person holding the camera turns to run]

Transcript ends.

Partial transcript from a video captioned, “🌈PSA from your local #LAFD118 queers!🌈”

[Interior shot of Station 118, the loft. Hen and Albert are sitting at one of the tall, circular tables, both of them looking vaguely annoyed. The truck bay is visible behind them.]

Albert: I feel like this is homophobic.

Buck, from off-screen: How is this homophobic, Al?

Albert: Because you’re making us - [He gestures between himself and Hen] - do a thing about this.

Buck, OS: I’m making you do this because you’re paramedics.

Hen: And because we’re queer.

[Buck enters the screen from the right to stand next to Hen.]

Buck: Okay, yes. But do you really want to have Chimney trying to get through this?

[Hen and Albert turn to look at each other. They nod.]

Hen: Yeah, okay. That’s fair. I can already hear all the jokes he’d want to make.

Chimney, OS: I have a list!

[Buck twists around to point a finger at someone off-screen.]

Buck: And I know each and every one of ‘em will summon the Mouth of Sauron into my inbox, so you’re not saying any of ‘em! Leave ‘em in the comments like everyone else.

Albert: Can we just get this over with?

Hen: How did you get them to approve this, anyway? Did you get them to approve it?

Buck: For your information, yes I did. And it’s community outreach and a safety thing and- Anyway, it’s all in the clear.

[Buck moves to stand behind Hen and Albert and claps his hands together. The two paramedics visibly wince from the noise.]

Buck: So we’ve all heard the jokes about someone - [Buck raises his hands to make air quotes for the next word] - accidentally falling off a bunk bed onto an inconveniently placed cucumber-

Chimney, OS: Or a conveniently placed one!

Buck: And then rushing to the ER.

[Hen closes her eyes, visibly trying not to laugh. Buck drops his hands onto Hen and Albert’s shoulders.]

Buck: And my friends here are going to tell you how to avoid, uh…

Albert: Having to be the next person telling us that you accidentally fell onto an inconveniently placed cucumber.

[Buck snaps his fingers and points at Albert.]

Buck: Yes! That.

Hen: And the first step- [She cuts herself off with a snort and then clears her throat.] The first step is to use only what you can safely remove yourself. Something with- with- Do I really have to do this?

Chimney, OS: Think of the greater good, Henrietta!

Hen: Call me that again and you’ll be the next one who lands on a-

Buck: Guys.

Hen: Sorry, sorry. [She clears her throat.] The first step is to use only what you can safely remove yourself, something with a large-

[Albert starts to laugh. He gets up from the table and walks off-screen, still laughing. Buck rolls his eyes and takes his seat.]

Buck: I should’ve bullied Eddie into doing this.

Partial transcript ends.

Transcript from a video captioned, “I can’t believe we actually have to say this. 😓🐯”

[Interior shot of an office. Buck sits at a desk with a computer, a plaque with his name on it, a couple framed photographs turned away from the camera, and two firefighting themed knick knacks. On the wall behind him is a map of the city of Los Angeles.]

Buck: Okay, I think I can get through it this time without using no-no words.

Eddie, from off screen: I hope so, capitán.

[Camera pans to the left. Eddie is shown leaning against the wall, arms crossed.]

Eddie: I don’t think Ravi wants to be stuck here playing cameraman for the entire shift.

Ravi, OS: I don’t.

Buck, OS: But you’re so good at it.

[The camera slowly pans back to Buck. No words are spoken but Buck raises his hands and nods.]

Buck: Okay, okay. Last go.

[Buck clears his throat, sits up straight, and places his hands back on the desk.]

Buck: Okay.

[Buck’s face goes stern. It does not look natural.]

Buck: You cannot keep tigers as pets in Los Angeles. Or anywhere else in California. Or anywhere in the US. I think. I’ll have to look that-

Eddie, OS: Buck.

Buck: It’s against the law, and it’s stupid, and it’s cruel to the tiger. If you or anyone you know owns a tiger - I can’t believe this is a thing I’m having to say - or any other restricted animals,  please call animal control. It doesn’t matter how cute it is as a baby, and I know they are very, very cute, it’ll grow up into a really big animal that deserves better than to be stuck in the kind of living space most of us can afford in this city.

[Buck looks slightly to the left of the camera. His face scrunches up and then clears as he nods again.]

Buck: Right, right, and it’s dangerous to you. Fangs, claws, rip and tear. Yadda yadda.

[Someone off-screen loudly sighs.]

Buck: Hey, I have my priorities. The innocent tiger over the idiot that tries to keep it as a pet in a studio apartment.

Ravi, OS: Didn’t this last one nearly kill two people?

[Buck points at the camera.]

Buck: That wasn’t his fault, he was a baby.

Eddie, OS: It was four hundred and twenty-five pounds.

Buck:  A very big baby.

[Another loud sigh comes from off-screen. The camera pans left again to show Eddie pinching the bridge of his nose with his eyes closed. His lips are moving without sound.]

Buck, OS: What?

Transcript ends.

Partial transcript of a video captioned, “I still don’t know what ice cream had to do with anything.”

[Interior shot of the Diaz kitchen, the camera is looking in from the dining room side of the breakfast bar. Buck and Abuela are moving around each other while cooking. Buck has on an apron over a colorful “I Am Kenough” hoodie.]

Buck: -it wasn’t actually ice cream then, it was just snow and ice. But Alexander the Great apparently liked his with honey and nectar. Vanilla and chocolate ice cream weren’t a thing until white people started invading the Americas.

Eddie, from off-screen: You and Chris called me basic for liking vanilla.

Buck: ‘Cause you are, babe.

[Abuela says something in spanish that makes Buck laugh as he goes to open the refrigerator. She stands at the counter, obviously looking for something.]

Buck: Uh.

[Buck takes a wooden stirring spoon out of the refrigerator. He holds up the spoon and stares at it in visible confusion.]

Abuela: There it is.

[Abuela reaches for the wooden spoon and takes it from Buck. Buck turns slightly to the camera and shrugs. He takes a stick of butter out of the refrigerator and closes the door.]

Buck: Um, anyway. What was I talking about?

Eddie, OS: White people invading the Americas.

Buck: Right! So anyway, vanilla and chocolate weren’t ice cream flavors until white people invaded the Americas…

Partial transcript ends.

Partial transcript of a video captioned, “Q&A time!”

[Exterior shot of the Diaz backyard. Buck and Eddie are sitting in patio chairs, the back of the house and part of the yard behind them. Hoover the dog has his head in Eddie’s lap. Eddie is petting him while frowning at Buck. Buck has a tablet in his hand.]

Eddie: Why are we doing this?

Buck: Because I like the attention.

Eddie: So why am I stuck doing this?

Buck: Because you love me.

[Buck turns his head to smile at Eddie. Eddie sighs.]

Buck: Okay, first question. [He looks down at his tablet. His face visibly brightens.] Oh! First question is, what happened to the tiger?

Eddie: It went to some sanctuary in Ohio. This one - [He points at Buck with the hand that was petting Hoover. Hoover raises his head and softly barks until Eddie resumes petting him.] - kept bothering people until they told him.

Buck: It’s the same sanctuary they sent Ming, the tiger from New York. Chris was upset, because he was hoping it would go to the LA Zoo. The next question is… [He looks at the tablet, grimaces, shakes his head.] Oh, no, sorry, not answering that one.

Eddie: What is it? [He leans in to read it for himself and then makes a face. He turns to the camera.] Our sex lives are none of your business!

Buck: Especially on an account sponsored by our bosses. Oh! What kind of dog is Hoover and how did we get him? He is a Picardy Shepherd and uh…

[Buck and Eddie share a look.]

Eddie: We got him from Hen, because she and her wife couldn’t keep him.

[Buck nods.]

Buck: Yes! I woke up from a post-shift nap and there he was. Eddie keeps bringing animals home.

Eddie: Which includes you.

Buck: Rude. [He looks at the tablet again.] Oh, God.

Eddie: What, is it another sex one?

Buck: No, worse. How did we meet?

[Buck’s face turns dour. Eddie smiles widely.]

Eddie: We met at work! And then this one spent a couple shifts being a total brat to everyone.

[Buck huffs.]

Buck: I was not that bad.

Eddie: Bobby compared you to a threatened tomcat, mi sol. Stomping around and hissing at everything, trying to mark your territory-

Buck: I was not that bad!

Eddie: And then I gave you a compliment and suddenly you were my best friend.

[Buck huffs.]

Buck: That is not how it went at all, stop lying to them. [He looks at the tablet again.] Oh. What is Taylor Kelly like in person?

[Eddie opens his mouth. There is a smash cut. Eddie is sitting back down, having gotten to his feet at some point. Hoover is now on Buck’s other side.]

Eddie: -and I was not jealous of her!

Buck: Of course not, babe. [He reaches over to pat Eddie without looking away from the tablet.] Let’s see, uh… Teek, I know this question is from you, and the answer is obviously Marjan. C’mon, she's Firefox. Can’t answer this one because of patient privacy. Not gonna- [He looks up at the camera.] Sorry, but our kids are none of your business.

[Eddie leans in again to look at the tablet screen.]

Eddie: ¿Qué pedo? Yeah, Gavin is adopted. No, you don’t get to know about his mother. Why would you even ask that?

Buck: Moving onto the next question. I should probably go through them ahead of time, if we do this again. Oh! What…

Partial transcript ends.

Transcript of a video captioned, “Trick-or-treating Safety Tips! #LAFD118 is hosting the yearly #LAFD Firehouse Haunt Fest! 👻🎃”

[Interior shot of the truck bay for Station 118. Buck and Eddie stand between the engine and the ladder. Behind them, firefighters are putting up various Halloween and autumn themed decorations.]

Buck: With Halloween coming up, the LAFD has some tips and tricks for how to have a safe and fun time while Trick-Or-Treating. The first and most important is that all the little ghouls need to have a grown-up with them. One that is paying attention!

Eddie: Make sure you’re easily visible. Use a flashlight or glow sticks so that people can see you.

Buck: Stay in a group, walk slowly - don’t run off! - and make sure everyone knows where you’re going.

Eddie: Try to stick to neighborhoods that you know and homes with the porch light on. 

Buck: Remain on well-lit streets and always use the sidewalk! If there isn’t a sidewalk available, walk at the farthest edge of the street and walk facing on-coming traffic, so you know to get out of the way.

Eddie: Don’t cut across yards-

Buck: That’s rude!

Eddie: Don’t use alleys and don’t run between parked cars. Obey all traffic and pedestrian regulations.

Buck: Walk, don’t run, across the street. Always look left - [Eddie turns his body to face stage left.] - right - [Eddie turns his body to face stage right.] - and left again - [Eddie turns his body to face stage left before turning back to the camera.] - to make sure there are no cars coming. And remove anything that might keep you from seeing those cars, like a mask.

Eddie: Don’t assume the drivers can see you. That’s why it’s important to only cross at intersections. Just remember that just because one car stops, it doesn’t mean the others will.

Buck: Grown-ups should check the treats when you get home. If something is unwrapped, that is a trick and should be thrown away.

Eddie: Sharing is caring, but make sure that the tiniest monsters aren’t being given any choking hazards.

Buck: The Los Angeles Fire Department wishes you a happy Halloween! And remember! Station One Eighteen is hosting the Firehouse Haunt Fest this year. If you’re not here, you’re lame!

[Eddie covers his face with a sigh.]

Transcript ends.

Chapter 11: A Kid (Un)Friendly Scare

Chapter Summary

In which Buck manages to accidentally traumatize a group of children. Again.

Buck whistled as he wheeled in his piece de resistance, the tune changing into one long tone of appreciation as he took in the decorations that were going up all over the station’s truck bay. There were large, fake, sticky spider webs stretched over the trucks and onto the awning structures being lifted up between them. There were plastic skeletons being put into place, along with bats and spiders and fake ghosts. There were, too, hay bales and pots of marigolds strategically placed all around.

He’d gone to pick up what would certainly be the crowning jewel of this whole thing without much concern, since the station had been taken offline. Besides, Bobby was here somewhere to supervise, having taken them hosting the haunted house as some sort of challenge and returning for the day to make sure it was done right in person.

“Lookin’ good, guys!” Buck called out, coming to a stop by one of the tables ladened with miniature pumpkins and (electric) candles.

“Yeah, no, I don’t think so,” Chimney said, shaking his head. Behind him, Albert shook his head with his face a mask of exasperation. The younger Han was wearing a pair of fake cat ears, though Buck had no idea where he got them from. “This is the Firehouse Haunt Fest, not the Fall Fest. Where’s the spooky, Cap? The macabre? The gore!?”

He grabbed a fog machine and sprayed it right into Buck’s face.

“We’ve got spider webs, bats, crows,” Eddie listed as he pawed through various bags of goodies, pausing to torment Chimney with the crow he just pulled out. “We’ve got fake blood. Does fake blood count?”

“Fake blood is just a start,” Chimney said, taking the gallon jug of the stuff. “This place should be festooned with blood.”

“Festooned?” Ravi repeated, coming over to hang off Albert.

“You know, decorated! Adorned! Covered! This place should be covered with fake blood and gore!”

“You do remember that this is supposed to be a kid-friendly haunted house, right?” Buck asked, leaning away from him a bit. “Less House of Wax, more Halloweentown.”

“I can’t watch that movie,” Chimney complained, making a face. “The guy that sells the flying brooms just creeps me out.”

“Filing that away to mock you for later,” Hen commented from where she was fluffing a fake ghost she’d just hung up. “You know how hard it is to clean up real life blood, Chim. Fake blood isn’t any better.”

“Point.” Buck pointed at her. “You’ll have to clean this up, so keep that in mind.”

“You mean we’ll have to clean this up,” Ravi said with a squint. “Right?”

“Right, that’s what I said. You guys will have to clean it up.”

He grinned at their unimpressed glares.

“Why are we the ones doing this, anyway?” Albert asked, digging into the bags that Eddie had been going through.

“Community outreach!” Bobby spoke up, appearing from behind one of the backdrops that was being put together and making his way towards them. It was weird seeing him in the station but not in uniform. ”Every year the department chooses a different house to host it.”

“It’s probably our fault that we got chosen. You know since they've got us doing so much community outreach,” Eddie said, gesturing between himself and Buck with a skeletal arm. Then he perked up. “Wait, no, it’s Taylor’s fault. All of this can be blamed on Taylor Kelly.”

“The two of you are so adorable,” Buck teased. It earned him a scowl from his husband, which he smiled prettily at.

“Last year the One Twenty-six hosted everything,” Bobby said as he rolled his eyes at their antics. “I am making it my personal mission to crush them.”

“Which explains why you’re here and not in Hollywood,” Hen commented with a smile.

“If you wanna crush ‘em, then blood is the way to go!” Chimney argued, waving the gallon jug around wildly enough that Buck was momentarily worried he was about to hit someone with it. “Kids love gore. Right, Buck? Eddie? Tell ‘em, would Chris prefer more or less Halloween gore?”

“I actually don’t know,” Eddie said with a frown. “The last couple of Halloweens, he ditched us to go hang out with his friends. When we told him about all of this-” He gestured around at the bay-turned-haunted house with the skeletal arm. “-he called it cringe.”

“He still said he wanted to come, though, so.” Buck shrugged. 

“Okay, but.” Bobby pointed at what Buck had rolled in. “What is this?”

“Oh!” Buck bounced on his toes and then whipped off the sheet he’d used to cover it up with. Beneath the sheet was-

“Is that a coffin?” Ravi asked, leaning over the table to peer at it.

“Feast your eyes,” Buck said as dramatically as possible. Eddie rolled his eyes. “On the newest star of the One Eighteen.”

He flipped open the lid, revealing the impressively realistic mummified corpse resting inside. It was dressed in tattered, dusty clothes and laying on a bed of straw.

“Good lord, Buck,” Bobby said, staring at it with his jaw hanging open.

“This is what I am talking about, people!” Chimney declared, excitedly throwing up his hands. “Where did you find it?”

“There’s a Hollywood prop house down the street from my old apartment,” Buck answered. “He was tucked away in a musty old corner.”

“For good reason, capitán.” Eddie’s face was scrunched up, nose and brow wrinkled. “He looks like the cryptkeeper.”

“He looks like he’s been dead… Two-hundred years,” Hen said.

“I thought you said Halloweentown.” Albert was frowning at the prop from the back of the crowding group. “This definitely looks like something cursed they’d find in an episode of the Librarians that they’d have to rescue people from.”

They all stared at him.

“What?” His shoulders rose up around his ears. Ravi gave him supportive pats on the back. “It was a good show.”

“The prop guy said it’d been used in a bunch of old Westerns,” Buck told them, moving on. “I figured, y’know, stick him in a vest with a cowboy hat. Maybe a six-shooter.”

He mimed shooting into the air with finger guns.

“Uh, I don't know about this,” Bobby said, uncertainty lacing his words. “This might be too intense for some of the younger kids.”

Buck glanced at the realistic prop and then shrugged at everyone else.

“It’ll be fine,” he said. “This guy’ll be a showstopper.”

“So why is Grandpops playing Cap Dracula?” Christopher asked, unwrapping a sucker and popping it into his mouth. He wasn’t wearing a costume, because he was apparently too cool for that now.

Chris had shown up with a group of his friends and a parent that volunteered to ferry them over. He and his friends had eaten - there were tables of refreshments at the back of the decorated truck bay - and then said friends had gone home or off to torment weak willed adults, whatever the kids did these days. But Chris had stuck around to offer the kind of cutting judgment and criticism that only a jaded teenager could conjure. Suffice to say, nothing they’d thrown at him as he went through impressed him much, especially Eddie’s apparently lame attempts to be a terrifying wolfman in a fake graveyard.

He thought the fake corpse, currently sitting in a rocking chair with a bowl of candy in his lap, was pretty neat, though. Buck always knew he was the cooler parent.

“Because he does a better accent than me,” Buck answered, adjusting the stetson on his head. He was dressed up as a cowboy, complete with hat, boots, big buckled belt, and ascot. Going by the heated way Eddie had stared when he first saw him in the outfit, Buck was gonna get his own treat tonight. “Plus, he was really, really excited to do it.”

That was an understatement, perhaps. Bobby had lit up when he heard about the 118 being chosen to host the Firehouse Haunt Fest this year, only to droop like a plant left to Eddie’s care once he remembered that he wouldn’t have any part of it. What was Buck to do? Not invite the man to get involved?

Screams erupted from the- Well, it was less of a haunted house and more a series of haunted tents. The last one was Chimney’s, who’d been very successful tonight with his jumpscares as a masked killer straight out of one of those overdone slasher films. Buck moved into position just as the newest group of costumed kids came sprinting out of the tents, still screaming, only to come to a wide-eyed stop when they spotted Buck, the corpse prop, and the bowl of candy in his lap.

“Howdy, partners.” He ignored his son snickering off to the side at the fake drawl he was putting on. “Congratulations on making it to the end of the Firehouse Haunt Fest. Come on over and get your reward.”

None of the kids moved to take any of the candy.

“Come on, now,” he tried again. “Reach on in and grab a handful. You’ve earned it.”

Still nothing.

“D- Doesn’t anybody want any?” Buck asked them, dropping the drawl.

“He’s creepy,” one of the kids, a girl in a fairy princess get-up, declared.

“Oh, hey, he- he’s not creepy.” He glanced at the prop. “Okay, m- maybe a little. But he’s harmless. He’s not even real, just a dummy.”

“I don’t like his arm,” the girl said.

The prop had been arranged so that it looked like it died gripping the edges of the candy.

“That’s okay,” he told her, kneeling down. “I can just move them out of the way. Come on, come closer.”

They crept closer like tiptoeing mice as he gripped one arm - it felt like dried jerky beneath his hand, like he’d read that actual mummies felt like, and he wondered what the makers had done to achieve that effect - and moved it to lay against the armrest of the rocking chair. It was stiff, Buck didn’t think it was supposed to be arranged like this, but he got it done easy enough.

“Hey, cowpoke, that tickles,” he said out of the corner of his mouth, dropping his voice. The kids laughed nervously. “He’s fine.”

He got up and went to the other side to do the same with its left arm. Except this time, he must’ve yanked it with a bit too much force or it wasn’t as securely connected as the other arm, because it came off in his hands at the shoulder. Buck stared at it in his hands, brain working overtime to comprehend what he was seeing.

“Are those worms?” one of the kids, an older boy dressed as a baseball player, asked.

“I think they’re tendons,” Buck whispered. But why would a fake prop have realistic looking tendons on the inside? There wouldn’t be a need to show them.

And its skin felt like dried jerky. Just like actual mummies did.

“Tendons?”

“Oh my God, he’s real!” Buck shouted, the realization slamming into him like an out-of-control steam powered locomotive. “He’s real! He’s real! He’s real!”

He dropped the arm onto the ground as the kids screamed and ran, falling back from it and frantically wiping his hands off on the denim of his jeans. Chris came over and he nudged at the arm with the bumpered end of a crutch.

“That is so cool,” he whispered, grinning in delight.

The police ended up being called, because duh. The haunt fest was also put on pause because, again, duh, with the police marking the truck bay out in yellow Do Not Cross tape until the coroner could arrive to pick up the actual, not-at-all-a-prop corpse. Which Buck had brought into the station.

“You called it, Buck,” Bobby said. They’d gathered to watch the coroners load up the body, costumes looking rather ridiculous under the fluorescent lights of the station now that they were back on. Hen’s mad scientist outfit, in particular, lacked a certain pizzazz without the bits that fluoresced under blacklight.  “He was a showstopper.”

“I just don’t understand,” Buck said with a frown. “Why would they rent me a real body?”

“Why would they even have a real body?” Ravi asked. He was dressed up as a circus lion tamer while Albert, standing next to him, was some sort of large cat.

“That’s LAPD’s problem, now,” Bobby told him. “We should get a start getting this set dec taken down and put away before B-shift gets in.”

“Wh- What? No! Pops, c’mon. Look at them all.” Buck gestured at the small crowd of costumed onlookers being kept at bay by officers and the tape. “They still want to come in.”

“Yeah, we can’t stop now!” Chimney argued, hockey mask pushed up to the top of his head. “We just started getting some good scares going.”

“Speak for yourself,” Eddie grumbled. Buck reached over to give him a supportive pat, only for his husband to cringe away from his hand.

“He was already a mummy,” Buck said, choosing not to be offended, like the adult he was. “It’s not like there’s foul play here.”

“Oh, there was foul play, alright,” Athena stated as she joined them. It was not the least bit surprising that she was one of the officers that responded, all things considered. “In the management of that prop house. Turns out, they had that body inventoried as a curio, not a dummy.”

“What’s a curio?” Chris asked, speaking up after spending the last bit of time sulking over the fact that no one would let him hold the dead guy’s detached arm.

“Something you collect just because it’s rare or weird,” Bobby answered. “A curiosity.”

“Ohhh.”

“The log had him listed as an old outlaw named Billy Boils,” Athena explained. “We’ll find out more about him once we pull the original purchase orders, but they’re in a warehouse in Altadena. So it’s gonna take a minute.”

“Well, keep us posted if you can,” Bobby requested.

“Will do. See you at home,” she told him, giving him a quick kiss before turning on her heel and strolling over to the coroners. “Alright, our work here is done.”

“I think we can all agree on one thing,” Buck said as the coroners slammed the doors to the van closed and got ready to leave. “This was not my fault.”

There was immediate disagreement from everybody. Everybody. He was even betrayed by his husband and their son. Buck glared at them all.

“Okay, but come on, look at all those people out there,” he argued, gesturing again to the costumed crowd waiting outside. “We can just reopen for a couple hours, right? And we have all this candy.”

“I think we’ve traumatized these kids enough for one day,” Bobby said. “So let’s get to it and start boxing everything up.”

“But- Wait.” Buck furrowed his brow. Why was he even arguing about this? “No, wait. I’m the captain. This is my station.”

“Yes you are and yes it is,” Bobby agreed, putting a hand on his shoulder and looking him in the eye. “And we had to call the police because you brought a dead body into your station. Then you traumatized a bunch of children with it.”

“Oh no.” The station’s phone began to ring, the sound of it somehow echoing through the truck bay. “Oh no.”

“Good luck.”

“I cannot believe you brought a dead body into the station,” Eddie nagged at him a few hours later.

“I didn’t know it was a dead body!” Buck started waving an arm for emphasis, remembered he currently had a knife in his hand, and sheepishly lowered it again. “They told me it was a prop. Why would I think it was an actual dead guy!?”

They were currently finishing up carving the pumpkins to go on the porch. There was one for each occupant of the house, including the cat and the dog, and bits of pumpkin guts on the dining table that Gavin was delighting himself playing with. There was a plate of s’mores sitting in the middle of the table since Chris wanted to make one for his mother for the ofrenda that he was helping Abuela put together in the living room. To go along with the s’more for Shannon, there was also a cigar for Edmundo the Senior and a packet of Skittles for Daniel.

Buck was still in his costume, which really wasn’t much of a costume at all without the hat. Eddie had peeled out of his werewolf get-up, make-up and all, before they left the station and Buck was thankful for that. He wasn’t certain how much longer he could go without pointing out that he thought his husband looked like Rowlf the muppet.

“Was your boss upset?” Chris asked, crutches tapping against the hardwood floor as he joined them in the dining room. He grabbed a s’more to munch on, deftly managing to avoid the pumpkin seed that Gavin threw at him.

“No,” Buck denied. Eddie fixed him with a disbelieving look as he carved out an eye. “She wasn’t!”

Chief Williams had just sounded so very, very tired. Or maybe exasperated was a better word for it. Buck got the impression that at this point she honestly hadn’t even been surprised that something like this happened, just vaguely annoyed that it was happening under her purview. He wondered, briefly, if the other shifts had to deal with this kind of thing or if it was entirely limited to their crew. 

Surely Reynolds and Mayfair had their own share of insanity to deal with. Okay, so Buck couldn’t remember them having any trucks explode or bridges collapse or arsonist probies or having to help passenger planes land on the interstate, but surely…

“This one’s done, mi sol,” Eddie announced, lifting up his pumpkin and turning it in the air, this way and that, to look at it. “Yours?”

“Oh, yeah.” Buck had been slicing out little whiskers in his poor attempt to mimic Senorita’s face before he got distracted. He hurriedly did the last one and then set aside the knife. “Let’s go put them out on the porch.”

It took several trips, because they’d gotten rather large pumpkins, and it took some negotiating because they couldn’t be in the way of Chris or Abuela. It meant they’d ended up less on the porch and more along the side of it, but that was fine. They could be seen easier from the street that way. They stuck LED candles in them and Buck took pictures to post along with ones of the ofrenda, because he was proud of his subpar pumpkin carving, before heading back inside.

“Your phone’s ringing,” Abuela said, pointing to where it sat on the coffee table and was, indeed, ringing.

Buck answered it with a, “Hey, Teek” that got interrupted by his friend’s loud, 

“You rented a dead body for Halloween!?”

Eddie ducked and ran from Buck’s glare.

Chapter 12: Pumpkin-Head

Chapter Summary

In which Buck is struck by the curse of Billy Boils.

The ordeal with having to choose five people on their shift to maybe get fired - something that luckily hadn’t happened, though he knew C-shift hadn’t been so lucky - had brought to Buck’s attention a couple of areas where their shift was lacking. Really, one of them was something he’d already realized a year ago, but that period of time had been a bit fraught, plus he hadn’t actually been captain - just acting - until recently, so he thought he could be excused for letting it go unaddressed for so long. But their shift was a bit understaffed, which was probably what allowed them to eke by without being hit by lay-offs, with some glaring gaps on the roster.

They should have had six people to the ladder truck, six to the engine, and at least two paramedics assigned to each ambulance, for a total of sixteen people on their shift. At least sixteen, that was the bare minimum. But they only had three paramedics, and more often than not only four people on the engine. That, though, wasn’t something he would likely be able to address anytime soon. But the other issues he’d noticed? Those he could do something about.

“Hey, Cap.” Ravi poked his head through the doorway of the office, looking uncertain. “Clarke said you wanted to talk to me?”

“Yeah!” Buck smiled at him and waved at one of the seats in front of his desk. “Sit down.”

“Uh, okay.” The other man sounded a bit hesitant as he did. “Is that my personnel file?”

“Um.” Buck glanced down at it. “Yes?”

“Oh, God, am I about to be fired?”

“What? No. What?” Buck shook his head. “There’d be someone from the union and HR here, if that was the case. No, I just wanted to talk to you about something.”

“Okay.” Ravi only looked marginally relieved by that statement. “What did you want to talk to me about, Cap?”

“Last year, when we lost Jones-” There was a pause where they both grimaced at the reminder. “-they had to scramble to find someone to fill in for him even for the short term. We had three people who were qualified to drive the engine: him, Javier Ortiz, and me. But then we lost him, Javier was needed for the ladder, and I was busy filling in for Pops.”

“And then we got Toby.”

“Right! But you see how the problem is still there, don’t you?” Buck asked him. He got a slow nod in response. “If something happens to Toby and Javier, or even if they just want a day off, we have to find a qualified floater or beg someone from another shift to fill in.”

“What does this have to do with me?” Ravi asked, in the tone of someone who absolutely knew the answer already and was hoping they were mistaken.

“Bobby had nothing but good things to say about your past evals-”

“Oh, God damn it,” was groaned into Ravi’s hands.

“C’mon, I’m not asking you to actually go for the job,” Buck told him. “Not unless you want to. I never did, but I had the license for it when I started here, and that meant I could drive the truck or engine in a pinch.”

“I did actually wonder about that,” Ravi commented once he’d uncovered his face again. “What if… What if I did want to take the job, though? What would that need?”

Buck beamed at him.

“Four years of working in the department,” Buck said. “Full-time, paid. And a valid California Commercial B driver’s license with either a Haz-Mat and Tank or Firefighter endorsement.”

“That’s all?” Ravi sounded dubious.

“Plus, y’know, the exam and the practical and the interview. It’s the same for both driver-engineers and apparatus operators. ” Buck shrugged and waved it away. “I’ve already cleared this with Williams and talked to both Toby and Javier. If you’re willing to do it, I’m gonna have you shadow Toby while you’re working on getting that commercial license. Clarke’s doing the same with Javier.”

“And I won’t have to switch shifts? Or stations?”

“No. No, no, no.” Buck shook his head. “That would kinda defeat the purpose of having you do it, right? We’d just be right back where we were. Like I said, you don’t have to go all the way, you can just get the license - which isn’t much harder to get than a regular driver’s license - and fill-in when needed. But being a driver-engineer does come with a pay increase, so.”

“I’ll take the money,” Ravi stated with a nod.

“Excellent!” Buck clapped his hands together, beaming at him. “So just-”

“Hey!” Chimney suddenly barged in and then retreated just as fast, until he was just poking his head around the corner. “Oops, sorry. The door was open, didn’t know you were busy.”

“Uh, it’s fine.” Buck frowned at him, shook his head, and then turned back to Ravi. “As I was saying, just go talk to Toby.”

“Got it, Cap,” Ravi said with a nod, before pushing himself out of his seat. He was out the door quickly, stepping around Chimney since the man was still lingering just outside.

“Okay,” Buck sighed. “What did ya want, Chim?”

“Halloween,” Chimney said, coming inside fully after looking back down the short hall that led to the rest of the station.

Buck was hesitant to ask what the man meant by that one-word statement, knowing damn well that it was inevitably going to be headache inducing. No one really wanted to work on Halloween, especially those with kids old enough to appreciate trick-or-treating and those who were still young enough themselves to have plans for that day. Last year, Buck and Eddie had actually volunteered to work on the holiday, since Gavin was so young and Chris was just going to abandon them for his friends, and there’d been a dozen people scrambling over themselves to switch shifts with them.

“What about Halloween?” Buck asked.

“I was just thinking,” Chimney said, taking the seat Ravi had just vacated. “It’s Hen and Karen’s first Halloween with Mara, right?”

“Right.” Buck could see where this was going and was realizing that his instincts had been correct; this was absolutely gonna give him a headache.

“So I was just thinking,” the other man said, repeating himself. “That it would be nice, y’know? If Hen could have the day off.”

“She’s not the only parent on this shift, Chim,” Buck reminded him.

“I know, but our kids- Well, Eddie said Chris ditched you guys for his friends. And Gavin and Jee, they’re young enough that they won’t remember. Or even notice, really,” Chimney argued. “But Mara’s old enough that it matters to her, and with everything they went through thanks to the councilwoman…”

“Yeah, yeah, fine.” Buck dragged a hand down his face. “Eddie can fill in for her.”

That was another thing he needed to bring up, and which he’d been putting off because he wasn’t sure if it would result in an argument or not. There was nothing stopping Eddie from getting fully certified as a paramedic, nothing except himself. In most situations where his husband would argue the need to watch his back, Buck would be standing on the sidelines, anyway.

“You are the best!” Chimney said, leaping to his feet.

Buck just grunted and waved him away, deciding he was done captaining for the moment until the next time the bell rang.

“So this is gonna be one of those weird ones,” Buck announced to everyone over the headsets. “Our patient has his head stuck in a pumpkin.”

“Not the worst thing someone’s been stuck in that we’d been called for,” Eddie remarked from his spot just behind Buck’s seat.

“How did he get his head stuck in a pumpkin?” Toby asked, cutting a quick glance at Buck before returning his eyes to the road.

“We’re about to find out,” Buck answered just as they pulled up in front of the address.

They clambered out of the engine, meeting Hen and Chimney on the sidewalk. They fell into step behind Buck as he led the way to the front door, which was answered by a teenage girl in a wheelchair. She wore an air of annoyance around her as she expertly backed up and turned on a wheel.

“So your dad’s stuck in a pumpkin,” Buck said, though it came out more like a question.

“He thought it would be funny to do Pumpkin-Head for us,” she replied.

“Pumpkin-Head?” Buck looked over his shoulder to the others and got a bunch of blank stares in return.

“It’s a thing he used to do when we were little,” the girl explained as she led them through the house. “And it was funny then. Now it’s just… Cringe.”

“Feel that one,” Eddie muttered under his breath,

They found their patient in the combination kitchen-dining room-living room, another teenage girl trying to get the rather large pumpkin off his head. She was not very successful, the pumpkin slipping out of her grip and sending him falling backwards onto the floor, almost hitting the table that was clearly being used as a carving station before.

“Alright,” Chimney said. “Still a little funny.”

“Tough pumpkin,” Buck commented. He figured it would be too easy for it to just burst open when they arrived. “Okay, let’s get him up, guys.”

He and Chimney took Mr. Pumpkin-Head under the arms and hauled him to his feet. The man was unsteady for a moment, very clearly disoriented since he had no idea what was going on around him.

“Dad? The fire department’s here. This is Captain Diaz,” the second teenager said, voice raised to be heard through the gourd. The dad thrust his hand out to shake Buck’s as he said something too muffled to make out, except he was facing entirely the wrong way. Buck just stepped over into the spot the man thought he was at to take it. “His name’s Franklin. Oh! I’m Rachel.”

“Nice to meet you,” Buck said, raising his voice as well. There was a muffled response from inside the pumpkin. “Uh, how about… Eds, that chair.”

Eddie glanced about, spotted the dining chair that Buck was talking about, and dragged it over. They worked together to get Franklin seated without the man toppling falling back on his ass, which was not as easy as it sounded. Then Buck gave it his own go to unstick the pumpkin, since he was - not to brag - a bit stronger than Rachel looked to be.

But it refused to let go of the man’s head.

“That thing is stuck,” he said, more to himself than anything else. “Alright, let’s uh. Let’s make room for Hen and Chimney to work. Ravi, Toby, go get, uh. Lube, a saw. Maybe a pumpkin carving kit. Anything that’ll help get this off.”

“Got it, Cap,” Ravi said as the pair hurried back to the engine. 

Eddie and the others, meanwhile, picked the table up and carried it a couple feet away. Franklin was saying something, a lot of something, but it was muffled too much for Buck to make out. Neither could Chimney, going by the lost expression he was wearing when he came over. Rachel laughed at them a little.

“He says he doesn’t understand how he could get it on so easy one minute,” she translated.

“And barely get it past his ears the next,” her sister finished.

Maybe Buck should go get his hearing checked, because there was no way he could’ve made that out.

“Gourds can be very unpredictable,” Chimney told him, before kneeling down with a pulse oximeter. “Okay, sir, I’m gonna take your pulse while my friends check you out.”

Eddie was on Franklin’s other side with a blood pressure cuff while Hen was finishing getting her gloves on. Buck stepped back because he knew when to get out of the way and let the others handle it, and this was definitely one of those times. All three of them had been doing this, or something like it, for longer than he’d been EMT certified, after all.

Franklin was saying something again. And once again, it was too muffled to make out. They looked to the girls once more for clarity.

“He says since he and my mom got divorced, he never gets us on actual holidays,” Rachel translated again. Hen came over with a stethoscope to check his breathing, Eddie stepping aside to give her room. “Like Halloween.”

“He wanted to make us smile,” her sister told them, all quiet-like, as if she didn’t want her father to hear her.

“I get it, sir,” Chimney said as he kept his eyes fixed on the pulse ox reading. “My daughter’s finally old enough to actually be into trick-or-treating, instead of us just showing off how cute she is to everyone. And I’m missing it. It’s kinda killing me. Pulse is good.”

“Got the lube!” Ravi announced to the world at large as he and Toby came back in, waving the tubes of lube in the air. Buck had to remind himself that he was the captain and they were at a scene and he could not say the joke he just thought of, no matter how much he was dying to say it. Ravi and Toby also had the bag containing the rotary drill saw and, in what was clearly someone preparing for the worst, the suction unit.

“Thank you.” Buck took the tubes of lube from Ravi, tossing one to Eddie.

“This is gonna be a little chilly, sir,” Eddie warned Franklin as they started applying the lube, digging the tips of the tubes in between human skin and pumpkin flesh to make sure everything was well coated.

“We’re gonna try and pull it off again, okay?” Buck warned Franklin, tossing the lube aside and grabbing hold of the pumpkin. Opposite him, Eddie did the same. “On three.”

Buck counted it and they pulled. Immediately, there were muffled protests from within the pumpkin.

“Stop! Stop!” Rachel said. Buck and Eddie both froze. “He’s saying it hurts.”

“This is really fused on there,” Eddie said with a frown.

“Try lifting it again.” Chimney knelt down beside Franklin, peering intently where pumpkin met human. “Just a little.”

Buck shrugged at Eddie and did as the paramedic asked. There was a noise of interest from Chimney as the man’s irritated looking neck was revealed.

“Hen,” he called over. “Check this out.”

“Oh,” she said when she came over, in the tone that no one wanted a medical professional to use. “Looks like dermatitis. Is your dad allergic to pumpkins?”

The question was directed to the girls, both of them shook their heads.

“He’s been doing Pumpkin-Head since I was a baby,” Rachel said.

“Any idea how old these pumpkins are?” Chimney asked.

“He said he bought them last month.”

Oof. A month was a long time for a fruit off the vine.

(So many jokes, all doomed to wither on the vine in the name of professionalism.)

“Bet they’re starting to rot,” Chimney said, more to Hen than any of the rest of them. “The bacteria and mold is probably causing his face to blow up like a-”

“Pumpkin,” Eddie finished for him.

“This is anaphylaxis,” Hen concluded, already moving. “I’ll grab an epi from the med kit.”

The muffled sounds of coughing and distress, along with Franklin’s frantic gesturing, demanded their attention. Franklin tipped over while trying to grab at his throat, landing on the floor with his legs flailing.

“I think he aspirated pumpkin guts,” Chimney guessed while they crouched around the patient. Ravi and Toby were both already moving, the former grabbing the saw and the latter the suction unit, which he handed to Chimney.

“Okay, um.” Buck tapped his knuckles against the pumpkin, ignoring his crew’s stares as he listened for the hollow sound he was seeking that indicated space between the wall of the pumpkin and Franklin. “Ravi, here. Score it, then we’ll break it into chunks.”

“Got it, Cap.”

Ravi worked quickly, the spinning blade of the saw cutting deep into the pumpkin. Once he and Buck both had deemed it scored enough, the two of them and Eddie worked their fingers into the gouges. Tearing the pumpkin apart was actually rather easy, the three of them tossing aside the pieces until Franklin’s swollen face was uncovered. 

Chimney didn’t waste any time. As soon as he was able, he was shoving the tube down Franklin’s throat and suctioning out bits of pumpkin. After several anxious moments, the man was sitting up and spitting out pumpkin seeds. They helped him into the chair he’d fallen out of, where his daughters immediately clung to him.

“No more Pumpkin-Head,” Rachel told him. “Ever again.”

“I promise,” Franklin said.

“We should take you to the hospital and get you checked out,” Hen said, reluctant to break up their moment. “You girls are welcome to come with.”

They were both quick to agree.

“Alright, let’s get this cleaned up,” Buck said, gesturing at the bits of pumpkin that littered the floor. “And then get him ready to go.”

“Oh, hey, I want to thank you guys,” Franklin said. “I feel so dumb, nearly being killed by a pumpkin.”

“That’s fine,” Buck assured him. “Do this job long enough, you see people get hurt in much dumber ways.”

As if it had been planned, he stepped on a piece of pumpkin. He slid, legs going out from under him, and came down hard onto his left shoulder. He was left blinking up at Franklin’s ceiling as he caught his breath against the sudden, sharp agony.

“Exhibit A,” Ravi declared with a dramatic sweep of his hand.

Buck ignored him. The pain in his shoulder was familiar, the awkward feel of it was familiar. He grabbed his radio.

“Dispatch, we need another RA unit,” he said, before letting go of it to grip at his shoulder. Eddie appeared at his side, looking worried as he stood over him. “Pretty sure I just dislocated my shoulder.”

This was a curse. Buck had been cursed by the ghost of Billy Boils, there was no other explanation. Even if Eddie was of an entirely different mind.

There’d been a lot of time to waste while waiting for the ER doctor to see him. Eddie rode the engine to the station to grab the captain’s truck, so Buck was left to his own devices. Which meant he was free to call Athena, who tutted at him in concern before updating him on the real corpse prop.

Athena had managed to pull the bill of sale from the prop house. It turned out that they bought Billy Boils from a carnival, who got him from a novelty shop, who, in turn, got him from a rodeo. The novelty shop burned down in ‘93, the carnival was wiped out by a hurricane in ‘97, and the rodeo ended after a stampede. Buck didn’t have a year for that one. 

The point of the matter was, he was cursed.

“You’re not cursed,” Eddie told him as they pulled into the parking spot for the captain’s truck.

“I tore off Billy’s left arm, babe. Right out of its socket,” Buck argued. “And then my arm, my left arm, gets popped out of the socket? That is not a coincidence!”

“It is the definition of a coincidence,” his husband retorted. “It definitely isn’t a curse. Those things aren’t real.”

“Oh yeah? Then go inside, right now, and say the Q-word.”

“No,” Eddie was quick to say. He followed it up with a defensive sounding, “That’ll just make everyone else upset and they’ll get in their heads about it.”

“Uh-huh.” Buck unbuckled himself and then flung open the door. “Maybe I should ask Abuela’s friend to take care of it. She’s a witch, isn’t she?”

“Curandera,” Eddie immediately corrected. “And no, she isn’t. Because magic isn’t real, either. C’mon, get inside, mi sol. I’ll grab you an ice pack. And something to wash down the meds they gave you.”

Buck headed for the captain’s office, because he knew there was paperwork involved in a firefighter getting injured at a scene. He figured he could get that done while waiting for the pain meds to kick in, and it wasn’t something that would tax him too much. Hen was sitting behind his desk, though, looking surprised as her head popped up from the computer screen.

“Buck!” she exclaimed. “I didn’t know if you’d be coming back today.”

“Doc said I could do light work,” he explained. Technically speaking, the man had said he could do light work when he returned for his next shift. Whatever. Eddie had been too busy arguing against reality to remember that. “Figured that covered the incident report.”

“Nah, I already took care of it. Made sure it sounded as stupid as possible, too,” Hen teased. Then her expression turned serious. “Hey, so, I was wanting to talk to you about something.”

“What about?”

“I know this is probably the worst time for it,” she said. “But I was hoping to ask for a shift off. For Chimney.”

“For- What?”

“I heard him talking to the pumpkin guy, about missing out on Halloween with Jee, and-”

Buck turned around in the middle of her sentence and marched out of the office to bellow, at the top of his lungs,

“Chimney!”

Utter silence fell over the station, except for the sound of boots hitting the metal stairs and then running across the bay. Chimney came skidding to a stop in front of him.

“What’s up, Cap?” he asked, sounding both confused and worried.

Buck gestured at Hen, sitting stunned and wide-eyed at the desk still.

“I cannot have you both taking Halloween off,” he told them, the pain in his shoulder making him grumpy. “Figure out which one of you is gonna work it.”

Then he stomped away, before he snapped at either of them. Eddie, blessed man that he was, met him halfway with the ice pack, the glass of water, and the pain meds. If they weren’t on duty, and in the middle of the station where everyone could see them, he’d make out with the man right there. Even if he was being rude by not believing Buck about the curse of Billy Boils.

(Hen and Chimney ended up deciding that neither of them were taking Halloween off. Which, whatever. Easier on him that way.)

Chapter 13: The Billy Boils Blues

Chapter Summary

In which Buck absolutely insists he is suffering from a curse. Eddie is not convinced.

Abuela tutted and fretted over Buck when he and Eddie got home from their shift. Chris wasn’t much better, hovering over Buck when he realized he’d gotten hurt and demanding to know what happened. The sweetness of that was undercut, however, by the way Chris laughed upon learning that Buck had slipped on a piece of pumpkin.

“It’s like one of those old cartoons,” Chris stated, while Buck glowered and his husband made a poor effort to cover up his own snickering.

The teenager was also not very receptive to the idea of Buck being cursed, having apparently grown into his father’s skepticism. The two of them shook their heads in doubt and scoffed in unison while Buck told Abuela about it, who did listen with all the seriousness that the situation was owed. She also gave him double portions of food, because that was how she expressed her care and concern.

Sleeping arrangements were going to be awkward and potentially painful. Buck was going to need to sleep sitting up, which would have been easier done in the recliner in the living room. Except then Senorita would, inevitably, curl up on his shoulder and be flung across the house. The next obvious solution, of course, was to steal all of Eddie’s pillows.

“Is that enough?” Eddie asked as Buck sat back on the small mound without ever looking away from his laptop. “Or should I ransack Chris’ room?”

“No, no.” Buck shook his head. “It’s good, thanks.”

Eddie nodded, which Buck only saw out of the corner of his eyes, and padded around the bed and out of the room. He returned a short time later with a fresh ice pack that Buck gratefully took from him to press against his shoulder.

“I don’t care how tired you are in the morning,” Eddie said as he slipped under the covers beside him, after turning off the bedside lamps. “I’m dragging you out of bed to take your meds.”

“Okay, Dad,” Buck mocked, wagging his head as he did. Eddie flicked him on the ear. “His name was William James McCurdy.”

“Who? Wait.” Eddie leaned over to look at the screen. “You’re reading about Billy Boils. Of course you are.”

“I found a Substack, it has all these articles about him and the Old West.”

Eddie let out an insincere sounding “yay” and then there was the sound of a drawer opening up. Buck glanced over to see his husband tugging out the sleep mask that he’d bought him early on in their relationship, after one too many nights where he kept Eddie awake with the light from his phone screen. It had “Fuck Off” written across it in white stitched lettering.

“He was a gunslinger and a bank robber,” Buck told Eddie. “His skin was covered in boils, hence…”

“Oh, cool, everyone’s been calling him by an old-timey schoolyard insult.”

“By all accounts, he was not a man to be crossed.”

“Ominous.” Eddie leaned in to kiss Buck, forcing him to turn away from the screen long enough for it. Then he pulled the sleep mask over his eyes and settled onto his lone pillow. “I was serious, mi sol. Try not to stay up too late.”

“Yeah, yeah.” Buck flapped a hand at him. “Wanna hear how he was finally caught?”

“You’re gonna tell me either way,” Eddie stated, because he knew how this worked.

“His own posse hogtied him, turned him in to the sheriff for the reward. But Billy had his revenge! All six of ‘em died sudden, horrible deaths.”

“Did anyone in the Old West die pleasant deaths?” Eddie asked. It was a rhetorical question, Buck could tell.

“He was a man not to be crossed.”

“So you said.”

“And I crossed him.”

“You’re not cursed,” Eddie said, rolling over onto his side. “G’night, Buck.”

Buck wasn’t certain when he fell asleep, he’d learned to avoid the shame of that knowledge long ago by not looking at the clock. He knew he hadn’t been sleeping for very long when he was torn out of sleep by the sound of his husband’s screaming. He woke up flailing and twisting in his sheets, thankful that the laptop had been moved out of his lap at some point.

“What!?” Buck asked, frantic. “Eddie, what’s wrong?”

“Um.” Eddie was standing by Buck’s side of the bed, fist pressed against his mouth. “You’ve got a little something on your face…”

Buck threw off the sheets and leapt to his feet to run to their en suite. He hurriedly smacked the light switch on, coming to a stop in front of the mirror. Somehow, seeing his face covered in boils in the reflection was not a surprise.

“It’s not that bad,” Eddie told him a little while later, after they’d moved to the dining room. 

Eddie had grabbed the first aid kit and was now swabbing ointment onto the boils while Buck sat on a stool at the breakfast bar. Abuela was cooking, diligently keeping her back to the sight of him as she scrambled some eggs. She had cringed the first time she laid eyes on him, before crossing herself. Hoover had let out a single bark before running to hide in Gavin’s room.

“You woke me up by screaming,” Buck pointed out. “I told you that Billy Boils wasn’t done with me.”

“Please,” Eddie sighed as he tossed the q-tip into the kitchen trash can, along with the nitrile gloves he’d pulled on. “Don’t start with the stupid curse again.”

“Billy Boils. Hello?” Buck pointed at his boil-covered face. “What are the odds that after I defile his corpse, I wake up and I’ve broken out in the exact same skin condition he suffered from!?”

“I’m guessing it’s probably just an allergic reaction of some kind.”

“To what? Bad juju?”

“We just had a call where a guy got a rash from rotten pumpkin guts,” Eddie reminded him. “That you fell into, as I recall.”

Laughter accompanied the sound of crutches tapping against the floor. Buck turned to glare at Chris, who didn’t even look apologetic.

“It’s still funny,” the teenage brat said.

“If it was the pumpkin, it would have happened right away,” Buck said, turning back to Eddie. “Not the next day.”

“Listen, boils can be caused by- by- by an infection,” Eddie told him, rolling his hand in the air. “You probably got something on you from the pumpkin or the dad, or from the hospital, and you’ve stressed yourself out so much with this stupid curse business that you managed to mess up your immune system.”

Buck opened his mouth for a retort, but a finger being jabbed into one of his boils made him yelp and jump, nearly falling off his seat. 

“Christopher,” Eddie scolded, rubbing at his eyes. “Please don’t poke your pops’ boils.”

“But they’re so gross.” Chris sounded far too delighted about that.

“Oh.” Buck scowled at them both as he dodged his son’s finger. “So I’m gross.”

“Yeah!”

“You’re not gross,” Eddie insisted.

“Oh yeah? Then kiss me,” Buck said. His husband flinched back, cringing. “What’s wrong, babe? You said I’m not gross, so pucker up and kiss me.”

“Yeah, Dad!” Chris urged. “Kiss him! Sha-la-la-la-la, kiss the-”

“Go wash your hands,” Eddie snapped at him. “And get ready for school.”

“No. I wanna see you kiss him.”

“You never want to see us kiss,” Eddie said, rolling his eyes. He did, however, lean in to peck a quick kiss on Buck’s lip. He kept his eyes closed the entire time, too. “There, happy?”

“No,” Buck complained. “That was barely a kiss. I took you to see the Dodgers at the World Series, I deserve more than that.”

“Listen, mi sol.” Eddie gripped him by the shoulders. Buck couldn’t help but note that the way he did it meant he neatly avoided coming anywhere near to touching Buck’s face with his bare skin. “This curse talk is spinning you out, which is not good for you.”

“Don’t worry, Buckito,” Abuela said. Buck turned on the stool to see that she’d turned off the burners and was plating the eggs and bacon that she’d been fixing. “I’ll call Rosario, she can come over and take a look.”

“Oh, madre de dios,” Eddie grumbled and threw up his hands.

“Do you think she can help?” Buck asked, ignoring his husband’s dramatics.

“She will certainly try,” Abuela said.

“One comment about payment or donations.” Eddie went around to grab the plates and carry them to the dining table. “Just one, and I am throwing her out of this house. I don’t care how old she is.”
