“Yeah, yeah, whatever.” Buck flapped a hand at him as he focused on Abuela. “How soon can she get here?”

Rosario arrived shortly after lunch. Buck didn’t have an exact image of what he expected her to look like, yet he was still surprised. She was a few years younger than Abuela, closer to Pepa’s age, and arrived in a flowery blouse and pink sweatpants with her graying hair up in a ponytail. She had a large canvas tote bag hanging from her shoulder, similar to the ones that Buck and Eddie used for grocery shopping.

Eddie was the one who answered the door, rolling his eyes at her behind her back when she came in. Abuela smacked him for it, already chattering to her friend in quick bursts of Spanish. Buck stood up from the dining table, where he’d been helping Gavin color, when the three of them came over.

“Ah,” was all the woman said when she saw Buck’s face, and then started unpacking her bag. 

The boils had increased in size since that morning. Buck was just thankful that Gavin had been more confused than anything else, and then easily distracted from trying to touch them. The boils hurt, but the pain meds for his shoulder helped with that just as well.

“Isabel told me you thought you were cursed,” Rosario said.

“Can you help?” Buck asked, all too aware that he sounded pathetic. Eddie rolled his eyes, again, and Buck threw him the finger when neither Rosario nor Abuela were looking.

“I will try,” the curandera said. “Take off your shirt.”

“Um. Why?”

“For this,” she answered, holding up a tiny tupperware with a single egg inside of it.

Buck refused to even look Eddie’s way, because he knew his husband would be the picture of “I told you so.” He was never going to live this down.

It was one of the oddest things Buck had ever experienced. Rosario rolled the egg all over his body, from the top of his head to his armpits and even all the way down to the soles of his feet. Even Eddie was weirded out by it, and he was just watching. And then, after she was done, she cracked the egg into a glass of water that she had Abuela fill up and bring to her. Several minutes were spent in silence as she examined the egg yolk sinking into the water, trailing whitish tendrils like a jellyfish taking a nosedive.

Whatever Rosario saw, or read, or intuited from the egg, she didn’t share with Buck. She just nodded decisively and then opened more containers, these holding sprigs of what looked like parsley and freshly cut flower blooms. Buck was stuck awkwardly standing there once more as she rubbed at his skin with both, before marching him out onto the back patio so she didn’t set off the smoke detectors as she burned first a bundle of white sage and then something that reminded Buck of the evergreen tree they bought for Christmas last year. She circled around him with both, fanning the smoke with a white feather and chanting prayers in Spanish.

“So is that it?” Buck asked after they’d gone back inside, Rosario packing everything away. “Is the curse gone?”

“It should be,” she told him. She lit up when Abuela approached her with a tupperware from the fridge, the see-through lid showing that it contained leftover tamales from last night. “Oh, Isabel, thank you.”

Eddie gave the interaction a narrow-eyed glare, arms crossed over his chest, before settling back on his heels with a nod.

“Now, you.” Rosario pointed at Buck. “Apply a warm compress to the boils several times a day, ten minutes at a time. And wash your hands and face.”

“Is- Is there anything I should wash them with? Specifically?” Buck asked her.

“Warm water and soap. You should also wash your pillowcase, your sheets, towels, anything that’s touched your face, to keep it from spreading.”

“The curse?”

“What? No.” Rosario gave him a weird look. “To keep the germs from spreading. You have boils.”

“...oh.”

“And make an actual doctor’s appointment,” she told him as she shouldered her tote bag again. “That infection looks severe.”

Oh.

“Are you done yet?” Ravi called, looking up from his phone. He was perched on the edge of their kitchen counter, kicking his heels against the cabinet doors.

“Just about!” Albert shouted back from the bathroom.

They were getting ready to go out to a Halloween party that Crawford from B-shift had invited them to. It was being thrown by a bunch of first responders that had to work on the actual holiday, like the two of them were having to do. Ravi was already dressed in the lion tamer outfit he’d worn to the Firehouse Haunt Fest, complete with top hat and whip.

At the moment, to waste time, Ravi was bouncing between playing games on his phone and bothering everyone else in the various group chats. One of them erupted into several all-caps messages from Eddie. It didn’t take long to figure out why that was.

“Oh, hey, the Dodgers won the World Series.”

“Sweet!” Albert cheered, and then stepped out where Ravi could see him. “How do I look?”

He, unlike Ravi, was not wearing what he wore to the Haunt Fest. Not exactly, anyway. It was still cat-themed, though it would be pushing the lines of kid friendly. He was wearing a leopard print waistcoat without a shirt, which meant Ravi happily got to eye up his boyfriend’s bare arms and the bits of chest that were uncovered. To go with it, Albert also had a pair of cat ears sitting on his head, a tail clipped to the back of his pants, and fingerless gloves that looked like paws.

“Like it would be worth it to be late. Or miss it entirely,” Ravi told him, shoving off the counter. “I like the whiskers, Alley Cat.”

“Thank you.” Albert beamed at him, the painted on whiskers moving with the smile. He’d also painted his nose black. “But I do not want to miss this, so c’mon.”

“Fine, fine.” Ravi grabbed his keys and wallet, tossing Albert his. “Crawford would probably bitch at us if we skipped out on the party to have sex, anyway.”

“I mean, it isn’t like we can stay out too late anyway,” Albert reminded him. “Sex can still be on the menu. Later.”

“That is a very good point.” Ravi grabbed his tail and used it to pull him closer for a kiss, being careful not to smudge the facepaint. “You are very smart.”

“Thank you.”

“What kind of cat are you supposed to be, anyway?”

“Uh.” Albert glanced down at himself and shrugged. “A good looking one.”

Fair enough.

Chapter 14: All Hallows'

Chapter Summary

In which this year's Halloween is more about the tricks than the treats.

Chapter Notes

This chapter was not meant to be this long!?!?

See the end of the chapter for more notes

The boils did not magically clear up by the time they had to go to work the next morning. Everyone’s reactions upon seeing Buck at the start of their Halloween shift were pretty much all the same: flinching and shouting and general horror. Captain Mayfair was the most understated, but even she cringed away from him the entire time they did the handover briefing.

Chimney, when he and the others got up to the loft, greeted him by shouting, “Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown!” at the top of his lungs.

“What happened to your face?” Ravi asked. He and Albert were looking particularly zombie-like that morning as they zeroed in on the coffee. Buck wasn’t certain if Albert was even awake, with the way he was using his boyfriend for support.

“Don’t get him started,” Eddie told them. And even though Buck wasn’t facing his way, he knew the man was rolling his eyes. “He thinks he’s cursed.”

“I tore the arm off Billy Boils’ corpse and then ended up with a dislocated shoulder and boils , Eddie!” Buck retorted. “What would you call it!?”

“The man raises a good point,” Chimney said. Eddie did not sound like he appreciated the sentiment.

“And besides, I’m not cursed anymore,” Buck assured them, “‘Buela’s friend took care of it.”

“I’m almost curious enough to ask for more, but I know better than that,” Hen told him. “Please tell me you’ve got an appointment with an actual doctor.”

“Tomorrow.”

“Good.”

“Maybe you should uh, stay back today, Cap,” Chimney said. He’d gotten far too close for Buck’s comfort and was peering up at the boils. “Don’t want to traumatize any more kids.”

“Chris complimented me this morning on my Halloween mask,” Buck told him, and then smacked his husband when the asshole laughed. “Eds!”

“I’m sorry.” Eddie did not sound the least bit sorry. “My kid’s funny.”

“Maybe those two should stay back,” Hen commented, gesturing at Ravi and Albert. The pair of them had collapsed into stools at the kitchen island, clutching mugs of coffee and looking mere moments away from pouring out onto the floor. “Apparently their couples’ costume this year is Night of the Living Dead.”

“What happened to the two of you?” Eddie asked them, raising his voice.

“Halloween party,” Albert groaned. His head fell forward to hit the island with a thud. Ravi kindly lifted it back up for him. “There was a punch bowl of something with gummy worms at the bottom.”

“He ate three of them,” Ravi added.

“Albert, Albert.” Eddie tutted. “You never eat the worm.”

“And then Crawford pulled out some green stuff,” Albert said. “The bottle was like, a skull? I don’t know. I think I had a couple shots of that. Maybe? It’s kinda fuzzy.”

“Green stuff in a skull. That sounds like- Oh, my God.” Buck stared at Albert. “That sounds like absinthe. Was Crawford trying to kill you!?”

Albert, in lieu of answering, just fell forward again with a groan.

Luckily for their youngest paramedic, the daylight hours of Halloween were rather calm. Kids were at school, adults were working, and everyone knew the holiday didn’t actually start until the evening, anyways. It meant that Albert and Ravi had time to revive themselves from the dead before the chaos really hit. And there would be chaos, there always was.

Everyone was visibly bracing themselves as the clock ticked closer and closer to the end of nautical twilight and for night to officially fall over the city. Buck had them make sure the trucks and ambulances were well-stocked, that they had everything they might need for whatever stupidity they’d be forced to deal with. He didn’t know if that stupidity would take the form of alcohol poisoning or bad falls or drunk drivers, and figured it was better to be prepared for all of it.

Then there was nothing to do but wait for it to hit, which Buck chose to do by claiming one of the chairs in the loft’s den area. Hen was on one of the coaches, talking to Denny over video as the Wilsons (and Jee-Yun) got ready to go out.

“Remember, it’s Halloween,” she was saying. “All the weirdos come out on Halloween. If you see a pack of teenagers without adults, or adults without children, head the other way.”

“It’s trick-or-treating,” Denny said. “Not the Purge.”

“Just keep your guard up, okay? You’re the big brother, so you have to help your mom look after the girls. And share your candy.”

“I will, Mama.”

“Speaking of the girls,” Chimney said, coming around to lean over Hen’s shoulder. “Where’s Jee-Yun?”

“You mean Toto?” Buck heard Mara say, followed by Denny trying to call Jee over. When the little girl refused, bluntly saying “no” to seeing her father, he had to cover up his snort of laughter with a cough.

“Sorry,” Denny said. Jee-Yun was barking in the background; they were all going as Wizard of Oz characters. “She’s busy.”

“Yeah, I can see that,” Chimney replied.

“Hey, Denny.” Karen sounded farther away from the phone than even Jee had, her voice raised to be heard. “Tell your mom we need to go.”

“Let me say hi before you do,” Hen said, and Denny passed on the message. A short moment later, Karen was saying,

“Hi.”

It was so short, so blunt, that Hen physically recoiled from her phone. It was also apparently the end of the call, because she dropped her phone into her lap with a despairing sigh.

“Is, uh. Is everything okay?” Buck asked.

“Yeah. Karen’s just unhappy that I’m missing Halloween with Mara to work.”

“Oh,” he said, and then he shrugged. “She’ll get over it.”

The Wilsons had been a unit since long before Buck came to LA. He knew that it was Chimney who introduced them, which meant that Hen had been a firefighter-paramedic the entire time Hen and Karen were together, the entire time they had Denny. That was a lot of Halloweens - and Valentine’s Days and Thanksgivings and Christmases and birthdays - that Hen had to work, because they couldn’t manage to get every single one of those off every single year.

Besides, they had Christmas off this year, and Buck was fairly certain that Karen would find that day far more important.

“You wanna see Gavin’s costume?” he asked, already digging out his phone.

“Duh.” Hen scooted over on the couch to make room for him. “But don’t sit too close.”

Buck rolled his eyes, sighed, and went over to show off his kid.

“He’s gotten so big,” Amy said.

“He has,” Bobby agreed.

Ahead of them on the sidewalk, Gavin and Chris were walking together. The little toddler was dressed as a firefighter, complete with plastic helmet and reflective hi-vis stripes, and was clutching at Chris’ crutch with one tiny hand and had a plastic pumpkin-shaped bucket dangling from the other. The teenager was not wearing a costume, and hadn’t bothered to do so for a couple Halloweens now.

Technically speaking, Chris was the one taking Gavin trick-or-treating. He had been very, very clear about that. Bobby was just there to supervise. Amy’s presence was unexpected, but it wasn’t unwelcomed. Chris was no longer quite so distrustful of the young woman, content now that his little brother’s biological mother had no interest in taking the tot away from them.

“I figured you would have other plans tonight,” Bobby commented. “I know May’s at some party.”

He was fully expecting to be woken up at some ungodly hour to go pick her up. Not that he minded, not truly. It was much better than any alternatives, and he was glad that she knew she could rely on him for that.

“Yeah, she invited me, but…” Amy shrugged and brushed strands of bright blue hair out of her face. “I just wasn’t feeling up to it.”

“This is probably more fun, anyway,” he said, and smiled when she laughed.

Ahead of them, Chris and Gavin turned to walk up to the next house that had its porch light on. Bobby and Amy paused on the sidewalk to watch them make their slow way to the porch and climb up the small set of steps. It was Chris who rang the doorbell while Gavin bounced in place. A woman in a witch’s hat opened it and immediately started cooing. Bobby couldn’t blame her, his phone had no less than thirty pictures, now, of Gavin in his costume. Plus a few dozen of him with Chris, taken from behind, as they trotted down the sidewalk together.

“Tricker treat!” the tot shouted at the top of his lungs, thrusting his bucket up. The first couple of houses, Gavin had been very unsure of it, needing Chris to gently urge him into saying the words. That was very much a thing of the past now, though.

“How’s school?” Bobby asked Amy while they watched Gavin’s bowl get filled even further. Chris made him say thank you before they turned around and made their way back down the porch steps. “Any idea what you want to major in, yet?”

The last time they’d talked about it, Amy hadn’t been certain. Everyone had assured her that she didn’t have to decide just yet, and that she could just get the required general education courses out of the way while she figured it out. But that was several Sunday dinners ago.

“Yeah, actually. I talked to May about it, and my advisor.” Amy smiled down at Gavin as he and Chris passed them by, reaching down to straighten out his firefighter helmet. “I think that I want to be a social worker.”

Bobby made an effort to not react to that, beyond simply nodding. He could guess, based on Amy’s history, why she would be drawn to that sort of career. But he certainly wasn’t going to say those thoughts out loud.

“The world definitely needs more of them,” was what he said instead.

The next house was across the street, and Bobby got to watch as Chris made sure Gavin looked both ways - left, right, left again, just like in that silly video Buck and Eddie did - before they crossed. Gavin was once again clutching to Chris’ crutch, as he had been all night. They made a couple more stops, with Gavin belting out “Tricker treat!” at the top of his lungs each time, before making it back to Buck and Eddie’s.

The smell of smoke the moment they stepped inside made Bobby’s adrenaline start pumping.

“Isabel!?” he called out. “Carla!?”

“In here!” Carla was in the kitchen, waving a towel at an open window. Isabel was muttering in spanish over a burnt casserole dish. “Dinner’s gonna be a bit delayed.”

“What happened?” Bobby asked, patting an uncertain looking Chris on the shoulder before heading into the kitchen to make sure everything was fine. Amy was already helping Gavin go through his candy at the coffee table, to make sure there wasn’t anything harmful.

“Oh, nothing bad,” was Carla’s cheerful answer. “We got a bit distracted outside with Hoover and the food was left in the oven for too long, that’s all.”

There was an odd note to Carla’s tone, an edge to her friendly smile. But Bobby wasn’t sure what to make of it, and he didn’t want to press her about it now. Not with the boys just in the other room.

“I hope the fact that the smoke detectors aren’t screaming is because you turned them off,” he said, looking for the one that hung up on the kitchen wall. “And not because I need to yell at Buck and Eddie.”

“I took out the batteries,” Carla said, pointing to where it sat on the counter. “There was too much smoke, so it kept going off.”

“I’ll put it back up when it’s cleared a bit more,” Bobby assured her. “How about I order something?”

“Pizza, please!” Chris immediately shouted from the living room. Gavin echoed him, crying out “Pizza! Pizza!” repeatedly.

“Pretty sure you have to, now,” Carla teased.

“Seems it,” Bobby agreed as he pulled out his phone. “Everyone okay with pineapples and anchovies?”

Chris just about tripped over himself in his rush to stop him.

By the time they’d gotten sent to put out a literal flaming bag of shit left on someone’s porch, Buck was officially done with the day. There were so many minor nuisance calls that he had to divide and conquer, which meant that it was only Toby and Eddie responding to this call; Hen and Ravi were dealing with a supposed candy thief suffering from anaphylaxis, while Chimney and Albert were dealing with a case of alcohol poisoning at a college party. That last one was neither minor nor a nuisance, which was why Buck sent two paramedics, but still.

“I am so sick of it,” the homeowner was complaining to Buck while they watched Eddie and Toby spray at the porch with fire extinguishers. It didn’t take long and they came over to awkwardly stand there, not interrupting the man’s spiel. “I’m a vice principal at Valley High and they pull this prank crap every year, with the eggings and the toilet paper. It’s too much.”

“We're good to go, capitán,” Eddie said, when there was a gap in the man’s ranting. He gave a thumbs up and everything.

“Awesome, let’s head out, then,” Buck said, already turning to leave. “Have a happy Halloween, sir.”

“Happy Halloween,” he heard Eddie say, followed by the homeowner’s frustrated,

“Well, who’s gonna stop these clowns from doing it again!?”

“Not our circus, sir!” Buck told him without even bothering to turn around.

“That guy was pissed,” Eddie commented when they were far enough away from the house.

“He was such a delight.” Toby’s words were laden with sarcasm. “I don’t know why anyone would- Gah!’

A man made-up like a realistic zombie jumped out from behind a bush at them. Toby leaped in the air and almost swung the extinguisher in his hand like a bludgeon before he caught himself. Buck and Eddie laughed at Toby’s reaction as the three of them continued on to the fire engine, leaving the zombie to wordlessly grunt and groan and then go back to his hiding place. They took their time putting the extinguishers away, wanting to catch the next person’s reaction to being jumpscared.

“Bet you his next victim doesn’t scream like a baby,” Eddie said, as they watched the unsuspecting group coming down the sidewalk.

And indeed, despite being dressed like an oversized infant, the next guy did not scream like a baby. Instead, when the zombie jumped out to scream at them, the big baby immediately punched him in the face, laying him flat out on the ground.

After making sure the zombie wasn’t concussed, they went back to the station and regrouped with the others. They had just enough time to restock on supplies before they were being sent out again. This time, it was something much more severe than the simple nuisance calls, and so they all went.

According to dispatch, a pair of girls were being chased in their car by a Mr. Pearson, who was actively trying to run them off the road. Dispatch heard them scream, then a crash, and then the call cut off. Those were not details that made for a pleasant situation, so Buck was preparing himself and the crew for the possible worst as they arrived in a cul-de-sac that might’ve been quite peaceful at any other time.

A pair of terrified teen girls ran up to wave them down when they hopped out.

“Hey, hey! We’re the ones who were on with nine-one-one,” one of the girls said.

Buck made a mental note to tell Maddie or Josh that they were both (relatively) okay, to pass on to whoever had been on the line with them.

“Tell us what happened,” he said as the group kept moving to the crash scene.

“We egged this guy’s house and we tried to drive away.” The girl was shaking as she spoke. “He chased us for several blocks.”

“He’s still in there,” the other girl said. “People tried to help get him out, but I think the door’s jammed.”

“Did he hit anyone?” Buck asked.

“Yeah, a trick-or-treater.” Shit. “He’s pinned against the car.”

“Someone check these ladies over,” Buck called. “Eds, you’re with me to get the driver. Hen, Chim, Albert, you’re on the kid. Everyone else, shore up the porch roof! Make sure it doesn’t come down on our heads.”

If only it were so easy.

Buck began to realize things were terribly wrong when Chimney suddenly shouted for Hen. Then Hen said Karen’s name. Buck picked up his pace to the car, which had run through a white picket fence, through a porch, and into the side of the house. He spotted Karen in her lion costume first, standing by the hood of the car.

And then he saw Denny, stuck between the car and the house.

“I tried,” Karen was saying as Hen sprinted past her to their son. “I couldn’t…”

Hen could not, absolutely could not be here for this, Buck knew. If he had known ahead of time, he would’ve kept her back at the station. But they were here now, she was here now, and there was no way that Hen was going to be standing on the sidelines, Buck knew her better than that. He also knew that they didn’t have the time to waste, trying to make her.

“Hen.” Buck tried to get her attention. Difficult to do with her so focused on her son. “Hen!”

“What!?” she snarled at him, like she was the lion.

“You’re on his vitals.” There was no way that Buck was going to get Hen to leave Denny’s side, not without a fight. The next best option was to give her something to do.

Hen stared at him for a moment and then frantically nodded, turning to Albert to bark out,

“Get me the Lifepak!”

“Is Mara okay?” Denny asked. He was awake, he was aware, those were all good things.

“She’s fine,” Chimney answered. “She’s with Jonesy, she’s okay.”

“I shoved her really hard. I didn’t mean to shove her so hard.”

“He pushed her clear,” Karen explained. “He saved her life.”

“Buck, no pulse. Driver’s gone.” Eddie had shattered the driver’s window while Buck was busy with Hen and everything else. “Isn’t this the guy from the flaming bag call?”

Buck leaned down to see for himself. It was indeed the vice principal from before. There was a massive bloody gash to his temple, presumably from him hitting his head against the steering wheel.

“Yeah. Go get a sheet for him,” Buck told Eddie. “And then go help with the roof.”

His husband’s answer came in the form of a nod before he was jogging off, passing Albert as the paramedic came back with the Lifepak. He passed it off to Hen, who hurriedly set it up.

“It hurts,” Denny cried. “Mama, my leg hurts.”

Good. Well, it was bad, but it was also good. Denny’s leg hurting meant that Denny could feel his leg, which ruled out some of the more severe possibilities they could’ve been dealing with here.

“Chim, start a line,” Buck ordered, before Hen had the chance to even think of doing anything more than what she was doing at that moment.

Chimney glanced between the two of them. Then he nodded and dove into his medical bag.

“Got it, Cap,” he said, slapping the supplies onto the hood of the car. “Starting with two mils of morphine. Al, get to the other side and check his leg’s circulation.”

Buck stepped away to let Albert through when he came around the car, giving him room to work. Eddie came back with a sheet for the driver and Buck threw it over him, before both he and Eddie went to check on the progress of the scaffolding being built to hold the porch roof, since the car had taken out several of its support beams and it was threatening to fall on top of the Denny and the paramedics.

If they removed the car before that support was in place, there was the risk of it collapsing down on them almost immediately.

There wasn’t much time given to Buck to oversee the hurried construction, though. Hen was soon calling for him, the Lifepak making concerning noises.

“What is it?”

“We’ve got to get this thing off him!” she said.

“We’re working on it, Hen,” Buck told her, and then pointed at the porch roof. “But we gotta make sure that doesn’t fall on him when we do.”

Hen glanced up and glared at the roof, like she was taking personal offense to it, before turning back to her son.

“How do you feel now?” she asked him. “Is the medication working?”

“Yeah, it doesn’t hurt anymore,” Denny answered. He had an IV running into the back of his hand. “Now I’m just cold.”

“Okay, wiggle your arms and legs for us,” Chimney said. “Can you do that, D?”

Buck wasn’t at any angle to see Denny’s limbs. But he saw Albert give a thumbs up from his side of the car, and he saw Chimney nod.

“That’s good news,” Hen said, and turned to Karen. “It’s not a spinal injury.”

The structure of the house creaked and cracked. Buck’s attention was stolen from Denny, who was groaning in pain as what he was pinned against shifted, and directed to Eddie. His husband looked up from what he was doing and shook his head.

“We’re going as fast as we can!” Eddie said.

“His stomach is warm. He’s bleeding internally!” Hen’s words had Buck spinning back around, just in time for her to shout to him that, “He’s in shock! Cap, we need blood!”

“Go faster!” Buck told Eddie and the others, and then grabbed for his radio. “Dispatch, we need whole blood on scene. Now.”

“I’ll have an RA unit there in fifteen minutes,” Maddie replied.

“That’s not soon enough, Mads,” Buck replied, but knew there wasn’t much else she could do. There was something he could do, though; he joined the others, picking up a piece of lumber and carrying it to its place, before grabbing a spare drill and some nails.

He focused on putting together the shoring, ignoring the commotion going on around Denny. There was nothing that Buck could do to help there, and he knew that. His attention and energy was better spent here, where he could do more than simply observe and be in the way.

“Cap!” Hen’s cry was distraught. Buck looked up from drilling to see that Denny was slumped over the hood. “How long before the blood lands!?”

“Dispatch said fifteen!” he shouted back, already refocusing on his task. It wasn’t what she wanted to hear, it hadn’t been what he wanted to hear, but it was the reality they were dealing with.

Moments later, Chimney was calling Eddie over. Buck didn’t even look his way before jerking his head in their direction, giving him the all-clear to go. They had the wooden support put together by that point, and they hefted it up and carried it to the porch and the car. Buck stepped back as Ravi and Clarke ran to get the jacks, and saw that Eddie was helping hook up a line from Karen to Denny.

They were doing a field transfusion, which explained why they called for the army medic.

Buck ignored that, though, just as he ignored the screeching of the Lifepak and the Wilsons’ increasing franticness. He focused, instead, on helping hold up the wooden shoring as the jacks got put into place. And then when he deemed the porch roof suitably supported, he sent Toby to get the winch hooked up. He focused on that instead, too, and he focused on eying the porch roof with held breath as they pulled the car out.

Denny was awake and aware again when they got him onto the awaiting gurney. They got him into the ambulance, Hen and Karen climbing in after. The doors slammed shut and they drove off.

And Buck and the others were left with the clean-up.

They could not immediately go to the hospital to sit vigil with Hen and Karen, however much they wanted to. They still had the rest of their shift to get through, an entire night full of strangers that could, at any moment, need their help. So they were stuck pacing the loft or the bay or the bunks or the captain’s office, wherever they happened to be, while checking and rechecking their phones for any news.

For once, Buck was thankful for Bobby’s sudden decision to retire back in the spring. Since the man wasn’t working, he was able to go to the hospital and keep them updated. Not that there was much to update them on, other than repeatedly telling them that Denny was still in surgery whenever someone - usually Buck or Chimney - bothered him for something new.

They didn’t receive more than that until after their shift had ended and they had descended upon the waiting room en masse. It was good news, thankfully, and came with the request that they stuck around to sign Denny’s new cast. Not that Buck and Eddie could stick around for very long; Buck’s appointment to take care of the boils was made for soon after they got off work, and it was at another hospital.

Buck was in decidedly better spirits when they finally did get home, even though his face was dotted with patches that covered up where the boils had been. Chris was already at school, but that was expected. What wasn’t expected was the way that Carla anxiously greeted them. It set Buck’s nerves on edge, and he knew it was doing the same to Eddie. Especially with the way that she lingered longer than she normally would have after they got home. But she didn’t say anything, not until Abuela took Hoover outside.

“Okay.” The word left Carla’s mouth like a sigh as she checked to make sure the back door was closed. Then she gestured for them to follow her down the hall, to Gavin’s room. The tot was wearing his plastic firefighter helmet and playing with the toy fire engine Bobby got him last year.

“What’s going on?” Eddie asked. “Is everything okay?”

“I’m sure everything’s fine,” she answered, but she didn’t sound like she believed it. “But I need to talk to you about something that happened last night.”

Buck felt his stomach squirm and tried to rationalize himself into calming down. Gavin was okay, Chris was okay - if he wasn’t, Carla would’ve told them first thing - and Abuela was okay. Hoover had greeted them as soon as they got home, and Senorita batted at them on their way past.

“Last night,” Carla said, “the dinner that Isabel was going to make kind of… Didn’t happen.”

“Okay…” Buck’s confusion was shared with Eddie.

“Everything was going fine, until Isabel stuck it into the oven,” she continued. “I didn’t even know that she had, I’d taken Hoover out. Then Isabel joined me and… And I guess she forgot about the oven. Not until the smoke detectors started screaming. I almost called you guys before I realized what was going on.”

“So she let dinner get burnt.” Eddie was frowning at the nurse. “That happens. I’ve done that.”

“If it was just forgetting about the oven,” Carla said. “If it was just the one thing, but…”

“I found one of the wooden spoons in the fridge the other day,” Buck whispered, dread uncoiling in his stomach.

“She couldn’t find the house phone this morning,” Carla told them. Her tone was resigned. “It was in the spice cabinet.”

“What are you saying?” Eddie asked, the words tight with tension.

“That I think it might be a good idea to make a doctor’s appointment for her,” the nurse said, the words crushing with how gentle they were. “Sooner than her regular check-up.”

“Why!?”

Buck sighed and prepared himself to break his husband’s heart, reaching over to take Eddie’s hand in his own.

“Because, baby,” he said. “She thinks ‘Buela might have Alzheimers.”

Chapter End Notes

😊😊😊😊😊

Chapter 15: Burdens

Chapter Summary

In which a reported abduction isn't what it seems, Eddie's feeling lost, and Buck worries.

Abduction cases are never pleasant to be called to, especially abduction cases that turned into hostage situations. In this instance, dispatch reported that an elderly woman had been taken. Currently, both the suspect and the victim were on the roof of the building that the 118 was pulling up to. Maddie informed them over the radio that Athena was already on site, having been in pursuit. Their job was to make sure that, if things took a turn for the worse, there wasn’t going to be a messy end.

When he got out of the engine, Buck could see someone close to the ledge of the building’s roof. Just the one person, and they didn’t look very elderly to him.

“Deploy the airbag there,” he ordered, pointing at the pavement just below the figure. The others were already scrambling to get everything out that they would need, but he got a few nods and a couple “got it, Cap”s.

“I only see the one,” Eddie commented, peering up at the building’s roof. “Is that the hostage or…?”

“I don’t know. Go help with the- Um.” Buck cut himself off as one of the lookie-loos that was hanging about suddenly joined them. Eddie took one look at the guy, shrugged at Buck, and left to help deploy the airbag. “Sir, you can’t be here.”

“My wife took my mother up there,” the guy said, gesticulating wildly.

“Your… Your wife?”

“She just sent me these.” The guy pulled his phone out of his pocket, messed with the screen a bit, and held it out. “I think it’s a threat.”

Buck took the phone from him, unsure what he was expecting. Text message ransom notes, a picture of an old woman holding that day's newspaper, something. What he wasn’t expecting was to see a photo of a vase. A fancy vase, but a vase nonetheless.

“I’m confused,” Buck told him. “What is this?”

“My mother!” the guy exclaimed. Buck glanced back at the vase on the screen. “I want her back, and I want no harm to come to her.”

“This is your-? Oh.” He drew out the word as his mind made the jump. “It’s not a vase, it’s an urn. But, wait. Dispatch reported your mother was abducted.”

People, living people, were abducted. Things, and remains, were just stolen. Which meant either someone lied or someone misunderstood.

“No, no, I never used that word,” the guy argued, taking back his phone. “I just- I expressed my concern for her state of mind. My wife is a little…”

He trailed off, but Buck filled in the blanks as he looked back up to the figure on the roof. Considering she stole her mother-in-law’s remains and took them up there to… What? Dump them? Drop the urn over the edge? Either way, she was little something, alright.

This also wasn’t as severe of a situation as they’d feared.

When Buck went over to share the slight change in plans, Chimney was busy playing spotter while the others finished setting up the airbags. He was tracking the woman’s pacing on the roof, relaying it over the radio. In perhaps the most unhelpful fashion possible.

“Okay, she’s over the bag. Okay, she’s not over the bag,” he was saying. “Okay, she’s over the bag. She’s not over the bag.”

“Stop that,” Buck told him, rolling his eyes. “Eddie, Ravi, go get the fly paper and head up to the southwest corner there.”

The pair nodded and jogged to the trucks.

“So what happens next?” Oh, goodie, the guy followed him. “Are you calling SWAT or something?”

“For an urn?” Buck scoffed. “No.”

“An urn?” Hen’s, brow furrowed behind her shades.

“His wife stole his mother’s ashes,” he explained, gesturing at the guy. The others stared, and he reached for his radio before SWAT actually did show up to send everything to hell. “Dispatch, this isn’t a kidnapping. It’s a theft.”

“A theft?” Maddie repeated.

“They took an urn.”

The silence that followed that statement was heavy. It was also soon broken by a woman’s ranting.

“-him that I am done living in Doris’ shadow. He needs to let her go or… or I’m dropping her right here. Tell him that.”

“Did you get that, Captain Diaz?” Athena asked.

“Tell her if she brings down the urn in one piece,” the guy said. “I- I’ll do whatever she wants.”

Buck stared at him and then wordlessly held out the mic of his radio. Because there was no way in hell he was playing telephone for this domestic squabble. The guy wasted little time putting his face to the mic.

“Uh, sweetheart? Sweetheart? Just bring Mother back down here,” the guy said. “Okay, I’m just concerned for both your safety. And you can have your crafting corner back, I’ll put Mother in the spare room. I swear!”

“You hear that?” Athena asked. Buck frowned and almost asked who she was talking to, when the wife responded. He wondered if her radio’s button was stuck again.

“Yeah, I’m hearing that now, she’s getting her own room,” the wife complained. And then, a few minutes later, “What, is this thing welded shut?”

“What are you doing?” Athena asked. It looked, from where Buck stood below them, like the woman was trying to open the urn. Below her, Ravi and Eddie were at the window and working to get it open.

“Stay back. If Trent wants his mommy down there, I’m gonna give her to him.”

The words had the guy, Trent, anxiously yanking at his own hair.

“The unpermitted scattering of human remains carries a fine, and up to six months of jail time.” The sergeant sounded close to losing her patience entirely. Buck was familiar with the tone, having been the recipient of it more than once. “Celeste? Celeste, stop. This is not about some space in a house for your crepe paper and yarn, this is about the space between the two of you. You both allowed her to come between you. Why give her more power, especially since she’s gone?”

“You’re right.”

“And you heard what he said. He wants to change.”

“Yeah, I still don’t buy it,” Celeste said. “Who cares if he can’t move on? I can. If it means that much to him, you can stay in the garage-”

Celeste cut herself off with a scream as she misjudged her footing and toppled backwards, right over the ledge and right into the fly paper that Eddie and Ravi had waiting. The urn, meanwhile, fell and fell and fell, to land on the airbag. Buck grabbed Trent by the arm before he could even attempt to get the urn himself, allowing Chimney to fetch it.

“What is that?” Chimney asked after he handed it over to Trent, who was looking very relieved to have it in his hands. “Ming dynasty?”

“Me dynasty. This is my inheritance,” Trent told them, holding the vase as lovingly as Eddie held Senorita. “This thing has been in my family for a hundred years, and it is worth a fortune. Celeste doesn’t know that. I figured if I put my mother in it, she wouldn’t go near it during the inevitable divorce settlement.”

That was actually kind of clever. But Buck was never going to tell the guy that he thought that.

“Am I under arrest?” Celeste had made it to ground level the safe way, escorted and in cuffs. Eddie and Ravi were both rolling their eyes as they joined Buck and the others.

“You’ll be booked,” Athena answered as she handed the woman off to another officer. “Your husband can bond you out of jail.”

“She can bond herself out,” Trent said. “We’re done.”

“The house is in my name!” Celeste retorted.

“You can keep the house!” Trent followed his soon-to-be-ex wife as the officer escorted her to a cruiser. “All I need is right here. Mother and I will be checking into a hotel. Oh!”

He tripped and fell, sprawling onto the pavement. The vase hit the ground and shattered. Celeste cackled at the man’s misfortune as she was led away. And Trent was left with a face covered in ash.

Eddie could not say for certain why he was here. It had been a very long time since he willingly stepped foot inside a church, any church, aside from the occasional wedding or a funeral. Or because they’d been called to it as part of the job.

This church was larger, more ostentatious than the one in his childhood that he was dragged to by his parents. The outside was reminiscent of a fortress with its towers, and it lacked much in the way of embellishments. On the inside, the sanctuary was cast in a myriad of colors by the light that filtered through the stained glass windows. Bas-relief carvings depicting the Stations of the Cross adorned the walls, along with paintings and sculptures and crosses. A crucifix was held suspended above the altar.

It all felt very Los Angeles -like to Eddie.

A church pew was a church pew, though, and the one he was sitting on now was as uncomfortable as any from his childhood. The discomfort of being here in general was very familiar, almost a physical weight. Faith never quite fit right, just like the clothes his mother used to make him wear to Sunday mass.

The sanctuary was big enough to fit hundreds of people, but there were only a couple present besides himself. They were farther up in the rows, closer to the altar and the hanging crucifix. He, though, sat near the very back. Close to the entrance, close to the exit, feeling very much like he’d snuck into a place that he didn’t belong and was trying to not get caught trespassing.

“You are looking very lost.” The sudden voice had Eddie startling in his seat. A priest was standing in the aisle, frowning down at him. That was a sight that Eddie was very familiar with, as well, though the priest of the church his family went to was nowhere near as young looking as this one. “I don’t think I’ve seen you in the congregation before.”

“I’m not a church person,” Eddie told him. “I haven’t been to confession in twenty-three years, not since middle school. Haven’t gone to church in just as long. But my father-in-law comes to this one, and I just…” He shrugged. “I don’t know.”

“Well, you’re here now,” the priest said, taking a seat beside him on the pew. “Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find it; knock and the door will be opened to you.”

Eddie frowned at the back of the pew in front of him for a moment, then he rolled his eyes with a scoff.

“Of course you’re already quoting scripture.”

“I am what I am,” was the priest’s simple response. “What has you so lost that you found yourself here?”

“My abuela might have Alzheimer’s,” Eddie answered after a beat. “I really don’t know why I came here.”

“Perhaps you came to our Father in the hopes that he could fix it,” the priest said. “Didn’t you do that with your parents when you were a kid? I know I used to think mine could just make it all better, no matter what it was.”

“My father told me on my tenth birthday that it was time for me to step up and be the man of the house.” He caught the priest’s grimace out of the corner of his eye. “Abuela was the only one who ever treated me like a kid, whenever she visited us.”

“It sounds like you’ve had to shoulder burdens and responsibilities for a very long time,” the priest said. He was gazing at one of the bas-reliefs. “Maybe that’s why you came here? He takes those who are weary and burdened, and He offers them rest. I think you might need that.”

When Eddie didn’t immediately reply, the priest let out a sigh.

“How about if we pray together?” he offered. “Pray for comfort, pray for health. It might help? Make you feel better?”

“I don’t know if it would, though.”

“That is usually where faith comes into it.”

Eddie shook his head.

“Coming here was a mistake,” he declared, getting to his feet. “I’m gonna go.”

The priest’s disappointment followed him all the way out of the church.

“Alright, so.” Buck let his hands fall against the counter top of the breakfast bar. Hoover laid down and curled up at the foot of the stool he was on. “What do we do?”

“What do we do?” Carla repeated. She was in the kitchen, washing the cup she’d been drinking out of.

They were the only two adults in the house. Pepa had swooped in and taken off with her mother, having taken the news of their concerns stoically but still obviously shaken by it. She was taking it better than Eddie, at least, who was… Buck didn’t actually know where Eddie was at the moment. He’d fallen into a pattern of hovering over Abuela one moment and avoiding her entirely the next.

“Abuela’s Alzheimer’s,” Buck said. “What do we do?”

“First off, we don’t know for sure if that is what’s going on,” Carla told him. “There are other possibilities it could be, and the doctors will run tests to rule ‘em out. It’ll definitely take more than one visit, that’s for sure.”

“Okay, but what if it is?” he insisted.

“Then we handle it,” was the nurse’s simple answer. “It’s not the end of the world, Buck. She wouldn't be the first client with Alzheimer’s that I’ve had, you know that.”

“That’s my point. I remember how Patricia was, I remember how much it wore on Abby,” he said. “And- And Red. I remember how much it hurt him when I tried to set him up with his ex only for it to turn out she had it, too. She forgot who he was in the middle of the conversation. She forgot who we were and was terrified of us because we were strangers in her house.”

Carla let out a sigh, fixing him with a soft look of sympathy.

“We’re a long time from that, Buckaroo,” she told him. “We’re nowhere near that point, yet.”

“But we will get there,” he said. “It doesn’t get better, Carla.”

He heard the way his voice cracked on the words. She sighed again before coming around to take the stool beside him.

“The first thing you and Eddie should do is talk to Chris,” Carla said. “He’s more than old enough to understand.”

“And Gavin?” Buck asked. “We were trying to figure out childcare for him before, but then you and Abuela both got upset with us about it. We can’t expect you to watch her and him.”

“Isabel isn’t going to just suddenly stop being able to take care of herself right after a diagnosis,” she chided. “I told you, we’re a long time from that point.”

“She forgot the oven was on,” he reminded her. “What if the next time it’s more than just burnt dinner?”

“You’re right,” she said with a nod. “But what I’m saying is that we have time. Gavin might even be in school already when she gets to the point where I have to focus all my attention on her all the time. We have time to figure this out.”

“I guess you’re right.” Buck covered his face with his hands and then dragged them down with a groan. “You’d know better than me.”

“I do,” she confirmed with a laugh. “At least about this. And I also know that you and Eddie are in a much better position than Abby was. She was dealing with it all alone, she chose to do it alone. The two of you have each other, plus a whole village to support you.”

Hoover perked up at Buck’s feet, first lifting his head with his ears at attention and then jumping up with his tail wagging. He trotted to the door, which opened moments later. Eddie came in and shut it behind him, petting at Hoover’s head with one hand as he toed off his shoes.

“Welcome home,” Buck called over. “Abuela’s out with Pepa.”

Eddie didn’t give much of an answer beyond an absent nod. He padded through the living room and the dining room to lay against Buck’s back, burying his face into his shoulder. Buck just reached up to stroke at his hair.

“I’m gonna head out, boys,” Carla said and gave both of them a pat on the arm. “I’ll see you tomorrow.”

“Drive safe,” Buck said, while Eddie lifted up a hand to wave. Eddie took her seat after spending a bit more time pressing himself into Buck. “Are you okay?”

Eddie shrugged.

“Dad called when I was on the way home,” he said. “He was talking about the two of them coming up here, but I told him to wait.”

Buck bit back the “oh thank God” that wanted to burst out of his mouth.

“Carla thinks we should talk to Chris,” was what he said instead. “And- And I think we should start looking for daycares again. For Gavin.”

“Probably a good idea,” was the listless response.

Buck gave a sigh and reached out, dragging his husband into him. Eddie didn’t resist it, and just buried his face into Buck’s chest.

Chapter 16: Control

Chapter Summary

In which Buck visits Maddie at work and Eddie does some introspection.

The elevator gave a soft ding as it reached the right floor and the doors opened. Gavin squirmed a little in Buck’s arms, eager to be let down and explore the new space he’d found himself in. Not that Buck was about to do that, the last thing any of the dispatchers needed was for a curious toddler to be getting in the way.

Maddie once described the new Metro Dispatch, when it was rebuilt after the fire that gutted the old one, as bright and shiny. There was much emphasis on the shiny aspect of it at the time. Buck had never been to that version of the dispatch floor, because at some point between then and when he visited his sister at work to talk about their father showing up, they’d decided to go for mood lighting or something. The floors were still shiny, and he wondered how they regularly polished them since it wasn’t like the floor ever closed, but it definitely wasn’t very bright anywhere except the break room and the conference room, both visible through the glass walls.

Linda Bates was just leaving the break room when Buck stepped out of the elevator, and she immediately changed course to intercept him.

“Oh, aren’t you just the cutest thing,” she gushed. Gavin shied away from the attention a bit, blinking up at her as he clutched at the fabric of Buck’s shirt. “Maddie showed us pictures of him in his Halloween costume. The helmet was adorable.”

“It was,” Buck agreed, casting a quick look around. He spotted his sister at one of the stations, and though she was in the middle of the call, she smiled and waved at him.

Linda chatted with him for a bit longer, or rather, she cooed over Gavin’s adorableness while Buck stood there and held him. She had to go back and start taking calls, though, so she dragged herself away to actually do her job. Buck went into the breakroom, setting the bag of food that he’d been carrying onto one of the round tables along with the diaper bag, and then putting Gavin down on the floor. The tot immediately started tugging at Buck’s pants in silent demand until he dug out a couple of the toy cars that were tucked away in the diaper bag. Gavin took them happily, setting his butt down on the floor and making the cars zoom around him.

A more responsible parent would probably be concerned about whether or not the floor was dirty. Buck was just thankful that Gavin wasn’t in a “run around and scream for no reason” mood. Those were always fun. Not. Especially whenever Hoover decided to add an accompaniment. Buck loved his kids and his dog, but after they - and that included Chris, who had joined in on the “fun” - decided to sing the song of their people at the top of their lungs after a twenty-four where he barely got any sleep, he begun to understand why Kronos just ate his children.

Buck busied himself reheating and setting out the lunch he’d brought for himself and his sister as he waited for her to finish up. He knew she hadn’t taken her lunch break for the day, had asked before even leaving the house with Gavin, so he didn’t feel much guilt about showing up here. Felt absolutely no guilt, in fact, when Maddie opened the door of the breakroom and Gavin leapt to his feet to run to her, squealing,

“A’t Maddee!”

“Gavin!” Maddie scooped him off the floor with a laugh. “My cutest nephew.”

“I’m telling Chris you said that,” Buck teased.

“Chris is my handsomest nephew,” was his sister’s immediate response. “What did you bring me? It smells good.”

“Leftovers from last night,” he answered. “Red beans and rice, with andouille sausage and tasso. Plus some of the cornbread that I baked.”

“I know I’m going to regret eating this later, but I do not care,” she declared as she sat down. “And what is my nephew eating?”

Buck wordlessly pulled out a Lunchable that he’d packed into the diaper bag. Maddie rolled her eyes, clearly not impressed by what he was feeding his son, but tore off the plastic covering all the same. She kept Gavin in her lap as he picked at the cheese and crackers and round slices of ham, stacking them together and then stuffing the creations into his mouth, and she accepted the plastic fork that Buck gave her along with a bottle of water from the break room’s fridge.

“You should visit me at work more often if it’s gonna be like this,” Maddie said. “Letting me sit here with my nephew while you serve me.”

“You get that almost every Sunday, is that not enough?”

“Nope. Besides, Bobby and Athena usually hog him. I don’t gotta fight ‘em this way.”

“Or, how ‘bout this? You-” Buck jabbed his fork in her direction, a piece of sausage speared on the tines. “-come visit us more often, and then you’ll get more Gavin time.”

“You drive a hard bargain,” she groused, immediately dropping the act with a laugh. “So, if you’ve decided to come visit, what is everyone else up to?”

“Chris is in school. I hope. I hope he’s in school.” Buck made a face. “He’s a teenager, he could be skipping.”

“He’s your teenager, he probably is skipping.”

“Hey, he’s Eddie’s son, too. And Shannon’s. It could be either of their faults if he’s skipping.”

“Blaming a dead woman for your son skipping school feels a bit gauche,” Maddie remarked, trying to entice Gavin into eating a bean.

“I fell on my face keeping Hoover from eating her s’more, she can deal with it. And…” He let out a sigh. “Eddie and Carla took Abuela to a doctor’s appointment.”

“Okay.” Maddie looked up from Gavin and frowned. Probably at whatever expression Buck was wearing. “Not okay. What’s wrong?”

“Abuela is… She’s… She’s been forgetting things recently. A lot of things.”

“She’s been- Oh.” Maddie slumped in her seat, mouth twisted. “Oh, Buck. Alzheimer’s? Or- Or something else?”

“Carla says they won’t know for sure until after the doctors have run their tests. Apparently they used to not be able to actually say for certain if it was Alzheimer’s until…” He wagged a hand in the air, not wanting to even mention the idea of Abuela no longer being with them. “But now there’s some marker in the blood, beta something, that they can look for.”

“How is Eddie handling it?” Maddie asked, concern marring her features.

“About as well as he handled me and the whole, y’know.” Buck made a twirling motion in the air by his temple with a finger. His sister scoffed and scowled at him. “Worse, probably.”

“Probably,” Maddie agreed.

It was not much of a secret, how much Eddie loved his abuela and how much she doted on him in turn. Even more than she did Chris and Gavin, and that was saying something. They all had been happily going through life with the impression that Abuela was an immovable institution that wasn’t going anywhere. Now they were going to be disabused of that notion, slowly and surely and oh so cruelly.

“Hey, um.” Buck wetted his lips. “Remember last year? When I asked about a spot at the daycare you take Jee-Yun to?”

“Yeah. What about-?” Maddie’s face dropped. “Oh. Yeah.”

“We’re not- We’re not there yet. I don’t think,” Buck said. “But I don’t want to wait until we are, until things are that bad, because Carla’s gonna have to focus on Abuela and I know Chris is going to be there, that he’d help with Gavin if we asked him to, but I don’t want to ask him to, I don’t want to do to him what Mom and Dad did to you, plus I know your daycare works with our messed up hours so I just-”

“Take a breath,” Maddie interrupted. Buck did, in through his nose and out through his mouth. “I’m pretty sure you’re still on the waiting list from the last time I asked. I’ll check with them, see if any spots have opened up. Or if they know of any good daycares that would also fit.”

“Thank you,” Buck breathed out.

“You don’t have to thank me for helping my brother and my nephew.” She rolled her eyes at him. By that point, Gavin was done with his Lunchable and was wiggling to be put down, immediately going to his toy cars again when he was. “Another daycare would probably be better, actually. One closer to yours. Unless he’ll be going to Durand, too?”

“I don’t know,” Buck admitted. “Probably not, since it’s Chris’ last year.”

“So a daycare near whatever school Gavin would be going to would probably be better than Jee’s,” Maddie told him. “That way, when he does start school, you won’t have to go through this again.”

“Yeah, that’s- That’s a good idea.”

“I thought so,” she said. “But let’s talk about something lighter. Like the call I just had.”

“Was it stupid?” Buck asked.

“So stupid,” Maddie answered. “Okay, so, this woman calls and reports that her neighbor a couple houses down is using their table saw with the garage door open.”

“She called about her neighbor’s table saw?”

“Yes, but no. She called because she was afraid the wind would somehow send the saw blade flying at her.”

Sometimes, Buck was very glad he never thought of being a 9-1-1 operator. He’d probably have gotten fired within the day.

Their return home from the doctor’s was not cheerful. It was in the early afternoon, Christopher already home from school, because it had taken that long to get through some of the tests that the doctor wanted to do. They weren’t even done, because they were going to have Abuela return to go over the lab work results and then more tests, just to clarify what it wasn’t.  

Abuela had not exactly been happy about going through the appointment, hadn’t been since Buck and Eddie came to her with their concerns. Everything they did that day was done to the soundtrack of her complaints and her insistence that she was perfectly fine, thanks very much. But the usual fire was absent from her words, as if she was only doing it just to do it and not because she was actually feeling it. Like even she was worried, and just simply didn’t want to admit it or think about it.

Eddie didn’t want to think about it, either.

When they got in, they were given the regular exuberant greeting from Hoover and Gavin. Abuela smiled and loved on them both as Edddie cleared a path for her, bodily picking the toddler up and out of the way, which always made the kid giggle and squeal. She didn’t stick around for very long, however, giving Buck and Christopher a quick hello each before retreating to her room.

She claimed it was so she could watch her shows in peace before dinner, but Eddie didn’t believe her.

“What are you two making?” Eddie asked, setting Gavin back down on the floor. When Senorita batted at him from her perch on the cat scratcher as he passed her by on the way to the dining room, he plucked her up in his stead. She immediately went limp in his arms. “Cookies?”

“We had the stuff for it without going to the store.” Buck gave him that beautiful sunshine smile of his. There were clouds around the edges of it, though. He was stirring away at a mixing bowl clutched in one arm. “Mine is snickerdoodle, and Chris’-”

“Chocolate chip!” Chris was perched on one of the stools they kept at the breakfast bar, using a hand to keep his mixing bowl steady on the counter as he used an electric hand mixer that Buck got two Christmases ago. It was from either Maddie or Karen, Eddie couldn’t remember.

“I’m not sure how much chocolate chip actually made it into the dough, though,” Buck said, teasing lilt to his voice. “Pretty sure I watched Superman there eat every other handful.”

“Not every other handful,” Chris argued. “You ate some, too.”

Buck stuck his tongue out at the teenager. The teenager stuck his tongue out in return. Eddie just sighed.

“I think my dough is about done and ready to be made into cookies.” Buck’s eyes flickered in the direction of the hall and Abuela’s bedroom, and then to Chris. They hadn’t had that talk yet with their son, using the excuse of wanting to wait for the doctor’s word before telling him anything. It was very much just an excuse, though, and Eddie knew that. They both did. “What about yours, Chris?”

Chris frowned down at his bowl of cookie dough very intently, before sticking his finger into it to scoop out a bit and pop into his mouth. Then he gave a firm nod, set the messy mixer aside, and held the bowl out to Buck. Once the dough was portioned out onto baking sheets, and those sheets were put into the oven, he didn’t bother sticking around for the cleanup.

“So.” Buck pulled one of the whisks off the electric mixer and started licking the dough off of it. When Eddie gently dropped Senorita onto the floor and held out a hand, he gave him the other. “How did the appointment go?”

Eddie stared at the whisk in his hand, the cookie dough coating it no longer appetizing, and tossed it into the sink with a sigh. Buck grimaced in apology.

“They asked the three of us questions,” he told his husband as he used his fists to prop himself on the counter. “Health, medicine, diet. Any of the, you know, changes we might have noticed. Then they put her through a bunch of tests for memory, problem solving, that stuff, before taking fluids. We’ve got another appointment for a psych eval and one for scans. They said they also wanted to do a spinal tap.”

“Good thing we’ve got good insurance and a captain’s salary,” Buck joked. Tried to joke, anyway; it landed flat between them.

“Yeah. Pretty sure we work the day they booked us for the scan and the tap. I can-” Eddie started, but his husband cut him off with,

“You’ll have the day off.”

“Mi sol,” he sighed. “I was going to say that I can ask Pepa to go with her.”

“Yeah, but you want to be there,” Buck countered as he came to stand next to him. “I know you do. Porter still owes us for working Halloween last year, he won’t mind.”

“Thank you,” Eddie whispered, leaning into the other man.

“What’s the point in being the boss if I can’t do things like this, right?” Buck pressed a kiss into his temple. “I haven’t decided what we should have for dinner tonight. Any suggestions?”

“Something spicy,” he said after a moment.

“We just had spicy last night,” Buck reminded him, and then laughed when Eddie just shrugged. “Okay, I’ll figure something out.”

Eddie turned his head to kiss him, before reluctantly pulling away. He padded down the hall, pausing for a moment outside Abuela’s closed door, the quiet murmur of one of her shows only just audible. Uncertain if she was even in the mood to see anyone at the moment, he continued on to his and Buck’s bedroom.

After he closed the door behind him, he went to his bedside table to pull out one of the drawers. Not the top one, the one where he kept the sleep mask and loose change and whatever else got thrown in. He went to the bottom one, the one where he kept everything important that didn’t have a better place, and pulled out the book inside.

Back in the spring, after the medal ceremony, when Bobby was acting weird, he’d given Eddie this book with the claim that it might come in handy. The Catholic Book of Prayers. Eddie had tried to give it back to him after the man’s heart attack, but the former captain refused. So it had sat in the bottom drawer of Eddie’s bedside table for months and months.

They’d talked before, him and Buck, him and Dr. Copeland, even him and Frank, of how much Eddie didn’t like it when things were completely out of his control. Session after session had covered everything leading up to his stupid, stupid decision to accept Lena Bosko’s invitation to that fighting ring. If something was wrong, he always wanted - needed - to do something about it.

From the way that Dr. Copeland would always segue those conversations towards his childhood, her thoughts and opinions on the matter were quite clear. Maybe she even had a point, because that priest the other day had mentioned going to his parents with the certainty that they’d fix everything and Eddie couldn’t remember how old he was when that stopped being true for him. With his father gone so often and the way he was expected to help out with the girls in his stead, maybe Eddie never had that luxury of trusting someone else to be able to take care of something. Not before moving to Los Angeles, anyways.

(Not before Buck.)

Eddie stood there for several moments, simply staring at the book in his hand. A sense of desperation had been gradually building up in him, the same as he’d felt after the lightning strike and after Buck told him about the truth of the motorcycle accident and after Bobby’s heart attack. But all of those times there’d be the hope that things would be okay after the storm passed. He could tell himself that he just had to keep steady hands on the wheel until the choppy waters turned calm again.

That was not the case here. Buck talked about Abby sometimes, much as Eddie would sometimes talk about Shannon. More now than at the beginning, when the wounds were still so fresh. And with Abby came Abby’s mother, shadowing the memories and stories.

Eddie knew that the storm was not going to pass any time soon. He knew that when the waters calmed that it would be because…

He sat down in the armchair in the corner of the room, grip tight on the book. Numb fingers opened the cover, flipped the pages, traced the contents list. He found what he was looking for on the page just before the foreword, under Devotional Prayers, and flipped through until he was almost to the very end of the book.

The words mocked him from the page, it felt like. And when he spoke them, voice barely more than a whisper, they felt awkward in his mouth and on his tongue.

“God our Father, source of all health…”

Chapter 17: Rhymes

Chapter Summary

In which Chris gets to visit the set of Hotshots.

Bobby’s oldest grandson - and wasn’t that a wondrous thing to be able to say? - was a fan of the awful, awful show that he was stuck advising for. He couldn’t for the life of him figure out why that was the case, except for how it probably wasn’t all that different from the melodramatic telenovelas that Buck would tease Eddie about watching. It no doubt had the same quality of writing, or so Bobby imagined. He only ever saw Hotshots piecemeal while it was being made and never the final product, because he refused to watch it on principle alone.

Anyways, Christopher was a fan of the show. And because Bobby endeavored to be the best grandpops he could be - again, the fact that he even had the chance to claim something like that was a gift to be treasured - he invited Chris to come visit the set. When he’d brought it up as a possibility one Sunday dinner, over yet another heart healthy meal of salmon and salad, the teen almost dragged him to the car then and there. He’d pouted, though denied that he was when it was pointed out, when Bobby told him it would have to wait until a weekend shoot. He pouted even harder when Buck and Eddie looked at each other, had an entire conversation with nothing but head tilts and eyebrows and shrugs, and then pounced on the opportunity to use it as an incentive to do good at school.

Not that Bobby, or really any of them, were worried that Chris wasn’t doing well at school. The most he’d gotten in trouble had been when he decided to start skipping Science Club a couple years ago. But Bobby wasn’t about to get in the way of their parenting, that wasn’t his job. His job was to spoil his grandkids at any and every opportunity provided. Hence, on this Saturday, he swung by the equestrian center where Chris had his horse therapy. The kid was very excited to see him, barely saying goodbye to Carla and Gavin in his hurry.

Bobby treated him to lunch first, since it was around that time. He took the opportunity to have something decidedly not heart healthy, the greasiest burger and the saltiest fries available at the diner they went to, making a very amused Chris promise he wouldn’t say a word to Buck.

Getting Chris onto the set was easy enough. Technically, very technically, against the rules, but still easy. Bobby tried to at least be friendly with everyone, especially the members of the crew, even if he didn’t exactly like the job he was stuck doing. He knew most of them by name and greeted them as they rushed by with their tasks, and just about everyone had heard about his grandkids at least once by now.

So while it was technically not allowed to just bring Chris onto the set, no one was about to say anything against it.

“This is so cool,” Chris gushed, looking around in awe. He was so distracted by his surroundings that Bobby had to gently pull him out of the way of a harried looking grip. “Will I get to meet any of the actors?”

“Probably.”

Brad definitely had the tendency to stick to Bobby like an unwanted mosquito. The chance that Chris was going to get through this day without meeting the man in person was very low. Bobby simply hoped that the actor’s personality didn’t turn Chris off from something he enjoyed so much.

“One of the girls at school says that her cousin works here,” Chris said, making a face so similar to Eddie’s at his bitchiest that Bobby was almost tempted to take a picture with his phone and send it to Buck. “She tries to act like she knows what’s gonna happen on the show, but no one believes her.”

“Probably for the best,” Bobby told him. “Hey, Hailey.”

The young woman came to a stop at the sound of her name, brightening at the sight of Bobby.

“Oh, hey!” was her cheerful greeting, smiling at the pair of them. “You’ve brought a guest.”

“This is Chris, my grandson,” Bobby told her. “Chris, this is Hailey, a PA.”

“You have your own PA?” Chris asked, stars in his eyes.

“No, no.” Bobby chuckled and shook his head. “She’s not my PA.”

“The number of coffees I bring you says otherwise,” Hailey teased. “Speaking of, that’s where I’m heading now. I’ll bring you one and steal one of Mack’s cokes while I’m at it. He won’t notice.”

The last bit was said with a wink towards Chris.

“Do you know what all they’re filming today?” Bobby asked before she could dash off. He usually just focused on the shoots he was needed for, some days not bothering to come to set at all and other days wasting time while waiting for them to get to a firefighting scene.

“A scene at the station and…” Hailey checked the papers she had clutched to her chest. “A medical call on the street mock-up.”

“Thanks, Hailey.” Bobby gave her a nod and a smile as she hurried away. “Alright, so the station is at stage six, this way.”

Bobby wasn’t often called to the Station 119 set, mainly being asked if they were doing a good enough job pretending as the stars and extras went through the motions of what an active station would be like. Occasionally they’d have an emergency happen at the station for the sake of drama. That wasn’t the case today, however.

“Bob!” was shouted almost the moment they stepped onto the sound stage, the accented voice cutting through everything else. Its owner came at them like a rough beast slouching towards Bethlehem. “Good to see you, mate!”

“Hi, Brad.” Bobby’s smile felt more like a grimace.

“And who’s this bloke?” Brad asked. “Did you go and get yourself an understudy, Bob?”

“This is Chris.” He put an arm around the teen’s shoulders, who was far too starstruck in that moment to manage a response. “My grandson. Buck’s son. He’s a fan of the show.”

“Well I am always happy to meet a fan,” Brad said with a broad grin. “I’ll get you something to go home with. As soon as Hailey gets back with my bloody coffee, anyway.”

The last sentence was bitten out harshly and impatiently, and Bobby grimaced at the vitriol. Chris, at least, hadn’t seemed to register it. He was just staring up at the actor and nodding jerkily, something he kept doing even as Brad was called away by that week’s director.

“So cool,” he whispered.

“C’mon, we’ll sit over here.” Bobby used his arm on Chris’ shoulders to steer him to where the folded chairs were all grouped. “We can watch it on the monitor there…”

There was a phrase that Buck remembered reading somewhere forever ago: history doesn't repeat itself but it often rhymes. It was supposedly Mark Twain who said it, but it probably wasn’t. There were a lot of people who might’ve said it, or who said the same thing but worded it just the slightest bit differently.

The reason that Buck was thinking of the phrase now was because he was getting a severe case of deja vu. A frantic mother called 9-1-1, informing dispatch that her young son had fallen down a drain pipe. History wasn’t repeating, but the rhyme was as clear as the seemingly endless blue skies above their heads. The others heard it too, Hen and Chimney and especially Eddie, the three of them falling into heavy silence that made Toby frown in the driver’s seat.

When they arrived at the house, Buck and them wasted no time as they headed straight for the backyard, walking through the thrown open gates of the picturesque white picket fence. The mother told dispatch that they’d had a construction company installing a pool, and it was very obvious with the equipment sitting out and piles of dug up dirt everywhere. The parents were crouched in a rectangular hole in the middle of the yard, presumably around the drain pipe that was just out of sight.

“Over here!” A frantic boy, a few years younger than Chris, came running to meet them. “It’s my little brother, he fell all the way down.”

“We only took our eyes off of him for a second,” the dad explained when they made it to him.

Buck glanced at Eddie and knew he was thinking the same thing he was, that it only ever took a single second of inattention. How many calls had they responded to where someone told them the exact same thing? 

“Let’s just make room,” Buck told him, thankful when Chimney started herding the two parents out of the way. The pipe was jutting a foot or so out of the bottom of the hole, enough that he wondered how the hell the kid ended up down there. Especially since, when he peered down the pipe, he could see the boy’s face.

It wasn’t the position of someone who tripped and fell headfirst. There was a black tarp nearby, but its end wasn’t folded or bunched up like it would be if the parents tossed it aside, so it didn’t seem like it had been covering the pipe. The pipe was high enough out of the ground that, unlike the kid in the well, it wasn’t likely he simply walked into it by accident. Did the boy just decide to go for a fun adventure? Did he play too much Mario? Read Alice in Wonderland one time too many?

“I’d say he’s about twenty feet down, and the pipe looks fairly narrow.” Buck certainly wouldn’t fit down there. He raised his head to face the parents. “Any clue where this goes?”

“No.” The dad shook his head. “The construction crew found it when they were digging up our pool. Said it was an old drainage pipe.”

Eddie crouched down next to him with the open camera kit and handed him the camera on its bright orange cord. Buck gradually fed it down into the pipe while his husband kept his eyes on the screen in the case.

“I don’t hear him anymore,” the mother suddenly said, sounding worried. She made to rush for the pipe once more, calling her youngest’s name - “Jack? Jack!” - while the others moved to stop her.

“Dispatch, Captain Diaz, One Eighteen,” Buck radioed once the camera was just above the trapped boy. “We need USAR at Fifty-two Seventy-three Ridgeford Drive for a trench rescue, ASAP.”

“Copy, Captain One Eighteen.”

“Hey, Jack, I’m Buck,” he called down the pipe. “Can you hear me, buddy? Can you tell me how you’re doin’?”

“It hurts,” a tiny voice replied.

“Aw, bud. Just hang in there, okay? Stay as still as you can, we’ll get you out.”

“Cap?” Eddie’s voice tore his attention from the kid down the hole. “Look at this.”

He was talking about the screen showing the camera feed, Jack’s frightened face perfectly visible. As Buck watched, the boy’s squirming caused him to drop a little bit farther down.

“Can you tell if the pipe narrows?” Buck asked, squinting in an effort to make out the details in the shadow below Jack. “He’s not falling very far, very fast, but is that because of friction or because it’s getting tighter the farther down he goes?”

“If it’s the latter, then we need to worry about positional asphyxia,” Hen commented, crouched down on Eddie’s other side. “Every millimeter that wedges him tighter could impair his breathing.”

“Dispatch.” Buck grabbed his radio again. “How long on USAR?”

“Estimated sixteen minutes, One Eighteen.”

Oh, cool. They could be getting there just in time to pull out a tiny, still warm corpse.

“Can we get O2 down to him?” Eddie asked.

“If it’s getting tighter, then it won’t help,” Hen argued. “If he can’t expand his lungs, then…”

“Then we dig him out,” Buck declared, and pointed. “There’s a backhoe right there.”

“And what if the pipe collapses?” Ravi asked, voice lowered as he joined their discussion. He and Albert had come in on the ambulance, the pair of them standing back up ‘til now. “It could bury him, right?”

“Then someone’s got to get down there,” was Eddie’s suggestion.

“Not you,” Buck immediately shot back. “Not that you could fit.”

“I can do it.” That was the older kid that had met them when they arrived. “I’m his big brother.”

“No,” Buck snapped, harshly enough that the kid flinched back. The words that threatened to come out of his mouth right then came with a PG-13 warning. At best. It took a lot of self-control to bite them all back. “We are not sending a- How old are you?”

“Ten,” was the mumbled response.

“We are not sending a ten year old down a hole to rescue anyone. What if you get stuck, too? Then we’d have two kids to rescue.” The older brother would be stuck upside-down, too, unless they wanted to try and use his feet to drag Jack out. “We’re using the backhoe. We’ll dig a parallel hole, cut into the pipe just below him.”

“So what USAR would probably be doing,” Ravi pointed out. “But still, it looks pretty old, Cap. If it collapses…”

“Pretty sure it’s steel.” Buck rapped his knuckles on it. “And I don’t see any rust, not up here or on the inside. Just dirt. Eddie?”

“I don’t see any,” his husband concurred, peering at the screen. “Should be structurally sound.”

“Then digging is our best option at the moment. Ravi, get some of the others and help clear a path for that backhoe. Eddie, we need to get something down there for him to grab hold of, keep him from falling farther.”

The pair of them nodded and hurried off to do as ordered, Ravi grabbing Albert and a couple of others from the ladder to start moving everything - kids’ toys, their gear, whatever - out of the way. Buck left Chimney and Hen to deal with the parents and the older brother as he jogged up to the backhoe. It had been several years since his last construction job, but he was confident he remembered how to use one of these things. And it beat the alternatives.

Send a ten year old down to rescue the kid. What the hell?

After far too long spent in the fake fire station, because the director of the week just had to get a specific shot perfect and so kept making the actors redo it, they moved to the street mock-up.
