This was a shoot that actually needed Bobby, since it was more emergency centric than the previous one. According to the script, it was about a pedestrian involved in a hit and run. Bobby wasn’t too clear on the details, and he didn’t truthfully care about the characters or their dialogues. He was just there to make sure they were convincing at what they did.

“Everyone at school is going to be so jealous of me,” Chris crowed, clutching the signed photograph that Brad had given him. They were riding on the back of a golf cart, because Bobby wasn’t about to make Chris walk all the way across the busy studio lot. “Can we stop by the store and get a frame for it?”

“Of course we can,” Bobby told him. 

They arrived at one of the false intersections of the street mock-up, which already had cast and crew busy preparing for the shoot. There were extras dressed in torn and scuffed clothing with make-up artists adding finishing touches to scrapes and bruises. Brad wasn’t there, thankfully: he and the other stars would probably be arriving on the engine, careening around the corner for maximum drama.

“Captain Nash?” The owner of the voice was a young woman in a sundress beneath a denim jacket, the fabrics of both torn and stained. A make-up artist was hovering around her, powdering at her face until they deemed it suitable and darted off. The young woman looked familiar, and it took a moment for Bobby to place her.

“Felisa Valdez, right?”

“Right!” She nodded. “You guys rescued me from a chandelier. And then from death by hot asphalt.”

“Abuela was upset with Dad,” Chris said. “Because he didn’t get an autograph from you.”

“Eddie,” Bobby supplied, and watched Felisa’s eyes go wide with recognition.

“You’re Christopher!” She nodded. “That’s why you look familiar. So is this a visit to the set or…?”

“Chris is, but I’m the technical advisor,” Bobby explained. “For all the firefighting stuff.”

“That explains why I haven’t seen you here before,” Felisa said. “And for my last scene, too. I’m dying today.”

She gestured down at herself.

“Well, rest in peace,” Bobby said, which made her laugh. “Who do you play?”

“Grandpops,” Chris groaned with a roll of his eyes. “She’s Autumn, Saint’s girlfriend.”

“I don’t watch the show,” Bobby told her, earning another laugh. Chris let out a startled yelp.

“They’re killing off Autumn!?”

“Spoilers.” Felisa placed a finger to her lips with a wink, and then glanced over her shoulder when the director started shouting. “Alright, gotta get to work.”

She went over to the street while Bobby led Chris to where the chairs were, beneath a canopy. As he watched, Felisa settled herself onto the pavement while talking to the director, nodding at something he was saying, before flopping backwards and splaying her limbs out.

The 119’s engine and truck came careening around the corner, lights and sirens blaring. Bobby held in his groan as Brad- Sorry, as Captain Race Banner leaped out, throwing a quippy one-liner before giving orders. A couple of the people playing paramedics, one of whom Bobby knew was Saint because Chris pointed him out, went to a car parked half on a sidewalk.

Bobby perused his copy of the script as he suffered through yet another indignity. The scene was basically that a car drove through a bunch of pedestrians, one of whom was Felisa’s character. It read as melodramatic, and it looked it as it was played out. Saint spotted his girlfriend laying on the pavement, shouted out her name, abandoned the car and its driver to dash across the street. Bobby tuned it out, only half paying attention as they had their final conversation and Saint argued with one of the others about intubating her.

In the chair beside him, Chris had gone silent. Not starstruck silent, like he had been with Brad, and it wasn’t the awed silence he had while watching the other shoot. This one was different, somehow. Heavier. His gaze was fixed on the actors in front of them, face drawn and pale. Worryingly pale.

Something was wrong.

“Chris?” Bobby whispered.

“I think…” Chris’ quiet voice trembled. “I think this is how Mom died.”

Bobby’s breath caught in his throat as he sat up in his seat. He turned back to the actors, who were doing another take of Felisa’s final conversation. He hadn’t been there when Shannon died, it had happened while he was suspended. It was only the aftermath that he witnessed, arriving at the hospital just in time to catch Eddie leaving the morgue.

Bobby hadn’t been there himself, hadn’t seen it himself, hadn’t known.  

“Chris…” He turned back to his grandson, who was doing his best to not look affected. “Do you want to leave?”

A moment’s hesitation.

Then a nod.

“Alright.” Bobby got up and then helped Chris get his crutches situated. “Let’s go then.”

The show could survive without him for the rest of the day.

The last thing Buck was expecting that day was for Bobby to arrive for a visit with Chris. He wasn’t certain about shooting times, but he’d figured they’d be at the studio all day. He definitely didn’t think his kid would be showing up looking as upset as he did.

“Hey, guys.” Buck jogged to meet them in the bay, Eddie following. “What’s up?”

Chris didn’t answer. Instead, he did something he hadn’t done in quite some time: fling himself at Eddie. Eddie caught him, sending Bobby a look of confusion and worry over the kid’s head.

Bobby let out a sigh.

“One of the scenes they shot today was a hit and run,” he explained. “Car running through some pedestrians. One of them was the girlfriend of one of the firefighters.”

Buck hissed in a breath as he understood exactly what happened. Eddie looked heartbroken.

“I’m so sorry, mijo,” Eddie whispered, half-crouched to press his face into Chris’ hair. “C’mon, let’s go upstairs.”

Chris didn’t argue as he let himself be half-carried to the loft. Buck and Bobby stayed behind.

“I didn’t know,” Bobby said. “I don’t bother to look at the scene details, and I didn’t even know one of the characters was anyone’s girlfriend.”

“Did he have a good day besides that, at least?”

“Yeah, he got an autograph from Brad.” Bobby rolled his eyes as he said the man’s name. “I meant to get a frame for it, I’ll pick it up later.”

“We were about to have dinner,” Buck said. “I can tell you about one of today’s call. Some kid was stuck in a well and his ten year old brother wanted us to lower him in to get him out.”

“You said no, right?”

“ Of course I said no," he told him. "I got to show off my hoeing skills, though."

Bobby's face was a twist of confusion and disgust.

Chapter 18: Stinky Cheeses and Dangling Stuntmen

Chapter Summary

In which it becomes apparent that they should all avoid the set of Hotshots for their own peace of mind.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Buck was in the middle of setting the table when there was knocking at the door. Sundays might have been the night of the week where they always had guests over for dinner, the extended members of their family that could make it, but the day didn’t have a monopoly on it. They hosted guests on other nights of the week; the Wilsons, Ravi and Albert, sometimes May, sometimes Amy, often Bobby and Athena, and people from Eddie’s Saturday veterans group, too. Tonight, it was Maddie and Chimney who were coming over.

The moment Eddie opened the front door, Jee-Yun was a squealing streak past his legs as she made a beeline for Gavin and Hoover. Maddie and Chimney came in behind their daughter, the pair of them rolling their eyes at her.

“Hey, Eddie.” Maddie stood on her tiptoes to wrap her arms around him in a hug. “How are you holding up?”

“I’m…” Eddie trailed off with a shrug.

“Yeah, I get that.” She looked around and frowned. “Where is Isabel?”

“Her room.” Buck pointed down the hall with a fork before placing it down on the dining table. “She didn’t really feel up to people, I guess.”

“Yeah. Yeah, I get that, too.”

The doctors hadn’t officially said it yet, but they all knew it was only a matter of time. Buck knew it, Eddie knew it, Abuela knew it. The samples of her blood that the doctors took and tested had an increase in beta-amyloid levels, and while that wasn’t enough for them to come out and just say the obvious, while they were still waiting for the results of the spinal tap and brain scans, it might as well have been.

“Nothing to raise the spirits like some good spirits,” Chimney declared, holding up the bottle of wine that they brought with him. Probably Maddie’s idea, still following the WASP-y habits ingrained into the Buckley siblings by their mother: they couldn’t go to someone’s house as a guest and not bring something.

“I actually have a Malbec breathing,” Buck told him, grabbing it off the table along with the wine glasses he’d set out. Because while he might not drink as much with the bupropion, due to the whole ‘heightened risk of seizures’ thing, it didn’t mean he went full teetotaler.

He poured a glass and started to hand it to Maddie, only for her to wave it off.

“None for me,” she said with an awkward laugh. Chimney hurriedly took it instead. “Trainer says I need to lay off the booze.”

“Uh, okay.” Buck could see Eddie frowning at her back, where he stood just behind the pair of her and Chimney. “Does he want you to lay off the dessert? ‘Cause we were gonna have Baked Alaska.”

“Baked Alaska?” Maddie echoed. The expression that she and Chimney made at that as they sat down at the table was not called for. “Since when do you make Baked Alaska?”

Buck cringed a bit, rubbing at the back of his neck, but it was his husband who answered for him.

“He’s been stress baking,” Eddie explained, and then slapped his stomach with a grimace. “And I have never used our gym equipment more.”

“I don’t make you eat it,” Buck sniped, which was better than admitting in front of Maddie and Chimney that focusing on baking was keeping him from totally freaking out over Abuela so that he could help Eddie through his freak outs over her. “But that reminds me!”

He went into the kitchen to grab the goodie he’d set out for them.

“You guys are taking home a lemon loaf, by the way,” Buck told his sister and brother-in-law, holding it up for them to see. Then he went to the fridge, where more wrapped up goodies were waiting. “And a walnut loaf. And… And a pumpkin loaf.”

“Seems like a lot of loaf,” Maddie commented.

“Don’t discourage him,” Chimney said, and then told Buck, “I love loaf.”

“Please, take some.” Eddie’s tone was grave, and Buck glared at him for it as he set the two loaves out on the breakfast bar next to the lemon loaf. “We’re being overrun by loaves. I’ve snuck a couple into Chris’ lunches, but I think he’s catching on to me.”

“You shut up,” Buck told him. “You’ve been eating them as fast as I’ve been making them.”

“There are twenty of ‘em in the fridge right now, mi sol, so that is a straight lie.”

“How dare you accuse me of doing anything straight.”

Eddie rolled his eyes at him and then poured himself a glass of wine, because Buck hadn’t gotten around to that before getting distracted by first the weirdness of his sister turning down the wine and then trying to offload some of the loaves that were piling up. He could admit that they were starting to become an issue, and was tempted to just throw a bunch into a basket to take into work with them. Carbs never lasted long around large groups of firefighters.

“I guess obsessive baking is better than other things you could be doing. Maybe,” Maddie said. “But I think you should take a deep breath and step away from the baked goods.”

“But I promised Chris we’d make chocolate peanut butter cookies,” Buck protested. Even Chimney perked up in his seat at that. Behind Buck, the oven’s timer went off, so he grabbed his oven mitts. “Oh! That would be the baked brie.”

There was silence as he pulled it out, and then his sister’s uncertain voice asking,

“You baked brie?”

“Yeah!” He didn’t bother setting it on the counter, instead carrying the tray out and over to the dining table. “Your favorite!”

Or, not her favorite? Maddie’s face was drawn and looking slightly green as he held the brie out to her.

“What’s wrong?” Buck asked, worried. Eddie shrugged when he looked to him for answers, and Chimney wasn’t meeting his eyes. “Why do you look like you’re gonna barf?”

“Uh, I just… I can’t really do the stinky cheese right now.”

“Brie is not a stinky cheese.”

“It is to me,” Maddie complained, leaning away from it. “So if we could just…”

“Uh, okay.” Buck stepped back and turned to put the brie on the breakfast bar, next to the loaves. “But you love brie? I mean, the only time I’ve ever seen you turn down brie was when you were pregnant with-”

The penny dropped; the tray clattered against the counter as it slipped out of his hand. He turned to fix wide eyes on his sheepish sister.

“That’s why you didn’t drink the wine!”

“That is why I didn’t drink the wine,” she confirmed.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“It’s just the first trimester,” Maddie said with a shrug.

“And you’re a blabbermouth,” Chimney added.

“You wanna rethink that argument, Chim?” Eddie asked. “‘Cause I remember you telling me about Abby within a shift or two of meeting me.”

“And you told a criminal about my dead brother before I even knew about him,” Buck reminded the man.

“I never said I wasn’t a blabbermouth,” Chimney grumbled.

“Plus, you punched me for not being a blabbermouth.”

“Moving on.” Maddie rolled her eyes at them. “I know you guys are going through a rough time of it with Isabel, so we didn’t want to rub our good news in your faces.”

“This isn’t good news.” Buck waited for their faces to fall before giving them his brightest smile and adding, “This is the best news.”

He tugged them both out of their seats and into a hug, wrapping his arms around them both and squeezing.

“If you tell anyone,” Chimney said, face mushed against Buck’s shoulder, “you’re dead.”

Eddie rolled his eyes at the threat. Buck just hugged Maddie and Chimney tighter.

The last time that Buck had reason to be on the set of Hotshots, he was party to the “borrowing” of the show's fully functional, if poorly stocked, fire engine. He couldn’t even be a proper tourist at the time, because they had the imminent crash landing of Athena’s plane as a priority to focus on. It didn’t seem like he would have the chance this time, either.

They were waved through the studio gates fairly quickly, and soon they were in a mock-up of a fake city that couldn’t decide if it wanted to be Los Angeles or New York or San Francisco. It seemed to change depending on the angle Buck looked at it and the “block” they were on, which was probably very much intentional. They came to a stop in front of a pair of blue plastic roadblocks, a woman in a hi-vis vest signalling for them to come to a halt. Just beyond it was the set-up for that day’s shoot, lights and cameras and everything else.

Bobby was waiting for them, looking as angry as Buck had ever seen him. The guy beside him, wearing a flannel shirt, was visibly panicked.

“This way,” their former captain said, sidestepping any greeting. “It’s Grady, one of the stunt guys. This is Mark, an AD.”

“There was an incident during a take,” Mark the AD explained as they followed in Bobby’s furious wake. “He fell off the aerial ladder.”

The aerial ladder, and the man dangling from it, came into view. Buck wasn’t paying much attention to the others, not until he heard Hen’s quiet “oh.” Then he realized that they had all come to a stop, heads tilted back and gazes fixed on the scene in front of them. Buck opened his mouth to ask what that was about, but then Bobby was talking again. His focus was entirely on Brad Torrance, who was chatting on the phone a few feet away, entirely unconcerned with the actual emergency occurring.

“Brad-” Bobby said the name with enough vitriol to make Buck flinch. “-decided to play with the controls, swung it fast enough to knock Grady off. Fried the gearbox, too, so we can’t just retract the ladder. Didn’t see him hit his head, he was just dangling and then he passed out.”

“Okay, then…” Buck peered up at their vic, dangling from the end of the extended aerial by his safety harness. “Ravi, tell Javier to bring the ladder around. You and Eddie are going up to bring him down.”

Unlike every other time he’d given orders on a call, no one immediately snapped into motion. They didn’t even acknowledge that they’d heard his words. He turned to look at them, only to find that they, too, had been entirely focused on Grady.

“Guys?” he prompted, waving his hand in front of Eddie’s face. His husband blinked and shook his head. “Person in need of help. Could we go rescue him?”

“Right, yeah.” Eddie gave the hanging stuntman one last moment of staring, and then he was turning around to jog towards the trucks with Ravi on his heels.

“Am I missing something?” Buck asked the others, who were all various degrees of grim.

“I guess you wouldn’t remember,” Bobby said. He was the only one who hadn’t looked up at Grady, always finding something on the ground-level to stare at, instead. Or glare at, in the case of Brad Torrance. “You dangled.”

“I dangled?” Buck asked, not getting it. Until he did, the realization striking him like lightning. Which was perhaps not an appropriate metaphor to use at that moment. “Oh, shit. And I sent Eddie to get him down.”

Trauma had a splash zone, as Copeland was so fond of telling them. Just because Buck was the one struck by lightning, it didn’t mean it wasn’t horrific for everyone else around him. He remembered being told that it had been Eddie who scaled the ladder after the lightning strike, Eddie who lowered him down to the ground. But all Buck’s memories of the incident after his smiting were secondhand, because he didn’t remember it himself.

Eddie was with Ravi when Buck found him, the pair of them pulling on the safety gear for climbing. They were to the side of the fake street, so the engine had room to get out of the way and allow the ladder to be maneuvered into position. Neither of them looked particularly bothered, Eddie certainly wasn’t wearing the shuttered expression he normally wore after being startled by fireworks, but Buck knew damn well that looks could be deceiving.

“Hey, Eds, if you want…” Buck glanced up at the dangling Grady, just barely visible around the corner of the building. “I didn’t realize, before. If you- If either of you want someone else to go up there, that’s fine. Toby wasn’t even with us then, he and I can go up.”

“It’s weird that you’re offering us an out to avoid trauma flashbacks to your death,” Ravi commented, tightening the straps of his helmet.

“I don’t remember it, I was dead at the time. Like you said.” Buck shrugged. “I just get freaked out by thunderstorms now. But you guys do remember it, so if this is too much…”

Eddie sighed and reached over to grab his shoulder.

“Capitán, I’m-” He glanced over to Ravi, who nodded. “We’re fine. If it was raining, maybe it would be different. But it’s a very sunny LA day.”

Buck looked between them, not seeing anything that countered his husband’s statement.

“Alright, if you say you’re fine to do this, then you’re fine to do this.”

Once their truck was in position, not quite nose to nose with the show’s, the ladder was extended until it reached Grady. That put it slightly lower than the ladder that Grady was dangling from, the one that Ravi was climbing. Eddie went up the 118’s aerial.

Buck watched from below as Eddie tried to get a response from the man. When that didn’t work, Eddie reached into the man’s firefighter costume and knuckled his sternum. That got a reaction, the stuntman startling awake to cling at Eddie.

“He’s responsive, Cap,” he radioed a moment later. “Coming down now.”

“Copy that,” Buck responded, and then side-eyed Bobby. “So how did this happen? Because there’s no way that you just let someone play with the controls like that.”

“I was talking to the director while Brad was doing a closeup.” Bobby shot a venomous glare at the actor in question, not that Brad seemed to be paying attention enough to notice it. “Next thing I know…”

He waved a hand up at Grady, who Ravi managed to pull back up onto the ladder with Eddie’s help. Now he was aiding the man in getting to the bottom, where Chimney and Albert were waiting to receive him.

“How’s Chris?” Bobby asked. “He seemed okay on Sunday, but…”

“Eddie took him to visit Shannon,” Buck answered. “They’ve talked about it before, what happened and how it happened. Pretty sure Chris just wasn’t expecting to have to see a near reenactment of it.”

“I wasn’t expecting it.” Bobby let out a sigh. “The next time - if there is a next time - I bring him with me, I’ll be sure to actually read the script ahead of time so I know what’s going on.”

“Yeah, Cap, about that,” Hen broke in. “What the hell?”

They turned to face her, saw she was pointing at something, and followed her finger. Buck’s eyes landed on an extra gawking at the actual firefighters doing their job. An extra that, for some reason, was made up to look as if he had a piece of rebar driven through his forehead. It wasn’t the exact same as Chimney, but it came pretty close.

“Seconded,” Buck said, unable to tear his eyes away from it. “Pops, what the hell? What’s even happening on this show that they had someone on the ladder and someone playing Chimney in his unicorn phase? At the same time.”

“You know, for the life of me,” Bobby said, “I would not be able to tell you. Firefighting, supposedly.”

“I want to blame Taylor for this, somehow,” Buck said. That was probably Eddie’s bad influence at work. “But I know that wasn’t in her book.”

“They probably yanked it out of the news,” Hen told them. “Shows like this do that all the time. I know Grey’s Anatomy does.”

When the pair of them stared at her, she shrugged and explained,

“Karen’s a fan.”

Bobby’s groan of annoyance cut off anything Buck might’ve wanted to say about that. The cause was easily identified, once he saw that Brad was coming over. Bobby’s expression was getting increasingly stormy, and Buck decided he did not want to be around for this.

“Y’know what, I bet Chimney will get a kick out of this,” he said. “Let’s go tell him about it.”

Hen nodded like a bobblehead, already hauling ass to where the Hans were waiting. Buck was not far behind her, and instinctively ducked when he heard Bobby’s raised voice, asking,

“What the hell were you thinking!?”

He did not want to be in Brad’s shoes right then.

Chapter End Notes

While writing this chapter, I realized I'd been spelling Brad Torrance's name wrong this entire time.

Chapter 19: This Time It Wasn't Chief Williams' Problem

Chapter Summary

In which important conversations are had, or at least attempted.

Buck knocked on the door, waited for a moment, and then knocked again before poking his head inside the room. Chris looked up from his tablet with a frown, brows slightly furrowed.

“Hey, Superman.” Buck tried for a smile. It felt a little stretched on his face, not sitting quite right. “Your dad and I, we need to talk to you about something. You got a minute?”

The teen’s frown grew deeper. Buck was apparently not doing that good of a job of hiding his nerves. Chris didn’t say anything, he just set aside his tablet and gave a nod. Buck was hesitant as he stepped inside, moving aside to allow Eddie in as well. Eddie went to the chair at Chris’ desk, pulling it out and carefully sat down.

Buck just stayed standing. A couple years ago, he would’ve been a pacing mass of nerves, so it was progress.

“What’s going on?” Chris asked, expression and tone both wary. “Which one of you is dying now?”

“Neither of us, mijo.” Eddie rolled his eyes. “We wanted to talk to you about Abuela-”

“Is Abuela dying?” The words were sharp and on the verge of panic, and Eddie hurried to reach out to place a calming hand on Chris’ shoulder.

“No, no.” He shook his head. “But she is… She’s sick.”

“How is she sick?”

“You know how, um.” Eddie looked to Buck for help, but Buck could only shrug. “You know how, as people get older, their… their memory isn’t as good?”

“Yeah.” Chris gave a slow nod.

“Your bisabuela’s been forgetting things more lately, that’s why we’ve been taking her to the doctor,” he gently explained. “She has something called Alzheimer’s-”

“Oh.”

Sometimes, it was easy to look at Chris and forget that he was closer to being a young adult than the little kid that Buck first met so long ago. Sometimes, it was easy to look at a kid and forget how much they knew and were aware of, how much Buck had known and was aware of at that age. The way that Chris said it, the heaviness to that little oh was enough to remind Buck, though.

Chris might not know the details, but he knew the broad strokes of it.

“Right now, she’s just having trouble remembering the small things,” Buck told him, moving to kneel by the bed. “A name, a word, an ingredient, that kind of stuff. And she’s been losing things easier. Misplacing them.”

Chris slowly nodded.

“But…” Buck glanced at Eddie, whose face was grim, and sighed. Chris was closer to being a young adult than a little kid. He knew the broad strokes, and it would not be fair to keep the details from him when he would inevitably see them in person. “But it will get worse. She’ll forget more things, bigger things.”

“She’ll forget me,” Chris said, voice small.

“Maybe.” Eddie sounded pained. “And Carla will eventually have to start helping her with things more. Which means that she won’t be able to help as much with you and Gavin.”

“You aren’t going to be stuck taking care of him, though,” Buck quickly assured Chris. Chris’ expression twisted, as if he was mildly insulted by that statement. “But more than that… More than that, Superman, Abuela might start acting differently. Acting scary.”

“What do you mean?” Chris asked him.

Even after Buck helped search for Patricia, even after they progressed from talks over the phone to sex and failed dates, Abby had been reluctant to open up about her mother’s illness. She’d been very insistent about going through it by herself, almost like a martyr. But Buck had still been there for some of it, and Carla had been there for even more, and they’d talked over the years.

It wasn’t the possibility of Abuela forgetting about dinner in the oven again that had him so worried.

“We’re not there yet, we’re not anywhere near there yet. But she’ll start getting confused about things, and maybe a bit frustrated because of that. She might start thinking that things are happening that aren’t.” Once, Buck tried to surprise Abby with a ride in a hot air balloon. She’d had to ditch him because Patricia was convinced that Carla was a stranger keeping her prisoner. “And she might, um. She might get really angry for no reason.”

The time that Patricia slapped her daughter for no reason was one of the things that, through unspoken agreement, neither Buck nor Carla had told Eddie about.

“It’s going to be scary,” Buck whispered. “For us and for her.”

“But like your pops said, we’re not there yet.” Eddie moved from the chair to beside Chris on the bed, pulling the stricken-looking teen into his side. “Okay? We’ve got plenty of time before we are.”

Buck wondered how much of that was Eddie trying to reassure their son, and how much of it was him trying to reassure himself.

“And having time means we can learn how to help her,” Buck told Chris. “Because that’s going to be very important, what we can do to help her.”

Chris swallowed and nodded, and then he was reaching for his tablet again. Buck looked up at Eddie, sharing a small smile with him. When he got up and moved to sit on Chris’ other side, he was not very surprised to find that Chris was pulling up Google.

Brad Torrance needed to be reined in. At this point it was very much a life or death matter, since the man had nearly killed Grady. Worse, he was entirely unrepentant about it, more offended over the public scolding from Bobby than recalcitrant for his actions. Over the months of working with him, Bobby could see the man’s ego getting bigger in real time. Which was an impressive feat, because it was already overinflated when they met.

Yelling at him for messing about with the controls while someone was on the aerial only helped insomuch that Brad promised not to do it again. Offhandedly, though, like it was a minor thing that was liable to be forgotten the next time the actor wanted to be authentic. And he’d barely apologized for Grady, saying only that,

“He’s fine, so it’s fine.”

It was pushing the limits of Bobby’s midwestern politeness. Hence why Bobby invited the man out to dinner. Hopefully the setting would be more conducive for getting the man to listen to him.

“Welcome to the Wolford Lounge,” the server, a young woman, greeted them excitedly when they walked in. The Wolford Lounge was upscale, the atmosphere relaxed and… Well, Bobby was going to say cozy, because the word he actually wanted was not one he desired to use in context with Brad. If the food here was good, he might consider this for the next date night with Athena. “I know I’m not supposed to say it, but I’m a big fan, Mr. Torrance.”

“Aw, you’re too sweet,” Brad told her, barely paying attention to the woman. “Maybe we have a little selfie after dinner, eh?”

“That would be amazing, thank you,” the server gushed. She led them to a table, with a vintage banker’s lamp of all things perched on the end. Once they were seated, she asked, “Can I get you gentlemen anything to drink?”

“Well, it’s on me,” Brad immediately said. “So bombs away.”

“Actually, it’s on the LAFD,” Bobby corrected him. Because this was technically work related, and his manners dictated that he couldn’t force the person he invited to pay for it.

“In that case, I’ll have your most expensive gin martini,” the actor said. Luckily he was focused on the server again, and so missed the face Bobby made at that before he caught himself. “Dry, stirred, with three pit-in olives.”

Did he say pit-in? Or was it pitted?

“And I’ll have a club soda,” Bobby said. “Thank you.”

“Okay, I’ll go put that in right away.” The server gave them both a smile, the one she sent Brad a bit bigger and brighter than the one for Bobby, before leaving them.

“Listen, Brad,” Bobby started once she was gone. “I really appreciate you taking the time to sit down with me.”

“Are you mad?” the actor asked. “I’m always up for breaking bread with Hollywood Bob.”

The chuckle Bobby let out was more out of politeness than actual mirth. Hollywood Bob? Lord Almighty…

“So, what did you want to talk about?” Brad asked him. “The show?”

“I do,” Bobby said. “Well, partly. Your behavior on the show.”

The actor’s face dropped.

“Oh,” he said, leaning back with a petulant groan. “I thought we'd already talked about this, Bob. Look, everything is fine, right? No harm, no foul.”

“No harm, no-?” Bobby shook his head and bit back the words that wanted to spill forth from his lips. “You could have killed him!”

“But everything was fine. Besides, that’s what the stuntmen are for, right? To do the risky stuff for us actors.”

“That doesn’t mean you just needlessly put them in danger,” Bobby ground out. “But more than that, Brad, it’s your behavior on the show in general.”

“Look, Bob, I want to be recognized by the public as an authentic fire captain,” Brad told him, looking a bit desperate as he leaned forward. “So to do that, I need someone like you, a leader of men, to guide me.”

“That is what I am trying to do. Right now. I am trying to guide you right now. Because you’re not acting like an authentic fire captain.” Well, that depended on the fire captain, but he wasn’t about to voice that thought. “You’re acting like a pomp-”

“Okay, I’ve got a club soda.” The server’s cheerful return cut him off. She set down napkins, then first Bobby’s drink and then Brad’s. “And a dry, stirred martini. Did we decide on any appetizers?”

“Tell me something, love.” Brad’s voice was tight, as was his expression.

“Yeah?”

“I know you’re only a waitress-” He ignored Bobby’s chiding “Hey!” for his rudeness. “-but do you, perchance, recall how many olives I ordered?”

“Three?” was the young woman’s nervous answer.

“So why are there four, bobbing around in my glass?”

“I- I just thought that, if you wanted three, then you might like a bonus one…” She trailed off with a nervous laugh.

Brad’s responding chuckle was sarcastic and sharp, barely lasting a moment before he was glaring at her.

“If I wanted four,” he told her, “I would have ordered four.”

“Brad, take it easy,” Bobby tried. This was the exact kind of behavior that he was talking about.

“I can take it back,” the server offered.

“No, it’s okay,” Bobby told her, though he was still focused on the man across from him. “We can just fish one out.”

“Yeah, fish it out.” Brad laughed, pulling the skewer of olives out of his drink to take one off. “Yeah, yeah, I’m okay.”

Bobby relaxed in his seat, confident that the crisis was managed and avoided. Falsely confident, apparently, because Brad was soon losing that cheer.

“Man alive,” he snarled. “Are you bloody joking?”

“What is it?” Bobby cautiously asked.

“This olive.” Brad held it up to show him. “It’s pitted.”

Seriously? Seriously? That was enough to set this guy off?

“I thought that’s what you said,” the server told him. “Three pitted olives.”

“No, love, I said three pit- in olives. I was very clear.” And then Brad raised his voice, almost shouting, as he asked, “Are you hard of hearing or are you just daft?”

“I- I can take it back to the bar and fix it,” the server stammered as she offered.

Brad threw the olive back into the martini, splattering the table, as he got up. His attempt at wiping it up was more akin to slapping aimlessly with the napkin.

“I’ll do it,” he told the server, brushing past her.

“I’m so sorry, Mr. Torrance, I-”

“It’s okay,” Bobby assured her. “You have nothing to apologize for.”

And if he sent a pointed glare at Brad, standing at the bar, as he said it, it wasn’t like it was noticed.

“I just didn’t understand,” the server said. “Maybe it was the accent. It was my mistake.”

“I think we have well-established that,” Brad said. “Is it your first day on the job, love?”

“Look, I’m-” Her voice broke with a sob and Bobby’s heart with it as he reached up to try and comfort her. “I’m so sorry.”

She ran off to the back of the restaurant, to hide from Brad and from the stares of the patrons. Brad watched her go with a hint of disgust.

“And there she goes,” Brad mocked. “She’s gonna bloody cry now. Boo-bloody-hoo.”

“Brad!” Bobby snapped.

“What?”

“That’s enough. You owe her an apology.”

“I owe her an apology?” was Brad’s incredulous response.

“Yeah, you do,” Bobby said, getting up from his chair and approaching him.

“What if I don’t feel like it?”

“If you don’t feel like it?” The absolute nerve of this man. “This! This was the behavior I was talking about, you pompous jerk! You want me to guide you into playing an authentic fire captain? The only thing I can buy you as right now is an entitled man-child. Now go tell her you’re sorry.”

“Or what?”

“Or I’m gonna kick your limey ass!”

Brad glared at him, and then stepped around to head for the exit instead of going to apologize to the poor woman. Bobby shook his head at the man’s retreating back and went to go make sure she was okay, because no one deserved that sort of treatment. Worse, she had been so excited to meet Brad Torrance, and they all got to watch that excitement be cruelly crushed.

(A small part of Bobby wondered if, now that he’d pissed off the show’s big name, he’d finally get assigned elsewhere.)

Except for the television playing in the living room, volume turned low, the house was quiet. Gavin was down for a midday nap with Hoover loyally watching over him, Chris was at school, and Buck and Eddie were at work. It was just Isabel and Carla, which was convenient.

Isabel did not want her boys to be here for this.

She’d noticed that something was wrong long before Halloween. Sometimes it felt like there was a fog over her mind. Sometimes she would lose entire words, having to stop in the middle of the conversation or switch languages mid-sentence to find the one she meant. How many times had she misplaced something that she had in her hands just moments before?

Once, not too long ago, she and Carla took Hoover for a walk around the neighborhood with Gavin. Mere blocks away, on a path that her feet had trod several times a week in the more than two years that she’d lived in this house, she had looked up and realized that nothing was familiar to her. She looked around and realized she did not know the path back home.

She hadn’t said anything to Carla at the time, or even afterwards. Denial and stubbornness, perhaps. But she’d known even then that something was wrong.

“Carla,” Isabel said. Her aide, her friend, raised her head with a smile from the kitchen, where she was pouring them both glasses of lemonade. “I need to talk to you about something.”

It was her tone, perhaps, or the set of her face. Whatever it was, it had Carla frowning.

“Of course,” she said, carrying the glasses out of the kitchen, through the dining room, and into the living room where Isabel sat in her chair. Carla placed the drinks down on the end table, within easy reach of Isabel, before taking a seat on the couch. “What about, hun?”

“The future,” was Isabel’s answer.

Carla’s face dropped.

“Oh.” She sighed. “Of course.”

“I know how bad it is going to get,” Isabel told her, and shook her head when Carla opened her mouth to speak. “No, don’t try to sugarcoat it. It will be bad, we both know this. This is how you and Buckito met, isn’t it? That… The woman, before Eddie.”

She glared at the coffee table. She knew that woman’s name, she was certain of it. Eddie had complained about her at length, years ago, after that train wreck. But the woman’s name just refused to come to her, regardless of how much she dug and clawed at her own memory.

“Abby,” Carla supplied. Isabel nodded, refusing to look her way just yet because she did not want to see the pity there. “Well, Abby’s mother, Patricia. The first time I saw Buck, he was embarrassing himself on the news. The first time I met him, we…”

She trailed off, and appeared uncomfortable when Isabel finally did look at her.

“Patricia had wandered off,” Carla quietly continued. “Abby was panicking, and Buck came over to help. It was the first time they met in person.”

“It will be bad,” Isabel said again. “I have seen it before. You don’t get to my age, with friends my age, without ever seeing it. Eddie might not realize it yet, but I’ve seen the way Buck has looked at me when he thinks I am not paying attention. The way you do. We know it will be bad, and we know that it will not get better.”

Carla let out a sigh.

“Yes.”

“I do not wish to be a burden on them,” Isabela told her. “So what are my options?”

“You could move in with Pepa, or with Ramon,” the aide offered, but Isabel shook her head.

“I told you, I don’t wish to be a burden on my family,” she said. “I do not want to put them through the worst of it. I love them too much for that.”

“There are facilities,” Carla said. “Abby’s brother, Matt, wanted to put their mother in one. But she insisted on having Patricia with her for as long as she was able.”

“The good ones are expensive,” Isabel countered. “And the bad ones are especially bad.”

“Isabel, what, exactly, are you asking for?”

“I told you,” she said. “What are my options?”

She stared at Carla, waiting for her to understand the question. The nurse aide’s face turned grim, mouth tightening into a line. 

“You have time before it gets that far,” Carla said. “You have time.”

“How bad was Patricia, at the end?” Isabel asked her. When no answer was forthcoming, she repeated herself. “How bad, Carla?”

“Bad,” was the quiet answer.

“I do not want to put my family through that. I do not want to lose myself like that. So, what are my options?”

Her aide, her friend, closed her eyes and drew in a breath. Then she let it out, slowly.

“California has an End of Life Option act,” she said, leaning forward  a little with her hands clasped in her lap. “But to qualify, the illness has to be terminal within six months and the person has to have the capacity to make medical decisions.”

“And I won’t have the mental capacity to make the decision by that point.” Not that she was comfortable about taking that path even if it were available to her. Suicide was a sin, after all, an unforgivable one. But she was facing down a nightmare, and would it not be more unforgivable to put her family through that hell when she could avoid it? “So what else?”

“There’s a directive, it’s not legally binding, but it’s a form that lets you communicate what you would want at each… At each stage of decline,” Carla said. “You can attach it to an Advanced Directive. There’s also the POLST, Physicians Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment. It’s similar, it’s a directive describing what kind of care you would like to receive. Or not receive.”

Isabel nodded. That sounded better, more acceptable. If God decided it was time, then it was time. There was no need for her loved ones to busy themselves with prolonging the inevitable.

“I can get copies of the forms and bring them with me,” Carla said. “Go over them with the three of you.”

Isabel nodded.

“Thank you, Carla. I think I’d like something to drink. Would you like some lemonade?”

Her aide, her friend, silently reached over to one of the glasses of lemonade sitting on the end table and held it out to her. Isabel took it from her, neither one of them saying a word.

The theme song from the Golden Girls erupting from the pocket of his uniform pants had Buck digging out his phone. He didn’t have to check the caller ID, because only one person on his phone had that set as their ringtone.

“Hey, Teek,” he answered. “What’s up?”

“It’s on TMZ!”

“Uh.” Buck blinked, more than a bit taken aback. “What’s on TMZ? Oh God, wait, Eddie and I aren’t that level of viral, are we?”

“No, Sunshine,” TK scoffed. Buck let out a sigh of relief. “You haven’t seen it yet?”

“Seen what?”

“I’m sending you a link,” his friend said, and then hung up.

Buck stared at his phone screen in confusion until, as promised, a notification from TK popped up. He clicked, he watched, he felt awe. And then he dashed through the station to where he knew Eddie was helping Hen wash the rig.

“Guys! Guys!” he shouted. “You have to see this!”

“Is this another cute animal video?” Eddie asked, setting down the sponge he’d been using. “Lemme guess, it’s that hippo from Cincinnati?”

“No, no, better,” Buck said, holding out his phone. “So, so, so much better.”

Hen took it from him, eyebrows going up when she saw Bobby on the screen. When she clicked play, all three of them gathered close to watch it, her eyebrows went sky high.

“Oh, my God,” she said. “He did not say that.”

“This can’t be real, can it?” Buck asked them.

“No, this has to be one of those deepfakes,” Eddie suggested. 

“Of Pops?”

“It says Harvey Levin posted it himself,” Hen pointed out.

“Why is it that everytime I visit, none of you seem to be working?” Bobby was in uniform as he strolled towards them. The three of them got up from where they’d perched on the side of the engine to watch, Buck bounding over to Bobby after taking his phone back from Hen. “What are you three doing?”

“We were watching the greatest British smackdown since the War of Eighteen Twelve,” Hen answered, and they laughed at the way Bobby groaned.

“It’s on TMZ,” Buck told him, bouncing in place. “TK sent me the link.”

“What are you doing here, Cap?” Eddie asked. “Did the people at Hollywood get pissed off and send you back or something?”

“I wish,” Bobby muttered. Louder, he said, “No, worse. So much worse. For you, at least.”

“What does that mean?”

“Just wait,” Bobby said, holding up a finger. And then-

“Hollywood Bob!” Brad Torrance’s shout echoed across the station. Bobby closed his eyes in exasperation, taking a deep breath. Eddie hurriedly took out his phone, not even attempting to be subtle about it as he started recording. “And company.”

“Um.” Buck stared at the actor, who walked in like this was an everyday occurrence, bags in hand. “Pops, what?”

“He talked to the chief,” Bobby explained, rolling his eyes out of sight of Brad. “He’s going to be shadowing you.”

“Shadowing- What?” Buck leaned in. “How did you yelling at him lead to me being stuck with him?”

“I am very sorry.” Bobby did not sound very sorry at all.

“Bob’s tirade blasted the entitlement right out of me,” Brad said as he joined them, dropping his bags to the floor. He threw an arm around Bobby’s shoulders; Bobby, in turn, stared at the arm like a venomous snake. “It was like a truth enema. No one has been that blunt with me since I was a young boy working at the Millwall docks. It’s just too bad that I can’t shadow Bob himself, but I guess you’ll do if I must.”

Wow. Buck could already see how his next appointment with Copeland would go: “Well, Doc, this famous guy with an exaggerated accent and an inflated ego proceeded to poke holes in my self-confidence like Swiss cheese…”

“But don’t you have a TV show to go star in?” Hen asked.

“They put me in a coma,” Brad told her. Too big to just kill off, probably, but too much off-screen drama to not do something. “So until Captain Race Banner wakes up, here I am!”

He grinned at them, arms out wide. Buck stared at him, and then at Bobby. Bobby smiled back, far too cheerfully, and patted Buck on the shoulder before telling him,

“Good luck.”

Chapter 20: Professional Opinions

Chapter Summary

In which it's all fun and games, until Buck loses his temper.

An email from the Mouth of Sauron - Tomas Wade, of the Community Liaison Office - dropped into Buck’s email not long after Brad was dumped in their laps. The request - an offer they couldn’t refuse, more like - to take advantage of the Hotshots actor being with them for their LAFD sponsored Instagram was not surprising. The entire point of it, after all, was the department squeezing the Diazes for all the good publicity they could.

They were just lucky that Buck’s attention whore tendencies meant he actually enjoyed doing those sorts of things. Really, Marjan - Firefox - had the right idea of it, though the mess with the roller coaster his probational year meant that Buck was not comfortable with using their rescues for internet fame like she did. 

There was something about doing the department dictated publicity reel with Brad that left a sour taste in Buck’s mouth, however. Probably the way that Brad did his best to slip into the melodrama of the show. Or the fact that the man’s ego was so large that it pushed everyone to the side. They normally managed to have a little fun with it, see: the trick-or-treating safety video, but this time he found himself having to grit his teeth and push through.

At the moment, they were watching an episode of Hotshots in the den area of the station’s loft, the entire crew gathered around. Because apparently Brad wanted their professional opinion on everything, which was a dangerous thing to ask for. The show wasn’t bad, not really. It honestly reminded Buck of a Michael Bay movie in a lot of ways, and those were always fun to watch. Also like a Michael Bay movie, it wasn’t necessarily good, either.

Brad himself was right by the television wearing, of all things, his character’s gray shirt uniform from the show. Buck was pretty sure he was reciting his lines as they watched, the dialogue also coming straight from a Michael Bay movie. On the screen, Captain Race Banner was removing a trapped woman from a burning car in the rain while throwing out corny one-liners - “Let’s get this baby open like a can of tuna!” - and carrying her away to safety just in time for the vehicle to explode dramatically behind them.

Cue credits and overly enthusiastic applause.

“So?” Brad asked, once the noise had died down. He’d moved to stand in front of the TV, looking all the world like a blushing school kid that just presented their first film. “What do you think?”

“It was exciting!” Albert threw out. He was stuffed into an armchair with Ravi.

“I really liked the music,” was Hen’s answer. She was on the couch in-between Buck and Chimney. Well, Chimney was more perched on the back of the couch, boots on the cushion. Buck’ll make him clean it later.

“The production value was off the charts,” the aforementioned paramedic said.

“Yeah.” Buck scooped a handful of popcorn from the bowl in his lap and held it out to Eddie, sitting on the arm of the couch beside him. “Super cool.”

Somehow, though, all those answers had Brad’s face falling.

“You hated it, didn’t you?”

“No one said that,” Eddie protested.

“It wasn’t very realistic,” Ravi said.

“But real life is boring!” Buck immediately countered. “And who wants that? This was fun.”

It wasn’t on the level of Backdraft, but then again, so few movies were.

“But as professionals, did anything bother you?” Brad asked them, straddling the coffee table to sit on it. “Did anything ring… False?”

“Um.” Buck looked around at the others, spotting the same reluctant expressions on all of their faces.  Just telling the man that literally everything about the firefighting in the show bothered him was probably rude. “This isn’t a big deal-” Yes it was. “-but usually we would put out an engine fire before attempting such a difficult extraction.”

Precisely to avoid the kind of explosion that happened at the end.

“That was the network,” Brad immediately countered, almost hissing the words.

“And also we wouldn’t call it a hydraulic ram,” Hen said. “We just call it a spreader, and we get it.”

“That was the network, too. They thought “spreader” was too provocative.”

“Okay, but how many actual firefighters are watching this?” Albert argued. “The people watching the show probably wouldn’t know what we meant by a spreader. They know what a hydraulic ram is.”

While Brad looked insulted by the mere suggestion that the real professionals wouldn’t give his show the time of day, Buck contemplated what Albert said. Whenever they hosted a school field trip, they explained the gear and tools they used to the kids. But not everyone had the chance to experience that, and addressing that sounded like the kind of thing the Mouth of Sauron would approve of. He dug out his phone, careful not to dump the bowl, and jotted down a note to get back to that idea later.

“I was just gonna say that you wouldn’t be blabbing so much to the driver in the middle of a rescue,” Eddie said, reaching down for another handful of popcorn.

“What blabbing?” Brad demanded.

“The speech at the end.” It was apparent that Eddie realized he’d said the wrong thing. “Uh, the ‘hotshots don’t get burned’ bit.”

He deepened his voice as he quoted it, almost coming across as mocking, which probably wasn’t helping matters any.

“Are you saying we should get rid of the speech?” Was Brad getting choked up at the idea?

“No, I’m just- In real life, we wouldn’t be standing around yakking, we’d be getting her out,” Eddie said. “I’m just saying, it seemed kind of, uh…”

“Extraneous.”

“Fake.”

Brad gasped sharply, reeling back. If he were wearing pearls, he’d probably have been clutching them at that moment.

“You said the F word.”

“No, no, no.” Eddie sounded desperate as Brad stood up. “F is for fun! Like Buck said!”

Buck scowled up at his husband for dragging him into this, not that the man noticed as he tried to do damage control.

“I think I need to pop to the loo,” Brad announced, sounding for all the world like he was about to start crying, and headed for the stairs.

“It’s my kid’s favorite show!” Eddie called after him. The actor seemingly ignored him, not stopping with his exit. When he was gone, Eddie drooped with a sigh. “Why is it Chris’ favorite show?”

“Says the man who watched El Conde: Amor y honor religiously,” Buck teased. His husband glared at him.

“You shut up. Also, that was a good show.”

“Someone who let Backdraft dictate his life choices should not be throwing stones, Buckaroo,” Chimney chided.

In lieu of a rock, Buck threw a piece of popcorn at his head. It bounced off and landed on the cushion between Chimney’s feet.

“Okay, but seriously.” Hen craned her neck, probably to make sure Brad wasn’t within earshot, because she next said, “Let’s get this baby open like a can of tuna? Seriously? Seriously?”

“More like a tuna melt,” Ravi quoted, which had Albert burying his face in Ravi’s shoulder to hide the laughter.

“Hotshots don’t get burned,” Chimney quoted, deepening his voice. It made his brother laugh harder. “They just get a little toasted.”

“I feel like we shouldn’t make fun of it behind his back,” Buck said, getting to his feet and crossing over to the railing so he could see down into the bay. He didn’t want Brad to overhear what they were saying. “But also, those lines were really cheesy. ‘I’m a life saver, not a heartbreaker’ level of cheese.”

Hen and Chimney both burst out in laughter at the memory.

“Chris would disown us if Eddie or I said those lines,” he finished.

“Yeah, but that’s because you’re not a Hotshot, obviously.” Albert had gotten his own laughter under control. Unfortunately “So you’re not cool enough to get away with it.”

Buck just rolled his eyes.

“How are you handling Brad with you?” Bobby asked. He’d come over to have dinner with them, since Athena was on duty. No one complained, especially not Gavin, who climbed into his grandpops’ lap when they sat down to eat, refused to be moved, and fell asleep curled up against Bobby’s chest. He was still there.

“Well.” Buck leaned back in his chair to make sure that Chris, who’d finished his food and went off to seal himself away in his room, wasn’t about to make an appearance. “Eddie made him cry.”

“What!?”

“I didn’t mean to!” Eddie defended himself as he cleared off the table.

“You said the F-word, babe,” Buck teased, and then explained to Bobby that, “Brad made the mistake of asking for our professional opinion on the show. And Eddie called it fake.”

“No, no. I said that the heroic speech seemed fake,” his husband argued. “That’s all!”

Abuela tutted from her spot at the head of the table. As Buck watched, she picked a piece of chicken off her plate and fed it to Hoover, who was sitting patiently beside her chair. He was very delicate as he took it from her, mindful of her fingers and his teeth.

“You better get me an autograph this time, Eddito,” she said, wagging a finger at him.

“Lo prometo, Abuelita,” he said, placing a kiss in her hair as he went by on his way to the kitchen.

“Brad’s got a thing about being ‘authentic.’” Bobby rolled his eyes as he said it and the air quotes, even through he wasn’t doing them, were loud. “He made you guys watch it?”

“Yeah. It wasn’t too bad.” Buck shrugged at the man’s incredulous look. “It was fun! Stupid and entirely unrealistic, but I liked that. If I wanted a documentary about what I do every day, I’d watch one.”

“This actually explains why you like Backdraft so much.”

“Hey! What is that supposed to mean!?”

“You know exactly what he meant by that, mi sol.” Eddie turned his head to smile at Buck over his shoulder as he loaded up the dishwasher, unperturbed by his husband’s glare. “How have you managed to stomach sitting through them filming it?”

“Lots of AA meetings,” Bobby answered, which yanked a bout of surprised laughter out of Buck. “Honestly, I tune out what they’re actually saying most of the time. I just tell them when they’re doing something wrong.”

“That’s probably not something to brag about, ‘cause there was a lot wrong in that single episode.”

“I’m only human, I can only do so much.”

“Pah!” Abuela flicked a hand at them. “Why let tiny things like that get in the way of a good story? Who cares if you wouldn’t do it like that in real life?”

“I do,” Bobby told her. “I care.”

“Pah!” she said again, getting up to give her plate to Eddie. “I hope you get me the autograph of this one, Eddie. I do not want a repeat of the last time.”

Because Buck was looking, he saw the pain that flashed across Eddie’s face at the repeated request.

“I will,” Eddie quietly answered, taking the plate from her.

They fell into an awkward silence as he rinsed it off and stuck it into the dishwasher with the rest, closing the door with a bit more force than necessary. When it was running, he whistled for Hoover and took him out back. Abuela watched him go before she turned back to Buck and Bobby.

“I asked him that already, didn’t I?” She sighed and didn’t wait for an answer, announcing, “I will be in my room.”

“Carla brought forms to go over with us and fill out,” Buck said, once Abuela’s door was closed. “Advanced Directive type things, for when…”

He trailed off, but Bobby nodded all the same.

“It must be terrifying,” Bobby whispered. “I suppose asking how you all are handling it would be a stupid question.”

“Yeah, probably.”

The other day, Buck found the Catholic Book of Prayers sitting out on Eddie’s bedside table. The copy that Bobby gave to Eddie, before his heart attack. It had a bookmark sticking out of it, marking the section titled “Prayers in Time of Sickness and Death.” Buck hadn’t commented on it, however much he wanted to, opting instead to let that sleeping dog lie. 

And for his part, there was still a hoard of loaves and other baked goods tucked away in the kitchen.

“So!” Buck chirped, all forced cheer. “How’s the studio without its resident Brit?”

“Like a vacation.”

Very rarely was life as an actual firefighter as glamorous as it appeared on TV. It was never more apparent than on calls like this one, when the ingloriousness of it slapped them right in the face. Or, as was the case today, in the nose.

They were summoned to an incident in downtown Los Angeles, at the sight of some road construction. Things had, somehow, exploded in a spectacularly messy fashion. Multiple cars were involved, but it luckily sounded like most of the drivers and passengers managed to make it out to safety on their own. When the 118 pulled up, it was to find a geyser spewing forth from the pavement in the middle of the mass of stopped vehicles.

“That doesn’t look good,” Hen commented as they hopped out of the engine.

“It doesn’t smell good, either,” Buck replied. It didn’t take much to guess what kind of water they were dealing with here. This stench was going to be stuck with them for the rest of their shift.

He was suddenly shoved aside as Brad pushed his way to the front to yell, as dramatically as possible,

“Thar she blows!”

The actor was in a spare set of turnout gear, because if he was going to be out on calls with them, then he was going to be as safe as possible doing it. Not that Buck was going to let the pretend firefighter run into anything dangerous, not even if Brad was the last person available, but one never knew what kind of situation could arise.

Ignoring Brad’s dramatics, Buck spotted a man in a hi-vis vest and safety helmet and headed that way.

“Are you the foreman?

“Henry Jennings,” the man answered, shaking his hand. “Department of Sanitation.”

“What’ve we got?” Buck asked him, moving around the stopped cars to get a better look at everything, though the spray was making visibility difficult. The foreman and some of the others followed behind him.

“About five-thousand gallons of wastewater.” That definitely explained the stench. “We were running pressure tests on the sewer lines.”

“Looks like they failed,” Chimney quipped.

“Went off like a bomb. His car blew up, but he’s okay.” Henry pointed over to where a man was sitting, shellshocked, off to the side. Without even a word from Buck, Hen and Chimney went to check him over. “Cars started crashing everywhere. I think there’s still people trapped in that one, pinned between two cars.”

Buck spotted which one he was pointing to, near the middle of everything. 

“Eddie, Ravi, we’ve got trapped victims,” he radioed. “The black SUV, between the copper and the blue sedan.”

“We’re on it,” Eddie replied.

“Any luck getting this water shut-off?” Buck asked the foreman.

“It’s a half mile away,” he replied. “Crews are working on it, but there’s too much running through.”

“Should’ve brought an umbrella.”

“Hey,” the foreman suddenly said, looking past Buck. Looking at Brad. “Do I know you?”

“No, no. No.” Brad shook his head. “I’ve got one of those faces, mate.”

Buck rolled his eyes and headed back for the engine. Brad and the paramedics, having returned from checking the driver over while he spoke to the foreman, followed him.

“How is he?” Buck asked them.

“Rattled,” Hen answered. “But fine, like he said.”

“Alright, good.” That was one more person he didn’t have to worry about. He couldn’t tell if there were more people in any of the other cars, so they would need to go through and check them individually.

“Cap,” Eddie radioed. “We’re gonna need more hands.”

“You’ve got ‘em,” Buck replied, motioning for the others to head that way. He was about to go as well, when Brad’s calling of his name stopped him.

“Can I come with?” the actor asked. “I’m good with the jaws.”

Buck bit back the immediate, instinctive response - “Fuck no!” - and spent a moment coming up with something more diplomatic. Something more akin to what Bobby might say.

“Maybe you should stay here and observe,” he suggested. “Watch how we do it and take notes.”

“Alright, yeah.” Brad nodded. “I’ll wait in the wings then, yeah?”

“Yeah,” Buck agreed, and then rolled his eyes the moment his back was to the guy.

It did not smell any better the closer they got to the SUV. When Buck got there, it was just in time to see them helping a man out through the roof of the vehicle and Eddie sliding in. There was water pouring out of the shattered window on the driver’s side.

“Check him over,” Buck told the nearest paramedic - Albert, in this case. He nodded and helped get the guy clear.

Over the water, a woman’s anguished cry could be heard.

“Eddie, what was that?” Buck asked over the radio.

“She’s got a laceration on her upper leg. Bleeding pretty good.”

“Right. Focus on that,” he told him. “We’ll deal with everything else.”

“Copy that.”

“There’s not enough space between the cars and the SUV, Cap,” Ravi told him, looking and smelling like a drowned sewer rat. “We couldn’t get to the doors to open them.”

Which meant there was no easy way to drain the water. At least it didn’t seem like there was an immediate threat of drowning at the moment, but it made treating the laceration difficult. Plus, sewer water, open wound.

Blegh.

“So we move the SUV,” Buck said.

“I’ll get the tow rope,” Chimney announced, already sprinting away.

It was an easy matter, getting the tow rope hooked up from the front of the fire engine to a hardpoint on the back of the SUV. From there, Toby eased the engine in reverse, dragging the SUV out from between the two cars with the squeal and crunch of metal. Buck directed, keeping an eye on the SUV, and waved Toby to a stop as soon as it was clear of both wreckage and geyser.

After that, they could get the doors open without problem. A flood of water came pouring out and Eddie switched with Hen, giving her access to the patient. It also freed up the others to go checking the other vehicles for anyone else who might be in need.

“Hey!” That was Brad’s voice. Where was he? “I got another one!”

Buck spotted the actor coming towards them from the mass of vehicles. He had an unconscious woman in his arms, carrying her without any apparent care.

“What the hell?” Buck whispered, heading that way. “Someone get- Albert, get that gurney over here!”

“Single car accident,” Brad recited as they worked to get the woman onto the gurney. “She was struck by the airbag. No signs of bleeding. Possible internal injuries.”

“Did you check her vitals?” Hen asked him.

“No.”

“How about for any head injuries?”

“I got her out of the bloody car,” the actor snapped.

Buck opened his mouth to say- He wasn’t sure what he was going to say. Nothing kind, certainly, with the anger coursing through his veins in that moment. But the woman on the gurney woke up and recognized the actor, which led to others on the scene realizing who he was and the crowd fawning over him.

Buck focused on getting the woman to the ambulance, calling for another RA unit for the woman in the car and getting her extracted. The ride back in the engine was uncomfortable, due to the stench clinging to them and the way that Brad yammered on about his heroics. Buck’s very apparent mood, to everyone except Brad, also did not help matters.

Several times, Toby glanced at him, only to grimace and return his eyes to the road.

Once they got back to the station, Buck hopped out and helped direct the trucks with backing into the bay. Then he stripped out of his wet, stinking gear and tossed them onto a wheeled rack. 

“Eau de sewer,” he heard Chimney complain. “Such a specific aroma.”

“Like sour milk and old fish guts,” Ravi said.

“Isn’t it glorious!?” The sound of Brad’s voice at that moment just made Buck angrier.

“Put your turnouts on here,” he ordered as he wheeled the rack to them. “Al, Chim, you’re on decontamination. The rest of you, wash the rigs. Brad!”

“Yeah? How can I help?” Brad eagerly asked as he shrugged off his coat. “Oh, I can get my PA to deliver scented can-”

“Shut the fuck up!” Buck snapped. Brad reeled back, eyes going wide with shock. The station fell utterly silent. “That stunt you pulled was the stupidest thing you could’ve done!”

“That woman was in danger,” Brad argued. “She was trapped in the car, she needed my help.”

“No, not your help,” Buck told him. “You could have paralyzed her! She needed a professional’s help. Someone who would know that we check for possible spinal injuries before moving anyone if we can help it. Someone who knew to put a C-collar on her first.”

“Okay, great.” Brad tugged out the small notebook he’d been taking notes in the entire time he was with them. “We tend to skip over these parts in the show, because they’re a bit tedious.”

Buck grabbed the notebook out of his hand and tossed it away. It sailed over Toby’s head to slap against the glass wall of the locker room and then land on the floor.

“Because you’re not a real firefighter!” he yelled. “You’re not a hero! You’re just an actor, a bad one at that. It’s only sheer luck that you didn’t injure that woman more. If you did something like that at a different scene, you could’ve put yourself in danger. Then my people would have to risk their lives to save you, too. And I am not going to risk their lives for yours!”

He stepped closer to Brad, and the man took a step back.

“You’re not a firefighter,” Buck repeated. “You’re an actor, here to watch actual firefighters. That is what you will do. You will put your ass on that bumper-” He pointed at the engine. “-when we arrive at a scene, and it will stay there until I say otherwise. But since you want some hands-on experience that badly, you can go help the actual firefighters make that bumper shine. Am I clear?”

“Got it,” Brad said.

“No.” Buck shook his head. “It’s ‘yes, captain.’”

“Yes, captain,” was the quiet response.

“Get to work,” Buck told him, and then turned on his heel.

He marched past the silent crowd of observers and headed for the showers, eager to wash off the stench and the anger.

Chapter 21: A Speech on a Runaway Nuclear Sub

Chapter Summary

In which the melodrama might specifically be a Brad Torrance thing.

Chapter Notes

cw: discussion of suicide and suicidal ideation, and some potentially tasteless jokes therein from Buck.

See the end of the chapter for more notes

There was an awkwardness lingering in the air following Buck’s public verbal flaying of Brad Torrance. None of them immediately spoke up after Buck stalked off to the showers, silently removing their turnouts and placing them on the rack as they were ordered. None of them, despite how much the smell of wastewater clung to their nostrils, were in a rush to go shower themselves. Not until Buck was done.

Now, they were getting the rigs washed down. Pieces of both the engine and the ladder truck were strewn across the bay, and members of the crew were scrubbing them clean. Others were taking sponges to the rigs themselves, from top to bottom. The inside of the cabs, too, were getting much needed attention since they’d sat in the seats with their dirtied turnouts.

Thankfully, it seemed that Buck had remembered to take them offline. There’d be no way they could respond to a call quickly enough with how things currently were.

Brad, in particular, was quiet as he polished the front bumper of the ladder truck. He’d changed out of his character’s costume and was now wearing a spare hoodie. The man looked every bit the definition of deflated following the dressing down, enough so that Eddie found himself tucking away his phone - he’d been switching between two threads of messages to gossip about what happened, one with Bobby, the other with Carlos and TK - to raise the man’s spirits.

“That’s some good chrome work, Brad.”

“Thank you for saying that, Edmundo,” Brad said, barely looking at him as he worked.

“No, I’m not just saying that. You could use that thing as a vanity mirror.”

“Well, I reckon when it comes to vanity, I’m a natural.”

Oh, wow. Buck really did a number on this guy. Brad was reminding Eddie of a balloon that someone popped and then left to lie in pathetic misery on the ground. He hadn’t realized the actor’s ego was that fragile, although he really should’ve.

“Hey, everybody on the team gets an earful from el capitán sometimes,” Eddie told him, trying for reassuring. “It’s part of the job.” 

That was an absolute lie. It might’ve been - almost definitely was - true when Bobby was in charge, but it certainly wasn’t the case with Buck. The only one of them that Buck ever talked to like that was Dalton Wolfe last year and he was a special case. Even then, Eddie was fairly certain he hadn’t done it in front of all of them as he did Brad. Partially because, altogether, he’d only been doing the captain job for a few months. Partially because he was still reluctant to dress down any of them like that, especially the ones who’d already been there when he started.

“But I’m not on the team, am I? I’m just an observer.” Brad countered. “No, what I really am is an impostor. The other Diaz had the right of it, I’m not actually a firefighter. I just play one on TV.”

“Come on, that’s not- Okay that might be true,” Eddie admitted. “But impostor’s a strong word.”

“I’m forty-seven years old,” Brad told him. “And I don’t have one real thing in my life.”

“Your show is real.”

“Hotshots?” The actor scoffed. “It’s a trifle with artificial sweetener.”

Ay, dios, even his self-pitying was pretentious.

“That tastes delicious,” Eddie tried. “Your show matters to people.”

“Who?”

“To your millions of fans and to um. To my son, Christopher! He’s a real big fan of the show.”

“Why don’t you bring him to the station?” Brad suggested, getting up to sit on the bumper he’d been cleaning. “Meet me in person?”

“He has met you in person, at the studio.”

Brad furrowed his brow, clearly trying to remember. Then his face lit up in recognition.

“Oh, right. The sprog that Bob brought with him.” He nodded to himself. “He’s a fan of the show?”

“He thinks you’re cooler than we are,” Eddie told him.

“My son was nine when I left, to test for a pilot for the CW,” Brad said. “It never went, but I never did quite make it back to England. He’s all grown up now, studying to be an architect. He’s getting married in the spring.”

“That’s great! Congratulations. Buck doesn’t even talk to his dad,” Eddie said, and then, “His birth dad, the one he grew up with. Not Bobby.”

“Mine doesn’t talk to me, either.” Oof. “Still holding out hope for the invitation, though.”

Brad pushed himself up from the engine’s bumper and walked off, and Eddie watched him go with a sigh. That conversation hadn’t really gone the way he’d wanted it to, not that he really knew how he’d wanted it to go. Maybe he should go check on his husband, see if he’d simmered down.

Buck was in the captain’s office, on the phone with someone. Someone important, from the sounds of it. And he apparently hadn’t simmered down, or maybe the phone call was just reigniting his temper.

“I know, ma’am,” Buck gritted out, fist pressed against the desk he stood behind. “I didn’t-... I didn’t ask to play babysitter!”

Eddie felt his brows skyrocket at the way his husband snapped at whoever he was talking to, and sat in one of the chairs in front of the desk. Buck barely acknowledged him.

“No one asked me about him being with us, Chief.” His tone was reined in again for the moment, thankfully. “He showed up and I was told-... I didn’t let him do anything! I told him to stay with the trucks and just watch us… Because I was busy doing my job? I had to oversee an extraction… You know we’re too understaffed for that, Chief… No, ma’am. I made it very clear that it won’t happen again.”

The call seemed to be winding down. A minute later, Buck was setting the phone back in its cradle, and then falling back into his chair with a puff of air. He carded his fingers through his curls, still obviously agitated, and gave Eddie a weak smile.

“Hi.” The tone was shorter than he meant it to be, judging from the way he immediately grimaced. “Sorry.”

“Bad phone call?”

“It’s all over social media, Captain Race Banner rescuing the woman from her car.” Buck rolled his eyes with a scoff. “So of course Chief Williams wanted to know what the hell I was thinking, letting him do something like that.”

This time it was Eddie’s turn to grimace.

“Ah,” he simply said. “Not to make it worse, but we might need to put Brad on suicide watch.”

“Hey.” Buck pointed at him with an exaggerated scowl. “I’m the only one allowed to make those jokes.”

“You never make funny ones,” Eddie retorted. “But seriously, I tried to cheer the guy up but I think I just made it worse.”

That had Buck frowning.

“Was I too harsh?”

“No.” Eddie quickly shook his head. “No, no. No. You should be like that more often. Maybe even in other aspects of our lives.”

“Get back to work.” Buck’s attempt at sounding scornful was ruined by his smile. 

“Yes, captain!” Eddie said, getting to his feet with a snappy salute.

His husband rolled his eyes at him.

“And keep Brad away from anything sharp,” Buck added.

“Seriously?”

“I told you, I get to make those jokes.”

Maybe Buck shouldn’t be making those jokes. Karma was clearly listening to him, judging from the call they were responding to.

There were calls that came in that firefighters dreaded. Anything to do with children, for example. Or certain areas of town that everyone knew was going to be a pain in the ass, just for the types of people that were bound to be involved. And then there were the calls that were, unfortunate to say, as routine as they were tedious, thanks to Los Angeles’ very nature as a city.

This one sent them to one of the overpasses crossing the Los Angeles River, which was today, as most days, decidedly lacking in the “river” part. Honestly, it was rarely ever much of a river, at least the portion that went through downtown. Just a large concrete canal that fed overflow directly into the ocean at Long Beach and served as a convenient spot for drag racing. When they reached this particular bridge, it was to find a man pacing on one of the concrete railings as a crowd of people gawked just a few feet away.

“What do we know about this guy?” Eddie asked as they all hopped out. Ravi and Toby immediately started herding the crowd out of the way.

“Just that the calls started about ten minutes ago,” Buck answered, before grabbing his radio. “Dispatch, send a crisis response team. And LAPD for crowd control.”

“Copy that, Captain One Eighteen,” the dispatcher responded.

“Hen, Chim, you here?”

“Right below you, Cap,” Hen answered. The fact that the concrete canal was almost always dry wasn’t just convenient for drag racing, it also made it convenient for them. He’d sent the ladder truck and one of the ambulances down below while the engine and the other ambulance came up on the bridge.

“Get that bag deployed, I don’t like how this guy’s looking,” Buck told her, then turned to Eddie. “Capture strap?”

“On it.” Eddie gave a nod and hurried back to the engine.

Brad had sat himself down on the front bumper of the engine, just as Buck told him to. That didn’t mean he wasn’t causing issues, though: someone in the crowd apparently recognized him, and now they were mobbing the guy. Toby and Ravi looked to Buck, clearly wondering what they should do about it; Buck just shrugged at them. It seemed like that was two problems solved, to him.

When Eddie came back with the capture strap, it was time to focus on the reason they were there.

“Hey, buddy.” Buck approached the guy on the ledge slowly, not wanting to spook him. Eddie was a half-step behind him. “Want to do us a favor and take a seat? Maybe we can have a chat, what d’ya say?”

“I think I’ll stay where I am,” the guy said, holding out his hand to keep them at bay. They both froze where they were. “And so should you.”

“We respect your space,” Eddie told him. “I’m Eddie, that’s Buck. What’s your name?”

“Craig,” he answered, continuing with the slow, careful pacing.

“What’s going on, Craig?”

“I just got laid off from work. That’s what’s going on.”

Craig came to a stop and then started to turn, to go back the other way. But his foot slipped, sending him falling onto the railing. He caught himself on his hands and knees, but it was enough to terrify Buck and Eddie, both.

“Guys.” Buck took the opportunity of the man’s distraction to quietly talk into his radio. “Is that bag ready?”

“Working on it,” Chimney replied.

Maybe they should start doing drills, see if they could speed it up some.

“I see that you have a wedding ring.” Eddie was wearing his shades, so Buck couldn’t see his eyes, but his face was angled towards Craig’s hand. A silver band was glinting on the man’s finger. “I’m guessing there’s somebody at home waiting for you?”

“You’d guess wrong,” Craig told him, pushing himself to his feet. “My wife left two months ago. There’s nobody at home but the TV. Nobody cares about me.”

“If that was true, we wouldn’t be here,” Buck pointed out to him. Craig paused to frown down at them. “Anything good on TV?”

“What?” Craig was looking at him as if he had two heads. Eddie was wearing a more subdued version of the same expression, tempered by familiarity.

“This one-” Buck used his thumb to gesture at Eddie. “-would miss his own funeral before missing an episode of one of his telenovelas.”

The nice thing about the Diazes was that, when they rolled their eyes, they put their whole head into it. Made it easy to know when they were doing it, even when Buck couldn’t see their eyes. Like now.

“At the moment, the one he’s watching is, uh…”

Eddie heaved a sighed, before saying,

“It’s Sed de venganza.”

“Right, that one.” Buck nodded. “And our son, he’s a fan of that Hotshots show.”

“It’s a good show.” Craig shrugged, a twitchy motion. “I watch every episode.”

“You’ll miss the next one if you fall,” Buck pointed out, and then a thought struck him. An idea that was so stupid, it wrapped back around to being genius. “Stay right there, don’t go anywhere.”

“What? Where is he going?” he heard Craig ask Eddie, after he turned and sprinted off to the engine.

“Everyone, make way! Give us room!” Buck shouted, flapping his arms to herd the mob of fans away from Brad. “Back away! Back away! Thank you.”
