Brad awkwardly retook his spot on the bumper, after he’d been standing around attending to his adoring fans. He looked for all the world like a dog that thought it was about to get scolded for piddling on the carpet. It was really starting to make Buck feel guilty for the way he laid into him.

“Sorry about that, Captain.”

“It’s fine, it kept them out of the way,” Buck said. “Remember how I said that lady needed a real firefighter’s help, not yours?”

“Yes…”

“Well this guy needs a fake firefighter. Specifically, Captain Race Banner.”

Brad was bewildered as Buck tugged him to his feet and guided him towards Eddie and Craig. Craig, for his part, was watching their approach wide eyed and slack jawed.

“You’re- You’re Brad Torrance,” Craig stammered in awe.

“Craig here is a big fan,” Buck informed the actor.

“I thought you’d be taller.”

“You’re standing on a ledge,” Brad reminded him.

“That’s true.”

“Craig here, he lost his job today,” Buck informed Brad.

“And his wife,” Eddie added, a bit quieter.

“Just the one?” Brad scoffed. “I’ve lost five.”

“Jobs?” Craig was stunned.

“Wives,” the actor corrected, walking towards the railing that Craig stood perilously on. “Not much luck on the job department, either, mate.”

Maybe Eddie’s quip about putting him on suicide watch wasn’t a joke at all. Jesus.

“What are you talking about?” Craig asked in disbelief. “You’re on a hit TV show.”

“Meaningless, disposable trash.”

Okay, yeah, concerning. Very, very concerning. Also not helpful. Brad was aware he was supposed to be talking the guy down, right? Not encouraging him into a swan dive?

“That is not true,” Craig protested as he crouched down on the railing. “When my wife left me, I binged the first three seasons. You’re my comfort, Captain.”

“I appreciate that, son, but you’re gonna have to switch the channel. Captain Race Banner is in a coma,” Brad replied. “And what the suits at the network don’t know yet is he’s never waking up.”

“You’re killing off Captain Banner?” 

“Afraid so.”

“Y- You can’t,” Craig protested as he shakily stood back up.

“Why would you care?” Brad asked him. “You’re about to end it all.”

“I’m considering it.”

“Great. I say we join hands. Go over together, eh?”

Red flag!

“Oh, mistakes were made,” Buck commented under his breath, to which Eddie frantically nodded in agreement. He grabbed his radio. “Uh, Chimney?”

“About twenty seconds more.”

“Do you realize how many people would be devastated if you did that?” Craig argued.

“Wait, is he talking Brad off the ledge now?” Buck asked. His husband shrugged, just as lost as he was.

“Two days on TMZ, tops,” Brad retorted. “Then they’d all forget about me.”

“You’re wrong,” Craig shot back. “I know it seems dark right now, but there’s one thing I can tell you. There’s a spark inside each of us. And if we just hold fast and refuse to let that spark die-”

“It’ll grow into a roaring flame nobody will ever put out,” Brad finished, perking up.

“What is happening here?” Eddie asked, just as lost as Buck felt.

“Season two finale,” Brad answered, flashing them a smile. “Captain Race Banner’s speech on a runaway nuclear sub.”

“It’s our son’s favorite show,” Eddie whispered, dread and horror lacing every word.

“You can’t kill off Captain Banner.” Craig was crouched down again, almost begging. “He’s what keeps the One Nineteen fire family together.”

Brad turned his head to look at Buck and Eddie; Buck nodded encouragingly to him. He even threw the man a thumbs up.

“Alright, Craig.” The actor turned back to him. “I’ll tell you what. I’ll promise you that Captain Race Banner will wake up from his coma. On one condition.”

“What’s that?” 

“You get down from there. Return to terra firma.”

“You swear?”

“Captain’s honor.” 

Brad held out his hand and Buck found himself holding his breath until Craig took it, letting the actor help him off the ledge. Buck waved for Albert, and he and Ravi escorted the man to the ambulance, ‘cause all jumpers got a reservation for a psych hold. Brad followed them, talking animatedly, while the crowd gave their applause.

“That was so stupid,” Eddie said, staring after them.

“It worked.” Buck leaned over the railing and gave those down below a thumbs up to indicate everything was good. “I mean, I totally thought we’d have to stop Brad from jumping, but it worked.”

Eddie just shook his head, muttering about how stupid it was the entire way back to the engine.

“I,” Chris said, excitedly bouncing in place, “am going to be the coolest kid in class.”

“What?” Bobby played up the faux insult. “Having a grandpops working here as tech advisor wasn’t enough?”

“No,” was the blunt answer. Hen burst into laughter beside them, desperately trying to muffle it.

Apparently, talking a fan off the literal edge was enough to offset being an absolute ass to restaurant staff, because Brad was back on set. Not that Bobby ever honestly thought he would be gone for very long, even if his ego constantly rubbed everyone around him the wrong way. Race Banner could’ve been stuck in a coma for another episode or ten, though.

But alas, they were filming the scene where he wakes up in the hospital. Not only that, but the idiots playing the roles of nurses and doctor were his idiots: Buck and Eddie for the former, Chimney the latter. And their acting was, sadly, about on par with the rest of the cast’s. 

While Chimney, or rather, the doctor explained to Race why he was in the hospital - an explosion at a bowling alley on orphan night, dear Lord - one of the phones in Bobby’s pocket buzzed. He’d been entrusted with Buck and Eddie’s, while Hen had Chimney’s. None of them were quite comfortable with turning their phones off completely, not with their history of disasters.

It was Buck’s phone that was buzzing, when he pulled them out. The name on the screen had Bobby glowering at it, even as he tucked Eddie’s phone back away. Almost everyone on Buck’s contacts list had a fun nickname of some sort. Fire Dad for himself, Dogheaded for Chris - a joke about how St. Christopher was depicted as a cynocephalus in iconography - and Literal Rocket Scientist for Karen.

Almost everyone on Buck’s contacts list had a fun nickname, not all of them. Margaret’s name, plain and simple, was glaring at Bobby from the screen. Margaret, not Mom. Bobby watched it ring, felt it buzz in his hand, and let it go to voicemail.

“How did I wake up?” Brad - Race Banner - asked, voice deepened for the American accent..

“In my scientific opinion,” Chimney - the doctor - said. “It’s a miracle.”

“Good thing I’m in the miracle business.”

Bobby cringed. Chris, beside him, was in awe.

There was a flurry of motion after the director yelled “Cut!,” everyone dispersing in various directions. Bobby waited, knowing that Brad would be coming his way, because he always did. Chimney ambushed him from the make-up station, apparently concerned that his delivery with the line was too much. A worry that betrayed his unfamiliarity with the show.

“So?” Brad asked when he did arrive, still in the hospital gown and sweats that the costume department put him in. “What do we think?

Buck’s phone buzzed again in Bobby’s hand, with a notification for a new voicemail message. Bobby wondered what was going on to have the Buckleys reaching out to their son like this, when they were usually so content to leave him be. Usually. Something like dread coiled in Bobby’s stomach as he realized one possibility, and he looked about for Buck in the post-shoot chaos.

“I think it was awesome!” Chris gushed, using his crutches to lean back and look up at Brad.

“Thank you.” Brad smiled at him. “But what about the scene? What are your thoughts?”

“I loved it,” Bobby answered, more focused on locating his son. “No notes.”

“Henrietta?”

“It was… Good,” Hen answered, not very convincing. “There’ll be music under it, right?”

“You hated it, didn’t you?” Brad was drooping before their eyes, fragile ego popped once more. “Where did I lose you?”

“No, you didn’t,” she told him. Brad didn’t look like he believed her. “You were in a coma, right? Well, when you opened your eyes…”

Bobby spotted Buck across the way, taller than most of the rest and looking ridiculous in his nurse costume as he and Eddie were chatting with Hailey, the three of them laughing at something. Abandoning Hen to Brad was probably unkind, but Bobby had other things to worry about. He hurried across the stage, dodging sethands, until he reached the Diazes.

“Buck.” He held out his phone. “Your mother called, she left a message.”

Buck looked curious as he took his phone back. Eddie, meanwhile, just looked annoyed. Those expressions changed, though, as Buck listened to the message that Margaret left him. Buck’s expression fell and Eddie’s turned concerned.

“Mi sol?” Eddie prompted, when Buck was just standing there, phone no longer pressed to his ear. “What did she say?”

Bobby knew the answer before Buck even spoke the words, quiet and lost.

“Dad’s dead.”

Chapter End Notes

I told you that my fics would never be a safe space for the Buckley parents.

Chapter 22: Let Me Open My Teeth (And Cradle You There)

Chapter Summary

In which Phillip Buckley has died.

Chapter Notes

Here! Have a really long chapter!

“I don’t know how I feel.”

Buck was in their backyard, curled up in one of the patio chairs with a leg tucked under him. In his hand was his tablet, Dr. Copeland’s politely concerned face on the screen. She’d managed to fit him in for an unscheduled session, as their regular one was a few days away still. 

“That’s perfectly okay,” Copeland said. “Especially when you’re still coming to terms with everything. Would you say that you’re numb?”

“I… No. Maybe?” Buck chewed on his lip. “I don’t think so. It’s like I’m feeling too much, and it’s all just this… Blur.”

“Your relationship with your parents has always been rather fraught. Even if it wasn’t, it would not be unexpected to have a storm of confusing emotions at a time like this. Is there any particular emotion, perhaps an especially strong one, that you can identify?”

He sat there and he thought about it, shifting through the storm that had been raging inside him since he heard his mother’s tired, tear-filled voice. Numb maybe would’ve been a good descriptor, actually. The kind of numb you got from trying to march through pelting rain, unable to see ahead of you, soaked through and freezing. The kind of numb that left you hurt and shaking.

But there was one emotion, cutting through the storm like lightning, that he could identify. It was white-hot and familiar, an emotion that was never far from him whenever it came to his parents.

“Anger,” Buck said, the word quiet and heavy. “I’m angry.”

“Are you angry with him for dying?” Copeland asked.

His laughter was sharp.

“No, I’m just…”

“Always angry at them,” she finished for him, when he trailed off.

“Yeah.” He chuckled. “Probably bad karma to be angry at a dead guy, right?”

“I know you’ve been there while Eddie and I went over this with Shannon,” Copeland chided, a delicate eyebrow raising slightly. “Rarely are we allowed to bury our emotions with those they’re associated with. We’re told not to speak ill of the dead because it’s considered impolite to tell everyone that they, for example, struggled with alcoholism or had a temper. But death does not erase how they still struggled with alcoholism, or that they still had a temper, and it does not erase how those who survived them were affected by their actions. Dying does not retroactively make us perfect.”

“Yeah, I- I know.”

That had been something Eddie had struggled with for the longest time, Buck knew. Believing that he wasn’t allowed to feel bitter and hurt and angry at Shannon after she passed, treasuring and hoarding a perfect image of her in his head for Christopher’s sake. But Shannon wasn’t perfect, however much Eddie loved her, and denying everything that made her imperfect and ignoring how those imperfections had cut at Eddie simply kept those wounds inflamed and unable to heal.

Eddie was allowed to be angry at her for the way she left, and came back, and then asked to leave again. Eddie was allowed to be hurt by it. It didn’t mean that the love he carried for her was lesser, nor that he was a bad husband or a bad father.

And Buck was allowed to still be angry at his father, even if the man was no longer around for it.

“Can you identify any other emotions?”

“Guilt.” The emotion pulled at him like water-logged boots, every step a drag.

“That, too, is understandable.”

She didn’t ask him why he would feel guilt. He’d told her about his father’s impromptu visit earlier in the year, about their meeting in the park that Buck himself had cut short. He’d told her about his father’s years-late answer to that question he asked at Bobby and Athena’s.

“He told me he loved me and I just left him,” Buck whispered. “And he was dying the entire time.”

Cancer. Leukemia. That’s what he had, according to Buck's mother. Taken by the same thing that had claimed his son. The worst part of it might’ve been how, when Buck thought back on that day, he could see it now. How thin his father looked, how worn and tired he had seemed.

He’d been dying, and Buck had barely given him the time of day.

“Let me ask you a question,” Copeland said. While Buck couldn’t see it, the motion of her shoulders told him that she was crossing her arms on top of her desk. “If he wasn’t dead now, or if you didn’t know he had died, would you still feel guilty about how that meeting went?”

“Yeah,” was Buck’s immediate answer. “I mean, I- I felt guilty afterwards, too.”

“But,” she said, stressing the word, “would you feel as guilty as you do now?”

“No,” he admitted.

“I told you, his death does not suddenly invalidate your emotions. Sometimes, hurts caused by those who love us - or who claim to love us - are worse than they would be if those same actions were done by someone else.”

“Yeah, I know.”

Again, not the first time they’d broached this topic. Not even the first time they’d talked about it in regards to someone he viewed through a paternal lens. He probably, almost definitely, would not have reacted so drastically if it hadn’t been Bobby, specifically, keeping him from returning to work after the embolism.

“Would you like to continue trying to identify your emotions?” Copeland offered. “Or would you prefer to move on and come back to it later?”

“Um.” Buck’s fingers tapped on the back of the tablet. “Move on.”

There was simply too much in that storm of emotions. Too much rain and wind and thunder. If he wasn’t careful, they’d spend the whole hour trying to name every drop.

“Alright,” she agreed easily enough. “The next important thing would be, I guess, the funeral. Are you going?”

“Memorial,” Buck corrected. “Mom had him cremated. But yeah, Maddie and I are both flying in.”

“It’ll be the first time you’ve been home since you left, right?” she asked. He nodded. “And how are you feeling about that?”

This time, there was no messy knot of emotions. There was only the one, thrumming like the string of a guitar.

“Anxious.”

Eddie felt a flash of warped deja vu as he watched his husband pack. A couple years ago, their situations had been reversed, sort of. It had been him packing to return home like the prodigal son while Buck watched, expressing his discomfort with the idea. Both of them were far too aware of the demons lurking in their childhoods to be happy about the idea of them returning to those settings on their own.

“It’s not too late,” he said. “I can still buy a ticket and come along.”

It would be expensive as hell, more expensive than it already was, and they probably wouldn’t even be on the same flight at this point. But he could still do it. He would be glad to do it.

“The station can’t be down three people,” Buck reminded him as he threw a sweater into his bag. “If you come, Chimney’ll come. And I don’t want to leave Hen scrambling for coverage or to be left shorthanded.”

“I just don’t want you to be there alone.”

“Maddie’ll be there.” Buck threw that sunshine smile at him from over his shoulder. “And so will Ma and Pops.”

“But I won’t be.”

“Hey.” Buck zipped up the bag and walked over to where Eddie was leaning against their dresser, to wrap his arms around him. “I’ll be fine, alright? I don’t think Mom’s going to be in the mood to start anything, anyway.”

Eddie let out a sigh and tilted his head forward to rest against Buck’s.

“You don’t know that, mi sol.” 

“Okay, you’re right, I don’t,” Buck admitted. Their breaths intermingled in the small space between them. “But like I said, Ma and Pops will be there with us. If she starts anything, they’ll cut her off. It’s not like we’re planning on spending more time than we have to at the house.”

“They keep hurting you,” Eddie whispered, reaching up to hold the back of Buck’s head, burying his fingers into his curls. “Every time they come back into your life, they hurt you.”

“I’ll be fine,” Buck said again, before kissing him. A quick peck that became more when Eddie refused to let him pull away.

It was an early start the next morning. Far too early, with Eddie pulling himself out of their warm bed after his husband. He grumped and grumbled the entire time he dealt with the electric shedemon in the coffee, his thank you coming out as more of a yawn than actual speech. Breakfast consisted of something quick and easy, made while Buck cradled a half-asleep Gavin to his chest.

Buck had, technically, already said his goodbyes to the boys the night before, since he was leaving so early. But Gavin was already up and about, if only barely - woken up by either the ruckus of them getting up and ready for the day, or by Hoover’s excitement over their unusually early start. He’d complained and demanded to be picked up, something Eddie knew that neither he nor his husband were going to deny their son, and now Gavin was well on his way to falling back asleep.

Honestly, Eddie was not far behind.

“I am not a bed,” Buck quietly complained, chuckling a little, when Eddie sat down in the chair next to him and then proceeded to lay his head on his shoulder.

“You’re not,” Eddie mumbled in agreement. “You’re a very good pillow. Right, Gav?”

Gavin didn’t answer, busy burying his face into his papa’s shirt as he was.

“You didn’t have to get up,” Buck pointed out. Eddie raised his head enough to blankly stare at him. “Well you didn’t.”

“Like I’m going to get any sleep while you’re gone,” he grumbled, then had to reach out and rescue his plate as Senorita leaped onto the table. “Hey now, little lady.”

“I blame you for her bad manners.”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Eddie said as he swapped the plate for the fluffy cat and cuddled her to his chest. She immediately started purring. “When are they picking you up?”

“Uh.” Buck glanced at the watch on his wrist. “Soon, I think.”

“That’s helpful.”

His husband just shrugged with his free shoulder as he went back to one-handedly eating his breakfast.

“Soon” turned out to be an accurate guess, however. They were just setting their plates into the dishwasher when Buck’s phone chimed. He went over to open the front door, still carrying Gavin, and stepped back to let Maddie in.

“You ready?” she asked, running her hand over her nephew’s hair. Said nephew grumbled and shifted.

“I just gotta go grab it all,” Buck answered. “I’ll put this one back to bed while I’m at it.”

“How are you holding up?” Eddie asked her, once it was just the two of them.

“Honestly?” Maddie let out a huff of air. She looked tired and drawn, dressed in an oversized sweater and sweatpants. “I have no idea. I mourned the parents I thought I had a while ago, but…”

“I get it,” he said, and then glanced at the hallway. “I wish I was going with you guys.”

“It’ll be okay.”

“That’s what he keeps telling me.”

She snorted, a soft little puff of air, and then she raised her hand, her pinky jutting out. Eddie rolled his eyes, but twined his own pinky around hers all the same, accepting the unspoken promise he was being given. It did, marginally, make him feel better.

“Alright, I’m good,” Buck announced, jogging into the living room with his bags. Three of them, including one that contained his funeral wear, and-

“What the hell is that?” Maddie demanded, pointing at the smallest of the bags.

“My carry-on.”

“It has knitting needles sticking out of it,” she said. “You’re bringing your knitting onto the plane?”

“I don’t think they’d appreciate me stress baking in the aisle, Mads.”

“Aren’t you on medication for this?” she asked, a bit exasperated sounding.

“Yeah! So imagine how I’d be right now if I wasn’t.”

“No thanks.” Eddie reached out to grip Buck’s shoulder, thumb rubbing at his pulse point. “Call me when you land, okay?”

“We have a layover in Chicago,” Maddie said.

“I’ll call you then, too,” Buck promised, giving him a quick kiss. “Don’t do anything stupid when I can’t be there.”

“I won’t, mi sol.”

“That includes hanging the lights up outside,” he said. “If you start decorating while I’m gone, wait to do the eaves until I get back.”

“Yeah, yeah. Vete, pendejo.”

Eddie stood on the porch as he watched Buck throw his bags into the trunk of Athena’s car. He stayed there, waving and aching, as they pulled away. And he hoped to God, or the universe, or whatever, that he wasn’t going to regret not going with them anymore than he already was.

It was very odd to be driving back into Hershey after all this time. The hours-long flight and the layover in Chicago, plus the three hour time difference, meant that they had pretty much lost the entire day. Buck was the one driving this time, in their rental. Privately, he thought Maddie was better suited, seeing as she’d been here more recently than he had, but she’d declined the offer. So here he was, following the GPS on his phone to their hotel.

“It doesn’t smell like chocolate,” Bobby commented from the backseat. He’d rolled down his window to stick his nose out, heedless of the chill. It probably didn’t bother him much, compared to a Minnesota winter.

“They shut down the factory a while ago,” Maddie said. She was in the back with him. “The Reese’s plant makes it smell like peanuts, though. And Etown still has the Mars plant, so it smells like chocolate.”

“The streetlamps are cute.” Athena was peering out the windows at them, looking at the Hershey Kisses shaped lights with interest. The closer they got to downtown, the more of them had Christmas decorations.

“We are known for one thing and one thing only,” Buck said. “And we’re gonna make sure no one forgets it.”

“Even though they don’t make their chocolate here anymore,” Bobby said.

“Semantics.”

It was Athena that picked their hotel, and it was her and Bobby who paid for the rooms. They ended up at a Best Western on Chocolate Ave that had not been there when Buck left town, with Buck sharing a room with his sister. He called Eddie and spoke to Chris and Gavin, while Maddie did the same with Chimney and Jee-Yun.

The next day was what Buck was dreading the most. Not the service for his father, but seeing his mother again. They made a stop for Athena to pick out a bottle of wine, to go along with the lemon loaves that Buck brought with them. Maddie also picked out a bouquet of flowers, and while Buck initially assumed they were for their mother, she left the bouquet in the rental when they got to the house.

“It looks the same,” Buck remarked, standing on the curb. He adjusted his grip on his wrapped up baked goods and tugged his coat tighter around himself; of all the things he didn’t miss about this town, winter was perhaps the thing he missed the least. “It looks the exact same.”

“I thought the same thing when I drove through on my way to Boston,” Maddie said as she stood beside him. Neither one of them were in any hurry to make the walk to the front door. “It needs repainting.”

She was right. There were a few spots where the paint was peeling or chipped. It was also lacking the tasteful white Christmas lights that their mother preferred to put up when the season came around. Buck could remember the strings lining the eaves and the windows, and following the sidewalk to the driveway. He’d always been jealous of the neighbors whose homes were a cacophony of bright colors.

They’d had that on the inside of the house, at least. They’d set up the tree in front of the living room window and decorate it with gaudy lights and gaudier ornaments. They’d do it together, Buck and Maddie, and Phillip, too.

Buck sucked in a breath and blew it out.

“Alright.” He raised his hand and stuck out his pinky. Maddie immediately hooked her own around it. “Let’s do this.”

Bobby and Athena, who’d been patiently waiting for them to find their courage, followed them as they trooped across the lawn to the front door, stepping through the brick entryway. The wreath that typically hung on the door at the start of December was also missing.

It was Maddie who knocked, looking for all the world like she was bracing herself for war. It would not be uncalled for, considering how the last couple of visits with their mother had gone. Buck was hopeful that those experiences would not repeat, that he wouldn’t explode like a grenade stuck in some idiot’s leg.

The way he was feeling, strung out and on edge, he would probably take out more than an ambulance.

When the door opened, when Buck laid eyes on his mother for the first time in more than two and a half years, his first thought was how old she’d gotten. She had not looked like this when she was last in Los Angeles, she had not looked this small.

“Maddie, Evan. You came.” Her smile was more of an attempt than a successful endeavor, and it slipped some when she saw Bobby and Athena with them. “And Robert and Athena.”

“We’re sorry for your loss, Mrs. Buckley,” Athena said. Margaret’s attempted smile wobbled and slipped even further.

“Yes, well.” Margaret dithered before stepping aside. “Come in.”

Unlike the outside, things had changed on the inside. Mostly small details that piled up. There was a new rug in the hall, he could see a new couch in the living room to their right. The dining table, in the room to their left, looked to be the same, but the checkered pattern table cloth on it was new, or so Buck thought.

“I uh, I’ve been baking,” Buck said, holding out the lemon loaves.

Margaret let out a little hum as she took them from him, and then the wine from Athena. She invited them to sit at the dining table as she took the loaves and the wine to the kitchen, and Buck could see an empty casserole dish on the counter when he peered through the doorway. He wondered how many saran wrapped dishes were in the fridge right now, brought over by well-meaning neighbors.

“I have orange juice,” Margaret said, raising her voice to be heard. “Would you all like some?”

“Yes, please,” Bobby responded, polite as ever.

“It is lovely to see you all again,” Margaret said as she carried a pitcher of orange juice to the table, along with glasses for all of them. Buck got up to help her. “I honestly wasn’t expecting you to come.”

“I told you that we would, Mom,” Maddie gritted out.

“You also said that your father and I were dead to you,” Margaret replied. “So I don’t see why you would care now that he actually is.”

Buck watched Maddie draw in a breath, and then another, making admirable efforts to stay calm.

“He was still my father,” was the answer she finally gave.

“You didn’t come with him when he visited LA,” Buck noted. Margaret just made a dismissive little noise. “He didn’t tell us he was sick.”

“He was diagnosed in February,” she said. That was just before he started calling Buck. 

“We saw him in April,” Maddie said.

“I don’t know what to tell you,” Margaret replied. “Maybe he just didn’t think you would care.”

“Mom.” Maddie lifted her hand to rub at her face. Their mother drew a breath in a hiss.

“That’s a new ring,” she stated, voice oddly flat.

“A new- Oh.” Maddie looked at the wedding band on her finger, along with the engagement ring. “Yes.”

“You’re married.”

“We got married in the spring.”

“I see.” Margaret’s mouth tightened. “And your father and I weren’t invited, of course.”

“Mom…”

“We were dead to you, of course we weren’t. Can’t even be told when we have new grandchildren.”

Buck shoved himself away from the table, feeling like he was a teenager again as he left without being excused. It was perhaps muscle memory that led to him stomping up the stairs to his room. What had once been his room, at least.

It definitely was not his room any more.

The dresser was the same, and the bed, and the table with the lamp beside it. But everything that had made it Buck’s room had been stripped away. The skateboard shelves, the signs, the giant letter E. He wondered if they’d packed it away in boxes to be stored in the attic, or if they’d gotten rid of it all. Donated, maybe, or simply set out on the curb for anyone to come and pick away at the remnants of his life in Hershey..

The closet was bare, save for some hangers and a box of junk that clearly had no better place to belong. The drawers of the dresser were in much the same state. Everything he hadn’t packed up and taken with him were all just gone, a realization that sent a pang through his chest even though none of it had really been all that important. It still would’ve been proof that he’d been here, though, that he had lived here and grown up here and bled here and screamed here.

A whim, or perhaps a hint of desperation, had him lifting up the mattress to look under it. And of course, that’s how Bobby found him.

“What are you doing?” the man asked, amusement and fondness in his voice.

“Oh, uh.” Buck let the mattress drop back down. “I was, um. Seeing if something I left here was still here.”

“Beneath the mattress? I don’t want to know,” Bobby said. “Is this your old room? I never would’ve guessed.”

“Yeah, they basically got rid of everything. Erased me like they did Daniel.”

They’d been thorough about it, too, since they’d gotten to what he’d tucked away between his mattress and box spring. In hindsight, it probably explained why his parents had not been surprised about Eddie. Which, ugh. There were worse ways for them to have found out, but still.

“I’m trying to imagine how it would have looked,” Bobby said, taking a seat on the bed. “I keep coming back to that loft you had.”

“A lot of that was Ali.” Buck took a seat beside him. “Uh. I was really into skateboarding at one point. I mean, really into it. I had like, five skateboards on my wall? A couple were turned into shelves.”

“Creative.”

“I thought it was pretty cool. I always wanted to stick glow-in-the-dark stars up there, but they wouldn’t let me.” He tilted his head back, to stare at the bare ceiling above him. “He said he loved me.”

“Phillip?”

“Yeah. He said he loved me, that that was why he and Mom kept me,” Buck said. “I asked him where that had been when I was growing up, but I never gave him a chance to answer. But the thing is, when I look back, I can see it. Flashes of it. When he bought me a new bike when I was a kid, and took me out for ice cream. When he taught me how to swim, or when he convinced Mom to let me play football in high school, or when he got me those skateboards. It was there, but it just…”

“Wasn’t enough?” Bobby asked.

“That makes me sound awful. I guess, it’s just- If he showed it all the time, that would be one thing, right? Or even if he’d never shown it at all, I could deal with that. But he only showed it sometimes, and all the rest of the time it was perfectly clear that Mom was the center of his world and I didn’t come into it at all. I mean, the only reason he got me that new bike was because Mom threw a fit and wanted the old one thrown away. And he just did it. Maybe he did love me, but he just… He didn’t love me enough.”

“What was wrong with the bike?”

“It was Daniel’s, I think.”

“Ah.” Bobby nodded. “You know, it seems like the One Eighteen just draws in people who have poor relationships with their parents. Ravi’s the only one I know that’s the exception.”

“Pretty sure Toby’s cool with his parents.” And then, after a moment’s thought, Buck added, “And Jones. His parents swung by the station a couple weeks after the anniversary, his mom made food for us.”

“I haven’t spoken to my mother in years,” Bobby said. “She does one of those travelling carny acts, claiming to heal people with the power of prayer.”

“Seriously?”

“Ann Hutchinson Ministries. She does it with my brother.”

“Pops, did you lie to us?” Buck asked with an overly dramatic gasp. “You said boys only had the one career option in your family.”

“Charlie always took after our mother more,” Bobby said. “I, meanwhile, followed in our father’s footsteps. The alcoholic fire captain.”

“Pops…”

“Come on.” He clapped Buck on the shoulder. “Let’s head back down and tag in, give your sister a break.”

They did not stay at the house for very long that morning, Buck and Maddie switching in and out to keep from hitting their breaking point with their mother. Eventually, however, they made a strategic retreat that had them all breathing a sigh of relief in the rental. This time, it was Maddie who took the driver’s seat, and she seemed to have a destination in mind.

That destination was a cemetery, about forty-five minutes away. Buck, for some neurotic reason, grew exceptionally nervous when he realized where they were. They parked on the edge of the grass, at the end of a long row of headstones. Neither Bobby nor Athena walked along with them, though they all four got out. Maddie led the way with the bouquet clutched in her hand, stopping on occasion to orient herself. 

The lonely looking headstone that Buck and Maddie came to a stop in front of was bereft of any flowers or decorations, a fact made even starker by the ones it sat between - the one on its right had a large and colorful array of flowers stuck into a vase, while the one on the left had a tiny little Christmas tree. The headstone itself wasn’t very ornate, and was actually rather simple: it was just Daniel’s name, and some dates, and an image of a dove at the top. Buck watched Maddie kneel down and place the bouquet in front of it, the winter wind biting at his cheeks.

“Um,” he said. “Hi?”

Maddie snorted out a laugh.

“I didn’t know what to say, either,” she told him. “I just talked about you. He named you, did I ever tell you that?”

“No,” Buck said, that fact leaving him feeling rather odd.

“He was insistent that they couldn’t name you something boring,” she said. “Or give you a weird name like mine.”

“It is weird.”

“Says the guy who willingly goes by Buck.” Maddie rolled her eyes and shoved at him. Then she turned back to the headstone and said, “I’m having another baby. We don’t know if it’s a boy or a girl yet...”

The service the next day was agonizing, in a way. Buck hadn’t been to a memorial or funeral service yet that wasn’t somehow agonizing, in truth. This one was uniquely bad, in that he was stuck sitting in the front row while Bobby and Athena found seats in the back, feeling uncomfortable and awkward in his funeral wear. And he had to suffer as people he didn’t even know or barely remembered came up to him and Maddie to offer condolences.

He still wasn’t certain where he landed, when it came to his feelings about his father being dead. The storm was still raging inside him, the rain still pelting against his skin, leaving him blind and numb. Sometimes, he wondered why he even bothered coming at all, if maybe it wouldn’t have been better to stay at home and figure it out without putting himself through this.

Then he looked at his mother, looking so small and alone, and the sight would rouse the little boy he used to be.

Which was weird, because Buck was starting to think he wouldn’t even care if she had passed. Not really. It was a thought that filled him with lead-weighted guilt. But while he could say with some confidence that Phillip did love him, even if all the love he spared for Buck was really just table scraps, he knew it wasn’t the same with Margaret. His mother looked at him and saw the ghost of Daniel haunting her, and she always would.

Maybe if it had worked, if Daniel had lived, she could’ve loved him. But it hadn’t, he didn’t, and her resentment and grief colored his entire childhood.

The people that came to the service were a mix of neighbors and old colleagues and students he used to teach. Buck didn’t know any of them all that well, only recognizing a few by their aged faces. There was one group, though, that lingered on the edges of the room after the service ended and they were stuck receiving well wishes. Buck wouldn’t have noticed them at all, except for the way they were staring at the Buckleys.

Or, no. At him.

“Who are they?” Buck asked Maddie, keeping the question a whisper.

“Who are who?” she asked, turning his head. “Oh.”

“Oh?”

“Our old neighbors.” She turned back, smiled at the newest stranger.

“I don’t recognize them.”

“You wouldn’t. They’re our old neighbors.”

“Our- Oh. Oh.” Buck craned his neck to look at them again. It certainly explained why they were staring at him, specifically. “Why are they even here?”

Maddie just shrugged.

Thankfully, none of them came up to talk, apparently content to gawk from afar. The guests all drifted out, leaving Buck and Maddie with their mother, while Bobby and Athena stood by the entrance. Ready to come intervene if they had to, no doubt.

“So,” Margaret sniffed. Just her tone had Buck’s hackles rising. “I suppose you’ll be leaving now.”

“Our flight’s tomorrow,” Maddie said, all forced patience.

“And I’m on shift the day after,” Buck added.

“Don’t even care that I’ll be alone for Christmas,” their mother sniped. “Probably won’t even come for my funeral.”

“Probably not,” Buck said, surprising even himself with his bluntness. “Because I’m not going to hurt myself for your sake.”

“You always were an ungrateful-”

“And you were an awful mother,” he said, sharply cutting her off. “And he was an awful dad! It was worse with him, though, because he could’ve been better, if he chose to. But he just kept choosing you! Now it’s too late to make any difference, it’s been too late. I lost the parents I could’ve had a long time ago. And you’re going to be alone for Christmas because of it, because you couldn’t love your kids.”

Margaret stood there, lips trembling. She didn’t say anything, though. No one said anything. Buck felt drained and tired as he left, Maddie following after him, to where Bobby and Athena were both waiting.

The flight back to Los Angeles was once again a long one. They boarded in the morning, and had a layover midway through. By the time Buck was standing in front of his house - still yet to be decorated with lights - the sun was long set and he was just desperate to go inside. He trudged up the drive to the front door, unlocked it, shoved it open.

And then froze at the sight in front of him.

Eddie, wearing naught but a button down, socks, and his tighty-whities, also froze.

“Buck!” he yelped and leaped to his feet, sprinting to turn off the radio. “You’re home.”

“And you are cheating on me with the fireplace shovel.”

Eddie stared at the small shovel still gripped on his hand, which he had been doing something with when Buck walked in, and tossed it away from himself. Then he smoothed back his hair as Buck dropped his bags and closed the door, patting at the dog when he trotted up to him.

“So- So- How was the flight?” Eddie managed to get out.

“Long,” Buck answered with a grin. “I like the get-up. I think you should dress like this all the time, babe.”

“Shut up,” was the grumbled response.

“Where’re the kids while you’re doing… Whatever this is.”

“I guess I have to make you watch Risky Business later,” Eddie said, and then sighed. “Chris and Gavin are at the Wilsons’. Abuela went with Pepa to see some of her other grandchildren.”

“Her least favorites,” Buck joked. “I noticed that no decorating happened while I was gone.”

“Chris insisted we had to wait until you got back,” his husband explained. “He wants to take Gavin to pick out a Christmas tree when we’re off.”

“We’ll mark it on the calendar,” he said. And then smirked as a thought came to him, eyes trailing over Eddie’s bare legs. “So we have the house to ourselves.”

“Yeah- Ah!”

Eddie yelped again when Buck suddenly picked him up, which quickly turned to laughter as he was carried down the hall.

“Last time we spoke, you were still trying to figure out your feelings regarding your father’s passing,” Dr. Copeland said, perched in her armchair. Buck sat on the off-gold couch, cotton candy pillow clutched in his lap. Eddie was beside him. “Have you made any progress?”

“Yeah,” Buck answered. “I mean, there’s the anger and the guilt. But I’m disappointed, too.”

“Could you tell me why?”

“Because now he’ll never be a better dad.”

Chapter 23: The Cold Front

Chapter Summary

In which it's the holiday season and the in-laws are in town.

Chapter Notes

It felt very weird to be writing Christmas chapters in April.

“So how many does this make?” Eddie asked over the headset.

“Uh.” Buck thought about it. “Counting the gingerbread mishap this morning, I think this is our twenty-fifth Christmas-related call.”

“Yes! That means we’re ahead.”

When the seasonal insanity started for real this year, someone stuck a scorecard up in the station’s kitchen with tally marks tracking how many Christmas calls each shift responded to. When they came in that morning, B-shift was behind at nineteen calls, while C-shift had been winning with twenty-four. Not that any of them would really be winning anything except some bizarre form of bragging rights.

Christmas itself was still days away and they were scheduled to work the day before. They’d also gotten stuck with that month’s full moon, which had just been a disastrous mess. Their shift came out of it with six holiday themed calls, including one involving an inflatable snowman that they’d all agreed to never talk about outside of therapy. Dr. Copeland earned her paycheck after that one.

The details for this call weren’t particularly clear, but it involved a tree, a cat, and maybe some minor to major impalement. Toby pulled the engine to a stop in front of a house bedecked in lights, with a team of shining reindeer pulling a sleigh in the front lawn. The ambulance, carrying Hen and Chimney, came to a stop behind them.

“I was always jealous of our neighbors’ lights as a kid,” Toby commented as they climbed out. “Then I started paying my own electric bill.”

“Yeah, our bill next month is going to hurt,” Buck agreed. “It always does. Worth it, though.”

It was a kid that answered a door, a girl around Chris’ age or maybe a little younger. She stepped back and yelled out,

“Mom! They’re here!”

“We’re in here!” a woman yelled back, and Buck led the way to the room her voice came from.

It was obviously the living room, based on the couch and the television. What drew Buck’s eye, however, was the large Christmas tree laying on its side, ornaments in various states of wholeness scattered around the floor and a toppled step ladder right beside it. Beneath it was a man that looked a bit worse for wear, with scratches all over his exposed skin from branches and needles and pieces of glass. There was also a small blood pool forming from the tree topper - a shiny, pointy star - sticking out of his shoulder, near his neck. 

“Hen, Chimney.” Buck just gestured at the man and they hurried to his side, digging through their bags. “What, uh. What happened?”

“Miss Mittens,” the woman answered. She pointed at the top of a bookcase where a sleek looking calico was cleaning herself, entirely unconcerned with the destruction and devastation below her. “She likes climbing the tree. We’ve been trying to get her to stop, but… Cat.”

“Oh, I know exactly what you mean,” Eddie said.

“I was trying to get her down,” the man added, face lined with pain. “Then she jumped and I lost my balance, and the tree fell, and…”

“You fell?” Chimney clarified. When the man confirmed it, Chimney pulled out a c-collar and started wrapping it around the man’s neck. “Doesn’t seem like you’ve got a concussion, at least.”

“This star is in there deep,” Hen said, eying the tree topper. “I think we’ll have to leave it in, let them take care of it at the ER.”

“Alright.” Buck nodded. “Anything else?

“There’s something wet here,” Chimney commented, patting the man down under the tree. “Can you feel your toes? Wiggle ‘em?”

“Y- Yeah.” The man grimaced a little.

“Not a spinal injury, then. Good.” Chimney pulled his hand out from under the tree, and then frowned at his glove. “Cap, this is blood. A lot of it. I can’t see where it’s coming from with the tree in the way, though.”

“Okay. Ravi?” Buck turned to him. “Go get the gurney?”

“On it!” the younger man said, and hurried back out to the ambulance.

“Eddie, Toby, help me with the tree.”

Buck winced with every ornament that crunched beneath their boots, but it couldn’t be helped. The three of them got into position and carefully lifted the tree up and off the patient, easing it back until it was standing once more. Now that they could see him clearer, it was more apparent how rough of a state he was in.

Also apparent was the source of the blood: there was part of a glass reindeer sticking out of the man’s thigh.

“I do not like where that is,” Chimney said, using the hand that wasn’t smeared with blood to pull a tourniquet from his bag. “Eddie, give me a hand?”

Eddie gripped the man by the shin and thigh, lifting up his leg enough for Chimney to wrap the tourniquet just above the glass ornament. Hen, meanwhile, was packing around the star and ensuring it didn’t move during transport.

“That reindeer was my mother’s,” the woman said, a bit mournfully.

“She never did like me,” the man said, lifting his head to glare at the ornament in his leg. “Bet the witch cursed it before she died.”

“Arnold,” the woman chided, sounding more exasperated than upset.

“You’re right,” the man, Arnold, sighed. “I shouldn’t be insulting witches like that.”

“I’m assuming you didn’t get along with your mother-in-law?” Buck guessed, stepping out of the way to let Ravi pass him with the gurney.

“Oh, we got along perfectly well,” Arnold said. “As long as she was in another state.”

That reminded Buck, he should ask Eddie if he knew what time Helena and Ramon were coming in tomorrow. Adriana and Sophia were supposed to be showing up, too, but he was fairly certain it would be later, closer to the holiday itself. Which was unfortunate, because Buck would much prefer them over Eddie’s parents. After all, they didn’t try to bully their way into parenting Buck’s kids.

(They also ganged up with him to tease and torment Eddie, but that was beside the point.)

It didn’t take long to get Arnold onto the gurney and then loaded up in the ambulance, to be taken away. His wife and daughter didn’t wait very long after they were told which hospital he was headed for, getting into their car and following him as soon as the last firefighter was out of the house and the door was locked. Buck couldn’t blame them, knowing he’d have been the same in their shoes.

From inside the house, Buck heard the crash of the tree toppling over again and was very thankful he and Eddie had their Christmas tree anchored to the wall.

It wasn’t often that Eddie cooked dinner. Not because, as some liked to jeer and joke, that he couldn’t cook. Because he could! Buck would be the first to tease him about his skills in the kitchen, but also the first to defend him against anyone else’s teasing about it, especially after that Valentine’s Day dinner. 

No, the reason that Eddie wasn’t often the one responsible for cooking was because he was living with Buck and Abuela. Both of them loved to cook, especially for other people. And Eddie loved to watch them in the kitchen, the pair of them working around each other while talking, with Bobby joining them on Sundays. Eddie loved to see how much his husband lit up at those times, every moment that brought a smile to Buck’s face a memory to treasure.

Just because Eddie wasn’t the one that usually cooked, though, it didn’t mean that he never did. Less now than he used to. Before they moved, before Abuela started living with them, he would cook more often to give Buck a break. That had been the intention today, but it was sadly not turning out that way.

“You’re stressed,” Eddie remarked, leaning against the wall and watching his husband fret about.

“I’m not stressed,” Buck argued, retrieving a toy from where it had been lodged under a couch cushion. “Why would I be stressed?”

The living room was bedecked in holiday cheer, a large Christmas tree looming in the corner and anchored to the wall with fishing wire. There were strings of lights hanging around the wall, and the colors played against Buck’s face to soften the edges even further. Eddie would happily watch his husband under any light, but normally Buck under the twinkling, colorful lights of Christmas was one of his favorites just because of the soft smile Buck would usually have.

That smile was nonexistent at the moment, however, replaced by a tight expression that reminded Eddie far too much of Shannon in El Paso.

“Mi sol,” Eddie sighed. He crossed the space to pull Buck into his chest. “If Mom and Dad do anything, we’ll just kick ‘em out. It’ll be fine.”

“Chris wants to see them,” Buck replied, leaning into him. “Abuela wants to see them, or at least your dad. We can’t just kick them out.”

“Please, if they say the wrong thing, ‘Buela will be the first one chasing them out the door.”

“That’s… Okay, that’s true.” Buck turned in his arms to kiss him, mouth tasting vaguely of peppermint from the candy cane he’d been tormenting Eddie with earlier. “Dinner’s smelling good.”

That would be the barbacoa that Eddie had in the slow cooker. It had been in there for hours now, pretty much the entire day, and would hopefully be ready just in time for his parents to arrive. He’d volunteered to cook today because his husband really had been stressing about Eddie’s parents coming, more so than usual. A lot more than usual, actually.

Buck normally just grumped and grit his teeth and rolled his eyes until they were gone.

“Oh!” Speaking of things that would stress out Eddie’s husband. “I might need to change my schedule for the next few months.”

Buck pulled away to frown at him.

“Why?” he asked, eyes flickering around as he clearly did his best to come up with a reason. “Wait, you’re not thinking of changing shifts because of Abuela, are you?”

“No, no.” Not yet, anyway. “Uh. I was giving the idea of getting paramedic certified a shot. We were basically down to one ambulance while you were in Hershey.”

Hen was capable of a great many things. But she couldn’t be fire captain and paramedic, the two roles simply demanded too much individual attention. Which meant that while she was captain in Buck’s stead, the only paramedics they’d had were Chimney and Albert. Hell, on regular shifts, one of them was typically being sent off on their own with only an EMT-trained firefighter as assistance. Or with Eddie.

“Oh! Okay.” His husband nodded. “Okay, yeah, that- Obviously that’s not a problem. I’ll look up the dates for the classes.”

“It’ll leave you short on people on those days, though.”

“We’re already short on people,” Buck retorted. “I got Williams to promise we’ll get a probie when they graduate, though. I was thinkin’ I’ll have Ravi train ‘em.”

“Don’t you already have him shadowing Toby?”

“He’s a smart guy, he can do both,” Buck said with a dismissive flick of the wrist. He was looking significantly less stressed than he’d been just minutes earlier, simply talking and being distracted doing wonders for him. “‘Sides, he’s been doing that for a couple months. Even Gavin could figure out what switch turns on the sirens by now. Actually, maybe that’s not a fair comparison. Our kids are geniuses, after all.”

Before Eddie had the chance to come up with a response, or even think of a joke, there was knocking at the front door. Both of them stiffened at the noise before they turned to it, Buck letting out a little groan as Hoover came running into the room with Gavin chasing after him.

“Are they early?”

“And the barbacoa's not done.” Eddie grimaced. “It’s still got thirty minutes.”

“If they complain, we’ll feed them dog food,” Buck told him, fixing on a smile and heading to let them in. The moment he opened the door, however, he immediately relaxed. “Pops! Ma! Oh, thank God.”

“I like that reaction,” Athena said with a laugh. She led the way inside, Bobby following loaded down with bags. Gavin, spotting them, start bouncing up and down while shouting,

“Nana! Grandpop! Nana! Grandpop!”

“Nevermind, I think I prefer this one,” she joked as she lifted Gavin up.

“We weren’t expecting you guys,” Eddie said, joining them at the door.

“That was obvious,” Bobby pointed out. He lifted up the bags. “We figured we’d bring everyone’s gifts before we fly out.”

The Grant-Nashes were flying to Florida for the holiday, to spend it with Michael and David. There was also discussion about going to visit Athena’s parents while they were there, something that had everyone wishing Bobby luck. The fact that Bobby and Athena weren’t going to be around for Christmas was undoubtedly not helping things for Buck.

“Who were you expecting?” Athena asked, fingers running through Gavin’s hair.

“His parents,” Buck answered, and got an understanding ah from them.

“I’ll stash these with the others,” Eddie said, taking the bags from Bobby.

They were storing all the presents in the garage-turned-home gym, so he took the opportunity to bring Hoover outside for a bit. When Eddie got back, it was to find that Chris had left the seclusion of his room and was now chatting with Bobby in the kitchen.

“Buck said you were making barbacoa?” Bobby asked, peering at the slow cooking with interest.

“And it’ll even be edible,” Eddie stated with a sniff, which got Chris to laugh. “Buck’s been stressing about my parents. He doesn’t normally, so I have no idea why he is now.”

“Yeah, it’s weird,” Chris agreed, making a face. “He normally just complains about them when he thinks we can’t hear.”

“It’ll be fine,” Eddie said when he saw Bobby turn a worry frown Buck’s way. “It’s not like we’re hosting his mother.”

That would have been a disaster. Eddie was secretly - at least as far as Buck and Maddie were concerned; he was pretty sure everyone else was well aware - glad that Phillip was dead. In a perfect world, Margaret would’ve followed her husband so that there was absolutely no chance of her showing up to darken her children’s lives again.

“I think it’s because of Abuela,” Chris stated. He was pawing through the pantry until Eddie, with a scowl, shut the door.

“You’ll spoil your appetite,” Eddie told him, ignoring his son’s pouting.

It probably was because of Abuela, come to think of it. Buck had even brought her up earlier. Usually, when Eddie’s parents were visiting, Buck provided quiet support while allowing Eddie and Abuela and, when she was there, Pepa to take the lead with handling them. But with Abuela’s diagnosis, Buck probably figured she wouldn’t be up to it this time. And no doubt Eddie’s parents would be even more overbearing because of it.

Which meant Eddie would have to husband up even more.

Bobby and Athena didn’t stay for long, taking their leave to head back to their temporary residence and finish packing for the flight. Buck was relaxed after their visit, smiling. He hung off Eddie, chatting in Eddie’s ear as he tore the barbacoa apart with a pair of forks and then drowned it in the liquid left in the slow cooker.

It, of course, did not last. Knocking at the door again, louder and more insistent than Athena’s own, had Buck drooping with a sigh.

“I’ll answer it,” Eddie told him, pressing a kiss to his temple. “Go tell Chris and Abuela.”

“Copy that, babe.”

Eddie watched his husband march off down the hall, grimaced as his father - and it definitely was Ramon - knocked once more. He squared his shoulders, patted Hoover as the dog padded along at his side, and answered the door.

“Mom, Dad, hi-” He stopped and stared at the bags that they were holding. “Did you get take-out?”

“It’s not Fu Chow’s,” Ramon said, brushing past him. “But it’ll do.”

“I told you I was cooking,” Eddie told them.

“Oh,” Helena said, setting the bags in her hands on the dining table. “Did you?”

“Yes.” He shut the door, with perhaps more force than necessary. “I even told you what I was making.”

“Well, you know. Now there’ll be more options,” she said. “Should the dog be inside while we eat?”

“We’re not kicking Hoover out.”

“Ramon!” Abuela’s voice cracked through the room like a whip. She came into the dining room a moment later, Hoover hurrying to her side. “[You brought your own dinner? Where are your manners? I raised you better than that!]”

“Isabel, hable ingles, please,” Helena said, rolling her eyes.

“She said it was rude of you to bring your own dinner.” Buck was scowling at the bags of Chinese food on the table. Gavin was perched on his hip, eying Helena and Ramon curiously but nowhere near as excited about them as he was with Bobby and Athena.

Helena’s expression tightened with a scowl before it cleared up.

“It’s fine. More options, like Helena said.” Ramon went to his mother, hugged her, and then looked her over. “You’re looking good, Mama.”

“Thank you. Buckito, can you put all of that in the fridge?” Abuela asked, making a sweeping gesture at the food that her son and daughter-in-law brought. “It can keep until later.”

“‘Course.” Buck set Gavin down, the tot clutching at him for a moment, and then gathered up the take-out on the table.

“Isabel-” Helena started, only for Abuela to cut her off with a,

“Pah!” She even held up her hand in Helena’s face. Eddie had to cover up a snort of laughter. “I have been smelling Eddito’s barbacoa for hours now. That is what we will all be eating.”

Eddie couldn’t help but grin as he moved to help Buck gather everything up. He gave Chris’ shoulder a squeeze when the teen joined them in the dining room, and followed his husband into the kitchen to put everything in the fridge. He caught Buck frowning, though.

“What’s wrong?” he asked, keeping his voice low.

“Nothing,” was the immediate answer. Buck managed to last two seconds under Eddie’s stare before breaking. “No, seriously, it’s…” He let out a sigh. “She forgot they were coming today.”

That took the wind out of Eddie’s sails.

“The decorations outside are... Interesting,” Ramon said later, when they’d all sat down for dinner. “The bunting along the fence, I mean. And the flags.”

The rainbow bunting, and the pride flags. Eddie hadn’t even thought about them still being up, he was so used to them being there now. They’d even twined some of the Christmas lights around the bunting.

“We had issues with one of the neighbors last year,” Buck answered. “Turned out they were homophobes.”

“Their brats threw eggs at the house. Buck can be petty,” Eddie said with a smile. He sat at one end of the table, Abuela at the other. “Gavin, Hoover has his own food, stop feeding him yours.”

“I told you,” Helena said. “He should be outside while we’re eating. Here, I’ll take him out.”

“Hoover’s fine,” Buck said, tone just short of being sharp, before she could get up. “As long as someone actually eats his food.”

He turned his head to give Gavin an exaggerated face, which had the tot laughing.

“I gotta say,” Ramon said, pausing to eat a forkful of barbacoa. “I was surprised when Eddie said he was the one who cooked. I figured it would be you, Buck.”

Something flickered across Buck’s face: the ghost of a scowl, an aborted eye roll.

“I can cook, you know,” Eddie said, stabbing into his food. “Obviously.”

Chris had spent the entire dinner stuffing his face instead of talking. It was very heartening.

“I just meant,” Ramon said, “that I figured it would be… more Buck’s thing, mijo.”

“We take turns,” Buck told him, a sarcastic smile on his face. 

“I’d be a bad husband, and grandson, if I expected him and Abuela to cook for me and the kids all the time,” Eddie pointed out, and didn’t understand why his husband huffed out a laugh.

“I’m getting a refill,” Buck announced, getting to his feet. “Babe, want another beer?”

“Por favor.”

“Can I have seconds, Pops?” Chris asked, holding up his plate.

“Here, honey, I’ll get that for you,” Helena said, already moving to take the plate from Chris.

Eddie watched Buck open his mouth, before shooting a look at Chris and then simply shaking his head. Choosing their battles was probably going to be the theme of this visit. At least it wasn’t too bad so far.

Chapter 24: The Language Used

Chapter Summary

In which Buck vents, and Helena Diaz pushes at limits.

“It was so bad,” Buck complained with a groan as he sank down in the chair, squeezing in between his sister and the arm. Chimney was sitting on the other end. “I shoulda gone to Florida with Ma and Pops.”

It was the next day, and while Ramon and Helena obviously had not stayed the night, thank God, there was the looming threat of them returning that got more dire as the clock ticked closer to noon. So Buck made the strategic decision to pack Gavin into the jeep and flee to his sister’s for lunch, and maybe the majority of the afternoon. He hadn’t been the only one with that idea, because Josh was also there when he pulled up.

Maddie and Chimney’s house was not as insanely decorated as Buck and Eddie’s, but that was because Buck had the tendency to go a bit overboard and his impulse control was Eddie. Therefore, “not as insanely decorated as Buck and Eddie’s” still left a lot of wiggle room. Before Doug, Maddie had loved Christmas just as much as Buck did, and in the years since her return from Boston, that had started to show again. Mainly in the form of a giant tree covered in twinkling lights and silvery tinsel that got everywhere, along with garland strung up all over the wall and stockings hanging from the fireplace mantle.

At the moment, Gavin and Jee-Yun were doing who-knew-what in the other room. There was the occasional crash or loud bang that paused the conversation, but the lack of cries meant it couldn’t be anything too terribly bad.

“What was so bad about it?” Maddie asked. She wasn’t showing yet. Buck was tempted to ask about the baby, but he wasn’t sure if Josh knew or not. “Besides the usual.”

“The usual,” Buck retorted. “They stopped and got Chinese for dinner. And I know that Eddie told Helena he was cooking, I was right there when he talked to her on the phone!”

“That bitch.”

“I thought you were getting along with them?” Chimney brow was furrowed. “She gave you that recipe, Eddie’s dad was actually tolerating everything. And they came down for Gavin’s birthday last year.”

“They were just as bad then, too,” Buck grumbled. “Pretty sure Helena’s campaigning for us to get rid of Hoover.”

“That bitch,” Maddie repeated with a small smile.

“And Ramon is tolerating,” he emphasized. “He definitely still doesn’t like it. Made some comment about how he thought cooking would be more my ‘thing.’” He lifted up his hands to do air quotes around the word. “Y’know, because clearly I’m the wife in this relationship.”

Josh, sitting in one of the arm chairs, scoffed and rolled his eyes and asked,

“What did you say?”

“That we took turns,” Buck answered, smirking. 

Josh guffawed and Maddie let out a long, drawn out,

“Eww.”

“I don’t get it,” Chimney said. Josh reached over and nudged him in the ribs, eyebrows doing some weird wagging thing. Chimney stared at Josh for a moment, uncomprehendingly, and then his face scrunched up in disgust. “Oh, God, I did not need to know that!”

“And I did not need to know you had sex with my sister,” Buck shot back. At the other man’s warning look, he followed it up with, “But my kid’s playing with the reminder.”

“True,” Josh agreed with a nod. “Politically, I’m tolerant of the heterosexual lifestyle. But I find the actual act to be rather revolting.”

“The worst part of what you just said,” Chimney said, pointing a stern finger at the dispatcher, “is that these two goobers don’t even know what you’re quoting!”

“That wasn’t a Glee quote, was it?” Buck asked his sister.

“No,” she scoffed. “Wait, have you ever watched Glee?”

“I think I watched the first episode.” Buck shrugged. “Maybe.”

Josh’s gasp of offense was far too dramatic, in Buck’s opinion.

“Yeah, yeah, whatever,” Buck grumbled. “I’ll get to it whenever.”

“No, seriously.” Josh sounded appalled. “Are you sure you weren’t raised Amish?”

“Just in Amish country,” Maddie said. “When are his sisters getting here?”

“Adriana’s coming in this evening, Sophia’s tomorrow,” Buck answered. “Pretty sure they’re staying until New Year’s, there was something about dragging Eddie out for sibling bonding time. I think they just want to get him drunk and embarrass him.”

“Maybe we could have a girls’ night.” Maddie tilted her head in thought.

“I’ll take Jee and flee for Hen’s that day,” Chimney said, which got a laugh from everyone else.

“I’d offer mine for refuge,” Buck told him. “But I have no idea when Helena and Ramon are going back.”

If it was up to him, they’d be gone the morning after Christmas.

If Eddie were a better brother, he would probably have picked his sister up from the airport. But seeing as he wasn’t, and also that LAX was a hellmouth, he didn’t. Adriana needed to pick up her rental and then check into the hotel room she was sharing with Sophia, anyways, so it was fine. Totally not at all deserving of the way she socked him in the chest when he opened the door.

“Hola a ti también,” he said, rolling his eyes and pulling her into a hug. “Brat.”

“Me cago en la leche,” she grumbled into his shirt.

“That’s Spanish Spanish,” Eddie couldn’t help but point out.

“Their swears are fun to say, so I don’t care. The traffic here is hell, I’m making Sophie drive when she gets in.”

“Have fun picking her up at the airport.”

“Que te folle un pez.”

Adriana was the youngest Diaz sibling, the baby of the three, and able to get away with just about anything. She and Sophia had both been lucky in that way, with none of the expectations that their parents laid on his shoulders and none of the disappointment for failing to meet them. Eddie was positive that Adriana was the one responsible for all the worst Spanish swears that both Buck and Chris knew.

“Chris! Gavin!” she shouted as she stepped around Eddie and into the house. “Your favorite tia is here!”

“But Dad said Tia Sophia would get here tomorrow,” Chris replied, standing in the doorway to the dining room and blinking guilelessly at them.

“Ay! The cheek on you.”

“Where’re my presents?” the teenager demanded, looking pointedly at Adriana’s empty hands.

“Why would I get my least favorite nephew anything, huh?” she retorted. “You’ll get them on Christmas, you greedy thing. If I like you enough.”

“Fine,” Chris sniffed.

“Fine.”

There was a moment of silence where they stared each other down, Eddie rolling his eyes at them while they weren’t looking, and then they were breaking into laughter and hugging. Ramon, sitting at the head of the dining table beside Abuela, let out a little laugh of his own.

“Look at you, you’ve grown!” Adriana gushed over Chris, messing his curls. “Growing up so big and strong and manly! You obviously get that from Buck.”

“Gracias, Adri,” Eddie dryly said.

“How was the flight?” Helena asked from the kitchen.

Adriana looked up and Eddie, thanks to where he was standing, got to see his sister’s face fall a little when she saw what their mother was doing.

“It was fine,” she said, and then under her breath so only Eddie and Chris could hear, “You couldn’t have warned me that she was cooking?.”

“Mom insisted,” Eddie said with a grimace. “Buck’s outside with Gavin and Hoover.”

Buck made the retreat not long after he got home from Maddie and Chimney’s to find the kitchen taken over. Eddie could actually see his husband biting his tongue before he disappeared out the backdoor, tablet in hand.

“So that’s where all the cool people are,” Adriana stated.

“But I’m right here,” was Chris’ immediate reply.

“I said what I said,” Adriana told him, tone haughty, before going to Abuela, who welcomed her in with a hug.

“It’s been too long,” Abuela said, letting her granddaughter pull away after a moment before pinching at her. “And you’re too skinny.”

Eddie didn’t say anything. He didn’t have to say anything, because his sister knew exactly what he would say. She turned her head with a warning glare that increased in venom when he smiled pleasantly in return.

“How are you, ‘Buela?” Adriana asked, turning back to smile brightly at her grandmother.

“I’m fine,” she insisted. “Everyone’s worrying too much.”

“That’s what you always say,” Ramon told her with a scoff. Adriana echoed it.

“Got any more stents put in without telling us, Papi?”

“No,” was the flat answer. “Chris, what about another game?”

Chris sent Eddie a look of suffering, then he sighed and drooped slightly where he stood.

“Okay, Grandpa,” he said.

“I’ll get the board,” Ramon said, getting out of his seat and heading for the living room.

“Chess,” Eddie explained to Adriana, when his sister shot him a questioning look. She frowned, nodded, and, after a glance at their mother, headed for the backdoor. Eddie followed her, relaxing the moment that the door closed behind him.

“Oh, God,” Buck intoned, looking up from his tablet. He was slouched in one of their patio chairs, a leg tucked beneath him. Gavin was shrieking as he sprinted back and forth across the grass, Hoover loping behind him. “You’re here.”

“Yes, yes, the prettiest of the Diazes has arrived,” Adriana declared, throwing out her arms. It was surely an accident that she managed to smack Eddie in the face when she did it. “You may rejoice, now.”

“That doesn’t make sense,” Buck told her. “Because I married the prettiest.”

“Aw, thank you, mi sol.” Eddie went over and kissed him, giving his sister the finger when she made melodramatic sounds of disgust. “We’ll have to rescue Chris in a bit, Dad’s got him playing chess again.”

“Chris not a fan?” Adriana asked, throwing herself into one of the empty chairs.

“He hates it,” he told her. “He’s good at it, but he hates it.”

“I’ll make a comment about the little horse guys being a choking hazard or something,” Buck said, dropping the tablet down onto his lap. The screen was taken up by a paused youtube video of a PBS documentary about the Gilded Age. Eddie wondered what rabbit hole led to that. “Your mom will throw it all out the door.”

“How bad have they been?” Adriana asked, and then laughed at Buck’s answering groan. “Yeah, I figured. How did Mom end up cooking?”

“Hell if I know!” Buck exclaimed. “I come back from Maddie’s and I find her invading my kitchen.”

“Hey, it’s another day you and ‘Buela don’t have to cook,” Eddie said, trying for peace. “You’re getting to sit out here and do nothing, and then you’ll get to go in there and eat.”

“That’s the only reason I’m not raising a bigger fuss,” his husband grumbled. “That and the fact that they brought their own groceries. But if she tries it on Christmas, I’m tossing her out. I’m serious, Eds, I have the whole meal planned and I will not -”

“I know, I know.” Eddie rubbed at Buck’s shoulders. The meal had been written down weeks ago on a piece of paper that was stuck to the fridge door, lines scratched out and rewritten as Buck and Abuela dithered on what to make. Eddie, of course, would be perfectly content to devour anything they set down in front of him. “I’ll make sure she knows that, too. It’ll just be you and Abuela in the kitchen, the entire day.”

“And maybe Chris.”

“And Chris.”

“Christopher Diaz!” Helena screeched from inside, loud enough for them to hear. The three of them all turned to the backdoor and then to each other.

“Speaking of.” Adriana was frowning. “What was that about?”

“I’m about to find out,” Eddie told her, heading inside. Hoover trotted up to hover anxiously at his side, no doubt as perturbed by Helena’s volume as the rest of them.

When he got into the house, he found Helena at the dining table, looming over Chris. The teenager was glaring up at her mulishly, which was mostly concerning for the way that Abuela was mirroring the expression. The chess set that Ramon had brought with him was set up on the dining table, a couple pawns making progress across the squares. Ramon himself was back in his seat at the head of the table, a stern expression on his face.

“Mom? Dad?” Eddie called out. “What’s going on?”

“What’s going on is the language our grandson is using!” Helena said.

“Well, we are a multilingual household,” he couldn’t help but point out. His mother was not amused, turning to glare at him.

“My grandson using such foul language-”

“I didn’t know Chris was learning German.” That was Adriana, who had followed him inside. Buck was right behind her, Gavin wiggling under his arm.

“This is not a joking matter.”

“Helena, it’s just cussing,” Buck said, barely hiding the way he rolled his eyes. “I know that Chris didn’t cuss at you. Right, Chris?”

“No, Pops,” was Chris’ answer.

“And that he knows the time and place for it,” Eddie added, and got a dutiful,

“Yes, Dad.”

Of course, while home might’ve been the place for it, in the middle of his abuelos’ visit was definitely not the time. Eddie had assumed that went without saying, but perhaps he needed to explain it.

“So you’re just fine with him talking that way?” Helena demanded with a huff.

“Mom, he’s been in the room while Abuela cooked,” Eddie told her. “The ship has sailed.”

“He has a point,” Ramon said, and quailed a bit when his wife turned on him. “Mama taught me most of the swears I know.”

“He’s a teenager, they cuss,” Eddie said. “Chris, go wash up for dinner.”

“Okay!” Chris got up and hurried out of the room, throwing him a thankful look.

“I’m not sure about having that out,” Buck said, casting an anxious glance at the chess board. It was overly acted, in Eddie’s opinion. “Gavin is still in the phase of stuffing everything into his mouth.”

That was not remotely true, and hadn’t been for several months now. But it had Helena quickly turning her attention and scorn onto the game, and then her husband, smacking at him until he got to his feet and started packing it away. Adriana covered up a laugh with a fake cough and Buck smirked as he headed down the hall with Gavin, no doubt to check on Chris.

“I’m going that way,” Adriana told Eddie. “I still haven’t gotten to hug my other nephew.”

Eddie took one look at his sister’s retreating back, then one at his parents, and quickly decided that she had the right idea of it.

Chapter 25: Merry Christmas from the Family

Chapter Summary

In which the author manages to make the 25th chapter be the Christmas chapter, and Abuela reaches the end of her patience.

Chapter Notes

I struggled getting this chapter written out. I am tired of staring at it, so I am flinging it out here now. Also, a reminder that this series is half fueled by my spite towards canon, so.

Christmas Eve shifts tended to follow a pattern, or so Buck found. The first part of the day tended to be busy and chaotic, with everyone in the city in a hurry to finish up last minute holiday preparations. Especially traffic accidents, those seemed to increase exponentially the closer the clock ticked to closing time for all the stores. Always, always, there were people who realized they forgot something or that they didn’t have enough of something, and had to race to the store to get it.

There would be a crescendo as evening drew closer, everyone in that bit more of a rush as the deadline loomed, and then it would taper off. The sun would set and most people would spend the night in their homes, with their families. Maybe some would go out and gawk at their neighbors’ lights. There would still be emergencies that needed responding to, still people that needed rescuing from ignoble situations. But compared to the daylight hours, it would be much calmer.

They weren’t at that point yet. The major stores still had an hour before they closed until the 26th, and the 118 was on the scene of an accident involving a trio of cars and their very stressed, very unhappy drivers. Buck wasn’t entirely certain what had happened, but one car got pincered by the other two, and now they were having to carry out an extraction while people shouted obscenities at each other at the top of their lungs. And all the while, someone’s radio was blaring Jimmy Buffet’s Christmas Island album at full volume.

(It was a simple fact of the world that one did not tend bar along the coast for as long as Buck did, even if the time wasn’t consecutive, without being very familiar with at least a few of the man’s songs. This album had been played on repeat the December he spent on the Gulf, to the point that if he had the wrong drink during this time of year he would get A Sailor’s Christmas stuck in his head for the rest of the day.)

Thankfully, there were officers on site that could deal with the civilians, so Buck didn’t have to pay them any mind beyond making sure they weren’t too injured. That had been fun, getting them to focus on something other than their vitriol for long enough to go through a concussion check. But now the 118 were pulling the cars apart so Eddie could get in there with the jaws, and Buck was stuck supervising with not much else to do.

At least until his phone began to ring in his pocket. It was Carla’s ringtone.

“What’s wrong?” he rushed out when he answered it, after a fumble that nearly saw it hitting the pavement.

“Your in-laws,” Carla growled out. “I called you because I wasn’t sure if you were all busy and I figured it was safer than distracting Eddie.”

“We’re on a scene,” Buck told her, calming down. “Car accident, nothing serious. What’s going on?”

Eddie was staring at him, brows furrowed and the jaws ready to go when there was clearance. Buck gave him a thumbs up, to assure him that it was nothing to worry about.

“I took Chris and Gavin to the park for a bit,” Carla explained. “To get them out of the house.”

“You mean to get them away from Helena and Ramon.”

“Well. Yes.” She laughed a little. “Adriana went with us. When we got back, they had Isabel in a right state.”

“What about?”

“A lot of things. Adriana will be able to give you the full rundown of it tomorrow. But Hoover was outside and had been since we left, apparently.”

“And when was that?” Buck asked, keeping his tone neutral despite the way he could feel his temper fraying.

“Just after lunch.”

That was hours ago. They’d left his dog outside by himself for hours. A dog that was used to being around people on a regular basis. Buck wasn’t certain that Hoover had actually spent any significant length of time by himself since Eddie got him from Hen.

The only saving grace was that the temperature stayed below sixty degrees all day, rather than the eighty degrees of last week, because they didn’t have any water set-up back there for the pooch to drink.

“Someone should lock Helena out,” he grumbled, because he knew it was her who did it. Carla snorted on the other end of the line. “Do I need to send Eddie home early?”

“No, boo, I’ll be fine,” Carla assured him. “Pepa will be over in a bit, and then I believe the plan is to go to midnight mass together.”

“Chris won’t want to go. If they try to force it-”

“He won’t have to go if he doesn’t want to.
