I’m pretty sure Adriana has no interest in going either, I might suggest that Chris go with her to pick up Sophia.” There was the sound of someone talking in the background, just loud enough that Buck could make out Adriana’s voice. “Nevermind, Adriana’s decided she is going to kidnap him and run away.”

“She’s welcome to keep him,” Buck joked. Carla laughed. “But everything’s okay?”

“Yes, Buckaroo. I just wanted to make sure you all knew there were issues. Nothing serious enough that I need one of you here, but…”

“But you might, later,” he finished for her. “I’ll try to keep Eddie back on calls, in case you need him, but we are still short handed so I can’t promise much.”

The phone call didn’t last much longer past that, beyond making sure again that Carla didn’t need one of them there right that minute. Buck focused back on the extraction, with the cars pulled apart and the doors popped open with the jaws. They got the patients - one of whom had a severe compound fracture - out and loaded into ambulances and sent away. It took both ambulances, and Eddie rode in one instead of taking the engine back to the station.

When Eddie got back, and when Buck informed of what the call had been about, his reaction was exasperation and annoyance. Curiosity, too, about what all had Abuela fired up. He agreed to hang back on calls, in case one of them needed to rush off to help Carla. Buck was reminded of all his dates with Abby that got interrupted or cancelled for the same reason.

Luckily, that Christmas Eve was following the pattern of the ones before. Unlike Halloween, things calmed down as nautical twilight fell over the city and day turned to night. They got to relax around the station, and even hit the bunks before midnight. Most of them did, anyway.

When midnight struck, not a creature was stirring throughout the firehouse, not even a mouse. Actually, that was inaccurate. There were at least two firefighters that weren’t snug in their bunks with visions of sugar-plums dancing in their heads. Buck was in the captain’s office - his office, which was still weird to think about - to fetch the present he stashed away that morning, behind Eddie’s back. Eddie, he knew, was somewhere doing the same.

It was their tradition, had been since their first Christmas Eve as a couple. They’d stay up late and then, when it struck midnight, they exchanged presents. The present that Buck got for Eddie this year also doubled for their anniversary gift, something he tried to do every year since their wedding. A new book for the first, a new sweater last year. This year was leather, and the present was tucked away in a large box wrapped in snowflake patterned paper.

With the gift in hand, he strode out of the office and into the truck bay. Eddie was waiting for him, the gift meant for Buck - flat, square shaped, wrapped in red with green stripes - clutched in his hands.

“Here.” Buck practically shoved Eddie’s gift into his chest and snagging his gift to unwrap it with all the care of a bear. “Merry Christmas, happy anniversary, yadda yadda.”

“There used to be romance to this,” Eddie griped, even as he started tearing into the wrapping.

“Oh, I’m so sorry.” Buck leaned in to kiss him. “Oh! A new cookbook? Some of My Best Friends Are Cookies. Weren’t you complaining about all the baking I was doing?”

“I complained about all the loafs of bread taking up space,” Eddie countered. He opened the box and pulled out the leather jacket inside. “Really, mi sol?”

“Leather is the traditional third anniversary gift. It was this or a new belt.”

“You could’ve gotten me leather pants.” The joke had Buck’s brain slamming to a stop, and his eyes automatically darted down to Eddie’s legs. Eddie noticed and he tapped Buck on the head with the jacket. “I am not going to wear leather pants.”

“Even if I asked really, really nicely?”

“Not even then.” Eddie tucked the jacket back into the box it came in and sat it down on a nearby bench, taking the cookbook from Buck’s hands and placing it beside it. Then he kicked the discarded wrapping paper aside, pulled out his phone, and started up some music. “Dance with me?”

“If I must.” Buck tried to put as much melodrama into the put-upon sigh as he could, and then laughed when Eddie rolled his eyes.

Buck’s dancing skills were greatly improved after his dance lessons from two years ago, and then with Eddie’s own lessons following. He didn’t have to look down at his feet even once, and neatly avoided stomping on his husband’s toes. They danced for a few songs in a row, the volume low enough not to disturb anyone.

Afterwards, Eddie took their gifts to their locker to be stowed away until their shift ended and Buck carried the wrapping paper up to the trashcan upstairs. And then nearly had a heart attack when he spotted Toby sitting at one of the tables, a bunch of playing cards in front of him. Apparently he was playing solitaire.

“Hey, Cap,” the red-haired driver-engineer greeted him, giving him a wave.

“Okay, I know why Eddie and I are awake.” Buck pressed his foot on the pedal to pop open the trash can’s lid and stuff the paper inside. “Why are you?”

“Nittel Nacht,” was the answer he got. “Every Christmas Eve, we stay up and try to be as invisibly Jewish as possible. I used to play chess with my mom, but I could never stay awake as long as she could.”

“Why?”

“Traditionally? It’s so that when gentiles-” Toby pointed at Buck with a card before placing it down on the table. “-get drunk and decide to do a little pogrom, we’re not caught sleeping in our beds.”

”Oh.” Now Buck felt a bit awkward. “Do you… I could stay up with you, if you want?”

“I’m good, Cap.”

“Alright.” 

After a moment, he headed downstairs where Eddie was waiting, the pair of them heading to the bunks to catch some sleep while they still could. They thankfully managed to catch a few hours, until they got yanked out for an early morning traffic accident. By the time they made it back, the next shift was already trudging in and looking particularly Scrooge and/or Grinch-like. Buck even got an actual “humbug” in response when he gave a reflexive “merry Christmas” to Captain Reynolds in greeting. 

Gavin and Hoover greeted them at the door, as always, and Abuela greeted them from the kitchen. The presents that had been stashed in the garage-turned-gym were all under the tree now, presumably a task carried out by Carla before she left for the night. Chris was still in bed, the excitement of Christmas morning dulled by teenage apathy, but he was roused easily enough.

After all of the house’s occupants had breakfast - pancakes for the humans, expensive canned food for Hoover and Senorita - they gathered around in the living room to tear into the presents while Buck took pictures to share with all the people that weren’t there. Chris made half-hearted gripes about the presents from Santa, as he did every year, but didn’t really seem to mind that he was still getting them.

Buck and Eddie both minded the gifts from Bobby, though.

“Are you serious right now?” Buck glared at the man through the phone screen.

“And a merry Christmas to you, too, kid,” Bobby snarked. He was standing in a kitchen, presumably Michael and David’s, already elbow deep in cooking. “Did you guys enjoy the presents?”

As if on cue, the toy that Gavin got from his grandpops, some horn shaped terror, let out a screechy howl. Hoover joined in with a howl of his own.

“You know, that is fine,” Buck said, pointing at it. Not that Bobby would be able to see Gavin at all. “Or at least it will be. The batteries on it will die eventually, or it’ll go missing, and he’ll forget all about it. But Chris’? That one might be unforgivable.”

“What did he get Chris?” Michael’s question preceded his appearance as he shoved his head into view.

“A helmet,” Eddie said. He was standing beside Buck in their own kitchen, Senorita lazilly puring in his arms.

“They got new helmets for Hotshots,” Bobby explained to his wife’s ex-husband. “I snagged one of the old ones.”

“We could get him an actual fire helmet!” Buck complained with a flap of his arm. Eddie leaned back to keep from being smacked. “But no, he unwraps a cheap prop from that awful show and it’s the best thing he’s ever gotten.”

“And I gave him a parent for Christmas,” Eddie added. “Twice!”

“The best thing, huh?” Bobby was grinning at the phone while Michael laughed. “Let me talk to my grandkids.”

“That sounds like rewarding you for bad behavior,” Buck told him, giving the man a squinty glare. “I don’t think I should do that.”

Bobby actually rolled his eyes and then hung up, which had Buck squawking in offense. And then Buck squawked even louder when Chris’ phone rang in the other room, the teenager answering it with a loud,

“Grandpops, it’s so cool!”

“It’s so cool,” Buck quietly mocked, wagging his head.

“Your son has awful taste in television,” Eddie said.

“Hey, do not blame this on me. I’m not the one that raised him on telenovelas.”

“And what is wrong with my shows?” Abuela asked. She’d joined them in the kitchen while they were distracted bickering. She was holding a bright red moleskine notebook.

“I don’t think there’s a right answer to that question,” Buck said.

“It definitely wasn’t that,” Eddie whispered into his ear. He got an elbow to the stomach for it.

“No, it wasn’t,” Abuela said, and then held out the book. “Feliz Navidad, Buckito.”

“Gracias, ‘Buela,” Buck replied absently as he took it from her. He flipped it open, curious to know what was in it. The answer was rather unexpected as he stared at a list of ingredients on the very first page. “‘Buela, is this… Are these recipes?”

“Si.” She nodded. “I thought I should make sure they were all written down, while I could still remember them.”

Buck blinked at her, eyes dropping back down to the book in his hands. Beside him, Eddie had gone utterly silent and still. And then, without a word, he left the kitchen and went down the hall, setting Senorita down along the way. Buck instinctively took a step to follow, but let him go with a sigh.

“I wish…” Abuela let the words trail off as she stared after Eddie. She shook her head and turned back to Buck, raising her hand and placing it on his cheek. “I know he will be okay. He has you.”

“Always,” he promised, swallowing a boulder of emotions. “Um. Carla said you were, uh. Upset yesterday? With Helena and Ramon?”

“Oh, pah.” Abuela waved her hand irritably. “That.”

“She told me about Hoover, but was it anything else?”

“It was Helena being Helena and Ramon being Ramon,” she stated, tone final. It was as if she thought that was all the explanation that was required of the situation. The sad part was that it really was all the explanation required. Then she tapped the book of recipes that Buck was still holding. “Go put this away. Helena does not get to see these.”

“Copy that.”

They had about an hour's peace after that, before the visiting Diazes invaded. Buck was surprised they got that much, but he wasn’t about to complain. All four of them arrived at the same time, Eddie answering the door while Buck and Abuela were getting started on the cooking. They came loaded with presents, which they passed out before Sophia and Adriana invaded the kitchen.

“And there’s my fourth favorite Diaz!” was how Buck greeted Sophia, which got him smacked by Adriana. “I love how you just assumed you ranked lower.”

“Oh, we all know the boys and Abuela take up those spots,” Adriana grumbled. Abuela nodded smugly as she chopped up veggies.

“It’s not too late, Buckito.” Sophia draped herself against his arm and batted her eyes at him. “Take my hand, run away with me.”

“No, no, take me.” Adriana pressed against his other arm. “We can ride into the sunset together.”

“Stop trying to steal my husband, you harlots,” Eddie snapped. Buck laughed and turned his head to spot him on the other side of the breakfast bar, setting a gift wrapped box down on the counter. “Get your own.”

“Uh, we’re trying!” Sophia gestured at her and Buck. “Go away.”

“You don’t want me, anyways,” Buck told her with a grin. “I’m needy.”

“Ah, true.” She nodded, letting him go to pet Hoover when he padded over. “Like a puppy that can’t be left alone.”

“Woof,” he intoned, and had her cracking up.

“Is that the present Sophia got you?” Adriana asked, crossing the kitchen to peer at it. “Oh, you and Buck.”

“Open it!” Sophia crowed, and her smile was far too wicked for Buck’s liking. Eddie didn’t see it, too busy peeling away at the wrapping paper to reveal a plain looking brown box with a hinged lid. He lifted it up, screeched, and hurriedly shut it again.

“Sophia!” He stared at her, wide-eyed. “¿¡Qué carajo!?”

“What did she get us?” Buck asked, curious, as he abandoned the food prep to look in the box for himself. When he opened it, he let out a startled “Oh” that Adriana, peeking around him, echoed. “This should probably go in the bedroom, babe.”

“This doesn’t bother you?” Eddie hissed.

“No.” Buck shrugged at his husband. “Quality ones are expensive and we needed more lube, anyway.”

“Buck! Abuela’s right there!”

“Edmundo.” Adriana reached up and cupped his face. “Abuelita’s had sex.”

Eddie’s face went bright red as Abuela cackled. He snatched the box off the counter and fled deeper into the house, chased by his sisters’ mocking laughter. Buck shook his head at them and went back to the food, purposefully bumping Sophia out of the way. She scowled at him for it.

“You’re both so mean to him,” he said.

“He makes it far too easy,” Sophia told him. “We need Christmas music. Where’s your radio?”

“Right there.” Buck used a knife to point at the retro-looking radio on the counter, a replacement for the one that met a gravity-assisted demise a few months ago. They all knew that Senorita was the culprit, but she’d refused to confess under interrogation. “It has bluetooth.”

“Muy bueno.”

He went back to dicing up veggies, not really paying attention as Sophia moved the radio to the breakfast counter, then pulled out her phone and started fiddling with it. Not until the radio started playing and the first song was-

“Mom got drunk and Dad got drunk at our Christmas party-”

“Seriously!?” Buck blurted out. “Montgomery Gentry?”

“Little sister brought her new boyfriend, he was a Mexican,” Adriana sang, or rather, screeched into his ear. Or she tried to at least, not quite managing to reach despite standing on the tips of her toes.

“We didn’t know what to think of him,” Sophia joined in on his other side. “‘Til he sang Feliz Navidad! Feliz Navidad!”

“This is why Eddie’s married and you’re spinsters,” Buck told them.

“I could play some Dixon Dallas instead.”

“Get out of here before you lose radio privileges!”

The pair of them cackled as they left, though they only made it as far as the dining room table. At some point, Adriana raided the cabinet for glasses and they’d brought a thing of eggnog with them, which was undoubtedly a poor omen. Eddie eventually crawled back out of hiding to dutifully ignore his sisters’ teasing, not that he was very successful. He got increasingly grumpier when Chris joined in, something that had Eddie coming to pout to Buck and Abuela about.

Then, Ramon and Helena began to invade Buck’s space. They moved in and out regularly, hovering right around where Buck and Abuela were working. Helena would offer to help while Ramon would just be right there. Their presence was enough to have Buck on the verge of growling like an actual dog, and he was thankful that Abuela would irritably shoo them away every time. Not that they were ever gone for long.

Throughout it, Buck’s phone was busy. Hen and Karen called to wish them a Merry Christmas, and then Buck had to call Bobby for help when something wasn’t tasting right. Afterwards, Buck called Maddie, who was hosting her own Christmas dinner with the Lees plus Albert and Ravi. She paused in the middle of telling him about Jee-Yun’s excitement over the gift he and Eddie got her to frown past him.

“What? Oh, yeah.” Buck glanced at Ramon, who was being chased out of the kitchen by Abuela, and glowered. “I don’t know.”

“How have they been?” she asked.

“Uh… Well, pretty much that,” he said. “Adriana and Sophia got into eggnog, so they haven’t been helpful.”

“Are they the ones singing? Or is Gavin strangling the cat?”

Buck snorted and picked up the phone so he could show Maddie what was going on in the dining room. The two sisters were flanking poor Eddie, tugging him back and forth by his arms as they sang along with the radio at the top of their voices. Hoover, ever helpful, was playing the part of backing vocals.

“Oh, God.” That was Chimney, sounding rather despairing. When Buck turned the phone back around, he saw he’d joined Maddie. “Is that what I’ll have to look forward to on your girls night?”

“I actually think the eggnog improved how they sound,” Buck said.

“Where’s Pepa?” Maddie asked.

“She has her own kids and grandkids, y’know. She’s with them.”

“Isabel.” Helena was in the kitchen again. Buck huffed out as a sigh as he set the phone down and tasted the food. It was nearly done. “Let me do that, I can-”

“That is enough!” Abuela snapped, slamming down the platter she’d been about to carry into the dining room. “Both of you, I’ve had it!”

“Mama-” Ramon, joining his wife, tried. But his mother wasn’t having any of it.

“No, it has been like this all day!”

Buck shared a look with his sister, whose eyes had gone wide and brows had gone skyhigh. Ravi and Albert were crowding in around her and Chimney, clearly interested in the drama going on. A quick check showed that Eddie had gathered up Gavin in his lap, but the little tot wasn’t as bothered by raised voices as he used to be.

“We just want to help,” Helena said.

“I don’t need your help, Helena!” Abuela said, waving a wooden spoon at her. “I am still perfectly capable of cooking dinner.”

“Mama,  no one’s saying that,” Ramon said.

“Aren’t you?” Abuela countered. “You asked- No, you both told me that I was moving to El Paso with you so you could take care of me, but my home is here. I am not moving in with you, I am not moving into a facility. You have been acting as if I am infirm and incapable of taking care of myself. You keep looking at me, you all keep looking at me, as if I am already dead! But I am still here, damn it!”

There was silence in the house as everyone stared at her. Buck swiftly ended the call with Maddie, making a mental note to apologize for it later.

“I am not gone yet,” Abuela said, much quieter. “I am still here.”

She shook her head and then stomped out of the kitchen for the backdoor. Eddie shoved Gavin into Sophia’s lap and got to his feet to chase after her. Ramon and Helena both started to, as well, but Buck stopped them with a firm,

“Help me get the food to the table.” When the two of them just stared at him, he repeated himself. “The food? It’s done, it needs to go to the table. You said you wanted to help.”

The Diazes didn’t speak as they shuttled food from the kitchen, with Adriana getting up to help as well. The only one who did was Chris, who grabbed Buck by the wrist before he could go back, asking in a quiet, worried voice,

“Is Abuela okay?”

“She’s fine,” Buck assured him. “She just got a little upset.”

“Is this… Is this like what you said?” Chris asked. “When you told me about it?”

“No, no, this is just… Trust me, I think she’s been holding that back for a while.”

Abuela and Eddie didn’t come back inside until everyone else already got their plates loaded up. When they did, Eddie walked her to her seat at the head of the table, pulling it out for her. She thanked him quietly, gave him a quick peck on the cheek as she sat down, and then held out her hands as Eddie took his own seat.

While Abuela led them in grace - Buck and Eddie and Chris staying silent, while Gavin happily babbled along - Buck shared a look with his husband. Eddie just shook his head.

Chapter 26: FirefightersDiaz_LAFD II

Chapter Summary

Some more transcripts of videos posted by @FirefightersDiaz_LAFD.

Chapter Notes

My gift to you in these trying times.

Transcript from a video captioned, “Firehouse Haunt Fest! 🎃👻🚒 (I think working in Hollywood has gone to Pops’ head a little)”

[Interior shot of Station 118. The truck bay has been turned into a makeshift haunted house, with a bunch of black tents between the fake spider web covered trucks. Various other Halloween decorations litter the area. The camera focuses on Bobby, dressed in a cheesy vampire costume.]

Bobby, Dracula accent: Come to Station One-Eighteen for the spookiest night of your lives.

[Bobby makes a sweeping gesture around himself, using the cape to emphasize the movement.]

Bobby, Dracula accent: I am Cap Dracula, and I shall be your guide for this journey. For behind these curtains- [Bobby gestures at the curtains of the first tent] -are thrills and scares that you cannot even imagine!

[Bobby makes a vague “blegh” noise at the camera.]

Bobby, Dracula accent: But beware! There are rules to be followed for everyone to have the best fright.

[Eddie walks onto the screen in a high-effort werewolf costume, carrying a poster that just has the number 1 on it.]

Bobby, Dracula accent: Rule one! There is to be no running, not even for your lives.

Eddie: You could get hurt that way.

Bobby, Dracula accent: Rule two! [Eddie drops the poster and reveals a second one with a large number 2.] No touching the set decorations. The ghouls have worked very hard on it.

[Eddie scowls at the camera.]

Eddie: Some of us have, anyway.

Buck, from off-screen: Stick to the script, Jacob.

[Eddie makes a pathetic attempt at a snarl and drops the second poster, revealing a third with a large number 3.]

Bobby, Dracula accent: And the third and most important rule! Everyone that comes must have a terrifyingly good time!

[Bobby laughs evilly. It is magnificent.]

Transcript ends.

Transcript from a video captioned, “A Public Apology”

[Interior shot of the 118’s captain’s office. Buck sits behind the desk, looking awkward. Small adhesive patches are dotted across his face. Someone starts snickering from off-screen and Buck glares at them.]

Buck: Stop laughing, Rav.

Ravi, from off-screen: I can’t. This is so stupid.

[Buck throws up his arms in clear agitation.]

Buck: Think how I feel! Let’s just get this over with.

[Buck clears his throat and crosses his arms in front of him on the desk, attempting an air of grave seriousness.]

Buck: As some of you might have heard, this year’s Haunt Fest had a… Complication.

Eddie, from off-screen: You brought an actual corpse in.

[Buck glares and points angrily at someone the camera isn’t looking at.]

Buck: I didn’t know it was an actual corpse! That’s the point here, okay? I rented a Hollywood prop. They told me it was just a prop. I had no way of knowing.

Eddie, OS: Except we all warned you it would traumatize the kids, capitán.

Buck: They weren’t traumatized. I mean… Not until I accidentally tore the arm off

Ravi, OS: And then started screaming, it’s real! It’s real!

Buck: I didn’t scream it.

Eddie, OS: You screamed it.

[Buck huffs]

Buck: The point here is, I am making a public apology.

Ravi, OS: Because the Mouth of Sauron told you to.

Buck: No, Chief Williams told me to and she is very scary. Anyways.

[Buck picks up a single sheet of paper off the desk. Then he drops it with a sigh.]

Buck: I apologize for any emotional distress I may have caused to the guests going through the Haunt Fest. And for those who could not participate due to, you know. The station becoming a crime scene. It was my bad. Mea culpa and all that.

Eddie, OS: Wow. Very sincere, capitán.

Buck: They said it was a prop!

Transcript ends.

Partial transcript from a video titled, “🦃 Turkey Day Safety Advice 🦃”

[Exterior shot of a rooftop. There are lawn chairs lined up along the edge in the background and a turkey fryer in the foreground next to a fire extinguisher. Buck and Eddie stand behind it in uniform. Eddie is in full turnouts, complete with helmet. He is holding a frozen turkey and a pike pole.]

Buck: Thanksgiving is coming up, and do you know what that means?

Eddie: A lot of kitchen fires.

Buck: Quite right, Firefighter Diaz!

[Eddie rolls his eyes while Buck smiles.]

Buck: According to the National Fire Protection Association, Thanksgiving is the peak day for cooking fires, with more than three times the daily average! 

Eddie: On Thanksgiving Day in Twenty-two, there were one thousand, six hundred, and ten such fires. A nearly four hundred percent increase over the daily average for that one day alone.

Buck: And here to help us tell you how to avoid becoming a statistic is- [Buck’s smile turns fixed as he holds out an arm.] -Brad Torrance, the actor from Hotshots.

[Brad Torrance walks onto screen. He waves, as if there is an audience to be waved at. When he talks, his voice is as deep as it is on Hotshots.]

Brad: Hello, I’m Brad Torrance. I play Captain Race Banner on Hotshots.

[Buck visibly twitches. Eddie looks away from the camera for several moments.]

Buck: And like I said, he’s here to help us keep you from becoming a statistic!

Brad: Always make sure your smoke alarms are working. That is very important.

Buck: Yes, yes it is. And always keep an eye on the stove and oven while they’re in use.

Eddie: But most of all, do not use a turkey fryer.

Buck: Bad things happen when you use a turkey fryer. Horrible burns for one thing, because it uses cooking oil that gets really, really hot.

[Brad’s face scrunches up.]

Brad: Is that all?

[Buck points at him and then grabs the fire extinguisher.]

Buck: No! No it is not. Because if you’re not careful enough. And none of you are. [Buck sternly points at the camera and then grabs Brad by the arm to drag him back several feet.] This can happen! Firefighter Diaz?

[The cameraman backs up as Eddie dangles the frozen turkey by a string from the end of the pike pole. From a safe distance he drops the turkey into the fryer.]

[Everything explodes into fire.]

Partial transcript ends.

Partial transcript from a video captioned, “Another q&a”

[Exterior shot of the Diaz backyard. Buck sits in a patio chair, tablet in hand, with the house behind him. Hoover the dog has his head in his lap. The atmosphere is gloomy and Buck looks tired. Even the dog looks sad. A bit of the sky is visible: there is smoke.]

Buck: Hi, everyone. We’re- Well, I’m doing another q&a. I actually went through them ahead of time, so there won’t be any surprise sex questions.

[He glances at the tablet. One hand is absently petting Hoover’s head.]

Buck: First question is, did we really film a scene on Hotshots? [Buck smiles at the camera. It is faint.] We did, yeah. Eddie and I played nurses, Chimney played a doctor. And that follows into the next question: How was Brad Torrance in person?

[Buck grimaces as he finishes reading the question]

Buck, muttering: Okay, maybe I didn’t vet them well enough.

[Buck smiles at the camera again. It is fake looking.]

Buck: Brad was fine. And I have no comment whatsoever on any video that may or may not have shown him being yelled at by my firedad. Next question!

[Buck’s face falls.]

Buck: How are we doing with the wildfires? Well. [Buck’s eye twitches.] My sister and her husband are staying with her in-laws. Hen and her family are in a hotel. They might’ve actually lost their house because it’s right in the middle of it. And I haven’t seen my husband in weeks, and I haven’t spoken to him in two whole days, so!

[Buck smiles again. It somehow manages to look like the exact opposite of a smile.]

Buck: But we’re safe! We’re fine! If a fire gets here, that means the entire city has burned. 

[Buck looks at the tablet again.]

Buck: The next question is a good one. Does Hoover know any tricks? He knows how to fetch and sit and…

Partial transcript ends.

Transcript of a video captioned, “Edit: I guess this is what I get for staying logged in on my tablet 🙄”

[Interior shot of the Diaz house, in the hall. The camera is facing the floor and wobbling as it moves. We enter another room.]

Chris, whispering from off-screen: So Dad just got home.

[The camera rises. It focuses on Buck and Eddie in the living room, sitting in front of the door. Buck is in casual wear; Eddie is in uniform. They are hugging each other. Hoover the dog is pawing at them.]

Chris, OS: He hasn’t even said hi to me yet. I just found them like this.

[Buck and Eddie are still wrapped around each other. They are currently rocking. Hoover gives up on trying for the attention and starts trying to wiggle between them.]

Chris, OS: They’re so pathetic.

Transcript ends.

Partial transcript from a video captioned, “H-O-T-T-O-G-O”

[Exterior shot of the Diaz backyard. Buck and Bobby are standing next to each other. Bobby is looking very confused.]

Buck: C’mon Pops, it’s like YMCA. Or the Macarena.

Bobby: Why isn’t Eddie doing this instead? Or your mother?

Eddie, from off-screen: I’m the cameraman.

Athena, from off-screen: And I just don’t want to.

[The camera pans to show Athena sitting at the patio table. She is relaxed and has a glass of wine in her hand as she watches the pair. The radio from the kitchen sits on the table. The camera pans back to Buck and Bobby.]

Buck: It’s not hard. Okay, watch me. H [Buck puts both his arms straight up.] O [Buck connects his hands together.] T [Buck spreads his arms out straight to his sides.] T [He bounces them slightly.] O [He raises his arms above himself again.] G [Buck makes a vague G shape with his arms. It looks more like a C.] O [He once again puts his arms above him in a vague circle shape.]

[Athena laughs from off-screen.]

Bobby: I already feel ridiculous and I haven’t even started yet.

Buck: It’s not hard!

Eddie, OS: Chris taught him how to do it.

Buck: And if I can learn, so can you! Okay, follow me.

[Buck demonstrates the motions again. Bobby, looking ruffled, copies them.]

Buck: See? And then you do this number…

[Buck sticks one arm in front of him and then the other, before folding them and then dragging his hands down his chest.]

Bobby: I am not feeling myself up.

Buck: You’re not- Where is your whimsy, Pops?

Bobby: It’s buried for the day.

[Buck turns to Bobby. His face is not in clear view, but the wide-eyed pout is still apparent. Bobby meets it full-on for only a second before sighing. Athena laughs again from off-screen.]

Bobby: Fine, fine. Show me it again.

Buck: Maybe it would be easier with the music.

[Buck pulls out his phone and fiddles with it. The radio on the table starts playing the song from off-screen.]

Partial transcript ends.

Chapter 27: He Has Unlocked the Dad Jokes

Chapter Summary

In which there is a conversation, then a time skip, then the author expands the cast.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Christmas Day

There was utter silence in the wake of Abuela’s outburst, a silence initially broken only by her footsteps as she made her way to the back door. They heard her shove it open and then it slammed shut a moment later. Eddie shoved Gavin into Sophia’s lap so he could get up to chase after her. His parents moved to follow, but he heard Buck stop them with a firm,

“Help me get the food to the table.”

If it had been Buck that stormed out after an outburst like that, Eddie knew, he would’ve been a mess of frenetic energy as he paced to work out his frustration. Eddie himself would not have been too much different, if more tightly coiled. But Abuela was not like either of them, however much she had contributed to the Diaz family’s stubbornness. When Eddie stepped out into the backyard, he found her simply standing at her garden and glowering down at the blooms: chrysanthemums, orchids, roses, and star-of-bethelehems.

She acknowledged his existence with a quick glance as he joined her, but she didn’t say anything in greeting. Eddie stayed silent as well, entirely uncertain of just what to say. Abuela had accused them all of looking at her like she was already dead, and Eddie could not lie and claim innocence on the matter. Because ever since Carla brought up her concerns, ever since the doctors confirmed them, he’d seen only the clock that was ticking down towards the end.

(“I felt like she saw me,” Buck had said about that death doula they’d met on a call, in the weeks after the lightning strike. “She saw me and not my corpse!”)

However much Eddie was hurting, it had been unfair of him to do that to his abuela. He owed her an apology, which was probably the best place to start.

“Perdóname, ‘Buela,” he told her. “I didn’t- I didn’t mean to make you feel like that.”

“I know you didn’t, gordito,” she said. She sounded weary. “It is nothing.”

“No, that- It’s no wonder you and Buck get along so well.” He shook his head. “It was bothering you, it was hurting you, and we weren’t seeing it. I should have seen it, instead of focusing on what I was feeling. And I should have been there for you.”

Abuela let out a harsh tsk, tilting her head to fix him with a sharp eye.

“You have not been there for me? Then who is it that has gone to every doctor’s appointment with me, hm? A secret twin? An identical stranger?” She had watched far too many of those shows of hers. “I am not so far gone that I have forgotten it was you that has gone to every one of them with me, so far.”

“Pepa and Carla have gone, too,” he reminded her.

“But not to every one,” she insisted. “This is difficult for all of us, I know. It is unfair to all of us. I did not mean to lose my temper like that.”

“You’re allowed, though.”

“As if I have ever needed permission to give anyone a piece of my mind.” Abuela sniffed, a bit haughtily, and then patted Eddie on the cheek. “This is especially difficult for you, I know, because there is nothing you can do. That has never been something you’ve handled well, but hopefully this time you won’t be getting into fights.”

“Abuela.” Eddie was a grown ass man with children, he did not whine. He didn’t!

“I know that Buck has already gone through this before,” she said. “That he’s helped someone he cared about through this before. He knows what’s in store for us, and I understand why he sees that when he looks at me. And I understand that you’re hurting and afraid. I just wish…”

“That we’d stop looking at you as if you were already dead,” he quietly finished for her.

“Yes. I have some time in these old bones, yet. I do not want to spend it all at my own funeral.”

Eddie opened his mouth to apologize again, but the word caught in his throat. Instead, he wrapped his arms around his abuela and pulled her close, to hold her as tightly as he dared. She wrapped her arms around him and didn’t pull away, not for some time. When she did, it was with some reluctance and an attempt at discretely wiping her eyes.

“Buckito should’ve gotten the food set out by now,” she said with a sniff. “I hope they have not started eating without saying grace.”

“Buck wouldn’t let them,” he assured her.

They made their way back inside, a slow and easy pace, with Eddie holding the door open for her. Everyone had already been served, or perhaps served themselves, but they were all sitting patiently, with the exception of Gavin, who was already chewing on a piece of ham. Someone, it was probably Buck, had even set out plates full of food for the two of them. Eddie walked her to her seat at the head of the table and pulled the chair out for her, receiving a quiet “gracias” and a quick peck on the cheek in payment.

He took his own seat between her and Buck, taking both of their hands in his own when they were offered. While Abuela led them in grace, her voice steady through the words she had spoken a hundred thousand times before, Buck caught his eye. The question was silent and unspoken, but loud all the same. Eddie shook his head in answer. They’ll talk about it later.

February

It wasn’t precisely planned, their going out for Valentine’s Day. Not by them, anyways. But Bobby came over and practically kidnapped Gavin and Chris, after the latter came home from school, with the declaration that he was taking them to May’s. And then Abuela chased them out the door with Pepa’s aid. Buck didn’t resist it too hard, though, and neither had Eddie.

In early January, Eddie was called up as one of those selected to help fight the blazes threatening to consume the city. He wasn’t the only one, the same special deployment list was used from when they were sent off to fight the wildfires in Texas. Except this time, Buck hadn’t been sent with him, because someone still needed to respond to all the everyday emergencies in the parts of Los Angeles that weren’t burning. And so, for weeks, Eddie had been so close yet so fucking far.

Buck would like to think he coped with the separation quite well; everyone else’s opinions on the matter were not to be trusted. Though, yes, there might’ve been a little bit of crying on both their parts when Eddie finally came home at the beginning of the week. Buck couldn’t deny that fact, no matter how much the two of them might want to, because their brat of a son posted video proof of it to the internet.

There’d been palpable relief from everyone else the day prior, when Eddie walked into the station for his first shift back. More so than for the others that had been drafted up and returned.

(Buck might’ve gotten a bit unbearable towards the end.)

“I don’t think this is quite what they had in mind, mi sol,” Eddie said, picking out a fry from the bag clutched between his knees. There was a bright purple flower tucked behind his ear, from the bouquet that Buck stopped to get him.

They were both perched on the hood of the jeep, overlooking one of the city’s beaches - the Santa Monica pier jutted out into the black ocean a bit north of them, a dark shape outlined by bright, fluorescent lights. A lack of time to make a reservation, plus the way everything had been thrown out of sorts, meant they’d made do with hitting a drive-thru. Neither of them really cared, in truth.

They were not the only ones at the beach. While it wasn’t as crowded as it typically was, even accounting for the off-season, it was still impressive just how quickly everyone went from “Oh, God, everything’s on fire and we’re all going to die!” to “What? Oh, yeah. Whatever.” Buck was pretty sure houses were still burning when the transition happened. 

“I don’t think I care,” Buck told his husband. The way he pressed closer to him was only partially because of the cool night air; it had rained the last couple of days, thankfully. “If they wanted us to have a fancy date night, they coulda done the work for it themselves.”

“Wow. So I’m not even worth the effort of doing it yourself anymore,” Eddie teased.

“Shut up.” Buck smacked him in the stomach; the thin cushion that had been there before was gone, something he’d taken note of before but still kept being surprised by. Eddie had come home to him haggard and worn. “Are you excited?”

In a couple weeks, Eddie would be starting the courses to officially be paramedic certified. They were supposed to have begun earlier, but things had been delayed on account of apocalyptic conditions. Plus, Eddie’s background as an army medic was transferring over as credit towards… Something or other, Buck wasn’t entirely certain. He just knew Eddie would be missing a lot of shifts until it finished, and then he’d actually be getting paid for the paramedic work he got shoved into so often.

“A bit,” Eddie said. He dug into his bag again, frowned when he came up empty, and didn’t even hesitate to reach into Buck’s for a fry. “It’s been a while since I’ve gone to school.”

“Eh, you and Chris helped me.” Buck bumped their shoulders together with a smile. “We’ll help you. Though I don’t think you’ll need it quite so much. Oh! We need to get you school supplies!”

“Oh, could I get a Superman lunchbox? Please? All the cool kids have ‘em!” Eddie pitched his voice high, making them both laugh. “You sure y’all will be okay without me? I heard the horror stories from last month.”

“It won’t be so bad this time, since we won’t be down so many,” Buck told him. It had been painful, because they were all stretched so thin and it seemed like so many people were taking the opportunity to be idiots. “We’ve got a new probie starting on Sunday, anyway. You’ll hardly be missed.”

Buck threw his husband a grin. Eddie scoffed and rolled his eyes.

“Know anything about ‘em?”

“Just what was on the paperwork I was sent,” Buck said. “Pops took me to the academy to watch the class, a couple weeks ago. Claimed it was for a scouting mission, but I didn’t have a clue what I was supposed to be looking for.”

Plus, Buck was fairly certain it had mainly been an attempt by Bobby to distract him from Eddie’s absence. Bobby spent the time as they watched the cadets run through drills making comments on each of them, and Buck dutifully jotted them down on the clipboard he brought along. It was close enough to graduation that the ones who couldn’t hack it were already long winnowed out, but there were one or two that he knew weren’t going to make it to the end of the year if they didn’t shape up, just by how they acted with the others.

The problem, mainly, was that Buck had no clue what to look for. Sure, by this point in his career, he knew the things that made a good firefighter on paper. But he was also well aware that they weren’t individuals existing in a vacuum, that the ability to fit in with the rest of the team was just as important. More important, even. It had been part of why Bobby recruited Eddie so hard, why he poached Ravi from B-shift and Albert from the 133. It had been the second biggest reason that Dalton Wolfe didn’t work out.

Buck knew what made a bad recruit, that was easy. But the specific things to look for in a good one? He wasn’t so good at that yet. He was just stuck hoping that the new probie would work out and it wouldn’t be as big of a disaster as the last one.

(No one from the recent group of graduates was related to any of the brass, that was something he’d made a point of checking.)

“Sounds like a good father-son bonding exercise,” Eddie quipped. “Hopefully this probie won’t start any fires.”

“That is literally my bare minimum,” Buck said. He sighed and let his head fall onto Eddie’s shoulder. “I missed you, baby.”

He could feel the smile on Eddie’s lips when they brushed against his hair, and he could hear it in his voice when he said,

“I missed you, too.”

Sunday shifts were not Buck’s favorite. Sundays were supposed to be reserved for days spent in the kitchen and evenings spent around the dining table, surrounded by all his family. Unfortunately, he chose a job with a shift schedule that did not allow them to get every weekend off. He wouldn’t trade it for the world, a nine to five desk job was pretty much his version of hell, but it still sucked at times.

As always, he and Eddie arrived at the station already in their uniform and earlier than the rest of their shift. Eddie took their bags with their change of clothes to their lockers, Buck losing sight of him when he went into the locker room. Towards the end of January, in the middle of what might have quite possibly been a fit of mania, Buck brought in rolls of privacy film that he’d paid for with his own money and spent a shift applying it to the glass panes between calls, because he’d taken one look at them in the middle of their previous shift and just finally had it with the lack of privacy. He couldn’t even remember what it was that finally pushed him to and then right on over the edge.

No one bothered him while he worked, everyone giving him a wide berth until he was done.

(It was possible he didn’t handle Eddie’s prolonged absence quite as well as he’d like to claim.)

Captain Mayfair was upstairs, sitting at one of the smaller tables with paperwork spread out in front of her as her crew finished up and prepared for the handover. She was looking more than a bit strained these days, the dark circles beneath her eyes steadily growing over the past month. She lived in Altadena.

Past tense.

“Morning Buck,” she greeted him, with just as much cheer as usual. “Yesterday wasn’t all that exciting, nothing really to tell you about. Everything’s in the book.”

The book being the logbook, where the captains jotted down everything and anything important that happened on their shifts. The calls they went on, incidents of note, if they went on a grocery run, if they exploded any vehicles, all of it written down and dated. Past ones were tucked away in a filing cabinet in the captain’s office.

“Aw, dang it Maria, now you’ve jinxed us,” Buck complained without any heat as he took the seat across from her. “How’s…?”

He trailed off. It was the same question he’d asked her at every shift change since the fires started. The answers she gave didn’t change very much, either.

“We’re all fine,” she said, the same answer. “Our insurance company is already being a pain. Did Tim tell you?”

Tim Reynolds was the captain for their B-shift, as large in form as he was in personality.

“He mentioned his daughter finally settled on a school, somewhere out east,” Buck said, a bit uncertain. “Why?”

“He’s thinking about retiring, mentioned it to me yesterday morning.”

“That’s…” Buck was gonna say it was a bit sudden, but it really wasn’t. The man had been here since before even Bobby, taking command of his shift sometime after Gerrard got the boot and the brass started cleaning out the house. “Did he say why?”

“Doc diagnosed him with COPD,” she said, both of them grimacing with it. “And the last of his brood is about to leave the nest.”

“How many kids does he have?”

“I don’t know. Seven? Eight? Too many.” Mayfair shook her head. “His poor wife.”

Personally, Buck thought seven or eight kids sounded perfectly fine. Then again, short of a medical miracle, he wasn’t the one that would have to carry them around for nine months before squeezing them out in a mess of screams and blood. That probably tended to color one’s opinion on these things.

There were things he had to do before his shift got started, instead of sitting around chatting. However much he enjoyed sitting around chatting. Most of it surrounded the new probie that would be starting today, including assigning them a locker and a gear cage, and making sure their turnouts were there. There was also the various paperwork that needed to be printed off.

By the time he got all of that done and started on breakfast for everyone who might want some, his shift had trickled in while the previous changed and hurried out. Hen, of all people, chose to invade the space for the morning. She usually spent it watching the morning news or chatting with Chimney. But Buck meant to check in with her, anyway, so this was more than fine.

“How’s the neighborhood?” he asked, turning his head to look at her over his shoulder.

“Mostly okay,” she said. Hen lived in Altadena, too. “We were extremely lucky.”

“No kidding,” Eddie added, pouring himself a cup of coffee. He opened his mouth to no doubt thank the machine as he did Hildy, caught himself, and then glared at Buck when he sniggered. “It was a nightmare.”

“He was a nightmare while you were gone,” Hen said, and it was Buck’s turn to glare at someone.

“I was not that bad!”

“I’m pretty sure you made Ravi cry.”

“I did not!” he protested. “Did I?”

“Uh, hi?” A woman’s cheery yet uncertain voice had him turning around. She stood at the head of the stairs, a denim jacket over a black top, a duffel bag hanging from her shoulder. Her hair was braided in tight plaits that fell to just below her chin and hung around her face. “I’m Maribel Frey, they told me to report to Captain Diaz? Someone downstairs told me he was up here.”

“That would be me!” Buck raised his spatula in a wave. “You can just call me Buck.”

“Okay, Captain Buck.”

He elbowed Eddie when his husband hid an amused snort in his coffee.

“Important questions first,” Buck said. “Anything you prefer to go by?”

“Everyone calls me Bell,” was the answer he got, along with a shrug.

“Bell it is, then. And anything you can’t eat?”

“I have a shellfish allergy?”

“My shrimpathies,” he told her, and grinned at the groan it elicited from everyone in the loft. “This is just scrambled eggs, though. You want some?”

“Sure!” Bell bounced a little as she said it.

“Then grab a plate,” he told her, and raised his voice to let the others know that, “Food’s done!”

Chapter End Notes

Unless they've changed it since then, 6x06 (Tomorrow/Henren Begins) placed the Wilsons' home on E. Mount Curve Ave in Altadena. If you want to look anything up for yourself.

Chapter 28: I Think She's Gonna Need More Than An Egg

Chapter Summary

In which the 118 horrifies the poor probie and the author is forced to wrestle with the question of whether or not he wishes to be cruel to a fictional little girl.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Bell was… Excitable, that was a good term for her. Cheerful, sunny, energetic, those were also excellent descriptors. She seemed to bounce along as Buck led her on a tour of the station after breakfast and introduced her to everyone. The paperwork he had her fill out for the station records didn’t dull any of it, either. He was fairly certain he caught her humming as she filled things out at one of the tables.

He initially intended for Bell to shadow Ravi, a declaration that earned him a flat and unimpressed stare from the younger man. But Hen didn’t waste much time before claiming the probie for her own, accompanying them on that station tour and then taking off with her after the necessary paperwork was all filled out. Buck couldn’t really claim to be surprised about it, either.

Over the years, he’d heard all sorts of horror stories about Captain Gerrard from both her and Chimney. It only made sense that Hen would take one look at Bell and take it upon herself to make sure the young woman had a warmer welcome to firefighting than she got. Buck just kinda left them to it, for the most part.

Also, Bell asked the weirdest things at times. Or maybe not weird, just… Unexpected.

“Is it true the One Eighteen’s cursed?” she asked, apropos of nothing as she was helping Eddie clean the kitchen; Hen not yet returned from taking a patient to the hospital with Albert. It was a statement that had Eddie freeze in the middle of wiping down the counter and Buck in the middle of finishing the after action report of the call they’d returned from.

“Yes!” Ravi answered without any hesitation from where he was trying to beat Toby at a racing game. 

“Only when someone says the q-word,” Chimney said. He turned and half-rose out of his seat to point a stern finger at Bell. “Do not say the q-word!”

“What’s the q-word?” Bell asked, scrunching her face up a little with the confusion.

“It’s, uh.” How did Buck answer that without saying the q-word? “Not loud.”

“Not- Oh! You mean qu-”

“Don’t!” Chimney shouted, loud enough it echoed off the beams. He put enough feeling into the singular word that Bell recoiled and blinked in shock.

“Ignore them,” Eddie told the probie, going back to wiping down the counter. “They’re a bunch of viejas with this stuff.”

“Oh yeah?” Buck cocked his head to the side and leaned forward on the table he was at. “Go ahead and say it, Diaz. I dare ya.”

“I wouldn’t want to upset Chimney,” was Eddie’s mumbled response towards the countertop. Bell was looking between them, frowning in thought with her eyebrows scrunched up.

“That’s what I thought.” Buck smirked at his husband and got flipped off in return. “Who’s saying we’re cursed?”

“People at the academy,” Bell blithely answered, after shaking her head a little. “When they read off my assignment, everyone acted like I was being marched off to Mt. Doom. Someone even played bagpipes on their phone. Did you know that bagpipes are awful?”

“Yeah, we did,” Buck said. There was a moment where all of them avoided making eye contact with anyone else, each of them remembering the same thing. Not a single one of them walked away from that day with a particular appreciation for the instrument, Buck was fairly certain about that. “Wait, is this why it’s such a pain getting floaters? There are people really saying we’re cursed? Why are people calling us cursed?”

“Cap, you got struck by lightning and died,” Ravi pointed out, setting down his controller to properly focus on the conversation.

“It was only for a couple minutes. I had a weird dream and then I woke up.”

“I got impaled through the head with rebar,” Chimney said, counting off on his fingers. “Stabbed. Nearly died from encephalitis.”

“Eddie got shot,” Ravi added.

“Oh my God,” Bell whispered, sounding a bit horrified.

“And buried alive in a well,” Chimney said, bobbing his head as he spoke. “Albert had that accident.”

“Does that count? That was before he started.”

“The ladder truck, the bridge collapse, the- Should we count Bobby and Athena’s cruise ship? It happened while they were on vacation.”

“I’m counting it, I got a medal for it.”

“You counted your stabbing, Chim,” Buck pointed out. “That was off-duty, too.”

“In that case, we can count their house getting arsoned,” Chimney said.

“Why didn’t anyone warn me?” Toby said. Buck was fairly certain it wasn’t actually meant for any of them, because the driver-engineer was staring at some point in the middle-distance.

“There was the time Buck and I got held hostage during the prison riot-” Eddie said, and got cut off by Ravi with,

“That time I had to wear someone’s blood-covered clothes and sneak through a prison riot!”

“Oh my God,” Bell said again, this time a bit louder.

“And that accident Hen had, when the light didn’t change,” Eddie continued, giving Ravi a nod in acknowledgement. Bell’s eyes were wide as they bounced from one speaker to the next. “Everything with the councilwoman’s son. Karen’s lab, maybe? If we’re counting Albert’s accident?”

“There was Douchebag.” Ravi spoke Dalton Wolfe’s moniker with as much disdain as possible. “And that Jonah guy.”

“What Jonah guy?” Toby asked, and then, “Wait, he was in that book, right? That paramedic?”

“Him, yeah.”

“Who’s Douchebag?” Bell asked.

“The probie we had before you, he set a bunch of houses on fire,” Eddie answered. “He was a douchebag.”

“I wonder if that’s why it took so long to get another probie,” Buck wondered aloud. “But- But there’s no way it’s just us, though, right? I- I mean, the other stations…”

Toby quietly shook his head at him. Buck grimaced and turned to Eddie.

“Do you think Abuela’s friend would come do an exorcism on the station?” he asked him. “Just in case?”

Eddie threw his rag at him.

When Hen started at the 118, so very long ago, that first day had almost soured it for her completely. She still recalled Gerrard’s complete and utter disdain as he literally looked down on her, the way he called her “prettier than most” and introduced her to the rest of the shift as their new diversity hire. The way he sat there at the dining table, later, and denigrated her ability to do the job when she’d barely had the opportunity to do the job.

She remembered, too, the oh-so-warm welcome she got from the others. The easy dismissal from (almost) all of them. The casual homophobia from Sal, Tommy’s remark about her supposed bitchiness after barely interacting with her. The way that their change of heart coincided so conveniently with Gerrard getting the boot and Cooks taking the reins for his very short tenure.

If it hadn’t been for Chimney and Athena, Hen didn’t think she would have lasted that first week.

So, when Bell stepped into the loft and introduced herself, Hen did not hesitate before deciding to take the probie under her wing. Even though she knew, she knew, that Bell would have a better time of it than she did at the start, she still wanted to make sure of it. And she figured Buck realized what she was doing, why she was doing it, because he hadn’t spoken a word against her hijacking everything.

The ambulance needed restocking after their last call, and Hen had Bell helping her with it. This was one of the things they all needed to know, even the ones that weren’t expected to ride the bus. Circumstances could - would - force them here anyway and a life could be lost one day simply because Bell didn’t know what someone meant when they asked for a tool, or because she had to take precious moments to locate it. Or because she didn’t know how to use the gurney.

(Buck still brought up the time that Ravi folded one up like a taco.)

“Hey, so,” Bell spoke up in the middle of Hen explaining what the bougie was and where they kept it. “Captain Buck and Eddie are both Diaz?”

“Yeah? They’re married.”

“That’s allowed?” the probie blurted out. “I mean, obviously it’s allowed. But it’s allowed?”

“It’s not disallowed.” Hen had laughed herself silly, when Buck passed on to her what Chief Williams had told him. That the sexism and homophobia of old was the reason Buck and Eddie could be on the same shift now, because no one had ever taken the time to even entertain the possibility of firefighters being married to each other for long enough to make any rules against it. “You didn’t know? The department has them doing that Instagram account together.”

“My Instagram feed’s all cute animals,” Bell admitted with a shrug. “Plus I mostly use TikTok.”

Hen wondered, briefly, if the brass ever contemplated putting the Diazes on there. Then she decided that Buck being given incentive to make content for TikTok was simply too much to contemplate, a nightmare in the making. 

“They used to be more obvious, before Buck was captain,” she told the probie. “Now they try to be more subtle about it. Not that the two have ever been subtle about anything.”

“What do you mean?”

“You’ll see,” Hen answered, trying her best not to sound patronizing. Because if Bell was gonna stick around, she was definitely going to get a front row seat to the Buck-and-Eddie show. “Like I was saying, the bougie goes in this cabinet here…”

There were some calls that Eddie immediately knew he would need to brace himself for, that they all would. He spent the time from the moment the alarms sounded to when they finally arrived onto the scene getting himself ready for whatever they might find. His usual spot on the truck had become the seat just behind the captain’s, back pressed up against it, and so he couldn’t see Buck’s face as he conversed with dispatch and gave them brief little nuggets of info.

The tightness in his voice was enough, though, to let Eddie know that Buck was bracing himself, too.

The engine had barely pulled to a stop before they were all jumping out. The building they had been called to was ablaze, flames and smoke rising to the night sky above. Buck was on the radio without hesitation.

“Dispatch, we’re on-scene. Bravo-Charlie side is well-involved,” he relayed. “We’re gonna need more RA units and definitely gonna need Animal Services when you can get ‘em.”

They were going to need Animal Services because the burning building in front of them was an animal shelter. If Eddie strained his ears, he thought he could hear howling and barking. He really hoped it wasn’t just his imagination, either.

A woman, cradling a medium-sized mutt to her chest like it was her newborn infant, rushed up to them.

“I got twenty-eight dogs still inside,” she announced.

“Okay,” Buck breathed out. “Toby! You, Clarke, and Perez, get those hoses set up! Hen, we’re getting a place set up for the dogs. The rest of you, search and rescue! Get in, grab a dog, get out. Eddie, take the rotary saw.”

“Got it,” Eddie said with a nod, joined by a chorus of “on it, Cap” and “copy that.” He jogged back to the engine, grabbing an oxygen tank and the rotary saw, along with an extinguisher. It didn’t take long to get himself geared up, and then he was leading the others inside after busting open the door.

He wasn’t sure what the first room was supposed to be: it was large, with chairs straight out of a public school. Maybe a room meant for the dogs to do meet-and-greets? The sprinklers were working overtime, raining down and thoroughly soaking through everything. It was dripping off the brim of his helmet like rain off a porch roof.

“She says they’re in two rooms.” Buck’s voice over the radio competed with the sound of the falling water and the echoing barks of distressed dogs. “The main kennel and from there, down a hall, is the quarantine room.”

Eddie radioed over an acknowledgement. The layout wasn’t complicated, and they came across what must’ve been the main kennel right away. Flames had started enveloping thankfully empty cages, and a blast from an extinguisher put them out easily. There was a tiny white dog in a cage, which thankfully wasn’t locked; Ravi yanked out the pooch with half-assed attempts at comfort, before jogging back outside.

It became a bit of a relay. Eddie would use the saw to open a cage, one of the others would grab the pooch to take it outside, and then he’d move to the next waiting pooch and firefighter. They made it through the main kennel and into the quarantine room that way, Eddie silently keeping up a headcount.

The last dog, number twenty-eight, was a tiny beagle curled up in the corner of a large cage. It whined a little when Eddie opened the cage, got to its feet, and then darted between his legs.

“We’ve got a runner!” Chimney helpfully declared.

Eddie gave chase after barely a moment’s hesitation, not waiting to face his husband and tell him that they left a dog to the fire. The beagle led him down one hall and then another, ignoring Eddie’s calls to it, and took a sharp right into what might have once been the shelter’s office space before the fire started eating away at everything. There was a cabinet tipped over and propped against a desk.

The beagle had gone there for shelter, no doubt propelled by ancient instincts about caves or something. It proved to be excellent instincts, too. An ominous wooden creaking had Eddie looked up, just in time to throw himself backwards to avoid being slammed by a flaming beam that had partially given way and swung down at him.

“Eddie.” Buck had either the best or the worst timing. “What’s it looking like in there?”

“The roof’s starting to go.”

“Then you should probably haul ass.”

“Nag, nag, nag,” Eddie muttered, to himself and not into the radio, as he crouch-walked to where the beagle was hiding. The little thing was hunkered down and visibly shaking, and it backed away when he reached a gloved hand towards it.

“Firefighter Diaz.” His husband’s tone was falsely pleasant, carrying a warning that he was rapidly approaching a thorough scolding that he would have to try and not smile through. “You better not be wasting time in there.”

“Oh, like you’re one to talk,” Eddie grumbled, and then thumbed his radio to reply to him. “I’m trying to get the last stray, capitán.”

“Then hurry up and grab him.”

Gee, why hadn’t Eddie thought of that?

He eyed the dog, eyed the sleeve of his coat and the gloves he wore, listened to the increasingly ominous sounds of structural failure around him. The decision was an easy one to make.

“Sorry about this,” Eddie told the beagle, and then grabbed the poor thing by the leg it had sticking out. It yelped when he pulled, a mouth full of sharp little teeth striking at his turnout-covered arm. It wiggled and barked at him as he got a better hold on it, clutching the little guy to his chest and getting to his feet.

Now, Eddie followed the captain’s order to haul ass. His speed was spurred on by the sound and feel of something finally giving right behind him, by the heat that billowed out around him. When he made it out of the smoke and into the clean night air, he found the others waiting for him in anticipation around the impromptu puppy corral of traffic delineators and orange safety fencing. They hurried to meet him halfway, Buck leading the group.

“You gave us a scare, boy,” Hen said. She stroked the dog’s snout with a gloved hand, and got a tiny little bark.

“Sorry ‘bout that,” Eddie told her, taking off his oxygen mask to let it dangle from the tank.

“She was talking to the dog,” Buck said. He was attempting to look stern, arms crossed and face set in a scowl. Eddie gave him his best smile and lifted up the beagle, until his husband rolled his eyes and took the dog from him. “Shut up.”

The dog strained up to lick at Buck’s face, its tail wagging a mile a minute. Buck laughed as it did, not in any obvious hurry to put a stop to it. Not until the shelter employee, her hand freshly bandaged up and kept protectively to her chest, joined them.

“Thank you so much,” she gushed, before waving someone over. “We’ll take him from here.”

“You hear that, buddy?” Buck asked the dog, scratching at its nape and holding it with the same care he did Gavin. “You’re gonna go with them now, okay?”

Someone from Animal Services took the beagle from Buck and stuck the wiggling thing into a cage. Eddie watched it get carried off to an awaiting transport, and he watched his husband’s face fall slightly.

“Hey, where is he going?” Chimney asked the shelter employee.

“El Segundo,” was her answer. “Our sister shelter’s pitching in, for the time being.”

“And then what?” Buck asked her.

“Same as usual,” she said. “We pray he finds a home.”

Buck huffed a little at that less than satisfying answer. He turned back to the rest of them and then huffed again, because Eddie was staring at him.

“What?”

“You know what,” was Eddie’s reply.

“You shut up,” his husband told him. “You’re the one who keeps bringing animals home.”

Eddie just raised an eyebrow, instead of pointing out that none of them had mentioned bringing home anything. Buck scowled and huffed and turned away to the rest of the crew.

“I want more hoses on that fire!” he shouted, ignoring Eddie’s laughter. “Get to it!”

Chapter End Notes

Fun fact: This fic is now longer than TWO Great Gatsbies.

Chapter 29: And Bingo Was His Name-O

Chapter Summary

In which the author decided to not be cruel to a fictional child, and ended up being mean to Buck instead.

“Alright,” Maddie said, settling onto the couch with a glass of lemonade. She’d come over sans Jee-Yun or Chimney, after seeing Athena. “Explain to me how this happened.”

“Well,” Buck started from where he was sitting on the living room floor. “When Chris was looking up ways to help Abuela, there were articles about games improving cognitive abilities.”

“I didn’t think I would be having this much fun,” Abuela commented. She was sat in her chair, controller in hand. On screen, her avatar was running around with a bunch of Disney characters.

Buck had no idea what she was doing, honestly. She’d been decorating a virtual house earlier, but now she was running errands for Prince Eric. It wasn’t the only game that she’d started playing, there were also a couple of Mario games, but this was the one she’d apparently decided was her favorite.

“We’ve also been doing board and card games,” Buck added. “You and Chimney are invited, but I gotta warn ya, the Diazes get pretty cut-throat when it comes to Uno.”

There was absolutely no mercy involved, especially not from Abuela. She’d slapped both him and Chris with Draw Twos and Draw Fours without even an ounce of hesitation or remorse.

“That’s all very sweet,” his sister told him. “But I was talking about that.”

She pointed at Buck. Or rather, at the beagle wiggling and flopping in his lap, little tail thumping against Buck’s foot as he gave the pooch belly rubs. The back door opened and closed, Hoover racing in with Gavin close behind. The beagle leapt to his feet and gave a yappy little bark in greeting.

“His name’s Blaze,” Buck told her with a grin, watching the tiny thing go up and start licking at Gavin’s face. The toddler laughed hard enough to fall onto his butt. “Because of how we met.”

“Yeah, Chimney told me about the fire,” Maddie said, waving away her brother’s words. Buck made a face at her. “But explain to me how that led to you taking in another dog.”

“Oh, that’s easy,” Eddie stated as he joined them. “We left the station after shift and he took us directly to the shelter in El Segundo. Didn’t even tell me what he was doing until we were passing the turn to go home. The dog still smelled like smoke when we got him.”

“Oh, like you’re one to talk, Eds,” Buck shot back at him. “I remember you calling and asking me to pick you up from the shelter, along with that one.”

He pointed at Senorita, who was stretched out along the back of the couch and watching the new addition to the household with wary eyes. She wasn’t quite sold on Blaze, yet. The initial introduction between cat and beagle had resulted in the latter fleeing for his life, to cower and whimper beneath a dining chair. They seemed to have reached an accord now, though, or at least a truce.

“I didn’t say I was any better,” Eddie shot back.

“It’s probably a good thing you haven’t responded to a fire at a group home,” Maddie commented, smiling over the rim of her drink. “God knows how many children you’d end up with then.”

“We don’t have room for any more, not unless someone shares.”

“The garage is fully finished,” Buck pointed out. “If we put up a wall, maybe install a bathroom…”

Eddie, notably, did not shoot down the notion out of hand. He actually seemed like he was contemplating the whole idea.

“I’m not sure how any social workers would feel about the kid not living in the house,” Maddie said.

“It would probably be okay if it was a teenager,” Buck said. It was a comment that earned three weighty stares. “Don’t look at me like that!”

“And just how much thought have you put into our next kid?” Eddie teased.

Buck let out a huff.

“Shut up,” he sniped. “Maddie was telling me about a kidnapping case before she got distracted by this adorable little fella.”

He reached out and gave Blaze scritches behind the ears. The little beagle twisted around to lick at him.

“A kidnapping case?” Eddie repeated, watching Gavin take off running down the hall. Hoover followed just behind him, loping along.

“Yeah, I took a call from… Well, from the kidnapper,” Maddie explained. Eddie’s eyebrows rose as he took a seat on the couch; Buck immediately shifted over to lean back against his legs. “I mean, it started out as a regular crisis call, with the caller sounding like he was considering self-harm, and I hate how that’s a regular crisis call. And then it got weird, with him saying he didn’t want to take her and how he thought he could save her.”

“Her being…?”

“A girl named Jayna. Units went to the location we traced him to, but there was no one there.”

Buck grimaced, focusing on Blaze to distract himself from the depressing turn of the conversation.

“I found a Jayna Whitlock listed as a missing person in Bakersfield,” Maddie continued. Bakersfield was just a short trip north of Los Angeles, an hour and a half by car if the traffic was good. “Athena got me a meeting with a hotshot missing persons detective, Amber Braeburn. She’s already got a lead, a possible suspect. Athena’s gonna look into it.”

“Ma’ll get the guy,” Buck declared with easy confidence.

“I hope so. It was weird, the guy’s voice sounded… Off, somehow.” His sister sighed, and then cut a glance at Eddie. “It’s nice to see you in person again, by the way. Buck’s been so much less annoying since you got back.”

“Hey!” Buck glared at his sister, but she just ignored him.

“Mi sol, I turned my phone back on at one point and was bombarded with three dozen text messages from you.” Eddie’s smile took the edge off the teasing. “Half of them were about Glee, of all things. About someone that looked like Chimney and the show being biphobic.”

“You were lucky, I was stuck on the phone with him for about two hours for that rant,” Maddie said, a bit darkly.

Abuela nodded along with her.

“Oh, I’m so sorry.” Buck drew the words out, wagging his head. “I thought two of the most important people in my life would want to hear my thoughts about the outrageous biphobia.”

“You know I like listening to you,” Eddie said, reaching down to pat his head. It was just patronizing enough to have Buck smacking the offending limb away.

“The singing twink called bisexuality a lie and that people used it to tiptoe back into the closet!” Buck was getting worked up again. “I couldn’t even keep watching past that.”

“Because you were too busy telling everyone how much it upset you,” Abuela said, not even taking her eyes away from the video game.

Buck blew a raspberry at her.

“I’d actually forgotten about it until you were ranting down the line at me,” Maddie commented, wrinkling her nose. “But that means you didn’t make it to the Turkey Lurkey Time.”

Buck craned his neck back to meet Eddie’s eyes and then they both turned to Maddie to ask, at the same time,

“The what?”

“You know, I’m honestly not even surprised,” Hen told Eddie as they both leaned against the loft’s railing and looked down at the bay below. “I’m more surprised it didn’t happen earlier.”

Below them, the trio of Buck, Albert, and Bell the probie were all fawning over Blaze the beagle. It had been like that all shift, though they hadn’t been on duty for very long, because the dog was adorable. For once, no one complained about being the man behind, because it meant they were also on dog duty.

“Buck always was trying to talk Bobby into getting a station dog,” Eddie commented.

“We always joked that Buck was the station dog,” Hen said. “I think that’s how we got that dalmatian statue. Why did Buck bring him to the station instead of leaving him at home?”

“Well, the reason he gave me was that Blaze is still a puppy, and he’s still adjusting to Hoover and Senorita and vice versa,” Eddie explained. “He didn’t want anything to happen while we weren’t there.”

“And the actual reason?”

“He’s attached,” he said with a laugh, and then waved down at Buck when his husband looked up at the sound. Buck beamed and waved back. “Should never have handed the thing to him, Buck was a goner the moment it started licking at his face.”

“You would know about winning Buck over with licking,” Hen said, and then smiled serenely at Eddie’s sputtering. “It did get you out of being yelled at, don’t think we all missed that.”

“He wasn’t gonna yell at me,” Eddie told her, once he was done choking on his own spit. “Not over something we all know he’d do himself.”

“That’s a good point,” she said, and then eyed him in consideration. “You all ready to go back to school?”

“It’s practically just a formality at this point. I’m already doing the job half the time.”

“I don’t know how we’ve been getting away with that for so long, pretty sure it’s against the regs somewhere.”

Eddie shrugged, honestly unsure on both counts. It probably was against the regs to have someone who wasn’t paramedic certified doing so many paramedic duties. No one had said anything, though, and Bobby obviously hadn’t cared about the semantics of it all. Eddie knew what he was doing, and that was good enough.

“Okay, so obviously you know the practicals already,” Hen said, smacking him lightly on the arm. “But the non-practical stuff, or the academy standard way of doing things that we ignore-”

“Like where to stick the angiocath to decompress the pleural cavity,” Eddie said, smiling as he remembered his very first day on the job. Buck got very embarrassed whenever he was reminded of how he acted around Eddie, back then.

“Exactly that, those kinds of things. If you need study buddies, Chim and Al and I have got your back,” she said. “You’re gonna be part of the cool kids club.”

“I will definitely take you up on it,” he said, and then, “Want to go play with a puppy?”

“Is that even a question?” Hen scoffed, pushing off the railing to head for the stairs. “Of course I want to play with a puppy.”

“I see what you mean, Hen.”

Bell’s statement has Ravi looking up from the cards in his hand. The five of them were gathered around the dining table, passing away the time while Buck cooked dinner. Downstairs, Toby and Javier were doing maintenance checks on the trucks, their voices occasionally carrying up. Blaze the beagle was curled up under the table, occasionally poking out his nose for whatever snack someone “accidentally” dropped to the floor.

“What did Hen mean?” Chimney asked, pushing a small pile of pretzels forward. “Raise.”

“Call.” Hen tossed in a few pretzels of her own.”Buck and Eddie, right?”

“Yeah!” The probie nodded, her tight braids bouncing around her face with the motion. “She said they weren’t very subtle, and I totally get what she meant by that now.”

The five of them all looked towards the kitchen, where Buck and Eddie were standing at the stove and pressed shoulder to shoulder. The latter was supposedly helping, but as far as Ravi could tell, he was just standing around and looking pretty. As they watched, Buck offered a spoonful for Eddie to taste and then huffed at whatever response he was given.

“It’s good. You always say it’s good,” Albert said, pitching his voice up and down and tilting his head back and forth as he mocked the two. He was in the seat next to Ravi, foot hooked around his ankle. “Because it’s always good. That’s not very helpful, Eddie. Then why do you keep asking me. Because you’re there.”

“It’s the same thing every time,” Ravi told Bell. “Every single time.”

“There’s less kissing here than when it happens at theirs, though.”

“Thank God,” Chimney muttered. “I do not want to see my brothers-in-law making out, thank you very much.”

Ravi heard Albert mutter something that sounded very much like “I don’t mind seeing it.” It wasn’t loud enough for the others to hear, or they were all choosing to ignore it. He was going with the former, Bell seemed the type to loudly acknowledge a comment like that one.

“Brothers-in-law?” Bell asked, giving Chimney a wide-eyed stare.

“He married Buck’s sister,” Hen explained. 

“So that makes you…” Bell trailed off as she pointed at Albert, who nodded.

“I have a flowchart somewhere,” Ravi told her. “I made it for Toby.”

“Toby had it worse,” Albert commented around a mouthful of pretzels. “Bobby was still here.”

“Who’s Bobby?” was the expected question from the probie, which got the simultaneous answers of,

“Our old captain,” from Hen and,

“Buck’s dad,” from Ravi.

“But not his actual dad,” Albert added. “His actual dad’s dead.”

“Oh.” Bell blinked. “I’m… Sorry?”

“You’d be the only one,” Chimney said.

“Don’t ask,” Hen advised, before the probie could even open her mouth. She laid down her cards. “But do give me your pretzels, please.”

Albert let out a groan, and then flung a pretzel at Hen’s face.

“Cap!” Chimney shouted. “Al’s throwing things!”

“None of you are my children!” Buck shouted back while Eddie laughed. “I don’t care!”

It was an hour before their shift ended, early enough that Captain Reynolds hadn’t even arrived yet for the handover. The morning had been calm and now Buck was playing with Blaze in the truck bay after taking him for a walk around the station to do his morning business.

“Hen mentioned something about going out tomorrow,” Eddie said as he joined the pair. “The two of us, her, Chimney, and Bobby.”

“That’ll be fun, the five of us haven’t really hung out together for a while,” Buck commented. Not that they didn’t hang out at all, obviously, but it was usually Buck and Eddie with Hen and Karen, or with Maddie and Chimney, or with Bobby and Athena, or with Albert and Ravi. Rarely did they have get-togethers as a unit anymore since Bobby’s heart attack. Which was something for Buck to put more in-depth thought into later. “I’ll ask Carla if she’s free. Wait, what about Al and Ravi?”
