“They said they had plans, apparently. They didn’t offer details and Hen didn’t ask.”

“Plans,” Buck repeated, and wagged his eyebrows up at his husband.

In his lap, Blaze suddenly perked up. Then, he shot off like a bullet for the bay doors. Buck scrambled to his feet and gave chase, Eddie following a bit behind, and caught up just in time to see the beagle tackle a little girl in a pink sweater who squealed in laughter. There was a man kneeling right beside the pair, who Buck guessed to be her father. Hen and Chimney were standing nearby, the pair of them looking torn between cooing over the sight and shooting Buck grim looks.

Buck, on his part, drooped where he stood. He recognized this reaction from the beagle well enough, having seen it with Hoover and Gavin and even himself. He knew where this was heading, and wouldn’t stop it even if he could.

“I’ve missed you, Bingo,” the girl said as she pressed her face into the dog’s fur.

“I’ve been calling him Blaze,” Buck said, a bit numbly.

“That suits him, too,” the father said, lifting his head up to look at them and explain that, “He got spooked by our neighbor popping off fireworks, squeezed out of the yard.”

“That happens a lot,” Eddie said. He bumped his shoulder into Buck’s to catch his eye, the pair of them thinking the same thing. “We’re not exactly fans of fireworks ourselves.”

“How did you know to find him here?” Hen asked.

“We’ve been checking pretty much every shelter on this side of town, including the one that burned down,” the father explained. “They recognized him, told us which one he’d been transferred to, but you beat us to the punch.”

“He’s very lucky to have people who love him so much,” Buck told the both of them, doing his best to shove down his emotions before they choked him.

“We do,” the girl said. She hadn’t diverted her attention from the dog for even a moment. Blaze - Bingo - had been happily wiggling the entire time they spoke, tail wagging so fast it could’ve been used as a propeller.

“Hey, uh,” Chimney spoke up, sounding uncertain at first. “Would it be okay if he said goodbye to him?”

He jerked his head at Buck.

“Sure,” the father said with a nod.

Buck knelt down in front of the beagle, feeling grateful for Chimney, and smiled when he gave his face a little lick.

“Okay, boy, I know we didn’t have much time together, but it was a good time,” he told him. “You can’t go running off on your people anymore, okay? ‘Cause then they miss you so much.”

He pet the beagle for a couple more moments, and then the father cleared his throat.

“We need to get you to school,” he said to his daughter, who let out a groan. “You’ll see him when you get home.”

Buck stood and watched the trio leave, the father carrying the beagle in his arms. The moment they were outside and no longer within earshot, he tossed his head back with a groan of his own. Hen laughed, not even bothering to cover it up, and Eddie gave him a comforting pat on the shoulder.

“This is your fault, Eds.”

“How is this my fault?” was Eddie’s offended response.

“You gave me the dog!” Buck retorted. “You knew what would happen!”

“I can’t even argue against that,” his husband grumbled.

Chapter 30: Without a Trace

Chapter Summary

In which Maddie is missing. (Again.)

The house was dark and silent when Chimney let the three of them in, loaded down with bags of leftovers. Dinner out with everyone had been a hit, and Buck was still riding from the social high of it. Since he wasn’t yet willing to go back to theirs, and with child- and abuela-care handled for a little bit longer, he and Eddie had simply followed Chimney to his and Maddie’s place.

(Carla and her husband were apparently in a fight, so she was avoiding going home until he’d moved onto the fretfully apologetic stage. It wasn’t the first time it happened, and it likely wouldn’t be the last.)

“We’re home!” Chimney called out, not very loudly, as he hit the lightswitch to illuminate the small foyer. “We brought steak frites and chocolate tart.”

“Yeah, on my dime,” Buck groused without any actual heat while they crossed the living room and into the kitchen.

“That’s what you get for being the captain,” the paramedic told him, turning on the kitchen lights and then dumping the bag he was carrying onto the island. “Bobby did it all the time.”

“Bobby didn’t have a grandmother, two children, a dog, and a cat to feed at home,” Eddie pointed out as he and Buck did the same with their bounty. “Maybe we should start doing a pool or something.”

“And a mortgage,” Buck added. He went for the fridge, not at all reticent about stealing a couple beers for himself and Eddie. “Hey, maybe we could afford it better if you stopped buying Hoover and Senorita all that fancy wet food along with the kibble.”

“Or you could stop buying name brands,” his husband shot back as he took the offered drink, not at all ashamed of the way he spoiled the animals at home. “It tastes the same.”

“No it doesn’t.”

“Mind getting down plates while you bicker?” Chimney asked, gesturing at the cabinets. He’d laid out the styrofoam clamshells and flipped them open. “It’s criminal to eat steak frites from a to-go box.”

Buck definitely didn’t mind eating anything from a to-go box, that was how he’d eaten many a lunch, dinner, and breakfast. Plus, it saved on the washing later.

“Maddie! I’m eating your fries!” he bellowed out.

Eddie winced and leaned away from him.

“Easy, Mr. Megaphone,” Chimney chided. “I got a sleeping toddler in the house. If she wakes up, it’s your job to put her back to bed.”

“Yeah, you’re just threatening him with a good time there, Chim,” Eddie pointed out.

Buck grinned at him and plucked a couple of fries from the clamshell meant for his sister.

“Where is Maddie, anyway?” he asked, leaning a little to look down the hall towards the bedrooms.

“Probably in the shower,” Chimney answered.

“There’s no water running,” Eddie pointed out.

“You’re right.”

Chimney dusted off his hands and headed down the hall, quietly calling out for Maddie. Buck, with his hands covered in grease and crumbs from the fries, turned to the kitchen sink to wash his hands. He froze, though, when he spotted a ring sitting on the back edge, by the dish soap. He picked it up, stared at it.

“What’s that?” Eddie asked him, peering at it over his shoulder.

“Maddie’s wedding ring,” Buck answered, somewhat distractedly.

She must’ve taken it off while she was doing the dishes, he and Eddie did the same with theirs, if they hadn’t forgotten to take them off their chains and put them back on after work. But it was odd that she would have forgotten to put it back on. The towel, which she probably used to wipe off the dishes in the drying rack, was neatly folded to hang off the edge of the sink. The empty sink.

The lightning strike had given him the ability to do more than basic arithmetic, but he still couldn’t get the problem in front of him to add up.

“She’s not here. Jee-Yun’s asleep, but Maddie’s not here.” Chimney had returned while Buck was distracted by the ring. He had his phone out, fingers tapping away at the screen while he spoke. “Why would she leave her alone for even a minute? That doesn’t make sense.”

It didn’t, not one bit. They all knew how suddenly disaster could hit, how quickly everything could go from alright to total nightmare. Maddie wouldn’t just leave Jee-Yun home alone.

She also wouldn’t just leave her wedding ring sitting by the sink.

Chimney held his phone to his ear. The sound of something vibrating reached all their ears from the dining table. He went over and picked up Maddie’s phone from where it had been laying.

“Okay,” the paramedic said. “Now I’m freaking out a little.”

“I found this on the sink,” Buck told him, holding up the ring. His stomach was curdling with worry. The other man’s expression as he came to take the ring from him said he was feeling much the same.

“Daddy?” Jee-Yun had gotten out of bed and crept into the kitchen while they were distracted. “Where’s Mommy?”

The three of them looked at eachother, uncertain what to say. And then Eddie moved to sweep Jee-Yun into his arms.

“Mommy’s gone out for a bit,” he told the little girl. His voice shook only a little, doing a much better job of hiding his concern than Buck would’ve in his place. “Let’s get you tucked back into bed. Okay, chiquita?”

“Okay…”

Eddie cast one last look at Buck, and then headed down the hall with Jee-Yun. The little girl laid her head against Eddie’s shoulder, blinking tiredly at Buck and Chimney until she was out of view.

They called Hen, who wasted no time in flying over. She checked in with Chimney, who’d taken a seat at the dining table and was just staring at the wall, and then she and Buck and Eddie started making phone calls. A lot of phone calls, to a lot of people and places.

“Nobody matching Maddie’s description at Presbyterian ER, either,” Hen announced after she finished her latest one.

“And according to Dispatch, her car hasn’t been involved in any kind of accident anywhere across the city,” Buck said, tapping his phone against his palm. 

“What about her phone?”

“No.” Chimney shook his head and set Maddie’s phone down. “There’s nothing here.”

“We’ve called every hospital in LA County,” Eddie said. “I started calling hospitals in Ventura and Orange County, just in case.”

“I think it’s time we call someone else, Chim,” Hen said, taking a seat beside him. “I think you need to file a missing persons report.”

“Ma’s already on it.” Buck’s announcement got a pair of surprised looks from the paramedics, though he couldn’t understand why. “My sister’s missing, Ma was my first call.”

“Listen,” Chimney said. “When we found out that she was pregnant, we made a deal. She said that she wouldn’t leave without telling me, and I told her that I would not treat her like she’s broken.”

“I know. She made me the same promise.”

“Chim,” Hen said, tone gentle and careful. “If she’s really out there having a mental health crisis, we need to get her help.”

“God.” The word left Chimney’s mouth like it pained him. “She was doing so well.”

“Was she?” Buck’s tone was sharp and cutting as he stared down his brother-in-law. “Was she doing well, or were you both just pretending that she was?”

He was thinking back, examining every interaction he’d had with his sister over the last few months. He thought about when he last saw her, when she was over just the other day and making fun of him with Eddie and Abuela. When he talked to her just earlier that day. She’d seemed fine, she hadn’t seemed like she was hiding anything wrong like the last time. She promised she wouldn’t hide anything from him this time.

He had known that something was wrong after Jee-Yun was born, even if he hadn’t known what it was. If something was wrong this time, he’d missed it entirely.

“She was,” Chimney swore as he met Buck’s eyes.

After a moment, Buck accepted his word with a curt nod.

“Postpartum psychosis comes on suddenly,” Eddie said. “It- It could be prepartum psychosis. That’s a thing.”

“Alright,” Hen said, and then gestured at Buck and Eddie. “You two-”

“I’m going downtown with Chimney,” Buck cut her off, digging out the keys to the jeep to hand to Eddie. 

“Fine. Eddie, you canvas the neighborhood. She could just be out walking around,” she said. Eddie gave a nod, but Buck doubted she was anywhere nearby if that was the case. He remembered how far Abby’s mom got, and how quickly, and she’d been far less fit than Maddie was. “I’ll stay here with Jee-Yun.”

“I’ll call Albert and Ravi, interrupt their night-in.” Eddie was already pulling out his phone. “They can help canvas.”

“C’mon.” Buck reached over the table to clap Chimney on the shoulder. “Let’s go.”

It had been the night before Phillip’s funeral. Buck and Maddie, the both of them trying to fall asleep on their separate full-sized beds of their hotel room. The day had been exhausting, mentally and emotionally: a morning spent dealing with their mother, and then being “introduced” to his dead brother. Buck felt wrung out, even though they’d spent the second half of the day playing tour guide through their hometown for Bobby and Athena.

Was a part of him buried in that grave? Buck wondered as he stared up at the ceiling. Maddie had said the cells - the stem cells from his umbilical cord, a middle of the night internet spiral told Buck that was what they would’ve tried for the transplant. An infant was far too young and small to donate bone marrow. - failed to graft. But they’d still been in Daniel, pieces of Buck had been in his brother. Were those pieces still there when he was buried?

Their room was as silent as it was dark, which was to say that it was only almost silent. There was light seeping through the gauzy curtains that covered the window. There was occasional traffic going up and down Chocolate Avenue, which was also US 422 and one of the only roads that went from Harrisburg to cut straight through Hershey and the other tinier towns adjacent to it. The heater was a lone drone, doing its best to keep the temperature somewhere near Buck’s preference.

He had never been particularly fond of winter weather. Snow was fine, even pretty, but it would be finer and prettier if it could somehow also be at least seventy degrees at the same time. And he was never especially skilled at walking across icy patches, something he readily blamed on his too long legs. It was hard to master the penguin waddle when his center of gravity was so oddly placed compared to everyone else.

“Buck?” Maddie’s hushed voice cut through the heater’s drone. “You still awake?”

“Yeah.”

There was the sound of bed covers rustling, and then the wall lamp between their beds flicked on. Buck blinked and squinted against the sudden brightness and sat up. Maddie was doing the same in the other bed, swinging her legs until her bare feet were on the floor. Buck mirrored her.

“I’ve been thinking,” Maddie said. She was wearing an overly large shirt and a pair of shorts, her hair kept in a ponytail by a scrunchie. Buck’s own pajamas consisted of a pair of sweats, a sweatshirt stolen from Eddie, and a pair of fuzzy socks. “Being here, visiting Daniel’s grave… I’m pregnant again.”

“I know, Mads. You told me that a couple weeks ago,” Buck teased.

“I’m pregnant again,” his sister repeated. She drew in a breath, let it out. “And if things happen again, like last time… I need you to know that I’m not going to hide it, I’m not going to lie to you. If there’s something wrong, I’m going to tell you.”

“And if… If you feel like you need to leave again?” he asked, hating how he sounded like a little kid even to his own ears.

“Then I’ll tell you first,” she said. “If I feel like I need to leave again, I’ll tell you first and I’ll tell you where I’m going. I won’t go as far, and I won’t cut you off.”

Maddie raised up her hand between them, all her fingers tucked into her palm except for her pinky, which was sticking out. Without a word, Buck twined his own pinky around hers.

Buck hadn’t been to Athena’s precinct very often.The last time he could remember being here was during the mess with Dalton Wolfe. The time before that was when he and Taylor were nabbed before they could go dumpster diving for evidence together. Back then, they’d gotten shuffled off to separate interrogation rooms, though Buck hadn’t been interrogated. In fact, he helped break the case by figuring out the biggest, most important clue on his own.

(Athena would probably disagree with his versions of events. Athena could be a buzzkill.)

“The last time you spoke to Maddie, how did she sound?” Athena asked. She and Bobby had met the pair of them at the precinct, and now she was perched on her desk while Chimney sat in the chair for visitors. “Was there any indication that…?”

“No.” Chimney shook his head. “I thought she sounded fine. Maybe I was just too caught up to even hear her.”

“Hey.” Bobby reached over and placed a hand on his back. “You didn’t do anything wrong.”

“I talked to her, I saw her,” Buck said. “I thought she seemed fine, too.”

A brunette woman in a leather jacket came rushing into the bullpen, looking harried as she made her way directly to Athena. Buck assumed she was Amber Braeburn, the missing persons detective that Maddie mentioned to him the other day. Athena had told them she was coming.

“Sorry,” she said. “Took me a second. Is this Maddie’s husband?”

“Yeah, hi.” Chimney stood and held out his hand to shake. “I’m Howard Han. Uh, people call me Chimney.”

“And…?” She glanced at Buck and then Bobby, standing by Chimney’s shoulder.

“Buck, Maddie’s brother.” He pointed at Chimney. “And his captain.”

“Bobby Nash, her husband.” Bobby nodded at Athena, and then at Chimney. “His former captain.”

“Right.” The woman made a face, the kind that people usually made when confronted with even a glimpse of the tangled mess that was the 118’s interpersonal relationships.

“So what more can we do?” Chimney’s question was tinged with desperation. “My friends are out looking for her, we checked all the hospitals…”

“First things first, why don’t you finish filling out that form so I can get it into the system.” Braeburn pointed at the missing person form that Chimney had been working on. “Did you bring a picture?”

“Yeah. Digital okay?”

“Absolutely, just keep writing.”

The smile she gave Chimney was almost lizard-like in its flatness, and then she took Athena aside to talk with the sergeant privately. Chimney sat down, pen working away at the form, which left Buck and Bobby by themselves.

“How are you doing?” Bobby asked him.

“My sister’s missing, Pops.” Buck shrugged, shoulders rising and falling limply. “Everyone’s thinking she’s run off again, but I… I don’t know.”

“You don’t think she did?”

“I can’t think of any other reason why she’d be gone.”

Bobby didn’t say anything. What he did instead was wrap an arm around Buck and pull him in close.

When Chimney finished up the form, he gave it to the detective. Then, the four of them went to an office - presumably Braeburn’s - while they waited for her to get it submitted. Bobby and Athena sat down in the chairs provided, but Buck was too wired up with anxiety. Chimney didn’t sit down, either.

“There’s something I haven’t told you two,” the paramedic said. “Something I probably should’ve put on that form.”

“Wait.” Buck stared at him. “You didn’t put it on the form!?”

“Put what on the form?” Bobby asked, politely interested.

“Maddie’s pregnant,” Chimney said with a sigh.

“Oh.” Bobby said, and then, after a moment, he widened his eyes and said, “Oh, wow.”

Athena side-eyed him and his totally unbelievable acting. Chimney looked between them, realized the same thing Buck had, and then turned to glare at Buck.

“I didn’t tell them!”

“She stopped drinking wine at dinner,” Athena pointed out.

“And Buck stopped serving fish,” Bobby added.

“She said the smell made her nauseous,” Buck sheepishly explained.

“Alright.” Braeburn had rejoined them, stepping into the office. “She’s in the system, APB’s going out now.”

“You should probably tell her,” Bobby urged.

Chimney sighed.

“Maddie’s pregnant,” he said. “She’s in her second trimester.”

“And I’m guessing you didn’t put that on the form,” Braeburn said.

“It might explain things, though. After we had our first child, Maddie suffered from postpartum depression-”

“Thyroiditis,” Buck interrupted, and then ducked his head a little. “It- It was postpartum thyroiditis. That’s why the meds they kept putting her on at first weren’t working.”

“Postpartum thyroiditis.” Chimney nodded to Buck. “And it was… It was pretty bad.”

“How bad?” Braeburn asked.

“She ran all the way to Boston,” he told her. “And she tried to drown herself.”

“I see…”

“But that was postpartum. She hasn’t shown any signs of depression or anything out of the ordinary since.”

“Mr. Han,” Braeburn said. “Did your wife say anything to you about the case we’ve been working on together?”

“Yeah,” Chimney slowly said, seeming as confused as Buck felt. “She was freaked out, but she said you got the guy.”

“Did she say anything about how we got him?”

“No…”

“He took his own life,” Athena said, sitting forward. “Maddie talked him into it.”

“Go Maddie,” Buck blurted out, laughing a little. It earned him four incredulous stares. “What? He kidnapped a kid and was gonna do God-knows-what to her. I don’t feel sad for him.”

For some reason, Braeburn glared at him for the comment. It was fleeting, there and gone again, but it was scathing for the moment that it existed.

“We have to take this into account,” she said, her face going neutral again as she turned her attention back to Chimney. “She was under a very unique stress. May I have a moment to talk to Mr. Han alone?”

“Yeah,” Bobby answered for them. “Chim, we’ll meet you outside.”

Buck followed him and Athena out of the office, through the bullpen of desks, and out into the hall. Athena stopped and turned, already speaking.

“Something about this isn’t right,” she said.

“I would say almost nothing is right about it,” Bobby said.

“She left her wedding ring,” Buck said, drawing both of their attention. “It was left on the back of the sink, like- like she’d taken it off when she washed the dishes and didn’t put it back on. Jee-Yun was in her bed, asleep. When Maddie left last time, she took Jee to the firehouse, made sure she wasn’t alone. And- And she promised that she’d tell me before she went anywhere this time, that she’d tell me where she was going. She promised she would tell me if there was something wrong.”

It was a pinky promise. He and Maddie did not break those.

Athena placed a hand on his arm, soft and comforting.

“It’s not just about her running away,” she said. “It’s the timing, the way it happened right after she helped stop a kidnapper. That’s too big of a coincidence.”

“A man’s dead,” Bobby argued. “He didn’t kill himself and then kidnap Maddie.”

“But what if he wasn’t working alone?”

“You suspect he had an accomplice?”

“She said something was weird about the guy’s voice.” Buck’s statement got Bobby and Athena’s attention again. “Wh- When she told me and Eddie about it, she said the kidnapper’s voice sounded off.”

Athena opened her mouth, and then focused her gaze on something past Buck and Bobby.

“Don’t say anything, I don’t want him to worry,” she said, just before Chimney joined them. “All set?”

“She gave me her card,” Chimney told them. “Told me to try her anytime, day or night. I get the feeling she thinks Maddie will be missing for a while.”

“Yeah, m- maybe.” How was Buck not supposed to tell him? “Hey, let’s get you home.”

“I feel like I should be doing something more.”

“You are doing exactly what you’re supposed to,” Athena told him. “You have one place to be right now, and that’s with your daughter.”

“Maddie told you to take care of Jee last time, remember?” Buck reminded him. “Just do that. C’mon.”

With a final glance to Athena, he started leading Chimney to the where they parked. And he bit his tongue the entire way there.

Chapter 31: Maddie's Not-So-Silver Hammer

Chapter Summary

In which Maddie is found. (Again.)

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The thing is, Buck totally intended to follow Athena’s directive. Except, on the silent drive back to Maddie and Chimney’s house, with him behind the wheel because Chimney wasn’t really in a state to be driving, he got to thinking. And while he’d learned to think through his actions before leaping headfirst into the first solution he came up with, thinking still got him into just as much trouble as not thinking.

Mostly, Buck was thinking about how much trouble was caused the last time by them not telling each other what was going on, what they knew. And while he could understand Athena not wanting Chimney to worry, the thought of keeping something like this from the other man felt a little too close to hypocrisy than Buck was comfortable with at the moment. Plus, he didn’t want to be punched again.

“What, uh. What did the detective say?” he asked, while trying to figure out how to broach the subject.

“She just asked me for more details about last time,” Chimney answered, the words coming out exhausted. “She thinks Maddie ran away.”

“She doesn’t know Maddie like we do,” Buck said, taking his eyes off the road just long enough to cut a glance at his brother-in-law. Chimney was leaning against the window. “And Ma, uh… Ma didn’t want me to say anything to you, because she didn’t want you to worry.”

Chimney blinked, made a face, and then sat up.

“Worry about what? I’m already worried.”

“Ma thinks that, uh. That there’s a chance the guy, the Weepy Caller or whatever they’re calling him on the news, that he might have had an accomplice,” Buck told him. “She thinks the timing’s weird. And she knows Maddie better than the detective.”

“She thinks Maddie was taken.” It wasn’t a question.

“She doesn’t know for sure, there’s no proof,” Buck hurried to say. “But it… It makes more sense than her leaving without telling us.”

Without telling me, Buck thought but did not say. He could tell from Chimney’s expression that he was thinking it, too, that he was remembering how he’d gotten a recorded message last time while Buck got a phone call.  Neither of them said it, though.

Eddie, along with Ravi and Albert, had spent the intervening time canvassing for Maddie. Now, though, with the sun having risen and no sign of her yet, Eddie swung by and picked Buck up so they could go home. They had a kid to get to school, and they needed to refill on caffeine.

“Did you find Aunt Maddie?” Chris asked, meeting Buck and Eddie just inside the door.

“Not yet,” Buck told him, reaching down to ruffle his hair. Chris allowed it with only a small scowl. “Your nana’s on it, though. Where’s Abuela and Carla?”

“Outside with Hoover.”

“You ready for school? Go get your stuff,” Eddie urged, and got a huff and a grumpy,

“I can help look.”

“We have a lot of other people looking, mijo,” Eddie said. “You can help by going to school.”

Another huff and an eye roll later and Chris was heading for his room, to grab his bag. Eddie shook his head in fondness and then made his way into the kitchen to get them both coffee. Buck followed, laying on his husband’s back while he got the Hildy started on brewing a new pot.

“What if someone did take her?” The question came out in a whisper and it hung, quivering, in the still air.

Buck had told Eddie all about Athena’s suspicions, just like he told Chimney. There hadn’t been any debate about it, he simply blurted everything out the moment the jeep’s doors were closed and they were on the road again. They’d both agreed not to spread it to anyone else besides Chimney and whoever Chimney decided to tell.

“Your sister killed the last guy who took her,” Eddie reminded him.

“Yeah,” Buck breathed out. “She did.”

The secret that he didn’t want to give voice to, though, was that he thought he might prefer the idea that his sister was taken. It wasn’t better, he knew that. It wasn’t a good thing if Athena was right, if that Weepy Caller guy had an accomplice and they decided to kidnap Maddie. But it would mean that Maddie didn’t choose to leave.

“Oh, don’t you both look awful,” was Carla’s cheerful yet worried greeting to them when she walked into the kitchen, Hoover trotting ahead of her and Abuela trailing.

“Thanks, Carla. Real helpful for the self-image,” Eddie snarked.

“You’re still pretty, boo,” she assured him, reaching up to pat his cheek. “Any news?”

“No.” Buck shook his head. “But she’s formally reported, and Ma’s on it.”

Abuela sighed and crossed herself, shaking her head as she continued on through the house. 

“The sergeant’ll find her,” Carla said with confidence. “I’ll go make sure Chris is ready and get his genius self onto school.”

“Oh.” Eddie blinked at her. “I was gonna do that.”

“Have either of you slept since last night?” she asked, and didn’t wait for the answer she already knew. “You’ll fall asleep at the wheel.”

“Don’t you have another client today?” Buck asked, a bit dumbly. “Or, wait. You’re not working on your day off, are you?”

“You’re my friends.” She emphasized the word. “I don’t have to be anywhere until noon.”

“Still…”

“Hush, it’s fine. I called Pepa, she’s coming over to sit with Abuela,” Carla told them. “You two go take a nap while you can.”

“If I can,” Buck muttered.

But she was right, they did need to get at least a little bit of sleep. However much Buck wanted to search and search and keep searching until Maddie was found, until she was safe at home, he had no idea where to go. Last time, they’d had Doug’s phone and then a gas station and then a rental agreement,  they’d had a trail to follow that led them straight to her. Hell, the same was true when Chimney went missing before his wedding.

Buck could spend all day spinning his wheels this time, and he’d still get nowhere.

Rick Romero was Athena’s oldest friend and one of her truest. She wasn’t certain there was anyone else she could trust more to have her back. Trust as much, maybe, but not trust more. And that trust came through once again when she told him that she wanted to review the autopsy of Richard Bullock, the Weepy Caller kidnapper-slash-serial killer who’d shot himself before they could bring him in, and he made it happen without any questions.

“Thanks for arranging this,” she told him as he climbed out of his car. They were meeting in the parking garage of the ME’s office.

“When Athena Grant calls,” he said, slamming the car door shut. “I come running.”

“Anybody else know we’re doing this?”

“Just the M.E.,” Rick said. “But don’t worry, I’m keeping this between us.”

“I appreciate that,” she told him. “Because I am really going out on a skinny branch here.”

Or maybe the branch wasn’t skinny at all. The added details from Buck, his own misgivings about how Maddie disappeared and what Maddie had told him, the fact that, according to Bobby, Buck wasn’t so certain she’d simply ran off, it all served to make Athena even more certain about what her instincts were telling her. Athena just needed proof, something undeniable that she could point at to get the bureaucratic wheels turning.

That’s why she and Rick were here now.

“I have to admit, I was surprised you wanted to review the autopsy,” he said as they went inside. “The guy shot himself on the air with Nine-One-One. Seemed pretty open-shut.”

“Maybe it’s a little too open-shut. I want to make sure he’s the one who actually pulled the trigger.”

According to Maddie, the caller’s voice had sounded off, somehow, that there was something weird about it. Without being able to ask her what she meant, there could be any number of reasons for why a person’s voice would sound off over the line. Anything from their mood, to drugs, to distress.

Hell, maybe the caller was using a voice modulator and that was what Maddie heard.

“Well, his finger was definitely on the trigger,” the coroner, Luann, told them. 

The body of Richard Bullock was laid out on the metal table, sheet covering him from the middle of the chest down. The y-shaped incision was stark against his pale, bloodless skin, and the sides of his head were less gory than when he arrived. There was still a hole going through it, though, and not a clean one.

“He has gunshot residue all over his right hand and temple,” Luann continued.

“So he did shoot himself,” Athena concluded, unable to suppress the disappointment. If there was no accomplice, if Maddie really had fled instead of being taken-

“I didn’t say that,” Luann said, cutting off her thoughts. She handed Rick a sheet with the lab findings on it. “I said his finger was on the trigger, but he had a healthy amount of trichloromethane in his system.”

“That’s chloroform,” Rick said, reading through what the paper said.

“We believe he used chloroform on his victims, to incapacitate them” Athena told Luann. “Could that account for it?”

“Not at these levels. My guess is, he was chloroformed repeatedly.”

“So he was drugged, somebody put a gun in his hand, and then manipulated his trigger finger?”

“I don’t put the puzzle together, Sergeant,” Luann said. “I only provide the pieces.”

And this was one big piece.

“So somebody kept him alive long enough to be a fresh kill when we got there,” Rick concluded.

Somebody that was still out there, too. Somebody that might have Maddie.

They had a trail to follow, now, leads they could chase down that they hadn’t seen before. They could go back to Jayna, the last kidnapping victim, and find out what she remembered. If she failed to come up with anything useful, there was Richard Bullock’s girlfriend, the same one who sent them to the trailer where he’d been living. Not that they’d found him there.

If he was just a patsy, that meant the real Weepy Caller was still on the loose, and they’d become their number one suspect in Maddie’s disappearance. 

It was hours and hours later, late in the evening, when they reconvened at Maddie and Chimney’s house. Buck’s sister had been missing for over twenty-four hours now, and he was slowly going insane with it. After an attempt at napping that was barely refreshing, they’d restarted the search by harassing every desk agent at LAX and Union Station, as well as the airports of John Wayne, Hollywood Burbank, Ontario International, San Bernardino International, and Long Beach. Because they had no proof that Maddie had been taken, just a suspicion.

Ravi and Albert had spent their time, when they resumed searching, going to every bus station in and around the city with a picture of Maddie. They’d had just as much luck as Buck and Eddie.

When they got back to the house and Hen let them in, they found Chimney pacing the living room with his phone pressed to his ear. The detective’s business card was clutched in his hand.

“I already called her office,” Chimney snapped at whoever he was talking to. “I need you to patch me through to her cell.”

“What’s going on?” Albert asked.

“He’s trying to reach that missing persons detective,” Hen explained to them.

Buck turned slightly and caught Eddie’s eye before asking,

“Did something happen?”

“Someone else might have been in the house when Maddie disappeared,” Hen said. “Jee-Yun said she heard someone crying.”

Immediately, Buck’s thoughts went to Athena’s suspicions of an accomplice aiding the kidnapper. The crying definitely made it sound like it. Except the caller, the one who cried, was supposed to also be the one who shot themselves.

“Have Detective Braeburn call me as soon as possible,” Chimney told the person on the other end of the line. “My name is Howard Han. It’s about a case, she’ll know.”

He hung up, dropped his arm to his side and turned to face them.

“They said her call went straight to voicemail.”

“It is getting late,” Eddie pointed out.

“Well, this can’t wait.”

“So, what are you gonna do?” Ravi asked him.

“If I can’t get the detective on the phone, then I’ll go to her,” Chimney said, already scrolling through his cell. “I just gotta get her address.”

That required a simple phone call to Josh at dispatch, who apparently didn’t even hesitate before looking it up for them. He was Maddie’s friend, after all, and he’d been keeping an ear out for anything that even sounded like it might’ve been her. Josh gave Chimney the address and wished him luck, and Buck didn’t hesitate to go with his brother-in-law.

When they got to Braeburn’s house, they ended up waiting on the porch for a while. Chimney pressed the doorbell insistently, and Buck waited impatiently to the left of him. He tapped his foot and paced a little, until the door opened and the detective greeted them.

“Mr. Han, and… Buck.” She looked taken aback to see Buck there, more surprised than she did to see Chimney.

“Sorry to show up on your doorstep like this,” Chimney said. “I’ve been trying to reach you all night.”

“No, it’s okay,” Braeburn replied. “I’m sorry, I was downstairs working. Reception sucks down there. Come on in.”

She stepped to the side and Buck followed Chimney in, through the foyer and then into a sitting room. Braeburn joined them after closing the door.

“So, what’s going on, Mr. Han?”

“Maddie didn’t leave on her own,” Chimney blurted out. “I think she was taken.”

Braeburn’s head jerked a little.

“What makes you say that?” she asked.

“Our daughter,” Chimney said. “She said that someone else was in the house."

“Uh.” Braeburn looked to the side. “Let me get you both some water.”

“Ma- Er, Sergeant Grant thinks the kidnapper had an accomplice,” Buck told her while he and Chimney followed her into the kitchen. It was small, with another doorway on the other side of the room that led to what might have been a utility room.

“Really?” 

Her voice had an odd tone to it, or maybe that was just Buck’s anxiety for his sister.

“Jee-Yun said she heard someone crying,” Chimney explained. “Someone not my wife.”

For a single moment, Braeburn seemed to freeze. And then she nodded.

“Let me get you some water, and then we can go downstairs,” she said. “I’ll take an official statement. You know, leave no stone unturned.”

Chimney pulled out his phone, which had started vibrating. He glanced down at it, and then grew visibly excited.

“It’s Athena,” he announced, before answering. Braeburn went to the kitchen sink while he talked to the sergeant, turning on the faucet to fill a glass. “Hey, Athena, did you find her?... Yeah. Buck’s with me… What?”

The last word sounded odd, to Buck’s ears. Purposefully flat. He was focused on the conversation that he was only hearing half of and not what the detective was doing, which was probably why it caught him by surprise when he glanced over to find Braeburn had shut off the faucet and was now pointing a gun at the pair of them.

A jolt of adrenaline went through Buck as he stepped closer to Chimney, putting himself in front of him and blindly reaching back to smack at him.

“Chim. Chim. Chim.”

“What? Oh.” Chimney had obviously noticed the current seriousness of their situation. “Athena, I’ll have to call you back. She has a gun.”

“I guess the sergeant figured it out?” Braeburn asked, far too casual for someone who was pointing a gun at Buck’s chest.

“Where’s my wife?” Chimney demanded, trying to step around Buck. Trying to; Buck moved to keep Chimney behind him. “Where’s Maddie? Maddie!”

“Sorry.” There was a movement in the doorway behind Braeburn. “You just missed her.”

And then a hammer rose up before coming down upside her head.

Braeburn collapsed forward, revealing Maddie right behind her. A blood splattered Maddie, bleeding from her throat. She stumbled, dropped the hammer, started to fall. Buck and Chimney were both there to catch her and lower her to the floor.

While Chimney fell into frantic paramedic mode, pleading with Maddie to keep her eyes open and using Siri to call 9-1-1, Buck tried to find something to use to staunch the bleeding besides Chimney’s bare hands. A towel, maybe, or even an oven mitt. It was why he noticed that Braeburn was not unconscious, merely rattled. She was still on the ground, but she was reaching for the gun.

Buck brought his foot down on her hand, hard, with all his weight. He felt delicate metacarpals and phalanges crunch, and the detective let out a cry of pain. He kicked the gun, sending it skidding farther away from Braeburn, and then kicked her head like a football for good measure.

“Chimney! Buck!” That was Athena, bursting through the house with her gun drawn. She wasn’t alone, with Romero and another cop right behind her.

“Her gun’s over there!” Buck pointed at it and went to grab the towel folded up to hang off the edge of the sink. He handed it to Chimney, who took it with hands dripping with Maddie’s blood and pressed it to her throat. “Where’s the-?”

“Right behind us,” Athena said, nodding to Romero as he went to secure the weapon. The other officer was securing Braeburn. “Scene’s secure!”

Chimney ended up riding in the ambulance with Maddie, obviously. Buck stayed behind to give a quick statement of what happened, before hitching a ride with Athena to the hospital. He called Eddie on the way, who was still with Hen and Albert and Ravi. 

The wait was agonizing. Buck’s time was split between pacing a hole and sitting in one of the uncomfortable chairs, bracketed by Bobby and Eddie. The moment one of the doctors came through the swinging doors, calling for Chimney, they were all on their feet. Buck didn’t pay attention to most of what she said, focusing instead on the gist of “she’s okay.” The cut to her throat had been deep enough to hit her artery, but it wasn’t so deep to sever her trachea or cause permanent damage to her larynx.

“And the baby?” Chimney asked.

“He’s just fine.”

Chapter End Notes

Baby Boy Han needs a name, 'cause I ain't naming him Robert Nash.

(Also, 2/3 characters named Robert Nash have died onscreen. That is not a good statistic for the child.)

Chapter 32: He Looks Nothing Like Taylor Kelly

Chapter Summary

In which we meet Bobby's mother.

A couple days after Maddie was kidnapped - again - and then rescued, Eddie started the classes to become a paramedic. In the weeks since, he and Buck had fallen into a new routine. He would hesitate to say that the new schedule was kinder, because he had four ten-hour days in a row, but he did have guaranteed weekends at the moment. He’d started taking Abuela and the boys out to the park or wherever, on the Saturdays and Sundays that Buck worked. And he’d even got to sit a more subdued Sunday dinner while Buck was on shift, something that had his husband pouting something fierce in jealousy.

His weekdays still started just as early, though. Earlier, even, because his commute to classes was longer than the commute to the station. He’d roll out of bed after slapping his alarm into silence, dragged himself through a shower, and then dressed for the day. In civvies, because he didn’t need the uniform for the lectures and the skills lab.

On days that Buck didn’t have to go into work, he’d see Eddie off at the door with a kiss and a brown paper bag that had lunch plus a little note inside that was almost always a stupid pun. On the days that Buck did go in, they’d part the same way, except in the driveway. And then there were the days that Eddie hated, the ones where he left the house before Buck came home, and they didn’t get to see each other until late into the afternoon.

His fellow paramedics-to-be were quickly able to pick up on those days, where he came in with a lunch that had no pun. Days where he was a little bit grumpier and a lot more tired, because he’d lost the ability to have a good night’s sleep without Buck in the bed with him a very long time ago. They teased him mercilessly for it, because one of them followed that stupid Instagram account and it wasn’t hard for them to guess why he was grumpier than usual on those days.

Luckily, today was not going to be one of those days. The same could not be said for tomorrow, though.

“You guys got everything for school?” Buck asked from the kitchen, where he was sorting out Eddie’s lunch. Everytime, Eddie said he could do it himself or buy something. Everytime, Buck would scoff and ignore him.

“Yeah, Pops,” Chris said with a yawn, half asleep in his cereal.

“Eds?” Buck prompted.

“Yes, mi sol,” Eddie dutifully answered with an over exaggerated eye roll. It got Chris to laugh, sitting across from him at the table, so he gave himself an imaginary pat on the back.

“Don’t you roll your eyes at me,” Buck said without turning around.

“I didn’t!” Eddie denied.

“He did!” Chris countered.

“You traitor.”

“He loves me more,” Buck bragged, coming over with the paper bag. “Okay, Chris, Carla should be-”

“Good morning, Diazes!” the woman in question greeted them as she opened the door, pausing to pat Hoover when the dog trotted up to her with his tail wagging.

“Right here,” Buck finished, bending down to smack a kiss into Chris’ curls. “Go get your stuff.”

Chris grunted and grumbled, but he pushed himself out of the chair and trundled into the kitchen to deposit his bowl in the sink. Then he went to his room, to grab his school bag and his crutches. Eddie could take his son to school on one day of the week, Friday, and only that day. The rest of the week it was Buck or Carla.

“Gavin threw the mother of all tantrums at bedtime last night,” Buck warned Carla. “Literally everything made him angrier. And louder.”

“Ah, the thankless threes,” she sagely said.

“I thought they were supposed to be terrible twos. He was an angel at two,” Eddie complained into his coffee. “Now my baby boy’s possessed by the devil.”

He was only half-joking there. Last night, when Gavin threw the third book across the room and shouted “No!” at the top of his lungs for the hundredth time, Eddie had asked Abuela if her friend did exorcisms. And then Abuela, his beloved Abuela, laughed in his face before hiding away in her room with the dog.

Speaking of Abuela, she shuffled into the dining room and tutted.

“You were no better,” she told him, and Buck laughed at his squawk of offense.

“I don’t have to take this,” Eddie huffed and stood up, grabbing his bagged lunch. “Have fun with el diablo, Abuelita.”

Abuela just sniffed haughtily and told him,

“My bisnietos are all angels for me.”

Religion, for Buck, was always just sorta there. A constant presence, especially nowadays with Abuela, but not something that was ever an actual fixture of his life. His family was nominally Episcopalian, and Maddie said that they used to go to church on occasion, but Buck didn’t remember doing it growing up. And for all that he fully believed in the universe’s ability to scream at them, the closest he’d ever gotten to being religious himself was when Eddie got shot and he found himself praying with every breath until the man woke up.

Buck wasn’t certain if the building they were arriving at was intended to be a megachurch or not, the large cross made out of piping that jutted from the roof certainly didn’t seem original to the structure, but it was definitely being used for one today. When the trucks and ambulance came to a stop at the entrance, there were people standing around being very… Odd. Swaying, crying, swinging their arms around. Others were meandering around or sitting wherever.

“What the heck?” Ravi blurted out, voicing all of their thoughts.

“Dispatch said some kind of miracle service went south,” Buck told him, and got the quip from Chimney of,

“They ever go north?”

“Thank God!” A young man in business casual wear ran up to them before Buck could reply. “Mervin Egan, I run facilities here.”

“What happened?” Buck asked as he continued to lead the way inside.

“Sister Ann was in the middle of her act- I mean, service.” Mervin caught himself, but Buck still heard a giggle come from Bell. The probie muffled it and ducked her head. “And then people started, I don’t know. Dropping, puking, dancing?”

“Isn’t that kind of normal?” Chimney asked him.

“Not like this.”

There was a large banner right by the doors, of an older woman in a white gown with her hands clasped in front of her in prayer. It was the words in gold above her, though, that had Buck almost tripping over himself: Ann Hutchinson Ministries. He didn’t have time to dwell on why the name was so familiar, though.

Inside was, initially, calm as they got through the foyer. Calm except for the screaming and crying that got louder as they reached one of the double doors to the auditorium. They burst open, letting out a wall of sound and a woman who puked onto the floor even as she stumbled out. There was one man muttering while hitting himself in the face with what might’ve been a collection plate until Chimney rushed over to stop him. Besides him, there were people standing stock still with their arms stretched out above their heads, people rolling in the aisles, people laid out where they’d fallen.

Utter chaos.

“Was there something in the communion wafers?” Chimney asked, to no one in particular.

“Too much Holy Spirit,” was Bell's exuberant contribution.

“Okay, uh, let’s start triaging and figure out what’s going on,” Buck said as he looked around to try and figure out where to start. There was a man laid out in the aisle, not far away from them; he was grinning up at nothing and giggling. His face, like so many of the others around them, was flushed bright red. “Hen, Chim, start with that guy. The rest of you, spread out and do what you can. Keep an eye out for whatever might be causing this.”

They spread out in all directions, and Buck did his best to keep track of the goings on around him. Someone fell down the stairs to his left, but Albert was already on it. In front of him, Hen and Chimney were sticking a c-collar on their patient, who was quietly giggling still. On the stage were Ravi and Bell, the pair of them splitting up to check on the people there.

Missing from the stage, however, was the star of the show. The woman whose name was just so familiar…

“Hey.” Buck caught Mervin’s attention. “The woman from the banner outside, Ann Hutchinson? I don’t see her anywhere.”

“I shooed Sister Ann and her son to the tour bus when everything went nuts, they’re fine.”

Sister Ann and her son- Oh.

Oh.

Oh, shit.

Buck was about to ask if Ann’s son was named Charlie, but his radio crackled into life with Bell’s voice.

“Hey, Cap? Running gas generators inside a building is bad, right?”

“Yeah, Bell,” Buck replied back, glaring at Mervin as he did. “Running gas generators indoors is very bad.”

“I had to,” Mervin said in defense of his stupidity. “Every time Sister Ann’s circus comes to town, I can barely keep up on the lighting package.”

“That doesn’t mean you had to keep them inside,” Buck snapped. He thumbed the button on his radio so he could speak to his team. “They’ve all got carbon monoxide poisoning. I want all of you in full SCBA gear and the building cleared out. Ravi, Bell, kill the generators and get the place ventilated.”

If he wasn’t very gentle about herding Mervin Egan out the door, well, he was at a church. He could just ask forgiveness later.

They got a spot outside for triaging the more severe victims while they waited for dispatch to send more RA units. While Albert, Chimney, and Hen focused on the worst of the patients, the others went through and herded the dazed churchgoers out the doors. For a lot of them, simply being outside in the fresh air did them a world of good.

“The fans are going,” Ravi announced as he exited the building, tugging off his mask. Bell was right behind him. “Five-hundred PPM and falling.”

“Good job.” Buck flashed them a grin and a thumbs up, and then stepped out of the way as the paramedics hurried out with a patient on a gurney.

He followed them to the triage and watched as they fussed over him, calling out stats to each other. They had the patient on oxygen and cranked it up higher, which seemed to be enough to rouse the guy. He came awake with a jerk, and was wheeled away to one of the awaiting ambulances.

“Oh, thank God,” Mervin blurted out. He’d been watching, too, with perhaps even more anxious tension than the rest of them. It was his ass on the line, after all. “Are these people gonna be okay?”

“Should be,” Buck told him. He was a bit worried about the guy that Bell found backstage, right next to the generators.

“This could’ve been a lot worse, huh?”

“You’re lucky it wasn’t.”

The statement had Mervin wincing.

“I’m coming, Jesus!” a woman shouted from up above. Buck looked up and spotted her climbing that giant cross on the roof. “I’m coming!”

“Oh, God,” Mervin gasped in dismay.

Buck’s response to the new development was a simple and concise, “aw, crap,” before grabbing his radio.

“Javier, get the aerial into position. Ravi, you’re going up. Toby, get on the roof and make sure that thing’s stable,” he ordered. Toby, close enough for Buck to hear his voice but not make out the words, said something that had people laughing. Buck turned to Chimney, still standing nearby, and jerked towards the cross. “Chim, go up with him?”

“Copy that,” the paramedic replied before hurrying off to deposit his medical bag and grab what was needed.

It didn’t take long to get the aerial ladder maneuvered into place, Javier using the controls to swing it around. Toby and Chimney used a fire escape and then an extension ladder to reach the roof and the base of the cross. The moment Buck spotted their helmeted heads over the edge, he was radioing to check in.

“It’s creaking, Cap,” Toby replied. “She’s making it top-heavy.”

“The two of you do what you can to keep it from falling over,” Buck told him, eying Ravi as the aerial was extended to put him even with the woman.

Ravi shouted something and got a reply back that had him rolling his head in clear exasperation.

“Cap,” he radioed down. “She thinks I’m Satan.”

“He doesn’t look anything like Taylor Kelly,” Albert said from just behind Buck. He shrugged when Buck turned to make a face at him. “Eddie isn’t here to say it.”

Albert was right, that was what Eddie would say if he was here. But thinking that just made him miss his husband, even though he’d seen the man just that morning.

“Try telling her you’re not,” Buck radioed back.

Ravi looked down at him, hand thrown out and the unspoken “really?” clear as day. He shook his head and turned back to the woman and spoke to her, but whatever he said was clearly not convincing since she didn’t stop climbing. The way the cross shook and wobbled, though, definitely had her pausing.

“Toby, how’re things looking?” Buck asked.

“We’re working on it,” was Toby’s terse reply.

“Ravi?”

“I’m trying,” Ravi replied. “She isn’t listening to me.”

The woman was now standing on the arm of the cross, clinging to the structure by a single hand. Her other was stretched out towards the sky above. Or to Jesus Himself, Buck wasn’t too certain.

And then the cross shook. Buck had no idea what it was made of, but it definitely wasn’t steel, because he watched the pipes that it was made of crumple and bend at one of the joints above Toby. The woman screamed and clung to it, seemingly made more cognizant of her situation now that adrenaline was pumping through her system.

Ravi was saying something to her, and whatever it was had her reaching out for him. But then the cross shook and she went back to clinging to it, shaking her head at Ravi. She was scared and seemed on the verge of hyperventilating.

“I can’t!” she cried out, loud enough for Buck to hear. “I’ll fall!”

“Sister Greta, be still.” Ann Hutchinson had a bullhorn- No, correction, she had the 118’s bullhorn, apparently having just grabbed it off their engine. “This is the time for you to come down from the cross. That work has already been done.”

There was a wry tone to her words, and Buck couldn’t decide if it actually reminded him of Bobby or if he was just making connections that weren’t really there.

“Save me, Sister Ann!” Greta, the woman on the cross, shouted down.

“You’re already saved, honey. Jesus is with you,” Ann replied. “All you have to do is go into His loving arms.”

“Oh cool, I’m dating Jesus,” Albert quipped, because Ravi was clearly the Jesus in this metaphor.

“I know you can do this, have faith,” Ann urged. The cross shook, bent, nearly tossed Greta off. “Believe! And reach out!”

And Greta did. For Ravi, at least. She reached out and took his hand, allowing him to help her off the cross and onto the ladder. He helped her down, where she was met by paramedics with a waiting gurney. Ann saw to her as she got loaded onto the ambulance, while Buck and the others started the task of loading everything back onto the engine.

“She’s kind of something, isn’t she?” Hen said, because Buck had been kinda staring at Ann the entire time.

“Should I call her Grandma?” he asked as Ann came over with the bullhorn. “Or Granny?”

“Wait, what?”

“I think this belongs to you.” Ann held the bullhorn out to Buck, smiling perfectly pleasantly. A man that might’ve been Charlie, Bobby’s brother, was beside her.

“It uh, it technically belongs to the city,” Buck said as he took it from her. “You’re Po- er, Bobby’s mom, right? Bobby Nash?”

It was a statement that had everyone staring at him. Ann even slipped off the sunglasses she was wearing to look at him better.

“How do you know Bobby?” she asked.

“Um.” How to answer that question without coming off as insane to a complete stranger… “He was the captain before me. Our old captain.”

She hummed and then nodded.

“Charlie,” she said to the man next to her, and then, “Excuse me.”

Buck stepped to the side, allowing the pair to head onto the tour bus. He and the others watched them go, before Chimney was breaking the silence with,

“That’s Bobby’s mom?”

“She wasn’t on the flowchart,” Bell complained.

“Because I didn’t know she existed to put on the flowchart,” Ravi shot back.

“Yeah, yeah, let’s finish packing everything up,” Buck told them, rolling his eyes. He had to figure out how to tell Bobby that his family was in town.

The future Grant-Nash house was coming along nicely. The roof and the outer walls were already done. Or as far as Buck could tell, anyways. It was abuzz with activity as workers went about their business, giving him and the stroller he pushed curious gazes. Most of them recognized him from prior visits, so he wasn’t stopped except for a quick hello.

The interior was no nearly as finished, with plastic sheets serving as temporary doors and the inner walls consisting of the studs and not much more. Buck found Bobby and Athena in what would be the kitchen, one day. Athena looked at him, and then at the grumpily tired child in the stroller, and put a hand on her hip.

“Did you walk all the way here with my grandbaby?” she demanded.

“I figured he can’t scream at me anymore if he’s exhausted,” Buck said with a shrug. “And it worked.”

Now, anyway. Gavin was perfectly fine giving his negative opinion about the plan for the half mile he was walking, and then for most of his time in the stroller.

“Carla called it the thankless threes,” he told Bobby and Athena. “And it has been very thankless so far.”

“Mmm. Harry was the same,” Athena stated.

“So was Brooke,” Bobby added, smiling.

“Speaking of your family, Pops, wanna guess who I met yesterday?” Buck asked. Bobby looked confused and slightly panicked. “We went to a call for a case of carbon monoxide poisoning at a, uh. Faith healing-”

“Oh, God. My mother’s in town?”

“Ayup. Ann Hutchinson Ministries.”

“What?” Athena sounded shocked as she turned on her husband. “When were you going to tell me that your mother wasn’t dead?”

“I didn’t say that she was,” Bobby replied as he moved to the island. It was mostly just a shape made of plywood at this point, with tool bags, drink cups, and counter samples sitting on it.

“I’m sorry, I guess I just assumed,” Athena shot back. Buck glanced between them and then backed up a little with the stroller. “Given the way you talk about her. Or rather, don’t.”

“I don’t talk about her because I don’t want to think about her, I don’t even want her in my life.” Bobby held up two counter samples, one white and one black. “Which countertop do you like? I think we should pick between these two.”

“Bobby.”

“Hank said we have to pick today to stay on schedule.”

“What about the granite?” Buck suggested, ducking slightly when it earned him Athena’s ire.

“I do like the granite,” Bobby agreed, setting the samples down and going to where the granite sample was sitting. “You can set a hot pan down on it no problem, no searching for a trivet.”

“That’s fantastic,” Athena snarked. “But you are not changing the subject.”

“Alright,” Bobby sighed. “What do you want to know?”

“When did you and Buck talk about her?”

“Hershey,” Buck answered. “When I was hiding from Mom…”

Athena’s countenance softened and she nodded, accepting that explanation.

“And why don’t you two speak?” she asked next.

“Because every time we do, I get this kink in my neck that lasts for like, a month,” Bobby complained, reaching up to rub at his neck as if the very mention of his mother caused him discomfort. Buck could sympathize. “She’s a fraud and a con artist. It’s embarrassing.”

“So you don’t think she’s sincere?”

“I think she sincerely enjoys living the high life. And those gullible people that she fleeces from town to town? They pay the bill.”

“When’s the last time you even spoke to her?” Athena asked.

“Back when she brought her carny act to the Twin Cities, just before Marcy and I were gonna get married. We went to see her. Marcy wanted me to invite her to the wedding.”

“And did you?”

“I went backstage. We talked for about three seconds, and then we were fighting,” Bobby said  “So, no. I did not.”

“And that was it?” was Athena’s next dubious sounding question.

“No. After the apartment fire-” Buck winced preemptively, because he knew this was going to be bad. “-I received a condolence letter on official Ann Hutchinson Ministry stationary. I didn’t even read it to the end.”

“Why not?”

“I was afraid there might be a pitch for a donation.”

“Bobby, she’s your mother,” Athena said. “Don’t you think it’s time that you mended fences?”

Buck cleared his throat, drawing their attention.

“Uh, Ma?” he gestured vaguely at himself.

“Point taken,” she admitted. “But still, Bobby. Maybe there’s a reason the One Eighteen responded to that call.”

“You think God poisoned a bunch of people with carbon monoxide to facilitate a reunion?” Bobby’s skepticism was clear as day.

“He works in mysterious ways.”

Bobby turned to Buck. Buck shrugged at him.

“I’m the one always saying that the universe screams,” he pointed out.

“I’ll go tell Hank that we’re going with the granite,” Bobby announced after a minute.

Buck and Athena watched him head outside, presumably to where Hank was. And then Gavin started screaming again.

Chapter 33: The Prodigal Son

Chapter Summary

In which it's Bobby's turn to suffer through parental drama.

“Would you guys want to go out and, uh. Kick it?” Buck winced as he heard himself, the words sounding awkward even to his ears.

Ravi paused in the process of squeegeeing the film-covered glass of the locker room walls to stare at Buck. Albert, who was sitting on the bench and had been bothering his boyfriend while said boyfriend did his chores, also stared at Buck.

“Go out and kick it?” Ravi repeated. “Are we about to be pranked?”

“Not as far as I know,” Buck told him, which was true. 

Part of being captain meant that he was no longer involved in the prank wars that occasionally broke out in the firehouse. He knew they still happened, because he wasn’t stupid. He had, after all, gleefully participated in the ones that went on behind Bobby’s back. But he pretended not to know about them and hid behind plausible deniability, made incredibly easy by the fact that Eddie’s role in them nowadays was the designated distraction. It mostly consisted of his husband saying, “I’m supposed to be distracting you,” and then Buck rolling his eyes before showing Eddie something new on his phone.

“I’ll make sure to check my boots for ketchup packets, later,” Ravi said, wrinkling his nose.

“Why are you asking us if we want to-” Albert made a face. “-kick it?”

“I thought it might be cool,” Buck explained with a self-conscious shrug. “It’s been a while since the four of us have hung out outside of the station together.”

Mostly, it was because Carla was pressuring them to go out and do stuff. Unspoken, but still so very loud, was the implication that there was a looming point in the future when it would be much harder to find the time. One day, far sooner than they would like, they could end up in the same situation as Abby had been.

(How many times were their dates interrupted or cancelled because Abby’s mother needed her? Buck honestly forgot the count.)

It wasn’t like Buck and Eddie never went out, they just didn’t go out as often these days. The last couple of times, before Maddie was kidnapped, was because they’d gotten pushed into it on Valentine’s Day and then Hen dragged them all out for dinner that Buck ended up paying for. It was also the first time they’d gone out and did something as a team since Bobby’s heart attack. And baseball season had literally just started, with no home games for the Dodgers yet, so Buck hadn’t taken Eddie to any yet this year. Which, now that Buck thought about, was what most of their nights out consisted of.

“We could do pick-up basketball?” Albert suggested.

“Eddie would probably like it,” Buck said, trying to keep his distaste from being too obvious.

Ravi, thankfully, made a face and shook his head.

“We could do frolf,” he suggested. At Buck’s blank stare, he clarified it with, “Frisbee golf. You just aim your disc at a basket and…”

He mimed throwing a frisbee, clicking his tongue as he did. Buck turned his head to look at Albert, who simply shrugged at him.

“What about drinking?” Buck knew he sounded a bit desperate, but the alternative was apparently frisbee golf. Is that what he and Albert did? God, what someone would do for love. “You like to drink, right?”

“In moderation,” Ravi answered.

“I know a great place. It’ll be fun.”

“Excuse me.” That was a new voice, not belonging to anyone that should’ve been at the station. Buck turned and saw Charlie, Bobby’s brother, standing awkwardly in the doorway to the locker room. He was dressed much like he had been at the miracle service-turned-disaster, business casual with a blazer and turtleneck. “You’re the captain, right? The one who knew Bobby?”

“Right, yeah,” he said with a nod. “Captain Diaz, but everyone calls me Buck.”

“I was hoping…” Charlie shuffled a bit in place. “I don’t have any way of contacting him.”

“Oh, um. I could…” Buck’s immediate thought, of giving the man Bobby’s phone number, was nixed just as quickly as it came. Bobby barely spoke about his living family, and what little he shared made it clear that the relationship there was pretty much  nonexistent. He probably wouldn’t appreciate Buck just giving his number to his family.

Buck knew that he wouldn’t, if the roles were reversed.

“I’ll- I’ll call him,” he said, instead. He didn’t think that Bobby was on set today, but even if he was, he’d take the excuse to leave it if he could. Maybe. “You can wait upstairs, if you want?”

Something about Charlie’s expression seemed to shutter, but he nodded.

“Alright,” he agreed. “Just… Tell him his brother would like to speak with him.”

There was an awkward moment as the other man shuffled away for the stairs, and then Buck was turning back to Ravi and Albert. The pair was staring at him with wide-eyes and he shrugged at them before pulling out his phone to call Bobby.

The man answered after only a couple rings.

“Aren’t you supposed to be working?”

“Funny thing about that, Pops.” Buck scratched at the back of his head as he spoke. “Um. Your brother is here? At the station?”

There was a beat of silence.

“Charlie’s there?”

“Yeah, he said he wants to talk to you. I could, um… Send him away? Give him a fake number? If you want?”

Bobby sighed.

“I’ll be right there.”

He hung up before Buck could reply, leaving him to look down at the screen of his phone with its background picture of Eddie curled up with Senorita on the couch, the pair of them taking a nap.

“Well this is going to be very awkward,” Buck declared. “Do you guys want to-”

“No, no, no,” Ravi and Albert both said at the same time, shaking their heads.

“We’ll stay down here,” Albert told him.

“Cowards.”

The time spent waiting for Bobby to get there was uncomfortable, to say the least. Buck did his best to fill the time with idle small talk as he got the man coffee, feeling like he was creeping across a minefield with every word. Charlie, for his part, spent much of the time comparing the station to the one Tim Nash worked at.

“They didn’t have a kitchen like this at Dad’s firehouse,” Charlie remarked as he looked around.

“That’s because none of Dad’s guys could cook.” Bobby was standing at the head of the stairs. He wasn’t in uniform and it hadn’t taken him long to arrive, so Buck wondered if the man had been at Casa de Diaz or just out and about.

“It’s good to see you, Bobby,” Charlie said, turning slightly in his stool.

“It’s good to see you, too,” Bobby replied, taking the seat next to him at the kitchen island. “How are you? How’s Deborah?”

Buck glanced between them and then busied himself with getting Bobby a coffee of his own. Part of him thought he should scurry away and not eavesdrop, while another part - the part that remembered all of his own experiences with estranged relatives popping into his life - made him want to hang around and hover. That part won over, supported by his curiosity.

“That’s a good question, I… Have no idea, actually.” Charlie chuckled, the sound self-conscious. “Deborah was two wives ago.”

“Two?” Bobby repeated.

“Life on the road, man.”

“Well,” Bobby said after a beat, nodding to Buck when he was handed his coffee. “I guess there’s only room for one lady in your life.”

Buck scurried off to the side with his own drink, out of the way but close enough to eavesdrop.

“Yeah, there is some truth to that,” Charlie said. “How about you?”

“Uh, Athena and I are almost five years married-”

“Six,” Buck corrected around a fit of fake coughing.

Bobby paused and then his eyes went wide.

“Six, thank you, Buck,” he said. “And she is a sergeant. LAPD.”

“First responders in the house,” Charlie said, and suddenly the similarities between the brothers weren’t just skin deep. That was the exact sort of dorky thing Bobby would say, supported by him laughing at it. “You have any kids?”

“Two step-kids, one adopted. He’s a firefighter, too,” Bobby said, eyes flickering towards Buck. “And I’ve got a couple of grandkids.”

“Wow, that is fantastic. I’m happy for you.”

“Thank you.”

“Another firefighter, wow. That’s, what? Five generations?”

“Yeah.”

“What are you doing now?” Charlie asked. “You’re not in uniform. The captain, Buck? He said you used to be captain.”

“I had a heart attack last year,” Bobby said. His brother’s wince encompassed his entire body. “And I reinjured my back the year before that. They moved me to light duty, technical advisor on that awful Hotshots show.”

“It really is awful, isn’t it?” Charlie laughed. “My brother, the Hollywood man. You know, I thought about reaching out so many times. But I just… I didn’t think you wanted me to.”

Charlie was probably right. It had never seemed like Bobby was very interested in rebuilding rotten bridges, not any of the few times he spoke about his mother or brother.

“It’s alright,” Bobby said. “It’s not like I was making a big effort, either. I’m sorry.”

“And yet it almost seems providential, doesn’t it?” Charlie said. He clasped his hands together in front of him, briefly, and tilted his head back for a moment like he was looking heavenward. “We had a carbon monoxide leak, and it was your old station that was sent to save the day.”

“Funny, you’re not the only one to say something like that.” Bobby’s eyes moved past his brother to land on Buck again. Buck hurriedly ducked his head and hid his face behind his drink as he failed to pretend he wasn’t listening to everything. “Athena said something similar.”

“Did she? She sounds like a smart lady.”

“Yeah. Anyway, firefighters go where they’re sent. You know that.”

Buck knew, for a fact, that if it involved literally anything other than his family, Bobby would be 100% on-board the “it’s a sign from [Insert Power of Your Choice]” train. Bobby believed in signs and portents, however much he liked to act the cautious skeptic.

“Well, Mom wants to see you,” Charlie said, and Bobby immediately started moving his head like he was trying to work a kink out of his neck. “Why don’t you just come to lunch? You and your wife?”

“I don’t think that’s a good idea…”

“We’re only gonna be in town for three more days.” Charlie reached into his blazer and pulled out a business card that he laid down on the island. “Here’s my number. Just think about it, please.”

He got up and then patted Bobby on the shoulder.

“Dad would be so proud of you,” he said.

Bobby’s smile was more of a strained grimace as he watched Charlie leave. Buck hesitated for a moment and then took the stool that Charlie vacated.

“I could make up an emergency?” he offered, once the older Nash was out of earshot. “Something happened with Abuela and you’re needed to watch Gavin?”

“Don’t tempt me,” Bobby told him. He reached down to pick up the business card - it was one for Ann Hutchinson Ministries - and then pulled back to rub at his neck with a pained grunt.

“Or,” Buck continued. “I could come with? Gavin’s throwing tantrums like it’s a competitive sport these days, that could get us out of there.”

“I don’t…” Bobby frowned with his whole face. “Mom used to be very… Hate the sin, love the sinner. I don’t know how she would be. About you and Eddie.”

“Oh.” Buck winced. “Yeah, okay. I don’t think we want Ma shooting her mother-in-law the first time they meet.”

Bobby threw back his head to laugh, only to grunt in pain again as that kink in his neck flared up.

Bobby was already regretting the most recent of his life choices before they even arrived at his mother’s hotel. It must’ve been madness that drove him to call his brother, and madness that drove him to agree to lunch with his mother. A part of him was ashamed to feel this way about his mother, this dread to spend any amount of time with her, because he knew that she wasn’t anywhere close to being as bad as Beatrice Carter or Helena Diaz or - God forbid - Margaret Buckley.

That didn’t mean she was good, though. That didn’t mean she was tolerable.

“Of course we couldn’t just meet them at the restaurant,” Bobby griped to his wife as the pair of them travelled the halls. “No, she’s got to show off her fancy hotel suite."

Athena scoffed and lightly smacked him with her shiny, golden clutch. She wore a sleeveless black jumpsuit and looked gorgeous. She always looked gorgeous.

“Remember what we talked about,” she lectured as they approached the right door, room 2400. “She reached out to us.”

(“Give her a chance,” Athena said. “Don’t go in there ready to fight. Maybe this could be the start of you two reconnecting.”

“Yes, dear,” Bobby promised, his fingers crossed behind his back.)

“I’ll try,” Bobby said and reached up to knock.

Charlie opened the door with a smile, dressed considerably more casual than he or Athena, in a cardigan that looked like it came out of Mr. Roger’s closet. Or maybe Buck’s, come to think of it.

“Bobby, you made it,” he greeted them. “And you must be Athena.”

“It’s nice to meet you,” Athena said, and she absolutely meant it.

“She’s just finishing up here,” Charlie said, letting them inside and gesturing deeper into the absurdly large, gaudily decorated hotel suite. There were chandeliers, rose gold shelves with various knick knacks on them, and an actual piano on the other side of the room.

Ann was at a table ladened with food, with various multi tiered serving trays. She was dressed in a white pantsuit and discussing something with a pair of personal assistants, the both of them already packing away despite her still giving out directions.

“The camera always has to be at eye level or above,” she instructed, and Bobby rolled his own eyes while no one was looking. “Nobody wants to see a cadaverous-looking faith healer.”

“Mother?” Charlie interrupted, prompting Ann to turn.

Bobby stared at her for a moment, and she stared back. She’d gotten older, wrinkles creasing her face and neck and hands. He’d known she’d gotten older, her and Charlie both, had seen it in videos and pictures. It was still so jarring to see in person.

“Bobby. You look well,” she said.

“Thank you. So do you.”

“And you must be Athena,” she said, walking closer. “I knew Bobby would be marrying up, but you are a jewel.”

A casual put-down. Subtle, Midwestern passive-aggressiveness that would rival even Margaret Buckley’s jabs. The comparison had him even more certain that it was the right choice to not take up Buck’s offer of joining them today.

“Well, so are you,” Athena replied, blinded by the compliment.

“Let’s sit,” Ann said, already turning to lead them to the sitting area of the room. Charlie followed, as did Athena.

“I thought we were going to lunch?” Bobby asked, not moving from his spot. Athena half-turned, gestured for him to come with.

“We are, but I made the reservation for three, so we could just sit and talk,” his mother explained as she sat down in a comfy chair. Bobby’s stomach curdled, because he did not see this going well. “Anybody want something to drink?”

God on high, yes. But he and Athena simply asked for water before Athena sat down on a green velvet couch. Bobby stayed standing, because that meant he could make a quicker exit when the time inevitably came.

“Here we all are, together, about to feast.” Ann clapped her hands together and laughed pleasantly. “It reminds me of Luke 15.”

“The Parable of the Prodigal Son.” Bobby took the glass of water that Charlie handed to him. “Is that how you see me?”

The tale of a rich father of two sons, and how the youngest left home after receiving his half of the inheritance early while the older, dutiful son remained. But the younger son was a fool who squandered it all away and had to come crawling back home to his father. The father threw a feast, to celebrate his youngest’s return.

(“But now we must celebrate and rejoice, because your brother was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.”)

“It’s a beautiful hotel,” Athena blurted out when it became obvious that a reply was not forthcoming.

“Well, our God is an abundant God,” Ann proudly declared.

“That’s one way of putting it,” Bobby sniped into his glass. He didn’t bother to be very quiet.

“Next time,” Athena said, gripping Bobby’s hand to tug him onto the couch with her, “we get to host. That is, if our house ever gets finished.”

“Are you building a home?” Ann gushed. “How delightful.”

“Someone burned the last one down,” Bobby told her.

“Not you, I trust.”

There went the subtlety. Bobby flinched with the words, hand flexing on his glass of water so tightly that he could swear he heard it creak. He set it down on the coffee table, before it could shatter.

“Excuse me?” Athena’s tone was a knife hiding in the folds of a skirt, just waiting for a reason to lash out.

“Just a joke, dear,” Ann said.

“You know, Ann,” Athena said after a beat. “When we first got together, Bobby and I, I didn’t know…”

“You didn’t know I existed.”

“I assumed you were dead until our oldest came to tell us that he met you on a scene,” Athena said. In the chair across from them, Charlie frowned and sent Bobby a questioning gaze that he ignored for the moment. “But I have done a little research.”

“Don’t worry,” Bobby told his mother. “She didn’t run your rap sheet.”

“You always did think I was a fraud,” Ann shot back.

“I think you are very good at what you do,” was his diplomatic response.

“What about you, Athena? Do you believe?”

“I’ve looked at some of your Youtube channel,” Athena said. “And, well. It’s clear that the people who come to you do get something out of it.”

“You wonder whether I’m actually healing the afflicted. There is a paucity of hope in the world today, and what is faith in God without having hope for something better?” As Ann spoke, Bobby couldn’t help but think about Eddie and his utter distaste for this exact sort of thing, the story he told of the charlatan that took advantage of Isabel’s grief and hope.
