Ann wasn’t much different, she simply had a bigger stage and a larger crowd to prey upon. “I give hope for healing, I stroke the fires of faith. Because I don't know how people can get better without hope.”

“The answer is no,” Bobby translated, once his mother was done preaching to them. “She doesn’t actually heal anyone.”

He got up and headed to the suite’s kitchenette to refill his glass.

“Maybe we should head for the restaurant?” Charlie suggested, getting up as well.

Ann did, too, but it was simply to move onto the couch beside Athena.

“Are you a churchgoer?” she asked, everything - from the words to her posture - superficially pleasant and welcoming.

Bobby glowered and prepared himself for the next passive-aggressive swipe.

“Southern Baptist,” Athena answered. “My mother almost had a coronary when she learned I was marrying a Catholic, of all things. I’m pretty sure she took longer to forgive me for that than she did for me dropping out of law school. But every Sunday that work allows, we go to church in the morning and then family dinner at our oldest’s in the evening.”

“The firefighter, right?” Charlie spoke up. “The one you said we met, but…”

He looked to Bobby in question. Bobby sighed before he answered.

“Buck, the captain,” he said, and was ready for the expressions on the faces of his mother and brother. They were probably doing the math in their head for the timing, and not coming up with an answer that made sense to them. “It was unconventional, taking him in.”

“Buck walked into the firehouse and the pair of them imprinted,” Athena teased from over the back of the couch.

“He needed at least one good parental figure in his life. And he ended up with two.”

“Does he go to church?” Ann asked.

“No, neither he nor his…” Bobby’s eyes met Athena’s. “Neither he nor the rest of his family, except his in-laws.”

(“God still loves them,” Ann said one day, shortly after she really started devoting her life to religion. “Any sin can be forgiven, you just have to ask for it.”)

“Tim would drag the boys to Our Lady of the Sorrow, to Sacred Heart.” Ann was talking to Athena, but it was impossible to miss that it was somehow a jab towards Bobby. “Anywhere, really, that he could get his sins absolved.”

“Really, Mom?”

“Mother,” Charlie admonished. “You said you weren’t going to bring up Dad.”

“Right, I forgot.” Ann’s tone was borderline mocking. “We’re not supposed to ever mention the name of the sainted Tim Nash.”

“Yeah, please don’t.” It took effort for Bobby to keep his tone even as he circled back around the couches to face down his mother. “He’s not here to defend himself.”

“If I recall, I’m the one who defended you from him.”

“Until you walked out.”

“You chose to stay.”

“Somebody needed to.”

“No they didn’t,” Ann denied as she stood up. “He made his own choices, and I will not apologize for making the right choice of leaving him. And I will not apologize for not crawling into that casket with him.”

“Like I did, you mean?” Bobby said.

“You did follow in his footsteps,” she told him. “Even knowing how his path ended, even after we all begged and begged for you to make different choices. Better ones.”

“Is this why you invited us here?” Bobby asked as Athena stood up, too. “To pick a fight?”

“Charlie.” Ann’s head swivelled around to fix her gaze on her oldest. “What does he mean, why I invited them here?”

“Blessed be the peacemaker,” Charlie quoted, a bit sheepishly.

“You arranged this?”

“Of course he did,” Bobby scoffed, that acrid feel of disappointment curling up in his stomach. “Why would I think, after all this time, that you would finally take even a little responsibility for walking out on us? I-”

“Responsibility?” Ann interrupted with a snap. “You want me to take responsibility for it? Fine, I do. Leaving him was the best decision I ever made in that marriage. He was a deadbeat husband, and a deadbeat father, and you chose to stay with him even though we both begged you to come with us. You have been angry with me since you were thirteen because I wouldn’t martyr myself for someone we were all better off without.”

“I’ve worked hard for so many years,” Bobby managed to grit out, “to accept my failing and the failings of those around me. To accept them, to forgive them. Dad’s especially-”

“Oh, so you’re admitting now that he wasn’t perfect? It only took forty some-odd years.”

“You were right,” Bobby told her. “I do think you’re a fraud, but not as a preacher. You’re a fraud of a mother.”

When he stormed out of the hotel suite, he didn’t look back.

Chapter 34: Wayfaring Stranger

Chapter Summary

In which one woman rises from the grave, and another is prepared for her own.

It was not the first time that Ravi and Albert had hung out with Buck and Eddie outside of work. Whether it be hanging out at Albert and Ravi’s to play video games, or the two of them dropping in at the Diaz house to eat the food Buck and Eddie’s abuela made, it was a semi-regular thing. The only problem being that, well.

Buck was kinda annoying when he drank.

In the past, Ravi usually managed to avoid it by allowing the others to bear the brunt of dealing with a tipsy or drunk Buck. It had barely been an issue since the lightning strike and Buck getting put on his meds, because he was cautious about mixing them with alcohol. But tonight, apparently, he’d decided to let loose a little. And now Ravi was suffering.

“So we get the tab paid,” Buck was saying. He was gesticulating as he spoke, nearly hitting Eddie a couple times. They were pressed close together, despite the fact that they’d gotten a rather large booth and there was plenty of space for the four of them. "We both run out to the parking lot, and there’s a boot on my front tire.”

“Damn.” Ravi halfheartedly threw a quarter at the tabletop. It barely bounced, landing pathetically to wobble against the wood instead of going into the shot glass they were using as a goal. “That sucks.”

Albert laughed beside him. They were sitting close together, yeah, with Ravi’s leg wrapped around his boyfriend’s, but not like Buck and Eddie. Those two were practically in each other’s laps.

“Yeah, so, obviously, at this point, I’m like, we’re not gonna make the game,” Buck continued. Eddie was hanging onto his every word, casually rolling a quarter between his finger and the table, even though he was there when the story happened. “Then Eddie pulls out the spare tire from the back and I kid you not, five minutes later, the spare is on, we’re driving down the road, and the old tire is sitting on the side of the curb. Boot still on.”

He leaned into Eddie, somehow managing to put even less space between the two of them. Ravi wondered how many more shots it would take before Buck was trying to crawl into his husband’s clothes.

“Isn’t that illegal?” Ravi asked.

“What? No, no, it’s not illegal.” Buck seemed legitimately offended by the question. “Eddie would never do something illegal. Eddie has a Silver Star.”

The man in question barked out a laugh before pressing a kiss into the side of Buck’s head.

“Thanks, mi sol.”

“I can’t believe you’re our captain,” Ravi bemoaned.

“Weren’t you in an underground fight club?” Albert pointed at Eddie with his empty glass as he asked the question. “Like, just a couple months before I got here?”

“Exactly, that was ages ago,” Buck said, coming to Eddie’s defense once again. “And he had a ton of stuff going on.”

“My wife died and I couldn’t talk to my husband.” Eddie threw his quarter and it bounced cleanly off the table to land in the shot glass with a clink. He did it with such ease that it was insulting, almost disdainful.

Buck threw up his arms with a cheer and then started slapping the tabletop obnoxiously with both hands.

“Drink! Drink!” he goaded.

“Have I mentioned how much I hate this game?” Ravi groused as the waitress swung by with a tray of fresh shots for all of them, the rims of the glasses salted and limed.

“The loser usually does.”

“Who even plays quarters, anyways?”

“Texans,” was Eddie’s answer. “C’mon, hermano. Bottoms up.”

Both Buck and Albert snickered at the wording. Ravi rolled his eyes, chose his shot, plucked the lime off it, and tossed it back while Buck pounded the tabletop with his fists and chanted Ravi’s name. The alcohol burned as it went down his throat, making him sputter and cough.

“You know what, I think I’m gonna switch to beer.” Ravi set the now empty glass down onto the table, waving away Buck’s attempts to get him to continue the stupid game. He wasn’t even the one playing, he’d simply been content watching Eddie win against Ravi and Albert. “You guys want anything?”

“Beers sound good,” Buck said. Eddie nodded.

“I’ll come with ya,” Albert offered, presumably to keep from being left alone with the double act.

It was crowded at the bar, and Ravi had to slide through gaps to reach it. He flagged down the bartender, ordered a quartet of IPAs, and settled in to wait, turning back to check on Thing 1 and Thing 2 at the booth. The pair of them were already lost in their own little world as Buck buried his face into the side of Eddie’s neck. Whatever Buck was doing, it had Eddie’s own face beet red as he laughed and tried to wiggle away. He couldn’t get far, though, because Buck’s arms were wrapped around him like an octopus.

“Why did we agree to this?” Ravi asked.

“Because they’re our friends,” Albert said. “And there was nothing good on TV tonight.”

“They’re our friends when they’re sober,” he countered. “When they’re drinking, they’re… That.”

His boyfriend took in the image of the two Diazes, Buck having peeled himself away from Eddie to ramble about something. Eddie was once again giving his husband his full attention and looking utterly besotted.

“Do you think they’d notice if we disappeared to make out in the bathroom for like, I dunno, half an hour?” Albert asked, nodding in thanks to the bartender when their IPAs were set out.

“That is a very good question, Alley Cat,” Ravi praised as he helped carry the drinks back to their table. “Absolutely worth investigating.”

(The answer was a very insulting no, but they both had fun finding it out.)

The house they were responding to was a nice one. The main structure itself was long,  maybe renovated not too long ago, and it sat on a large plot of land with white fencing and other, smaller buildings that might have been garages and sheds. It was probably a farm in a past life, but there was neither livestock nor crops immediately visible when they pulled up.

“Right, this one was automated,” Buck told the others as they crossed the yard to the doors. “Elmer Caldwell, has a med-alert pendant. Dispatch said he has hypertension and a coronary stent.”

“So he might’ve had a heart attack,” Hen concluded. “Does he live alone?”

“Got a wife, but I guess she’s not here.”

At the very least, no one was responding to their shouts. And the door, when Buck tried to open it, was locked.

“Do we break down the door?” Bell asked, all bubbles and cheers at the prospect. Buck found himself smiling.

“Assuming he’s in the house,” Albert pointed out.

“That’s true,” Buck admitted. “Go around, see if there’s any doors or windows that are open or unlocked. And keep an eye out for our guy, if he is outside.”

They split off, pairing up as they searched because the buddy system was important. Buck went with Ravi, going around the house and then across the paved drive towards a fenced in garden. There were several beds of plants, one of which looked freshly done. Their patient, Elmer, was on the ground beside it. There was a knocked over folding stool, a bag of soil, and a tray of plants straight from the store.

“Sir?” Buck approached him with Ravi, while they waited for the others to converge on their location. “We’re here to check you out.”

“Me?” Elmer regarded them with confusion, and he was panting a little. “I didn’t call anyone.”

“Your pendant did, sir. Come on, let’s get you up.”

They got the stool righted, and then he and Ravi hauled him up to sit on it. It did not do anything to soften the man’s demeanor, though now the guy’s hand was to his chest.

“What a nuisance,” Elmer complained. “My wife makes me wear it.”

“He’s got shortness of breath and chest pain,” Buck explained to Hen and Chimney when they joined them, the others close behind.

“I don’t have any chest pain.”

“You’re clutching your chest,” Ravi pointed out.

“And you look like you’re in pain,” Buck added, and then nodded to the paramedics. “Check him over?”

“It’s not a heart attack!” Elmer insisted, a bit agitated.

Hen and Chimney weren’t deterred, however, the pair of them kneeling on either side of him. Hen put him on oxygen and Chimney got his vitals, which were moderately worrisome but not horrible, considering his medical history. Until they were, and the guy was bent over in even more pain.

“Ravi, gurney,” Buck instructed, and the younger man rushed off.

“I’m thinking angina,” Hen stated over the frantic beeping of the Lifepak they had hooked up to Elmer. “Most likely from exertion.”

Buck frowned and looked at the nearest garden bed, the one that looked the freshest. How bad off was this guy’s heart, that putting a couple plants down could render him like this?

Albert pulled out the nitro spray and handed it to Hen, who tugged off the oxygen mask she’d put on Elmer. A single, quick spritz under the tongue, and the Lifepak was soon calming down. Still worrisome, because the nitroglycerin was a treatment, not a cure, but he’d be okay getting to the hospital.

“I guess your wife was onto something after all,” he commented. For some reason, it Elmer’s head jerking up and him uttering a panicked sounding,

“What!?”

“The medical pendant,” Buck said, gesturing at it. “It-”

And then a hand grabbed his ankle. He looked down to see a woman had half-risen from the garden bed. He screamed. Everyone screamed, including Elmer and Ravi, who’d returned with the gurney, and Toby, who’d come with him. Buck was not certain whose scream was the shrillest, but if anyone asked him later, he’d say it was Albert and definitely not himself.

“What is this?” the woman asked, looking around, as they helped her sit up. She was still buried from the waist down. “Elmer?”

“Hello, Suzanne,” was Elmer’s resigned, and disappointed sounding, greeting.

“Ma’am, do you know how you got here?” Buck asked while Albert got her hooked up to a Lifepak.

“Where is here?” Suzanne asked. “Am I in the garden?”

“You were under the garden,” Chimney clarified for her.

“The last thing I remember, we were eating sweet potato soup,” she said. “But it smelled funny, and- and I started to feel dizzy…”

Hen looked up from where she was wrapping a blood pressure cuff around Suzanne’s arm. She was glaring at Elmer.

“It didn’t have a bitter aftertaste and burn a little going down, did it?” she asked.

“Yeah. How did you know?”

“Sounds like cyanide.”

“Ravi, Toby, keep him from running.” Buck grabbed his radio while the pair held the failed murderer in place. “Dispatch, we need LAPD at our location.”

Which quickly turned into a request for the coroner, when Elmer keeled over and died right then and there. His heart, and the stress, and more than a little bit of karma.

“So,” Maddie prompted, setting down her glass of juice onto the patio table. Her voice was remarkably clear, for someone whose throat had been sliced open last month, and the scar left behind was a line of knotted, healing tissue. “How’s paramedic school going?”

“It’s going okay,” Eddie answered, sipping at his own drink. He watched as Gavin and Jee-Yun chased Hoover around the backyard, all three of them making a ruckus in the lengthening shadows of the early evening. “Kinda boring? It’s mostly been review for me.”

He sat in the back of the room during the lectures, and spent much of his time texting people. Buck almost constantly, Carlos sometimes, but a surprising amount was spent chatting with TK. The former New Yorker had turned into a stay-at-home dad after the pair took in his half-brother, which took quite the adjustment, and Eddie was getting the sense that he was missing adult interaction.

“You’d think the army medic thing, and then everything you’ve done at the One Eighteen, would count as credit towards something,” Maddie said.

“It does, I think. I dunno.” Eddie shrugged at her. “What about you? You’re looking… Tired.”

That was a polite way of putting it. There were shadows under her eyes, gradually getting bigger since her release from the hospital. He’d seen Bobby and Abuela both exchanging looks behind her back at Sunday dinner, clearly contemplating how much time to give her before ambushing her with care and concern.

Maddie’s jaw set in a familiar way, almost a mirror image to her brother, and then she relaxed with a sigh.

“I’m having nightmares,” she quietly confessed. “I’m at work, on the dispatch floor, and then I take a call and… My throat is open and bleeding, again.”

“Trauma nightmares are always fun,” Eddie quipped. Maddie laughed, not with much exuberance or feeling, but it was better than nothing. “I had them after the sniper, they’re actually why Buck forced me into seeing Copeland.”

“What were yours about?”

“Honestly? Your brother.”

“Seriously? You get shot, and your nightmares from it are about Buck?”

“I don’t actually remember much about being shot. That time, at least. The most vivid memory I have from it is Buck’s face covered in blood, and I was just so certain he was hurt. My brain just took that and ran with it.” Eddie shrugged at her. “And if it makes you feel better, Buck’s been having the occasional nightmare about you.”

According to Buck, it was Doug that took Maddie in his nightmares, and they couldn’t find her until it was too late.

“It doesn’t, actually,” she said, and immediately followed it up with, “Is that why I’ll sometimes get texts at four or five in the morning?”

“And your nightmares explain why you’re responding to them at four or five in the morning.”

“Point.” Maddie looked up at the sky, at the sun that was more than halfway past the horizon, and sighed. “I should probably get Jee home, get her fed, a bath, all that.”

She did not seem very enthused about doing any of it. In fact, her expression went tight when she talked about going home. Eddie had a suspicion why that might be.

“Abuela’ll talk you into staying for dinner, anyway,” he said. “You can stay longer, you know that.”

“I think I will,” she said, the smile she gave him a bit wobbly. “I can keep you company a bit since both our guys’ are doing overnights.”

“And you could stay the night,” he continued. “If you want.”

“Eddie, I couldn’t…”

“Sure you can,” he insisted. Maddie seemed hesitant, like she wanted to accept the invitation but couldn’t bring herself to do so. “Y’know, when we finally moved out of the house on Bedford, Buck was upset, but also relieved. ‘Cause he wouldn’t have to pretend like he wasn’t expecting for Jonah Greenway to leap out every time he passed Chris’ door.”

Buck worked very hard, in those last couple of months they spent in that house, to hide it from Chris. But Eddie saw how he would quicken his pace to hurry past the door, how he would veer to the far side of the hallway from it. Because there was a certain violation to being attacked in your own home that a person did not easily get over.

“I keep checking the locks, on the nights Chimney works,” Maddie finally said. “I was doing the dishes before she attacked me and now it takes twice as long to wash them if I’m in the kitchen alone, because I keep stopping to make sure, you know? Sometimes I’ll just leave them sitting in the sink until Chim gets home.”

“That sounds like something to talk to your therapist about,” Eddie teased, words coming out sing-song. Then he laughed and leaned away when Maddie reached over to smack him. “You and the princess can take our bed.”

“What? No, it’s your bed. Jee can share with Gavin, I’ll take the couch.”

“Maddie, Buck won’t be here tonight,” he reminded her. “I’m not going to sleep very well anyway, bed or couch.”

“God,” she groaned at him. “You’re both pathetic.”

“I know,” was his cheerful reply.

Bobby couldn’t rightfully say what drove him to go to that church the 118 responded to the other day, he couldn’t say what made him decide to listen to his mother’s sermon in person. Maybe it was the universe screaming at him, as Buck would insist, or God Himself touching his heart. Either way, he was there to watch as his mother collapsed on the stage and was there to keep her heart beating until help arrived.

And now here he was, in yet another hospital waiting room. Athena had arrived to keep him company, and so had Buck. Because they all had intimate knowledge of how miserable it was to sit in these uncomfortable chairs alone. Because they loved him and did not want him to sit there alone.

“It’s good that you were there,” Athena told him, after he got done telling her and Buck what happened.

“She was made to get up there and preach,” he said. “And she would never have found it if she’d stayed married to my dad.”

“Do you miss him?” Buck asked from his other side, the words loud in the hush of the waiting room.

“Yeah,” he confessed. “Sometimes I think I’m the only one who does.”

Tim Nash was an angry and mean drunk, Bobby could admit that. It was an unavoidable truth, up to the moment he died. But Tim Nash wasn’t always an angry drunk, he was also Bobby’s dad, and his hero. And he figured out of everyone, Buck would understand that mess of twisted and confused feelings.

(“When I look back, I can see it. Flashes of it,” Buck had said, the pair of them sitting in his childhood bedroom that was stripped bare of his childhood. “When he bought me a new bike when I was a kid, and took me out for ice cream. When he taught me how to swim, or when he convinced Mom to let me play football in high school, or when he got me those skateboards. It was there, but it just…”)

Athena placed her hand on his shoulder in sympathy, and then she frowned in thought.

“How’s that kink in your neck?”

“It’s like cement,” Bobby told her.

“Oh, boy.” Athena’s fingers dug in, trying fruitlessly to ease the discomfort. “You are not joking.”

“It just means she’s alive.”

“Bobby!” his wife tutted, while Buck barked out laughter.

Bobby spotted his brother approaching them from the direction of their mother’s room. He looked a mess, tired and with his suit rumpled. Bobby stood, eager and anxious to hear what he had to say.

“How is she?” he asked.

“She’s stable,” was Charlie’s answer. “She’s, uh, she’s fighting with the doctor.”

“Has this happened before?”

“Oh, gosh, no,” his brother lied.

“Charlie.”

The other man sighed and seemed to shrink more.

“Not on stage,” he admitted. “Never on stage.”

“How sick is she?”

Charlie drew in a breath, crossed his arms in front of his breath. He didn’t meet Bobby’s eyes as he explained that,

“Her oncologist says it’s terminal. She was diagnosed last year.”

Her oncologist. Cancer. It seemed like it was always cancer.

“When were you going to tell me?” Bobby demanded.

“Never,” Charlie told him. “That’s what she wanted. But then a complete stranger showed up at the church and he knew you, knew who we were to you… It felt like a sign, you know?”

“How are you holding up?”

“It’s the end of the world as I know it, but that’s what I get for devoting my life to Mom.” Charlie had always been closer to Ann than Bobby. He was the dutiful son who followed their mother everywhere, town to town and church to church, even to the cost of everything else. “Maybe you got lucky, Dad set you free a lot earlier.”

“I’m not so sure of that.” Neither about the luck, nor about being set free. 

“She wants to see you,” Charlie said. Then, before Bobby had the chance to express his skepticism, followed it with, “And yes, it really is her asking this time.”

Ann was powdering her face when Bobby walked into her room. There were wires trailing from her, and an oxygen cannula hooked under her nose. She looked small in the bed, and surprised to see him there.

She probably didn’t expect him to show, which was more than fair.

“How are you feeling?” he asked.

“Much improved,” she answered, setting her oversized compact onto the wheeled table every hospital room seemed to have. “Actually, I’d like you to do me a favor? Speak to the doctors, tell them you’re the, uh. LAFD fire captain and that I’m doing fine. Because I have to be in Vegas tomorrow afternoon.”

“I’m retired. Mostly,” Bobby told her. “And you should probably cancel that anyway, shouldn’t you? Charlie told me you’re not fine.”

Her expression froze, and then melted a little.

“He told you about the cancer? That snitch.” She laughed lightly. “Die in a hospital bed, or die on the road. Not much of a choice, is there?”

“You could stay in LA instead of travelling the country,” he said. “Get sustained treatment here.”

“Honey, it’s stage four.”

Bobby’s heart skipped, dropped, broke. He was surprised by his own pain over the news, because just the other day he was so angry at her, because he spent actual decades actively avoiding contact with her. He was not surprised by his own pain over the news, because this was his mom.  

“No treatment is gonna do anything for me at this point,” Ann said. “It would take a miracle. And yes, I recognize the irony.”

“I’m sorry,” Bobby whispered.

“I’m not. I’m going home to my Savior, where there is no sickness and no toil,” she said. “When I meet Him, it’ll be a joyful day for me.”

“I think He’ll have some questions for you.”

“And I’ll answer them, and He’ll answer mine,” she said. “It meant so much to me that you came to the church tonight.”

“I wanted to apologize. I didn’t want that to be the last thing I said to you.”

“That I was a fraud of a mother? I’ve heard worse.”

“Honor thy father and mother,” Bobby quoted, kneeling down beside the bed so he wasn’t looming over her. “I haven’t been fair to you. I’m glad that you didn’t climb into Dad’s coffin with him, and you were right to get out when you did.”

She smiled at him and reached a hand to cup his face.

“You and Charlie were the best parts of that marriage. The best parts of Tim and I,” Ann said. “I’m sorry I left you there with him, I should have taken you with us regardless.”

“I would’ve hated you if you did that.”

“I’m your mother, I was supposed to do what was best for you. If you hated me, if you raged, so what?” She shrugged and dropped her hand. “Charlie said I have more grandchildren, and even great-grandchildren. Tell me about them.”

“May and Harry were Athena’s,” Bobby answered, a bit hesitant.

“And Buck and his husband are the ones with my great-grandchildren,” she said, and then laughed at whatever expression was on Bobby’s face. “They have an Instagram, dear. It was very easy to find them.”

“And you’re…?”

This time, it was her turn to hesitate.

“They’re your family, and I’m dying,” she said. “And it’s never been my place to judge that sort of… Thing.”

Bobby sighed. It was better than Ramon’s attitude, at least.

“They named their youngest after me,” he told her. “Gavin Robert….”

Chapter 35: Cat Got Your Tongue

Chapter Summary

In which Eddie makes a sacrifice for a good cause, and trauma chooses the worst moment to pop up.

“I’m thinking about trading in the truck.”

Eddie’s statement was calm and matter-of-fact, and it came completely out of left field. Unfortunately for Buck, the unexpected announcement hit just as he was drinking his coffee and he ended up choking and sputtering. Abuela reached over from her spot at the head of the table and started patting his back, which was more than his kids did. Both Chris and Gavin found his predicament amusing enough to openly laugh at him. Considering that mere minutes before, Gavin had been making his sudden hatred of pancakes everyone’s problem, Buck was willing to look past the insult.

“You okay?” Eddie asked, peering at him.

“Y- Yeah, fine.” Buck cleared his throat. He took the paper towel that his husband handed him and used it to mop up the spewed coffee. “You’re thinking about getting rid of the truck? But you love that thing, babe.”

Maybe love was a strong descriptor, but Buck remembered how proud Eddie had been of the thing when he first bought it with the money from that stupid fight club. Not that Buck had known at the time that that was how Eddie managed to afford the impulsive purchase. Eddie had just shown up with the big beast of a vehicle, simply because the AC crapped out on his old one and he’d seen the dealership as he drove past.

It was one of the many signs that something was up with Eddie at the time.

“I don’t love how much of a gas guzzler it is,” Eddie said.

“You’ve had that thing for five years and you’re just now noticing?” Buck asked, a bit exasperated.

“You’re usually driving me around to places!” His husband threw up his hands. “We carpool to work, to the grocery store, wherever. I didn’t notice how much gas it ate up until now, now that I’m driving myself across the city just about every day.”

“Dad’s a passenger princess,” Chris said with a laugh.

Eddie let out what could only be described as an outraged squawk.

“Where did you even-!?”

“Don’t worry.” Buck stood up with his empty plate and rounded the table to pat Eddie on the shoulder. “You’re the prettiest passenger princess, and I love driving you around.”

“Wanna go check out cars with me?”

“Absolutely, princess.”

“I will stab you with this fork,” Eddie threatened, brandishing the utensil at Buck.

“Abuela!” Buck called over his shoulder as he went to rinse off his plate and then stick it in the dishwasher. “Your grandson’s threatening me!”

“Sorry, Buckito, I don’t remember that happening,” Abuela replied, and then made a vague gesture to her head. “The Alzheimer’s.”

This time it was Buck’s turn to squawk in outrage.

With breakfast done and after making sure Eddie had his bagged lunch for the day, it was time for Buck to take off for the station. It was still weird, even weeks later, even after he’d gone through this before with the wildfires and whenever Eddie was injured, to be driving into work without Eddie in the passenger seat. It always left Buck feeling off-balanced, somehow, and the silence left in his husband’s absence was never quite filled by the radio.

As usual, Buck was the first of his shift to arrive. He and Mayfair went through the handover, going over anything she deemed important enough to tell him herself instead of simply hoping he’d read it in the log. She looked more rested nowadays, since she and her husband managed to wrangle their insurance into submission enough to get a payout. They were currently living in a cheap apartment, much like Bobby and Athena since the arson, but he didn’t know if they were planning on rebuilding their home or if they were going to sale the lot and find somewhere else.

Afterwards, he fetched the paperwork from the office that he should’ve completed before the end of his last shift, but which he’d opted to put it off. He was powering through it, and taking longer because he chose to sit at one of the hightop tables and chat with people, when Chimney came stomping up the stairs. The paramedic was talking to Hen, and looking worried. It became very clear why when Buck heard the last part of his sentence.

“-nearly died five weeks ago!”

“Why are we talking about Maddie?” Buck asked, sitting up. “Is she okay?”

“Maddie’s… Fine.” Chimney could have been more convincing. “She decided to go back to work today.”

“Today today,” Hen added.

“I walked into the kitchen this morning and she was dressed for work,” Chimney continued. “She has my full support, but I’m still worried. She hadn’t even mentioned wanting to go back to work before today.”

“Is she still having the nightmares?” Buck asked.

“Every night, apparently,” Chimney answered, and then, “Wait, you knew about them?”

“She mentioned ‘em to Eddie. Did you not…?”

“No! Not until this morning.”

Considering that the nightmares had to be bad enough to wake up Maddie, since she was responding to his middle-of-the-night check-in texts long before his alarms went off, Buck found himself wondering how Chimney could have possibly not known about them before this morning. Buck certainly hadn’t managed to sleep through Eddie’s trauma-induced nightmares after the shooting. Then again, he didn’t know how Maddie was with nightmares, maybe she just wasn’t as obvious about them as Eddie.

Buck made a mental note to check in with his sister later, to see how she was handling her first day back. He made another mental note to check in with Josh, too, because Buck’s sister was far too similar to himself and would undoubtedly understate any issues, and the other dispatcher could be depended on to rat her out if he was concerned enough. Buck felt it was fair, because he knew Maddie wouldn’t hesitate to use Chimney for the same purposes.

Their first call of the day was to a high-rise apartment building. A fire on the seventh floor was started by a mishap with popcorn. They rushed for their turnouts, pulling them on in quick and efficient moves, before clambering into the trucks.

There was the usual crowd of on-lookers when the 118 arrived. It was difficult to tell if they were people from the building or people who sniffed out something exciting and just wanted to watch. There wasn’t any smoke pouring from the building itself yet, so it was hard to tell for sure.

“One Eighteen.” Maddie’s voice sounded scratchy over the radio, hoarse. It had Buck frowning. “I’m showing you arriving at Eighty-Three Forty Wilshire.”

“Copy that, dispatch. One Eighteen on-scene,” Buck replied as he hopped out. He started shooing the crowd of people out of the way, sending them shuffling off with, “LAFD. Step back, step back.”

“We need search and rescue for a nine year old named Chance and his dad,” Maddie said. Her voice was still hoarse sounding. “He doesn’t know the apartment number, but it’s likely above the fire floor. The bedroom he’s in is filling up with smoke.”

Maybe Buck was just spoiled by Chris, because the kid had been and still was very smart, but what nine year old couldn’t even give at least a floor number? Maybe that should be the next Instagram video he bullied Eddie into doing with him, things parents should make sure their kids know in case of an emergency.

“Do we know if anyone else is still inside?” Buck asked.

“Negative. Just Chance and his dad.”

“Copy that,” he replied, and then turned to the others to give out instructions. “Ravi, you and Bell head up to find the kid. Start on the eighth floor and work your way up. Hen, Chimney, Albert, get a triage site set-up.”

“Copy that,” was echoed amongst all of them as they rushed off, the paramedics for a clear spot nearby, while the other two went for the oxygen tanks in the engine’s compartments.

“Everyone else!” Buck raised his voice to be heard by those farther away. “Handlines to seventh!”

The hardest part of being captain, or at least the part that Buck had found to be the hardest so far, was the part where he just stood around and watched. He’d given the orders, and now he was just waiting for them to be carried out. Ravi and Bell were inside, Hen and Chimney had the triage area set up and were working through anyone that needed seeing to, and Toby and the others were hooking up the hoses and starting to run them up. Now all there was for Buck to do was stand around and wait for something to happen.

Buck was awful at standing around and waiting for something to happen.

“Cap, we’re on eight,” Ravi radioed.

“Anything yet?”

“Negative.”

“Alright, keep looking,” Buck instructed, and then he switched channels. “Dispatch, is there any way we can narrow this down? Can the kid see us? Is the apartment near the stairs, the elevator?”

“One moment, One Eighteen,” Maddie responded, and then went silent as she no doubt switched to Chance to ask those very questions.

One of the windows facing them, a few floors above the fire, was suddenly billowing out smoke. It hadn’t been before. Buck stared at it, head tilted, as he wondered if that was the kid’s apartment, if he’d opened it on Maddie’s instructions. He hadn’t heard any glass shattering, so he didn’t think it broke under the heat.

But there was the possibility that the window had been left open by the occupants of that apartment, and the smoke just finally reached it. It was a big enough possibility that Buck was hesitant to send Ravi and Bell to it, on the off chance it just meant they missed Chance entirely.

“Buck, he can see your rigs,” Maddie said. “I’m gonna have him wave a blanket out the window.”

“I’ll keep an eye out,” Buck told her, scanning the rows of windows. He kept coming back to the one with the smoke, now certain that it was the one.

But there was no blanket hanging from the window.

“Dispatch, I don’t see a blanket,” Buck prompted, after a handful of moments passed. No one replied to him. “Dispatch? Maddie?”

A tremor of worry ran through him when his sister still didn’t reply. She wouldn’t just ignore him, not in a situation like this. There was something wrong, he knew there was, but he couldn’t spend the time focusing on it. Not when there was a child in danger.

He just had to go with his gut on this one.

“Ravi, tenth floor, Alpha side,” Buck radioed up. “It’s a middle unit. Dispatch said he’s in the bedroom, so he probably won’t answer. Just knock down doors until you find him.”

“Copy that, Cap.”

“Captain One Eighteen.” That was Josh. He’d taken over the call for Maddie. Now Buck knew for certain that something was wrong. “Chance is going to hang a blanket out the window.”

“Copy that, dispatch,” Buck replied, and then watched as a blanket was dangled out of the window with the smoke. He relaxed a bit with the knowledge that he hadn’t made a mistake. “I see it.”

Once again, he was stuck waiting. Toby and Javier radioed down to him on occasion, keeping him updated on their progress with fighting back the fire on the seventh floor. They were doing well, for how much it had spread before their arrival.

“Cap, we have eyes on the kid and his dad,” Ravi reported. “Grabbing them and getting out.”

“Understood,” Buck replied. “Dispatch, we have Chance and his father. They’re coming out now.”

“Understood, One Eighteen,” Josh replied.

When Ravi and Bell came down, they went straight for Hen and Chimney without a glance Buck’s way. Chance, the kid, was red faced and coughing in Bell’s arms, while the father was still not stirring. It had Buck frowning, because Maddie hadn’t actually said what was up with him.

He sent Chimney and Hen off with the father and the kid, which unfortunately left Albert by himself. By that point, the fire on the seventh floor was well in hand, though. They’d switched out for extinguishers and pikes, and were hunting down any remaining hotspots. So Buck grabbed one of the others and sent them to assist Albert, because there didn’t seem to be anything too severe that couldn’t be covered by an EMT.

(He could not wait until Eddie was through with paramedic school, both because then he’d be back at the station and also because they wouldn’t be scrambling quite so badly to fill the gaps.)

“Dispatch,” Buck reported. “Fire has been knocked down and is under control, doing overhaul now.”

“Understood, One Eighteen.” It was Sue who answered him that time, and she sounded hesitant. “Captain, is Chimney there?”

“He left on the bus with Chance and his dad,” Buck replied. “Why?”

“Maddie’s… Lost her voice.”

By the time that they’d cleared the scene, the fire out completely and everyone treated that needed treating, it had been long enough for Hen and Chimney to get their patients admitted, fill out the paperwork, and return to the station. Their turnouts were already hanging up in their gear cages when Buck hopped out to direct the trucks into the bay. When that was done, when the trucks were parked and his own turnouts were put up, he stomped up the stairs to the loft and found the pair of them playing cards at the dining table.

Everyone else was showering away the sweat and grime of a job well done, except for Albert, who had only handled triage instead of heading into the fire, and Hendrix, who’d been the man behind. They were both downstairs, though, so there wasn’t an audience to watch Buck break the news.

“Chim.”

His brother-in-law looked up and then his smile fell. Buck’s expression must’ve given it all away.

“What is it?” Chimney demanded.

“You’re cutting out early,” Buck told him. “Maddie lost her voice. She might still be at dispatch, Sue said she was pretty upset, but that was a bit ago.”

“Shit. Okay, okay.” Chimney scrambled to his feet and pulled out his phone. “I’ll call- I can’t call her, she lost her voice. I’ll call Sue!”

Buck stepped aside to allow him to rush past, heading for the locker room with his phone pressed to his ear. He turned back to Hen, who was gathering up the cards as she frowned after her friend.

“How bad is it?” Hen asked.

“Bad enough Josh took over on their end,” Buck said.

She let out a hum.

“I’m sure everything’s fine.”

“I’m sure everything’s fine, mi sol,” Eddie said, echoing Hen’s sentiment from the day before. For once, he was the one driving Buck around; they were on their way to a car lot to trade in the truck, something that Buck still couldn’t believe was happening. “Do they have any idea?”

“It’s psychogenic, apparently,” Buck said, looking back through the texts from his sister. Her dismay and stress was almost audible. “They took a CT of her neck, did bloodwork, everything. There’s nothing physically wrong, at least nothing to affect her vocal cords or the nerves there. She took her first call since Braeburn and her voice just… Left her.”

Amber Braeburn, former missing person detective, was currently waiting in jail for her trial. Well, at the moment, she was waiting until they could decide if she was competent to stand trial. There was something about childhood trauma and mental issues and a bunch of other stuff that Buck didn’t really care about, because she abducted his sister and then tried to kill her, so any sympathy for the bitch went the way of the dodo.

“Is it okay that you’re skipping a labs day for this?” Buck asked.

“Oh no, I might miss how to do a successful REBOA in a moving vehicle.” Eddie’s voice dripped sarcasm. “Actually, I wish that’s what we were doing. It’d be fun. All I’m missing today is being asked to help the instructor demonstrate how to administer medication.”

“You’re such a teacher’s pet,” Buck teased.

Eddie rolled his eyes as they pulled into the car lot.

They’d already emptied the truck of everything, spending the morning combing through it to make sure. All they’d have to do was pick its replacement, sign the paperwork put in front of them, and then pay whatever the difference was. The first step was the hardest one, because Eddie…

Well, he might’ve been the one to decide to trade his truck in, but he was very much dragging his heels about it. Because he was a Texan, born and raised, and he loved his stupidly large truck. And he very much did not love the alternatives with the better gas mileage.

“I like the color,” Buck commented as they stared at the blue car in front of them.

“Of course you do.”

“What does that mean?”

“That you’d like anything if it was bright enough.”

Buck opened his mouth to argue, only to immediately close it again. Because Eddie was right, he did like things that were brightly colored. But the joke was on him, because Buck had long ago accepted whimsy into his life. And this car was a very pretty blue.

“It has good reviews,” Buck said, swiping his thumb across the screen of his phone as he scrolled through the page he found. “Good safety ratings, good mileage.”

“It’s a Prius.” Eddie spoke of it in much the same tone as he did Taylor Kelly, with scorn and disdain. “A used Prius. Who knows what’s wrong with it.”

“You can look through it before buying,” Buck reminded him. “And you’re the one who decided to do this, no one’s forcing you.”

“The numbers on the pump when I filled up the truck yesterday are making me,” Eddie grumbled. Then he sighed. “Yeah, okay. This one.”

Eddie treated the trip to fetch the salesman like it was a funeral march, and then he hyped up his beloved truck like it was his actual first born. The salesman’s face when Eddie insisted on inspecting the Prius himself was hilarious, though. Fetching the paperwork when Eddie was done was very much an excuse for the salesman to run away.

“There, there.” Buck gave his morose husband a pat on the shoulder. “It’ll be okay, it’s for a good cause.”

“Bite me.”

“Happily, we have a new car to break-in. Or…” Buck frowned as he reconsidered, eying up the backseat of the Prius. “Actually, no. We’d never manage to fit into that backseat for anything fun.”

Eddie heaved out a sigh of despair.

Chapter 36: Thirty Minutes or Less

Chapter Summary

In which someone is definitely not getting their pizza, and the author corrects the issue of Maddie's brother barely being involved in Maddie's storylines.

Honestly, it wasn’t the most insane looking thing Buck had seen on this job. It was no bus sticking out of the side of an office building, or a jet fighter parked in someone’s living room, or a hotel tilted at a near perfect 45° angle. What it was, however, was a pizza delivery guy doing a horrible parking job at a parking garage. His car was sticking half-out of the side of the eleventh floor, by Buck’s count, and kept from falling the rest of the way by prayer and one of those barrier cables made up of steel wire ropes pulled as taut as it could be.

“Oh, someone’s garlic knots are gonna be late,” Hen commented as they all craned their necks to gawk.

Garlic knots actually sounded pretty good right now. Maybe Buck could order in today, give himself a break from cooking for the thankless masses.

“Long way down, Cap,” Ravi added. “Rescue cushion?”

Buck turned his head to shoot him an incredulous stare.

“For a car? It’ll burst like a balloon,” he said. “We’re gonna have to go up and secure it before that cable breaks. Chim, Toby, go harness up. Quickly.”

“Copy that!” Chimney said, as he and the driver-engineer jogged back to get the gear. “Thirty minutes or less!”

“Why not me?” Ravi asked.

“Because your idea was stupid,” Buck told him. “C’mon, let’s grab the hooks and straps.”

It was a group effort to get everything up to the car. The entire time, Buck kept an eye on its precarious position, wincing every time the wind blew too hard or he heard something creak. And then it was a matter of anchoring the car to the support beams of the garage, which was potentially even more anxiety-inducing. Because if they took too long, the cable might give before they had the car secured. But if they rushed it, they could end up being the reason the car finally went.

“Hen, Ravi, how are we doin’?” Buck asked.

“Almost there, Cap,” Hen answered as she ratcheted a strap until the tension was nice and tight.

Ravi didn’t answer, too busy attaching the hooks to the car’s back axle.

Buck nodded to them both and got as close to the car as he dared without a line, which was probably closer than Bobby would’ve preferred him to be, if Bobby had been there. The driver looked very frightened, which was understandable for someone who was in danger of plummeting several stories into the pavement below. The window was rolled down, so Buck was able to check in with the guy.

“Hey, sir.” He gave the driver a smile as he leaned a little over the in-tact portion of the safety barrier. “I’m Captain Buck Diaz, LAFD. What’s your name? How’s it hangin’?”

He winced as soon as the words were out of his mouth

“Ozzie, sir,” the guy replied. “I’m… Hanging. How high up am I?”

“Uh.” Buck did the mental math on that. They were on the eleventh floor, and a story was about ten feet tall, but the ground floor of the garage was a bit taller than the rest… “Hundred-ten, hundred-twenty feet. But don’t you worry, Ozzie, my guys’ll get you right out of there. Just sit tight.”

“Sit tight. Yeah, yeah, got it.”

The guy nodded a bit frantically, but he wasn’t moving enough to be worrisome just yet.

“Axle’s secure, Cap!” Ravi reported, and was followed by Hen’s,

“So’s the anchor.”

Buck nodded to them and stepped back, letting Chimney and Toby approach the car. They had helmets and their safety harnesses on, with lines attaching them to anchor points on one of the support beams, just like with the car. Buck lingered close enough to have a good vantage point of what was going on, but not where he would be in the way.

“His name’s Ozzie,” he mentioned to Chimney as he went past, and he got a nod in reply.

“Hey, Ozzie, it looks like quite the collision,” Chimney said as he got up to the driver’s door. Toby was across from them, peering through the passenger side window. “Did you hit your head at all?”

“No, no.” Buck saw Ozzie shake his head as he answered. “I hit the gas.”

“Alright. Can you do me a favor?” Chimney asked him. “Can you wiggle your fingers and toes for me?”

Ozzie raised his hands, one at a time, and quickly wiggled his fingers where they could see. The guy’s feet were blocked from Buck’s view, obviously, but Chimney must have been satisfied with whatever he saw. He nodded and then tried to open the driver’s door. Emphasis on try: however much he pulled, and he gave it his all, it refused to be moved.

“Doesn’t look like your door’s gonna budge,” Chimney said through gritted teeth. He tried the door to the backseat, and got the same result.

“Toby.”

Buck just had to say his name and Toby was giving the door on his side a try. It opened easily, if with a bit of an ominous creak, and then he hunched back down to be level with an increasingly anxious seeming Ozzie.

“Okay, sir,” Toby said. “Now just unbuckle your seatbelt and then carefully slide towards me, and I’ll get you out.”

“Slide!?” Ozzie yelped. “No, no, the other guy said to sit tight. What happened to sit tight?”

“Um.” Toby’s head popped over the roof of the car to shoot Buck a look that made it clear he was a bit lost on how to proceed. Buck shrugged in response and Toby’s expression went flat before he ducked down again. “He did, you’re right, but that was then. Now we’re getting you out, and I need you to move over here.”

“I- I have a heights thing,” Ozzie said. “There’s a name for it.”

“Yeah, it’s acrophobia,” Chimney offered.

“I’ve got acrophobia!”

“Well, sir.” Toby sounded a bit helpless. “I’m gonna put a capture strap-” He tapped the one he had slung across himself. “-on you, it’ll keep you from falling.”

“Nu-uh.” Ozzie shook his head. “No way-”

His words turned into a high pitched scream as the car suddenly rocked forward. Ravi lunged for the tie-downs, as if he would actually manage to singlehandedly hold the car back.

“The rope’s on tight!” Ravi said, and Buck knelt down to get a better look at what was going on.

It was not anything good.

“The axle’s coming off.” It didn’t matter how tight the rope was if what it was attached to was no longer attached to the rest of the car. “The whole rear suspension is going:”

“Must have hit a lot of potholes on that pizza route,” Hen commented.

“Must have,” Buck agreed as he stood back up. The thing must’ve already been on its way out, and the weight of the car combined with the pull of the rope just stressed it to its breaking point. “Toby! He needs out of there. Now.”

“You heard him, sir,” he heard Toby tell Ozzie. “Just slide over and I’ll get you out of there.”

“You know what.” Ozzie’s voice was tight, and he was sitting still as could be in his seat. “Just leave me.”

“That would be against my religion.”

“No, it’s cool, it’s fine. It’s kosher. God’ll allow it,” Ozzie said. “I deserve it, you know?

“For a car accident?” was Chimney’s incredulous reply to that.

“I- I weasel out of everything. Speeding tickets, my marriage. It’s just time to face the music.”

“Cap!” Toby straightened up as he addressed Buck. “You’re Catholic adjacent, you wanna give it a try?”

“Listen, Ozzie,” Chimney said, before Buck could make his attempt at convincing the guy to not die. “It’s just one step, man.”

“No, no.” Ozzie shook his head. “It’s fate. Weasel’s going down with the ship.”

Here, again, was the difference between being just another firefighter and being the guy in charge. If it was him in Toby’s shoes, Buck would just go in and grab the guy and pull him out. But he was well aware of how precarious of a position the car was in right now, and how easily it could fall if it had to hold up any more weight. Buck might’ve been comfortable putting himself at risk like that, but he wasn’t gonna tell someone else to do it.

That did leave him short on options, though.

“Chim, any ideas?” he asked.

“We could…” Chimney looked the car over. Buck could tell, just from a shift in his posture, when he thought of something. “We could weasel our way out. Ozzie, you’re about a thirty-two inch waist, right?”

Ozzie’s response was a nervous, quizzical,

“Yeah…?”

Chimney’s idea was to have Ozzie climb through the back and out the trunk. Buck was, admittedly, uncertain about the idea - it would involve a lot of movement inside the car, and he had no idea how much of that it could take before the axle snapped completely off and the car did its best impression of a lemming being filmed for White Wilderness. Unfortunately, it was the only idea any of them had so far to get a resistant Ozzie out of the car, or at least the only one that wouldn’t put any of Buck’s people in danger.

Thankfully, Ozzie managed to wiggle in between the front seats, slowly and carefully, and then pull the backseat down. The trunk was popped open with a halligan, and Ozzie came crawling out with a bit of help from them to stand on wobbly legs. He immediately wrapped his arms around a very uncomfortable Buck as he repeatedly thanked them all.

“Sir,” Hen broke in, rescuing Buck. “You should let us check you out at Presbyterian.”

“Why?” Ozzie asked. “I feel incredible.”

“Protocol,” Buck explained as the sound of approaching police sirens reached his ears.

Ozzie’s face fell a bit.

“There’s something I have to do real quick,” he said.

It turned out, whatever it was he had to do, it required him to not be there. Buck and the rest watched him take the stairwell down, leaving them all rather confused. There was nothing to really do about that, however - he was aware and ambulatory, he was refusing care, their hands were tied - so Buck had them start packing up.

And then, the axle finally snapped. The car immediately fell more than a hundred feet into the pavement below. Buck heard the crash of metal and then, because their life was dramatic enough that the rumored curse on their station had to be real, something exploded. They rushed over to find that the car had landed on top of another car, and now they were both burning.

“Who the hell parks right beneath this?” Buck asked as they all stared down at it.

“Him, I’m guessing,” Chimney said, pointing at the cop looking on at the wreckage in sheepish despair.

Also down below them was Athena. She was with Ozzie and, for some reason, the latter was now wearing handcuffs. Buck was very curious how that happened, but sating his curiosity was a low priority.

“Alright, let’s… Take care of that, now,” he told the others. “And then I’m ordering pizza for everyone.”

It was an announcement that earned him several cheers.

(Buck did manage to badger the details out of Athena, while everyone was busy either putting out the fire or putting away the gear. Apparently, Ozzie had been in traffic court - remotely - while out doing deliveries. He was in traffic court for driving with a suspended license. He’d been driving while appearing for court for that charge.

Buck didn’t think Ozzie was getting his license back anytime soon.)

There was rarely any excuse needed for Buck to drop in on his sister. That hadn’t always been true, especially back when Doug was still a fixture in her life. But it was something that became true after she came to Los Angeles, even after she moved in with Chimney. It was especially true after her return from Boston, when they both welcomed every chance to see each other again after months where they couldn’t.

He didn’t make unannounced visits often, though. There was Chimney to consider, after all, and the fact that they lived on the other side of the city from him. And they would usually invite the other over at least once every other week, and they talked every day, so it wasn’t like he needed to just barge into her life to see and check in on her. Not like he did those months after Jee-Yun was born and Maddie was silently struggling.

Maddie was silently struggling once again, though, and so he made the drive from West Adams to Los Feliz. The driveway was full with both her and Chimney’s cars, so Buck parked his jeep on the curb. He grabbed his offering of a tupperware of baked goods and bounded for the door.

It was Chimney who answered his knocking, appearing only momentarily surprised.

“Cookies?” Buck offered, holding out the tupperware. “Well, cookimisu.”

“Cookimisu?” his brother-in-law repeated, taking the offering as he stepped aside.

“Tiramisu cookies,” he explained. “They’re from the cookbook that Eddie got me for Christmas.”

“I will be having tiramisu cookies, then.” Chimney was already tearing off the lid to stuff one into his mouth. “Maddie’s out back.”

“Thanks, Chim.”

Maddie was curled up in a chair just outside their backdoor. She raised her head when she heard him come out, looking utterly miserable. Buck didn’t hesitate before kneeling down and pulling her into a hug, and she hugged him back just as fiercely.

“How have you been?” he asked, already knowing the answer.

She pulled away and shook her head, face twisted with her frown. Then she picked up the tablet that was sitting in her lap and, after tapping away for a bit, held it up so he could see the notes app that was taking up the screen and what she’d written on it.

We did exercises. Nothing worked.

“Nothing worked today,” Buck countered, easing into the chair beside her. “It’s… It’s physical therapy, y’know? It’s hard at the start.”

But there’s NOTHING PHYSICAL.

“No need to shout,” he teased. She rolled her eyes and smacked him on the arm with the tablet. “Hey, listen, all your thoughts and fears and anxiety and everything, they’re all just- just bits of electricity and chemicals being passed between neurons. They’re absolutely physical.”

She stared at him for a long moment and then typed one single word.

Bullshit.

“Okay, yeah, I was really leaning into the semantics there,” he admitted. “Have you guys talked about- Uh, shit. Um, I didn’t mean to…”

Maddie rolled her eyes again, an actual smile haunting the edges of her mouth, and then flapped her hand for him to move on.

“Any plans for therapy?” Buck asked. “Therapy therapy, I mean.”

She frowned and started typing. He watched her for a bit, watched as she typed and shook her head and typed some more. The message she wrote out, when she finally raised her tablet, was far shorter than Buck expected. She must’ve deleted and retyped it.

Chimney mentioned exposure therapy. Just go and talk to Braeburn?

“Why would you have to? I didn’t talk to that Freddie kid.”

His sister looked at him in confusion, and then her face cleared with realization.

The bomber? Why would you?

“Do you remember, after the fire at Metro Dispatch, when Pops first shoved me into being captain?” Buck asked. He waited for her to nod before he continued. “That shift was the first time I sat in the front seat of either truck since, y’know.”

He gestured at his leg, stretched out in front of him.

But you could still do your job.

“Eh.” Buck waggled his hand. “I froze, the first time. Just sat there like a scared bunny, waiting for everything to explode. And I’d freeze every time I had to get in. Or, I mean, not every time. When the alarm went off, I didn’t even think about it until I was already in the seat. The adrenaline, you know? And the rush. I guess it didn’t give my brain a chance to freak out until I was already sitting down.”

Maddie’s frown grew deeper, and then started furiously typing away on her tablet.

It’s not the same. You got hurt in the truck.

“Under the truck,” Buck corrected. “But sure it is. It’s- It’s… Copeland said it’s what the brain associates with the trauma that matters. Eddie sometimes gets freaked out if I get ketchup on my face, because he remembers my face being covered in blood. My brain associated the front seat with the explosion, and yours made the connection between taking someone’s nine-one-one call and getting hurt by Braeburn.”

What did you do?

“Copeland told me to sit in the front seat between calls,” Buck said. “I’d talk to Eddie or Hen or whoever decided to sit with me. Eventually, my brain realized that the front seat didn’t mean fire and destruction and pain. Maybe you can do that with calls.”

Maddie nodded in thought and then her face twisted again as she reached up to touch her throat. It took a moment, and then Buck realized what his sister already had.

“Ah, right.” He winced. “You need your voice before you can do that. Maybe… Maybe you can talk to Sue or Josh, see about sitting in on their calls?”

Maybe.

“But!” Buck slapped his knees. “You know I can talk enough for the both of us. Wanna hear about the guy who called about bugs under his skin? It was after Chimney left.”

Maddie nodded like a bobblehead.

I feel like I’m being babysat.

Eddie laughed at what he read on Maddie’s phone, and shook his head.

“You’re not!” he promised. “But Buck’s on shift, Abuela’s at church. You just gave me an excuse to get out of the house.”

They were at the park, him and Maddie with Gavin and Jee-Yun. Eddie made the decision on a whim when he texted Maddie to check-in with her and she told him the plans for the morning. It hadn’t taken much thought at all before he was packing Gavin into the Prius. He’d asked if Chris wanted to go, poking his head into his oldest’s room where the teen was still curled up in bed, only to get a series of grunts that he translated into a firm no.

I like the new car btw. Very bright.

“Buck liked the color,” Eddie told her and then dropped his voice to a whisper. “Between you and me? That’s half of why I picked that one.”

Maddie covered her mouth with a hand as she laughed, the sound coming out breathy. Her phone chimed and he managed to get a glimpse of Athena’s name, but before he could sate his curiosity by snooping over Maddie’s shoulder, his own name was being called.

“Daddy!” 

Gavin sounded upset, and it was enough to have Eddie immediately jumping to his feet. He spotted the tot quickly, sitting on his butt near a slide. He was crying, too, and that had Eddie jogging across the playground.

“Hey, hey, mijo, what’s wrong?” Eddie asked, kneeling to check on him.

Gavin raised up his hands to show his palms, the pair of them scraped and bleeding lightly.

“Hurts,” Gavin sniffled.

“Aw, no.” Eddie took Gavin’s wrists between his fingers, loudly smacking a kiss to each palm before picking him. “We’ll get them cleaned up in no time. Okay, buddy?”

“Okay.”

Eddie turned to go back to the bench that he and Maddie were sitting at, and where the diaper bag with the small first aid kit was left behind, and expected his sister-in-law to still be there. She wasn’t, though. He didn’t see any signs of her anywhere, either.

“Where did Maddie go, huh?” he asked Gavin.

“Dunno,” was Gavin’s answer. “Aunt Maddie go poof?”

“I think she did go poof,” Eddie agreed.

Calling for her wouldn’t do any good, he didn’t think, not when she wouldn’t be able to answer. He could text her, though, and he decided to do that after he’d taken care of his kid. He’d just grabbed the diaper bag to dig out the first aid kit when he heard Maddie cry out,

“Jee!”

Once again, Eddie was rushing across the playground, diaper bag still clutched in his hand and Gavin bouncing on his hip. He found Maddie clutching at Jee-Yun in the middle of some of the equipment.

“What’s going on? Is everything okay?”

“Yeah, everything’s fine,” Maddie said. Maddie said. “I- I lost track of Jee, freaked out a bit.”

“Mommy can talk!” Jee-Yun excitedly told Eddie.

“I can hear that,” Eddie said with a grin.

“The adrenaline, I guess.” Maddie stood up and wiped at her face. “Gave my brain something else to freak out over.”

“Whatever works.”

“So what happened with you?” she asked Gavin, poking at his side.

“Fell, scraped his palms,” Eddie answered, and Gavin held out a hand with a little,

“Ow.”

“Well that won’t do, will it, Jee?” Maddie asked. The little girl shook her head, hair flopping everywhere. “Okay, let’s take care of that.”

“And while we’re doing that,” Eddie said as they went back to the bench, “we can tell everyone the good news.”

Chapter 37: Happy HEN Day

Chapter Summary

In which Buck did, actually, forget Hen's birthday. But it doesn't count.

Chapter Notes

As is tradition at this point, here is a chapter on my birthday. One about a birthday, even.

This was as quiet as the house got when its occupants were awake and home. There was the low murmur of voices from the living room, where Abuela was watching TV as she knitted. There was splashing water in the bathroom and the occasional burst of laughter as Eddie gave Gavin his post-dinner bath. There was laughter from Chris’ room and the occasional whoop of celebration or cry of dismay as he played one of his games.

The kitchen, where Buck was, was much the same as he rinsed off dishes and put them in the dishwasher, making sure he put them in such a way that he wouldn’t have Eddie nagging at him about it later. Hoover laid on the floor by his feet, letting out sighs so heavy one would think he worked fulltime. And on the counter was Buck’s phone, propped up so that he could easily see the screen and the person whose face filled it while they complained.

“That cartoon dog is driving me insane. It’s got me dreaming in Australian accents,” TK was saying. “Last night I was having a very, very nice dream, and then Carlos started talking. He sounded like the fudging- Shut up.”

“I didn’t say anything,” Buck said.

“I can see you smiling.”

“I’m always smiling.” He shrugged. “I just find it funny that, before, you’d make fun of me for censoring myself. And now…”

“Shut up, shut up, shut up,” TK chanted. “I can imagine Grace’s face if my four year old brother-slash-adopted child starts repeating cuss words he heard from me, I don’t want to see it in person.”

“Just blame it on someone else, it’s what I do. But c’mon. Dream, Carlos, accents.”

“Yeah, yeah. Anyway, Carlos takes off his shirt-”

“Oh, one of those nice dreams.”

“And then he opens his mouth and he sounds like the Crocodile Hunter. It was just so wrong that it woke me right up. Carlos was working, so he wasn’t even there to make up for getting interrupted before the good part.”

“Your life is suffering,” Buck snarked as he put in the detergent for the dishwasher and then closed it.

“It is!” TK agreed. “I didn’t realize how much of being a parent is just being forced to watch the same thing over and over.”

“Tell me about it.” Buck pressed the buttons and let the dishwasher do its thing. “There was a month, just before Eddie and I got together, when the only thing Chris wanted to watch was Finding Nemo.”

“I’m gonna try to get him to watch something else tomorrow,” TK said. “If I have to sit through another episode of that blue dog and her adorable family, I’m gonna start raiding medicine cabinets.”

“Teek,” Buck scolded.

“Relax, it was a joke. I’m not gonna actually leap off the wagon just because Jonah wants to watch Bluey for the thousandth time. I mean, I probably won’t.”

Buck made a face at the screen, which only succeeded in TK rolling his eyes at him. Then, Buck frowned in thought and asked,

“Don’t you think it’s weird that he has the same name as the guy who technically killed me twice?”

“Well now I do. Thanks for that, Sunshine.” TK huffed. “C’mon, anything fun happen at work? Nancy didn’t have anything new when we talked, which makes it hard to live vicariously through her.”

Because TK no longer worked as a paramedic and was being a stay-at-home dad. When they were first trying to adopt his half-brother, the social worker for his case initially rejected them. She was worried that their jobs were too dangerous, even TK’s. And Buck would normally disagree with her, because paramedics typically had a much safer job than firefighters.

Except this was TK.

“We had to rescue someone from their own bed,” Buck said.

TK stared at him through the phone screen.

“How…?”

“I’m not sure. It was one of those beds that the mattress lifts up and there’s a storage compartment, and that’s where he was trapped. He said he was tidying up.” Buck folded his arms on the countertop and shrugged. “I don’t really know. What I do know is that, when we got there, there was a couple having sex on the bed.”

“Oh my God.”

“It was his fiancee. With his cousin.”

“Oh. My God.”

“And he also got fired.”

“His life is more suffering than mine.” TK almost sounded awed. “No, wait, he’s not stuck in Bluey hell. I still win.”

Buck rolled his eyes and then straightened up with a smile when Eddie walked out of the hallway with Gavin in his arms. The toddler was wrapped up in one of those hooded bath towels, this one made to look like a lion with little ears and a mane.

“There’s my little guy!” Buck leaned forward to press a kiss to the top of Gavin’s head. He mostly got fleece. “How was the bath?”

“All clean!” the tot announced, throwing up his arms.

“We’ll see how long it lasts,” Eddie said. “Hey, are we doing anything for Hen’s birthday tomorrow?”

Buck froze, blinked, ran that question through his mind once, twice, three times.

“Hen’s what now?”

“Her birthday. It’s tomorrow.” Eddie said it slowly and enunciated the words, like Buck was stupid. Maybe he was. “Did you forget?”

“I- Well- How did you remember!?”

“We’re Facebook friends.”

“How old are you?” TK asked.

Buck had a Facebook, but it had been so long since he even thought about it, much less logged onto it. Before Eddie started at the station, certainly. Before Hen found him tolerable enough that she’d even want to be Facebook friends with him.

“I can’t believe I forgot Hen’s birthday,” Buck said, shaking his head at himself. “Alright, let’s get ya to bed, little guy. Pops might have to make a trip to the store.”

There was a possibility that what Buck had planned qualified as a dick move and made him a bad friend. He got past that by telling himself that it was really no different from any of the other pranks they’d played on each other over the years, and that everyone would find it funny in the end. Probably.

There were other things going on today, which made his plan even easier. He spent the time after the handover brief getting everything set up and ignoring the curious glances that he garnered from everyone else. They grew even more curious as he had everyone gather around him in the bay, one of the rolling toolboxes in front of him with a blanket covering the top.

Hen was the last one to arrive, cutting it rather close. She walked into the station, spotted how they were all grouped up, and headed their way instead of the lockers.

”Ah, there she is,” Chimney said.

“We’ve been waiting for you,” Buck told her.

He saw Hen’s face light up at the words.

“Hey, fellas,” she said, smiling from ear to ear. “What’s all the buzz?”

“Oh, it’s a special day,” Ravi answered.

“It is?”

Buck hadn’t told any of the rest of them what his plan was for the morning, but they must’ve guessed. Otherwise, they’d be wishing Hen a happy birthday right then. Hell, Hen was clearly expecting something, just from the way she drew that question out.

“Alright, since everyone’s here, gather ‘round!” Buck raised his voice, and the strays drifted towards them. He clutched at the clipboard in his hand. “A few announcements this morning. First off, Reynolds is gonna retire this year. So b-shift will be needing a new captain.”

“Why is he retiring?” Albert asked. He was standing between his brother and Ravi.

“Health reasons,” Buck answered. “COPD.”

Everyone there grimaced in sympathy, even Bell, who’d only been doing this for a couple months. COPD was one of those looming specters that haunted all of them in this job. The chances that they’d end up developing it increased every time they responded to a fire. Statistically speaking, it was inevitable that at least one of the people in the station right then would end up with it.

“But!” Buck hurried them along from the drab topic. “Today is a big day for all of us!”

Everyone grew a little excited. He saw Hen start to beam, which made him feel somewhat guilty for what he was about to pull.

“Today is HEN day,” Buck said.

“Cap,” Hen said, “you don’t have to-”

“The new high-efficiency nozzles have arrived!” He gripped the blanket and whipped it off, revealing the quartet of new nozzles. Hen’s face dropped like a rock, perhaps the same face she made when she first learned Santa Claus wasn’t real, while everyone else whooped in excitement. “The chief wants more data, so we’re testing them along with the One Twenty-three.”

“Yes.” Chimney rushed forward to grab one. “New toys.”

“And finally,” Buck said, and looked Hen in the eye. “Happy birthday, Hen! There’s cake upstairs.”

Everyone froze. Everyone. Buck saw Chimney, wide-eyed and pale-faced, mouth the word ‘birthday?’ to himself. It was not a reaction that was missed by Hen, who gave them all an icy glare.

“Thank you, Buck. It’s nice to know one of you remembered,” she sniped. “I’m gonna go change and then get some of my cake.”

“Hen, wait!” Chimney tried, but she ignored him as she marched off for the locker room. It looked for a moment that he might chase after her, but he just drooped where he stood.

“I can’t believe we forgot her birthday.” Albert winced as he said it.

“Speak for yourself.” Buck gave a prim sniff and stood with his back straight, nose in the air, and then he lied that, “I remembered it.”

Chimney scoffed and told him to,

“Stuff it.”

When Hen was done changing into her uniform and stomped up the stairs to the loft, the iciness that she left with had not thawed. She ignored Chimney entirely and sat on one of the stools at the kitchen island, where her cake was sitting out. Buck cut a slice off, put it onto a saucer, and then set it in front of her with a fork.

“It’s a German chocolate cake without the nuts,” Buck told her. “You know it’s not actually from Germany? It’s named after some guy named German.”

“I did not know that,” Hen said, using her fork to dig out a bite. “What I do know is that you, Athena, and Eddie are the only ones that remembered my birthday today.”

“Really? Not even Karen?”

“Not even my own mother.”

“But- But she was there!” Buck said. “You literally came out of her!”

“And yet. This is really good, by the way.” Then she reached over and smacked him on the arm. “I hate surprises, you know that.”

“It was a prank,” he insisted. “I mean, we literally get the high-efficiency nozzles just in time for your birthday? H, E, N? It was too perfect.”

“You’re still a shit.”

“I know.” Buck beamed at her. “Hey, I was gonna ask you to do me a favor, but now I don’t think I should.”

“You’re gonna ask me for a favor on my sucky birthday?” Hen pursed her lips and shook her head at him. “What is it?”

“Well, uh. The annual reviews are coming up,” he said. His first time doing it since becoming captain.

“That’s gonna feel awkward, you reviewing my performance. But then I get to give you feedback, so.”

“Yeah, no, I’m not doing that,” Buck told her as he shook his head. “That was Pops’ thing, and it can stay his thing. No, um. Chimney’s my brother-in-law.”

“I know, I was there for the wedding,” Hen said, and then, “Oh, conflicts of interest. Are you about to ask me to do his for you?”

“Yeah, I am. If Eddie wasn’t at paramedic school, I’d ask you to do his, too.”

Hen let out a hum, and then turned her head slightly to fix Chimney with a stare. She nodded to herself as she chewed a bite of cake.

“Sure, I’ll do it,” she said.

“Thank you. Are you gonna go for it?”

Hen shot him a quizzical frown, brow furrowed.

“Go for what?”

“Oh, the captain’s position for b-shift,” Buck clarified. “Are you gonna try and get it?”

Hen didn’t answer right away. She took another bite of cake and took her time chewing it, and then another.

“Maybe,” she finally said. “I’m not sure.”

“Why not?” Buck blurted out. “You wanted it before.”

“I just… I don’t know.” Hen shrugged at him. “I’m not sure I want it anymore.”

“Well, that’s- That’s fine,” he said, while making a mental note to sic Bobby on her at some point. This seemed like a conversation that Bobby would do better at than Buck. “We’d all miss you too much if you switched shifts.”

“Assuming you all even remembered me,” she said, side-eyeing the others.

 Buck winced.

“Still upset, then?” he asked.

“Oh, yeah.”

There was a man stuck on the wheel of a tractor-trailer. Which, sadly, wouldn’t be uncommon, except for the fact that the tractor-trailer wasn’t barrelling down a highway when it happened. It hadn’t even pulled out of the company’s loading bay.

“My jack was jammed,” the driver explained when they arrived. “We couldn’t get him out.”

The “him” in question, their victim, was wedged between the wheels of the tractor and the trailer. His position looked awkward and painful, bent over the wheels but half-twisted, an arm over his head. Also, he was behind the tires, somehow. He smiled when they approached.

“Hi,” he said. “Again.”

Hen bent down to get a better look at him and then, surprised, asked,

“Archie?”

“You know him?” Buck asked her.

“We all do.”

“We do?” At least Chimney sounded just as confused as Buck felt.

“My fiancee cheated on me,” the guy said. And then, when they still drew a collective blank, added, “On top of me.”

“Oh.” They all nodded.

“Archie, the guy in the bed,” Buck said, remembering him now. “Hey.”

“You people ought to be ashamed of yourselves.” Hen glared at them, and then knelt down beside Archie. “Are you in pain?”

“It’s not super comfortable,” he answered.

“How did this even… Happen?” Buck asked.

“I was looking for my nut,” Archie said, and Buck was glad he had so much practice at staying professional. “And I got caught when he, you know, rolled his tires.”

“Dumbass was lurking in the undercarriage,” the driver said.

“I wasn’t lurking,” Archie protested.

“Then why couldn’t I see you?”

“Because nobody ever does.”

Well, that was depressing.

“Alright, we’re gonna need…” Buck stepped back to look the whole thing over. “Cribbing, airbags for the tractor and the trailer, the jack, and the hydraulic wrench. Bell, get chocks under those tires, keep them from rolling more. Hen, Chim, do your thing.”

He led Ravi and Toby to the other side of the truck, where they could work without getting in the way of the paramedics. Kneeling down, he did a once over for where best to put the airbags. It would really suck if, instead of lifting it off Archie, they just crushed him further.

“Toby, an airbag under the stand there.” He pointed it out. “Ravi, airbags and cribbing under the tractor. We’ll jack it up and then get the tire off.”

“Got it, Cap,” they chorused, rushing off to grab everything they needed.

Buck waited while they set everything up, getting it all into position. Even when it was, he still waited, until Hen gave the all-clear with a,

“Cap! He’s stable!”

“Lifting the trailer,” Toby announced.
