He pressed the big button on the controller and the airbag began to fill. The trailer lifted up and up with groans and rumbles.

“One shoulder’s free!” Chimney shouted from the other side.

“Okay, that’s enough, Toby,” Buck said. “Ravi, the tractor.”

“Here it goes,” Ravi said, and activated the hydraulic jack.

Buck eyed the tractor as the jack lifted it up. When he felt it was high enough, he had Ravi stop the jack.

“Let’s get that tire off,” he said as he stood.

Ravi stood as well, picking up the hydraulic wrench from where he’d set it down. This was, again, a downside of being captain: Buck didn’t get to play with the big toys nearly as often, now. Instead, after Hen warned Archie about the vibrations, Buck got to stand back and watch someone else use the big toy to remove the tire.

Archie wobbled when he first stood up, and would have fallen if not for Chimney catching him. Bell chose the time to approach him, something clutched in her hand.

“I found this over there,” she said, pointing at where he’d been pinned. “Is this your missing nut?”

Archie stared at her, then at the nut in her hand, and with an aura of utter defeat, took the nut from her.

The benefit of being captain, almost making up for having to watch other people use the big toys, was that Buck didn’t have to handle the clean up. Instead, as Hen and Chimney half-carried Archie to plop him on the back of the ambulance for a proper check-over, Buck supervised the others picking up the airbags and cribbing and chocks to be put away. He also kept an ear on the paramedics.

“Are you living out of your car?”

The question from Hen drew Buck’s attention completely. He’d tuned out everything she’d been saying until that point, because she didn’t need him hovering over her, but that meant he missed the context.

“Just until I find another place,” Archie said.

“Archie, you’re not invisible,” Hen said. “You’re making yourself disappear, and that’s your fault. It’s okay to take up space in this world. Instead of making yourself smaller, put your chest out, make a noise. Stand up and tell the world that you’re here, that you exist, that you matter. That it’s your birthday and it’s not okay that everyone forgot.”

Everyone was staring at her now, cringing slightly.

“Well, um, it’s not my birthday,” Archie awkwardly said.

“It’s- It’s a metaphor,” Hen told him.

“Hen, listen-” Chimney tried once again.

And once again, Hen showed him her back, cutting him off with,

“Nope, it’s too late.”

“Oh.” Archie stood up. “It’s your birthday, isn’t it? Well, happy birthday, Hen.”

“Thank you, Archie.” 

She beamed at him, but the smile fell when she looked their way. Buck scooted to the side, separating himself from those that deserved her ire. He gently tugged Bell with him, because it wasn’t her fault she didn’t know when Hen’s birthday was. Hen glared at the others, and then headed for the ambulance’s cab.

“I think she might still be upset, guys,” Buck said.

“You think!?” Chimney snapped. “The drive here was like the Arctic.”

Buck patted him on the shoulder as he passed him by, heading for the engine’s cab.

“Shoulda baked her a cake,” he told him.

Chapter 38: The Wheels on the Bus

Chapter Summary

In which Buck is stuck watching as Hen plays hostage negotiator.

Buck got home closer to nine than to eight, and the house was already settling in for the evening. He was not fond of half-shifts, because they always felt like a waste of a day. They were scheduled to work another tomorrow, but the overnight half. Whether that was better or worse, he couldn’t say.

At least he’d be there to take Chris to his horse riding in the morning.

As always, Buck was greeted at the door by Hoover. The pooch leaned against him, tail frantically wagging, as Buck patted at his head. Eddie was on the couch, feet up on the coffee table and Senorita the cat looking quite content in his lap. When he paused in his petting of her, she butted her head against his hand.

“Demanding,” Eddie tutted, even as he followed her bidding. “How was it today, mi sol?”

“Awkward,” was Buck’s answer. He managed to gently push Hoover off him enough to be able to actually walk into the house, shutting the door behind him. “How was bedtime tonight?”

Eddie threw his head back against the couch with a groan.

“He did not want to sleep. Went through three stories, checked under the bed twice, and sang the song.”

“Gotta make sure the dust bunnies aren’t growing teeth,” Buck joked as he sat down beside Eddie. “Is Sir Bun keeping watch?”

That was what Buck came up with when, seemingly overnight, Gavin was suddenly afraid of the dark. He’d get upset the moment the light was turned off and he was alone in his room, when it hadn’t bothered him before, and only calmed down when the light was on or if Buck or Eddie were with him. Did that mean they did what was, perhaps, one of the worst things they could’ve done and let him sleep in their bed for a couple nights in a row?

Absolutely.

But they also went out and bought him a nightlight to go with the glow-in-the-dark stars that were still on the ceiling and started leaving Gavin’s door open just a little. And when that wasn’t enough, when Gavin suddenly decided there were monsters under his bed, Buck - sleep deprived and desperate - came up with the idea of knighting the atrociously vibrant orange rabbit plushie in a bullshit ceremony involving a knitting needle and entrusting him with the sacred duty of slaying any monster that dared to crawl out of their hidey-holes. So now Gavin refused to sleep unless he had Sir Bun with him and the nightlight on, but he did go to sleep.

“Sir Bun is tucked in right next to him,” Eddie said. “Chris thinks we should get him a sword.”

“Sir Bun doesn’t have fingers,” Buck pointed out. “How will he hold it?”

“I don’t think Chris thought that part through all the way,” he said. “Why was work awkward today?”

“Have I mentioned that I love you?” Buck sunk down on the couch so he could put his chin on Eddie’s shoulder and bat his eyes at him. “That you are the best, most wonderful husband in the whole wide world?”

“Not often enough,” answered the wonderful husband in question. “How does this relate to work?”

“I was the only one who remembered Hen’s birthday.”

“You didn’t remember it, I reminded you,” Eddie said, and then, “Oh. Oh no.”

“Yeah. I kinda felt guilty for the prank I pulled on her at the beginning of shift, acting like I didn’t remember and then, psych! Here’s the cake,” Buck said. “Except it wasn’t a prank for anyone else. Even Chimney forgot it. Even Karen forgot it.”

“Oof.” Eddie winced.

“Yeah, Hen said it was me, you, and Athena that remembered.”

“Not even Bobby?”

“I… I mean, if Ma remembered it…”

But, the more Buck thought about it, the more uncertain he became. Hen hadn’t included Bobby in that list, and she never once mentioned whether or not he’d reached out to her at any point afterwards. Surely he would’ve remembered it, though. Buck forgetting was sucky, but he’d once made a store run for eggs only to come back without them. Half his life was structured around routine and noted down reminders.

Bobby didn’t have that problem, though. So surely…

He pulled out his phone and pulled up Bobby’s contacts. It rang a few times before the other man answered, his smiling face taking up the screen. Buck could see enough of him to know he was in uniform, and it looked like he was outside.

“Hey Buck, Eddie.”

“Hi, Pops,” Buck said. Eddie gave him a wave. “Are you guys filming? Kinda late.”

“Night shoot. We’re on a break now,” Bobby said. He looked off camera and smiled to someone with a, “Thanks, Hailey.”

“You’re welcome,” said the unseen Hailey.

“So.” Bobby paused to take a sip from the drink Hailey must’ve given him. “Not that I’m upset to hear from you, kid, but what’s up?”

“Uh, just… You wished Hen a happy birthday today, right?”

Bobby’s entire face froze. For a moment, Buck worried that the call messed up, except he saw someone walking by in the background. And then, slowly, Bobby’s eyes grew wide.

“Oh, God.”

Buck immediately turned his head to look at Eddie.

“You’re the best husband,” he said. “Please never leave me.”

“Everyone except me and Athena forgot,” Eddie explained to Bobby. “Buck managed to slide in under the wire, because I reminded him the night before.”

“I baked her a cake!”

“And Athena couldn’t remind me?” Bobby’s question was not directed at them, that much Buck could tell. “I’m going to order her some fancy chocolates.”

He ended the call abruptly.

“I felt so bad last night,” Buck told Eddie as he put his phone aside. “Now? Not so much. I mean, I still feel bad for Hen, but…”

“You’re gonna be lording this over them for as long as you can, aren’t you?”

“Hells yeah.”

“You’re welcome.”

Hen carried the offended air with her into their next shift, dragging it wherever she went and chilling the station with an arctic front. The only ones she showed any warmth towards was Buck and Bell, the others all got some degree of wintry reception depending on how close she was to them. Toby just got a cold shoulder, for example, but Chimney might as well have been crewing the HMS Terror.

Not very long into their shift, they were called out for a police chase. This one involved a metro bus being held hostage by someone with a knife, and it hadn’t actually ended yet when they were called out. Which meant they’d be trailing behind it so that they could respond the moment the bus came to a stop and they got the all clear.

The best ending of this was that the guy came to his senses, allowed the bus driver to stop the bus, and turned himself in without anyone being hurt. Not far behind it was the ending where the bus ran out of gas and, once again, the guy came to his senses and let himself be arrested without any violence. But Buck had seen the end of police chases before and he knew it was far more likely that the end to this would be very messy, so he had both ambulances come with them.

And he knew, the moment the information came through the tablet, that the messy end was what they were getting.

“Bus is stopped,” Buck announced to the others in the engine’s cab.

“By itself?” Bell asked, sounding hopeful.

“Spikes and a car barricade.”

“For a bus!?” Ravi sounded horrified, rightfully so. “Is anyone…?”

“Dunno yet,” Buck answered.

The bus had come to a stop in the middle of a three-way intersection, cordoned off by officers and members of SWAT. In its wake was a trail of destruction and the remnants of the police cruisers that it had smashed through with its momentum. But the bus was rightside up, when it could have very easily been overturned when the spikes blew out the tires, so they at least weren’t in the mass casualty event that he’d been preparing himself for.

Athena was waiting for them when they parked.

“Where do you want us?” Buck asked when he clambered out.

“Standing by,” Athena answered. She led him and the others to the edge of the perimeters, talking as they went. “Dispatch says that our hijacker has already stabbed one hostage with a carving knife.”

“What about over there?” Buck pointed at the wrecked cruisers. He was pretty sure one was on fire.

“Everyone got clear,” she said. “No injuries there.”

That was lucky. That also meant the burning car was a low priority. And the car could keep burning, because Buck was not putting his people in the middle of all this if he could help it.

“Spikes and a barricade for a bus, Ma?” He couldn’t keep the exasperation out of his voice, nor the judgment.

“It wasn’t my idea.”

“What has the guy been saying? Any demands to, I dunno. Lower the bus fare?”

“No demands,” Athena said as they came to a stop. “Reports are that he was raving about how he matters and he won’t be walked over and something about taking up space in the world.”

As one, everyone who’d been on the call from the other day turned their heads to fix Hen with a disbelieving stare. Hen met Buck’s eyes, her own so very wide, and then asked Athena,

“Did they get a description of him?”

“Why?” was Athena’s bewildered question.

“Because Hen might’ve talked the guy into this,” Buck answered, and got a nasty glare for it.

Athena made a call over her radio, and soon the woman overseeing the operation was approaching them with someone that Buck assumed was her second-in-command. She had an evidence baggie in her hand, and inside that baggie was the shattered remnants of a coffee mug. Enough of it was still whole to make out most of the picture emblazoned on it.

“This was left at the bus stop where the suspect first got on,” she explained as she held it out. “We think they belong to him.”

The picture was a photograph, and while half of it was gone, Archie was still perfectly recognizable.

“It’s him, Cap,” Hen said, and Buck nodded in agreement. “Commander? I need you to let me talk to him.”

“He’s armed and dangerous,” the commander protested.

“He might be armed, but he’s not dangerous,” Hen argued. “We’ve rescued him twice already. Trust me, he wants to be rescued again.”

The commander frowned, and then looked to Buck.

“Captain?”

Right. This was gonna be his decision, wasn’t it?

If it was a burning apartment building, Buck would not be so hesitant to send his people in. They each accepted the risks of charging into a fire the moment they entered the academy and again when they started their probational year. They were trained in how to respond to them, drilled in how to traverse those dangerous settings as safely as they could. They wore gear specifically designed to protect them if - when - the worst happened.

But this was not a burning apartment building. This was a hostage situation, involving a lot of guns and anxious  trigger fingers. And Buck was not okay with risking any of them in this.

“I don’t like this, Hen,” Buck told her. “I don’t want any of you in there until we get the all-clear, too many things can go wrong.”

“There’s someone bleeding out in there, Cap. Things have already gone wrong,” Hen pointed out. “But maybe I can keep things from getting worse.”

Damn it.

“Okay,” he sighed and then, louder, “Yeah, okay.”

They took Hen to get outfitted with a SWAT vest, with Chimney going with her. That left Buck at loose ends, uncomfortable with what was occurring but unable to do anything about it. He stood next to Athena and the others as they watched Hen begin her approach towards the bus, Chimney rejoining them.

“Archie!” Hen called out. “It’s Henrietta Wilson. Hen. I hear you have somebody in there that needs medical treatment.”

She pressed close to the bus doors, and Buck could see her mouth moving. He wasn’t close enough to hear what was being said, but the doors opened shortly after. And then he watched, heart in his throat, as she got onto the bus and those doors closed behind her.

“Did you know,” Buck said, eyes focused on the bus. Most of the windows were cracked, but he could make out the people inside, including Hen and Archie with the knife. “That you can stab through Kevlar?”

“I did, actually,” Athena said. “Her vest has ceramic plates in it.”

That made him feel marginally better. Marginally.

Buck was stuck watching. He watched as Hen talked to Archie. He watched as she edged past him, far too close to his knife, and then knelt down to, he guessed, check on the stabbing victim. He watched as Archie talked to her.

“Alright, Cap.” Hen’s voice crackled across Buck’s radio. “I’m sending out our patient for a massive transfusion protocol. Meet us at the door with a gurney.”

A look at Chimney and the paramedic nodded, dashing off for the ambulance. Albert and Ravi jogged after him.

When they got the gurney to the bus’ doors, Hen met them with the patient. Ravi and Albert got him onto the gurney and then Hen stepped back, the doors closing once more with her on the wrong side. The paramedics rushed to the ambulance, but Buck’s eyes were still stuck on the interior of the bus.

Hen was arguing with Archie, who was looking increasingly agitated. Too agitated, in Buck’s opinion, and he was swinging the knife around carelessly as he paced. Archie started shouting, suddenly and loudly enough that everyone, including Hen, recoiled in fear.

“The guy’s loaded up,” Chimney announced as he rejoined them in the front row. “Al’s working on him, and Ravi’s driving.”

Buck was not surprised that Chimney elected to stay behind, with Hen still in the danger zone. With a wound like that, they’d just be keeping pressure to slow the bleeding. Albert was more than capable of that, and more than capable of handling anything that came up before they reached the ER.

And honestly? If things went pearshaped, Buck was very relieved that Chimney would be here for it.

“Something’s happening,” Athena suddenly said.

The doors on the bus were opening again and, as they watched, the passengers and the driver quickly filed out with their arms in the air. SWAT rushed forward to meet them and check them over for weapons. Athena nodded to Buck and stepped forward to do her job.

Hen was still on the bus, though. She was talking to Archie, who moved on from agitation to what appeared to be despair. Buck couldn’t decide if that was better or worse, being familiar with both states. 

Then Hen held out her hand, and Archie took it. They were still holding hands as they stepped off the bus together, as they stopped. As Archie reached into his pocket.

The reaction of the approaching cops was immediate, with the commander giving out the order. Buck could do nothing but watch, and listen, as they opened fire, as Hen tackled Archie to the ground, as the pair of them laid there and didn’t get up right away. He ran forward, stuck only on the fact that he’d let her go in there, that it was because of him that she was in the line of fire.

It was only seeing Hen sitting up that kept him from panicking entirely.

“What were you doing?” she was asking Archie.

“I was giving you your birthday present,” he said, holding out his hand.

“A keychain?” was Athena’s incredulous response as she, and the other officers, holstered their weapons.

“A keychain?” Buck repeated, the panic morphing into anger. “You almost shot her over a fucking-”

“Buck.” Athena’s sharp tone cut him off. She didn’t even bother turning her head to look at him, nor did she waste her breath scolding him for not staying back. “Archie Mullin, you are under arrest.”

Buck didn’t spare any of his attention on Archie or the officers carting him off. His attention, instead, was zeroed in on Hen, who was looking at the keychain dangling from her hand with something like disturbed bewilderment. It was a keychain from that Cluck & Pluck fastfood joint, with its overly cheerful cartoon chicken.

It didn’t take a genius to figure out why Archie had chosen that particular item to give her.

“Are you okay?” he asked her.

“Yeah.” Hen looked up from the keychain and gave him a grimace that might’ve been meant as a smile. “I’m fine.”

Buck’s eyes slid to the scars on the bus, left by the bullets as they ricochetted off. Hen looked at them too, and then back to him.

“I’m fine, Buck,” she repeated.

“I owe Pops so many apologies,” he muttered as they went back to the others, to where Chimney was no doubt anxiously waiting to look her over himself.

Hen threw back her head and laughed.

Chapter 39: Safety Net

Chapter Summary

In which there is yet another emergency involving a bus, Athena has decided it's time to start emptying the nest, and Ravi takes a mistake to heart.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

“How are they not berries!?” Chimney’s complaint came in over the headsets as they raced to the newest emergency. “It’s in the name! Straw- berry. Rasp- berry. Black- berry. But a banana counts as a berry!?”

“Are you still going on about that?” Buck asked, turning slightly to look back at him.

“Yes!”

“Who decided they weren’t berries anymore?” Bell asked. She was sitting just behind Toby in the driver’s seat, so Buck could see her in profile.

“Botanists,” Chimney answered with a scoff.

“Okay, so what is a berry?” Ravi asked, sitting right next to Chimney.

The seat directly behind Buck, the seat Eddie had basically claimed for his own when Buck gained the captaincy, was empty.

Buck frowned in thought as he tried to remember the botanical definition. He’d learned it once, when he was arguing with TK over whether or not a tomato was a fruit or a vegetable. (It was both, as it turned out.) But that was a while ago, and it wasn’t like it was information necessary to his everyday existence.

“It’s a, uh. It’s a fleshy fruit-” You’re a fruit, Eddie would have immediately said if he were there. “-that grows from one flower with one ovary, but doesn’t have a pit. So pumpkins, watermelons, and cucumbers are also berries.”

“They are not!” Chimney denied. “Raspberries are berries and Pluto’s a planet, damn it.”

“It’s all kosher,” Toby said with a shrug. “Unless there are bugs on it.”

“Gross,” Bell said, making a face at the idea.

“And that is why I wash all the veggies I cook with,” Buck stated. He glanced out the windshield and straightened up in his seat. “Put your game faces on, we’re here.”

A couple weeks ago, when that guy with the awful life hijacked a bus and the cops pulled that boneheaded move to bring it to a stop, Buck had been trying to prepare himself for a mass casualty event as they arrived on the scene. Thankfully, the only injury of concern ended up being a stab wound to the abdomen. No one even ended up being shot, despite both Archie’s and the cops’ best efforts.

But now, it seemed, they were about to face what Buck was so worried about that night. According to what dispatch could figure out, a car hit the brakes and came to a stop. The metro bus behind it, however, did not. Things collided, then more things collided into those things and, well, they had that messy end.

They piled out, everyone already throwing themselves into motion. The bus that had caused this mess was slightly angled, with cars smashed into its tail end (which was on fire) and another car sticking out of its side. Buck couldn’t see the cars in front of the bus, but he didn’t imagine it would look any prettier. It seemed a lot of the drivers and passengers involved in the accident were out, gathered off to the side, but he very doubted it was all of them.

“That fire is right at the fuel tank!” And that fuel tank was filled with natural gas, like most of Los Angeles’ metro buses. Buck really wished it was one of the G-Line buses, instead. Those were all electric, which meant they wouldn’t have been as likely to turn into a bomb. “Get a couple inch-and-a-halves on that fire, gimme a water curtain. And somebody turn off that fuel supply.”

There was a flurry of voices as they recognized the orders and moved to follow them. As Buck came around, he could see the other half of the crash, now. A pair of cars were crushed between the bus and a moving truck. One of the cars was pushed so hard by the bus that it had gone up the back of the one in front of it and was now almost sticking straight up. 

“The brakes went out, I couldn’t stop.” That was the driver of the bus, judging from his uniform. He was bleeding heavily from a wound to the head, and Hen was looking very concerned about it. “I tried to get everyone out, but there’s still some passengers towards the back.”

That wasn’t a surprise, Buck knew that there was no way everyone was able to get to safety, but he still wanted to curse.

“Chim!” he called out instead. “Go on the bus, make sure everyone’s off. Ravi, get these other cars checked and cleared.”

Ravi nodded and ran off to the nearest car, grabbing Bell and a couple of the others to help him. Chimney, once geared up, made his way to the front of the bus and peered through the window.

“Cap, I got eyes on the stragglers,” he radioed. “Looks like one’s pinned to the seat. I’m going in.”

Buck didn’t bother replying as Chimney climbed inside. Instead, he turned towards where Toby and the others were hooking up the hoses. They dragged them to position and turned them on, pressurized water spraying out in cones to drown the flames. Albert, wearing SCBA gear to keep from scorching his lungs, dove forward to shut off the valve.

“Fuel’s off!” he radioed.

“Go help your brother on the bus,” Buck ordered. The younger Han nodded and jogged to the bus doors. “Ravi, gimme an update.”

“I’ve got a driver, Cap,” Ravi replied.

Buck looked and spotted him on the other side of that car nearly sticking straight up. His attention bounced between Ravi at the car, to the hoses knocking down the flames, to the people still on the bus. One of the passengers was stepping off, aided by Albert, and the fire was almost extinguished.

But, of course, things did not keep going their way. There was suddenly the orange light of flames inside the bus, with smoke pouring out.

“Cap, the car’s on fire,” Albert announced, not that Buck really needed that announcement.

“Get everyone off that bus, before combustibles start combusting,” Buck ordered over the radio. 

“Driver unconscious, pulse stable.” Ravi’s words came out in a rush, all in one breath. Buck could see that he had the driver’s side door of that car open, a ladder brought around to reach it.

Buck eyed the fire on the bus, getting increasingly anxious the longer it burned. Toby had a hose directed on it, but Buck didn’t think it was doing much good. It didn’t look like the water was actually reaching the flames well to do a good job of putting them out.

Albert suddenly jumped out of the bus, turning to help Chimney out with who Buck hoped was the last passenger. The passenger had a gash to his leg that was making him limp and was being helped along by Chimney. Buck rushed forward to meet them, and to hurry them.

“Bus is clear, Cap,” Chimney reported, which was very good.

“Get goin’ and keep goin’,” Buck instructed, moving along with them. “Ravi, how ya doin’?”

“Still extracting, Cap.”

That was very much not good enough. It was a fact emphasized a few moments later when something towards the back of the bus ignited enough to have flames bursting out of the windows. Time was not their friend here.

“Faster, Ravi,” Buck barked into the radio, and then turned to everyone else to shout, “Move back! Get away from the bus!”

Hoses were shut off and dropped as Buck’s people listened to him. The civilians that had been watching were herded by the police that were playing crowd control. From around the other end of the bus, Ravi and firefighters that had been clearing the cars came pushing a gurney with a woman laying on it. Buck met them and took a hold of the gurney, to help them get away that little bit faster.

“I think she has a fractured femur, and she has lacerations,” Ravi relayed to Buck. And to Albert, when he jogged over. “ABCs are good, but she’s not responsive. Could have been the airbag.”

Albert had a stick of smelling salts, and he waved it under the woman’s nose. She woke up quickly.

“You’ve been in an accident, ma’am,” the younger Han told her.

“My daughter?” the woman asked, struggling to sit up, and Buck’s heart dropped.

So did everyone else’s, he could see.

“Stay still, ma’am,” Albert instructed, but there was no way she was going to listen to him.

“My daughter was with me, she’s three months old,” she said. “She was in the back seat.”

Buck was already moving before she was finished talking, almost sprinting for the car. He heard Ravi say there was no one else in the car. He heard Chimney and Hen shout for him. But what he was focusing on was that the bus was about to explode, and there was a baby in the danger zone.

The smoke made visibility awful, and it irritated his lungs, but again, that didn’t matter. When he reached the car, it was obvious why Ravi had missed that there was a child in danger. Everything that was in the car was piled up in the backseat, bags and trash and just general junk. It was piled high enough that he couldn’t see through to the other side.

A little hammer, a keepsake from Bobby and kept in his turnout coat for this very reason, shattered the window. He reached in carelessly, popping the lock and yanking open the door before haphazardly throwing everything out of his way. When he uncovered the infant, strapped in her car seat, she immediately started crying.

“Hey there, sweetie pie,” he cooed, reaching in to start extracting her. “Let’s get you to your momma, okay?”

It was a change in the noises coming from the bus that alerted Buck that his time was up. The hissing that he had only barely paid attention to was getting louder, fiercer. There was the groaning of metal in great distress.

He dove forward, covering the baby with his body as the timer finally went off. He felt the heat as it enveloped him, he saw the orange gouts of flame engulf everything. But the turnouts he wore were developed with eventualities like this in mind, they were the product of more than a hundred years of firefighters trying to figure out how to run through fire and not get burned.

The fire went over him, around him, but it didn’t touch him. And the fire didn’t stay long, it quickly devoured the gas in its hunger and receded with its stomach full. Mostly. Some of the junk in the backseat had caught, which meant he opted to simply cut the straps anchoring the car seat rather than waste time figuring out the buckle.

Buck carried the car seat to where everyone else was waiting, and held it while Hen undid the buckle and took the infant out to be laid in the arms of her very relieved mother. And on the other side of the pair, he saw Ravi standing there.

A very distraught looking Ravi.

“Okay, okay, hold on,” Buck demanded, between laughs. “The bakery gave you the wrong cake?”

“They gave us the cake for the Shapiros,” Maddie said. “Whoever they are.”

“Soon to be very confused parents,” Eddie said. “Hopefully not disappointed ones.”

His sister had come over that afternoon with Jee-Yun, and now the two of them were sitting at the dining table with Eddie and Chris, the latter doing his homework. Jee-Yun was playing with Gavin, with Hoover dutifully playing the role of chaperone. Abuela was out with Carla visiting church friends, in an endeavor at keeping the Diaz matriarch socially active.

(That morning had not been a good one. Abuela had misplaced the remote to the television in her bedroom, and Buck helped her look for it. Which would have been okay, but she was… Crabby would be a good word for, maybe. She snapped at him a lot, which was very unusual for her, and even raised her voice at one point.

They’d found the remote in one of the kitchen cabinets, and Abuela apologized for being short with him. Buck was just grateful that neither Eddie nor Chris were home for it.)

Apparently, the other day, Maddie and Chimney did a gender reveal with a cake. Even though they already knew they were heaving a boy. Maddie said it was because Jee didn’t know and she was promised a cake reveal so they could all find out together. It was all very cute.

Until they cut the cake and it was pink inside, instead of the intended blue.

“Pink used to be the masculine color, y’know,” Buck said, leaning back in his chair.

“We know,” Eddie said at the same time as Maddie, the pair of them grinning at each other over the table. “Hey, maybe the cake’s right after all. Maybe the kid’ll realize they are a girl.”

“Assigned female at cake,” Buck joked. It was a bad joke, but it got Chris and Eddie to laugh, so he counted it as a win. “But hey, it’s not the worst gender reveal disaster. At least you didn’t start any wildfires.”

“I’d almost prefer the wildfire,” Maddie said, and Buck shot her a light scowl for it. It was a bit too soon for that kind of joke, in his opinion. He really didn’t want to be stuck without Eddie for a month again. “I had to sit down and explain to Jee that, actually, the cake was a lie and she’s getting a baby brother, not a sister. She didn’t quite get it, I don’t think, after we spent so long telling her that the cake would tell us if they were a boy or a girl.”

“We had Chris just as gender reveals were becoming a thing.” Eddie bent down and picked up Senorita off the floor beside his chair, cradling her in his arms as he absently stroked her fur. “But we never had one. Hell, we didn’t even know he was a boy until he was born.”

“You didn’t?” Chris asked, lifting his head up from the packet he was filling in.

“Your mom wanted it to be a surprise.”

Chris tilted his head, expression turning that mix of thoughtful and wistful as it always did whenever they talked about his mother these days. He opened his mouth, maybe to ask more, but they never found out. Because, before he could get the words out, the front door opened up and a pair of very annoyed seeming Grant children came trooping in.

“Please, just let yourselves in,” Buck deadpanned. “Totally not a mistake you’ve made before, May.”

“We saw Maddie’s car out front,” May said, coming over to the dining table and dropping into a chair with a huff. “Kinda figured you weren’t doing any gross roleplaying in the living room with her here.”

“We have two kids and my grandmother living with us,” Eddie said. “We don’t get to do anything fun in the living room.”

“Well, sometimes…” Buck trailed off with a grin.

“Gross,” was said by four different people at varying levels of volume.

“What’s got you both looking so…” Maddie waved a hand at them. “Like that.”

“Our mom,” Harry said. He hadn’t taken a seat and it was making his growth spurt very obvious.

“What? Did she take the cops’ side in something again?” Buck asked.

“No, she kicked us out of her dream home,” May said.

Buck and Eddie looked at each other, and then to Harry in the hopes that he could clarify.

“May won’t have a room in the new house, and my room is actually the guest room.” Harry scoffed. “I’m taking bets on if she’ll give me suitcases on my eighteenth or when I graduate.”

“In this economy?” Eddie asked. His nose was all scrunched up in offense. “What if something happens and May gets evicted?”

“I asked her that!” May exclaimed. “Apparently, we’re supposed to be her safety net now. She owns a home in the year twenty twenty-five, and she’ll get a police pension plus Bobby’s, but she needs me to be her safety net.”

“But Grandma gets stuck in a hotel,” Harry said. “Not even the Beverly Hills. If Grandma needs a safety net, Mom’s sticking her in a Blue Ribbon Inn with three and a half stars.”

“And a free continental breakfast.” May rolled her eyes. “Rebuilding gave them the chance to figure out what works for them, she said. Apparently what works for them is finally being rid of us. Neither of us asked to be born, Mom.”

“She’s sounding like me,” Buck commented to his sister. “Hey, Chris? I promise we won’t kick you out when you graduate.”

“Thanks, Pops.”

The night was not going the way that Albert had hoped it would.

Ever since the call with the bus, he’d noticed that his boyfriend’s mood was turning rather morose. Albert had done everything he could to pull him out of it, but it seemed Ravi was simply stuck on what happened. The latest attempt, the one he was certain would work, was to walk out of the shower in just a towel and then drop it when he stood in front of Ravi on the couch. It was the advice that Buck had given him, which was how desperate he’d gotten.

It hadn’t worked. It was more than a little insulting that it hadn’t worked.

“I think I need to go,” Ravi suddenly said, and Albert’s heart turned to ice.

“W- What? Go?”

“No, I mean...” His boyfriend wasn’t really looking at him. “I mean quit. The One Eighteen.”

“Jagi,” Albert sighed. He knelt down and picked the towel back up to wrap it around his waist again. This didn’t feel like a conversation to be had with his bits in the wind. “Is this about what happened with the bus?”

“I just keep seeing the baby,” Ravi said. “I just keep thinking that she could’ve died.”

“But she didn’t,” Albert reminded him.

“Because Buck went in there and pulled her out.”

“So what’s the problem?” he asked. “The baby’s fine.”

“The problem is that I  could’ve gotten Buck killed,” Ravi said. “The problem is that it was my job to clear the car and I missed a baby. The problem is that I- I… The problem is that I shouldn’t be out there.”

“You weren’t the only one at that car,” Albert tried pointing out. “Tanika, Javier, they were both there, too, and neither of them saw the baby, either.”

But Ravi just shook his head.

“I was the one who cleared the car,” he said again. “I’m- I’m gonna tell Cap that I need to quit.”

“Ravi,” Albert sighed, reaching out to cup his boyfriend’s cheek.

But he couldn’t think of any arguments to get through to him.

Chapter End Notes

How many readers will see "Jagi" and assume I typo'd Ravi's name, I wonder.

Chapter 40: Cough, Cough

Chapter Summary

In which the 118 responds to a fire at a research lab.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Thursday morning started normally enough. Buck woke up beside Eddie, the pair of them went through their morning routines of getting the kids up, doing their morning work-outs, and having breakfast. And perhaps it was Buck’s fault for not questioning things right away when he got out of the shower and found Eddie putting on his uniform.

He definitely did question it, however, when his husband slipped into the front passenger seat of the jeep instead of getting into his Prius.

“What are you doing?” Buck asked him, freezing in the middle of buckling himself up.

“Going to work,” Eddie said simply, smiling oh-so-prettily at him.

“Eds.” Buck gave him a flat stare. His husband’s smile intensified. “You don’t go to work today, you go to school.”

“But it’s so boring!” Eddie exclaimed, throwing his hands up and tossing his head back. “It’s labs today. I’ve spent a decade and a half doing more complicated things in a single day than we’ve done all semester.”

He turned in his seat and clutched at the sleeve of Buck’s shirt.

“I am bored, mi sol,” he said. “If you loved me, you’d let me come to work again. Just for the day, just one shift. I’ve already told the instructor I’m not coming in today.”

“Oh my God, you’re such a drama queen.” Buck loved him so much. He leaned across the center console to kiss him, just for being cute. “What did you tell them? That you were five seconds from exploding?”

“I told him I was sick.” Eddie let go and sat back. “Cough, cough.”

“Cough, cough.” Buck rolled his eyes. “Let’s hope we don’t do anything to earn a spot in the news, ‘cause that’d be awkward.”

Not that Buck was really complaining about Eddie deciding to play hooky at the station. He’d missed going into work with him, after all, and the morning drive to the station was a lot more fun with Eddie in the passenger seat.

Mayfair had the most subdued reaction to seeing Eddie, she simply rolled her eyes and started with the handover. Hen and Chimney, though, immediately started asking questions when they clocked him. And then they laughed when Buck told him that he was skipping school because he was bored, the pair of them immediately badgering Eddie and teasing him mercilessly for it.

Buck left them to it, until it was time for the morning briefing. Which wasn’t much, really. The expected weather, where there was road construction, that sort of thing. But when he was done, not everyone dispersed.

“Hey, Cap?” Ravi wasn’t looking much better than he did at the end of their last shift.

Albert was beside him, looking miserable. It was a detail that had Buck even more worried. 

“Yeah, Rav?”

“Can I talk to you?” the younger man said, and looked around. “In your office?”

“Uh.” Buck caught Albert’s eye, and saw how anxious he seemed about whatever this was. “Okay, sure.”

Buck led Ravi to his office, after Albert’s offer and going with them, too, was rebuffed. Once there, Buck closed the door and went to the desk, but he didn’t sit down. Neither did Ravi.

“So, what’s up?” he prompted.

“I need to quit,” Ravi blurted out.

Buck’s brain threw up error messages as it tried to parse the very short statement. Quit? Why did Ravi need to quit?

“What?” he managed to get out.

“I need to quit,” Ravi repeated, drawing in a deep breath. “I shouldn’t be out there anymore. As a firefighter.”

Buck stared at him.

“Is this… Is this about the baby?” he asked. Ravi didn’t answer, averting his eyes instead, and Buck decided, fuck this. “Sit down.”

Ravi didn’t move.

“Sit. Down.” Buck barked out

It was more falling than sitting, but Ravi’s ass ended up in the chair all the same.

“Explain to me, right now,” Buck ordered, “why you want to quit.”

“I was the one who cleared that car,” Ravi said. “I missed an entire baby. I almost killed her. I almost killed you. I can’t- I shouldn’t be out there. So I’m quitting.”

“No.” It was a simple statement, and Ravi had no business looking so confused by it. “You are a great firefighter.”

“I messed up-”

“We’ve all messed up,” Buck said. “There are people in this station who’ve messed up worse than you, with actual consequences. And- And you didn’t mess up, not really.”

“Really?” Ravi scoffed. “I missed an entire infant.”

“Rav, I saw that backseat. It was filled with junk, and there was no sign of the baby until I’d already dug her out and she started crying. You had no way of knowing she was buried there until the mom woke up and said something, so why in the hell would you ever think to dig through all of that just to check? When you had a critical patient right next to a ticking time bomb?”

“I almost got you killed.”

Buck couldn’t help it, he just had to roll his eyes.

“No,” he said, drawing the word out. If a bit of condescension trickled into his tone, well... Whatever. Tough cookies, Panikkar. “I nearly got myself killed. I’d already decided it was too dangerous to go near that bus, and I went anyway. That was my decision.”

“Because-”

“Because you had no reason to even think there was someone else in that car,” Buck interrupted, finishing Ravi’s sentence with what was factually correct. “I’d tell you that you made a mistake, and that you’ll learn from this and do better next time, be a better firefighter for it. But you didn’t make a mistake. Sometimes we miss things, and it’s no one’s fault. You’ve gotta push the doubt away. ‘Cause it’s like a virus and the second you let it in, it’ll eat you alive.”

Ravi didn’t answer. His head was down, and his eyes were focused on the front edge of the desk.

“Resignation not accepted, Ravi,” Buck told him. “Now get out and get started on your chores.”

The younger firefighter mumbled out a “yes, Cap” as he got up and followed the order. Buck sighed, shook his head and rolled his eyes at Ravi’s retreating back, and went to go bother his husband.

“When I said I was bored of the paramedic labs, I didn’t mean I wanted this,” Eddie said over the sound of sirens and tearing duct tape.

It had been nice to have Eddie on calls with them again. They hadn’t gone on any serious ones, not until the one they were responding to now, but Buck had still been delighted at having his husband on the truck with them. He hadn’t missed him as much as he had during the wildfires, he did get to go home to him, after all, but he’d felt his husband’s absence at the station keenly.

“One day you’ll learn not to test the EMT gods, Firefighter Diaz,” Buck teased. He couldn’t see Eddie’s face, since Eddie was in the jump seat right behind him, back to back, but he could imagine the almost petulant glower. “Dispatch, what exactly is this place we’re going to?”

“SoCal Tech Biomedical Research Laboratory,” Maddie replied. “It’s an independent facility. Fifty-five on staff, janitors to microbiologists.”

“You just said a lot of words I didn’t like,” Buck said. “Sounds like we’re gonna need hazmat.”

“They’ve got that covered, their containment team is setting up now.”

“What awful things should we be expecting? Something out of Resident Evil?”

“They’re pretty tight-lipped.” Despite the seriousness, Maddie sounded amused. “Their virology units run Tier Four precautions.”

“And that’s out of how many tiers?” Ravi asked from the back.

“Four,” Hen answered. Buck wondered if she knew that from Karen, or from her time in med school.

There was a tap at Buck’s shoulder and he grabbed the roll of duct tape that Eddie was offering him, after making sure the others - with Toby as the sole exception, since he was busy driving - were all sealed up. Then he ran the tape along the ends of his coat sleeves and over his gloves, so that his sleeves were sealed up tight.

“The lab is designated for lethal and exotic viruses.”

“Eds-” Buck started, only to be immediately interrupted by Eddie with,

“Do. Not. Say it.”

“You lied about being sick-”

“I said don’t!”

“What qualifies as a lethal and exotic virus?” Chimney asked.

“Don’t answer that.” There was a faint tremor to Bell’s words. It had Buck frowning. “Please do not answer that.”

Unfortunately, however much Bell may have wished that they remained ignorant, they couldn’t. Knowing might be worse than not knowing, but Buck would much rather be fully aware of the dangers he was about to lead his people into instead of sending them in blind.

They pulled up in front of the lab to find the sidewalks and green areas were filled with lab personnel milling about. A command tent was set up in the road, and there were people in bright blue containment suits walking in and out of it. The director of the lab, Dr. Francis Banting, met them as they climbed out, and he hovered anxiously as Buck instructed Albert to go set up a place to treat any injuries.

And he informed them what viruses qualified as lethal and exotic.

“SARS,” Banting said as he listed off the viruses they had stored in the facility. “Dengue, Marburg, West Nile.”

“So all the worst ways to die,” Hen helpfully summarized.

“I don’t see any smoke,” Buck noted as he handed Toby the duct tape.

“It’s below our feet,” Banting explained. “The fire broke out on Sublevel Three.”

“And what’s on Sublevel Three?”

“Just one thing. CCHF, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever.”

“That’s not scary sounding,” Bell said. That tremor in her voice was more present, now. “Not- Not terrifying at all.”

“It’s Ebola’s nastier cousin.” Hen seemed to have taken up the position as the person really making the terribleness of the situation clear. “Super contagious and fatal, usually from uncontrollable bleeding.”

“I wouldn’t call it Ebola’s nastier cousin,” Eddie said. He was looking at Bell as he spoke. “The average fatality rate for Ebola, world wide, is about half of infected patients. For CCHF, it’s only a little bit under a third.”

“Only a little bit under a third,” Toby repeated. “Only one in three people who get it die.”

He was done with the duct tape, the ends of his turnout coat’s sleeves all taped down, and he handed the roll back to Buck. Buck stuck it into his coat pocket, making a mental note to put it back where it belonged on the truck later.

“Maybe two in five,” Eddie hedged. “It’s endemic to places that don’t exactly have Los Angeles hospitals, man, what do you want from me?”

Buck smiled at his husband and shook his head, before getting them all back on track.

“How many people work on sublevel three?” he asked the doctor.

“Eight,” Banting answered. “But only two are badged in: Allen and Roz.”

“And they haven’t gotten out?”

“No.” Banting shook his head.

“Okay!” Buck raised his voice a little. “We go in, we get out. Fast. CO2 cans for the fires, the hose run off might spread things.”

He waited for everyone to nod.

“Everyone gear up. Full SCBA, then we head down,” he said. “Toby, Bell-”

“Hold on!” Banting interrupted, lunging forward a bit as if to stop them from going. “You can’t just head down. There are protocols, air locks. Your equipment might not be sufficient.”

“Sir, you called us to rescue your people and put out the fire.” Buck snagged the ID badge off Banting’s blazer, since the guy mentioned being badged in, and then turned back to the others. “Toby, Bell, grab the backboard. We’ll get the CO2.”

The main entrance of the lab was at the end of a cement walkway that ran across the road, and the hazmat team was sticking their plastic curtains over it. The other end, where the stairs were, was where they were setting up the decontamination tent. Buck got the feeling they were entering a maze, but they luckily had a voice with an internet connection.

“Okay, Buck.” Maddie had obtained a copy of the lab schematics. “Let me know when you’re in the atrium.”

“We’re there.”

“You see the elevator?”

“I see it.”

It was at the end of a long, brightly lit hall. Plaques and pictures lined the walls. Buck led the way to it as Maddie continued to speak.

“You’ll need credentials to access SL Three.”

“Done and done.”

Buck took out Banting’s ID badge and slapped it against the screen beside the elevator. The doctor’s information flashed onto the screen, with the edges turning green. It switched to a notice that read BIO - SAFETY LEVEL 4 as the elevator doors opened. They climbed in, anxious energy thrumming through the air inside the metal box.

When the doors opened again, they were at another long hall. This one was far more utilitarian, with reinforced walls, and darker than the one above. The floor might’ve been marble, and it reflected both the lights from their helmets and the lights ensconced upon the walls.

“At the end of the hall, you’ll see the first of three interlocking doors.”

“Kinda hard to miss it,” Buck snarked, because it was the only way he could keep his nerves from showing through in front of people counting on him. His hand twitched with the urge to reach out and take Eddie’s, who was a comforting presence at his back.

Every step Buck took felt like he was leading them all into the setting of a survivor horror film.

“That’s the cold zone. Locker room, shower. From there, door two takes you through a peroxide decon.”

He hoped it wasn’t as unpleasant as it sounded.

“What’s past that?” he asked.

“The hot zone.”

Did they have to give them such ominous names?

An electronic screen, identical to the one by the elevator upstairs, was beside the first door. Buck slapped Banting’s ID onto it, the man’s info once again popping up framed in green. He opened the now unlocked door, hearing the screech of fire alarms and spotting a man laying facedown on the ground in the middle of the room.

“There,” he said, stepping out of the way. Hen and Chimney immediately rushed for him, dropping by his sides with their med kits.

“Sir?” Hen tried rousing him. “Sir, can you hear me?”

“I got chest rising,” Chimney announced from the man’s other side. “And his lips are pink.”

“Got an open laceration on his head. The pink could be from a TBI.”

While they addressed the patient, Buck took a look at their surroundings. Door number two, the one to the peroxide decon, was standing wide open. Through a large glass window, he could easily see the lab and the flames burning through the hot zone. But he didn’t spot anyone inside, so he deemed it a lower priority for the moment.

“Okay,” Buck said, turning back to the unconscious man that he was guessing was Allen. “Let’s get him on the backboard.”

Toby brought it over and, through a group effort, they rolled the man onto it without moving his spine. This way, the blood flowing from his wound and which had been pooling on the floor was much more obvious. Being moved was enough to rouse the man, his eyes blinking up to stare at them.

“Sir?” Buck leaned down a bit. “Can you hear me? Are you Allen?”

“Yeah,” Allen said. “B- But Moira…”

Buck would’ve loved to ask him who the hell Moira was, but Allen’s eyes fluttered closed again and he went limp as he returned to unconsciousness. It didn’t look like he’d lost enough blood for that, so Buck was betting it was a definite TBI.

“Guy outside said Roz,” Chimney reminded them.

“We could’ve missed her and never knew it.”

Buck pointedly did not look Ravi’s way when he said it. He did, however, spot Bell off to the edge of the group. Their face masks made it difficult to make out expressions, but her anxiety was clear just from the way she kept looking around, as if checking for danger. It made his next decision easy.

“Bell,” he said, catching her attention. “You and Toby are taking him outside. Get him through decon, and then to Albert.”

“Yeah.” Bell hurriedly nodded. She sounded very relieved. “Copy that, Cap. Decon, then Al. Got it.”

“Okay. And when that door closes behind them, I’m opening the next.”

They gathered in front of door number three, and watched Toby and Bell depart. The door clicked shut, and Buck slapped the badge on the appropriate scanner to unlock. The others rushed in with their CO2. But he was still focused on the now closed first door.

“I should have left her outside,” he thought aloud, not to anyone in particular.

Eddie gave his shoulder a comforting pat all the same, before he followed the rest.

“Alright, dispatch,” Buck said into his radio as he took stock of his people knocking down the flames. “We’re in the main lab. What am I looking at?”

“To your left-” Buck assumed that his sister meant to his left if he was standing at the door. Which he was. “-is the specimens room and a storage area.”

That way was sealed with large glass doors. There were flames on the other side, doing its own decontamination. There were also glass cages, some of them empty, some of them with rats inside. The specimens.

“And to the right?” he asked, turning to the heavier looking door.

“The cryo room, where they keep the viruses on ice.”

Yeah, they weren’t going in there if they could help it.

“Start with the specimens,” Buck ordered, pointing to the left door. “Save the rats, then go around.”

“Copy that, Cap,” Hen said, already moving. “Come on, Ravi.”

“Eddie, stick with me.”

“Copy that,” his husband said, as if he hadn’t already been doing that.

The fire was put out rather easily, and quickly. The lab darkened as the orange light of the flames went away, replaced by lingering smoke and the spray from their extinguishers. Buck kept an eye as they went for the two missing victims, but was seeing no sign of them.

Not until Ravi got a jump scare at one of the windows for the cryo room. A woman in a balloon-like hazmat suit appeared out of the fog inside. She started banging on the glass and calling out to them.

Buck and Eddie rushed to the side with the door, but the screenlock for it was dead. It didn’t even react when Buck slapped Banting’s ID onto it.

“It’s melted.” The woman’s voice was muffled by her suit and the door, but still audible.

“Can we use the halligans?” Buck asked Eddie, who shook his head.

“No,” he said, running a gloved hand along the edges of the door. They could hear Ravi trying (and failing) to break the window on his side. “This is where the CCHF is, this is probably the most securely sealed room on the floor.”

That was very much not optimal.

“Are you Moira?” Buck heard Ravi ask from the other side, and he rounded the corner in time to hear her reply,

“God, no. I’m Roz.”

“Dispatch, we’ve found Roz,” Buck reported into his radio. “But she’s in the cryo room, and the door’s not opening, the windows won’t break. We need a way in.”

“There aren’t any other doors or windows on here.”

“Anything, Maddie. Give us something, even if it’s dumb.”

“Okay, uh… Look up.”

Buck and Eddie both did, and their helmet lights shining on the vent above. Buck hadn’t even thought of that.

“Will the vent get us into the cryo lab?”

“Not directly,” his sister told him. “The level you’re on is a sealed concrete box. All the air’s funneled to giant HEPA filters, except for the air in the cryo room.”

“It’s a box within a box,” Eddie said. The most securely sealed room on the floor.

“Right. But the vent above you runs alongside the vents for the cryo room.”

Which meant they could cut a hole between the two, and get into the room that way.

“What do you think?” Buck asked Eddie, but it was Chimney who answered with,

“I am always ready to get my Die Hard on.”

“Then up you both go.”

Eddie was not made to be a Bruce Willis stand-in, and he was not meant to be crawling through vents. Yet here he was, living an action movie cliche, with Chimney right behind him. Maybe he should’ve gone to the paramedic lab, after all.

“Hey!” Buck called up after them through the hole (formally a vent) they’d used to pull themselves into the ducts. “At least you won’t catch encephalitis this time!”

“Your husband thinks he’s funny,” Chimney complained.

“He is,” Eddie shot back with a grin, though the paramedic couldn’t see it. “This is our stop, I think.”

The electric saw he brought did a good enough job cutting through, filling the air with sparks as it did. He made a square in the metal and knocked it over, before crawling through the brand new hole. It left him in an intersection of ducts, but there was a vent nearby.

This section of ducts was just for the cryo room, so there couldn’t be very many options for what they were above.

Eddie knocked the vent out of its frame, sending it clattering to the floor, and then stuck his head out. The cryo room, alright. And there was Roz in her balloon suit.

“Hello, Roz,” Eddie greeted her when he’d jumped down. “I’m Eddie, and I’m gonna lift you up.”

“Oh, I- I can’t.”

Not the response he was expecting from someone begging to be rescued not five minutes ago.

“Why?”

“I need this to breathe.”

Roz held up a hose attached to her suit. It trailed along the floor, away from her, and it reminded Eddie of an umbilical cord.

“You can’t take off the suit, can you?” he asked, though he already knew the answer.

“Not for a million bucks.”

That was understandable. There wasn’t anything Eddie would do for a million bucks. He had his hands full with just one Buck.

“What happens if you disconnect the hose from your suit?” Chimney asked, head sticking out of the vent.

“Then it cuts off my air supply.”

A problem. But their only other option was to leave her to die, so that really only left them the one choice. 

Eddie asked her a final question:

“How long can you hold your breath?”

Getting her through the vent and into the ducts was a bit awkward with her in her suit, but they managed. They crawled as quickly as they could, because they did not have time to spare. The longer they took, the longer Roz went without fresh air.

“Eddie, how ya doing?” Buck asked.

“We’re almost there,” Eddie responded.

And they were, the vent they used to get into the vents to begin with were right there. Chimney went out first, and then Eddie, and then they both helped Roz to the ground.

“Do you need a hand?” Chimney asked.

“No, I’ll get her out,” Eddie said. “Go help Buck.”

“Copy that.”

Eddie half-carried Roz into the decon chamber that served as the exit. The moment the glass door closed behind them, he was ripping off the hood of her suit. She collapsed onto her knees and then onto the floor, heaving in mouthfuls of air.

“Just breathe,” Eddie instructed, helping her sit up. “Even breaths, there you go.”

Roz was still catching her breath when, a couple minutes later, the lab exploded in fire. The glass in the doors shattered, debris rushed in, and Eddie instinctively covered Roz with his body. An alarm, ominous in its deep tone, began to drone.

“Buck,” Eddie breathed out, horror filling his veins. He leaped to his feet and rushed for the lab.

A glass wall slammed down in front of him, cutting him off.

“No.” Eddie shook his head in vain denial, patting around for a latch or a handle or something. “No, no, no.”

There was no latch, no handle, nothing he could find to get this wall out of his way.

“Tell me how to get this open,” Eddie demanded of Roz.

“You don’t,” Roz said, and he did not accept that. “That wall means the lab’s in automatic lockdown.”

“Is it the whole building?”

“No. Just them.”

Okay, prioritize, Eddie told himself. There was a civilian, he had to get her out.

“Let’s go,” he told Roz, almost yanking her to her feet. “Out to decon.”

“I know where it is,” she said, pulling out of his grip. “We run drills, I’ve got it.”

“Okay, go.”

He watched her go for the hall they’d come in through, yanking off his mask and helmet as he did. The lab was sealed, that meant the risk of him breathing anything was minimal. And it was CCHF, anyway, a disease transmitted by ticks.

The air was fine where he was.

Through the glass window in the wall, Eddie could see the devastation in the lab. Nothing was untouched, and most of his view was blocked by smoke or something like smoke. It looked as if part of the ceiling had come down. But there was no sign of Buck or the others.

He grabbed his radio, thumbed the button.

“One-Eighteen, sound off.”

The response was nothing but silence..

“Buck?”

Silence

“Ravi?”

Silence.

“Hen?”

Silence.

“Chim?”

Silence.

“Buck?” Eddie tried again, voice cracking. “Mi sol?”

Silence.

Chapter End Notes

Chapter 41: Hold Your Breath

Chapter Summary

In which Eddie is separated from the others, and Buck goes outside his comfort zone.

Moira was still nowhere to be found. They raced around, putting out the fires and searching as they went, but it was proving fruitless. Buck hadn’t seen any sign of another person in this lab, and neither had Hen or Ravi.

“Eddie,” he spoke into his radio. “How ya doing?”

“We’re almost there,” Eddie responded.

That was something, at least. The search moved on, and Chimney joined them a couple minutes after. Eddie didn’t, and Buck figured he was getting Roz out of the lab.

There was a door, with flames visible through its skinny, rectangular window, and what sounded very much like screaming. Buck tried to get a good look inside, but really couldn’t. And no one responded to their calls.

Because it wasn’t a person screaming, as they found out when they forced the door open with halligans. There was a pipe engulfed in fire, and tanks of whatever they used to make the cryo room a cryo room were venting. The screaming wasn’t screaming, it was the sound a tank made as it was about to explode.

“That doesn’t look good, Cap,” Hen said.

“Fuck,” Buck swore, turning and pushing at her. His heart was pounding in his chest, and he had to get them all out of here.”Move, move, move!”

He herded them back down the short hall they’d come, towards the way they came in. They needed to get clear, they needed to-

“What about Moira?” Ravi had hung back.

“We’ve looked everywhere,” Buck told him. “We are leaving.”

“But she’s still in here!”

“Ravi, I don’t care!” Buck snapped. “I told you to move!”

“You heard him.” Chimney grabbed Ravi by the collar and tugged him forward. “Let’s go!”

They raced for the lab exit, but they didn’t move fast enough.

Buck felt the explosion before he heard it, the force of it lifting him off his feet and into the air. The last thing he thought, before darkness took him, was that maybe they really were cursed.

“Mi sol?”

Jell-O, Eddie repeated to himself as the silence over the radio continued unbroken. He was Jell-O, he was Jell-O, he was Jell-O.

“Dispatch, there’s been an explosion and I am cut off from my team.” Eddie pressed his forehead against the window, and stared into the destroyed lab. He slammed his helmet into the glass, and it didn’t even make a pleasing sound. “A security wall came down. I need another way through.”

“No,” Maddie said, and the word had Eddie curling his lip. “If the security wall was triggered, I’m not sure anyone’s getting out of that room.”

“Maddie, you’re not understanding me.” He will not snap at his sister-in-law, he will not snap at his sister-in-law, he will not snap at his sister-in-law. “I ask you for another way through, you give me another way through. That is how this works.”

“The automatic lockdown seals everything. It’s part of their safety protocols.”

“Fuck the protocols!” And he snapped at his sister-in-law. “There’s gotta be something on the truck that’ll get me in.”

He pushed off the window and started marching for the exit.

“No, Eddie-”

“I am getting back in there!” And he was getting Buck out.

“We will get them out!” Maddie said. “But we can’t risk injuring yourself. Or them! I have someone on scene who’s gonna help us.”

Eddie paused.

“Who?”

When Athena first heard what happened - an explosion at a research lab, the 118 trapped - her immediate reaction was to be thankful that Bobby was across the city from it. She was not sure if she could handle it, if he was trapped in there with the rest of them. She was already a mess of worry and fear as it was.

And anger.

“What do you mean you can’t open it?” she demanded, hounding the steps of the lab’s director through the command tent that had been set up.

“I mean that it’s just not possible right now,” Dr. Banting said.

“Then make it possible. You run this place, don’t you?”

“Yes, which means my first priority is keeping people safe,” he said. “Do you have any idea what’s on the other side of that door?”

“A bunch of people who are very dear to me.”

“Then maybe I should be dealing with someone else,” he said, doing his best to dismiss her as he headed outside.

Athena felt her temper flare.

“You are dealing with me,” she snapped as she stormed after him. “Now how do we get to them?”

He stopped walking and turned to face her.

“Sergeant, you have to understand.” Banting didn’t even look regretful as he spoke. “There is a very dangerous virus down there which may have been aerosolized in the explosion. If we raise the door right now, we risk releasing it on the public.”

Athena was distracted momentarily by the sight of LAFD turnouts on the walkway above, swarmed by blue hazmats. It was Eddie, of all people, who should not have been there at all. He was supposed to be at paramedic school or whatever.

He glanced down at her briefly as he marched towards decon. His face was a mask of stone, but there was anger seeping through the cracks. Which meant that he was as worried as she was, if not more.

“So what can we do?” she demanded of Banting, who’d tried to use the moment to run away.

“We just have to wait,” was his unsatisfying answer. “Until the filtration system can recycle all of the air in the lab.”

“And how long is that gonna take?”

“Well. Maybe a day,” he said. “Maybe a little longer.”

Yeah, no. That was not an acceptable time frame. Athena just had to figure out how to shorten it.

Consciousness returned to Buck slowly. Feeling first, the all encompassing ache of his body from being tossed like a ragdoll. Sound next, the drone of the alarms and the creaking of metal and someone’s voice, though he couldn’t quite parse the words yet. Sight came after, and he blinked his eyes until his blurry vision came into focus and he saw the utter devastation of the lab.

“...please respond. One Eighteen, do you copy?”

Maddie. That was Maddie.

“This is Captain Diaz, One Eighteen,” Buck answered as he pushed himself up and did a mental check of himself. It didn’t feel like anything was broken, but shock and adrenaline did wonders at hiding that.

“Buck.” Maddie seemed to have poured all her relief into his name. “Is everyone okay?”

“There was an explosion in the lab.” 

Buck began patting himself down. Nothing sticking out, nothing misaligned, nothing coming back wet. He went to his gear next, doing his best to check for damages with gloved fingers that felt clumsier than usual.

“We’re aware. Any idea what exploded?”

“A refrigerant. At least it knocked the fire out.” No tears in his turnouts, not cracks in his SCBA mask, no- His fingers froze partway through checking the hose that connected his oxygen tank to the mask. His fingers froze on a hole in the hose. “Um. Um. Stand by for status.”

Fuck. Fuck, fuck, fuck-

Wait.

Buck held his breath as he patted down the pockets of his turnout coat, looking for- Yes! The roll of duct tape was still there. He yanked it out with trembling hands, fumbling with the end until he could peel it and tear off a piece to wrap around the hose. Then he stuck another piece over it, for good measure, and then a third.

He didn’t find any other holes in the line, so crisis averted. Maybe.

“One Eighteen, sound off!” he ordered as he stood. “Chim?”

“I’m good, Cap!” Chimney called out from somewhere.

“Did Eddie make it out with Roz?”

“Yeah.”

Thank God.

“Hen?” Buck called. “Ravi?”

“Here Cap!” Ravi was at the exit, which was now blocked by a glass wall. “But there’s a little problem. The door’s broken.”

Ravi frantically pressed the button beside it, which was alive with red light. Buck stared at the glass wall, at the security wall, heart heavy and stomach roiling. He might not know for sure what it meant, but he could take a confident guess.

“I don’t think it’s broken, Rav,” Buck said. He could see Roz’s abandoned bubble suit on the other side. “I think it’s sealed.”

“We’re locked in?” His words were laced with the same growing panic that Buck was trying to suppress.

“We’re quarantined.”

(Don’t breathe in. Don’t breathe out. Hold your breath.)

Hen hadn’t responded yet. Buck glanced about for her and opened his mouth to call out once more. But then he saw her limp form several feet away and rushed to her, Ravi right behind him. There were metal shelves on top of her, and she didn’t respond. She didn’t even move when they uncovered her, but at least she was breathing. Shallow, but better than nothing.

“Chim!” Buck called out. “Kinda need you!”

“I’m right here, Buck.”

Wait. Buck had been far too distracted to notice it earlier, but… Why wasn’t Chimney’s voice muffled?

He stood from where he’d been crouched beside Hen and slowly turned, dreading what he would see. It was worse than he feared, Chimney standing there with his face completely uncovered. His helmet wasn’t even anywhere to be seen.

“Chim,” Buck said. “Where the hell is your breather?”

Chimney lifted up his shattered SCBA mask to show them.

“Must have gotten blown off,” he said, dropping it onto the floor.

(Don’t breathe in. Don’t breathe out. Hold your breath.)

Buck felt numb as he grabbed his radio and thumbed the button.

“Dispatch, One Eighteen accounted for. Wilson’s unconscious, and… And Han’s SCBA is compromised.”

“Did you say compromised?” Maddie just about screeched.

“Yeah, but don’t worry. I still have my face,” Chimney joked to her, heading over to Hen. “Alright, let’s get her flat.”

“How about your med kit?” Maddie asked as they worked to turn Hen over. “Do you have it?”

“His and Hen’s,” Buck answered for Chimney.

“Then grab any PPE you can find. And Chim, please, don’t take another breath until you’ve got it on.”

(Don’t breathe in. Don’t breathe out. Hold your breath.)

“Athena!” Eddie called as he took the steps to the ground two at a time. 

He spotted the sergeant as he was marched towards decon, arguing with the director. He hadn’t seen Albert or the ambulance, and could only assume the younger Han took Allen on to the hospital. Which was probably for the best.

“Eddie. I thought you were being deconned?”

“I was, now I’m not,” Eddie said, falling into step with her. “Is there any news?”

“Chimney’s mask came off.”

“What?” He stumbled for a step. “How do we know? Do we have eyes on them?”

“Buck told us.” Athena stopped when Eddie did, and took in his obvious relief. “You didn’t know?”

“They took my gear away, I haven’t heard anything,” he told her. “So has Chimney been exposed?”

“That’s what I’m trying to find out.”

The explosion could have aerosolized the virus, Eddie had realized while he was being decontaminated. Respirators could do it, too, if a CCHF patient was on a ventilator. It wasn’t something he had to be concerned about when he was in Afghanistan, because they didn’t have that kind of equipment on base, so he hadn’t thought of it as a possibility before.

Eddie followed her into the command tent for the hazmat team, the sergeant calling out for Dr. Banting and hurrying over when she spotted him.

“That thing on Sublevel Three,” she said. “Hemorrha- Whatever it’s called.”

“Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever.”

“We have a man inside breathing it. How do you tell if he’s been infected?”

“He’d start showing symptoms,” Banting answered. “Fever, of course. Bleeding, confusion, tachycardia. It generally progresses from there.”

“Progresses to what?”

“Death. By organ failure or blood loss, whichever comes first.”

“Stop,” Eddie snapped, clenching his fists. By the man’s tone, it was clear he’d already written Chimney off as a lost cause. “Maybe that’s true in places without proper medical services, but not here. There were two and a half thousand cases in Turkey over a handful of years, and only a hundred and thirty-three deaths. There were forty-one cases in one outbreak, and only a single person died from it.”

The man looked taken aback at Eddie correcting him, and clearly had not been expecting them to actually know this shit. He also looked worried, but that was to be expected in this situation.

“I served in Afghanistan as a medic, I was trained on this,” he said. “And we won’t even know for sure if Chimney’s sick until days from now.”

“How many days?” Athena asked him, instead of the director.

But it wasn’t Eddie who answered.

“Typical incubation for CCHF is three to seven days.” There was an army officer behind them, several other uniformed soldiers filing in and relieving the civilians there of their stations. Old instincts had Eddie standing to attention. “Colonel John Hartman, US Army Infectious Diseases.”

An explosion at a Tier 4 lab would definitely garner their attention. Eddie was just surprised they’d gotten there as fast as they did.

“Colonel, Sergeant Athena Grant, LAPD,” Athena introduced herself, after Banting did. “This is Firefighter Diaz-”

“Formerly Staff Sergeant Diaz,” Eddie added, and the colonel gave him a respectful nod. “It’s my team that’s stuck inside, sir.”

“And we’re here to get them unstuck,” the colonel said.

“How?” Banting asked.

Colonel Hartman explained it to them as they moved from the command tent set up by the lab’s hazmat team to the army’s own. The 118’s trucks had been moved off to the side, and military humvees were parked in clean, precise rows in their place. Up above, on the walkway, army soldiers in tan hazmat suits were moving equipment into place.

“Modular clean room, submicron filters and 6,000 FPM air showers,” the colonel said. “We build it from the isolation unit right to the front door of the lab.”

“So you’re tunneling them out,” Athena summarized.

“We are. And we have biosensors detecting pathogens. The DOD doesn’t mess around with lab leaks.”

“To be clear,” Banting broke in. “There is no leak.”

“No, just a potentially aerosolized, incurable virus.”

“Sir, what’s the ETA?” Eddie asked. 

“If my guys beat our record, I’d say about two hours.”

“Athena.” The group came to a halt at the sound of Maddie’s voice from Athena’s radio. “I’m patching you in with the One Eighteen.”

“Go ahead,” Athena said. “I’ve got some good news for them.”

“I wish we had good news for you.”

Eddie’s knees just about buckled with how much relief he felt at the sound of Buck’s voice. Athena had said they’d heard from them directly, that was how they knew about Chimney’s mask. But being told and actually hearing from them himself were two entirely separate things.

“It’s Hen,” Chimney said. “She’s got a collapsed lung.”

“What do you need?” Athena asked.

“An OR,” was Chimney’s response. “If she doesn’t get a chest tube in the next ten minutes, she’s gonna stop breathing.”

Eddie turned to Hartman at the same time as Athena, but the colonel shook his head. His face was grim.

“No one’s that fast,” he said.

According to Athena, it would take two hours for the military to get to them. Then however long it would take for Hen to be decontaminated and cleared, before she could even be taken to an OR. She didn’t have that long.

Which meant Chimney would have to do it himself.

They cleared off one of the tables that was somehow still standing, and then hauled her onto it. It was as gently done as they could manage, and after making sure her SCBA mask was sealed and unmoving.

“What’s next, Chim?” Buck asked.

“I need a spray bottle,” was the answer. “And a cup or some kind of container.”

“It’s a lab,” Ravi said, already rushing off. “I’ll find something!”

“Buck.”

Buck hurried to grab his radio to reply.

“Eddie!?”

“How is she doing?”

“Uh.” Buck had to refocus past how relieved he was to be hearing his husband’s voice right now. “Breathing’s shallow, but still breathing. What about up there? How’s it looking?”

“Army’s starting to build their yellow brick road.” It was Athena that answered, and he tried not to feel disappointed.

“Any idea how long they’re gonna take?” They said two hours, but surely they were trying to go faster than that.

“Mobile Command just went up,” Athena said. “I’ll radio once I find out.”

And then, a moment later,

“We’re right outside, Buck,” Eddie said. “Good luck in there.”

Buck closed his eyes and took a moment, before turning back to the mess with Hen. Chimney was muttering to himself and wiping at his forehead with a bare hand, before shaking his head as if to clear it before going back to digging through his medkit.

“Chim?” Did he look flushed? Sweaty? There wasn’t enough light to tell for certain, maybe it was just Buck’s paranoia. “You okay?”

“I’m fine, I’m fine,” the paramedic said, and then fumbled to get his phone out when it started ringing. “It’s Maddie.”

“Answer it. What are you looking for? I’ll find it.”

“A scalpel.”

Chimney handed him the kit, and then walked a bit away to answer the call. Buck dug through it, locating a fresh scalpel in its wrapping. Ravi returned from his scavenger hunt just before the call ended.

“Buck.” Why did Chimney sound like that? “You got that scalpel?”

Buck held it up for Chimney to see.

“You should hang onto it.”

“Uh.” Buck cocked his head, not understanding. “Why?”

“Because you’re gonna be using it.”

“I’m- What? No.” Buck shook his head. “You’re the paramedic, this is- this is your stuff. I’m just EMT trained.”

Chimney sighed, the kind of sigh that encompassed the whole body.

“Maddie pointed out,” he said, “that if I’m infected, then I could spread it to Hen when I cut into her. It’s too risky for me to do it.”

“No. No. Chim, you are asking me to do field surgery. To- To stick a tube into her lung. I don’t- Chimney, I don’t know how to do that. I don’t know what to do here.”

“I’ll walk you through every step,” Chimney promised. “But you have to do it. Okay?”

This was very much not okay. But Buck wasn’t being given very many options, especially once Chimney sequestered himself in the specimens room. Somehow, the glass walls and doors of that room were still intact.

“Alright,” Buck said once he and Ravi got Hen out of her turnout coat and onto her side. “Chimney, what am I doing?”

“Lift up her arm,” he said. Ravi did it, pulling Hen’s arm so it was over her head. “And you’re gonna cut the side of her shirt open.”

Right. Right, of course, Buck knew that.

He grabbed the scissors he’d found in the kit and began to cut, starting from the bottom hem. His hand trembled at the start, and he tried to ignore it. Eddie’s voice coming over the radio again helped calm his nerves a little bit.

“Ninety minutes on the tunnel.”

Buck paused long enough to thumb his radio and respond with,

“Copy. I’m gonna be busy for a bit, babe.” He dropped his hand from the radio and went back to cutting, until there was a long slit in Hen’s shirt up to her armpit. “Chimney, what now?”

“You’re gonna count her ribs. Stop when you feel the space between the fourth and fifth rib.”

“Chim.” Buck tried to keep from snapping at the man. “Counting from the top or the bottom?”

“Top, sorry. I’m not used to doing it like this.”
