Buck wasn’t used to doing this at all. He counted ribs until his finger landed in the correct space.

“And now?”

“Sterilize the area with ChloraPrep.”

Done.

“Ravi, take the sterile water from the med kit. Dump it into the beaker.”

Done.

“Buck, take the tube out of the spray bottle Ravi found and sanitize it.”

Done.

“Go for your scalpel. You’re gonna cut between her ribs. Aim for the size of the tube. If it’s too big, we risk exposure.”

“Right, right. Okay.”

Buck took a deep breath (don’t breathe in, don’t breathe out, hold your breath) and brought the scalpel to the spot he’d disinfected. It was shaking, because his hand was shaking. God, he wished Eddie was here. Or Bobby. Either of them would know what they were doing better than he did.

Either of them would be a much better choice for this.

“Buck,” Chimney urged when he was frozen for a bit too long.

“Okay. Okay. Cutting between her ribs. Okay.”

The scalpel was sharp. It didn’t cut through Hen’s skin like a hot knife through butter, it sliced through it like water. Flesh parted as if it was being unzipped, blood pouring out in the blade’s wake. When the incision was the right size, or so Buck hoped, he could not get the scalpel away from himself fast enough.

“Now what?” Buck asked again.

“Now’s the hard part,” Chimney said. “You’re gonna stick your finger in and break through the muscle.”

Stick his finger into- Buck swallowed the bile that rose in his throat. If it was anyone else he was doing it to, if it were a complete stranger, this wouldn’t be as awful. But this wasn’t a complete stranger.

It was Hen.

“How- How far do I…?”

“You’re gonna have to push really hard. Until you’re through.”

Buck put a gloved finger to the incision and closed his eyes as he shoved it in. It was wet, meaty, warm. He felt things tear, and he heard something squelch. It was intimate in a way he never wanted to be with anyone.

“Cap,” Ravi said, sounding worried. “She’s not breathing.”

“I just- I just need to-” Buck twisted and pushed and felt something give, felt his finger breach the other side. “I’m in.”

“Ravi, clamp the tube and hand it to him,” Chimney instructed. “Buck, you’re sticking it inside the incision.”

“How- How far into the incision?” Buck asked.

“As far as your finger went.”

Buck ignored the red covering his finger as he took the clamped tube from Ravi. He fed it into the incision, shoved it in, until he thought it reached far enough. The next step was to secure it with the silk tape, until it was air tight. When he unclamped it, blood started gushing into the tube.

“Put the other end into the beaker and seal it, quickly.”

When that was done, when the blood was pouring into the beaker, it was just a matter of waiting. Waiting and holding their breath as they watched for Hen’s chest to rise. Waiting and holding their breath until Hen took one, too.

When she did, it was a deep, gasping breath. Her eyes opened and her head rolled as she tried to get a fix on her surroundings.

“She’s breathing, she’s awake,” Buck reported into the radio.

“Let the record show that Buck did everything,” Chimney said. “I’m just his incredible mentor-”

His words were cut off by his coughing. Wet coughs that shook his whole body. He took off the disposable mask he’d been wearing and stared at the inside of it dumbly, brow furrowed as if he couldn’t quite comprehend what he was seeing. And then something dark began trickling out of his nose.

Chimney met Buck’s eyes through the glass, as both came to the same awful realization.

Chapter 42: The B Word

Chapter Summary

In which everyone realizes just how dire the situation truly is.

“Hey, honey. Not sure I’m gonna make it home for dinner. I think I picked up a little bug at the office.”

That statement, Chimney’s failed attempt at making light of this, echoed through Eddie’s head as he followed Athena through the hazmat tent. It didn’t make sense. None of this made sense. CCHF took days to incubate, days to get to the point that Chimney was at now. It should not have progressed this quickly.

“You don’t need to read it,” Banting was saying, shoving a tablet at Roz. “You just need to sign it.

“I already signed an NDA,” Roz said. She was in an isolation chamber, kept separate from the rest of the tent.

“Well, this one’s more comprehen-” Banting noticed them coming and turned, looking panicked. “Oh, hello.”

Eddie used to have a very unhealthy way of dealing with his anger. He would force it down, stuff it into a little box and do his best to ignore it. Until there was too much of it, until it achieved fusion under the weight of itself and exploded. Punching a man harassing him over a parking spot. Screaming at the love of his life in a grocery store. It got so bad, at one point, that he sought recourse in organized violence. Those fights were just as much about venting the rage and hurting himself as they were about seeking out control when it felt like he had none.

Years of therapy helped him find other avenues for both. Healthier avenues. Now, when that anger threatened to overflow, he’d talk it out with Buck. Or he’d settle in with Gavin and play with him until the anger melted into tranquility. He’d find something constructive to do.

But sometimes…

Eddie brushed past Athena and tore the tablet out of Banting’s hands, tossing it aside blindly. He grabbed the man by the collar and lifted him up, until the man’s terror-etched face was mere inches from his own.

“Talk,” he barked. “Now.”

Sometimes violence was the constructive outlet.

“I- I don’t-” Banting tried for denial, but fell silent with a whimper when Eddie gave him a good shake.

“What is in that lab, Dr. Banting?” Athena asked, much more calmly than Eddie.

“I- I- I told you, it’s Crimean-Congo hemo-”

“No,” Eddie snarled, shutting him up. “No, it isn’t.”

“The incubation period for CCHF is three to seven days.” Eddie hadn’t even realized that Colonel Hartman had followed them. “We have a man in there who’s been exhibiting symptoms within the last hour.”

“Oh, my God.” Roz looked horrified. “You didn’t tell them?”

“Tell us what?” Eddie demanded, lifting Banting up higher. The doctor was kicking his feet where they dangled in the air, occasionally hitting Eddie’s shin.

“Eddie.”

Eddie glanced at Athena, whose stern expression was fixed on him and the doctor. She inched an eyebrow up in expectation and he, grudgingly, let Banting go. The doctor stumbled a little as he regained his footing, hand going to his throat.

“You need to start talking, Dr. Banting,” Athena said. “Or he will be the least of your concerns.”

“I just- I want to make it very clear.” The doctor was breathing heavily as he edged away from Eddie. “I was unaware of what was going on in that lab until this morning, when Dr. Blake approached me.”

“Who’s Dr. Blake?”

“Moira Blake,” Roz answered. “She’s awful.”

“That’s the third person we were trying to find,” Eddie said. “Allen mentioned her when he woke up briefly.”

“Oh, she was off the property,” Banting said. “I terminated her as soon as I found out.”

“Found out what, Dr. Banting?” Colonel Hartman asked.

But it was Roz who answered.

“Moira had been performing gain-of-function research on the virus. She sped up the incubation period.”

Oh, God. Oh, God. No wonder Roz had looked horrified.

“Without authorization,” Banting said, a clear attempt at saving himself from the consequences about to fall upon all of them.

“So you ended her career, and then a fire breaks out in the lab where she worked,” Athena said. She did not sound nearly as fearful as she really should’ve. Nor nearly as angry. “And you didn’t think to mention that?”

“I was waiting to hear back from HR.”

“She made a bioweapon.”

Eddie’s statement had Athena drawing in a sharp breath. Her eyes widened. There was the appropriate fear.

“That’s- That’s an overexaggeration-” Dr. Banting tried for denial.

“She made a bioweapon,” Eddie repeated, prowling towards Banting. The doctor retreated, which only meant his back was against Roz’s isolation chamber and he had nowhere to run. “And you were waiting to hear from HR? She was your employee, in your lab, and you didn’t know she was making a bioweapon?”

“I can’t know what every-”

“Athena, give me your gun.”

“That’s enough,” Colonel Hartman barked. Eddie kinda hated the way it was enough to bring him to a complete stop and have him standing at attention, like he was back on base in Afghanistan. “Dr. Banting, you are now in my custody. Soldier.”

Eddie wished he could enjoy the sight of one of the soldiers dragging Dr. Banting away. But he couldn’t. Not just because his husband and their friends were trapped in that lab, with a loose bioweapon. But because of what the colonel said into his radio.

“E-team, E-team, this is Colonel Hartman. Terminate all extraction protocols and evacuate this building right now.”

“What? No,” Eddie said. “You can’t just leave them in there to die!”

“You called this virus a bioweapon yourself, Staff Sergeant. We have a pandemic in a bottle, and I am not risking popping that top.” The colonel turned to a nearby soldier, waiting for orders. “New objective: we’re evacuating all civilians within an eight-mile radius of this facility.”

“What about my team?” Eddie demanded as the soldier hurried out to start the evacuation procedures. “What about my husband?”

“I am very sorry.”

Jell-O. Eddie was Jell-O. His feet were Jell-O, his legs were Jello-O, his stomach…

“You’re sorry?” Athena snapped. “What are they? Canaries in a coal mine?”

“They’re heroes,” the colonel said. “And we are thankful for their sacrifice.

He was Jell-O, Eddie thought to himself as he watched the colonel walk away, as he tried to keep the panic at bay. His stomach was Jell-O, his chest was Jell-O, his head-

From the isolation chamber behind him, Roz declared,

“There’s a cure.”

In Ravi’s medical opinion, as limited as his medical knowledge was, Chimney looked like shit. He’d moved so he was sitting on the floor, propped up against a table and right next to a rat in a cage that was happily racing itself on its wheel. He was sweaty and clammy looking, even in the poor lighting, and after he’d wiped away the blood from his face, he stuffed a bit of gauze up his nose to catch the bleeding.

“Chim,” Ravi said, getting his attention. “How are you feeling?”

“Like a rat in a cage,” was the paramedic’s answer, along with another bout of bloody coughing.

“He’s awake and oriented,” he relayed into the radio for Maddie’s sake.

Maddie was hanging off every update they had about Chimney. Ravi didn’t know which was worse, to be stuck at dispatch, only able to listen; to be stuck outside, unable to get in; or to be stuck in here, and only able to watch.

“Keep him awake,” Hen said. Her voice was weak and she hadn’t bothered trying to move from the table-turned-impromptu surgery bed, but she was awake and breathing. That was a vast improvement from before. “No matter what.”

“Buck?”

It made something in Ravi’s chest ache, to see the way Buck perked up so obviously at the sound of Eddie’s voice. He hadn’t heard anything from Albert since they entered the lab. He’d taken Allen to the ER, surely, but what about after that? Did he even know what was going on? Was he at the station, completely oblivious to them becoming trapped? Did he come back and was now waiting outside like Eddie?

Ravi didn’t know. Ravi would very much like to know.

“Hey, Eddie.” Buck’s smile was audible in his voice, even though Ravi couldn’t make it out with the SCBA mask.

“How’s Chim?”

“Awake, aware, and bleeding from every orifice.”

“Not every orifice!” Chimney corrected.

“How long until we’ve got our exit?”

“About that…”

The change in Buck’s demeanor was instant and obvious. He went completely still, all of his constant little motions ceasing entirely. Except for the fist he had clenched at his side: Ravi saw it trembling minutely.

“What does that mean?” Buck asked, and there was clear effort at keeping his voice steady.

“Things have changed, mi sol,” Eddie said. Ravi had been around the Diazes long enough to know that the use of the endearment here was not a good sign. Ever since Buck became captain, they’d started going to great lengths to keep from giving the brass any reason to think they couldn’t work together, and part of that meant they kept their pet names for each other outside of the station. “Chimney got too sick, too quickly. The incubation period for CCHF is supposed to be days, not hours. That other woman we were looking for, Moira, decided to play mad scientist.”

“Eddie,” Buck said, and then repeated himself with words that were starting to shake, “What does that mean?”

“It means the army decided it’s too dangerous to get you out. The colonel doesn’t want to risk setting loose another pandemic.”

Ravi felt the full weight of that statement settle across all of them. He felt the despair creep into his chest like kudzu vines until he was nearly suffocating with it, and saw it mirrored in the others. He saw it in the way Chimney closed his eyes and let his head fall forward. He saw it in the way Hen tried to bury her face in her arm. He saw it in the way Buck dropped his hand from his radio and tipped his head back to look up at the ceiling. 

Help was not coming. They weren’t getting out of here. They were going to be stuck watching Chimney die, and then they were going to watch each other die. They might even be left here after that. His parents were going to be mourning over an empty casket while he was left to rot in a sealed lab.

Suddenly, Ravi hoped that Albert was sitting ignorant at the station. Better for him to be told after, than for him to carry the knowledge of it happening with the inability to do anything.

“But Moira also made an antiviral. Roz says it’s stored on the same floor.”

Laughter bubbled out of Buck’s throat. He sounded like he was on the verge of hysteria.

“I’m married to a drama queen…”

“Where?” Ravi asked Eddie. “I’ll go and get it.”

“Roz and I will guide you.”

Ravi hurried through the wreckage of the lab as quickly as he could, following Eddie’s directions through the halls. Occasionally he would have to backtrack, having gone the wrong way. Occasionally, he would come across a path blocked with debris and had to waste time clearing the way.

But he got to the room that the antiviral was stored in. He could see the refrigeration unit containing it through the window in the door, and cleared the bits of duct work and destroyed equipment that had been piled in front of it. The halligan he brought with him worked as a key and he soon had the door swinging open.

“Firefighter,” a man’s unfamiliar voice said over the radio. It drew Ravi to a confused halt just inside the (intact, untouched by the explosion) room. “Do not make another move.”

“Who is this?”

“This is Colonel Hartman, United States Army. I am ordering you to stand down. Right now.”

“This is Captain Diaz, Los Angeles Fire Department,” Buck said, voice harsh over the radio. “Ravi is my firefighter, not one of your soldiers.”

“Then you should advise him to stop,” the colonel replied. “If he opens that freezer, you both face charges of domestic and international terrorism. Do not access that antiviral. If you disobey my order, there are beds waiting for you in supermax. Do you understand me?”

“I understand you were gonna leave us here to die, so fuck your threats,” Buck spat, with so much vitriol even Ravi flinched. “Ravi, don’t worry about it. I’ll get it myself.”

“I’m already here, Cap, I might as well go ahead and do it,” Ravi replied as he crossed the room to the freezer. “If the colonel wants to stop me, he can come in here and do it himself.”

There was a security camera in the corner of the room, near the ceiling, and Ravi figured it was a safe assumption that was how the army was watching him. He gave it, and them, the finger. The freezer was tall, standing not-quite in the center of the room. It had a touch screen with a number pad and a message in orange at the top: PASSCODE ACCESS ONLY. Between that and the number pad was a line of five gray circles.

“What’s the code?” he asked.

“It’s five digits,” Eddie replied. “One seven eight seven five.”

“Firefighter.” The colonel sounded pissed. “Do not do this.”

Ravi couldn’t help himself as he replied,

“I’ll wear my Medal of Valor to the trial.”

The screen chirped as he pressed the numbers in sequence, a grey circle filling in with each one. 1-7-8-7-5. The message at the top changed to a friendly green FREEZER UNLOCKED and there was a buzzy blorp of a sound. The lid to the freezer lifted up with a hiss and fog poured out. A rack rose out of it with far less fanfare than Ravi felt there should have been, since he was facing terrorism charges for this.

An empty rack.

“Guys? It’s not here.”

“What do you mean it’s not there!?” was Maddie’s panicked response. He’d forgotten she was listening in, too.

“You’re looking at the right spot?” Eddie asked. He didn’t sound any better than Maddie. “Q3?”

“It’s completely empty, Eddie,” Ravi responded. “There’s nothing here.”

The antiviral was gone, and so was all of his hope.

Eddie watched as, on the screen, Moira walked off with the antiviral. And there was no one he hated more at that moment.

They were in the army’s command tent, all of them, even Roz. Eddie guessed that the army figured, since the disease was progressing so quickly, they’d know by now if she was infected. They’d gathered the security footage from before the fire, to find out what had happened to the antiviral. The answer was not much of a surprise, somehow.

“It’s confirmed, Buck,” Athena said. She’d switched to her phone to talk to the ones inside, putting it on speaker so they could all talk and hear. Maddie patched her through. “The employee who started the fire took the antiviral with her. She smuggled it out in a tumbler, of all things.”

“My tumbler,” Roz was apparently compelled to add. She was a bit sore that Moira decided to steal her things, on top of the attempt on everyone’s life.

“She’s got about a ninety minute head start on us.”

On the screen showing the inside of the destroyed lab, Eddie could see Buck. He was staring up at the security camera, at them. Eddie could also see Chimney in the specimens room with Ravi checking his vitals, and Hen on the table that they’d placed her on so Buck could do field surgery. 

As Eddie watched, Buck turned partially around to look at Chimney.

“Eddie said the mortality rate for this thing was one in three,” he said, turning back to look at the camera. “That means two in three people survive this.”

“That’s the average, Buck,” Eddie said, leaning in to speak into the phone. “It’s higher in places with the proper medical infrastructure, lower in places without it. It depends on if they have what they need to treat the symptoms and keep the patient from going into organ failure or choking on their own blood for long enough to recover.”

“We don’t have what we need for that, do we?” Buck’s voice was small and quiet.

“No. And with how fast it’s going, I don’t think it would even matter if you did.”

“Normal treatment is just palliative care,” Roz said, leaning in as well. “That was the point of our research, to find a better treatment.”

“Which it looks like Moira Blake did,” Athena said. “And then walked out the door with the one and only dose.”

“Okay, so. How long would it take to make a new dose?”

“It would take weeks to replicate it with a functioning lab,” Roz said. “We don’t have that time. Or a functioning lab.”

Buck turned again, this time in the other direction, to look at Ravi as he left the specimens room and went over to Hen. There was something on Buck’s air supply hose, but the lighting wasn’t good enough for Eddie to make it out. It looked like it might be duct tape…

“What’s the plan, Colonel?”  Buck asked as he turned back to the camera again.

“The plan?” the colonel asked, looking taken aback at the question.

“Chimney’s got a deadly disease, Hen’s got a tube in her chest.” Buck gestured to the both of them in turn. “Is there a plan?”

“We’re exploring our options, Captain.”

A new voice, a new person here to undoubtedly make everything worse instead of helping. This one was a man in an FBI windbreaker, who was flashing his credentials around.

“Now who’s this guy?”

“Special Agent Mark Santos, FBI,” the newcomer introduced himself.

“FBI?”

Eddie couldn’t really see Buck’s expression, thanks to the breather he was wearing, but he could picture it well enough from both the tone and the way he rocked back slightly.

“The breach of a Tier Four biolab is a national security concern,” Santos said. “I’ll be running the investigation and response from here on out.”

“Cool, fuck the colonel. He’s useless. Open the door and get us the hell out of here.”

“We can’t break quarantine,” was Santos’ completely predictable response. Eddie clenched his fists and told himself not to do anything stupid. “Not until we know what we’re dealing with.

“Uh, I think we all know what we’re dealing with.” The “you idiot” was left unsaid, but it was much implied by Buck’s tone. “It’s CCHF.”

“That’s what it started out as, but we still don’t know how virulent this strain is.”

Buck was silent for a long moment, simply staring up at the camera.

“So it’s the old plan,” he finally said. “Except you’re going to take notes while you watch us die. Like we’re a bunch of lab rats.”

“I urge you not to look at it that way, Captain-”

“And I urge you to bite me,” Buck replied, turning his back on them as he went to check in with Hen.

That was definitely duct tape on his air supply hose. Why was there duct tape on his air supply hose?

“We’ll find and apprehend Dr. Blake,” Santos promised. “Once she’s in custody, I am confident the military can safely resume extraction.”

“You mean you’ll be pulling out our bodies,” Buck shot back. He sounded angry, and Eddie was thankful for it. Anger was better than resignation. “The colonel didn’t want us using that antiviral. Even if you get it, you won’t use it on any of us.”

Santos didn’t say anything, and neither did Hartman. When the silence stretched on, Buck audibly scoffed over the line.

“Yeah.”

“I’m gonna hang up and go now, Buck,” Athena said. “I will talk to you soon.”

“Whatever you say, Ma.”

Before Athena could drop the line, though, Eddie snatched the phone out of her hand.

“Buck, why do you have duct tape on the air supply line for your tank?”

“Uh.” Everything, from Buck’s tone to his change in body language, was sheepish. “Don’t worry about it?”

“Buck.”

Eddie couldn’t hear the sigh, but he watched how his husband slumped in place.

“The explosion tore a hole in it.” Buck’s words sent ice through Eddie’s heart. And he saw on the screen as everyone else’s heads snapped towards Buck. “But- But it’s fine! I got it patched up, and I’m not feeling anything but pissed off.”

Eddie swallowed, throat and mouth suddenly dry.

“Tell someone if it changes.”

“You got it, babe,” Buck replied, giving the camera a sarcastic salute. “The moment I start dying, I’ll let you know.”

Athena took the phone from Eddie and ended the call - her hand was trembling, he noticed - and then headed out of the tent. Eddie followed her, and picked up his pace when she did.

“I know we aren’t just walking away,” he told Athena, keeping his voice low.

“We’re not, we’re going to be driving away,” the sergeant replied.

“Buck was right, they're never gonna give Chimney that antiviral.”

“I know,” Athena said as they reached her cruiser. “They’re all expendable to those motherfuckers. So we’re gonna find that crazy bitch and get our hands on that dose before anyone else in there gets sick.”

She yanked the driver’s side door open, and then jerked her head at Eddie.

“Now get in,” she barked.

“Yes, ma’am,” Eddie said, jogging over to the other side. “Getting in, ma’am.”

The tires screeched when they peeled out of there.

Chapter 43: (Don't) Breathe

Chapter Summary

In which Athena interferes with an investigation, Buck has to be MacGyver, and Karen looks through the IKEA catalog.

Athena worked as fast as she could once they pulled away from the lab, and the government presence there. She called up Officer Williams, someone she knew she could trust and depend on, and asked for a favor. He would tell her the moment there was a hit on Moira Blake’s car, and he was out there looking for it himself.

She worked as fast as she could, drove as fast as she could without gaining unwanted attention, but others still outraced her.

“How did they get here so fast?” Eddie asked, peering Moira’s house through the windshield of the cruiser. It was crawling with both the FBI and the military, along with LAPD officers. “There’s no way they knew who’d taken the antiviral before we saw that footage.”

Eddie turned to Athena, the scowl that etched itself onto his face over the day growing deeper.

“There’s no way, right?” he asked.

“Maybe HR reached out to them,” Athena replied with a scoff. She threw open her door and started getting out. “Stay here.”

This was the benefit of working with Eddie in the current circumstances. He knew, better than anyone, the dangers they were facing in their competition with the military. So instead of arguing with her, instead of making any sign like he intended to follow her, he just nodded and watched her go.

People had the tendency to accept things at face value. If someone looked as if they belonged, no one was going to question them. Here, at this moment, she wasn't suspicious. She was a member of the LAPD, helping execute a search warrant. No one paid her any mind. One person even kindly lifted the yellow tape up for her to pass under.

But there was a limit to this shield, a point where it became obvious she no longer belonged. That point was reached as she crossed the lawn on her way to the front door. She was stopped by a tired looking grunt in an FBI polo, balancing a shallow crate of investigative tools on a single arm, a bag clutched in his other hand.

“No entry,” he said. “ERT’s still got the scene.”

The Evidence Response Team. They were the FBI’s version of Crime Scene Investigators. He must’ve been one of them, judging by what he was carrying.

“They said you needed a hand,” Athena improvised.

Be friendly, be helpful. People were always more willing to work with you if you were friendly and helpful.

“Oh, they usually send me rookies for that.”

Right, her chevrons. Most people, those who weren’t first responders, wouldn’t bother looking twice at them. Hell, most people probably couldn’t say what rank they signified without looking it up. But here, with this man, they served to make it more obvious that she didn’t belong.

“No one should ever feel like they outrank lending someone a hand,” she bullshitted as she took the crate off of him. He looked relieved; he wasn’t going to question someone being helpful. “I heard there was some kind of manhunt. Any signs of life in there?”

“Nah.” The man shook his head. “If you ask me, no one’s been home in days.”

“Now that’s disappointing.” Thank God. If this luck kept up, she’d actually pay the tithe at church on Sunday. Maybe even more than the 10% they always tried hounding her for. “All this circus and no clowns to be found.”

Give them all wigs and red noses, she was surrounded by clowns.

“Yeah, well.” The man shrugged as he started off again for the open van parked on the curb, Athena dutifully following along. “The good news is that the place is as neat as a pin. We already shot photos.”

Athena glanced down at the crate in her hands and spotted a camera. Maybe she’d pay triple the usual tithe on Sunday.

“We should be in and out, unless they start pulling down the walls,” he said as he put the bag inside the van.

“Where do you want this?” she asked.

“Oh, there is great.”

She placed the crate where he indicated, taking her time. When he turned around, to talk to another agent, she took the chance to oh-so-casually pop out the camera’s SD card. She couldn’t rush back to the cruiser, that would definitely attract attention, so it took far longer than she was comfortable with before she was climbing back behind the wheel.

“That’s it?” Eddie demanded.

“That’s it,” Athena confirmed, closing the door. “We’ve got everything we need.”

“You didn’t even go inside, Athena.”

His tone was borderline rude, but she was choosing to be magnanimous and not say anything. Circumstances and all that.

“I didn’t need to.” She pulled out the SD card and held it up. “Someone already documented the scene for me.”

Eddie stared at it, a smile slowly breaking out on his face.

“You stole the crime scene photos.”

“They can make more.” Normally, she’d feel guilty for the tongue lashing that the FBI grunt was about to receive. But she’d happily throw him under a bus at the moment, if she needed to, so he was actually lucky. “Now let’s get out of here.”

If the SD card had anything, anything, that could help them, the entirety of Athena’s next paycheck would go to Sunday’s tithe.

Buck hadn’t honestly thought their situation could get any worse. They were stuck in a destroyed lab, with a virus that some crazy lady experimented with to make even deadlier, and the people outside that could get them out were choosing to watch them die. 0/10 stars, this party was awful.

But to his surprise, though he wasn’t sure why he was surprised at this point, his circumstances actually managed to get worse.

”Any fever?” Maddie asked. “Headache? Fatigue?”

“You’re giving me a headache,” Buck told her. “And I’m getting kinda tired of you tele-nursing. Does that count?”

“Buck.”

Eddie just had to go and draw attention to the duct tape on his air hose. He just couldn’t let it go.

“I’m fine, Maddie. No fever, no sensitivity to light, no headache, no chills.”

Buck dropped his hand from the radio and rolled his eyes. When he turned around, it was to Ravi, Hen, and Chimney all staring at him.

“I’m fine!” he insisted. He pointed at Chimney, separated by the glass doors of the specimens room. “You are not. So let’s- So let’s take care of that.”

“How?” Ravi asked.

“I know Eddie said we don’t have what we need to treat the symptoms here, but there has to be something we can do.” Buck was not putting any of their pictures up on that wall beside Jones’. He refused. “He’s losing blood. So- So we put him on fluids, hook him up to an IV of saline.”

He grabbed his radio again and thumbed it on, so both Maddie and Hen could hear him ask,

“How much saline would Chimney need to replace the blood he’s losing?”

“A lot of it,” Maddie answered. “Two to five liters per twenty-four hours. How much do you have?”

“Got plenty on the rig,” Hen told her. “But down here? Only the one.”

“That won’t be enough.”

Yeah, no shit, Maddie.

Buck looked around, trying to figure out a solution to the scarcity. Because there had to be something. None of them had gotten this far in life simply by giving up when things got tough.

“I tried to convince Eddie to let me buy Chris a chemistry set, once.” Buck buried his hand into a pocket of his turnout coat to feel for the necklace in it, the chain with his St. Christopher medallion and wedding band. “We’re trapped in a giant one. So- So…”

He thumbed the radio once more to ask,

“How do they make saline?”

The answer to that was simpler than Buck was expecting. It shouldn’t have been a surprise, saline was just salt water. Getting the measurements right was the tricky part. Too much water or too much salt could both be disastrous.

And the equipment that they would need to create the solution was also pretty basic.

“All the mad scientist items as requested,” Ravi declared as he returned, successful, from the scavenger hunt he’d been sent on. He carefully sat the fruits of his labor, which included a beaker and a hot plate, on a table beside some jugs of sterilized water before asking Hen, “What else do you need?”

“Sodium chloride, non-iodized salt,” she answered. “They use it for cell cultures.”

“On it!” Ravi declared, jogging off again.

“Okay, what goodies are in here.” Buck’s words were more to himself than anything as he started digging through Chimney’s medkit. Contrary to what he’d told Maddie earlier, they didn’t have Hen’s: the packet of saline in it had burst, soaking everything. Most of it was salvageable, but not all. “Looks like… Three rolls of gauze, and some trauma dressings.”

“Not much stanching power,” Hen said. “What about vasopressers?”

“None in here. And the pharmacy box is on the rig.”

Vasopressors were meds that constricted the blood vessels. They mostly used them to increase blood pressure, like in cases of shock or cardiac arrest. In this case, they would have helped slow Chimney’s bleeding.

“I got the salt!” Ravi declared as he rushed back, holding it above his head like a trophy.

“Okay.” Hen reached for her radio, laying beside her head on the table. “Maddie, we’re about to DIY some saline.”

“If you don’t get the ratio perfect, it could stop his heart,” Maddie cautioned.

“Ravi, go look for a defibrillator. Just in case,” Hen said. “In a place like this, they’ve got to have an AED mounted somewhere.”

Ravi nodded, and once again jogged off to complete his next task.

“Maddie, you’ll help me with the math here?” she asked.

“Normal saline is .9%,” Maddie said in answer. “That’s nine grams of salt per liter.”

“Alright, Cap, measure exactly nine grams,” Hen instructed. Buck grabbed the graduated cylinder that Ravi had found and started measuring out the salt. “Then boil a liter of water, bring it to a summer, and pour the salt in.”

“I can follow that recipe,” Buck told her. “It’s pretty much like baking.”

“This is nothing like baking, Buck.”

“You’re right. This is much easier than baking.”

“Cap!” Ravi called out. “Found the defibrillator.”

Buck turned to look, spotting him across the room.

“Awesome, Rav! Bring it over here.”

“Th- That part’s gonna be tough,” Ravi said.

“Why?”

“It’s on the other side of the…”

Ravi trailed off. And then he toppled sideways, falling onto a knocked over cabinet with a crash that sent his helmet skidding across the floor. Buck dropped what he was doing, barely giving it a thought enough to be thankful nothing spilled, and sprinted to his side, sliding to a stop beside him.

“Cap!” Hen shouted. “Cap, is he breathing!?”

“No!” Buck didn’t see his chest rising at all. He reached under the collar of Ravi’s coat, pressing his fingers around and praying as he tried to feel for- Yes! A pulse, a jackrabbit heartbeat. “He has a pulse! I’m not- I’m not seeing any symptoms, he just isn’t…”

He wasn’t getting any oxygen. How long had they been in here? If this was a fire, they would’ve been switched out by now, replaced by fresh bodies with fresh gear. But they’d been sucking on their oxygen for over an hour, now. Much longer than their tanks could last.

“His bottle’s empty,” Buck said, checking the gauge on Ravi’s tank. The needle was in the red, practically on zero. “Hen, check yours!”

Buck didn’t bother checking his own. It might not have been as low as Ravi’s, since they’d had him running around and using more of his oxygen than they were, but he knew it was getting there. They’d been so concerned about not breathing in the virus that they hadn’t paid any mind to their need to breathe at all.

“I’m at five psi!” Hen replied after a moment. “He’s got three minutes before there’s the risk of brain damage.”

Okay. Think, Buck. Think. There had to be something here they could use to either refill or replace Ravi’s supply. Did labs carry oxygen tanks? Would they even have-

Wait.

“Roz was hooked up to oxygen, where… That!” There were blue hoses dangling from the ceiling. Blue was a good color, right? He doubted it meant water here. “Maddie, these blue hoses. They’re for oxygen, right?”

There was a beat, as Maddie no doubt found the answer for him.

“They’re the pressure suits’ air supply lines,” she said. “They run through parallel compressors on level two, and provide a constant stream of filtered air.”

“Awesome!” Buck scrambled up to grab the nearest one.

“But I don’t know if the hose coupling will match his tank.”

“I’ve got duct tape, it’ll be fine.”

It was, after all, saving his ass at the moment. Hopefully.

Buck pulled the hose to Ravi, thankful that they were meant to stretch at least most of the way across the room. Maddie, it turned out, was right to be worried: the hose was just a hair wider than Ravi’s hook-up, and he could hear air hissing as it escaped. There wasn’t much else to do but wrap it up in tape, as tightly as he could manage.

And then Buck was holding his breath again as he watched and waited for-

Ravi drew in air with a loud gasp, eyes popping open as his head lifted a bit. Buck let out the breath he was holding, gripped the sides of the other man’s head and tapped their visors together, before standing up.

“Stay there and just breathe, Rav,” he instructed. “Hen, your turn.”

Hen’s tank received the same treatment as Ravi’s, a blue hose attached with layers of duct tape. To do his own, he had to shoulder his tank off so he could get to it. He took the opportunity to add more tape to the ad hoc patch job, to be safe.

“Was I sleeping?” Ravi asked with a groan.

“Yeah!” Chimney answered. “And stealing my thunder.”

“What I started to pass out, I thought…” Ravi sat up and shook his head. “I don’t know what we’d have done if I picked it up, too.”

“Force the two of you to play rock-paper-scissors over the antiviral,” Buck joked as he got the oxygen tank back on. “Okay, the saline. Nine grams of salt, liter of water. Boil, then let simmer.”

“Boil, simmer, then the salt,” Hen reminded him.

“Boil, simmer, then the salt,” Buck repeated as he searched for somewhere to plug in the hot plate. “Boil, simmer, then the salt…”

The next stop, after Moira’s house, was in Altadena. It was the first time since before the wildfires that he’d been to Altadena, as he’d been stationed on the other side of everything. The devastation was still more than apparent to see, with swathes of black burn scars and brown empty lots where homes used to be.

The Wilsons were in the middle of one of the few groups of houses that escaped unscathed. Somehow. Coming here made perfect sense to Eddie, even before Athena explained it as they drove. In that awful movie, Backdraft, they consulted an arsonist to catch an arsonist. He and Athena were going to consult a scientist to catch a scientist.

But first, they had to do the hard task of catching Karen up to speed.

“I know,” Athena said when they were done, and Karen was left to numbly absorb it all. “It’s a lot to take in.”

“Aside from the fact that Buck got to third base with her chest cavity, Hen’s okay,” Eddie said. “Last we heard.”

“She’s locked in a Tier Four lab, with a novel virus and no cure,” Karen bit out. “That doesn’t sound okay.”

“She isn’t the one coughing up blood. Okay’s relative right now.”

“And- And what about Chimney?”

“They’re keeping him comfortable,” Athena told her. “While we try to find the woman who made the antiviral treatment.”

“What do you know about her?”

“This-” Athena handed her the SD card. “-is everything we’ve got.”

“...and what is this?”

“Crime scene photos,” Eddie answered.

“Forensic photos of her home from the search,” Athena expanded.

“She stole them from the FBI.”

“I transferred custody.”

“Buck gets it from you, doesn’t he?”

Athena gave him a flat look, before turning back to Karen.

“We’re hoping that you might have something around here that could let us take a look at what’s on there,” she said.

“You said there’s only one dose of the antiviral?” Karen asked as she stood up from the couch.

“She used the other one on a rat,” Eddie said.

“Then I guess we need to thank God that only one of them is sick.”

“Yeah…”

Eddie glanced at Athena and caught her eying him back. The exchange must’ve been grim-looking enough to pique Karen’s concern.

“What?” she asked, glancing between them. “What is it?”

Eddie sighed before answering.

“The explosion tore a hole in Buck’s line,” he said. “He patched it, but…”

Karen closed her eyes and drew in a breath. When she opened them again, they’d gone steely and her expression was set in stone.

“Then we should be extra quick about it,” she said.

Karen went and fetched her laptop, bringing it out to the kitchen. She set it on the kitchen island and, once it was booted up, inserted the SD card into one of the ports along the side. When it was loaded, she pulled the file up and clicked on the first picture, one of Moira’s living room.

“For crime scene photos, it doesn’t look like much of a crime scene. More like an IKEA catalog.” She clicked on to the next photo, this one of twin salt and pepper shakers, positioned neatly side-by-side and right in the middle of a woven mat on a table. The next picture was of a kitchen counter, drawers pulled out to show the disturbingly organized contents. “She clearly lives at the lab and the house is just a place to shower, change clothes, and occasionally order takeout.”

That sounded a lot like how Buck described his old loft, before he moved in with Eddie and Chris.

“That’s a lonely way to live,” Athena commented.

“Maybe not,” Karen replied. “I’m guessing people don’t interest her.”

“Because she’s a psychotic bitch,” Eddie spat out.

“Neither of us are going to argue with you there,” Athena said.

Karen clicked on to the next photo, this one of a bookshelf. They looked like a mixture of biographies and what might’ve been self-help books, if one wanted help being completely unlikable. Eddie didn’t recognize any of them, except for the Marie Curie biography.

Buck had it sitting on their own shelf at home.

Something about them clearly caught Karen’s attention, though. She was leaning in for a closer look, but refocused on Athena when the sergeant pulled out her phone.

“Williams, tell me you found something,” was how Athena answered. A moment later, she lowered her phone and set it to speaker. “Her car? Where is it?”

“Right next to me,” Williams answered. “In the parking lot of SoCal Tech Biomed.”

“No one thought to check and see if her car was still there!?” Eddie just about shouted.

“We know she stole the ID badge of one colleague, and she stole the tumbler and handbag of another,” Athena said, motioning for Eddie to shut up. “Maybe that’s not the only thing she stole. Take a look around, see if there’s any empty parking spots nearby.”

“Uh… Yeah. One two spots down. Belong to a R. McLeod.”

“Roz,” Eddie guessed. “Her keys were probably in her bag.”

They really should’ve thought of that earlier. He figured they could be forgiven, though, circumstances and all.

“You did great, Williams,” Athena said into the phone. “See if you can find the car that goes in that spot. Our suspect might be in it.”

“Alright, Sergeant. I’ll let you know what I come up with.”

“I think I got something,” Karen declared when Athena put her phone away. “Photos on her wall.”

Eddie went back to peering at the laptop screen over Karen’s shoulder. Like the rest of her house, the photos on Moira’s wall were aligned neatly with perfect right angles and even spacing. There were a bunch of old-timey looking portraits in black and white, which made the colored photo in the middle stand out even more. It was of a girl with a blue ribbon, in front of a science project.

“Who is that?” Athena asked. “Tween Moira?”

“Look who else is up there.” Karen started pointing at the other pictures, identifying who they showed. “Samantha Blum, pioneer for RNA research. Alexander Fleming, penicillin. Jacques Durand, peptide synthesis.”

“Hijo de puta.” Eddie closed his eyes and pinched the bridge of his nose as he started to realize what was going on here.

“They’re all scientists,” Athena said.

“Not just any scientists, they’re all Nobel laureates,” Karen said. “They’re like the rock stars of science.”

“It’s a wall of fame. And Moira put herself right in the middle of them.”

“But you don’t win a Nobel prize for starting a pandemic.”

“She’s Jonah Greenway,” Eddie groaned. “Douchebag started fires because the actual job was more boring than he expected and he wanted excitement. But Greenway hurt people so he could get credit for saving them, so he could be a hero.”

“She wants credit for providing the cure for a disease she created,” Karen concluded.

“Where would you go if you had the next big cure?” Athena asked, clearly thinking aloud.

“You wouldn’t give it to the government,” Eddie said. They were just as likely to squirrel the antiviral away for a rainy day, and then erase anything crediting Moira for the work.

The superstrain of CCHF that Moira made wouldn’t be much of a pandemic. It was too deadly and progressed far too rapidly to spread very far. Not like COVID or the flu or HIV, all of which had a period of time where the person was infectious but didn’t show any symptoms. A period that lasted days or, in the case of HIV, weeks to months.

This superstrain only had an hour before symptoms showed, and it was only airborne if it got aerosolized. Ticks were how CCHF was normally spread, but this strain would kill off its hosts before the parasites had any chance to feed, and they wouldn’t feed off a corpse. It wasn’t a good candidate to be the next pandemic. But as a weapon? Someone, somewhere, was salivating at the thought of it.

(Eddie was coldly certain that was why they weren’t letting Buck and them out of the lab. A new weapon had to be properly tested, after all.)

“You wouldn’t give it to anyone,” Karen stated, tearing Eddie out of the dark train of thought he’d gone down.

“No,” Athena agreed. “You’d sell it.”

Chapter 44: Rhino Rocket

Chapter Summary

In which a psychopath is located, MacGyver once again saves the day, and Eddie asks someone unexpected for a favor.

Ravi took the thermometer out of the beaker with the homemade saline, tapping it on the edge before reading it. They’d moved the beaker off the hotplate they’d used to get the water boiling, and put it on a bunsen burner he had managed to scrounge up. They wanted it warm, but they didn’t want it too warm, hence the change in heat sources.

“It’s 104.5 degrees,” Ravi reported to Hen.

“Still too hot,” she said. “It’s gotta be under ninety-eight before we can give it to him.”

“Good thing we’re not going anywhere,” Ravi remarked, sticking the thermometer back in. He picked up his phone where he’d set it on the table, debating with himself.

“You should call him.”

Ravi turned to her and shrugged.

“He’ll just worry,” he said.

“He’s probably worrying already,” she argued, looking up at him from where she was laying on the table. “With other couples, I’d say it would change things for them if you called. That if you make it out of here, it would be harder for them each time they have to watch you leave. It’s why I’m not calling Karen yet, as much as I want to. But for the two of you…”

He chewed on his lip for a moment, and then thumbed his phone to life. The contact he wanted was near the top of the list, the second to last person he’d texted. It was with a request for a stop at Monty’s on his way home.

“Rav!” was how Albert answered. He sounded frantic, and Ravi imagined he looked frantic, too. It wasn’t a video call; Ravi didn’t want to worry Albert even more by letting him actually see the mess they were in. “Oh, thank God.”

“Hey, Alley Cat.”

“Don’t you-” Albert broke off, spitting a litany of Korean that went by too quickly for Ravi to parse. Hen was snickering behind him. “Are you okay?”

“I am… I’m more fine than the others,” Ravi answered, because it was true. Chimney was actively dying, Hen had a tube in her chest, and they were all waiting for Buck to start puking blood. “Have you been, um. Have you been listening over the radio?”

“I kinda left mine charging back at the station,” Albert answered, sounding sheepish. “I got there with Bell, and then Tanika told us that something had happened.”

“You left it at the- Where are you now?”

“Outside the lab. I don’t know what I was expecting to do, I just… Took the ambulance and rushed here, sirens blaring.”

Ravi felt the smile creep over his face. He was in love with this idiot.

“I really wanted to hear your voice,” he said, and resisted the urge to glance at Hen. He didn’t want to know what face she was making behind her breather, didn’t want to know if it was fond or sad. “But I’m really glad you’re not here with me.”

“I’m right out here waiting.”

Ravi opened his mouth to reply, and found that he couldn’t. The silence behind him from Hen was heavy.

“Ravi?”

Albert sounded worried again. His head was no doubt filling with all sorts of possibilities for why Ravi wasn’t saying anything.

“I’m still here,” he quickly answered. He pulled out the thermometer and checked it, just to have something to do. It was still too hot.  “I’m just, uh. I’m waiting for our homemade saline to cool.”

“Homemade saline?”

“Yeah. For Chimney.”

A moment of silence, where Ravi could hear the wind and distant chatter in the background.

“How is he?”

“He’s…” Ravi looked over to where Chimney was hunched over on himself and decided to lie. “He’s fine, Al. Joking and everything.”

“He’ll be cracking jokes on his death bed.”

“Yeah.” This time Ravi couldn’t resist the urge to check on Hen, and he knew the expression she wore behind her breather was heartbreak. “Yeah, he probably will.”

Buck checked the lone bag of saline they had, which hung from an improvised IV stand. It was fitting with today’s theme, at least. The bag was emptying quickly, and their cooked up replacement still wasn’t ready.

“Hey.” Buck lightly kicked Chimney in the thigh until the man lifted his head to stare balefully at him. The poor lighting was surely to blame for Chimney’s worrisome complexion, Buck decided. “No napping, you’re on the clock.”

“I think I deserve a nap.”

“What do you mean?” Buck crouched down in front of Chimney, and reached out to poke him in the shoulder. From this angle, it was impossible to miss how bad he looked. The piece of gauze in his nostril was far more red than it was white, now. “Ravi and I have been the ones running around doing the heavy liftin’. You and Hen have just been lying down on the job.”

“You’re still young, you’re supposed to be the ones running around while your elders rest,” Chimney tiredly argued. “Hey, was Gavin difficult?”

“Difficult?”

“You know…” Chimney’s shoulders lifted in a limp attempt at a shrug. “All the moms keep telling me that a boy is easier. All the dads keep saying that a boy is harder.”

“Oh, in that case, Gavin’s a right terror,” Buck joked. “I don’t know, Chim. Pops would probably be better to ask, I just have Chris to compare him to and the times I’ve babysat Jee-Yun. But the diapers are more dangerous, I never had to dodge artillery fire while changing Jee.”

Chimney chuckled weakly.

“I’ll remember that,” he said. “You know, I hated my dad so much for leaving. And now I’m about to do the same thing.”

“Chim, no, you…” Buck shook his head as he tried to come up with a reply. “Did- Did you hate your mom?”

“What?” Chimney gave him a squinty glare. “No. She was sick, she didn’t- Oh.”

“Not that it matters.” Buck took hold of Chimney’s leg and gave it a light shake. “We’re all gonna get out of here. You’re not going anywhere but home.”

“Buck, c’mon,” the other man scoffed. “This thing is moving fast, and I’m running out of time. So I need you to listen to me. Please.”

“Chim…” He sighed and dropped his head a little. “Yeah, okay.”

“Maddie’s gonna want to shoulder it all. She’s gonna tell everybody she’s fine, and everyone’s gonna believe her. ‘Cause she’s Maddie,” Chimney said, his words as serious as his blood-covered face. “But you and I, we know her better than that. I know you’re not gonna leave her alone, I know you’re gonna take care of her and the kids. I know you will.”

“Of course, Chim-”

“But I need you to promise me it, okay?” Chimney’s stare was beseeching. “Promise me.”

Chimney raised up his hand, pinky finger sticking out. Buck was struck by the memory of Eddie making Maddie the same promises, years ago now, before she went back to Boston. He sighed and hooked his pinky around Chimney’s.

“I promise,” Buck said. “Not that it matters. We’re all getting out of here.”

The way that Chimney started to cough immediately after Buck said that, globs of bloody phlegm flying out of his mouth, had to have been on purpose. The timing was just too good, otherwise.

When Officer Williams called to report that he had located Roz McLeod’s car, Athena did not let grass grow beneath her feet or her tires. She crossed the distance in record time, taking corners roughly enough that Eddie grabbed whatever he could get ahold of and held on for dear life. He looked relieved, and a little bit green, by the time she was pulling the cruiser to a stop just beside William’s.

The officer himself was glancing through the windows of a bright blue car, but he came to meet her half way when she got out.

“I think this is the first time I found a stolen car before anyone’s reported it stolen,” he remarked. “The parking attendant says it’s been here less than an hour.”

“I don’t suppose he saw which way she went after she parked.”

“He was slammed,” was the officer’s unfortunate, but expected, answer. “Yogalates class down the street just let out.”

Yogalates. Yoga pilates. That might have been one of the whitest things Athena had ever heard of, and she was married to a man from Minnesota who once served a casserole topped with tater tots for dinner.

“Did you see anything inside?” Eddie asked, peering through the windows of the car.

“Just a pack of mints and some tissue with lipstick on it,” Williams said.

Tissue with lipstick- Oh.

“She was blotting, which means she was worried about her appearance,” Athena stated. And if Moira was worried about her appearance, that meant she was intending to meet someone she wanted to make a good impression on. Like a potential buyer for the antiviral. “Eddie, can you pull up that list of Big Pharma addresses?”

“I could,” Eddie said, straightening up. He was looking up at something. “But I think we should start with that one.”

Athena turned to see what he was pointing at, and then felt very dumb. The parking lot they were in was right next to a tall office building, and at the top of the building was a large sign that read: Martel-Harvey Pharmaceuticals.

The lobby for the building, when she and Eddie went in, wasn’t quite gaudy. It was open, airy, with a central staircase that split off into two at the first landing. There were various uncomfortable looking comfy chairs dotting the place and a reception desk made of what looked like black marble or a knockoff of it, right by the base of the stairs.

“I can’t believe she just walked in,” Eddie said as they did just that. “And, what? Said ‘I have a science experiment I want to sell’?”

“Who knows,” Athena remarked as she went to the receptionist. “Hi, excuse me. We’re looking for Moira Blake. Five-nine, red hair.”

“A bit loco,” Eddie added, twirling his finger over his ear.

“You got here fast,” a man in an expensive looking suit said, hurrying down the stairs. “She’s in the conference room. Walked in off the street to set a pitch meeting. Which, red flag.”

So apparently she did literally just walk in and say she had a science experiment to sell.

“What do you mean, we got here fast?” Athena asked, a sinking feel at the pit of her stomach.

“I just called five minutes ago.”

Fuck.

“Who did you call?” Eddie sounded like he already knew the answer, just like her, but wanted to kill his hope entirely.

“Nine-one-one.”

Again: fuck.

“Show me,” Athena ordered, and followed as the man led her to the stairs. Eddie started to follow, but she stopped him. “Stay here, watch the door. I think we’re gonna have company.”

He scowled, but nodded, and stepped back to hover by the reception desk. As Athena turned away, she saw him pulling out his phone. His other hand was buried in a pocket.

The man in the suit led her up several flights, to a large conference room. Two sides were taken up by windows, showing a view of the city, and there was a long conference table. Roz’s bag was in one of the chairs, which meant Moira was here. She just wasn’t anywhere to be seen at that moment.

“But- She was just here…” the man said.

Athena grabbed the bag, placing it on the table to rifle through it. But the tumbler, and the antiviral, was also nowhere to be found.

“Hi.” A woman’s voice, uncertain sounding.

She turned, spotting Moira having just reentered the room. She had a disposable paper cup and a doughnut of some sort.

“Hi, Moira,” Athena said. “You’re under arrest.”

“I swear,” Moira said, trying to play stupid and innocent. “I thought the pastries were for everyone.”

“I figure we’d start with assault, arson, attempted murder.” She was not in the mood to entertain this woman’s bullshit today.

“Wow.” Moira dropped the attempt to act innocent, at least. “All that, and you’re not even out of the A’s yet.”

“And we both know that isn’t your purse.”

“God, no. It’s hideous.”

She thought she was funny. Athena hated when they thought they were funny.

“I’m gonna need that antiviral,” Athena said, resting her hand on her holstered gun.

“My life’s work?” Moira sounded, and looked, offended by the idea. “He was about to pay me millions for it.”

“I was not,” the man, standing next to Athena, immediately denied.

“Still, it’s my only bargaining chip.”

“Where is it?” Athena demanded.

“You know.” Moira was talking to the man again, and if Athena had the time to care, she’d probably make an effort to get his name. “I figured you called the police when you didn’t come back.”

“You hid it.”

But where did she hide it? There wasn’t a lot of options in this room, but she also left the room to get the-

The nearby watercooler, standing just between the two of them, burbled as a bubble of air rose to the top. There was a cabinet at the base of it. Moira’s eyes flickered to it. Because she thought she was a genius, but she was actually kind of an idiot.

To prove that she was an idiot, she dropped everything and tried to make a break for the cabinet. Athena had her gun out and pointed at her in moments.

“Stop!” Athena barked, and Moira froze with her hands in the air. She looked terrified, and Athena felt a flicker of pleasure over it. To the company man, she said, “Do me a favor and check that container.”

In the cabinet, filled with the same kind of disposable cups that Moira was holding moments earlier, was the tumbler. The man took it out, holding it gingerly.

Athena enjoyed putting the cuffs on Moira. She enjoyed yanking her around by the arm, with a grip that was no doubt leaving bruises. The psychopath complained the entire time, because she honestly thought she was getting a Nobel prize instead of a prison sentence out of this, but Athena ignored her.

They’d just reached the stairs when Eddie came rushing up.

“Wrong way,” he said, nudging her into changing directions. “You got the vial?”

“Yeah.” Athena held up the tumbler. “The FBI’s here?”

“Just downstairs. So we’re going up.”

Eddie literally meant up. They climbed and climbed, until they ran out of stairs, and then they found a ladder. All the way to the roof.

“This was your big idea?” Athena shouted, because he’d led them to a dead end.

“No.” Eddie sounded like he was dreading something as the sound of helicopter blades got closer. “That was.”

Her hair blew in the wind as the helicopter reached them and started to land on the building’s pad. She stared at it, at the Channel 8 News logo on its side, and then turned to glare at Eddie.

“You called her!?”

“I don’t like it either, okay!?” he snapped back.

“There is no way I am getting in that death trap!” Moira argued, struggling in their grips.

“Listen, psycho bitch,” Eddie snapped at her. “You either get in that helicopter, or I throw you off the roof.”

Normally, Athena wouldn’t think that threat had teeth, but these were not normal circumstances. Moira definitely believed him, because she went wide-eyed behind her glasses and gave a meek little nod. And she didn’t struggle as Eddie dragged her to the helicopter, pausing for a moment to pull open the cockpit door.

“Hola, Diaz!” Taylor Kelly shouted from within. Athena could see her tapping away at her phone in the copilot’s seat.

“Witch,” she heard Eddie reply as he shoved Moira into the helicopter. There was no gentleness involved, either.

“I gotta make a call, too!” Athena told him, pulling out her phone.

Eddie glanced back at her and just nodded, before climbing in as well.

By the time Santos and his agents reached the roof top, the chopper was in the air and flying away.

“Are you sure about this, Chim?” Buck asked as he fiddled with his phone. “Hearing is one thing. Seeing you right now…”

“Are you calling me ugly?” Chimney asked, all fake offense.

“I always call you ugly, man.”

“I want to talk to her,” the paramedic said. “I want… I want to see her.”

Buck nodded in understanding and hit the call button. It rang a few times and then Maddie’s face filled the screen. She was in the break room, the dispatch floor visible through the glass behind her.

“Hey, Mads.” He gave her a wave that might have been off screen to her. “Chimney wants to talk to you.”

He turned the phone around so it was facing Chimney.

“Hi. It’s good to see your face.”

“Yeah, I think this is a good look for me,” Chimney said. Buck rolled his eyes, not that either of them saw it. “How’s work going?”

“You know, the usual.”

“Yeah, same here. I think I might pass out from boredom.”

Okay, no. Buck was not gonna stay here and hold the phone for however long this was gonna last. Trapped or not, he had better things to be doing. Namely, literally anything else.

“And that would be very bad,” Buck said, taking Chimney’s hand and forcing his fingers around the phone. “Maddie, keep him awake while I check on the saline.”

He didn’t stick around to listen to whatever she said next, nor Chimney’s reply. Except, maybe he should have. Because it felt like no sooner did Buck step out of the specimens room that he heard gagging and groaning from behind him, and Maddie shouting from the phone.

The phone that was now on the floor while Chimney, bent over beside it, was pouring blood from his nose like a faucet.

“Chim!” Buck rushed over, doing his best to keep the panic at bay when he saw how much blood was already on the floor. “Ravi! Get the gauze!”

“We’re out of gauze!” Ravi replied a moment later.

“Then bring me a towel! Or a sock! Anything!” Buck shouted back. “Okay, Chim, just uh... Stay calm, alright? Don’t panic.”

The side-eye he received for that was well-deserved, and a little bit heartening.

“Here!” Ravi was suddenly shoving torn up bits of what might’ve been a triangular bandage, the kind of thing normally used to make slings.

Buck wasn’t complaining. He just forced it into Chimney’s hand, and then pushed his hand towards his face.

“Just hold that to your nose, okay? Just- Just hold it there,” he urged. “Hen, Rav, where’s the saline!?”

“Not there quite yet!” was Hen’s reply.

Buck stifled the cursing he wanted to let out. He wasn’t sure they had time to wait for the saline to cool down to a temp that was safe enough to be pumped into Chimney’s veins. He pressed more of the bandage scraps into Chimney’s nose, and did his best to slow down the flow.

Ravi came bursting into the room with the beaker, shouting,

“I got the saline!”

“Oh thank God,” Buck blurted out.

He scrambled to his feet and rushed to the now empty, shriveled IV bag of saline hanging from the impromptu stand. It was not a particularly neat process to get the new batch of saline into it, as the things were not exactly meant to be reused. They were meant to be emptied and then tossed.

By the end of it, though, they had the refilled bag hanging from the stand. Even if it was needing to be clamped shut.

“Can one of you check his pulse?” Hen requested from the other room, where she was laid out on the table still.

Buck knelt down beside Chimney, pressed his fingers to the man’s neck. It was high, but that was to be expected.

“It’s at one-thirty,” Buck called back to her.

“You’re sure?”

“Yeah.” Something about her voice worried him. “Why?”

“The capillaries in his nasal cavities are dissolving,” she said. “The saline bought us a few minutes, but he’s losing blood faster than we can replace it.”

“The bleed is coming from way up there, Hen. We need a Rhino Rocket.”

“We don’t have one!”

A Rhino Rocket was… Okay, it was basically a tampon. Much like they packed severe enough wounds by stuffing gauze into them, the Rhino Rocket was a bit of foam that was inserted up into the nostril. And like a tampon, that bit of foam would expand as it absorbed the blood, which would also put pressure on the bleed.

“Okay, so- so what else!?”

“I don’t know!”

Rage flooded Buck’s veins, leaving no space in him for the fear and the anxiety. There was just the rage, and the absolute refusal to simply give up. He stormed across the room to the door, to glare at Hen.

“No! That is not good enough!” he snapped at her. “You need to help me come up with something that we can-”

“Cap!” Ravi sounded panicked. “He’s unconscious!”

“Fuck,” Buck swore, running back to them. “Get him onto that table.”

There were things on top of that table, expensive looking things. Some of them broke when Buck swept them all to the floor without a care. The two of them hauled Chimney off the floor and laid him out on top of it, on his back. The impromptu IV stand was too short to be useful now, so Buck had to grab the bag and hold it up.

“BP’s falling off a cliff,” Ravi reported. “He’s fifty-four palp.”

That was low. That was really, really low.

“Start compressions,” Buck ordered, too busy keeping the saline flowing to do it himself.

Hen was making pained noises from the main part of the lab, but Buck didn’t have any more attention to spare for her. It was all focused on Chimney, and on Ravi pressing at his chest. At least until he heard wheels squeaking across the floor and Hen shouting for them to,

“Move!”

She was using an office chair to get herself and her oxygen set-up into the specimens room with them.

“What the hell, Hen?” Buck blurted out, even as he moved out of her way. “You have a hole in your chest to keep your lung from collapsing!”

“So we’re gonna do this fast,” she replied as she wheeled herself to Chimney’s side. She had one of their spare IV lines, and was tearing it out of its packaging. “It’s mostly from his left nostril, right? Ravi, fill a syringe with water.”

“Sterile water?”

“Any water.”

Ravi nodded and ran off to do as he was asked. Hen, meanwhile, fed the end of the IV tubing into Chimney’s nose. It didn’t take long for Ravi to return with the syringe, he just used the sink nearby.

“What are we doing, Hen?” Buck asked her.

“I’m gonna use the water to expand the cuff on this line and fill up his nasal cavity,” she explained as she took the syringe from Ravi and placed it at the port, and then began pushing the water. “If we’re lucky, it’ll stop the bleed.”

“A homemade Rhino Rocket.”

“Exactly. Shears?”

“Right here,” Ravi said, and handed her a pair of trauma shears from the kit. She used it to clip the end of the tube off.

And then they were stuck playing the waiting game once more. That was what they’d been doing this entire time, after all. They waited and they waited until-

There was a happy sounding chirp.

“BP’s rising!” Ravi announced. “Fifty-eight palp!”

Chimney’s eyes fluttered open with a groan, and then he looked at Hen in confusion.

“You’re not supposed to be in here,” he said. “What’s going on?”

“I told you that we’re all getting out of here, that’s what,” Buck told him.

He went and scooped up his phone from the floor, thankful the blood hadn’t reached it yet. Maddie was still on the line, her worried face filling the screen. At the top was a text notification, and for once Buck found himself breathing easier.

“Hey Mads,” he said. “I’ve got really good news.”

“Is he okay?”

“He’s stable, but that’s not the good news,” he said. “Ma’s got the antiviral, and she’s on her way.”

On a sidewalk a block away from Martel-Harvey, Athena waited for her ride. The helicopter wasn’t a safe way to escape from the government stooges and get back to the lab unaccosted, she’d realized. The army would chase it down with their own air support and bring it to ground somewhere. Then they’d take the antiviral, throw them all into a cell, and go back to watching Chimney die, followed by everyone else in the lab.

But that very fact would serve to keep the army distracted, keep them looking elsewhere while she snuck around behind them. If they thought she was in the air, they would never think to look in the streets. It would give her enough time to get the cure to where it needed to be.

Hopefully.

A truck came to a stop on the curb, right in front of her. The locks popped and she grabbed the handle to yank the door open, to be greeted by the smiling driver.

“Hey, baby,” Bobby said. “Sorry to keep you waiting.”

“I think you got here just in time,” Athena said as she climbed in, slamming her door closed behind her.

He held out his hand and she took it in hers.

And then he hit the gas.

Chapter 45: Sleight of Hand

Chapter Summary

In which there is a (rather boring) chase involving helicopters.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

When Eddie called Taylor, she’d sounded surprised at first. Understandably so, because he had her number blocked for the past couple of years. Plus, he hated her very much, and so never made any efforts to reach out to her for any reason other than to berate her for something.

When Eddie explained the situation to Taylor, as quickly but concisely as he could, the surprise switched to interest. Which again made sense. The reporter was a vulture, and this corpse of a story was too juicy for her to resist. It was one of the reasons he had called her, out of all the other options.

When Eddie asked her for the favor, Taylor said yes right away and it was his turn to be surprised. But it made sense, he had to admit that. As much as he hated her, Buck was her friend. Eddie remembered how upset she had been, when Buck was struck by that bolt of lightning and no one knew if he would be okay. So it made perfect sense that she would come through now.

It didn’t mean that Eddie liked her now, and it didn’t mean he wasn’t loathing every moment spent in her presence.

“You’re Dr. Moira Blake, right? M-O-I-R-A B-L-A-K-E?” Taylor asked over the cacophony of the rotors. She’d been tapping away at her phone the entire flight. “The woman who made the super strain and the antiviral.”

“And future Nobel laureate,” Moira replied.

“She’s a crazy bitch,” Eddie told them, and ignored the woman’s protests and complaints. 

“Let me make sure I have the highlights,” Taylor said. She raised her hand, lifting up her fingers as she listed everything off. “Dr. Blake develops the disease and the cure, gets fired, then sets fire to the lab and steals the cure. First responders arrive, get trapped due to an explosion, and are exposed to the disease. Army arrives and then the FBI, both refuse to let the trapped firefighters - note to self, put emphasis on them all being Medal of Valor recipients - out of the lab, and make it clear they won’t use the cure on any of them.”

It left a cold feeling in Eddie’s chest, that this disaster, this near tragedy, could be summed up so simply and casually. Taylor made it sound like a traffic report, almost. The 110 will be backed up today because of construction work, and Firefighter-Paramedic Han is bleeding to death from his nose.

“That’s… Pretty much it,” Eddie told her, reaching into his pocket. It held the chain with his St. Christopher medallion and wedding ring, and he rubbed his thumb over them both.

“You said the FBI agent in charge was Santos. What was the colonel’s name?”

“Civilian aircraft.” The voice of the colonel in question came in over the radio. “This is Colonel Hartman of the United States Army. You are impeding a military operation, and are to land immediately. Copy?”

“Nevermind.”

“Uh. What do you want me to say?” the pilot asked.

“Let me do the talking, Trent. Just focus on flying,” Taylor told him, and then asked the colonel, “How do you spell that?”

There was a beat where the only noise was the rotors and the wind.

“What?”

“How do you spell your name? With or without an E?”

“I repeat, you are to land immediately. We are providing you with an escort. Over.”

“Oh, yeah, you definitely talked our way out of this,” Eddie snarked as a military helicopter rose up behind them like a shadow from the depths and immediately repositioned itself to their right. “Talk to your boss downstairs, maybe he can get us a good lawyer.”

“Your jokes never get old, Diaz,” Taylor said, without an ounce of sincerity.

“They’re motioning for us to land,” Trent, the pilot, commented. “What do you want me to do?”

“The point is to waste their time. Show us some fancy flying.”

“We’re in a news chopper, Taylor, not a jet fighter.”

Nevertheless, Trent banked hard to the left and dove down a little. They flew with no destination in mind, simply with the intent of leading their pursuers on a merry chase over the city. That didn’t change when a second helicopter joined the first, the pair taking turns dropping down from above to cut them off. It was very obvious that they were being herded along somewhere, and their pilot made no efforts to avoid it.

“I don’t think we’re gonna get a choice about landing soon,” Trent announced to them.

“How far are we from the lab?” Eddie asked, because that was what mattered.

“Far enough,” Taylor answered, and then pointed outside. “I think they want us to go there. Try not to park it in the seats this time, Trent.”

“We were crashing!”

They landed in the field at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, the two military helicopters harrying them the entire way until their rotors were slowing to a stop and their struts were touching grass. Columns of soldiers marched down the steps in a controlled rush, FBI agents following along.

“Exit the aircraft!” Colonel Hartman ordered over a megaphone. Santos was right beside him. “And surrender the vial!”

“They’ll drag us out if we don’t,” Eddie said, and then slid the door open.

“Is all this for me?” Moira asked as he dragged her out with him.

“Hello!” Taylor greeted them brightly, phone clutched in her hand. It was restarting, Eddie noticed. “I’m guessing you’re Colonel Hartman, and you’re Special Agent Santos?”

“Sergeant Grant, come out!” Hartman was opting to ignore Taylor, apparently. That was always the sensible path to take. “Or we will come in and get you!”

“Uh, about that…” Eddie said, hands raised.

“What does that mean?” Santos demanded, and then let out a curse when he was able to see inside the helicopter. “She isn’t here.”

“Staff Sergeant,” Hartman barked. Muscle memory had Eddie snapped to attention at that tone coming from an officer of his rank. “Where is Athena Grant?”

“Not here, sir,” Eddie replied. “We took off in a helicopter, sir, it wasn’t all that subtle of an escape. Half of you were right there to watch us go.”

“Since we’re all here, though,” Taylor said. “Would either of you like to make a statement on the record?”

From the twin glares on both Hartman’s and Santos’ faces, Eddie was guessing the answer to that was a very firm negative.

One of the doors to the lab had a hatch, used to transfer things in and out while minimizing the risk of exposure. Buck knew this, because Athena texted it to him, along with the notice that she was not only on site, but she was on her way down to the lab. Which meant Buck was scrambling to find the door she was talking about.

He found it just as Athena arrived on the other side, looking like something out of a scifi movie in her hazmat suit.

“I’m here to make a deposit,” she announced as she shoved the package into the hatch.

Buck waited until he heard the chirp indicating her side was closed before yanking it open, finding the vial and a large syringe.

“You are the best, Ma,” he gushed to her, tapping his visor against the window separating them.

“I know,” she said. “Are you…?”

“No.” He shook his head. “I’m not feeling anything.”

“Good. Go save Chimney.”

Buck nodded and turned to go, just as a pair of men in beige hazmat suits entered the hall Athena was in. He felt kind of giddy with it, with the fact that they’d managed to snag the antiviral and keep it out of the military’s grasp. It was the same kind of feeling he got whenever he got away with a prank.

Chimney and the others were right where he’d left them, looking no better, but also not significantly worse. Ravi and Hen, the latter of whom had taken over holding the IV bag for him, both visibly perked up at his return.

“Let’s hope this is an actual miracle,” Buck told them.

“Rush a miracle man…” Chimney mumbled.

“Get rotten miracles,” Buck finished for him.

He tugged the cap off the syringe’s needle, dropping it onto the floor without a single care. He stuck the needle through the vial’s top, pulling back the plunger until the syringe was filled. And then, with his breath held, he stuck the syringe into Chimney’s IV, and injected the antiviral.

The waiting game continued again.

When Athena was marched into the command tent by a very annoyed Special Agent Santos, along with a pair of unfriendly soldiers, she was greeted by the sight of Eddie looking very perturbed about being stuck in close proximity to Taylor Kelly. The reporter, for her part, was observing everyone serenely, but with keen interest in her eyes, while her pilot from the news chopper seemed very uncomfortable to be there. Moira was still handcuffed, but looked for all the world like nothing about this situation bothered her.

She was probably still waiting to be awarded a prize.

“Athena!” Eddie exclaimed when he saw her. “Is Buck…?”

“He says he’s fine.”

The words seemed to ease his mind only a little, not that she could blame him. She wasn’t going to start counting her chickens until they were all out of that hellhole of a laboratory beneath them.

“Have you seen an arrest warrant yet, Sergeant?” Taylor asked, clapping her hands together. “Because I sure haven’t.”

“I have not,” Athena confirmed with a shake of her head. “I’m thinking Agent Santos here is just being a little dramatic. I doubt anyone’s actually under arrest.”

“That’s great,” Moira said, and Athena turned her head to pin her with a glare.

“Except for you. You are definitely under arrest.”

“You obstructed a federal investigation,” Santos told her, all smarm. “Did you really think we were gonna let that stand?”

Athena scoffed.

“Do you think your bosses are gonna let you stand up in open court and tell this country just how close we came to another pandemic?”

“Oh, I don’t think court’s what they have to worry about,” Taylor stated, examining her fingernails. “I think they should be more concerned with the email scheduled to be sent off just in time to become tonight’s top news story.”

Santos paled.

“I am not concerned about the legality, or the publicity,” the colonel said. “Sergeant Grant, you wasted the planet’s only dose of the antiviral on a man who’s already sitting at death’s door. A man who-”

“Is looking lively,” Eddie interrupted, pointing at the screen showing the security footage of the lab.

On it, Athena could see Chimney sitting up and waving at the camera. She could also see Buck giving the camera both fingers.

“See?” Moira spoke up, ruining the moment. “I’m a genius.”
