“So if he’s cured, there’s not much of a reason to keep them stuck in there,” Taylor stated, giving Moira a sideways glare. “Is there?”

Santos huffed, turned, pointed an angry finger at Taylor.

“I want that email deleted, Ms. Martin, before it gets sent to anyone.”

Taylor glowered, mouth pulling into a thin line. For a moment, Athena wasn’t certain she was going to agree, wasn’t certain she’d agree in Taylor’s place. And then-

“As soon as they’re all out,” the reporter said.

The Special Agent stormed out of the tent, the colonel following more sedately while barking orders at people. 

The pilot frowned at Taylor.

“Your last name’s Martin?”

“Shut up, Trent.”

“Bunny suits are back!” Ravi announced, with far more cheer in his voice than had been present before.

Buck walked over to see for himself. Sure enough, a trio of soldiers in the beige hazmat suits were making their way down the hall on the other side of the security wall. The one in the lead was waving around a detector, which was in a matching beige camo pattern. A second of the trio had a tablet clutched in his hands, and was peering at it intently instead of watching where he was going.

“Thank God,” he said, feeling the tension start to bleed out of his shoulders. “I hope that means we’re all getting out of here soon.”

“Thanks for not letting me quit this morning,” Ravi suddenly said. “I’m really glad I didn’t.”

“Rav.” Buck threw his arm over the other man’s shoulders. "I’m really glad for it, too. ‘Cause I don’t think I could’ve kept those two alive by myself.”

A shrill alarm cut through the air, and then the security wall began to rise a moment later. The other members of the 118 were on the other side, in full SCBA gear and carrying a pair of backboards. The moment the wall was retracted fully, they were swarming into the wrecked lab.

Eddie, at the front of the group, went directly for Buck. He didn’t say anything, just rushed him and threw his arms around him, their visors clinking together. The last of the lingering tension and anxiety and panic melted out of Buck entirely, leaving him lightheaded and thankful that he had Eddie to lean on.

Falling over now would not be a good look for him.

“Okay,” he said after a moment, reluctantly pulling away. “Hen needs to get out ASAP. She had a collapsed lung, and she has a tube from a spray bottle sticking out of her chest.”

“Is that what this is?” Hen asked, lifting it up. The beaker attached to the end of it was half-filled with blood that frothed.

“Got it!” Toby said, heading for her with one of the backboards.

Once they got everyone unhooked from their blue umbilical cords keeping them tethered to the lab’s ceiling, it was a frenzy of motion getting everyone out. Hen first, with Ravi helping carry her, and then Chimney. The latter, for whatever reason, had a passenger.

“I thought Jee-Yun could use a pet,” the man explained as he clutched the cage containing the white rat from the specimens room.

“You’re the one explaining it to Maddie,” Buck told him. “Not me.”

“If they even let you keep it,” Eddie added.

Getting decontaminated was… A process. Buck was stripped and sprayed and scrubbed so thoroughly that, if he still had any ounce of body shame left in him, he might have been embarrassed. As it was, he simply enjoyed finally being out of his gear and breathing clean air again. 

At least until he was shoved into what basically amounted to pajamas and shuffled into another cage inside a tent. This cage was smaller, with walls made of plastic. Ravi was in the one beside him.

“Freedom tasted so sweet,” Buck bemoaned as he put the chain with the medallion and wedding band back around his neck. He’d managed to snag it before they took off with his clothes and turnouts, to either burn them or decontaminate them further, and nearly took someone’s hand off when it seemed like they were going to try and take the chain away. “For the five seconds we got to taste it.”

“He’s being dramatic, that’s a good sign.”

Buck spun around where he stood at the sound of Bobby’s voice, spotting him coming into the tent with Eddie and Athena and Albert, the latter of whom dashed forward to Ravi’s cage. They immediately pressed up to their sides of the plastic and started talking to each other in words too quiet to hear. Buck turned away to give them their privacy, going to the farthest side of his plastic cage to talk to the other three.

“I was nearly used as a lab rat by the army, Pops,” Buck said. “I’m allowed to be dramatic.”

“You think your day was bad?” Eddie pulled up a chair and sat down. “I called Taylor Kelly for a favor.”

“I fingered Hen!” Buck immediately countered and was confronted with three almost identical faces of disgust.

“Did you have to phrase it like that?” Athena asked, all suffering.

“Yes. Wait, what do you mean you called Taylor?”

“It’s a long story,” the sergeant said. “Eddie can tell you later.”

“Does that mean I’m not gonna be stuck here for long?”

“You shouldn’t be,” Bobby said. “Probably just long enough to make sure you aren’t going to suddenly start showing symptoms.”

“We’re going to check on Chimney and Hen, before they get shipped off,” Athena said. “We’ll be back.”

Buck watched Bobby and Athena leave, and then almost collapsed with a groan into the chair provided for him. The exhaustion of the day was catching up to him, and he desperately wanted to be in bed.

“I cannot wait to get home and see our kids,” he told Eddie. “What did you mean you called Taylor for a favor? What sort of favor?”

“An escape helicopter."

“A what?”

Chapter End Notes

Did you really think I was gonna kill Buck? In the fic fueled by spite against canon and the showrunners? Come on, now.

Chapter 46: Tentative

Chapter Summary

In which Buck touches base.

It wasn’t often that Buck sat on Dr. Copeland’s couch alone. Usually, he and Eddie had their sessions together. It differed from what she did with her other clients, and it wasn’t the same as couples counseling. Their lives were so intertwined, so many of their traumas shared, that it had made sense when they started.

But for this, Buck was there and Eddie wasn’t. Eddie wasn’t even waiting outside like he normally would have been, instead he was at one of his paramedic classes. Because this was more than just a normal session with their therapist.

“It wasn’t- It wasn’t all that scary at first, you know?” Buck told her, fingers digging into the fluffy pink pillow that he held in his lap. The one that reminded him of cotton candy. “It was scarier for Eddie than for me, when the explosion happened.”

“What makes you so sure of that?” Copeland asked. “Have you two talked about it?”

“Only a little,” he admitted. Mostly, they’d talked about what Eddie was doing with Athena the entire time. “But I know what it’s like to be on both sides of something like that. The explosion happened, and he couldn’t know if any of us were alive until they heard from us. But when I woke up, I could see for myself.”

“You said it wasn’t frightening at first,” she quoted. “But that fact didn’t stay true. When?”

“When I saw the security wall, when Ravi couldn’t get it to open,” he said. “When I realized we were locked in. That’s when I started feeling anxious, you know? When we go into any structure, we always make sure to have a clear egress. A way to get out in a hurry, if we have to.”

“But with the lab going into lockdown, you didn’t have one.”

“Yeah. That’s when I started getting a little scared. Then I had to do the surgery on Hen, and I- I’m just EMT trained. If you need someone to put in an IV, intubate a patient, do CPR, deliver a baby. Any of that, I’m your guy.”

“None of that sounds like surgery.”

“‘Cause it’s not,” Buck said. “I can’t- I can’t even remember if I’d ever used a scalpel on an actual person before Hen. I had to cut my friend open and then- I stuck my finger through her chest wall, doc. I felt it tear.”

“That sounds… Gruesome,” Copeland commented. She looked a little green.

“It was. And then Chimney started bleeding from everywhere, and things just… I- Honestly, I wasn’t scared at that point. When Eddie said they’d decided to keep us there. I just felt angry. Angry and so fucking hopeless.”

They talked about it a bit longer, the entire rest of their session. And they talked about afterwards, what he did when they finally did let him out. How he spent an entire day clinging to everyone and anyone he could. How Eddie spent the time clinging to him just as much. How he’d just started bawling like a baby in the middle of Eddie telling him about the helicopter chase and how much it had freaked out his husband, along with Ravi and Albert.

“Have you had any other moments like that?” Copeland asked.

Her gaze was sharp, her voice was sharp. It felt much like it had when they’d first started talking about those pesky suicidal tendencies of his, when they were talking about the full breadth of his coma dream. The way she asked now was much the same as when she asked him, bluntly and seriously, if he wanted to die.

(The answer to that was still no. A much firmer no than it had been even then.)

“No,” Buck said, as he said then, and watched her relax minutely.

“Our time is up,” she said, glancing at the clock on the wall. “Actually, it was up five minutes ago.”

“Oops.”

“I will email the results, and my professional opinion, to Chief Williams.”

“Did I pass?” Buck asked, putting the cotton candy pillow aside and standing up.

“Tentatively, yes,” she said, and it was his turn to relax. “When’s your next check-up appointment with Dr. Weaver?”

Dr. Weaver was the doctor that was officially prescribing his bupropion. He went in periodically for Weaver to check and make sure that the bupropion was still helping him, that none of the more concerning side effects were potentially rearing their heads, and to renew his prescription when both of those things were true. The appointments were stretched further apart now than when he was first put on the meds.

“Next month, just after our regular day. Why? Should I try to get it moved up?”

“No.” Copeland shook her head as she moved to her desk, setting her pen and note pad down on top of it. “Next month is good. It’ll give us more time to see how you’re… Settling, emotionally speaking.”

“You mean to see if it’ll all catch up to me and I have a breakdown.”

Her lips twitched into a smile.

“Quite.”

Buck wasn’t certain if he was a good captain. He was trying. God, was he trying. So much of his time felt like it was spent trying to find that Goldilocks zone between the coworker that was their friend and the boss that they needed to listen to. Sometimes, he worried that he fell too far on one side than the other. Because it was hard to look at people that had been his friends for years, people who’d been in this job and at this station longer than him, and order them around or reprimand them if needed.

It was easier with Bell. She’d always known him as Captain Diaz. Buck never walked away from her feeling like a little kid wearing their father’s uniform as a costume.

He only really had Bobby’s example to follow. Sure, he’d met and worked with other captains, but never for long enough to really get to know what they’d do in one situation or the other. The closest was when Chimney and Hen took their turns wearing the captain’s hat, and the lessons he took from their tenure was mainly what not to do.

Don’t become an egotistical asshole. Don’t treat people that have done this job for years like they were probies. Don’t brush off someone that may be in need of assistance just because they’re acting like an asshole.

The lessons from Bobby were more numerous, and honestly more helpful than a bunch of what-not-to-dos. From the basic day to day aspects of the job, to things like the importance of forcing everyone to spend at least one meal together. A lot of times, on a scene, Buck found himself asking what Bobby would do in his place and go from there.

Sometimes, though, he would ask himself what Bobby would do and found the answer unsatisfactory. This was one of those times.

Altadena used to be a gorgeous place to live. It would be again, eventually, once everything healed as all things did. Buck had not realized just how lucky Hen and Karen were, until he found himself parking in front of a row of houses surrounded by brown dirt lots and blackened lumber skeletons. It was the middle of the day, so Denny and Mara were both in school, but Karen’s car was parked beside Hen’s.

Not much of a surprise, really: Hen hadn’t been home from the hospital for long.

Karen answered the door when he knocked, with a warm smile and a warmer greeting as she let him in.

“Here to check in on Hen, I guess,” Buck told her when she asked. “Talk to her about something. And apologize. Is she awake? Is she even in the mood for visitors?”

“God, yes, please!” Hen’s voice preceded her as she made her way into the living room. “I am going stir crazy.”

She was moving with some stiffness, Buck noticed. Her hand clutched the side of her chest and she winced a little when those muscles pulled too much. Buck grimaced as he remembered the feel of those muscles around his finger.

“It’s been like having three children in the house,” Karen complained, though the words were nothing but fond. “And the youngest is the most mature of the bunch.”

“You are beautiful and I adore you and I would not be able to function without you,” Hen told her as she eased herself onto the couch. “Hi, Buck.”

“Hey, Hen.” He gave her an awkward wave and then hurriedly sat down in one of the comfy chairs. “How’s, uh. Everything?”

Hen snorted.

“Everything’s fine,” she said. “Sore. Stitches will be in for a bit.”

Buck hadn’t seen her since she was still in the hospital, a week ago now. After the military decided they weren’t liable to spread the disease around, Hen and Chimney had both been sent off for medical treatment. Both of them spent a few days being poked and prodded by doctors.

“Yeah, n- no doubt.”

“What were you wanting to apologize for?” Karen asked, voice carrying over from the kitchen.

Buck hadn’t even realized she left the room.

“Please don’t tell me it’s for us getting stuck in that death trap,” Hen said, already glaring at him in disapproval. “Or for cutting a hole in me.”

“Hey, I’m the one that had to stick his finger into you,” he joked. “Really, you should be apologizing to me.”

Her snort was echoed by her wife’s as Karen brought her a glass of water.

“Did you want anything?” Karen asked him, still standing.

“Nah, I’m good.”

“So if not for that,” Hen said. “Then what do you want to apologize for?”

“I kinda, um. Lost my temper with you,” Buck said, feeling awkward and sheepish. “Snapped at you a bit. In the lab.”

“You mean when Chimney was bleeding out.”

“Yeah.”

Buck couldn’t say he was very proud of the way he’d acted in that moment. Hen had been just as trapped as him, just as scared as him, and he knew how brains froze in circumstances like those. Even when a person was trained for it. But he’d asked for something, anything, they could do to buy Chimney a little more time.

And all he’d gotten in answer was a frantic, “I don’t know!”

He’d gotten so angry at that moment. Angry over the fact that his friend was dying, and he didn’t know what to do. Angry at the fact that his friend was dying, and Hen couldn’t give him an answer for what to do. Angry at the fact that they were stuck there, unable to do anything but buy time for a rescue he didn’t even know was coming.

Buck didn’t know what he would’ve said to Hen if Chimney hadn’t lost consciousness then. He didn’t think it would’ve been very kind.

“You don’t need to apologize.” Hen shook her head at him as she said it. “We were stressed, afraid. Emotions were high. I’ve snapped at people, too, at times like that. I’ve snapped at you during moments like that.”

“Still.” Buck shrugged. “You didn’t deserve it.”

“You’re forgiven.” 

She rolled her eyes and he stuck her tongue out at her.

“That’s not the main reason I came over, though,” he said. “Seeing how you’re doing, obviously, but…”

He drew in a breath as Hen looked at him in curiosity, eyebrow raising.

“You need to get cleared by a therapist before you can come back.”

Hen’s face immediately pulled in a scowl.

“Is this the brass’ orders?” she asked. Her tone made it clear just how pleased she was with this.

“No,” Buck admitted. “I mean, Chief Williams agreed, but… It’s mine. I’m the one saying it.”

Hen’s scowl grew deeper.

“Why?” she demanded. “We’ve never needed it before.”

“That was with Bobby.” Buck shrugged. “And I think Bobby was wrong not to make it a requirement, sometimes. I think a lot of things could’ve been avoided if he had. I- I should’ve done this after- after Jones. I mean, one of us died, and we all just came back to work like it was nothing.”

“Buck.” Hen sounded annoyed. “I don’t need to see a shrink.”

Karen scoffed. Loudly. Hen glowered up at her wife.

“Last night I dreamed that I woke up and we were still in that lab, that we’d never actually gotten out.” Buck picked at a loose string on the cardigan he was wearing. “This isn’t just you. Copeland said I was ‘tentatively’ cleared to come back. I’ve already told Ravi, and I’m going over to Maddie and Chimney’s after this to tell him. He’s probably not going to take it any better than you are. But when we were in there… I was more than just scared, Hen.”

Hen glowered a moment longer, and then the expression melted away with a sigh. She rubbed at her face, looking twenty times more tired than moments before.

“I know,” she said, quieter now. “I think that was the most hopeless I’ve ever felt.”

“It’s kinda crushing,” he said.

She nodded in agreement.

“I emailed you a list of all the current department approved therapists,” Buck said.

“We’ll find one,” Karen told him. She had her hand on Hen’s shoulder, rubbing at it comfortingly.

That went easier than Buck was dreading. He hoped it would be the same with Chimney.

Even before everything went completely tits up at the research lab, Buck remembered how anxious and frightened Bell had been. It got worse when she went inside with them, to the point that he was honestly grateful that Allen’s head wound gave him an excuse to send Bell out. Of all the things he regretted that day, not leaving her outside, or maybe even not leaving her as the person behind at the station instead of Tanika, was one of the most prominent.

It was also the one that he could, 100%, blame himself for.

Even days later, Bell still seemed bothered. Strictly speaking, only the four of them trapped in the lab needed to be cleared by a therapist before coming back. Trauma had a splash zone, though, and they’d all had working radios that night. On his first day back, when the start of shift brief took a more serious tone than usual, he strongly suggested they talk to someone. But he thought Bell might need more than a strong suggestion.

“Hey, Bell?” Buck waited until he was sure he had the probie’s attention. She paused in what she was doing, helping roll up the hoses with the others, and looked up at his voice. “I want to talk to you about something.”

His comment ignited the usual bouts of teasing, jokes about being called to the principal’s office and how she was in trouble. Bell mostly brushed them off, but even he could tell that her anxiety was ratcheting up as they walked to the captain’s office.

She took a seat in front of the desk and Buck, after a moment’s thought, took the one beside it. He chewed on his lip for a moment while she played with one of her plaits, trying to decide how to approach this. It was never very easy, he knew. Honestly, he was dreading Bell’s first loss on a call, because he remembered how hard it had hit him.

“How’ve you been?” he blurted out, for a lack of anything else to say.

“I’m… Good,” she said.

“That sounded convincing.” He tried to go for teasing, and managed to mostly stick the landing. “Wanna try again?”

Bell dropped her eyes and her hand to her lap.

“I don’t… I don’t think I can do this job.”

Buck drew in a sharp breath. Somehow, he wasn’t surprised by her words.

“This is about what happened at the lab,” he stated. She nodded. “I noticed that you were a bit… Scared. Even before everything happened.”

“My parents both had COVID,” she said. “They’re fine. Now. But I spent a while only seeing them over video while they were in the hospital. Mom used to go hiking all the time, and now she gets winded getting the mail. And Dad still complains that nothing tastes right.”

“And then I drag you to a lab filled with deadly diseases.” Buck consoled himself with the fact that there was no way he could’ve known ahead of time. Except he could have asked earlier, couldn’t he? “I’m sorry.”

Bell just gave him a little shrug.

“If you… If you don’t think this job is for you,” he carefully said. “There’s nothing wrong with that. It’s why first year firefighters are called probies. It’s the year you try it out for real and decide if you can stick it out. Because the instructors at the academy can try as hard as they want, some things you have to just experience in the real world.”

“Like a mad scientist nearly killing you.”

“Like that,” Buck agreed. “It was a scary day, yeah. Scared the hell out of me. But you’ve been here for a couple months now, you know that isn’t the normal.”

“Like a bridge collapse isn’t it?”

He smiled grimly.

“Gossip or stories?”

“Javier told me,” she said. “When I asked about the guy’s picture on the wall.”

“Yeah, that’s… That sort of thing is closer to normal for us than a disease getting loose in a lab,” he said. “And it’s scary as hell, it always is. Anyone that tells you differently is an idiot.”

Buck had been that idiot, once upon a time. But the job broke him of that very quickly.

“I don’t know if I can do that,” Bell told him. “I- I haven’t even seen a big fire yet. I thought I could do it, I did it just fine at the academy, but now…”

“Like I said, this job isn’t for everyone. There’s no shame in realizing that includes you. But!” Buck got up and rounded the desk, to paw through a drawer for a business card. He held it out for Bell to take. “That’s the information for Frank, one of the department therapists. Eddie and my sister have both seen him. I think Chimney and Hen have, too.”

“Um.” Bell stared at the card in her hand. “Okay.”

“You’re rattled still, and you should talk it out with people before you decide anything. Trust me when I say that you can really regret making impulsive decisions because of big emotions.”

“Does that have anything to do with the thing between you and the last captain?” she asked, raising her eyebrows at him. “Everyone kinda talks around it.”

He shrugged, waggled his hand in the air. Because depending on what thing they were talking around, it could be the time he learned that lesson for himself, or it could be something else entirely. 

Bell got up with a nod, and headed for the open door. Just before she reached it, a thought struck Buck. She stopped when he asked her to hold on.

“I trust Frank,” he said, swallowing against a suddenly dry throat. “But if he does something, anything at all, that makes you uncomfortable, you get up and leave immediately. And you tell me. Okay?”

Bell frowned, confusion clear. But she nodded and agreed, and he let her go.

Chapter 47: Closure

Chapter Summary

In which Bobby and Athena solve a mystery.

Chapter Notes

Your regular reminder that this series is motivated by spite towards the show, and Tim Minear in particular. So have some Bathena in your Buddie fic.

It started with a phone call from Buck. Not very strange, in and of itself. It was the content of the call that struck Bobby as odd.

“Hey, Pops, there’s a guy here who’s looking for you,” Buck had said. “He, um. He says he wants you to help keep his sister out of prison.”

He wasn’t working that day - shooting for Hotshots had wrapped up for the season, so he was free for a couple months. Athena, too, was off. Which meant the phone call from Buck had been a little bit ill-timed, but it could’ve been worse. They were lazing in bed together and weren’t yet in the middle of anything.

But what Buck said snagged the attention of them both, a fish hook caught on the latest catch, and it didn’t take any discussion at all before they both agreed to meet this Gary person, whoever he was. There was a hole-in-the-wall of a diner, not far from the firehouse, that Bobby had Buck send the guy. He was already at a booth table when the two of them walked in, a mug of coffee in front of him. Bobby’s first impression of the man was that he looked tired, in a way that was far too familiar.

“I didn’t know you’d retired,” Gary said when they’d sat down across from him and ordered. “If I had, I wouldn’t have just shown up like that.”

“Semi-retired,” Bobby corrected. He nodded and smiled at the waitress when she brought his and Athena’s own coffees. “And I don’t know where else you would’ve gone to find me.”

“That’s… True, I guess.”

“Buck said you were hoping Bobby could keep your sister out of prison,” Athena said. She reached over for the packets of sugar, handing Bobby one for his coffee before tearing into her own. “What was she arrested for?”

“Um.” Gary winced. “Stalking, breaking and entering. Attempted kidnapping.”

Athena paused in her motions, sugar pouring out of the packet and into her coffee. She half turned her head to meet gazes with Bobby, the both of them on the same wavelength, the both of them questioning just how Bobby could keep the woman out of prison with all of that. It sounded more like she needed a good lawyer than she did a technical advisor for a television show.

“Who did she try to kidnap?” Bobby asked him, taking a sip of his coffee. He didn’t even have to say anything before Athena was offering him one of the tiny things of creamer.

“Her dead son,” was the eyebrow raising answer to Bobby’s question. “Who she has become convinced is not dead, but living in Santa Clarita.”

Nevermind, maybe not a good lawyer. It sounded like this guy’s sister needed a good doctor.

“Sounds like there’s a story there,” Athena probed, tone purposefully casual.

“My nephew Micah died eight years ago in a house fire,” Gary told them. “Leah was there when the fire broke out. She couldn’t get to him, and by the time the firefighters got there, it was too late.”

“My husband’s fire company.”

“That’s right.”

“Leah, Micah… Oh. I think I remember that fire,” Bobby said, thinking back on it. “The house was fully involved when we got there, already a loss. I wouldn’t have sent anyone into it if her husband hadn’t said they were still inside. We found her on the second floor, trying to reach the nursery. The floor gave out just as I walked into the room. I would’ve gone with it if Tommy hadn’t grabbed me.”

It was not a memory that Bobby thought he could ever forget. The sight of the crib falling through the floor, already engulfed in flames. The way Leah knew the moment she spotted him walking out empty-handed.

“After that, Leah’s marriage fell apart. She couldn’t hold a job. Some days, she could barely get out of bed,” Gary explained. “Basically, all the terrible things you think would happen to someone after the worst thing imaginable happens to them.”

Bobby did not have to imagine. Athena placed her hand on his arm and he placed his own over it, giving her a small smile in reply to her worried glance.

“But I got her a job,” Gary continued. “At a catering company I own. I found her a place to live. It took time, but slowly, she began to put her life back together.”

“Until something happened,” Bobby guessed, though it was an easy thing to guess. “Something that triggered her.”

Gary let out a sigh.

“We worked a birthday party a few weeks ago,” he said. “For a nine year old boy.”

“Micah would’ve been that age, wouldn’t he?”

“Yeah. It was even the same birthday.” Gary’s words had both Bobby and Athena wincing. “As soon as I realized, I tried to send Leah home. But she insisted that she could handle it, that I was being silly. And then four days later, she’s calling me from jail.”

“That is quite the quick spiral,” Athena commented.

“She’s convinced that this boy is her son and that he was stolen from her by this other mother. I’ve tried to reason with her, but she just says, ‘Gary, you don’t understand. You weren’t there that night.’”

“So you went looking for someone who was there that night.”

“You came looking for me,” Bobby said.

“I’m just desperate,” Gary told them. “And I just hope that maybe… Maybe she’d listen to you.”

Again, Bobby and Athena turn their heads to meet the other’s gaze. Again, the pair of them are on the same wavelength. They don’t even have to talk about it.

“We’ll see what we can do,” Athena promised, as much of a promise as that could be, and that was that.

It’s Athena that goes to speak with Leah at the jail. They both agreed that, while Bobby was the one who’d been there that night, the police sergeant was the one better equipped to question Leah. So she went and waited, until a guard escorted the woman in her orange jumpsuit to her seat on the other side of the glass. She picked up the phone on her side, and Athena did the same on hers.

“Hello, Leah. Thank you for agreeing to talk to me. My name is Athena.”

“Gary told me you were coming,” Leah said. “He said you’re a police officer. He also said Captain Nash would be here, but…”

She craned her neck, like she was trying to spot Bobby hiding somewhere.

“He’s busy getting the reports on the fire, but we thought I’d be the better one to talk with you,” Athena explained. “Your brother is very worried about you.”

“He thinks I’m crazy. I’m not crazy,” Leah insisted. Athena had met few crazy people who would admit to it. “I just did what any mother would’ve done. Probably went about it the wrong way, but…”

“Can you tell me about this boy?”

“Micah.”

“The police report says that his name is Cameron Myers.”

Pulling up that report was one of the first things Athena had done, once they’d left Gary at the diner. It was a very interesting read, but she knew that they needed Leah’s side of everything, too.

“Well, of course the police report says that, because that’s what she’s been calling him,” Leah said. “But my son’s name is Micah.”

Both statements were true, without a doubt. It was whether or not they were the same boy that was the question.

“Why do you think that this boy is your son?”

“I wasn’t certain at first. I kept telling myself I was imagining things, but when I saw him at the party…” Leah’s lips trembled for a brief second. “He looked so much like Micah. I couldn’t catch my breath for a moment. And- And I would’ve chalked the whole thing up to some crazy coincidence, until I handed him the bag and I saw the birthmark. A tiny little heart on the inside of his wrist. I used to tell him it connected his heart to mine, and that it meant that, no matter where he went, he would always carry my love with him.”

“And that’s when you knew for sure?”

“That’s when I allowed for the possibility,” she said. “I kept telling myself that I was crazy, that it couldn’t be real. I mean, I didn’t even know these people. But it turns out that I did. Her, at least.”

“You recognized her?” Athena sat up a little.

“I saw a picture of her at a prenatal yoga class. We did it together, nine in the morning, Tuesdays and Fridays.”

“You were in prenatal yoga class together?”

“Until she stopped coming. I remember hearing from the other moms that her pregnancy ran into trouble, that she’d lost the baby.”

Athena was beginning to see the assumed motive, now.

“That’s when you began to think she went after yours,” she said.

Leah nodded.

“There are stories of women so desperate, they’ll cut one out of another woman,” Leah said. “How much easier would it be to just wait until the baby’s born? Steal him from his crib.”

“Start a fire.”

“Exactly. If you’re desperate enough, you’ll do things you never thought you were capable of doing.”

Like trying to kidnap a child in broad daylight. It was all there in the police report. Leah went to one of Cameron’s little league games, and tried to take him away while insisting that his mother - Heather Myers - was the actual kidnapper. Other people that were there intervened, keeping her in place until the police arrived.

“I know what I did was reckless and stupid, but I’m not wrong,” Leah insisted. “I thought I buried my son, but I didn’t. He’s alive.”

When Athena didn’t say anything right away, she saw Leah’s face drop a little.

“You think I’m crazy?”

“No.” Athena thought she was desperate to deny the truth of her child’s death, even years later. “But I promise you this. If your son is alive, I’ll bring him back to you.”

“Do you want to explain to me,” Bobby said, as he watched his wife at work, “why you’re doing this in the unfinished kitchen of our unfinished house, instead of at the apartment?”

“Because the apartment-” Athena paused to slap another printed out picture onto the wall. “-doesn’t have a good spot for this.”

Bobby let out a little hum.

“You’re right, I really do need to replace that rolling board.”

His wife turned enough for him to see her rolling her eyes, as if she wasn’t the one turning the wall of their future kitchen into a conspiracy board, before getting back to work. The folding table that the workers had been using was not spared, either. Athena’s laptop was there, with a printer hooked up to it. There were Post-Its and a cup of sharpies, along with a pair of lanterns.

Athena frowned at one of the photos she was sticking to the wall and then went to the laptop, pulling up one of Heather Myers’ social media. Whatever she found, it had the frown deepening.

“She posted every day until March Seventeenth,” she said, tapping the screen. “And then not again until May Ninth.”

“Six weeks is a large gap, when she was doing it every day.”

“So… Maybe she did lose her baby? But not before he was born.”

There was another photo printed out, one of Heather with baby Cameron, the pair of them with matching green shamrocks painted on their cheeks. A Post-It note went beside it, labeling it as the last photo of Cameron before the fire on April 6th, 2017.

“This is going to be an all-nighter, isn’t it?” Bobby guessed. Athena just hummed in a response, busy with her mystery. “I’ll order us something to eat.”

“I think I almost have it figured out,” she said. “Something happened to Heather’s baby in those six weeks she didn’t post. Probably on March Seventeenth or Eighteenth.”

“That isn’t quite the evidentiary bombshell that you seem to think it is.”

“But even after she started posting again, things were different.” Athena started pointing at the photos on the wall as she talked. “The cute matching outfits were gone, no more daily photo shoots, and she stopped showing his face.”

“You’re the one who said the internet was full of - and again, quoting you - creepy ass stalkers,” Bobby pointed out. “Buck and Eddie go out of their way not to post our grandchildren anywhere public, either.”

“But it’s the change in behavior,” Athena argued. “A drastic change, after a long absence?”

“You’re right, it is suspicious. But only because you’re already looking for something.”

The look his wife gave him, for insinuating she might have been coming at this from a biased position, was not a happy one. Then she twisted her mouth as she glared at the wall of photos.

“Did you see the baby in the crib?” she asked.

“No. The crib was on fire when we got to the nursery, Athena. And like I said, the floor gave out pretty much the moment I put my foot down.” He grimaced at the memory. It was the closest he’d come to falling off that wagon in those eighteen months of sobriety, before that plane crash sent him sprawling entirely. “You know, this sounds like the Sodder children.”

“Sodder children?”

“Christmas Eve, Nineteen Forty-five. The Sodders lived in a house with nine of their kids-”

“Dear lord,” Athena said.

“They had ten,” Bobby added. “The house caught fire in the middle of the night, the official report blamed it on the Christmas lights, the Sodders and four of their children escaped. The bodies of the other five were never found. They spent their lives believing the fire was arson and that their kids were kidnapped.”

Athena stared at him.

“Buck heard it on a podcast or something.” Bobby shrugged. “He told me about it while we cooked one day.”

“Well, luckily, there are very quick ways to solve this particular mystery.” Athena turned back to him, a hand on her hip. “I’ve got an exhumation scheduled for in the morning.”

“That was quick.”

They’d only been on this for a couple days.

“It helps to know people.”

“It is 8:07 AM, and we are exhuming the grave of Micah Hamilton to obtain a DNA sample,” Athena said into the camera Officer Williams was holding. “I’m going to go check on the doc. You keep recording.”

“Got it, Sergeant.”

They were at the cemetery Micah was buried at, a backhoe digging up the dirt. On the street at the bottom of the hill, they had a tent set up for the coroner to do her thing. Bobby fell into her step beside her, and then sighed when a car came screeching to a stop and Gary stepped out.

“I’ve got it,” she told Williams, and went to intercept Gary. “What are you doing here?”

“I came to put an end to this insanity,” he spat at her. “You’re digging up a baby’s grave?”

“It’s the only way we can be sure.”

“No, I am sure. I’m sure that my sister is crazy. Clearly it’s contagious.”

“Your sister is traumatized,” Bobby told him, in that patient, gentle way of his. “She’s still grieving. I don’t think she ever got closure about what happened.”

“We got closure! Micah’s dead and buried!” Gary’s glare slid past the two of them, to land on the two men carrying a tiny casket to the coroner’s tent. “I’m gonna put an end to this.”

He followed the casket to the tent, with Athena and Bobby right behind, and burst inside. Williams was already there with the camera.

“Stop!” Gary shouted. “This is my nephew’s casket, and I do not consent to this.”

“I’m very sorry for your loss,” the coroner, Luann, told him. “But his mother hired me. Please, let me do my job.”

“No! You don’t understand what you’re doing.”

“Gary,” Athena said, trying to calm him down. “You really shouldn’t be here for this part. I can call you with the results.”

“There aren’t going to be any results.”

“What?” Bobby said, at the same time she asked, “Why?”

“The casket is-” Gary looked over, they all did, as Luann flipped the lid open. “-empty.”

Athena, and the rest of them, simply stared at it. Williams shut off the camera. Inside the casket was just a framed photograph, and a sandbag.

The Sodder children, indeed.

“We didn’t know how to tell my sister,” Gary admitted. “The fire, it just… There was nothing left to bury.”

“No wonder Leah still thinks her son might be alive.” Bobby sounded on the edge of being angry. “You didn’t tell her anything? She didn’t get to see any of this?”

“Her husband and I decided everything. She was upset. We didn’t want to make it worse.”

So, the exhumation was a bust, and  just gave Leah’s suspicions more credence. But there were other avenues to check.

Bobby knew that this was not going to be pleasant. He and Athena sat at one of the tables in the room at the jail meant for visitation. The first time he saw Leah in eight years was when the guard brought her in and escorted her to a seat at the table. The last time he saw her, she was in a hospital bed and he was still soot covered.

She’d asked him how he kept going, with the loss of his children. He told her that he lived in the belief he’d see them again. He hoped that hadn’t contributed to where she was now.

“Gary said you exhumed the grave. He was so mad I gave you permission,” Leah told them. “It wasn’t my son in there, was it?”

“No,” Athena said with a shake of her head.

“The casket was empty,” Bobby said. “Just a photo of Micah. He was small enough, and the fire hot enough that night, that there was nothing to bury. Your brother and your ex-husband just… Didn’t want you to hurt more.”

“No.” Leah shook her head in denial, and Bobby’s heart ached. “There was nothing there because my son isn’t dead. He didn’t die in a fire. That woman has him.”

Athena sighed.

“I have DNA test results here,” she said, placing her hand on the folder she’d laid on the table. “There was a match.”

“A match to what? You said there was nothing there.”

“There was still Cameron,” Bobby said, as gently as he could. “You said you thought he was Micah, that Heather Myers kidnapped him. The easiest way to prove it was to test their DNA.”

“I went to them, and I explained the situation. Heather agreed to allow for buccal swabs to be taken from her and Cameron.” Athena opened the folder as she explained, turning it around so Leah could see the results for herself. “We tested Cameron’s sample against your sample and hers. And hers… Hers was a match, Leah. Cameron is her son.”

“I’m sorry, Leah.” Bobby couldn’t help but feel like they were killing her child again. “But Micah is gone.”

Leah’s face crumpled with a sob.

“I was so sure. When I saw him, I… I felt it. I felt him.” She closed her eyes, gathered herself. “You think I imagined all of it. Don’t you?”

“I think,” Bobby said, choosing his words carefully, “that if I found there was any chance Robert and Brooke were alive today, I’d follow it, too.”

“The district attorney is sympathetic,” Athena told her. “He’ll consider a diversion program. If you comply, the charges could be dismissed. And you could get back to your life.”

“What life?” Leah quietly asked.

“Leah.” Bobby considered reaching out to her, but knew the guard would step in if he tried. “I know it’s hard, I do. But you’re still alive, and you still have your brother. You still have reasons to live for, if you just find them.”

However much he believed them and knew them to be true, the words still felt like nothing but air.

Bobby’s fist rapped on the door. The reaction on the other side was immediate: barking and claws tapping against hardwood; giggling and little feet thudding along; someone cursing in PG rated words as they lumbered for the door. The door swung open and Buck’s face lit up.

“Pops! Ma!” He reached down without looking, catching Gavin as the toddler sprinted for freedom. “What are you doing here?”

“Do we need a reason to visit?” Athena asked, raising a pointed eyebrow until Buck stepped aside and let them in.

Hoover immediately gravitated towards them, but thankfully didn’t invade her space.

“We came to see our grandkids,” Bobby said, taking Gavin from Buck.

“Oh, wow. At least I know where I rank now,” Buck said, all mock offense as he shut the door.

“As if that was ever in question,” Athena teased.

Buck rolled his eyes and then ducked away when she went to smack him for it.

“Eddie’s out back,” he said. “He bought a new grill today.”

“What happened to your old one?”

“The bottom rusted out,” Chris said, making his way from the hall and into the dining room. “‘Cause Pops left the lid open and it rained.”

“It hardly ever rains!” Buck protested. “How was I supposed to know it would just suddenly decide to?”

“There’s this thing called a weather app,” Bobby pointed out.

The grown adult and father of two stuck his tongue out at him.

“What about it, huh?” Bobby asked Gavin. “Wanna go see what Daddy’s grilling up?”

Gavin smiled and nodded, and so that’s where they went.

Chapter 48: Fire-Breathing

Chapter Summary

In which Athena is getting irritated with choices, the 118 run into a familiar face, and Chimney is indecisive about his career advancement.

There were three paint swatches stuck to the wall of the Grant-Nash’s new entry hall with blue painter’s tape. Buck was told that they were different shades of white, but he wasn’t seeing it. He was just seeing white on white, no matter how hard he stared at them.

“I still don’t get it,” Harry said, echoing Buck’s thoughts.

Athena made a frustrated sound, and Bobby covered up his face to hide his amusement.

“The contractor wants us to pick out the final wall color,” she said, gesturing to the swatches. “So he put up these three whites to choose from.”

“Are the other two shades of white in the room with us?” Harry asked his sister.

“Shrimp colors,” May whispered to her brother, and the pair of them started snickering..

“Are you sure he didn’t accidentally put three of the same color on there?” Buck asked.

“Alright, how about this. I’ll close my eyes,” Bobby said, doing so as he spoke. “And then just randomly pick one.”

He thrust his finger out at the wall. No one said anything.

“Well?” Bobby asked, eyes still closed. “Which color?”

“You hit the wall, Pops,” Buck told him.

“Oh.” His arm dropped like the browning leaf of a houseplant left for too long in Eddie’s care.

“Unbleached chalk it is,” Athena declared, marking the middle swatch with a marker. Buck wondered if that was the actual name of the color, but didn’t feel like looking to check. “Dear Lord, let this be the last decision we have to make this week.”

“I believe your mother’s quickly approaching the end of her rope,” Bobby told them as they followed Athena around the corner and into the kitchen.

“You think you’re a decisive person,” she said. “And then outlet plugs.”

“Don’t ask,” Bobby advised, obviously catching the confused and curious expression Buck was sporting.

Buck decided to follow Bobby’s advice, opting instead to look around the kitchen. The room was large, about the size of the living room and kitchen of the old house, combined. There were three different sets of glass doors that led to the backyard, and a fireplace on the end opposite the stove and sink.

“You’re gonna have a bigger dining area than us,” he stated, walking the length as Athena passed out Starbuck cups to the other three.

(He’d just kinda invited himself over, so there wasn’t any Starbucks for him.)

“We’ll have to get a table to match,” Bobby said.

Buck cut a glance his way, and then sniffed haughtily.

“I’m still hosting Sunday dinners.”

“Every other one,” Bobby immediately countered.

Buck spotted the other three rolling their eyes.

“Maybe I’ll get to eat with everyone at the table here and not at a counter,” Harry remarked to his sister, making no effort to be subtle.

“It’s their dream dining room,” May said. “We probably won’t have anywhere to sit at all.”

The pair, in sync, turned to their heads to stare at their mother, expressions disturbingly identical to Athena at her least impressed. Athena side-eyed them and then shook her head.

“Maybe we’ll start inviting Hen and Karen,” she said. “You two can eat In-n-Out outside.”

“Oh!” Buck snapped his fingers, interrupting the grumblings of his step-siblings. “Hey, Pops? I’ve been meaning to sic you on Hen.”

“Why?” Bobby asked, in the tone of a man who wasn’t sure he actually wanted to know the answer to his question.

“I’ve mentioned Reynolds is retiring, right?” Buck waited for the other man to nod. “I asked her if she was gonna go for the spot. She told me she wasn’t sure she wanted it anymore.”

Bobby and Athena shared a look, both of them perplexed and vaguely concerned.

“She was excited to be captain before,” Bobby wondered aloud. “What changed?”

“We’ll talk to her,” Athena promised.

Buck threw them a smile and a salute.

When the earthquake struck, Buck knew the shift following was going to be a pain in the ass. It didn’t matter if it was a baby of a quake, just a 2.5, nor that earthquakes were so common in California that Buck once saw Abuela grab a lamp before it fell without even bothering to look up from her book. All that mattered was that there was an earthquake, and people would inevitably freak out and go crazy about it.

Buck never thought crazy would cover fire-breathing, but that’s what they were responding to. They pulled up to a dentist’s office, the engine and the ambulance, and the dental assistant met them at the door.

“Dr. Stevens was drilling,” she explained as she led them to the operatory. “And then her mouth turned into a hellmouth.”

“How badly is she burned?” Hen asked. 

It was her and Chimney’s first week back after the mess at the lab, both of them having gotten the all clear from Frank. Chimney seemed mostly okay, for someone whose nasal capillaries were literally dissolving. Buck wondered just what was in that antiviral. For regular CCHF, or so he read, it took weeks to months to recover from it if it didn’t kill you. But despite being hit by a ‘roided up version, Chimney was up and going like nothing had happened.

In contrast, Hen still had stitches in and winced in obvious discomfort whenever a motion tugged on them. She was on light duty, and glowered at Buck every time he reminded her of that.

“No, no, no, she isn’t burned,” the dental assistant clarified as they entered the operatory.

“Oh,” Hen said, drawing up short. “He is.”

The dentist was perched on a stool, looking shellshocked. His entire face was red and starting to blister, except for where his mouth had been covered by his disposable face mask. His eyebrows were beyond saving.

“I- I don’t know what happened,” Dr. Stevens stammered. “It was a normal root canal.”

“Okay, Doc.” Chimney sat down his medkit and dug out gloves. “Let’s check out those burns.”

“You better take care of her, too.”

The “her” he was talking about was the fire-breathing patient, who had gone unnoticed so far because they were fixated on the dentist. The blue dental drape on her chest was pockmarked with burn holes, and she was trying to talk to them. Except, for some reason, she couldn’t.

“Oh,” Hen said, peering at her. The woman’s mouth, and the skin around it, was in a similar state to the dentist’s face. “Looks like the bite block melted from the heat.”

The woman, who looked so very familiar for some reason, let out a distressed cry that Buck felt really summed it up. Her mouth was stuck open, thanks to the plastic between her teeth, her jaw unable to close and unable to move.

“Looks like your burns are superficial,” Chimney told Dr. Stevens, and then turned to address Toby and Bell, who’d just come in with the gurney. “Let’s get him to the ambo. Irrigation and lots of gauze.”

“But I have a waiting room full of patients,” Dr. Stevens protested.

“Sir,” Buck said to him. “In ten, twenty minutes, you’re going to be in too much pain to see any of them.”

He motioned for Toby to come help get Dr. Stevens onto the gurney, whether the guy liked it or not, and turned back to the fire-breather herself. Which was weird. He’d seen a fire breather’s act in person once, and they used paraffin oil. And Buck, for various reasons that shall not be dwelled upon, knew that farts were ignitable, thanks to the gases produced by digestion, like methane and hydrogen.

Nothing that was supposed to come out of a person’s mouth was ignitable.

“Ma’am,” Hen said to their other patient, “are you having any trouble breathing?”

The woman’s response was garbled. 

“She said just opening her mouth,” the dental assistant translated. After another garbled word, she followed it with, “Exactly.”

“How are you doing that?” Hen asked the assistant, while Buck was once again trying to figure out just where he knew this patient from.

“I spend a lot of time around mouths.”

“Ma’am,” Buck interrupted, curiosity literally (not really) killing him. “Are you an actress?”

He didn’t need a translation, the volume and the way she shook her head at him was answer enough.

“Sorry, sorry.” He patted the air. “You just look familiar.”

“Right. Let me see if we can get your jaws free,” Hen said, pulling out a penlight to better see the inside of the patient’s mouth. “And Buck will shut his.”

The words were accompanied by a vicious side-eye.

“But why did she turn into a fire-breathing dragon?” the dental assistant asked.

“Dental drills can throw off sparks, can’t they?” Buck asked, picking up one of the dental tools to look at.

“You would still need something flammable in her mouth,” Chimney pointed out, then asked the dental assistant, “Were you all using ether?”

“No, just water.”

“That’s weird,” Buck commented. Something must’ve gotten into the water and contaminated it. Which meant… “Chim, you got a red tag?”

“Yes, I do.” Chimney was already digging one out, along with a marker. “No more dental procedures until the Health Department can inspect it.”

“Hey, Cap? Could you grab me a drape from over there?” Hen asked, gesturing where there was a small stack of them. “I wouldn’t want to strain myself and tear a stitch.”

Buck made a face at her, but went to grab it nonetheless. When he went to put it over the patient, though, he paused. His eyes went between her face and the drape as he finally made the connection.

“Blue!” he blurted out. “I knew you looked familiar.”

The others looked at him oddly, so while he got the drape situated over her, he sheepishly explained that,

“She’s the lady who overdosed on tooth cream a few Christmases ago.”

“The Smurf!”

Chimney’s declaration got an angry, muffled reply from the patient.

“Lorna,” the dental assistant translated. “And I don’t think she likes the Smurf reference.”

“Okay, Lorna, just keep as still as possible,” Hen instructed. “I’m gonna try to cut through that bite block.”

Lorna let out muffled cries of panic.

“No more-” the dental assistant started to translate.

“Drill, yeah,” Chimney finished for her. “Don’t worry, she’s just using a saw.”

What Hen used was, technically, their drill. But the drill bit in it was a circular saw blade. A tiny one. Chimney kept Lorna’s head steady while Hen worked, the saw blade whirring as it cut through the melted plastic. When she got through the last of it, Lorna let out a relieved breath.

“There we go,” Hen said, switching the drill to her other hand as she reached gloved fingers into Lorna’s mouth to pull out pieces of blue-purple plastic. “That feel better?”

“Actually, yeah,” Lorna said, intelligible for the first time since they got to the scene. “My tooth stopped hurting.”

She reached into her mouth and, after a yank, pulled out another piece of melted plastic. Bloody spittle followed it. Sticking out of the plastic was a whole tooth, bloody roots and all.

“Oh,” she said. “That explains it.”

“Good news,” Buck told her. “You don’t need that root canal anymore.”

He didn’t think she appreciated the comment.

“I don’t understand,” Buck stated dumbly. He felt rather dumb at the moment, too. “How is this harder the second time?”

He and Chimney were surrounded by torn plastic wrapping and wooden pieces and various tools. They were attempting - key word, there: attempting - to put together the crib for the future Baby Boy Han, actual name pending, since Jee-Yun’s was donated years ago. It was not going well. At all.

“What do you mean, how is it harder the second time?” Chimney sniped at him. “You didn’t help the first time. You were busy baby proofing our upper cabinets.”

“Thank God he’s not doing that this time,” Maddie commented from the kitchen.

Buck twisted his head around to sneer at her.

“He did that at home, too. When we were about to get Gavin,” Eddie said. He was very distinctly not helping with putting together the baby furniture. Instead, he sat at the island with Maddie, a mug of tea in his hands. “Abuela had very many things to say about that-”

“I learned two new swears!” Buck cheerfully informed Maddie and Chimney.

“And then, one day,” Eddie continued, “it gets a little too quiet in the house. I walk into the kitchen to find Gavin on the kitchen counter, trying to get a cabinet door open.”

“Speaking of.” Buck tilted his head and listened, nodding contently when he could hear Jee-Yun and Gavin playing in the former’s room. “No idea how he got on the counter, by the way. I still think Hoover helped him.”

“What?” Chimney asked, mocking tone to the question. He paused to glare at the crib piece in his hand, before grabbing the screwdriver that had been discarded on the floor. “Do you think Hoover stood there and let the kid use him as a stool? Hold this for me.”

“You joke,” Buck said as he held the crib piece steady for Chimney. “But I think Hoover would totally do it.”

“And Senorita would just watch,” Eddie added.

“Senorita would fetch Chris,” Buck corrected. “And then they’d both just watch.”

“I’d like to think Chris would stop him if Gavin was climbing on counters, instead of just watch.”

“Is it a boy thing?” Maddie asked, giving her stomach a worried frown. “Jee didn’t do anything like that.”

“Jee-Yun once TP’d the inside of our house,” Eddie countered. “I don’t know if it’s a boy thing. I can’t remember Adrianna and Sophia doing something like that, but Chris didn’t, either.”

“Babe,” was all Buck said.

“Yeah, yeah, mi sol. Shut it.”

“And I can’t judge by how Buck was,” Maddie said. “I’d like to think we’re not such shitty parents that our kid feels the need to act like that.”

“Here, here!” Chimney thrusted the screwdriver into the air before going back to the task of putting together the crib.

“Hey, you never said.” Buck poked at Chimney until his brother-in-law couldn’t ignore him anymore. “You thinkin’ about going for the b-shift captain, when Reynolds retires?”

“You looking to get rid of me?” Chimney joked.

“Yes,” was Buck’s dry answer. “That and I’d like to know if I need to headhunt for a paramedic.”

Maybe he could steal Crawford or Rosen away? As soon as he had the thought, Buck was dismissing it. They were too familiar with A-shift to go for it.

“Hold on, B-shift captain?” Maddie sounded very interested in the conversation, suddenly.

“Yeah, Reynolds is retiring. Health reasons. He announced it around Hen’s birthday. Did I not mention that to you?”

“No,” his sister huffed. Whoops. “Chimney didn’t say anything, either.”

The words were pointed, with some noticeable ire.

“Thanks, Buck,” Chimney grumbled. “I didn’t say anything because I don’t know if I’m gonna go for it. Last time I was captain, it didn’t go so well. I was awful.”

“Yup,” Buck said, nodding his head.

Chimney scowled at him.

“You didn’t have to agree so fast.”

“You didn’t have to make me wash your car,” Buck immediately countered. “I wasn’t even the probie, Eddie was. You should have been making him wash your car.”

“Love you, too, Buck,” Eddie deadpanned.

“What about Hen?” Chimney asked, clearly trying to draw the heat away from himself. “She hasn’t said anything to me. Do you know if she’s going for it?”

“To be determined,” Buck answered, and then shrugged at their collective quizzical expressions. “I got a similar answer to yours when I asked.”

“Does your pregnant wife get to have an opinion?” Maddie asked, leaning forward a bit to better look at them. “We have one kid and another on the way, and a mortgage. You’re going for it.”

“What about Hen?” Eddie asked.

“She could’ve been a doctor by now,” was Maddie’s sharp answer. “Their house is paid off and she’s married to a literal rocket scientist.”

“Are you going to apply for me if I don’t?” Chimney asked, twisted around to stare incredulously at his wife.

“Yes! Maybe.” Maddie frowned and laid a hand on her stomach. “That might be the hormones snapping, actually.”

Buck snorted, shook his head, and grabbed another part of the crib to stick onto the rest.

Chapter 49: Methane in the Tap Water

Chapter Summary

In which Buck touches base and Athena tries to nudge her friend.

While the earthquake was tiny, just a 2.5, it was big enough to cause a host of problems. It contaminated one of the city’s water reservoirs with methane gas, hence why Lorna started spewing fire from her mouth. The water the dentist used was from that reservoir, and when he started drilling into her tooth, the sparks ignited the gas.

Not that Buck and them knew about it right away. It wasn’t until after another call involving water catching fire that they saw the announcement on the news. Buck immediately texted everyone who wasn’t currently at the station, in all caps and with proper spelling,

METHANE IN THE TAP WATER!!!!!!

He even called Carla, to make sure she saw both the text and the news report. Not because he was particularly afraid of the water somehow setting their house on fire, though he was seeing how it was a distinct possibility. Nor was he concerned about them drinking it, because methane did pretty much nothing except make you burp. No, his concern was the fact that the methane wouldn’t stay in the water.

It acted much like carbonation did in drinks. It bubbled up to the surface and was released into the air, something that was sped up when water was heated. And while drinking methane infused water did nothing, methane gas could build up somewhere without proper ventilation, a distinct problem with outhouses back in the day. It would displace oxygen, and it was easily ignitable.

Buck didn’t know if the burners on the stove would be enough to ignite it, and he didn’t want to find out.

Meanwhile, it had been some time since the conversation he had with Bell, the one where she voiced her doubts regarding the job. He knew she’d gone to see Frank at least once, because he’d asked her a few days later. It was probably time to check in with her again, though, and make sure he wasn’t accidentally leaving his first proper probie out to dry.

Buck decided to talk to her after yet another methane-water call, this one simultaneously worse and better than the dentist one. Better, because the woman wasn’t burnt. Worse, because her entire bathroom caught fire and she was trapped on the wrong side. He’d had to send Ravi down through a skylight to get her out.

“Bell!” he called out, once the trucks were parked and everyone was stowing away their gear. His own was already hanging in his cage.

Bell looked up from stepping out of her turnout pants, and he jerked her head for her to come over. She hurried to finish getting out of her turnouts, and then came jogging across the bay to where he waited. Some of the others turned their heads to watch her go, and a couple jeered, but most of them didn’t pay any mind once they realized it didn’t involve them.

Hen, he noticed, kept watching.

“Yeah, Cap?” Bell asked once she reached him.

“Just touching base,” Buck said, opting to ignore Hen for the moment. “Have you seen Frank any more?”

“A couple times,” she said with a shrug.

“Cool. How has that been? Not- Not that you have to tell me what you guys talked about, but has it helped at all?”

“I… I guess? Maybe?” Another shrug, this one smaller and less sure. “We talked about, y’know, the lab. My parents.”

“Half of my therapy sessions are about my parents,” he said, and she let out a surprised giggle. “Talking is good, though. Eddie can tell you what happens when you decide not to talk about things. But have you guys gotten around to, you know…?”

She did, thankfully, seem to know what he was referring to.

“Some, yeah. He pointed out that I couldn’t really know if I can handle it or not until I’m there, handling it or not,” Bell said. “What was your first big, awful call?”

“Plane crash, just off Dockweiler Beach,” Buck immediately answered. “Liberty Flight Forty-Six. We were trying to get people out as it sank.”

Then he tilted his head in consideration. 

“The water was on fire then, too,” he said, and then shook that thought away. “Like I said before, if you decide this job isn’t for you, there’s no shame in that. But you’ve been a good firefighter so far, and we like having you around.”

Bell tugged at one of her plaits and ducked her head in that embarrassed way people did when receiving praise, and he let her go. Almost immediately, Hen was invading Buck’s space.

“So,” she said, making a failed attempt to sound casual. “What was that about?”

Buck thought about what to answer with for a moment, and then told her,

“None of your business.” He smiled brightly at the way she glowered. “If she wants to tell you, she can. But I’m not violating her privacy because you’re curious. Or…”

He squinted at Hen, and then frowned.

“I’m not Gerrard, Hen.”

She sighed and relaxed some.

“I know,” she said. “I just don’t want her to go through the things I did.”

“Choosing not to be insulted by that,” he told her. “I don’t know why you’re worried about me doing anything. It’s not like I’m gonna make her wash my car!”

The last part was louder, so the words carried across the bay, Hen cringing at the volume. The response from Chimney was quick.

“Let it go!” he shouted.

“Never!”

“She was on my case almost right away,” Buck recounted with a laugh.

“Why?” Amy asked. Her hair, previously, had a single streak of color in it: pink, then blue, then red. Now, though, the entire top layer was a vibrant green.

Gavin’s biological mother was over to get as much time with him as she could, since the school year would be ending soon and she’d be in Barstow with her aunt for the summer. She didn’t have her own car yet, so she either got rides with May or used an Uber. Buck and Eddie were already planning for one of them to give her a ride back to the dorms.

Currently, they were sitting on the floor of the living room with a mess of Lego Duplo blocks. Gavin liked Chris’ Legos, much to Chris’ annoyance and sometimes terror, so they’d gotten Gavin the Duplo blocks to appease him and keep him from destroying his big brother’s Lego creations. Again.

“Because her first captain was a-” Eddie cut himself off and glanced down at Gavin, who was sitting between his legs and slamming a pair of blocks together. “He was kinda awful. For a lot of reasons.”

“Pops isn’t like that, though.” Chris sounded insulted on Buck’s behalf, and Eddie decided to sneak him an extra cookie after dinner. 

Chris stuck a figurine - different from the tiny yellow men of the regular Lego sets, larger and more cartoonish - into a car. Gavin made grabby hands for it and Chris gave it to him without a word. The tot started rolling it along the floor, purposefully ramming it into Eddie’s calf and laughing loudly every time.

“She knows,” Buck told Chris, defending his friend, and reached out to stop Senorita from batting a block under the couch. “She’s just worried.”

“If she knows, then she shouldn’t be doing it,” was Chris’ sass filled retort.

Buck barked out a startled laugh.

“How’re your finals going, Amy?” Eddie asked, changing the topic.

(Mostly because he agreed with his son, but that was neither here nor there.)

“Okay. I think so, at least.” She was putting together a Bluey set, one that Buck got just to set off TK. Eddie knew that was the reason, because Buck outright told him it was. “I’ve only taken a couple so far, Monday and Tuesday were study days.”

No classes, no finals, just days the students had off to prepare. Eddie and Buck only knew that because of May.

“How’re you doing on the social worker deal?” Buck asked her. “You said you were gonna talk to your advisor about what degree to get for that.”

“Oh!” Amy visibly perked up, looking excited. “It turns out that USC’s gonna have an actual social work bachelors the school year after next. My advisor told me to stay undeclared for now and just get my gen ed requirements out of the way.”

“Nice!” Buck leaned across the mess of Duplo blocks and gave her a high five. “I don’t think I ever even got that far.”

Eddie glanced at his watch and grimaced.

“I think we missed your bed time, mijo,” he told Gavin.

“No,” Gavin replied, shaking his head.

“Yes.” Buck poked him in the stomach, an act that made the three year old laugh. “Amy, I’ll take you back to the dorms after we get his toys away and him to bed.”

Chris leveraged himself up with a grim expression.

“We should take Hoover outside,” he told Amy.

The dog, upon hearing his name, got up and trotted over, tail wagging. Amy, who’d been here for a couple bed time routines since Gavin became possessed by the devil, did not question or argue. She just followed Chris and the dog to the back door.

“Cowards!” Buck called after them with a laugh.

Truthfully, Eddie kinda wished he could join them. The nightly bedtime routine had become something of a chore not long after Gavin’s third birthday. It was better than it was a couple months ago, but he still made his displeasure about going to bed known, as well as having to pick up his toys.

Tonight was… Not the worst, and not the first time that they’d ended up chasing him around the house to get him into his pajamas. It also wasn’t the first time they’d had to explain to him that throwing his toys was not acceptable behavior, and throwing his toys at them was even less so.

Eddie’s eye was still smarting from a well-aimed Duplo block as he left the bathroom to pad into the kitchen. Chris was in his room, Buck had just left with Amy, and Abuela-

Abuela was in the kitchen, about to fill an empty glass with water from the kitchen faucet.

“Oh, hey, Abuela, no.” Eddie hurried over to stop her. “The methane, we’re not supposed to drink the water until it's cleared up.”

Abuela stared at him in confusion, not quite comprehending what he was telling her. And then her face dropped as she set the glass down on the counter.

“I was supposed to know that, wasn’t I?”

Eddie’s heart clenched and he didn’t answer. Instead, he opened the fridge and took out one of the things of juice that they had. The Brita pitcher was unfortunately empty, probably why Abuela went for the tap.

“It’s fine,” he finally said as he filled up her glass with apple juice. “No harm done.”

“No harm done this time,” Abuela muttered darkly, taking the glass from him when he held it out to her. “Gracias, Eddito.”

“You’re welcome, ‘Buela.”

Eddie waited until she left, until he heard her door close. Then he buried his face in his hands, suddenly feeling so very tired.

Even though Buck specifically asked Bobby to do it, and even though Athena said they both would, she ended up going to talk to Hen alone. It wasn’t unusual, they went to each other's for wine nights all the time. She was worried, too, that showing up with Bobby would make Hen feel ambushed. Hen wasn’t dumb, if they were both there, she’d quickly realize what was going on.

So Athena left Bobby at the apartment, and she and Hen sat at Hen’s kitchen island with glasses of white wine and a charcuterie board of cheese and fruit. Chimney had taken Jee-Yun, Denny, and Mara to the movies, and Karen was also out. It was a good environment for a probing mission, although Athena was smarter than to immediately start asking why her friend suddenly changed her tune about being a captain.

No, she waited, and then eased into the topic with,

“Buck mentioned that the B-shift captain is retiring? Something about COPD?”

“Yeah.” Hen nodded, popped a piece of cheese into her mouth, then washed it down with wine. “He announced it a couple months back.”

“So there’ll be a captain’s position open. You thinking about trying for it?”

“I might.”

“Might?” Athena’s eyebrows rose. “Not too long ago, you were gunning for the job.”

“What if I don’t want it?”

“Why wouldn’t you go for a promotion?”

“Why did you turn down a promotion?” her friend shot back. “I remember you turning down that bump to lieutenant.”

Shoot. Athena wasn’t expecting Hen to bring that up, although she really should have.

“I turned it down because I realized that wasn’t the job I wanted.” There, the simple truth. “It would have been more about paperwork than protect and serve. More riding a desk than out patrolling.”

“And you never regretted that decision?”

Athena shook her head, mouth too full of wine to answer verbally. 

“Turning down a promotion, that’s kind of like the end of the road for your career, right?” Hen asked. “Wherever you are is where you’re gonna be for the rest of your life. No more advancement. You never felt stuck?”

“Not until now,” Athena said, and they both laughed. “That sounds like a perfect argument for why you should try for the job.”

“What if I like where I am now?” her friend said. “Right now, it’s hands-on. I don’t need to tell someone what to do, wait for them to do it, and then inevitably step in because they’re doing it wrong.”

“Bobby was hands-on,” Athena pointed out. “Buck’s hands-on.”

“Sometimes, if the call’s big enough, and never for medical calls,” Hen said. “When Ortiz’s kid died-”

“God.” Athena drained her wine glass and refilled it.

“I rode in the ambulance, trying to revive him. I abandoned my firefighters at the scene because I was too busy being a paramedic to be a captain.” Hen swirled the wine in her glass, staring at it as she did. “Besides, it was one thing to be captain of our shift. But B-shift? That would be a big change. People I don’t really know, different hours from most of my friends.”

“Maybe that would be better,” Athena said. “Buck’s talked about how weird it is, giving orders to you guys now.”

“It’s weird having him give us orders. I still catch myself thinking of Bobby as Cap, and I forget it’s Buck now. Sometimes it’s like, you were a probie yesterday, why are you telling me what to do?”

Athena thankfully managed to keep her grimace off her face. She’d listened to Buck voice a fear of that exact thing to Bobby several times. It was a good thing, then, that she’d come alone. Although she doubted Hen would’ve said something like that if Bobby were here.

“He hasn’t been a probie for a long time,” Athena pointed out.

“No, he hasn’t. Makes me feel old.” Hen laughed. “Buck’s a good captain, though. He’s no Bobby, but he’s far better than the ones we got stuck with before.”

“But,” Athena said, deciding they’ve veered off-topic enough. “You, B-shift captain.”

“I don’t know, ‘Thena.”

They both looked up and turned slightly in their seats at the sound of someone unlocking and opening the front door.

“That must be Karen,” Hen said, getting out of her seat and entering the living room. “Or not. What happened to the movie?”

“You know that expression, beer before liquor, never been sicker?” Chimney and the kids were the ones that had come in, not Karen. Mara was looking downright miserable. “Just substitute the beer and liquor for nachos and cotton candy, and you get the idea.”

“I don’t think we can go back to the movie theaters,” Mara told Hen, stepping forward to get a hug.

“It was kinda epic,” Denny commented, which told Athena just how bad of a mess was left for some poor theater worker to clean up. “Hey, Athena!”

“Hi, sweetheart.” Athena bent down slightly to hug Jee-Yun when she came running up, and then hugged Denny. “Hey, Chim.”

“Athena.” Chimney gave her a nod and a wave.

“Go lie down in my bed,” Hen told Mara. “I’ll get you something to try and settle your stomach.”

“Okay.” Still looking the epitome of misery, Mara trooped off in the direction of the bedrooms.

“Give me a second, ‘Thena,” Hen said. “And we’ll-”

“Nah.” Athena waved her off. “Focus on your girl. We’ll have other wine nights.”

She walked herself to her car, and made the journey to the apartment. An apartment that they would, hopefully, be moving out of very soon. The house was almost finished, it even had electricity and running water.

Bobby was reading a book on their couch, legs stretched out onto the coffee table and crossed at the ankles. He looked up when she entered and smiled. It dimmed, though, when he saw the expression on her face.

“She doesn’t know if she wants it,” Athena said, sitting down beside him and immediately curling up into his side. “I think you’ll have to talk to her.”

She felt, more than heard, him sigh.

Chapter 50: Wet Stuff on the Red Stuff

Chapter Summary

In which the Diazes have a difficult morning, Eddie visits the station with Gavin, and Maddie saves the day.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The morning was not going well.

Buck watched Abuela slam another cabinet door, shaking her head and muttering in Spanish. Almost every word out of her mouth was a swear, spoken sharply and angrily. It was better than ten minutes ago, when she was shouting.

Senorita was perched on her cat tree in the living room, watching the whole preceding with an anxiously twitching tail, her ears directed towards the kitchen like furry, fleshy satellite dishes. Hoover was beneath the dining table, as out of the way as possible, with his stomach to the floor.

“Abuela,” Buck tried again, for what felt like the umpteenth time. “What are you looking for? I can help.”

“The- The thing!” Abuela snapped, tone sharp with frustration.

“Yeah, you- you said that.” Patient. He had to be patient. This was far worse for her than it was for him. “But what thing?”

“It’s-” Abuela let out a frustrated noise as she slammed another cabinet closed. “The thing. You know, the…”

She trailed off, grumbling in Spanish again. Buck was about to ask her to at least describe what she was looking for, or even tell him where it was supposed to be, when he heard the door open. He let out a relieved breath when he laid eyes on Carla, who’d finally arrived, and hurried over to her.

“Sorry I’m late, I- What’s wrong?” she asked, clocking that something was up just by the expression on Buck’s face.

“It’s- It’s a bad morning,” he told her, keeping his voice low. “She’s trying to find something, but she can’t tell me what. She’s just getting more and more upset and- I managed to convince Eddie to go ahead and take Chris to school early, and he took Gavin with him. But I- I have no idea what to do, Carla.”

Eddie had insisted on being the one to stay and try to help Abuela with whatever was wrong, pointing out that Buck being late for work was much worse than Eddie being late for his paramedic labs. But Buck remembered how much this sort of thing tore away at Abby, could see how it was tearing away at Eddie, and stubbornly argued until he got his way. It helped that he pointed out how the one that didn’t stay would either be late anyway, to bring Gavin back to the house, or they would have Gavin with them for the day.

“The first thing you need to do is breathe,” Carla instructed, motioning with her hands. She wasn’t satisfied until he took a deep breath, and then another. “Now, have you managed to get her to try and describe it?”

“Not yet.”

“Okay. So that’s where we start.” With a nod, she sat her purse down on the table by the door and strode through to the kitchen. She slapped on a bright smile and, in her friendliest tone, said, “Isabel, Buck tells me you can’t find something.”

“It was supposed to be right there!” Abuela pointed at one of the drawers by the stove. “But it isn’t and I can’t find it and I can’t even tell you what I’m looking for!”

“So we don’t start there,” Carla said. “What were you wanting to do?”

Abuela paused.

“Breakfast,” she said, a bit calmer now. “I was going to make breakfast. Eggs.”

“So it’s something you cook with! See, we’re halfway there,” Carla said, still smiling. “Do the eggs go in it, or…?”

“No.” Abuela shook her head. “Not the skillet or the bowl, I found those. I know those. Memoria de pollo, but it’s not all gone.”

“Then it’s a-”

“What is it in Spanish?” Buck blurted out, interrupting Carla. It was the phrase that she used just then that made him think of it, one of those cliches you hear growing up that stick in your head. She could’ve just as easily translated it into English, “memory of a chicken,” but she didn’t. She went with the language she grew up hearing it in. “You- You keep trying to tell us in English. What is it in Spanish?”

She looked startled, blinking her eyes repeatedly. He got the impression she hadn’t even thought of doing that. Then she furrowed her brow and, after a moment, snapped her fingers.

“Batidor!” she exclaimed, raising her hand like she was brandishing it.

Oh!
