“Whisk,” Buck translated for Carla, already heading for where he knew it was. It took him only a moment to locate it, grab it, and bring it back. “Here you go.”

“Gracias.” Abuela sounded relieved as she took it from him.

“Why was it in the bathroom?” Carla asked as she looked at him funny.

“Gavin was playing with it last night, and it became a bath toy.” Buck shrugged. “It wasn’t worth the argument at the time.”

She just nodded, because she perfectly understood what he meant by that.

“I am sorry, Buckito, for…” Abuela’s words were quiet as she gestured around herself. “I should not have- I am too old to be acting like that.”

“‘Buela,” Buck said, placing his hands on her shoulders. “I once got so frustrated I sued Pops and the fire department.”

“Speaking of.” Carla poked him in the arm. “You’re gonna be late if you don’t get a move on.”

“Right!” 

He pecked a kiss on Abuela’s cheek and hugged Carla, then rushed down the hall to grab his work bag. Thankfully, he was already dressed in his uniform. After a pause for Abuela to do her usual routine of crossing him, knowing better than to argue against it, he was dashing out of the house and to the jeep. He pulled out his phone as he went.

“Maria, hi!” Buck said when the C-shift captain answered. “I’m so sorry, but I’m running late and-”

“The other Diaz already called.” Mayfair sounded amused. “I’ll see you when you get here.”

He loved his husband. So, so much.

Buck managed to arrive at the station on time, technically, in that A-shift hadn’t officially started yet. In practice, he was very, very late, to the point that most of C-shift was already changed and leaving. He got heckled for it when he climbed up to the loft, after a quick chat with Mayfair.

“We’re not about to respond to a fire you started, are we?” Hen asked him. She was at the coffee maker, pouring herself a cup.

“No.” Buck rolled his eyes as he collapsed into a stool at the island. “This morning has just sucked.”

“What happened?” Hen asked.

When Buck cut a glance to the dining table, where Albert and Ravi were talking with Toby, she frowned and came closer.

“Abuela,” he said, keeping his voice low. He didn’t really feel like sharing their difficulties with Abuela’s Alzheimer’s with the entire station. “She couldn’t find the whisk, and couldn’t remember the word for it, and got frustrated. Mostly with herself.”

Hen grimaced.

“She’s getting worse?”

“There’s no other direction to go.”

She gave him a sympathetic smile and his arm a comforting squeeze, then headed for the stairs with her coffee. Presumably, he guessed to get a start on inventorying the ambulances. He probably should have sent Albert off to help her, but that could wait.

Thankfully, the calls they responded to throughout the day weren’t anything serious. A fall, a minor traffic accident, a kitchen mishap. They’d just gotten back from one where a kid called 9-1-1 to report their kitchen was on fire, only for it to turn out to be nothing more than a smoking toaster and a noisy smoke detector, to find Eddie and Gavin waiting for them in the loft.

“My little guy!” Buck exclaimed when he spotted them on the couch, sweeping a giggling Gavin up and smacking a kiss onto his cheek. He gave one to Eddie, too. “And my big guy.”

“It’s nice to know where I rank in your priorities.” Eddie was smiling as he said it, so he obviously wasn’t too bothered. He wasn’t any better than Buck, anyways. “Gavin was a big hit with everyone at my labs today. We decided to stop by on our way home. Didn’t we, mijo?”

“Yeah!” Gavin nodded, curls bouncing with it. “Wanna see the big trucks.”

“And it’s nice to know where I rank in your priorities,” Buck laughed, before sobering up and smiling grimly at his husband. “You were putting off going home.”

“Yeah,” Eddie quietly admitted, averting his gaze to the floor for a moment before looking back up. “How…?”

“She was fine when I left.” Buck shrugged. “It was the whisk. That’s what she was looking for.”

“Ay, Dios.”

Eddie buried his face in his hands. Buck adjusted his hold on the toddler in his arms and sat down beside his husband.

“Hey, it’ll be fine,” he said, pressing into Eddie’s side. “We’ll get through this.”

Eddie lifted his head and sighed, and then leaned his weight against Buck.

“That’s kinda what I’m afraid of,” he said.

Eddie and Gavin didn’t stay for very long. Long enough for Gavin to be doted on by everyone else, and then be allowed to clamber all over one of the trucks. Buck made Eddie promise to text him when he got home, to tell him how Abuela was doing. The answer, half an hour later, seemed to be that she was still embarrassed over how she acted that morning.

It wasn’t Abuela’s fault, not really. But it also reinforced the fact that they needed to find Gavin a daycare, so Carla could focus on her.

Late in the evening, they responded to a fire. A large one. Which was very much not ideal, because there was still methane in the water. The 118 was the first at the scene, pulling up to a building that looked far more involved than the 30% reported by dispatch. It was a commercial building, and the workers were scattered around the parking lot and sidewalks.

But the 118 was the first at the scene, the 133 showing up a minute later, and Buck’s stomach dropped as the realization struck him. Because he was the first captain to the fire, which meant-

“Oh, God,” he intoned as he hopped out. He flinched along with everyone else as something exploded inside the building and fire billowed out of a window, the workers screaming in surprise and fear. “I’m the IC.”

“Good luck,” was all an unsympathetic Hen said as she got out of the ambulance.

Buck could panic about it afterwards.

“Hen, Chimney, Albert, see if anyone’s hurt and how badly. Ravi, Toby, Bell, four-inch lines,” he ordered, and then grabbed his radio to make sure everyone heard him as he said, “Engine water only.”

There was a chorus of “Copy” and “Got it” from everyone as they fell into motion.

“Dispatch, One Eighteen on-scene and assuming command,” he said, after switching channels. “It’s a commercial building, right? Anything I should know?”

“It’s a recycling building,” Maddie said, voice coming through his radio. “One of the employees called Nine-One-One after a spark from some machinery started the fire. The wing that’s burning stores combustibles-” Buck winced. That explained the explosion. “-but no high hazards. Do you see the east wing?”

“What about it?” Buck asked, already dreading the answer. Especially with the large sign that read, Recycle Batteries Here.

“It’s the e-waste unit, specializing in lithium-ion batteries.” Fuck. “So if the fire reaches that wing…”

“It’ll burn for a week and we’ll be breathing toxic fumes,” he finished for her. “Is the hydrant supply safe? Or is it- What the hell is he doing!?”

Buck dropped his hand from the radio as he shouted. The 118’s hoses were already hooked up to their engine, ready to start spraying, but the 133 were still setting up. Across the street, firefighters from the 133 were attaching their hose to the hydrant.

“Hey!” Buck shouted again as he hurried over. “Stop! We don’t know if-”

Too late. The firefighter opened the valve. The hose running along the pavement filled up as the water rushed through it and up to the top of the 133’s engine, where another firefighter was at the ready. They opened the hose’s nozzle, let the water loose-

And suddenly had a flamethrower in their hands.

“Shut that off!” Buck bellowed angrily, voice carrying without the need of the radio.

The idiot, thankfully, listened this time. He shut the valve, cutting off the supply of tainted water. The hose flattened as the pressure dropped, and the firefighter on top of the 133’s engine stopped their Ray Bradbury routine.

“Cap!” Hen shouted as she jogged over. “The flames are jumping!”

“It’s like a tinderbox!” Chimney added as he came over as well.

“Dispatch, we need a source of water,” Buck relayed into his radio. “Preferably water that doesn’t burn.”

“Most of the city is on the same water system, the methanated one,” Maddie said. “But some neighborhoods pull from groundwater wells. Cal West Water company is one, it’s nearby and they don’t source from Headworks.”

“Dispatch,” Chimney cut in. “Where’s the nearest hydrant?”

“About ten blocks.”

“Okay.” Buck let go of the button as he thought. “So maybe we don’t need a refill.”

“Just a longer straw,” Hen said.

“Or a chain of them,” Chimney said. “Hose relay. We bring the water to us.”

“Okay, yeah, that’s good. Do what you can with what we have until we have that water,” Buck ordered. The other two nodded, running off to pass on his orders to everyone else. He grabbed his radio, pressing down the button before speaking. “Dispatch, we’re gonna do a relay. But we need more engines.”

“Copy you, One Eighteen,” Maddie replied. “You’re point-seven miles from the source. The longest hose on the engine is seven hundred fifty feet, so we’ll need-”

“Five more engines,” Buck finished for her, doing the math in his head. 0.7 miles is 3,696 feet. 750 goes into it a little less than five times. Five engines would have enough hose to get the water to the 118, without them having to send someone up with a hose of their own. “We’re using water from our engine and the One Thirty-three’s for now, but it’s not gonna last long.”

“I’ll get it there,” Maddie promised. A moment later, Buck heard her rattle off engine numbers over the open channel - 121, 94, 144, 153, 134.

It was a race against time, and they were losing. They sprayed what they had, them and the 133, and it killed the fire where it hit. But there was so much fire, and it was hurried along by the combustibles within the facility. Buck watched as it spread, bit by bit, to the east wing. He directed them to spray there, to draw a line there and keep it from going any farther.

But there was so much fire, and not enough water. The 133 ran dry first, and then the 118. Their hoses dribbled sadly onto the ground. The fire was free to resume its meal of building and batteries, and it surged forward to gorge itself.

“We’re dry,” Buck told Maddie. “And the east wing is starting to catch.”

“Captain One Eighteen,” Maddie responded after a moment. “Your lifeline will be there any second.”

Those seconds ticked by. One, and then another, the fire chewing through the east wing with every one that passed. And then, finally, the 134’s captain himself came sprinting out of the dark and the smoke, dragging the hose along with him. At 750 feet, it was more than long enough to reach the 118’s engine, and Buck helped carry it the rest of the way.

“We’re plugged in!” Buck told Maddie, once he and the other captain got the hose hooked up.

“One Twenty-one, charging the line!” an unfamiliar voice said over the radio.

“Ninety-four, opening gate,” came another.

Then it was the 144, the 153, the 134. Buck held his breath and then let it out in relief when he saw the hose go from flat against the pavement to filled up as the water shot through. It reached the engine, and poured into the empty tank.

“Go! Go! Go!” Buck shouted to the ones on the hoses.

The sprays of water jetting out to slam into the flames would have been the most beautiful thing he saw all day, if he hadn’t woken up next to Eddie that morning. Already he could see the difference, the fire’s progress slowing to a crawl and then getting forced back. It was going to be a very long night, he could already tell that, but at least it wasn’t hopeless.

“We’ve got water,” Buck reported. “Thank you.”

“You’re welcome, One-Eighteen,” Maddie replied.

Now that they could actually fight the fire, Buck was free to focus on other things. Such as the paramedics. Albert was by a group of workers, wrapping someone’s arm in gauze.

“Some minor burns, smoke inhalation,” he told Buck, when Buck went over. “Nothing major. I don’t think any of them even need a trip to the ER.”

“Good.” Buck nodded and moved on, pausing when Albert called out to ask,

“Where are you going now?”

“To piss off the One Thirty-three’s captain,” was Buck’s answer. “And yell at whichever idiot didn’t listen earlier.”

He didn’t know what his face looked like as he stalked towards where the 133 were grouped up, but two people dove out of his path.

Chapter End Notes

Anyone not following my Tumblr missed a rant about the hose relay scene.

Chapter 51: Building Collapse

Chapter Summary

In which it's Bobby's turn to talk to Hen, and the 118 responds to a building collapse.

Chapter Notes

This would've been written and posted earlier, but I had a crash out the other day.
(Everything's fine, don't worry about it.)

“The last time I saw him that pissed off was when he went off on Brad,” Hen recounted with a laugh.

“What did the guy’s captain do?” Bobby asked. “The One Thirty-Three, you said?”

He was, ostensibly, showing off the new house to Hen. That’s what he invited her over for, and he was, actually, doing that. It just so happened that it wasn’t the only reason he invited her. But he figured she’d be suspicious if he showed up at her door so soon after Athena.

“The One Thirty-three, yeah.” Hen nodded as she looked around the large, long kitchen and dining room. “He just stood there and watched, kinda shellshocked. You’re gonna be able to fit a big table in here.”

“I’m going to take Buck with me to pick one out, along with whatever kitchen stuff we still need,” Bobby said. “As someone who’s been yelled at by Buck, I can’t blame the captain for that reaction. It’s like being attacked by a Golden Retriever.”

“Right? He sent the idiot scurrying away with his tail between his legs. Ten minutes later.”

“That’s what he gets for ignoring the orders of the IC. I’m glad Buck did alright with that, the first time can be overwhelming.” 

Bobby tapped his fingers along the granite countertop of the kitchen island. Would broaching the topic now be too soon? Too obvious? Though, really, Hen was neither stupid nor oblivious, so it probably didn’t matter.

Might as well go ahead, then.

“Any word on who all’s gonna try for the B-shift captaincy?” he asked, trying to keep his tone as nonchalant as possible.

Hen scoffed and rolled her eyes.

“I knew there was an ulterior motive to this,” she said.

“What do you mean? I’m just looking for gossip,” he tried. She just side-eyed him. “Alright, fine. Buck and Athena both have asked me to talk to you about it.”

“Buck did?”

“Why is that a surprise?” Bobby asked in return. “Not too long ago, you wanted to be the captain.”

“The captain of our shift, Cap,” Hen said. Bobby raised an eyebrow at the title. “Like I told Athena, switching to B-shift would be a much bigger change.”

“So?” Bobby countered. “Buck’s the captain of the One Eighteen’s A-shift instead of you, so that means you’ve lost all interest in a promotion?”

“I don’t know. Maybe.”

“Chimney managed to stay friends with everyone while on a different shift.”

“I wouldn’t say Chimney was friends with most of us during those months,” Hen said. “And he has the advantage of being smack dab in the middle of our twisted little family. That’s like saying Eddie has managed it while taking the paramedic courses. Because of course he has, he regularly saw almost everyone outside of work.”

“I don’t understand, Hen,” Bobby admitted. “Almost three years ago, you were excited at the idea of someone believing you could be a captain. You were perfectly willing to be captain last year. What happened?”

“Last year happened!” she snapped, and looked surprised at herself.

“Ortiz.”

“Yes, her. Do you have any idea how it felt to be screwed over because of politics? For the brass to have no confidence in me? For them not to have my back?”

Bobby opened his mouth, paused, and then shook his head.

“No,” he admitted. “I don’t.”

“It was crushing, Bobby. I thought it would be different. A black fire chief, a woman battalion chief. I thought it would be different! But it wasn’t. It was the same story as always. If it wasn’t Buck, then it would’ve been Gerrard. The man who got the boot for how awful of a person he was. The chief was more willing to back him than me.”

“That was politics, Hen, like you said,” Bobby tried. “Gerrard and Ortiz are friends, it has no bearing on you as a person.”

“Of course it doesn’t,” she spat. “But it does on them. If it was Buck as captain that day, I have no doubt they wouldn’t have even considered skipping him over for someone else.”

“Maybe. You don’t know that. Ortiz was grieving and angry and petty, and Simpson tries too hard to be on the politicians’ good sides,” Bobby pointed out. “What is this really about?”

“Bobby-”

“No, Hen. I can tell you’re avoiding the actual reason.”

Hen swallowed and averted her gaze to look out one of the french doors into the backyard.

“I don’t think I could take it if I tried, only to lose it again,” she admitted. “Years and years and years, it felt like everything about this job was stacked against me. I told you how much it meant to have my boss telling me that I had what it took to be captain. But what if you’re the only one who thinks that?”

“Buck does, too. And Athena.”

“The three of you are biased,” she said. “I just keep thinking that if they actually thought I could do it, they would’ve fought harder for me. What if no one in the brass thinks I should be captain? What if I keep slamming into that wall, to be rejected again and again?”

“You don’t know for sure that’ll happen.”

“And as long as I don’t apply for it, I can keep living in a world where I can pretend my bosses have faith in me.”

“Ah. The coin flip.” Bobby nodded as Hen looked at him in confusion. “It was a metaphor Buck used the day Gavin was dropped off at the station. I asked him why he hadn’t talked to Eddie about having more kids. He said that it was like a coin flip, as long as he didn’t flip it, as long as it stayed in the air, it could be heads or tails. But-”

“But it lands, and you’re stuck with what you get. If he asked Eddie, and Eddie said he didn’t want more kids, then that would be that.”

“And as long as you don’t apply for the captaincy, you can’t be rejected.”

“Yeah,” Hen sighed.

“And as long as you don’t apply for the captaincy, you’ll never be a captain.”

“Yeah,” she said again. “I know.”

“I kinda feel bad,” Buck said, having just gotten off the phone with Bobby. “I mean, I was pretty much just handed the job.”

“Mi sol,” Eddie tutted.

He lifted up Buck’s legs so he could sit on the couch,setting them in his lap. Immediately, Senorita leaped onto first the back of the couch and then to Eddie’s shoulders to curl up. They were in the living room, putting off going to bed just yet and simply enjoying the quiet of the hour.

The day hadn’t been a bad one. Mostly they spent it trying to find Gavin a daycare that could fit in with their twenty-four hour schedules and which wasn’t too far out of their way. There actually was one not too far away, just a few blocks, and in the right direction. They had plans to go check it out the next time they both had the day free.

“I was!” Buck insisted. “It’s not like I- Ow! Hey!”

Eddie had grabbed some of his leg hair and pulled. Buck pouted at him and kicked at his thigh with a heel.

“You went through all the official parts, too,” Eddie pointed out. “The test, the exercise, the interview. If you hadn’t passed all that, would they have kept you on as captain or would they have replaced you with someone else?”

“Stop making sense while I’m trying to feel guilty.” The way Eddie rolled his eyes was simply rude. “I never applied for the job, though. They just summoned me to the chief’s office and asked me if I wanted it.”

“Because the alternative was the potential for a lawsuit and a PR disaster.”

“Exactly! I didn’t earn it on merit- Ow! Stop that!”

“Stop talking shit about my best friend,” Eddie retorted, tossing away the strands of leg hair he just yanked out. “I get protective about him, y’know.”

“Yeah, yeah.”

“Now tell me about the guy you chewed out.” Eddie poked at him. “It gets me all hot and bothered when you tear into someone else.”

Buck threw back his head with a laugh.

“Just some idiot at the One Thirty-three that didn’t listen when I told everyone not to use the hydrant,” he said. “Ended up spraying fire onto the fire before he turned it off.”

“Firefighters with flamethrowers. I’m pretty sure I read that book in school.”

“That was what I thought!” Buck lifted up his hand and kept it there until Eddie gave him the high-five he was asking for, shaking his head with a fondness that made Buck ache. “I kinda felt bad afterwards. Pretty sure the guy was crying by the end. And I think I scared Bell.”

“You made him cry?” Eddie laughed.

“I think so! It was dark and he practically ran away when I was done, but I’m pretty sure I saw the beginning of tears.”

To be fair, Buck had hammered on the fact that the firefighter on the hose could’ve been severely injured and it would’ve been the idiot's fault for not listening. Because Buck had seen how the firefighter on the hose had reacted to suddenly having a flamethrower, the way he treated it like he suddenly had a live snake writhing in his hands. It was a miracle that no one was injured, really, if not that firefighter, then someone that happened to get in the way of his frightened flailing.

“They should have the methane out of the water soon,” Eddie said. His thumb was rubbing circles into Buck’s ankle. Buck was fairly certain he didn’t even know he was doing it. “Hopefully the next shift will be calmer.”

“Eddie.” Buck groaned. “Did you really have to say that?”

“Say what?”

“You jinxed us.”

Eddie gave Buck a flat stare, and then pulled at his leg hair again.

Buck was already composing the mocking text he was going to send Eddie after this as they pulled up to the scene. They didn’t have very many details on hand, just the bare minimum, but it was enough to convey how much this was gonna suck. A high rise apartment building collapsing was never not gonna suck.

“One Eighteen, on-scene,” Buck reported as he climbed out of the engine. He glanced over as the 133 pulled up as well and huffed out a breath. Wasn’t their station closer? “What do we know?”

The apartment building looked absolutely wrecked. Cracks ran up almost its entire structure, and there were gaping holes blown out of the sides. Pieces of it had come down to crush cars that had hopefully been empty, one of them an LAPD patrol cruiser.

“We received twenty-eight calls reporting sounds of explosions on the lower level,” Maddie responded. Explosions on the lower level explained why the building looked like this; the foundation was pretty much taken out. “Still working on the cause.”

“I have a guess,” Chimney quipped as he checked over a dust-covered resident, looking shellshocked as they huddled on the pavement.

It was probably the same guess as Buck’s.

“Meyers, shut off the water! Clarke, the utilities!” he ordered. “I don’t want to add more methane to this, and I do not want any sparks.” 

Methane in the water didn’t stay in the water. It bubbled up like carbonation and was released into the air, where it could build up without proper ventilation. The lower level of an apartment building would probably have the laundry room, and it almost definitely didn’t have enough ventilation. 

And now any enclosed space in the wreckage could turn into a bomb.

“Ravi, Toby, ground ladders on Bravo side.” That part seemed steadier. “Start getting people out that way.”

“Got it, Cap!” Ravi chirped out, hurrying off with the driver-engineer.

“Bell-” Buck started, only to be interrupted by Hen’s,

“We’re gonna need more than a ground ladder.”

She was staring up. Buck followed her gaze and spotted a young woman up above, stranded in what might have once been an apartment’s corner room. There were just jagged, broken walls left, so it was hard to say.

“Help!” the trapped woman shouted. “Up here!”

“Step back from the edge!” Hen shouted back. “We’re coming!”

“My mom’s hurt!”

“Javier!” Buck barked out, spotting him a few feet away.

The sound of his name had him snapping into motion. He ran to the ladder truck and clambered up to the controls for the aerial.

“I’m guessing you’re going up there?” Buck asked Hen and Chimney, and didn’t really need them to answer. “Be careful. I don’t like how this building is looking.”

Eventually, it might settle onto its own weight again and reach something close to stable. As it was now, however, he did not trust it to stay standing, and the act of settling could trap and crush anyone inside. If he could justify it to himself, he wouldn’t be sending anyone into that death trap. But none of them chose this job to stand on the sidelines while people were in danger.

“Dispatch, do we know how many people were supposed to be in this building?” he asked while Hen and Chimney jogged off to the ladder truck.

“There is, or there were, two hundred and fifty-five apartments,” Maddie answered. “We’re waiting for the tenant list, but there should be somewhere north of three hundred people.”

“Copy that. Bell!” He waited for the probie to stumble to a halt and rush over. The 144 and the 153 had arrived, he noted, which meant more people to help with extraction, and more paramedics to get people through triage. “There’s a clipboard inside the engine, by the captain’s seat. It has a pen, and there’s sheets of paper. You are going to gather the names of every resident that comes out of that building, and their apartment number. Understood?”

He remembered that first big call of his, the plane that crashed off the coast. There was a woman whose job was to simply keep track of everyone they pulled out. It was protocol for events like these, but he wasn’t certain if the official person for it had arrived yet.

“Yeah! You got it, cap!” Bell nodded, a plait coming loose from under her helmet, and then hurried to the engine.

“Dispatch,” Buck said, thumbing his radio as he went to where Albert and the 133 paramedics were setting up the triage tent. He saw a couple of them freeze at the sight of him and then hunker down like scared bunnies. “Who’s in charge of gathering tenant names there?”

“That would be Maddie and Sue,” Linda answered.

That wasn’t much of a surprise. Buck knew that Sue tended to put Maddie into that sort of role, since her experience as an ER nurse helped her sort through chaos better than some of the others.

“I’ve sent Firefighter Frey to get the names and apartment numbers of everyone who’s gotten out so far.”

“That’ll be a big help, I’ll tell them,” she said. “Captain, we’re still getting calls from people trapped in the upper floors.”

“We’ll get ‘em.”

Buck helped get the triage tent up, and then spent his time keeping an ear on his radio and an eye on the chaos surrounding him. Mostly, he was tracking who went in and who came out, to the best of his ability. Toby and Ravi were bringing people they’d managed to rescue with the ground ladders, most of them scraped and bruised but ambulatory. He saw Hen and Chimney returning with the woman they’d gone to help, along with someone else on a gurney.

It was because he was paying attention that he noticed the woman, covered in dust and as scraped up as any of the other residents, sprinting towards them before she gave a shrill shout of,

“Help! Help! Help me!”

He reached her just a moment after Chimney, who caught her and started looking her over.

“Did you hit your head at all?” the paramedic asked, getting a negative in return. “Does your neck hurt? Any kind of pain at all?”

“No! No! My boyfriend, he’s in the laundry room,” she said. “The lady told me I- I should go and get- I should get-”

“Okay, okay, just breathe,” Chimney coaxed. “Where’s the laundry room?”

“The basement.” She started crying. “There’s so much blood.”

“That was probably where the explosion happened,” Buck guessed. “Ma’am, here. Take a seat over here.”

There were foldout chairs set up at the tent, and Buck and Chimney guided her to a free one. She was upset, very upset, so there was a limited amount of time they had to get information from her.

“You said there was a lady with him?” Chimney asked.

“Yes,” the woman answered. “The police lady. Um- Um - Sergeant Grant.”

Buck felt his heart stop, drop, restart.

“Hen!” Chimney called. “Panic attack, can you take over?”

“Yeah, okay.” Hen sounded confused as she came over. “Where are you going?”

“Ma’s in the laundry room with her boyfriend,” Buck answered for him.

From the expression on her face, Hen went through the same reaction he did.

“Sounds like the boyfriend’s hurt pretty bad.” Chimney stood and shouldered his medkit. “I’m gonna go lend a hand.”

“Be careful,” Buck instructed, stepping out of Bell’s way as she came to get a patient’s info.

“Captain One Eighteen,” Maddie’s voice came over his radio. “Do you have anyone free?”

“Yeah.” Buck flagged down Ravi before he could go back to the building. “What do you need?”

“We received a call from a Flint West before it disconnected. His ex-wife confirmed he’s in unit Nine-Twelve.”

“Okay. Is this guy injured?”

“Likely. I’ve been trying to call, but no answer.”

“We’ll find out.” If he was injured enough that he could no longer answer his phone, then he might need a paramedic to get him stabilized enough to move. “Albert!”

The paramedic straightened up from where he was helping a patient. When Buck waved him over, Albert patted the man on the shoulder and jogged to him.

“Flint West, unit Nine-Twelve,” he told him and Ravi. “Trapped, might be injured.” 

“Got it, Cap.” Ravi nodded, and then smacked Albert on the arm with the back of his hand. “C’mon, let’s gear up.”

Buck watched them go and was about to move on to the next thing requiring his attention, when a thought struck him. A question, really.

“Why didn’t Ma radio to tell us she needed help?” he asked no one in particular. “Why did she send someone out to get us?”

Hen and Bell frowned, but neither gave him an answer.

Chapter 52: Search and Rescue

Chapter Summary

In which Buck happily hands off the baton, Chimney finds a mess in the basement, Ravi and Albert discover their civillian has moved, and Eddie sees the news.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

It would never not be weird, in Buck’s opinion, to be in a huddle with other captains and have them looking to him for leadership. He was gonna start telling Toby to drive slower if this kept happening, so some other firehouse could get to the scene first and then that captain could be the incident commander. As it was, he was in full “fake it ‘til he made it” mode.

“We’ve got a couple dozen people out of the top floors so far,” said the 144’s captain, a stern looking woman whose coat named her Snow. “It’s slow going. Everything’s stable up there for now, but there’s also pieces of floor missing.”

“No risks,” Buck told her, and he could hear the accusation of hypocrisy from people that weren’t even there. “I don’t wanna have to rescue our own people in the middle of this.”

“Triage is going fast,” Captain Cooley, the 153’s captain, said. He was middle aged and gray at the temples. “But we can’t do much of anything for most of them, not here.”

“I’ve already requested more RA units.”

“Ivory and Vince Hooper, ten-oh-two.” Bell, standing nearby, had the clipboard in hand and was relaying names and apartment numbers over her radio to dispatch. “Betsy Fitzgerald, Faye Morgan, Maggie Contreras, twelve-twelve. Abigail, Cliff, Ariel, and Phoebe Pittman, eight-thirteen. Those’re the new ones.”

“Thank you, Ms. Frey,” Buck heard Sue reply. “We’re marking them off now.”

“Diaz!”

At the sound of the new voice, Buck spun around and let out a relieved breath. Chief Williams was marching towards him, utterly unbothered by the chaos around her. He met her halfway, glad to be handing the baton off.

“Chief.”

“Dispatch said we’ve got most of them accounted for so far?”

“I think so,” Buck said. “I’ve had my probie gathering their information, the ones that could give it. Between her and dispatch, we’ve got a little less than three hundred accounted for so far. We still have people trapped in the building, upper floors and basement.” He gestured as he spoke, pointing towards the ninth floor, where he knew Albert and Ravi were heading, and the basement with Athena and Chimney. “My guys, along with the One Thirty-three’s and the One Forty-four’s, have been going in and out.”

“Any black tags?”

“Not yet.” He caught her looking at the cars crushed by pieces of concrete. “Pretty bad injuries, though. A couple might not make it past the ER, and there’s one we sent off that might not make it that far. I’m pretty sure we’ve got half the ambulances in downtown ferrying people around, and I’ve already asked for more. We were sending them to LA General and First Presbyterian, but dispatch said their ERs are filled. Byrne Memorial still has beds, and I told them to take the less critical patients to hospitals farther away, like LA Regional and Mont Grove.”

The chief’s mouth drew into a tight line as she tilted her head to look up at the building.

“At least it’s not tilted over,” she said. Buck was pretty sure she hadn’t meant for him to hear it. “Any idea how this happened?”

“Methane’s our best guess.” They both grimaced. “Callers said there were explosions on the lower floors. The laundry room’s in the basement, and a resident said there was a lot of blood. Sergeant Grant and the older Paramedic Han are in there, trying to help a patient.”

“Call log said it was Sergeant Grant that called everything in.” Williams kept staring at the building for a moment longer, and then she gave a firm nod. “Alright. This is a mess, but it sounds like you’ve done a good job handling it. Where’re the other captains?”

“Over there,” Buck said, pointing. The other three were conversing amongst themselves, arguing about something.

“Tell me where you’ve got people while we walk,” she ordered, already in motion.

Buck hurried to keep up, talking as he went.

“I’ve had the One Fifty-three handling the triage…”

Chimney imagined there were bombed out buildings in war-torn countries that looked friendlier than the basement of this apartment complex. The hall he was in resembled more and more an artificial cave, with flickering light fixtures hanging by bare wires and ductwork spearing the floor. Pieces of the wall and ceiling and floors above provided partial barricades that he had to duck beneath or ease around. There were cracks crawling across what still stood, and he knew that one good shake could have all this coming down upon his head.

He paused at one of the hanging lights and frowned at it. Buck had sent Clarke to shut off the utilities, so these lights should be dark. Either she hadn’t done that, or the basement had another power source. An emergency back-up generator of some kind, maybe.

The laundry room, the presumed source of the explosion, was in much the same state. Rubble was piled up in the middle and along the edges, and burnt out washers and driers were crushed beneath it or somehow survived against the walls. But the doorway, which was burnt and charred, was clear.

“Hang in there, Donnie.” That was Athena’s voice. Chimney spotted her by one of the piles of rubble, from which someone was partially sticking out. “You’re doing great.”

“Athena!”

She turned and he saw relief on her face.

“Oh, thank God.”

“You alright?”

“Yeah. But I’ve got two trapped, one bleeding out,” she said as she stepped out of the way so he could see. There was a man in the middle of the rubble pile, looking pale beneath the cement dust. The first one had a hand pressed to a wound on the man’s shoulder. “That’s Donnie. His girlfriend Crystal is the one I sent out for help.”

There was something about the other guy, the one that was trapped but not bleeding out. Something familiar that was tickling Chimney’s brain.

“Are you-” Chimney squinted. “Cop cart guy?”

The last time he’d seen him, the guy was practically tenderized meat. According to the rumor mill, the kid was a bit too pushy in regards to people putting their shopping carts in the cart corrals, and someone lost their patience with him. It was around the same time as Brad Torrance playing guest at the station and Phillip Buckley dying, so there’d been more important things demanding Chimney’s attention.

“Retired,” cop cart said. “I’m a civilian now.”

“This is Graham,” Athena supplied. “He’s been holding pressure on the wound, but what we really need is a tourniquet.”

Chimney looked over again at where the wound was located. High up on the shoulder, more on the torso. A tourniquet wouldn’t do any good there, but he wasn’t gonna say that right then. Instead, he checked in with Graham.

“Can you wiggle your fingers and toes for me?” he asked. With the way they were both pinned, he needed to be sure.

“Yeah.” Graham lifted his free hand and wiggled his fingers. His legs were out of sight, so his word would need to be enough.

“Good, not a spinal injury then.” Chimney dug into his medkit and tugged out the actual right tool for Donnie’s wound. “This is a hemostatic pad. It’ll help get the blood to clot and stem the bleed. Okay?”

“Yeah. Yeah, okay.” Graham nodded and held out his hand. When Chimney gave him the pad, he quickly passed it over to his other and slapped it onto Donnie’s wound like Indiana Jones swiping treasure off a pressure plate.  “Got it.”

“Good man.” Now that the bleeding would, hopefully, slow down, it was time to replace the blood already lost. “Donnie, we’re gonna set up an IV, alright? Get some fluids in you. Then we’ll call for heavy rescue.”

“An IV?” Donnie’s voice was weak. “How?”

“Through your foot,” was Chimney’s answer as he rounded to where Donnie’s legs were sticking out a little. Something was wedged beneath the heavy slab that was trapping him, which kept it from crushing him entirely.

“His foot?” Graham was craning his neck in an attempt to see.

“It’s what I’ve got.”

Chimney yanked the guy’s shoe off, and then his sock. The top of the foot, the dorsal venous plexus, and the sides of the ankle and leg, the great and small saphenous veins. Those were the veins he needed to find a good sticking candidate out of.

“There’s a problem with calling for heavy rescue,” Athena told him. “I couldn’t get through on my radio. Too much concrete, maybe.”

“You can get Buck and them when we’re done here,” Chimney said. “Right now, you can be my extra hands.

The climb up to the ninth floor was nowhere near as easy as it could have been. The stairwell still existed, mostly. Ravi didn’t really trust it, and there were spots that they had to climb over chunks of building. A couple times he and Albert had to help people over those same pieces of debris on their way to evacuating, and radioed for others to come pick them up.

The ninth floor was mostly intact. By which Ravi meant the walls were still standing and there was still a floor. He was fairly certain the lack of a roof was not original to the design, though it did allow sunlight in to illuminate their way.

“Buck said Nine-Twelve, right?” Albert asked, pointing at each placard with an apartment number on it.

“Yeah. It should be…” They rounded a corner. He saw first 913, and then 912 farther down. “I see it!”

Albert pulled out the ax he’d tucked with the rest of the gear.

“You or me?”

“After you, Alley Cat.” Ravi stepped aside with a grin.

His boyfriend rolled his eyes and then slammed the head of the ax into the door, right by the handle and latch. The lock broke and the door swung open.

“LAFD!” Ravi called out as he entered. The room was much the same as the rest of the building, missing roof and all. “Flint!”

“Ravi!”

He heard the shout just a moment before he lost his balance, teetering on the edge of a giant hole. Albert suddenly grabbing him by the harness was the only thing that kept him from toppling over.

“Okay, that was my bad.” He let out a shaky breath as he peered down. “I wasn’t looking where I was going.”

“Cap, we’re at Nine-Twelve,” Albert relayed over the radio as he joined Ravi in looking. “But Nine-Twelve isn’t here.”

“What does that mean?” Buck asked.

“He means Nine-Twelve is now, uh… Would you say that’s the seventh floor?”

“I think so, yeah.”

“He means Nine-Twelve is now Seven-Twelve.”

There was a beat of silence.

“Be careful,” Buck said after a moment. 

“Will do, Cap.”  Ravi let go of the radio and nudged Albert. “Ready for some rock climbing?”

“We haven’t done that in a while,” Albert commented as he helped Ravi get out all the ropes and such. “Next date?”

“Sounds good to me.”

They anchored themselves to piping along the wall, after making sure it wasn’t liable to just tear off. It was a short drop down the two floors, made difficult only as they avoided pointy ends and unstable debris. When they reached their destination, they unhooked themselves and started searching.

“LAFD!” Albert shouted.

“Are you here, Flint!?” Ravi called out.

“Over here!” Albert was kneeling beside an antique looking wardrobe, which was wedged amongst some pieces of concrete. “I found him!”

There was a little gap, through which Ravi could see an old man.

“This is crushing me,” the presumed Flint managed to say, voice weak.

“We’ll get you out of here, sir,” Ravi assured him, though he had no idea how they’d manage it.

The wardrobe wouldn’t budge. Nor would any of the pieces of debris. Not that Ravi was willing to try too hard there, because he was a bit afraid that they’d collapse on poor Flint and crush him entirely.

“Do you think…” Albert frowned and then yanked the wardrobe doors open.

“Are we going to Narnia?” Ravi asked, even as he helped his boyfriend dig out the contents. “Please don’t tell me we’re going back into the closet.”

“I’m kinda hoping that there’s not any debris behind this.”

Once everything was out, Albert took the ax in hand and Ravi took the moment to admire him with it while he swung. The back of the wardrobe came apart easily in only a couple swings, revealing the man’s legs.

“Alright, sir, can you-” Albert cut himself off as Flint started turning in the little space he had, to start climbing through the wardrobe. “I guess you can. No spinal injuries, then.”

Between the two of them, they pulled the old man out easily enough. He collapsed with a huff when he was free, taking a seat on the floor.

“Deep breaths,” Ravi advised.

“I didn’t think you bums would ever find me,” Flint said. “Thank you.”

“Your ex-wife told us where you were.”

“Marge?” Flint sounded surprised. “She hasn’t spoken to me in years.”

“She spoke to Nine-One-One, at least,” Albert said. “But are you-”

Rumbling cut Albert off. He and Ravi dove over top of Flint to cover him as something exploded beneath them, shaking the building and sending debris raining down.

Sometimes, Eddie thought, being a pet owner was truly an inglorious thing. Take, for instance, the humble litter box. It was hard to declare themselves the apex anything when they would regularly kill their knees as they scooped out their cats little landmines before Hoover could do it for them. Or Gavin, who they’d once had to intercept before he crawled into it to explore the curious sandbox.

To put salt in the wound, Senorita seemed to delight in waiting until they’d just finished up before casually stepping inside and dirtying it again. Buck claimed she would maintain eye contact as she did it in an act of dominance. Eddie told him he was a weirdo for watching their cat poop.

Or take the backyard. It was Hoover’s bathroom. It was also the place where Gavin played and they would occasionally host people. That meant they’d go around and scoop up the dog’s much larger landmines, to be thrown into the trash.

That was what Eddie was currently doing, or just finishing up doing. It was a chore he typically foisted onto Buck, usually while smiling and batting his eyes and wearing his tightest jeans. It was a chore he would have happily foisted onto Christopher, except Hoover also liked to dig and that combination sounded like a humiliating disaster waiting to happen. Eddie didn’t think his son would ever forgive him if he tripped while carrying a bag of dog poop.

“You’re lucky I love you,” Eddie told Hoover as he came in. “You filthy, disgusting animal.”

“Funny,” Abuela said. She stepped out of the way as Eddie went to the kitchen sink. “I think I’ve heard you call Buck the same thing.”

“I say it with more love when I’m talking to Hoover,” he shot back as he washed his hands. “It’s with annoyance when I say it to Buck.”

“Right.” She rolled her eyes at him, which was simply insulting, and tugged out one of Gavin’s cups from the cabinet. It was bright orange, and had large handles for him to grip. From the fridge, she pulled out the apple juice to fill it up. “Take this in there to Gavincito?”

“Happily.” 

Eddie shut off the faucet, dried his hands, pecked a kiss onto his grandmother’s cheek, and took the cup. Gavin was in the living room, as was Chris. The former was on the floor with his toy fire engine, happily crashing it into some of his other toys. The latter was on the couch, remote in hand.

“Dad!” Chris said.

“Here you go, buddy.” Eddie set the cup on the coffee table. “What is it, mijo?”

His oldest didn’t say anything, he simply pointed at the TV. It seemed that he stopped on the news, which was currently playing a story about a building collapse downtown. On the screen, firefighters from several different houses were scurrying around.

“It is a race against time to find survivors trapped in the rubble of this collapsed apartment building.” It was Taylor Kelly reporting. Eddie had to fight the urge to grab the remote and change the channel. “Resources are stretched thin as crews work to save those trapped or buried. First responders from multiple firehouses are on the scene, with hopefully more on the way to help conduct search and rescue.”

The camera panned around, occasionally lingering on crushed cars, bright red fire engines, and firefighters pulling people out of the debris. Eddie spotted Buck in the background, talking into his radio. He looked stressed.

“Right, then.” Where were his keys? There they were. “Chris, watch your brother.”

“Tell Pops I said hi!” his son called after him.

Chapter End Notes

If you're interested at all, I procrastinated by compiling a list of the hospitals that are mentioned in the show.

Chapter 53: Fixing Death

Chapter Summary

In which Chimney fixes death, Eddie surprises his husband, and everyone gets out of the death trap

The building roared and rumbled, plumes of concrete dust exploding outward. Everyone outside reflexively ducked, each of them expecting more pieces of the building, if not the entirety of it, to come falling down upon all their heads. When it quieted again and the dust settled to show the building still standing, Buck let out a sigh of relief.

“What was that?” Bell asked, clutching at the clipboard and staring wide-eyed at what used to be an apartment building.

“Methane explosion,” was Buck’s grim answer for her. He grabbed his radio and thumbed it on. “One Eighteen, sound off. Where is everyone?”

“Wilson here,” Hen immediately answered. “I’m at triage with Clarke and Meyers.”

“Klein, just outside of Alpha side,” Toby followed. “I’ve got Hendrix with me and a couple civvies.”

“Perez and I are to you left, Cap,” Javier said, the pair of them waving when Buck turned to check.

“Albert and I are still on the seventh floor,” Ravi responded, just as Buck was about to raise them specifically. “We’ve got Flint with us.”

“Do you have a way out?” Buck asked.

There was a pause. It wasn’t very heartening.

“We’ll find one,” Albert finally answered.

That wasn’t an acceptable answer, in Buck’s opinion, but it was probably the best they could give him at the moment. He had a bigger problem to worry about, anyway, that being the fact that not everyone had checked in yet.

“Chimney?” Buck tried. “Chimney, do you copy?”

Nothing.

“Cap!” Hen was jogging towards him from triage. “He’s not answering.”

“I know.” Buck glared at the building, and then heaved out a breath. “Grab Clarke and Meyers, go see what’s going on. But if that building shifts again-”

“We’ll come straight out,” she promised as she ran off, but he wasn’t certain if she actually meant it or not.

Buck prayed to whichever power decided to listen today that he didn’t end up regretting that decision.

Chimney had been in worse situations than his current one, some of them very recent. At least he wasn’t bleeding out because some mad scientist’s vanity project was eating away at his capillaries. But just because he’d been in worse fixes didn’t mean things in the apartment building’s laundry rooms were all sunshine and roses.

Actually, there was actual sunshine now, beaming through the holes in the broken ceiling. So that was a bright side.

The not-so-bright side was that the last explosion shook the building and brought more of it down. Not on their heads, thankfully, but their exit out of there was blocked off by large pieces of cement and concrete and just general building. Which meant they were stuck until someone came to rescue them because, just like Athena said earlier, their radios couldn’t get through.

But that was not Chimney’s immediate worry at the moment. No, his immediate worry was how bad Donnie was looking. He’d gotten the IV inserted into the great saphenous vein in the man’s foot - not the preferred location, for reasons including an increased chance of a deep vein thrombosis, and he really hoped the guy wasn’t diabetic - and now Athena was holding the bag of saline for him in lieu of an actual stand.

“Just keep squeezing that,” Chimney instructed. He went back to his bag, to dig out the next thing he’d need to keep this guy alive. “Gently and evenly.”

“Does anyone know we’re down here?” Athena asked. She adjusted the arm holding the IV bag, lifting it a bit higher.

“Buck and Hen both do, so I like our chances.” After all, Buck had essentially out-stubborned everyone into surviving when they were stuck in that lab, and Hen would never leave him behind. “How’re we doing, Donnie? Feel that saline cocktail kicking in yet?”

Donnie’s slurred answer was not heartening, even more so with how he trailed off after only a couple words - “I, uh…” - and then fell silent. Chimney, worried now, got up to get a closer look. It looked like he fell unconscious.

“Graham, shake him for me,” Chimney instructed.

Mr. Cop Cart nodded.

“C’mon. Stay awake, guy.” He shook Donnie, the man’s head limply listing back and forth. “Oh, I think he’s out.”

Shit.

“What can I do to help?” Athena asked.

“What you’re doing now,” was Chimney’s answer. 

He grabbed the blood pressure cuff and stethoscope he dug out, sticking the cuff around Donnie’s leg, just above his foot. The bell of the stethoscope went just under it. He inflated the cuff and then let it deflate, listening for the Korotkoff sounds with the stethoscope and tracking the needle on the cuff’s gauge.

The results were not good.

“Fiftty-four over thirty,” he told Athena.

“What do you think?”

“I think he’s about to arrest.”

“Well, CPR is not an option,” Athena stated, glaring at the debris resting on top of Donne.

“Maybe we can defib him.” Chimney’s medkit had an AED. It was just a matter of getting the pads where they needed to be on Donnie’s torso. “Graham, can you reach his chest? Not just his side.”

“Uh.” Graham turned as best he could while trapped and stretched out with his free hand, the one not keeping pressure on Donnie’s wound. “I- I think so.”

“I lost his pulse,” Athena announced. She had her fingers pressed to Donnie’s ankle.

Then they’d have to use what they had and hope for the best. Chimney pulled out the AED and opened it up. The defibrillator pads were squarish and white, attached to the machine by wires that he really hoped were long enough.

“Graham, I’m gonna give you these defib pads,” he said as he straightened, holding them out for the man to see.

“Is he gonna die?” Graham’s voice trembled.

“Not if you stay calm and help me. And if he does, then I’ll fix that, too.”

“Fix death?”

“I do it all the time,” Chimney assured him. “Now, one pad needs to go on the front right of his chest-” He mimed doing it to himself. “-and the other on his left side. Can you do that?”

“Uh, yeah.” Graham nodded, holding out his hand for the pads. “Left side, right front. Left side, right front.”

The pad for Donnie’s left side was easy enough. It was the one that needed to go on Donnie’s chest that was the problem. Graham strained himself as he stretched, and for a moment Chimney wasn’t certain he could reach. Until-

“Got it! They’re on!”

“Good. Next important thing,” Chimney said. “You cannot be touching him when I shock him. When I say “clear,” your hands go up. Got it?”

“Yeah, yeah, yeah.”

They nodded to each other, and then Chimney knelt down to turn on the AED. Donnie’s heartbeat, when the screen lit up, was the concerning spikey hills of ventricular tachycardia. The blood loss sent the guy into hypovolemic shock, which was what they’d been trying to prevent with the saline. But for the saline to be effective, for it to be circulated to where it needed to go, the heart had to be pumping properly.

“Charging. Clear!”

Graham’s hands shot up into the air, one of them covered in blood. Chimney hit the button and the machine sent electricity surging through the wires, the pads, and into Donnie. A moment, one where no one breathed, and then Donnie’s heartbeat strengthened and returned to normal sinus rhythm.

“Okay! We’re back in sinus,” Chimney declared. “Graham, hand back on that wound. Donnie! Can you hear me?”

The answer he received was a mumble, but it was still an answer.

“How much time did that buy him?” Athena asked, voice low and words quiet.

Chimney figured the grim expression he gave her was answer enough.

“Ravi, Albert,” Buck barked into his radio. “Where are you?”

It had been far too long since he’d last heard from them, and even longer since he last laid eyes on them. Contact with Hen and them was lost - apparently the radios weren’t getting through from the basement; they’d sent Clarke topside again long enough to pass that along - and the building was crumbling as he watched. None of those facts were doing nice things to his nerves at the moment.

“Bravo wall, Cap,” Ravi finally answered. “Look up.”

Buck did, spotting him and Albert, along with someone that must’ve been flint, standing behind the broken wall of an apartment on the seventh floor. Albert waved down to him.

“What happened to the way you came?”

“Ceiling came down and we lost our anchor point,” Albert answered. “We’re trying to reach the stairwell, but everything’s blocked.”

Something exploded again, shaking the building. More of it fell to the ground, sending everyone scurrying for cover. At the end of the street, Williams was shouting something at someone.

“It’s really unstable up here.” Ravi sounded about as stressed as Buck felt.

“Tell me about it,” Buck replied. He scanned the building, trying to find some safe way to get them out. There wasn’t any that he could immediately see, but he was not simply giving up. “Chief Williams called for more USAR-”

“There’s no time for that.”

Buck paused, frowned, turned, and was somehow entirely unsurprised to see his husband standing right fucking there in his turnouts. The man had the audacity to smile and wave at him.

“What the hell are you doing here?” he demanded.

“You looked stressed on the news, capitán. Thought I’d come lend a hand,” Eddie replied. “Chris says hi, by the way.”

Buck rolled his eyes, but he couldn’t keep his smile at bay.

“Chimney and Ma are in the basement with at least one critical patient,” he told Eddie, motioning to that direction. “Hen’s trying to reach them with a couple of the others, but the radios aren’t working down there.”

“And Ravi and Albert are up there,” Eddie said, tilting his head to look up at them.

“They said their way to the stairwell was blocked, and I am not sending more people up there to clear the way,” Buck said. “But there’s too much debris out here. We’d have to clear it for the ladder to get close enough to reach ‘em with the aerial.”

“By the time we got the path clear, we wouldn’t need it. The building would be at our feet.”

“Exactly.”

“Okay, so.” Eddie frowned at the building, his face a mask of concentration. “If Bobby was here, what kind of stupid stunt would you pull right now that would have him yelling at you?”

“Seriously?”

“As serious as- Oh!” Eddie turned his head to face Buck. He was grinning. “Is the line gun still on the truck?”

Buck blinked, and then his smile grew.

(The line gun was, indeed, still on the truck. It almost wasn’t, though. Buck and Javier had, just the other week, talked about whether or not they should take it out to make room for something they might actually use. Luckily, they’d stuck a pin on that topic when the alarms interrupted them and never got back to it.)

“Chief,” Buck said into his radio as he and Eddie rushed for the ladder truck, and the compartment that held the line gun. “We’re about to do something very stupid.”

He heard Williams sigh through the line. Which meant that she thumbed her radio on just so that he could hear it. But she didn’t tell him off or order him not to, and it was a fact that had both him and Eddie grinning wider.

The building across from the apartments was a parking garage. Eddie had come in the 118’s battalion truck. Both of these facts meant it was very easy to quickly transport the line gun to where it needed to be, the roof of the garage.

“Cap,” Ravi radioed while they were getting set up. “Please tell me you’ve got us a way down from here.”

Eddie looked to Buck, face pleading, and Buck nodded to the unspoken question.

“We might have a way,” Eddie radioed back.

There was a beat of silence, the confusion almost audible all the way across the street.

“Wow, Cap,” Albert said. “That was a good Eddie impression.”

“He’s such a smart ass,” Buck told Eddie as he handed him the line gun.

(They’d done rock-paper-scissors to decide who would get to use it. Buck did not pout about losing, and anyone who argued otherwise was getting assigned latrine duty for the next chili day.)

“Aren’t you supposed to be at school?” Ravi asked.

“It’s the weekend, and I got a bit of FOMO watching the news,” Eddie responded. “We’re on the parking garage across the street.”

Buck waved.

“It’ll take too long to get the ladder to you,” he told Ravi and Albert. “So Eddie’s gonna use the line gun.”

Across the way, he saw the pair look at each other and then, after grabbing Flint, duck out of sight.

“Fire away!” Ravi radioed.

Eddie readied the gun, took aim, and fired. The hook flew across the air, rope trailing behind it, to smack into the wall just behind where Ravi had been standing. Buck took the other end of the rope and tied it to the battalion truck, through the windows of the doors.

“We’re ready when you are,” Buck told them once he was certain everything was secured.

They had Flint harnessed up and perched on the broken wall. And then Flint was no longer on the wall, and was instead hurtling along the line as he screamed his head off. He was still screaming when Buck and Eddie caught him.

“He’s clear,” Eddie told them once they got him out of the harness.

The apartments shook again, sending up more plumes of dust and throwing down more pieces of debris. Buck could see Ravi and Albert talking to each other, the both of them glaring and gesturing. It wasn’t hard to guess what that was about.

“Stop arguing,” Buck snapped at them over the radio. “Albert, then Ravi.”

“Nice to know who you care about more,” Ravi quipped back as he used one hand to push Albert off.

Buck rolled his eyes. They’d barely caught Albert before Ravi was following along, the piece of floor he’d been standing on crumbling just as he reached the midpoint of the line. Ravi and Albert hugged each other as soon as the former was free from his harness, and then the pair of them hugged Eddie.

“Yeah, yeah, celebrate later,” Buck said. He undid the rope’s knot and simply threw it over the side of the parking garage, to dangle in the street. “We’ve still got work to do.”

“He needs to pick up the other kids,” Eddie stage whispered. “They’re about to miss curfew.”

They reached ground level again just in time to catch Tanika Clarke jogging for their trucks. The way to the laundry room, where Chimney and Athena were, was blocked off by fallen debris, she said. Heavy slabs of concrete and cement, too heavy for Clarke and the other two that went, Hen and Meyers, to move on their own with just halligans and hooks.

After grabbing the drills, a couple backboards, and his other firefighters, they delved into the building’s basement. With how wrecked it was, and with how dark it was, it resembled a cave more than a man-made structure. Clarke led the way, their beams of light bouncing along. At the end, Hen and Meyers were still doing their best to move the giant slab blocking the way.

“We’ve got it,” Buck said, jerking his head to give the go ahead for the drills.

“I’m not gonna argue.” Hen was clutching at her side, and Buck narrowed his eyes.

“Did you pull a stitch? I told you, light duty.”

“Is this really the time?” she shot back, and then turned her head when his husband laughed. “Eddie?”

“Didn’t want to miss the fun,” was his answer to her unspoken question.

Between the drills and the extra manpower, the slab didn’t last very long. They broke there to the other side, clearing the debris out of the way, to reveal the laundry room. As wrecked as everywhere else, Buck saw Athena and Chimney first, then the piles of rubble in which two people were trapped.

“Told you I liked our chances,” Chimney told Athena.

“I wasn’t expecting everyone,” she said.

“We’ve got two patients needing extrication.” Chimney fell into work mode. “The first one is Donnie. He’s conscious, but barely. We had to bring him back from V tach. He has a severe wound to the shoulder, so be careful when you clear the debris. Second patient is Graham-”

“Cart guy?” Hen blurted out, peering at him.

Buck shrugged at the confused and questioning look Eddie shot him, because he didn’t know, either.

“That’s the one,” Chimney said. “Minor burns, but seems to be okay.”

“Okay.” Buck clapped his hands together. “Let’s clear some space and get him out.”

Extricating Donnie from the rubble was easy. Mostly, he was pinned by another large piece of what used to be the floor above. Once they managed to leverage that up, it was just a matter of yanking him out and onto a blackboard, where the paramedics fell upon him.

“That wound’s gonna need packing,” Chimney said.

“Five hundred CCs?” Eddie asked.

“Perfect,” Hen replied.

“Get him outside first,” Buck barked at them. He shot the ceiling a distrustful glance. “I don’t want anyone in here longer than they have to be.”

“Got it!” Albert nodded to Toby and Javier, and the pair picked up the backboard.

“The first RA to Byrne!” Buck instructed as they hurried out.

“You next, Graham,” Athena said to the second guy. “You are officially relieved of your laundry room duties.”

“Copy that, Sergeant,” Graham replied.

Buck decided he just did not have the energy to ask for context, and they definitely didn’t have the time. They got the debris out of the way, piece by piece. With the way that Graham was in an upright position, they focused on what was in front of him, under the assumption that - if his legs weren’t asleep - he could just walk out.

Too bad about the complication.

“Yeah,” was all Graham said as they stared at the piece of rebar sticking through the right side of his stomach.

Blood soaked through the fabric of his shirt, but for as long as he’d been stuck like this, there wasn’t as much of it as Buck would’ve expected. The debris must’ve put pressure on it, he thought. It also must’ve missed his kidney, though not by much.

“Are you in pain?” Hen asked.

“A- A little,” was his answer. “Not as bad as Donnie.”

“That’s his adrenaline talking,” Athena stated.

Hen crouched down to look at what they were working at. Buck joined her, seeing where the rebar stuck out of the debris behind Graham and into his back. He wondered how the hell he got impaled like he did at the angle that it was.

“Looks like it just missed his spinal cord,” Hen said.

“It must’ve.” Chimney sounded defensive, just a little bit. Checking for spinal damage was probably one of the first things he did. “He can move all his extremities.”

“Must’ve nicked his abdominal aorta.” Hen felt along Graham’s stomach, and Buck saw her grimace. “It’s warm to the touch.”

“Why didn’t you say anything?” Athena asked.

“I knew I was dead,” Graham said. “But Donnie needed help more than me.”

“So you just sacrificed yourself?”

“It was the right thing to do.”

“Are you dumb?” Bell blurted out. Her eyes went wide and she slapped her hands over her mouth.

“Gonna have to do a remedial on bedside manner,” Buck teased as he stood up. “But she’s not wrong. Ravi, we need to cut this rebar.”

“As close to his body as possible,” Chimney added. “And we need all the fluids we’ve got.”

“Um, I’m- I’m feeling kinda… chilly…” Graham’s head drooped forward, eyes fluttering closed.

“Shit.” Buck dove forward and crouched to shove his hands against the guy’s stomach, around where the rebar jutted out. He must’ve been right about the pressure of the debris slowing the bleeding. “We don’t have much time.”

“Starting the line, wide open,” Eddie said, sticking the IV into Graham’s arm. He handed the bag of saline to Bell. “Keep it above his head. Squeeze, let go, squeeze again, let go. Got it?”

“Bolusing, got it!” Bell nodded, holding the bag up as she bolused.

“We get him free, get him stabilized, and then get the hell out of here,” Buck said. “Where’s the saw?”

“Ravi went to grab it,” Athena said.

Right, because they hadn’t brought it with them. They hadn’t thought to bring it with them. Thankfully, Ravi was quick, and he was soon back with the saw in hand. Buck couldn’t see, but he felt the saw cutting through the rebar. The metal vibrated between his hands.

He found himself suddenly holding up more of Graham’s weight a moment before Ravi said he was done. As quickly as possible, they got Graham transferred to the second backboard, where Chimney set about hooking him up to the Lifepak while Hen got a blood pressure cuff onto him.

“His BP is fifty-three over thirty-nine,” Hen said, followed by Chimney’s,

“Heart rate one-forty. He’s tachycardic-” The AED’s rhythmic beeping changed tones, turning more frantic. “Nevermind, he’s in asystole.”

“Starting compressions.” Eddie placed his hands on Graham’s chest while Hen bagged him, putting the oxygen to Graham’s mouth. “Buck?”

“Keeping pressure.” Buck hadn’t moved his hands from around the rebar. “Go ahead.”

Compressions were routine, in their way. Eddie did thirty, and then checked for a pulse. Thirty more, another check. After the third round, Chimney pushed epinephrine - adrenaline - to kick things into gear. After the fourth round, though…

“Chim-” Buck started, but Chimney shook his head.

“We’re not calling it,” he said as he took over from Eddie. “Not yet.”

“Okay.” Buck glanced up at the ceiling above. “But we can’t stay here for much-”

The tone of the Lifepak changed again, slower, less shrill. Chimney scrambled to feel at Graham’s neck, and slumped with visible relief.

“Got a pulse,” he said.

“Cool. Now let’s get the fuck out of here,” Buck said. “Before this place comes down on our heads.”

None of them argued, and most of them had never moved faster.

Chapter 54: FirefightersDiaz_LAFD III

Chapter Summary

Some more transcripts of videos posted by @FirefightersDiaz_LAFD.

Transcript from a video captioned, “Your help would be paw-some. 🐕”

[Interior shot of an animal shelter. Buck is sitting on the floor with a pug in his lap. The pug’s short tail is wagging while Buck pets it. Other dogs can be heard barking in the background.]

Buck, waving: Hi, everyone! Say hi, Mr. Toodles.

[Buck lifts one of the pug’s paws to wave at the camera.]

Eddie, from off-screen: Mi sol.

Buck: Yeah, yeah. 

[Buck clears his throat.]

Buck: As some of you might have heard already, the Wilshire Animal Shelter burned last week. But don’t worry, all the animals got out safely. Including this little guy.

[Buck makes the pug wave to the camera again. The pug does not seem to care. His tail is still wagging.]

Buck: We are currently at the El Segundo shelter, which took in most of the displaced animals. But they are very overcrowded and underfunded. So it would be very, very awesome if you could give these cute little guys a home. It doesn’t even have to be forever - but a forever home would be even more awesome!

[Buck lifts up the pug, hands covering most of its torso.

Buck: Wouldn’t that be awesome, Mr. Toodles?

[The pug yips, seemingly in agreement.]

Buck: But even a temporary home would be good. The shelter is letting people foster dogs until they get adopted or the Wilshire shelter is repaired. So if anyone in or around Los Angeles is feeling lonely, or charitable, or wants to bribe their way into my heart, come down to the El Segundo shelter and make a new furry friend.

[The video blurs as the camera is turned. Eddie’s face suddenly takes up the screen. Sarah McLachlan’s “Angel” begins to play.]

Eddie: Please. Please come get a dog. Buck’s already tried to bring one of them home, and I don’t trust him not to try for more. We don’t have room for all these dogs.

Buck, OS: We could make room

Eddie: Please.

Transcript ends.

Transcript of a video captioned, “Pour one out for the truck.”

[Exterior shot of the Diaz house. The person holding the camera is on the porch and facing the driveway, where a large Ford truck is parked. Eddie is visibly forlorn as he stares at it.]

Buck, from off-screen: Eddie finally realized that his truck is a gas guzzling glutton.

Chris, OS: Nice alliteration, Pops.

Buck, OS: Thank you! Go get ready for school.

Chris, OS, voice getting quieter: Yeah, yeah…

Buck, OS: So we’re gonna trade the truck in for something a bit more reasonable.

[The camera turns. Buck’s face takes up the screen now.]

Buck: He’s a bigger man than me. I like my jeeps, thanks.

[The camera turns back to Eddie.]

Buck, OS: Babe, are you crying!?

Eddie: No!

Buck, OS: I think he’s crying.

[The video cuts to later in the day. The truck is gone, replaced with a bright blue Prius. The camera is closer to the driveway. Eddie is halfway onto the screen, arms crossed as he stares at the Prius.]

Buck, OS: There, there.

[Buck reaches out and pats Eddie’s shoulder.

Buck, OS: Your frugality is a big turn on.

Eddie: I can never show my face in Texas again. I’m going to be disowned.

Buck, OS: You are such a drama queen.

Transcript ends.

Transcript of a video captioned, “🎈🎂 It’s HEN Day! 🍰🎈”

[Interior shot of Station 118, the truck bay. Hen can be seen inside the back of one of the ambulances. The camera is moving towards her.]

Buck, from off-screen: Today is a very special day.

[The camera has reached Hen. It gets shoved into her face. Hen recoils.]

Buck, OS: It’s Hen day!

Hen: What the hell are you doing?

Buck, OS: Wishing you a happy birthday.

[The camera turns slightly as Buck enters the screen beside Hen. He throws an arm around her shoulder.]

Buck: She’s a bit upset, because everyone but me sucks. So I want you all to wish her a happy birthday.

[Hen scowls at Buck. Her mouth is twitching like she wants to smile.]

Hen: Don’t you have a job to be doing?

Buck: The boss gave me a fifteen minute break for this.

[Hen rolls her eyes while making an obvious effort to not smile. She shoves at Buck, an act that causes the video to wobble.]

Hen: Get off me, Cap.

[She climbs farther inside the ambulance.]

Buck: Fine. I’m gonna go eat the rest of your cake.

Hen, OS: Do it and you die.

[Buck’s face takes up most of the screen.]

Buck: She loves me.

Transcript ends.

Transcript for a video captioned, “And he makes fun of me. Edit: You said you weren’t gonna share this! I’m married to a liar!”

[Interior shot of the Diaz kitchen. Buck is holding a fluffy black cat in one arm while flipping through a recipe book. He seems unaware that he is being recorded.]

Buck: What are you thinking? Cow, pig, or chicken?

[The cat meows.]

Buck: You raise a good point, m’lady, pizza does sound good. But we already ordered out once this week.

[Buck flips to another page.]

Buck: We could do shrimp. Do we have shrimp? I think we actually cooked all the shrimp on Sunday, nevermind.

[The cat meows.]

Buck: If I go out to get shrimp, I might as well get the pizza. Or In-n-Out. A burger sounds good, too. 

[Buck closes the recipe book, picks it up, and shoves it onto a shelf with others.]

Buck: You’ve convinced me. Burgers for dinner it is!

[Buck turns to the camera. He freezes and his eyes go wide]

Buck: Hi, baby. Uh. How long have you been standing there?

Eddie, from off-screen, sounding like he’s laughing: Long enough.

Buck: What do I have to do to keep you from sharing that video with anyone?

Eddie, OS: That sounds like bribery, mi sol.

[Buck pouts at the camera as he clutches the cat.]

Eddie, OS: I think we can come up with something.

Transcript ends.

Transcript of a video captioned, “Public Service Announcement! 🔥📢”

[Interior shot of Station 118. Buck is standing in front of the kitchen island. His expression is stern.]

Buck: If you are in Los Angeles and you get your water from the Headworks Reservoir, do not use it. Not for cooking, not for laundry, not for showers. Drinking is fine, but you’ll be gassy.

[A burp from off-screen, close to the camera.

Buck: Like that. Thank you, Ravi.

Ravi, from off-screen: You’re- [Another burp.] You’re welcome, Cap.

Buck: While you’re probably seeing a lot of reports of water burning, the biggest danger is that the methane won’t stay in the water. It can build up in your homes, and then explode.

Chimney, OS: And that’s bad!

Buck: And please be extra cautious with fire safety. The water in the hydrants come from the same place as the water in your homes. Which means we can’t use it on fires, unless we want to make the fires worse.

Albert, OS: And that’s bad!

Buck: So try to avoid using tap water if you can. And please, keep it away from any open flames.

[Ravi burps from off-screen.]

Transcript ends.

Partial transcript for a video captioned, “Incoming nephew!”

[Interior shot of a hospital gift shop. Buck is looking between two stuffed animals, a bear and an elephant.]

Buck: I’m just saying, it’s the first toy I’m giving him. It has to be good, Eds.

Eddie, from off-screen: He’s not gonna care, mi sol. 

Buck: But I do!

[Eddie audibly sighs.]

Eddie: He’s gonna smother himself on either of those.

[Buck’s eyes go wide and then he hurriedly places both stuffed animals on the shelf.]

Buck: Right! Right! Can’t murder my nephew on his first day.

[A chime is heard. Buck digs out his phone and turns it on.]

Buck: Aw, that’s cute. The kids’re cooking with Pops.

Eddie, OS: They’re breaking in the new kitchen?

Buck: Yup. Ma wants to know if he’s here yet…

[Buck types away at his phone, tongue poking out between his teeth.]

Eddie, OS: He’s Chimney’s kid, he’s gonna take his sweet time coming out.

[Buck laughs as he puts away his phone.]

Buck: You don’t know, he’s Maddie’s, too.

Eddie, OS: If she’s anything like you, that just means he’s gonna be a foul, heathenistic, morning person.

Buck: Love you, too, babe.

Eddie, OS: Do we even know what his name’s gonna be? I haven’t heard anything.

[Buck opens his mouth, then he furrows his brow.]

Buck: They haven’t said anything to me, either. Huh. But it took them forever to decide on one, last time.

[Buck gives a small shake of his head.]

Buck: C’mon, help me pick out something that won’t kill an infant. Balloons are okay, right? And flowers?

Eddie, OS: You’re gonna give the baby flowers.

[Buck glares at the camera.]

Buck: No, I’m getting my sister flowers. Now c’mon. ¡Ándale!

Eddie, OS: ¡Arriba! ¡Arriba!

[Buck looks confused.]

Buck: What?

Partial transcript ends.

Chapter 55: Incoming Nephew

Chapter Summary

In which a daycare is considered, recipe books are given, and a nephew is met.

The wide building was definitely colorful on the outside, painted a bright and cheery yellow with blue trimmings. There was a playground in the back, surrounded by privacy fencing. Buck only knew it was a playground because some of the equipment was just tall enough to stick up above the fence. That, and the sound of children shouting and laughing that carried through the air. There was a large tree in the front along with a sign that had the daycare’s name, Lilypad Daycare. There was a cartoon frog on a lilypad serving as the dot on the i.

It wasn’t on the normal route they took to the station, so Buck hadn’t really noticed the place before, not until he got serious about finding Gavin a daycare. Space had luckily opened up just recently. It was their first choice, mostly because of its proximity, but also because everything Buck found about it pointed to good things. But they needed to actually check it out for themselves.

“You ready to check this out, bud?” Eddie asked Gavin.

The tot, clinging to Eddie’s hand, gave the place a curious stare. At Eddie’s question, he gave a silent nod.

“Alright then, little guy.” Buck smiled down at him. “Let’s go.”

There were two sets of doors, and they had to wait after coming in for the second set to be unlocked with a buzz before they could open them. Just inside was a hall straight out of a school. Tiled floors, mineral-fiber ceiling, art work pinned to boards on the wall. The office was to their left, small, with glass walls. There were two women inside, and one of them - maybe a decade or so older than Buck, with grey-streaked hair in a bun - got up and came out to greet them.

“Hi! You must be the Diazes, right? We talked on the phone the other day.”

“Right! That was me.” Buck held out his hand for her to shake. “I’m Buck, this is Eddie.”

“Hi.” Eddie smiled as he took his turn to shake hands.

“And this little squirt-” Buck reached down and scooped up Gavin, who squealed. “-is Gavin.”

“Nice to meet you, Gavin.” The woman smiled and held out her hand to him, who stared at it for a moment before gripping her fingers. “I’m Mrs. Hess. Debra. I’m the director.”

She pointed at the name badge attached to her sweater, with her name written in the same “fun” font as the sign out front.

“So,” she said. “You said you were trying to find a daycare for Mr. Gavin?”

“Yeah.” Buck nodded. “It’s been difficult, ‘cause, well. We’re firefighters, so our schedules aren’t the nine-to-five most daycares do.”

“Right now, I’m taking paramedic courses, so I’m not doing twenty-fours,” Eddie added. “But that’s only for a couple more weeks, and then I’m back to the same schedule he’s on.”

“I used to work nights while going to school during the day, I totally understand,” Debra told him. “It’s why I opened up this place. What have you been doing before now? If you don’t mind me asking, of course.”

Buck glanced at Eddie, who grimaced before answering.

“My abuela,” he said. “She lives with us, so she’d watch him while we were at work. But she’s- she got diagnosed with Alzheimer’s, so…”

“I’m sorry.” Debra’s face scrunched up in sympathy. 

“We have a home aide helping her, the same one that used to help with our oldest,” Buck added. “But she really needs to focus on Abuela, and not on Gavin. However much she’s complaining otherwise.”

“On the phone you said he was three?”

“Yeah. His birthday’s in March.”
