“We split them by age groups. The room he’d be in is this way.”

She gestured for them to follow, before leading them down one of the halls. Buck and Eddie both peered around as they walked, seeing posters with cartoon characters and more art work clearly made by children, along with a fire extinguisher and AED stuck to the wall. They passed what must’ve been the dining area - or was it cafeteria? - with round tables and then the kitchen, before taking a turn.

“We accept children from two years old all the way up to fourteen,” Debra informed them as they walked. “We don’t have many kids on the older end, mostly siblings of one of the younger kids. You said you have another child?”

“He’s fourteen, but he’s pretty self-sufficient these days,” Eddie said. “Hel- Heck, he’d probably watch Gavin during our shifts if we asked.”

“Not that we would,” Buck hurriedly tacked on.

“He sounds like a good kid,” was all she said. Buck and Eddie both beamed at her. “This is the room Gavin would be in.”

The room was long and subdivided up with short bookcases, and most of the floor was carpeted. There was a nook clearly meant for reading and another for playing, with tubs of toys cleanly tucked away. Part of the room was taken up by tables and chairs, the kind one would find in an elementary school classroom. On one end was a white board that stretched along the wall.

Gavin started squirming in Buck’s arms, demanding to be let down so he could explore. The moment his feet touched the ground, he was running off to dig through the toys.

“Everyone’s outside playing right now, but this is one of the rooms for the kids not old enough to be in school yet,” Debra said. “When it’s full, there’s twelve of them.”

“It looks like a classroom,” Eddie remarked.

“It is, basically. It’s also the only room that’s used throughout the day during the school year,” she said. “During the school week, the older kids arrive in the afternoon and are picked up when their parents or guardians get off work. We don’t have very many that stay overnight, or on the weekends.”

“Where, uh. Where would he be overnight?” Buck asked, peering around the room.

“There are mats for nap time during the day,” she said, gesturing at the back end of the room. That carpeted area was a notably bare space in the room. “But for overnight we have a room with beds. The sheets get washed every morning.”

“Uh-huh, uh-huh.” Buck nodded. “And fire safety?”

He heard Eddie bark out a laugh, and he stuck his tongue out at him.

After they peeled Gavin away from the toys, they continued the tour. It looked good, certainly. And it was within their budget, thank you captain’s paycheck. Most of their hangup was about the overnight portion and how Gavin would handle it.

They decided to give it a trial run, dropping Gavin off at the daycare while Eddie was doing his paramedic classes and labs. And if Gavin handled it okay, then they’d try the overnights.

(There was no question about whether or not Buck and Eddie would handle it okay, because they already knew they wouldn’t.)

“It’s looking homey,” Buck remarked as he stepped into the Grant-Nash kitchen.

There was actual furniture in the house now. New furniture, not just what Bobby and Athena got for the apartment. Hell, half of that got replaced. Like the couch, for example, and the dining table. Despite what Buck had been championing for, Bobby hadn’t gone for some outrageously long table. The one he’d settled on was just large enough for a Sunday dinner.

With the furniture, he could now see that what he’d thought was just the kitchen and dining area was also the den. The end with the fireplace got the couch and such. It was basically how the old house was set up, only flipped and without the wall in the middle separating it.

“Still needs a few touches,” Bobby said as he glanced about, too. “The walls are kinda bare. Upstairs especially.”

They’d printed out some photos that had been saved digitally, mostly thanks to phone back-ups, and they had copies that May and Michael had given them. There were still a lot that they couldn’t replace, something that Buck, who’d spent so long with a life that fit inside a jeep and who was never really attached to stuff, couldn’t really imagine. Bobby’s medal and the accompanying placard had both been casualties, but Buck didn’t think he mourned them for even a moment.

“That’s not all that’s bare.” Buck set down the box he’d been lugging around onto the kitchen island. “Don’t think I didn’t notice.”

He jerked his chin at the counter, specifically where the cookbooks would have been. 

“Yeah.” Bobby casually shrugged. “Haven’t gotten around to getting everything I need just yet. The kitchen at the apartment was not anything special.”

“I can take care of some of it, at least,” Buck told him, and then pulled out the first thing in the box.

“Buck,” Bobby tutted as he took the recipe book from him. “Did you- This is the same as one that we had before the fire.”

“I could remember a couple of them.” Buck pulled out others, setting them aside on the counter. “A couple are copies of ones we have at the station."

“The Firefighter’s Cookbook and the New Firefighter’s Cookbook.”

“Yeah, I couldn’t remember which one of those you had, so I just got both.” Buck shrugged at him, and then took out the last one. “And also this one.”

“What’s- Buck!” Bobby set aside the book he’d picked up to take the new one. “I don’t even- Really?”

“I thought you might like it.”

“You thought I might like-” The former captain broke off with a laugh, shaking his head. “You thought I might like a cookbook by Snoop Dogg?”

“There’s a recipe for a fried bologna sandwich that sounded good.” Buck grinned at the man. “And he’s got one for baking recipes coming out.”

“Please remember that captains get randomly tested, too.”

“Yeah, yeah.” He reached into the box again, grabbing the last of what he’d brought over in the box. It was wrapped in paper to keep it safe. “Eddie and I dragged the kids out for new pictures a little while ago.”

“Oh?” Bobby perked up, setting aside the cookbook.

“Yeah. Gavin did not appreciate having to sit still through it.” Buck unwrapped the paper, showing the pair of framed photos. “One of the four of us, one of Chris and Gavin.”

Bobby took them both, and simply smiled down at them for a long moment. Then he placed them on top of one of the cookbooks and dragged Buck into a bonecrushing hug.

“Thank you, kid.”

“‘Course, Pops.” Buck patted him on the back. “Y’know, I haven’t even been upstairs yet.”

“Come on then.” Bobby stepped back and cleared his throat. “I’ll show you.”

Buck avoided mentioning the conspicuous shine to the other man’s eyes as they went.

When Maddie started having contractions, she was visiting the Diazes with Chimney and Jee-Yun. Buck wasn’t certain who panicked more, him or Chimney, but it definitely wasn’t Maddie. Maddie just told them to stop being idiots and to help her to the car.

Buck and Eddie took the kids - Chris and Gavin and Jee-Yun - over to Bobby and Athena’s, while Eddie called Pepa. Their group chat was popping off like crazy, mostly because Maddie decided to announce that she was in labor with “btw baby’s coming” and then stop responding. It was up to Buck to tell them which hospital Chimney was taking her.

The last time, when Jee-Yun was born, Buck had been busy with that awful pile-up and then Albert’s accident. He wasn’t certain if it was better or worse than this time, because at least he was distracted then. This time he was stuck pacing the hospital, no doubt stretching his husband’s patience to its limit.

At least Eddie could entertain himself by filming Buck’s spiral for posterity.

It took most of the day for the new Han to arrive, from just before lunch to well past dinner. Buck wasn’t certain if it took Jee that long, mostly because Maddie had spent a lot of that labor under the assumption that her contractions were simply more Braxton Hicks. A nurse came into the waiting room, where almost everyone had gathered, a little after eleven in the evening to tell them that Maddie could have a couple visitors before they were all getting kicked out.

There wasn’t a mad scramble to decide who it would be, not even from the Lees. The others were almost of a single mind that it should be Buck and Albert. Which was good, because Buck had no compunctions about choking someone out with the string of the balloon he bought from the hospital’s gift shop.

“Hey, guys,” Chimney greeted them from where he was half-bent over Maddie in the bed. “Buck, you know that balloon says Get Well Soon, right?”

“It was this or a I’m Sorry For Your Loss with a smiley face on the back.” Buck shoved the balloon at him. “And flowers for you.”

He set the flowers down on the side table and pressed a kiss to Maddie’s hair. The angle let him see his nephew better, the tiny thing wrapped up in a powder blue blanket and looking very unhappy about being here.

“Thank God. He looks nothing like you, Chim.”

Chimney gave a fake laugh and the bitchiest face he could manage while still beaming at his wife and son.

“Does he have a name yet?” Albert asked as he came over to see the new addition, too. “I seem to remember you couldn’t decide on Jee’s until right after.”

Maddie and Chimney shared a smile.

“We do, actually,” she said.

“Did you name him after me?” Buck asked.

“No,” Chimney said, drawing out the single syllable.

Maddie rolled her eyes and held out the baby for Buck to take. He was careful as he took him from her, cradling him like he had Jee-Yun when she was a little bit older and Gavin the day he was left at the station. The littlest Han wiggled a bit and grumbled before settling again, his head nestling perfectly in the crook of Buck’s arm..

“He has the cutest little hat,” Buck cooed. “So what did you name him?”

“Daniel Kevin Han,” Maddie said. Her smile now was smaller, and a bit shaded. Chimney’s was the same. “We haven’t told the Lees, yet.”

“John’ll cry,” Albert stated with absolute certainty.

Chimney nodded in agreement.

“Like a baby,” he said.

Buck ignored them, too busy gazing down at his new nephew.

“Hello, Danny,” he whispered softly. “You’ve got cousins to meet.”

 

Fin.
